Name of a protégé of the Aśvins in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> 2. {@Dhānaṃjayya,@} pupil of {@Amāvāsya Śāṇḍilyāyana,@} according to the Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) viii. 5, 26. {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Transla- tion of the Rigveda, 3, 160; Hopkins, {%Journal of the American Oriental Society,%} 17, 89; Sieg, {%Die Sagenstoffe des Ṛgveda,%} 129, suggests that he may be identical with {@Khela.@}</F> <F>2) {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 373.</F>
{@Aṃhasas-pati.@}¦ — This is the name of the intercalary month in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā (vii. 30; xxii. 31). See {@Māsa.@}

{@Akra.@}¦ — In several passages of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> this word means, according to Geldner,<sup>2</sup> ‘horse.’ Roth<sup>3</sup> suggests that ‘riding horse’ is the precise sense. {%Cf.%} {@Aśva.@} <F>1) i. 143, 7; 189, 7; iii. 1, 12; iv. 6, 3; x. 77, 2.</F> <F>2) {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 168, 169.</F> <F>3) {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgen-%} {%ländischen Gesellschaft,%} 48, 118. {%Cf.%} Max Müller, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 32, 414.</F>

1. {@Akṣa,@}¦ ‘axle,’ is a part of a chariot often referred to in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later. It was apparently<sup>2</sup> fastened to the body of the chariot ({@Kośa@}) by straps ({%akṣā-nah,%} lit. ‘tied to the axle,’ though this word is also<sup>3</sup> rendered ‘horse’). The heating of the axle and the danger of its breaking were known.<sup>4</sup> The part of the axle round which the nave of the wheel revolved was called Āṇi, ‘pin.’ <F>1) i. 30, 14; 166, 9; iii. 53, 17; vi. 24, 3; x. 89; 4, etc.</F> <F>2) Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 246.</F> <F>3) Rv. x. 53, 7. {%Cf.%} Roth, St. Peters- burg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>4) Rv. i. 164, 13.</F>

2. {@Akṣa.@}¦ — This word occurs frequently, from the Rigveda onwards, both in the singular and plural, meaning ‘die’ and ‘dice.’ Dicing, along with horse-racing, was one of the main amusements of the Vedic Indian; but, despite the frequent mention of the game in the literature, there is considerable difficulty in obtaining any clear picture of the mode in which it was played. <div n="P"/>(1) {%The Material.%} — The dice appear normally to have been made of Vibhīdaka nuts. Such dice are alluded to in both the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and the Atharvaveda,<sup>2</sup> hence being called ‘brown’ ({%babhru%}), and ‘born on a windy spot.’<sup>3</sup> In the ritual game of dice at the Agnyādheya and the Rājasūya ceremonies the material of the dice is not specified, but it is possible that occasionally gold imitations of Vibhīdaka nuts were used.<sup>4</sup> There is no clear trace in the Vedic literature of the later use of cowries as dice.<sup>5</sup> <div n="P"/>(2) {%The Number.%} — In the Rigveda<sup>6</sup> the dicer is described as ‘leader of a great horde’ ({%senānīr mahato gaṇasya%}), and in another passage<sup>7</sup> the number is given as {%tri-pañcāśaḥ,%} an expres- sion which has been variously interpreted. Ludwig,<sup>8</sup> Weber,<sup>9</sup> and Zimmer<sup>10</sup> render it as fifteen, which is grammatically hardly possible. Roth<sup>11</sup> and Grassmann<sup>12</sup> render it as ‘con- sisting of fifty-three.’ Lüders<sup>13</sup> takes it as ‘consisting of one hundred and fifty,’ but he points out that this may be merely a vague expression for a large number. For a small number Zimmer<sup>14</sup> cites a reference in the Rigveda<sup>15</sup> to one who fears ‘him who holds four’ ({%caturaś cid dadamānāt%}), but the sense of that passage is dependent on the view taken of the method of playing the game. <div n="P"/>(3) {%The Method of Play.%} — In several passages of the later [Page1-003+ 49] Saṃhitās and Brāhmaṇas lists are given of expressions con- nected with dicing. The names are Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, Āskanda, and Abhibhū in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā.<sup>16</sup> In the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā,<sup>17</sup> among the victims at the Puruṣamedha, the {%kitava%} is offered to the Akṣarāja, the {%ādinava-darśa%} to the Kṛta, the {%kalpin%} to the Tretā, the {%adhi-kalpin%} to the Dvāpara, the {%sabhā-sthāṇu%} to the Āskanda. The lists in the parallel version of the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa are {%kitava, sabhāvin, ādinava-%} {%darśa, bahiḥ-sad,%} and {%sabhā-sthāṇu,%}<sup>18</sup> and Aksarāja, Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali. From the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>19</sup> it appears that another name of Kali was Abhibhū, and the parallel lists in the Taittirīya and Vājasaneyi Saṃhitās suggest that Abhibhū and Akṣarāja are identical, though both appear in the late Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa list. The names of some of these throws go back even to the Rigveda and the Atharvaveda. Kali occurs in the latter,<sup>20</sup> and Lüders<sup>21</sup> shows that in a considerable number of passages in the former Kṛta means a ‘throw’ (not ‘a stake’<sup>22</sup> or ‘what is won’<sup>23</sup> and this sense is clearly found in the Atharvaveda.<sup>24</sup> Moreover, that there were more throws ({%ayāḥ%}) than one is proved by a passage in the Rigveda,<sup>25</sup> when the gods are compared to throws as giving or destroying wealth. <div n="P"/>The nature of the throws is obscure. The St. Petersburg Dictionary conjectures that the names given above were applied either to dice marked 4, 3, 2, or 1, or to the sides of the dice so marked, and the latter interpretation is supported by some late commentators.<sup>26</sup> But there is no evidence for the former interpretation, and, as regards the latter, the shape of the Vibhīdaka nuts,<sup>27</sup> used as dice, forbids any side being properly on the top. Light is thrown on the expressions by the descrip- [Page1-004+ 52] tion of a ritual game<sup>28</sup> at the Agnyādheya and at the Rājasūya ceremonies. The details are not certain,<sup>29</sup> but it is clear that the game consisted in securing even numbers of dice, usually a number divisible by four, the Kṛta, the other three throws then being the Tretā, when three remained over after division by four; the Dvāpara, when two was the remainder; and the Kali, when one remained. If five were the dividing number, then the throw which showed no remainder was Kali, the Kṛta was that when four was left, and so on. The dice had no numerals marked on them, the only question being what was the total number of the dice themselves. <div n="P"/>There is no reason to doubt that the game as played in the Rigveda was based on the same principle, though the details must remain doubtful. The number of dice used was certainly large,<sup>30</sup> and the reference to throwing fours,<sup>31</sup> and losing by one, points to the use of the Kṛta as the winning throw. The Atharvaveda,<sup>32</sup> on the other hand, possibly knew of the Kali as the winning throw. In one respect the ordinary game must have differed from the ritual game. In the latter the players merely pick out the number of dice required — no doubt to avoid ominous errors, such as must have happened if a real game had been played. In the secular game the dice were thrown,<sup>33</sup> perhaps on the principle suggested by Lüders:<sup>34</sup> the one throwing a certain number on the place of playing, and the other then throwing a number to make up with those already thrown a multiple of four or five. This theory, at any rate, accounts for the later stress laid on the power of computation in a player, as in the Nala. <div n="P"/>No board appears to have been used, but a depression on which [Page1-005+ 60] the dice were thrown ({%adhi-devana, devana,%}<sup>35</sup> {%iriṇa%}<sup>36</sup> ), was made in the ground. No dice box was used, but reference is made to a case for keeping dice in ({%akṣa-vapana%}<sup>37</sup> The throw was called {%graha%}<sup>38</sup> or earlier {%grābha.%}<sup>39</sup> The stake is called {%vij.%}<sup>40</sup> Serious losses could be made at dicing: in the Rigveda a dicer laments the loss of all his property, including his wife.<sup>41</sup> Lüders<sup>42</sup> finds a different form of the game referred to in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.<sup>43</sup> <F>1) vii. 86, 6; x. 34, 1.</F> <F>2) Av. 3. {@Akṣa.@}¦ — In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (vii. 3, 1) this word seems to denote the nut of the Vibhīdaka ({%Terminalia bellerica%}).

{@Akṣata@}¦ or {@Akṣita.@} — In one passage of the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> dealing with the {@Jāyānya,@} mention is made of a remedy for sores designated both Akṣita and Sukṣata, or, according to the reading of the Kauṣika Sūtra, Akṣata and Sukṣata, while Sāyaṇa has Akṣita and Sukṣita. Bloomfield<sup>2</sup> renders ‘not caused by cutting’ and ‘caused by cutting.’ Formerly<sup>3</sup> he suggested ‘tumour’ or ‘boil.’ Whitney<sup>4</sup> thinks that two varieties of Jāyānya are meant. Ludwig<sup>5</sup> reads with Sāyana {%akṣita,%} which he renders by ‘not firmly established’ in the invalid. Zimmer<sup>6</sup> finds in it a disease Kṣata. <F>1) vii. 76, 4.</F> <F>2) {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 17, 562.</F> <F>3) {%Journal of the American Oriental%} {%Society,%} 13, cxvii. {%et seq.%}</F> <F>4) Translation of the Atharvaveda 442.</F> <F>5) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 500.</F> <F>6) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 377.</F>

{@Akṣu.@}¦ — The word occurs in two passages of the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and one of the Rigveda.<sup>2</sup> Roth<sup>3</sup> renders it by ‘net,’ while Böhtlingk<sup>4</sup> suggests ‘axle of a car.’ Geldner<sup>5</sup> sees in it a stake or pole used with a fishermen's net ({@Jāla@}),<sup>6</sup> the pole of a wagon,<sup>7</sup> and the pole of a house, whether vertical or horizontal, he leaves uncertain (see {@Vaṃśa@}).<sup>8</sup> Bloomfield<sup>9</sup> takes it as a covering of wickerwork stretched across a beam and sloping down to both sides — like a thatched roof, and this best explains the epithet ‘thousand-eyed’ ({%i.e.,%} with countless holes) ascribed to it. In the other Atharvaveda passage<sup>10</sup> he accepts the sense ‘net,’ and doubts if the word in the Rigveda is not an adjective ({%a-kṣu%}) as it is taken by Sāyaṇa. See also {@Gṛha.@} <F>1) viii. 8, 18 ({%akṣujālābhyām%}); ix. 3, 18.</F> <F>2) i. 180, 5.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>4) Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>5) {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 136.</F> <F>6) Av. viii. 8, 18.</F> <F>7) Av. i. 180, 5.</F> <F>8) ix. 3, 18.</F> <F>9) {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 598.</F> <F>10) Av. viii. 8, 18. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 153, 265; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 506, 526; Oldenberg, {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 179.</F>

{@Agasti.@}¦ — This form of {@Agastya's@} name occurs once in the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> where he appears as a favourite of Mitra and Varuṇa. <F>1) iv. 9, 3. {%Cf.%} {@Sieg,@} {%Die Sagenstoffe des Ṛgveda,%} 127, n. 5.</F>

{@Agastya.@}¦ — This is the name of a sage, of mythical character, who plays a great part in the later literature. He was a {@Māna,@}<sup>1</sup> and therefore is called {@Mānya@}<sup>2</sup> and son of Māna, and only once is there a reference<sup>3</sup> to the legend prevalent in latter times that he was a son of Mitra and Varuṇa. <div n="P"/>His greatest feat was the reconciliation of Indra and the Maruts after Indra had been annoyed at his proposing to give the Maruts an offering to the exclusion of Indra. This feat is the subject of three hymns of the Rigveda,<sup>4</sup> and is often referred [Page1-007+ 62] to in the Brāhmaṇas,<sup>5</sup> though the exact details and significance of the legend are variously treated by Oldenberg,<sup>6</sup> Sieg,<sup>7</sup> Hertel,<sup>8</sup> and von Schroeder.<sup>9</sup> <div n="P"/>He also appears in a strange dialogue with Lopāmudrā in the Rigveda,<sup>10</sup> which appears to show him as an ascetic who finally yields to temptation. Von {@Schroeder@}<sup>11</sup> regards it as a ritual drama of vegetation magic. <div n="P"/>In another passage of the Rigveda<sup>12</sup> he appears as helping in the Aśvins’ gift of a leg to Viśpalā. Sāyaṇa holds that be was the Purohita of {@Khela,@} and Sieg<sup>13</sup> accepts this view, while Pischel<sup>14</sup> thinks that Khela is a deity, Vivasvant. <div n="P"/>Geldner<sup>15</sup> shows from the Rigveda<sup>16</sup> that Agastya, as brother of Vasiṣṭha — both being miraculous sons of Mitra and Varuṇa -introduces {@Vasiṣṭha@} to the {@Tṛtsus.@} There are two other references to Agastya in the Rigveda, the one<sup>17</sup> including him in a long list of persons, the other alluding to his sister's sons ({%nadbhyaḥ%}),<sup>18</sup> apparently {@Bandhu,@} etc. In the Atharvaveda<sup>19</sup> he appears as connected with witchcraft, and in a long list of sages.<sup>20</sup> In the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā<sup>21</sup> cows, with a peculiar mark on their ears ({%viṣṭya-karṇyaḥ%}), are associated with him. <F>1) Rv. vii. 33, 10 (Agastya), 13 (Māna).</F> <F>2) Rv. i. 165, 15 = 166, 15 = 167, 11 = 168, 10; 165, 14; 177, 5; 184, 4 (Mānya); i. 189, 8; 117, 11 ({%Mānasya sūnu%}).</F> <F>3) Rv. vii. 33, 13. {%Cf.%} Geldner, {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 138 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>4) Rv. i. 165; 170; 171.</F> <F>5) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vii. 5, 5, 2; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 7, 11, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 1, 8; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, x. 11; Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xxi. 14, 5; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, v. 16; Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, xxvi. 9.</F> <F>6) {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgen-%} {%ländischen Gesellschaft,%} 39, 60 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>7) {%Die Sagenstoffe des Ṛgveda,%} 108-119.</F> <F>8) {%Vienna Oriental Journal,%} 18, 152-154.</F> <F>9) {%Mysterium und Mimus im Rigveda,%} 91 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>10) i. 179. {%Cf.%} Sieg, {%op. cit.,%} 120-126; Oldenberg, {%op. cit.,%} 66-68.</F> <F>11) {%Op. cit.,%} 156-172.</F> <F>12) i. 117, 11; {%cf.%} i. 116, 15.</F> <F>13) {%Op. cit.,%} 128.</F> <F>14) {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 171-173.</F> <F>15) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 138, 143.</F> <F>16) Rv. vii. 33, 10. 13.</F> <F>17) vii. 5, 26. {@Agara.@}¦ — This rare word is found as ‘house’ in the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) ii. 15. {%Cf. āgara,%} ‘chamber’ (?), n Av. iv. 36, 3; Bloomfield, {%Hymns of%} {%the Atharvaveda,%} 407. Agāra occurs also in Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra, i. 7, 21.</F>

{@Agni-dagdha.@}¦ — This epithet (‘burnt with fire’)<sup>1</sup> applies to the dead who were burned on the funeral pyre. This is one of the two normal methods of disposing of the dead, the other being burial ({%an-agnidagdhāḥ,%} ‘not burnt with fire’).<sup>2</sup> The Atharvaveda<sup>3</sup> adds two further modes of disposal to those —  viz., casting out ({%paroptāḥ%}), and the exposure of the dead ({%uddhitāḥ%}). The exact sense of these expressions is doubtful. Zimmer<sup>4</sup> considers that the former is a parallel to the Iranian practice of casting out the dead to be devoured by beasts, and that the latter refers to the old who are exposed when helpless.<sup>5</sup> Whitney<sup>6</sup> refers the latter expression to the exposure of the dead body on a raised platform of some sort. <div n="P"/>Burial was clearly not rare in the Rigvedic period: a whole hymn<sup>7</sup> describes the ritual attending it. The dead man was buried apparently in full attire, with his bow in his hand, and probably at one time his wife was immolated to accompany him, in accordance with a practice common among savage tribes. But in the Vedic period both customs appear in a modified form: the son takes the bow from the hand of the dead man, and the widow is led away from her dead husband by his brother or other nearest kinsman. A stone is set between the dead and the living to separate them. In the Atharvaveda,<sup>8</sup> but not in the Rigveda, a coffin ({%vṛkṣa%}) is alluded to. In both Saṃhitās<sup>9</sup> occur other allusions to the ‘house of earth’ ({%bhūmi-gṛha%}). To remove the apparent discrepancy between burning and burial, by assuming that the references to burial are to the burial of the burned bones, as does Oldenberg,<sup>10</sup> is unnecessary and improbable, as burning and burial subsisted side by side in Greece for many years. <div n="P"/>Burning was, however, equally usual, and it grew steadily in frequency, for in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad<sup>11</sup> the adornment [Page1-009+ 56] of the body of the dead with curd ({@Āmikṣā@}), clothes, and ornaments, in order to win the next world, is referred to as something erroneous and wrong, and in the funeral Mantras of the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā<sup>12</sup> only burning seems to be contemplated; the verses which refer to burial here really alluding to the burial of the ashes in the burying-ground ({%śmaśāna%}).<sup>13</sup> The body was wrapped in fat,<sup>14</sup> as we learn from the funeral hymn in the Rigveda, a goat being apparently burned with it,<sup>15</sup> to act as a guide on the way to the next world. According to the Atharvaveda<sup>16</sup> a draft-ox was burned presumably for the dead to ride with in the next world. It was expected that the dead would revive with his whole body and all his limbs ({%sarva-tanūḥ%} {%sāṅgaḥ%}),<sup>17</sup> although it is also said<sup>18</sup> that the eye goes to the sun, the breath to the wind, and so forth. <div n="P"/>Before burial or burning, the corpse was washed,<sup>19</sup> a clog ({%kūdī%}) being tied to the foot to prevent the deceased returning to earth.<sup>20</sup> <F>1) Rv. x. 15, 14; Taittirīya Brāh- maṇa, iii. 1, 1, 7; {%dagdhāḥ,%} Av. xviii. 2, 34.</F> <F>2) Rv., {%loc. cit.;%} = {%nikhātāḥ,%} Av. xviii. 2, 34.</F> <F>3) {%Loc. cit.%}</F> <F>4) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 402.</F> <F>5) Rv. viii. 51, 2.</F> <F>6) Translation of the Atharvaveda, 841.</F> <F>7) x. 18. The interpretation of v. 8 is a famous crux, see Patnī.</F> <F>8) xviii. 2, 25; 3, 70.</F> <F>9) Rv. vii. 89, 1; Av. v. 30, 14; xviii. 2, 52.</F> <F>10) {%Religion des Veda,%} 571.</F> <F>11) viii. 8. 5.</F> <F>12) xxxv. {%Cf.%} also Kauśika Sūtra, 80 {%et seq.,%} which treats the Atharvaveda hymns, xviii. 1-3, as intended for burning only.</F> <F>13) Av. v. 31, 8; x. 1, 18; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 2, 8, 5; 4, 11, 3.</F> <F>14) Rv. x. 16, 7.</F> <F>15) Rv. x. 16, 4. But {%aja%} may mean ‘the unborn part,’ as Weber prefers to take it, Proceedings of the Berlin Academy, 1895, 847.</F> <F>16) xii. 2, 48.</F> <F>17) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iv. 6, 1, 1; xi. 1, 8, 6; xii. 8, 3, 31. {%Cf.%} Av. xi. 3, 32. This fact probably explains the use of {%śeṣaḥ%} in Rv. x. 16, 5. The dead enjoy sexual pleasures in the next world; see Muir, {%Sanskrit Texts,%} 5, 307, n. 462.</F> <F>18) Rv. x. 16, 3.</F> <F>19) Av. v. 19, 14.</F> <F>20) Av. v. 19, 12; see Roth, {%Festgruss%} {%an Böhtlingk,%} 98; Bloomfield, {%American%} {%Journal of Philology,%} 12, 416. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 401- 407; Roth, {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen%} {%Morgenländischen Gesellschaft,%} 8, 468 {%et%} {%seq.; Siebenzig Lieder,%} 150 {%et seq.;%} Olden- berg, {%Religion des Veda,%} 570 {%et seq.;%} Caland, {%Die altindischen Todten- und%} {%Bestattungsgebräuche;%} von Schroeder, {%Indiens Literatur und Cultur,%} 40-42; Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythology,%} 3, 413- 423; {%Rituallitteratur,%} 87 {%et seq.;%} Mac- donell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} 165, 166; Pro- ceedings of the Berlin Academy, 1895, 815 {%et seq.%}</F>
{@Agni-bhū Kāśyapa@}¦ is mentioned in the Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> <F>1) {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 374.</F>

{@Agni-śāla.@}¦ — This term, which designates part of the sacrificial [Page1-010+ 49] apparatus,<sup>1</sup> is applied in the Atharvaveda<sup>2</sup> to a part of an ordinary house, presumably the central hall where the fire- place was. <F>1) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xix. 18.</F> <F>2) ix. 3, 7. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Hymns. of the Atharva-%} {%veda,%} 598; Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 154.</F>

{@Aghā.@}¦ — In the wedding hymn of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> it is said that cows are slain in the Aghās, and the wedding takes place at the {@Arjunīs@} (dual). The Atharvaveda<sup>2</sup> has the ordinary {@Maghās@} instead. It is impossible to resist the conclusion that the read- ing of the Rigveda was deliberately altered because of the con- nection of the slaughter of kine with sin ({%agha%}) — possibly, too, with a further desire to emphasize the contrast with {%aghnyā,%} a name for ‘cow.’ Moreover, in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> occurs the formula ‘Svāhā to the Maghās, Svāhā to the Anaghās.’ See also {@Nakṣatra.@} <F>1) x. 85, 13.</F> <F>2) xiv. 1, 13.</F> <F>3) iii. 1, 4, 8. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Naxatra,%} 2, 364; Pro- ceedings of the Berlin Academy, 1894, 804; Jacobi, {%Festgruss an Roth,%} 69; Winternitz, {%Das altindische Hochzeits-%} {%rituell,%} 32; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 742; Thibaut, {%Indian%} {%Antiquary,%} 24, 95.</F>
{@Aghāśva.@}¦ — The name of a serpent in the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) x. 4, 10. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 95.</F>
{@A-ghnyā.@}¦ — See {@Māṃsa.@}

{@Aṅka.@}¦ — The Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> and Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> refer to two Aṅkas and two Nyaṅkas as parts of a chariot. The meaning of these terms is quite obscure. The commentators refer them to the sides or wheels. Zimmer<sup>3</sup> compares the Greek <lang n="greek">ἄντυγες</lang><sup>4</sup> and thinks that the Aṅkau were the upper border of the body of the chariot ({%kośa, vandhura%}), and the Nyaṅkau the lower rims for greater security. Oldenberg<sup>5</sup> confesses that the exact sense is impossible to make out, but considers that the terms at once refer to parts of the chariot and to divinities, while Böhtlingk<sup>6</sup> takes the term as referring to divinities alone. <F>1) i. 7, 7, 2.</F> <F>2) ii. 7, 8, 1. {%Cf.%} Pañcaviṃśa Brāh- maṇa, i. 7, 5.</F> <F>3) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 251, 252.</F> <F>4) {%Iliad,%} v. 728. {%Cf.%} Smith's {%Dic-%} {%tionary of Antiquities,%} 1, 578.</F> <F>5) {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 29, 364, on Pāraskara Gṛhya Sūtra, iii. 14, 6.</F> <F>6) Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>

{@Aṅga.@}¦ — The name occurs only once in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> in connection with the {@Gandhāris, Mūjavants,@} and {@Magadhas,@} as distinct peoples. They appear also in the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> in the compound name {%Aṅga-magadhāḥ.%} As in later times they were settled on the Sone and Ganges,<sup>3</sup> their earlier seat was presumably there also. See also {@Vaṅga.@} <F>1) v. 22, 14.</F> <F>2) ii. 9.</F> <F>3) {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 35; Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 446, 449; Pargiter, {%Journal of the Royal%} {%Asiatic Society,%} 1908, 852, inclines to regard them as a non-Aryan people that came over-sea to Eastern India. There is nothing in the Vedic litera- ture to throw light on this hypothesis.</F>

{@Aṅga Vairocana.@}¦ — He is included in the list of anointed kings in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> His Purohita was {@Udamaya,@} an Ātreya. <F>1) viii. 22. {%Cf.%} Oldenberg, {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen Gesellschaft,%} 42, 214.</F>

{@Aṅgārāvakṣayaṇa.@}¦ — A word of doubtful meaning found in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.<sup>1</sup> It is rendered ‘tongs’ by Max Müller and Böhtlingk in their translations. The St. Petersburg Dictionary explains it as ‘a vessel in which coals are extinguished,’ and Monier-Williams as ‘an instrument for extinguishing coals.’ The smaller St. Petersburg Dictionary renders the word ‘coal-shovel or tongs.’ {%Cf.%} {@Ulmukāva-@} {@kṣayaṇa.@} <F>1) iii. 9, 18.</F>

{@Aṅgiras.@}¦ — The Aṅgirases appear in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as semi- mythical beings, and no really historical character can be assigned even to those passages<sup>2</sup> which recognize a father of the race, Aṅgiras. Later, however, there were definite families of Aṅgirases, to whose ritual practices ({%ayana, dvirātra%}) references are made.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) {%Cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} ii. 156-169.</F> <F>2) Rv. i. 45, 3; 139, 9; iii. 31, 7, etc.; Chāndogya Upaniṣad, i. 2, 10.</F> <F>3) Av. xviii. 4, 8, but this may be mythical; Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xx. 11, 1; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vii. 1, 4, 1. {%Cf.%} Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} 142, 143.</F>
{@Aṅguṣṭha.@}¦ — As a measure of size this word appears in the Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad (iv. 12; vi. 17).

{@A-cyut.@}¦ — He acted as Pratihartṛ at the Sattra celebrated by the Vibhindukīyas and described in the Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) iii. 233. See {%Journal of the American Oriental Society,%} 18, 38.</F>

{@Aja, Ajā.@}¦ — This is the ordinary name for goat in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and the later literature. The goat is also called {@Basta, Chāga,@} {@Chagala.@} Goats and sheep ({%ajāvayaḥ%}) are very frequently mentioned together.<sup>2</sup> The female goat is spoken of as pro- ducing two or three kids,<sup>3</sup> and goat's milk is well known.<sup>4</sup> The goat as representative of Pūṣan plays an important part in the ritual of burial.<sup>5</sup> The occupation of a goatherd ({%ajapāla%}) was a recognized one, being distinguished from that of a cow- herd and of a shepherd.<sup>6</sup> <F>1) {%Aja%} in Rv. x. 16, 4; i. 162, 2. 4; Av. ix. 5, 1; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxi. 9, etc.; {%ajā%} in Rv. viii. 70, 15; Av. vi. 71, 1; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiii., 56, etc.</F> <F>2) Rv. x. 90, 10; Av. viii. 7, 25; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, iii. 43, etc.</F> <F>3) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vi. 5, 10, 1.</F> <F>4) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iv. 1, 6, 1; v. 1, 7, 4. {%Cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%Vedische%} {%Mythologie,%} 3, 364, n. 4.</F> <F>5) Rv. x. 16, 4, etc. {%Cf.%} p. 9.</F> <F>6) Vājasaneyī Saṃhitā, xxx. 11; Tait- tirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 9, 1.</F>

{@Aja.@}¦ — The Ajas are named in one verse of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as having been defeated by the {@Tṛtsus@} under {@Sudās.@} They are there mentioned with the {@Yakṣus@} and {@Śigrus,@} and Zimmer<sup>2</sup> conjectures that they formed part of a confederacy under Bheda against Sudās. The name has been regarded as a sign of totemism,<sup>3</sup> but this is very uncertain, and it is impossible to say if they were or were not Āryans. <F>1) vii. 18. 19.</F> <F>2) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 127, {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 173.</F> <F>3) {%Cf.%} Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} 153; Keith, {%Journal of the Royal Asiatic%} {%Society,%} 1907, 929; Aitareya Āraṇyaka, 200, 21; Risley, {%Peoples of India,%} 83 {%et seq.%}</F>
{@Ajakava.@}¦ — This name of a poisonous scorpion occurs once in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) vii. 50, 1. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 99.</F>

{@Aja-gara@}¦ (‘goat-swallower’) occurs in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and in the list of animals at the Aśvamedha,<sup>2</sup> or horse sacrifice, as the [Page1-013+ 55] name of the boa-constrictor. Elsewhere<sup>3</sup> it is called Vāhasa. It denotes a person at the snake feast in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) xi. 2, 25; xx. 129, 17.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5, 14, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii, 14, 19; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 38.</F> <F>3) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 13, 1; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 34.</F> <F>4) xxv. 15, in the form of Ajagāva, with which {%cf.%} {@Ajakāva.@}</F>

{@Aja-mīḍha.@}¦ — The Ājamīḍhas, or descendants of Ajamīḍha, are referred to in a hymn of the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> Ludwig<sup>2</sup> and Oldenberg<sup>3</sup> deduce from the use of this patronymic that Ajamīḍha was the seer of that hymn. <F>1) iv. 44, 6.</F> <F>2) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 123, 135.</F> <F>3) {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgenlān-%} {%dischen Gesellschaft,%} 42, 215.</F>

{@Aja-śṛṅgī.@}¦ — This plant (‘goat's horn’), equated by the com- mentator with Viṣāṇin (the {%Odina pinnata%}), is celebrated as a demon-destroyer in the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> Its other name is {@Arāṭakī.@}<sup>2</sup> Weber<sup>3</sup> suggests that it is the {%Prosopis spicigera%} or {%Mimosa suma.%} <F>1) iv. 37.</F> <F>2) iv. 37, 6.</F> <F>3) {%Indische Studien,%} 18, 144. {%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 408, 409; Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 68; Caland, {%Altindisches Zauberritual,%} 89.</F>

{@Ajāta-śatru.@}¦ — He is mentioned as a King of Kāśī (Kāśya) in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka<sup>1</sup> and Kauṣītaki<sup>2</sup> Upaniṣads, where he in- structs the proud Brāhmaṇa Bālāki as to the real nature of the self. He is not to be identified with the Ajātasattu of the Buddhist texts.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) ii. 1, 1.</F> <F>2) iv. 1.</F> <F>3) {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 213; Hoernle, {%Osteology,%} 106; Keith, {%Zeit-%} {%schrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen%} {%Gesellschaft,%} 62, 138.</F>

{@Ajñāta-yakṣma,@}¦ the ‘unknown sickness,’ is mentioned in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> Atharvaveda,<sup>2</sup> and Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā.<sup>3</sup> It is referred to in connection with Rājayakṣma. Grohmann<sup>4</sup> thinks that the two are different forms of disease, hypertrophy and atrophy, the purpose of the spell in the Rigveda being thus the removal of all disease. From the Atharvaveda<sup>5</sup> he deduces its identity with {@Balāsa.@} Zimmer,<sup>6</sup> however, points out that this [Page1-014+ 42] conclusion is unjustified, leaving the disease unidentified, which seems to accord with its name. <F>1) x. 161, 1 = Av. iii. 11, 1.</F> <F>2) vi. 127, 3.</F> <F>3) xiii. 16.</F> <F>4) {%Indische Studien,%} 9, 400.</F> <F>5) vi. 127. 3.</F> <F>6) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 377, 378. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Bloomfield. {%Hymns of the Athar-%} {%vaveda,%} 342; Atharvaveda, 60; Jolly, {%Medicin%} (in Bühler's Encyclopædia), 89.</F>

{@Ajina.@}¦ — This word denotes generally the skin of an animal -{%e.g.,%} a gazelle,<sup>1</sup> as well as that of a goat ({@Aja@}).<sup>2</sup> The use of skins as clothing is shown by the adjective ‘clothed in skins’ ({%ajina-vāsin%}) in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>3</sup> and the furrier's trade is mentioned in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā.<sup>4</sup> The Maruts also wear deer-skins,<sup>5</sup> and the wild ascetics ({%muni%}) of a late Rigveda hymn<sup>6</sup> seem to be clad in skins ({@Mala@}). <F>1) Av. v. 21, 7.</F> <F>2) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, v. 2, 1, 21. 24.</F> <F>3) iii. 9, 1, 12.</F> <F>4) xxx. 15 ({%ajina-saṃdha%}); Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 2, 13, 1 ({%ajina-%} {%saṃdhāya%}).</F> <F>5) Rv. i. 166, 10.</F> <F>6) x. 136, 2. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches%} {%Leben,%} 262.</F>
{@Ajira.@}¦ — He was Subrahmaṇya priest at the snake festival of the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) xxv. 15. See Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 35.</F>

{@Ajīgarta Sauyavasa.@}¦ — This is the name given to the father of {@Śunaḥśepa@} in the famous legend of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> perhaps invented for the occasion, as Weber<sup>2</sup> suggests. <F>1) vii. 15; 17. {%Cf.%} Śāṅkhāyana Srauta Sūtra, xv. 19.</F> <F>2) {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 460; Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>
{@A-jyeyatā.@}¦ See {@Brāhmaṇa.@}
{@Aṇīcin Mauna.@}¦ — He is mentioned as an authority on ritual, and contemporary with {@Jābāla@} and {@Citra Gauśrāyaṇi@} or {@Gauśra,@} in the {@Kauṣītaki@} Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) xxiii. 5.</F>

{@Aṇu.@}¦ — This is the designation in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> and the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad<sup>2</sup> of a cultivated grain, {@apparently@} the {%Panicum miliaceum.%} <F>1) xviii. 12.</F> <F>2) vi. 3, 15 (Kāṇva), where see Dviveda's note.</F>

{@Atithi@}¦ (‘guest’). — A hymn of the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> celebrates in detail the merits of hospitality. The guest should be fed before [Page1-015+ 50] the host eats, water should be offered to him, and so forth. The Taittirīya Upaniṣad<sup>2</sup> also lays stress on hospitality, using the expression ‘one whose deity is his guest’ ({%atithi-deva%}). In the Aitareya Āraṇyaka<sup>3</sup> it is said that only the good are deemed worthy of receiving hospitality. The guest-offering forms a regular part of the ritual,<sup>4</sup> and cows were regularly slain in honour of guests.<sup>5</sup> <F>1) ix. 6.</F> <F>2) i. 11, 2.</F> <F>3) i. 1, 1.</F> <F>4) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, vii. 3, 2, 1.</F> <F>5) {%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%American Journal of%} {%Philology,%} 17, 426; Hillebrandt, {%Ritual-%} {%litteratur,%} 79.</F>

{@Atithi-gva.@}¦ — This name occurs frequently in the Rigveda, apparently applying, in nearly all cases, to the same king, otherwise called {@Divodāsa.@} The identity of the two persons has been denied by Bergaigne,<sup>1</sup> but is certainly proved by a number of passages, when the two names occur together,<sup>2</sup> in connection with the defeat of {@Śambara.@} In other passages<sup>3</sup> Atithigva is said to have assisted Indra in slaying Parṇaya and Karañja. Sometimes he is only vaguely referred to, while once<sup>5</sup> he is mentioned as an enemy of Turvaśa and Yadu. Again<sup>6</sup> Atithigva is coupled with {@Āyu@} and {@Kutsa@} as defeated by {@Tūrvayāṇa.@} <div n="P"/>A different Atithigva appears to be referred to in a Dānastuti<sup>7</sup> (‘Praise of Gifts’), where his son, {@Indrota,@} is mentioned. <div n="P"/>Roth<sup>8</sup> distinguishes three Atithigvas — the Atithigva Divodāsa, the enemy of Parṇaya and Karañja, and the enemy of Tūrvayāṇa. But the various passages can be reconciled, especially if it is admitted that Atithigva Divodāsa was already an ancient hero in the earliest hymns, and was becoming almost mythical. <div n="P"/><sup>4</sup> <F>1) {%Religion Védique,%} 2, 342 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>2) Rv. i. 51, 6; 112, 14; 130, 7; iv. 26, 3; vi. 47, 22.</F> <F>3) Rv. i. 53, 8; x. 48, 8.</F> <F>5) Rv. vii. 19, 8. There is no ground for assuming the reference here to be to a later Atithigva.</F> <F>6) Rv. i. 53, 10; ii. 14, 7; vi. 18, 13; viii. 53, 2.</F> <F>7) Rv. viii. 68, 16. 17.</F> <F>8) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 123; Bloomfield, {%American%} {%Journal of Philology,%} 17, 426, who renders the name ‘presenting cows to guests.’</F> <F>4) Rv. vi. 26, 3.</F>
{@Ati-dhanvan Śaunaka.@}¦ — He is mentioned as a teacher in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad<sup>1</sup> and the Vaṃsa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) i. 9, 3.</F> <F>2) {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 384.</F>
{@A-tṛṇāda.@}¦ — This term (‘not eating grass’) was applied, ac- cording to the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, to a newborn calf.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) i. 5, 2. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 268.</F>

1. {@Atka.@}¦ — This word occurs frequently in the Rigveda, but its sense is doubtful. Roth, Grassmann, Ludwig, Zimmer,<sup>1</sup> and others render it as ‘garment’ in several passages,<sup>2</sup> when the expressions ‘put on’ ({%vyā%} or {%prati muñc%}) or ‘put off’ ({%muñc%}) are used of it, and when it is said to be ‘woven’ ({%vyuta%})<sup>3</sup> or ‘well- fitting’ ({%surabhi%}).<sup>4</sup> On the other hand, Pischel<sup>5</sup> denies that this sense occurs, and otherwise explains the passages. He takes the term to mean ‘axe’ in four places.<sup>6</sup> <F>1) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 262.</F> <F>2) i. 95, 7; ii. 35, 14; iv. 18, 5; v. 55, 6; 74, 5; vi. 29, 3; viii. 41, 7; ix. 101, 14; 107, 13; Sāmaveda, ii. 1193.</F> <F>3) Rv. i. 122, 2.</F> <F>4) Rv. vi. 29, 3; x. 123, 7.</F> <F>5) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 193-204.</F> <F>6) Rv. v. 55, 6; vi. 33, 3; x. 49, 3; 99, 9. {%Cf.%} Oldenberg, {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 94, n. 1.</F>

2. {@Atka.@}¦ — In two passages of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> this word is regarded as a proper name by Roth, Grassmann, and Ludwig. But Zimmer<sup>2</sup> explains it in these passages as the ‘armour of a warrior as a whole,’ and Pischel<sup>3</sup> thinks that in both cases an ‘axe’ is meant. <F>1) x. 49, 3; 99, 9.</F> <F>2) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 262, 297.</F> <F>3) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 195.</F>

{@Aty-aṃhas Āruṇi.@}¦ — According to the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa (iii. 10, 9, 3-5), this teacher sent a pupil to question {@Plakṣa@} {@Dayyāṃpati@} as to the Sāvitra (a form of Agni). For this impertinence his pupil was severely rebuked.

{@Aty-arāti Jānaṃ-tapi,@}¦ though not a prince, was taught the Rājasūya by {@Vāsiṣṭha Satyahavya,@} and thereupon conquered the earth. When Vāsiṣṭha reminded him of his indebtedness, and claimed a great reward, the warrior replied irascibly that he intended to conquer the {@Uttara Kurus,@} and that Vāsiṣṭha would then become King of the Earth, Atyarāti himself being his general ({%senā-pati%}). Vāsiṣṭha replied that as no mortal man could conquer the Uttara Kurus he was cheated of his reward. [Page1-017+ 53] He consequently procured Atyarāti's defeat and death at the hands of {@Amitratapana Śuṣmiṇa Śaibya.@}<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, viii. 23. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 214.</F>

{@Atri.@}¦ — Neither Atri himself nor the Atris can claim any historical reality,<sup>1</sup> beyond the fact that Maṇḍala V. of the Rigveda is attributed, no doubt correctly, to the family of the Atris.<sup>2</sup> The Atris as a family probably stood in close relations with the {@Priyamedhas@}<sup>3</sup> and {@Kaṇvas,@}<sup>4</sup> perhaps also with the {@Gotamas@}<sup>5</sup> and {@Kākṣīvatas.@}<sup>6</sup> The mention of both the {@Paruṣṇī@} and the {@Yamunā@} in one hymn<sup>7</sup> of the fifth Maṇḍala seems to justify the presumption that the family was spread over a wide extent of territory. <F>1) For Atri in the Rigveda, see Mac- donell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} 145. {%Cf.%} also Av. ii. 32, 3; iv. 29, 3; Mantra Brāh- maṇa, ii. 7, 1; Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, iv. 36, etc.; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, ii. 2, 4.</F> <F>2) {%Cf.%} Rv. v. 39, 5; 67, 5; Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, xxiv. 3; Aitareya Āraṇyaka, ii, 2, 1.</F> <F>3) {%Cf.%} Rv. i. 45, 3; 139, 9; viii. 5, 25; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, viii. 22.</F> <F>4) {%Cf.%} Rv. i. 118, 7; v. 41, 4; x. 150, 5.</F> <F>5) {%Cf.%} Rv. i. 183, 5.</F> <F>6) {%Cf.%} Rv. x. 143, 1.</F> <F>7) Rv. v. 52, 9, 17. {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 128, 142; Bergaigne, {%Religion Védique,%} 2, 469; Oldenber, {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen%} {%Morgenländischen Gesellschaft,%} 42, 212- 215; Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 3, 310.</F>

{@Atharī.@}¦ — This word occurs only in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> and the sense is doubtful. Roth,<sup>2</sup> followed by most interpreters, renders it ‘point of a lance,’ but Pischel<sup>3</sup> thinks that it means ‘an elephant.’ <F>1) iv. 6, 8.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>3) {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 99.</F>

{@Atharvan.@}¦ — The name in the singular denotes the head of a semi-divine family of mythical priests,<sup>1</sup> of whom nothing his- torical can be said. In the plural the family as a whole is meant. In a few places an actual family seems to be referred to. Thus, for instance, they are mentioned as recipients of gifts in the Dānastuti<sup>2</sup> (‘Praise of Gifts’), of {@Aśvattha's@} [Page1-018+ 56] generosity; their use of milk mingled with honey in the ritual is referred to;<sup>3</sup> and a cow that miscarries ({%ava-tokā%}) from accident is dedicated to the Atharvans, according to the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) See Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} 141. In the Vaṃśa of the Bṛhad- āraṇyaka Upaniṣad, ii. 6, 3, Atharvan Daiva is characteristically the pupil of Mṛtyu.</F> <F>2) Rv. vi. 47, 24.</F> <F>3) Rv. ix. 11, 2.</F> <F>4) iii. 4, 11, 1. {%Cf.%} Vājasaneyi Saṃ- hitā, xxx. 15. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Athar-%} {%vaveda,%} xxxv. {%et seq.,%} who (p. xxxviii) takes {%avatokā%} as a woman, and the Atharvans as the hymns; Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 2, 174 {%et seq.%}</F>

{@Atharvāṇaḥ.@}¦ — This expression<sup>1</sup> is used with {@Aṅgirasaḥ,@} to denote the Atharvaveda. The compound {@Atharvāṅgirasaḥ@} is employed in the same sense. <F>1) Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 12, 9, 1; Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xvi. 10, 10; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 4, 3, 5 {%et seq.%}</F>

{@Atharvāṅgirasaḥ.@}¦ — This is the collective name of the Athar- vaveda in several passages<sup>1</sup> of the later Brāhmaṇas. It occurs once in the Atharvaveda itself,<sup>2</sup> while the term Atharvaveda is not found before the Sūtra period.<sup>3</sup> The compound seems, according to Bloomfield,<sup>4</sup> to denote the two elements which make up the Atharvaveda. The former part refers to the aus- picious practices of the Veda ({%bheṣajāni%});<sup>5</sup> the latter to its hostile witchcraft, the {%yātu%}<sup>6</sup> or {%abhi-cāra.%}<sup>7</sup> This theory is supported by the names of the two mythic personages {@Ghora Āṅgirasa@} and {@Bhiṣaj Ātharvaṇa,@} as well as by the connection of Atharvāṇaḥ and {@Ātharvaṇāni@} with healing ({%bheṣaja%}) in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>8</sup> Moreover, the term {%bhesajā%} (‘remedies’) designates in the Atharvaveda<sup>9</sup> that Veda itself, while in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>10</sup> {%yātu%} (‘sorcery’) conveys the same meaning. The evidence, however, being by no means convincing, it remains probable that there existed no clear differentiation between the two sages as responsible for the Atharvaveda as a whole. <F>1) Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 12, 8, 2; Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, ii. 9; 10; Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, xi. 5, 6, 7; Bṛhad- āraṇyaka Upaniṣad, ii. 4, 10; iv. 1, 2; 5, 11; Chāndogya Upaniṣad, iii. 4, 1. 2; Taittirīya Upaniṣad, ii. 3, 1.</F> <F>2) x. 7, 20.</F> <F>3) Śāṅkhāyana Srauta Sūtra, xvi. 2, 9, etc.</F> <F>4) {%Journal of the American Oriental%} {%Society,%} 11, 387 {%et seq.; Hymns of the%} {%Atharvaveda,%} xviii. {%et seq.%}</F> <F>5) Av. xi. 6, 14.</F> <F>6) Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, x. 5, 2, 20.</F> <F>7) Kauśika Sūtra, 3, 19.</F> <F>8) xii. 9, 10; xvi. 10, 10.</F> <F>9) x. 6, 14.</F> <F>10) x. 5, 2, 20. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 2, 177.</F>

{@A-dṛṣṭa.@}¦ — ‘The unseen’ is a term used in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and the Atharvaveda<sup>2</sup> to designate a species of vermin. The sun is also described as ‘the slayer of the unseen’ ({%adṛṣṭa-han%}),<sup>3</sup> and as a counterpart a ‘seen’ ({%dṛṣṭa%}) is mentioned.<sup>4</sup> In one passage<sup>5</sup> the epithets ‘seen’ and ‘unseen’ are applied to the worm ({@Kṛmi@}), their use being no doubt due to the widespread theory of diseases being due to worms, whether discernable by examination or not.<sup>6</sup> <F>1) Rv. i. 191, 4 = Av. vi. 52, 2.</F> <F>2) vi. 52, 3.</F> <F>3) Rv. i. 191, 9 = Av. vi. 52, 1; Av. v. 23, 6.</F> <F>4) Av. ii. 31, 2; viii. 8, 15.</F> <F>5) Av. v. 23, 6. 7.</F> <F>6) Kuhn, {%Zeitschrift für vergleichende%} {%Sprachforschung,%} 13, 135 {%et seq.;%} Bloom- field, {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 313- 315; Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 98.</F>

{@Adma-sad.@}¦ — This expression ({%lit.%} ‘sitting at the meal’), found several times in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> is usually rendered ‘guest at the feast,’ but Geldner<sup>2</sup> adduces reasons to show that it means ‘a fly,’ so called because of its settling on food. <F>1) i. 124, 4; vi. 30, 3; vii. 83, 7; viii. 44, 29; {%adma-sadvan,%} vi. 4, 4.</F> <F>2) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 179, 180; but {%of%} Oldenberg, {%Vedaforschung,%} 90.</F>

{@Adri.@}¦ — Zimmer<sup>1</sup> deduces from the use of this word (‘rock,’ ‘stone’) in a passage of the Rigveda,<sup>2</sup> that sling-stones were used in Vedic fighting. But the passage is mythical, referring to Indra's aid, and cannot be used with any certainty as evidence for human war. More probably it merely denotes Indra's bolt. See also {@Aśani.@} <F>1) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 301. {%Cf.%} Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>2) i. 51, 3.</F>

{@Adhi-devana.@}¦ — The place where the dice were thrown is thus designated in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>2</sup> according to Lüders.<sup>3</sup> Roth,<sup>4</sup> followed by Whitney, takes it to mean ‘gambling-board.’ See {@Akṣa.@} <F>1) v. 31, 6; vi. 70, 1.</F> <F>2) v. 4, 4, 20. 22, 23.</F> <F>3) {%Das Würfelspiel im alten Indien,%} 11-13.</F> <F>4) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>

{@Adhi-rāja.@}¦ — The word occurs fairly often throughout the early literature,<sup>1</sup> denoting ‘overlord’ among kings or princes. [Page1-020+ 47] In no passage is it clear that a real over-king is meant, as the word {%rājan%} may mean king or merely prince, a person of royal blood. On the whole it seems most probable that the word connotes no more than ‘king’ as opposed to ‘prince.’ <F>1) Rv. x. 128, 9 Av. vi. 98, 1; ix. 10, 24; Taiturīya Saṃhitā, ii. 4, 14, 2; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhita, iv. 12, 3; Kāthaka Saṃhitā, viii. 17; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 1, 2, 9 ({%adhirājan%}); Śatapatha Brāh- maṇa, v. 4, 2, 2; Nirukta, viii. 2.</F>

{@Adhi-ṣavaṇa.@}¦ — The two Adhiṣavaṇas<sup>1</sup> are usually understood, as by Roth<sup>2</sup> and Zimmer,<sup>3</sup> to designate the two boards between which the Soma was pressed. Hillebrandt,<sup>4</sup> however, shows from the ritual that the boards were not placed one over the other, but were placed one behind the other, the two serving as a foundation upon which the Soma was pressed by a stone. This theory seems to account best for the etymological sense of the name ‘over-press,’ as well as for the use of the word as an adjective (‘used for pressing {%upon%}’). But according to the procedure as witnessed by Haug<sup>5</sup> in the Deccan, the shoots of the plant are first placed on the skin, one of the boards being then laid over them and pounded with a stone. The shoots are then taken out and placed upon the board, the second board being then laid over them. <F>1) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xviii. 21; Av. v. 20, 10; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 9, 4, 1; 5, 3, 22 ({%adhiṣavaṇe%} {%phalake%}); Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vii. 32 ({%adhiṣavaṇaṃ carma,%} ‘the skin upon which the pressing takes place’; {%adhiṣavaṇe phalake,%} ‘the boards on which the pressing takes place,’ etc.).</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>3) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 277.</F> <F>4) {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 148 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>5) See Haug, Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, 2, p. 488, n. 10.</F>

{@Adhī̆-vāsa.@}¦ — This word<sup>1</sup> denotes the ‘upper garment’ of the Vedic Indian. Its exact nature is not described, but as the king in the ritual set forth in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> puts on first an undergarment, then a garment, and finally an upper garment, it presumably denotes some sort of cloak or mantle. <F>1) Rv. i. 140, 9; 162, 16; x. 5, 4; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, v. 3, 5, 22 ({%prati-%} {%muñc,%} ‘put on’); 4, 4, 3 ({%ā-stṛ,%} ‘spread out’), etc.</F> <F>2) v. 3, 5, 19 {%et seq.%} <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 268.</F>
{@Adhyāṇḍā.@}¦ — This is a plant mentioned with many others in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (xiii. 8, 1, 16).

{@Adhri-gu.@}¦ — This is the name of a man twice referred to in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as a protégé of the Aśvins and of Indra respectively. <F>1) i. 112, 20; viii. 12, 2. {%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%Journal of the American Oriental Society,%} 17, 90.</F>

{@Adhvaryu.@}¦ — In one passage of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> Hillebrandt<sup>2</sup> thinks that the five Adhvaryus who are mentioned do not designate actual priests, but refer to the five planets which move about in the heavens like the Adhvaryu priests on the sacrificial ground. See also {@Graha.@} <F>1) iii. 7, 7.</F> <F>2) {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 3, 423.</F>
{@An-agni-dagdha,@}¦ ‘not burnt with fire.’ See {@Agni-dagdha,@} ‘burnt with fire.’

{@Anaḍ-vāh@}¦ (lit. ‘cart-drawer’). — This is the common<sup>1</sup> name of oxen as employed for drawing carts ({@Anas@}). Such oxen were normally castrated,<sup>2</sup> though not always. Female draft cattle were also used ({%anaḍuhī%}), but rarely.<sup>3</sup> See also {@Go.@} <F>1) Rv. x. 59, 10; 85, 10; iii. 53, 18; Av. iii. 11, 5; iv. 11, 1, etc.; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, i. 14; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 1, 4, 17, etc.</F> <F>2) {%Cf.%} Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xv. 1, 5 ({%anaḍvān sāṇḍaḥ%}).</F> <F>3) Av. iv. 11; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, v, 3, 4, 11. 13. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 13, 151, n.; Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 226.</F>

{@Anas.@}¦ — This is the term<sup>1</sup> used to designate the draft wagon, as opposed to the chariot ({%ratha%}) for war or sport, with which it is sometimes expressly contrasted,<sup>2</sup> though Indra is once said to be ‘seated in a wagon’ ({%anar-viś%})<sup>3</sup> instead of on a chariot. Though Uṣas, Goddess of Dawn, sometimes rides on a chariot ({%ratha%}), the wagon is her characteristic vehicle.<sup>4</sup> Of its con- struction we know little. The bridal wagon on which Sūryā, the daughter of the Sun, was borne in the marriage hymn in the Rigveda had a covering ({@Chadis@}).<sup>5</sup> The axle-box ({@Kha@}) is also [Page1-022+ 56] mentioned.<sup>6</sup> In the Atharvaveda<sup>7</sup> Vipatha appears to denote a rough vehicle used for bad tracks. The wagon was usually drawn by oxen ({@Anaḍvāh@}), as in wedding processions.<sup>8</sup> The wagon of Dawn is described as drawn by ruddy cows or bulls.<sup>9</sup> <F>1) Rv. iv. 30, 10; x. 85, 10; 86, 18, etc.; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 1, 2, 5, etc.; Chāndogya Upaniṣad, vii. 15, 1; Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad, iii. 8, etc.</F> <F>2) Rv. iii. 33, 9.</F> <F>3) Rv. i. 121, 7.</F> <F>4) Rv. ii. 15, 6; iv. 30, 11; viii. 91, 7; x. 73, 6; 138, 5.</F> <F>5) Rv. x. 85, 10.</F> <F>6) Rv. viii. 91, 7; Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa, i. 3.</F> <F>7) xv. 2, 1.</F> <F>8) Rv. x. 85, 11</F> <F>9) Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} 47. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 246; Geldner, {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 4.</F>
{@Anās.@}¦ See {@Dasyu.@}
{@Anitabhā@}¦ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> is taken by Max Müller<sup>2</sup> to denote some river. <F>1) v. 53. 9.</F> <F>2) {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 32, 323; but {%of.%} {@Rasā.@}</F>

{@Anu, Ānava.@}¦ — Grassmann and Roth<sup>1</sup> see in these words designations of people foreign to the Aryans. But it is clear<sup>2</sup> that they denote a special people, the Anus, who are mentioned with the {@Yadus, Turvaśas, Druhyus,@} and {@Pūrus,@}<sup>3</sup> with the Druhyus,<sup>4</sup> and with the Turvaśas, Yadus, and Druhyus.<sup>5</sup> It is also a fair conclusion from their mention in a passage of the Rigveda<sup>6</sup> that they dwelt on the Paruṣṇī. The inference that the Bhṛgus were connected with this tribe is much more doubtful,<sup>7</sup> for it rests solely on the fact that in one place<sup>8</sup> the Bhṛgus and Druhyus are mentioned together, and not Anus and Druhyus. Ānava is used as an epithet of Agni,<sup>9</sup> but also in the sense of ‘Anu prince,’<sup>10</sup> in one case in conjunction with Turvaśa.<sup>11</sup> <F>1) St. Petersburg Dictionary.</F> <F>2) Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 125.</F> <F>3) Rv. i. 108, 8.</F> <F>4) Rv. vii. 18, 14.</F> <F>5) viii. 10, 5.</F> <F>6) Rv. viii. 74. 15, compared with vii. 18, 14.</F> <F>7) Oldenberg, {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen%} {%Morgenländischen Gesellschaft,%} 42, 221, n. 1.</F> <F>8) Rv. vii. 18, 4.</F> <F>9) Rv. viii. 74, 4. {%Cf.%} Rv. v. 31, 4, where the Anus prepare the chariot of the Aśvins.</F> <F>10) Rv. vii. 18, 13.</F> <F>11) viii. 4, 1. Apparently as prince also in vi. 62, 9. {%Cf.%} {@Kuruṅga.@} <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 205; Hillebrandt, {%Vedische%} {%Mythologie,%} 3, 153; Macdonell, {%Sanskrit%} {%Literature,%} 154.</F>

{@Anu-kṣattṛ.@}¦ — This word occurs in the list of victims at the Puruṣamedha,<sup>1</sup> and means, according to Mahīdhara,<sup>2</sup> ‘an attendant on the door-keeper,’ and, according to Sāyaṇa, ‘an attendant on the charioteer’ ({%sārathi%}). See also {@Kṣattṛ.@} <div n="P"/>3) On Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, {%loc. cit.%} <F>1) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxx. 11; 73; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 9, 1.</F> <F>2) On Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, {%loc. cit.%}</F>

{@Anu-cara.@}¦ — This is a general expression<sup>1</sup> for an ‘attendant’ (the feminine being Anucarī),<sup>2</sup> but it is not often used. <F>1) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxx. 13; Tait- tirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 7, 1.</F> <F>2) Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 5, 4, 27 (apparently slave girls are meant, 400 being enumerated).</F>
{@Anu-mati.@}¦ See {@Māsa.@}
{@Anu-rādhā.@}¦ See {@Nakṣatra.@}
{@Anu-vaktṛ Satya Sātya-kīrta@}¦ is mentioned as a teacher in the Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa Upaniṣad (i. 5, 4).

{@Anuvyā-khyāna@}¦ is a species of writing referred to in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.<sup>1</sup> Śaṅkara interprets it as ‘explana- tion of the Mantras.’ As the term, in the plural, follows {@Sūtras,@} this interpretation is reasonable. Sieg,<sup>2</sup> however, equates the word with {@Anvākhyāna,@} ‘supplementary narrative.’ <F>1) ii. 4, 10; iv. 1, 2; 5, 11.</F> <F>2) {%Die Sagenstoffe des Ṛgveda,%} 34.</F>
{@Anu-śāsana@}¦ in the plural denotes in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (xi. 5, 6, 8) some form of literature; according to Sāyaṇa, the Vedāṅgas.
{@Anu-śikha@}¦ is the name of the Potṛ at the snake festival in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) xxv. 15. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 35.</F>

{@Ante-vāsin,@}¦ ‘dwelling near,’ is the epithet of the {@Brahma-@} {@cārin@} who lives in the house of his teacher. The expression does not occur before the late Brāhmaṇa period.<sup>1</sup> Secrecy is often enjoined on others than Antevāsins.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, v. 1, 5, 17; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, vi. 3, 7; Chāndogya Upaniṣad, iii. 11, 5; iv. 10, 1; Taittirīya Upaniṣad, i. 3, 3; 11, 1.</F> <F>2) Aitareya Āraṇyaka, iii. 2, 6; Sāṅkh- āyana Āraṇyaka, viii, 11.</F>

{@Andhra@}¦ is the name of a people, and is mentioned with the {@Puṇḍras, Śabaras, Pulindas,@} and {@Mūtibas,@} as being the outcasts resulting from the refusal of the fifty eldest sons of {@Viśvāmitra@} to accept his adoption of {@Śunaḥśepa.@}<sup>1</sup> It may fairly be deduced [Page1-024+ 48] from this statement that these people were recognized as non- Aryan, as the Andhras certainly seem to have been.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vii. 18; Śāṅkh- āyana Śrauta Sūtra, xv. 26, where instead of {%udāntyaḥ%} (‘beyond the borders’) the reading is {%udañcaḥ%} (‘nor- thern’), but the former is obviously correct. The Sāṅkhāyana omits the Pulindas, and has Mūcīpas.</F> <F>2) Vincent Smith, {%Zeitschrift der Deut-%} {%schen Morgenländischen Gesellschaft,%} 56, 657 {%et seq.,%} who places them originally in Eastern India between the Kṛṣṇā and Godāvarī rivers; {%cf.%} Rapson, {%Catalogue of Indian Coins,%} xv., xvi.; Bhandarkar, {%Bombay Gazetteer,%} 1. ii. 138.</F>

{@Anyataḥ-plakṣā@}¦ (‘with wave-leafed fig-trees on one side only’) is the name of a lake in Kurukṣetra according to the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> where it occurs in the story of Purū- ravas and Urvaśī. Pischel<sup>2</sup> places it somewhere in Sirmor. <F>1) xi. 5, 1, 4.</F> <F>2) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 217.</F>

{@Anya-vāpa@}¦ (‘sowing for others’). — The cuckoo is so called<sup>1</sup> from its habit of depositing its eggs in the nests of other birds <F>1) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 37; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 18.</F>

{@Anvā-khyāna.@}¦ — From the literal translation (‘after-story’) the meaning of ‘supplementary narrative’ seems to follow. In two<sup>1</sup> of its three occurrences in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa this sense is hardly felt, the expression being used to indicate a subse- quent portion of the book itself. But in the third<sup>2</sup> passage it is distinguished from the {@Itihāsa@} (‘story’) proper, and there must mean ‘supplementary narrative.’ {%Cf.%} {@Anuvyākhyāna.@} <F>1) vi. 5, 2, 22; 6, 4, 7 (the reference is to vi. 6, 4, 8).</F> <F>2) xi. 1, 6, 9. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Sieg, {%Die Sagenstoffe des Ṛgveda,%} 34.</F>

{@Apa-cit.@}¦ — This word occurs several times in the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> It is held by Roth,<sup>2</sup> Zimmer,<sup>3</sup> and others to denote an insect whose sting produced swellings, etc. ({%glau%}). But Bloomfield<sup>4</sup> shows that the disease, scrofulous swellings, is what is really meant, as is shown by the rendering ({%gaṇḍa-mālā,%} ‘inflammation of the glands of the neck’) of Keśava and Sāyaṇa, and by the parallelism of the later disease, {%apacī,%} the derivation being from {%apa%} and {%ci,%} ‘to pick off.’ <F>1) vi. 25, 1; 83, 1; vii. 75, 1; 77, 1.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>3) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 97. So also Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, {{, 342, 500->3, 342, 500||20241111|Dr. Dhaval Patel, Andhrabharati|https://github.com/sanskrit-lexicon/csl-orig/issues/614|}}.</F> <F>4) {%American Journal of Philology,%} 11, 320 {%et seq.; Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 503, 504. {%Cf.%} Jolly, {%Medicin,%} 89; Whitney, Translation of the Athar- vaveda, 343.</F>
{@Apa-śraya.@}¦ See {@Upaśraya.@}

{@Apa-skambha.@}¦ — The word occurs only in one passage of the Atharvaveda, where the tip of it is mentioned as poisoned. Roth<sup>1</sup> suggests that the fastening of the arrow-point to the shaft is meant. Whitney<sup>2</sup> inclines to this version, but suggests corruption of text. Zimmer<sup>3</sup> follows Roth. Ludwig<sup>4</sup> renders the word by ‘barb.’ Bloomfield<sup>5</sup> thinks it means ‘tearing (arrow),’ a sense deduced from the etymology. <F>1) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} The passage is Av. iv. 6, 4.</F> <F>2) Translation of the Atharvaveda, 153.</F> <F>3) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 300.</F> <F>4) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 512.</F> <F>5) {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 375.</F>
{@Apācyas.@}¦ — The kings of the ‘Westerners’ are referred to in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (viii. 14) in connection with those of the {@Nīcyas.@}

{@Apāna.@}¦ — The word appears repeatedly in the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> and later as one of the vital breaths ({@Prāṇa@}), usually with Prāṇa, and often with one or more of the other three. Its original sense<sup>2</sup> appears to have been ‘inspiration.’ Its con- nection with the lower part of the body ({%nābhi,%} ‘navel’), which is found already in the Aitareya Upaniṣad,<sup>3</sup> is not unnatural. <F>1) Av. ii. 28, 3; v. 30, 12, etc.; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xiii. 19; 24, etc.</F> <F>2) See Caland, {%Zeitschrift der Deut-%} {%schen Morgenländischen Gesellschaft,%} lv. 261; 56, 556-558, correcting Ewing, {%Journal of the American Oriental Society,%} 22, 249 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>3) Aitareya Upaniṣad, i. 4, etc. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Deussen, {%Philosophy of the Upani-%} {%shads,%} 263 {%et seq.%}</F>

{@Apā-mārga.@}¦ — A plant ({%Achyranthes aspera%}) used frequently<sup>1</sup> in witchcraft practices, and for medical purposes, especially against {@Kṣetriya.@} It is described in the Atharvaveda<sup>2</sup> as ‘revertive’ ({%punaḥ-sara%}), either, as Roth<sup>3</sup> and Zimmer<sup>4</sup> think, because of its having reverted leaves (a view also accepted by Whitney<sup>5</sup> ), [Page1-026+ 46] or because, as Bloomfield<sup>6</sup> holds, it wards off a spell by causing it to recoil on its user. <F>1) Atharvaveda, iv. 17, 6; 18, 7; 19, 4; vii. 65, 2; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxxv. 11; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 7, 1, 8; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, v. 2, 4, 14; xiii. 8, 4, 4.</F> <F>2) iv. 17, 2.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>4) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 67.</F> <F>5) Translation of the Atharvaveda, 180.</F> <F>6) {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 394. {%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Journal of the American%} {%Oriental Society,%} 15, 160, 161; Weber {%Indische Studien,%} 18, 94.</F>

{@Apa-lamba.@}¦ — By this word<sup>1</sup> is denoted a brake or drag, let down (from {%lamb,%} ‘hang down’) to check the speed of a wagon. <F>1) Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 3, 4, 13. {%Cf.%} Caland and Henry, {%L'Agniṣṭoma,%} 50; Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.;%} Eggeling, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 26, 79.</F>

{@Apāṣṭha.@}¦ — This word occurs twice in the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> denoting the barb of an arrow. <F>1) iv. 6, 5; v. 18, 7 ({%śatāpāṣṭha,%} ‘huṅ- dred-barbed’). {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches%} {%Leben,%} 300; Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the%} {%Atharvaveda,%} 375.</F>
{@Api-śarvara.@}¦ See {@Anan.@}

{@Apī.@}¦ — Ludwig<sup>1</sup> finds an Apī whose sons are described as not performing sacrifice ({%a-yajña-sāc%}) and as breakers of the law of Mitra-Varuṇa in the Rigveda.<sup>2</sup> Roth<sup>3</sup> and Grassmann take the expression used ({%apyaḥ putrāḥ%}) as referring to the sons of the waters. <F>1) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 158, 159.</F> <F>2) vi. 67, 9.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v., apya.%}</F>

{@Apūpa@}¦ is the general word from the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> onwards for a cake, which might be mixed with ghee ({%ghṛtavant%}),<sup>2</sup> or be made of rice ({%vrīhi%}),<sup>3</sup> or of barley ({%yava%}).<sup>4</sup> In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad<sup>5</sup> there is a difference of interpretation. Max Müller renders it as ‘hive,’ Böhtlingk as ‘honeycomb,’ Little<sup>6</sup> as ‘cake.’ <F>1) iii. 52, 7.</F> <F>2) Rv. x. 45, 9.</F> <F>3) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 2, 3, 12, 13.</F> <F>4) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iv. 2, 5, 19.</F> <F>5) iii. 1, 1.</F> <F>6) {%Grammatical Index, s.v.%}</F>

{@Apnavāna@}¦ appears only twice in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as an ancient sage, coupled with the Bhṛgus, to whose family Ludwig<sup>2</sup> con- jectures him to have belonged. <F>1) iv. 7, 1; viii. 91, 4.</F> <F>2) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 128.</F>

{@A-prati-ratha@}¦ (‘he who has no match in fight’) is the name of an obviously invented Ṛṣi, to whom is ascribed by the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> and Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> the composition of a Rigveda hymn<sup>3</sup> celebrating Indra as the invincible warrior. <F>1) viii. 10.</F> <F>2) ix. 2, 3, 1. 5.</F> <F>3) x. 103.</F>

{@Apvā.@}¦ — A disease affecting the stomach,<sup>1</sup> possibly dysentery, as suggested by Zimmer,<sup>2</sup> on the ground that the disease is invoked to confound the enemy.<sup>3</sup> Weber<sup>4</sup> considers that it is diarrhœa induced by fear, as often in the Epic.<sup>5</sup> This view is supported by Bloomfield,<sup>6</sup> and was apparently that of Yāska.<sup>7</sup> <F>1) Av. ix. 8, 9.</F> <F>2) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 389.</F> <F>3) Rv. x. 103, 12 = Av. iii. 2, 5 = Sāmaveda, ii. 1211 = Vājasaneyi Saṃ- hitā, xvii. 44.</F> <F>4) {%Indische Studien,%} 9, 482; 17, 184.</F> <F>5) {%Indische Studien,%} 17, 184.</F> <F>6) {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 327.</F> <F>7) Nirukta, ix. 33. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 86, 87.</F>

{@Apsas.@}¦ — This word usually refers to the body, meaning ‘front part.’<sup>1</sup> In one passage of the Rigveda,<sup>2</sup> however, the adjective ‘with a long front part’ ({%dīrghāpsas%}) is applied to the chariot ({@Ratha@}). <F>1) See Pischel, {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 308-313; 2, 245, 246.</F> <F>2) i. 122, 15. {%Cf.%} Roth, St. Peters- burg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>

{@Abhi-krośaka@}¦ designates one of the victims in the Puruṣa- medha, meaning, perhaps, ‘herald.’ The commentator Mahī- dhara<sup>1</sup> renders it as ‘reviler’ ({%nindaka%}). <F>1) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxx. 20. {%Cf.%} Anukrośaka, Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 15, 1.</F>
{@Abhi-jit.@}¦ See {@Nakṣatra.@}
{@Abhi-pitva.@}¦ See {@Ahan.@}

{@Abhi-pratārin Kākṣa-seni@}¦ is mentioned in the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> the Chāndogya Upaniṣad,<sup>2</sup> and the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa,<sup>3</sup> as engaged in discussions on philo- sophy. The Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa<sup>4</sup> further reports that his sons divided the property amongst themselves while he was yet alive. He was a Kuru and a prince. <F>1) i. 59, 1; iii. 1, 21; 2, 2. 13.</F> <F>2) iv. 3, 5.</F> <F>3) x. 5, 7; xiv. 1, 12. 15.</F> <F>4) iii. 156 ({%Journal of the American%} {%Oriental Society,%} 26, 61).</F>

{@Abhi-praśnin.@}¦ — This term occurs after {@Praśnin,@} and followed by {@Praśnavivāka@} in the list of victims for the Puruṣamedha given in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> and the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā.<sup>2</sup> The commentators, Sāyaṇa and Mahīdhara, see in it merely a reference to an inquisitive man. But there can be little doubt that the term must have had a legal reference of some sort —  perhaps indicating the defendant as opposed to plaintiff and judge. <F>1) iii. 4, 6, 1.</F> <F>2) xxx. 10.</F>

{@Abhi-śrī@}¦ (‘admixture’). — This word<sup>1</sup> designates the milk used to mingle with the Soma juice before it was offered. <F>1) Rv. ix. 79, 5; 86, 27. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 227; Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} i. 211.</F>

{@Abhi-ṣavaṇī.@}¦ — Zimmer<sup>1</sup> renders the expression in the Atharvaveda<sup>2</sup> as a pressing instrument, but it appears to be merely an adjective, (waters) ‘used in pressing.’<sup>3</sup> <F>1) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 277.</F> <F>2) ix. 6, 16.</F> <F>3) {%Cf.%} Whitney's Translation of Av. ix. 6, 16.</F>

{@Abhi-ṣeka@}¦ (‘besprinkling’). — The Vedic king was conse- crated after his election with an elaborate ritual, which is fully described in the Taittirīya,<sup>1</sup> Pañcaviṃśa,<sup>2</sup> Śatapatha,<sup>3</sup> and Aitareya Brāhmaṇas,<sup>4</sup> and for which the Mantras are given in the Saṃhitās.<sup>5</sup> The consecration took place by sprinkling with water ({%abhiṣecanīyā āpaḥ%}).<sup>6</sup> Only kings could be consecrated, the people not being worthy of it ({%anabhiṣecanīyāḥ%}).<sup>7</sup> The sprinkler ({%abhiṣektṛ%}) is mentioned in the list of victims at the Puruṣamedha.<sup>8</sup> The Abhiṣeka is an essential part of the {@Rājasūya,@} or sacrifice of royal inauguration, being the second of its component members. <div n="P"/>9 {%Cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%Rituallitteratur,%} 143-147; Eggeling, {%Sacred Books of the%} {%East,%} 41, xxvi; Weber, {%Über den%} {%Rājasūya.%} <F>1) i. 7, 5.</F> <F>2) xviii. 8 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>3) v. 3, 3 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>4) viii. 5 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>5) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, i. 8, 11; Kāṭh- aka Saṃhitā, xv. 6; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃ- hitā, ii. 6; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, x. 1-4.</F> <F>6) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, v. 3, 5, 10-15,</F> <F>7) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 4, 2, 17.</F> <F>8) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxx. 12; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 8, 1.</F>

{@Abhīśu@}¦ is a common Vedic word<sup>1</sup> denoting the ‘reins’ or ‘bridle’ of the chariot horses. The use of the plural is due to the fact that two or four horses, possibly five ({%daśābhīśu%} ‘ten- bridled’),<sup>2</sup> were yoked to the car. <F>1) Rv. i. 38, 12; v. 44, 4; vi. 75, 6; viii. 33, 11; Av. vi. 137, 2; viii. 8, 22; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxxiv. 6; Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, v. 4, 3, 14 (where it = {%raśmayaḥ,%} ‘reins’), etc.</F> <F>2) Rv. x. 94, 7.</F>

{@Abhy-agni Aitaśāyana.@}¦ — This man was, according to the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> unfortunate enough to quarrel with his father, {@Aitaśa.@} The result was that he and his progeny were called the worst of the {@Aurvas.@} In the version of the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa,<sup>2</sup> the {@Aitaśāyana Ājāneyas@} take the place of the Abhyagnis and the {@Bhṛgus@} of the {@Aurvas,@} the latter being probably a branch of the former family. <F>1) vi. 33.</F> <F>2) xxx. 5. {%Cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 2, 173.</F>

{@Abhyā-vartin Cāyamāna@}¦ appears in a Dānastuti (‘Praise of Gifts’) in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> and as conqueror of the Vṛcīvants under the leader {@Varaśikha.@} It is probable though not abso- lutely certain, that he is identical with the {@Sṛñjaya Daivavāta,@} mentioned in the same hymn<sup>2</sup> as having the {@Turvaśas@} and {@Vṛcīvants@} defeated for him by Indra. In this case he would be prince ({%samrāj%}) of the Sṛñjayas. Daivavāta is mentioned elsewhere<sup>3</sup> as a worshipper of Agni. <div n="P"/>Abhyāvartin is also referred to as a Pārthava. Ludwig<sup>4</sup> and Hillebrandt<sup>5</sup> maintained that he is thus a Parthian, the latter using the evidence of the two places mentioned in the descrip- tion<sup>6</sup> of Daivavāta's victories, {@Hariyūpīyā@} and {@Yavyāvatī,@} as proofs for the western position of Abhyāvartin's people in Arachosia, in Iran. But Zimmer<sup>7</sup> is probably right in holding that the name Pārthava merely means ‘a descendant of Pṛthu,’ and that its similarity to the Iranian Parthians is only on a par with the numerous other points of identity between the Indian and Iranian cultures. <F>1) vi. 27, 8. 5.</F> <F>2) vi. 27, 7.</F> <F>3) iv. 15, 4.</F> <F>4) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 198 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>5) {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 105; 3, 268, n. 1. {%Cf.%} Grierson, {%Journal of the Royal%} {%Asiatic Society,%} 1908, 604 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>6) Rv. vi. 27, 5. 6.</F> <F>7) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 133 {%et seq.,%} 433; Bergaigne, {%Religion Védique,%} 2, 362.</F>

{@A-bhrātaraḥ@}¦ (‘brotherless’). — The lot of girls without brothers is referred to in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as unsatisfactory — apparently they became prostitutes. The Nirukta<sup>2</sup> expressly forbids marriage with a brotherless maiden, probably because of the risk of her being made a {%putrikā%} (‘adoptive daughter’) by her father — that is, any son of hers being counted as belonging to her father's, instead of to her husband's, family. See {@Ayogū.@} <F>1) i. 124, 7; iv. 5, 5. {%Cf.%} Av. i. 17, 1.</F> <F>2) iii. 5 ({%abhrātrī%}). <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Athar-%} {%vaveda,%} 259; Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 328.</F>

{@Abhri@}¦ (‘spade’) is a Vedic word<sup>1</sup> of frequent occurrence. Various possible materials and forms are enumerated in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> It may be made of bamboo or of the wood of Vikaṅkata or Udumbara. It may be a span or a cubit in size. It is hollow, and either one or both edges are sharp. From this it would appear that the handle was made of some wood, but the head of some metal. <F>1) Av. iv. 7, 5. 6 ({%abhri-khāte%} is ‘dug out with a spade,’ not ‘prepared ground’ with Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}); x. 4, 14; {%hiraṇya-%} {%yībhir abhribhiḥ,%} ‘with golden spades’); Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, v. 22; xi. 10; xxxvii. 1; Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xvi. 6; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 3, 2, 15, etc.</F> <F>2) vi. 3, 1, 30 {%et seq.%}</F>

{@Amatra@}¦ was a vessel into which the Soma, after being pressed, was poured,<sup>1</sup> and out of which the libation to the god was made.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) Rv. ii. 14, 1; v. 51, 4; vi. 42, 2, etc.</F> <F>2) Rv. x. 29, 7. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 278; Oldenberg, {%Ṛgveda Noten,%} 1, 61.</F>

{@Amalā.@}¦ — This plant<sup>1</sup> is probably the {%Emblica officinalis,%} or Myrobalan tree; also called {@Āmalaka,@} or {@Āmalakā.@}<sup>2</sup> <F>1) Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa, i. 38, 6.</F> <F>2) The reading in Chāndogya Upani- ṣad, vii. 3, 1, is {%vāmalake,%} which may give {%ă˚%} or {%ā˚.%}</F>

{@Amā-jur@}¦ is an epithet<sup>1</sup> denoting maidens ‘who grow old at home’ without finding husbands, or, as they are elsewhere called, ‘who sit with their father’ ({%pitṛ-ṣad%}). A well-known example of such was Ghoṣā.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) Rv. ii. 17, 7; viii. 21, 15; x. 37, 3.</F> <F>2) Rv. i. 117, 7. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altin-%} {%disches Leben,%} 305.</F>

{@{{Amā-vāsya Śāṇdilyāyana->Amā-vāsya Śāṇḍilyāyana||20170912|Dr. Dhaval Patel|https://github.com/sanskrit-lexicon/CORRECTIONS/issues/410|}}@}¦ is mentioned in the Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> as the teacher of {@Aṃśu Dhānaṃjayya.@} <F>1) {%Indische Studien,%} iv. 373.</F>
{@Amitra-tapana Śuṣmiṇa Śaibya@}¦ is the name of him who killed {@Atyarāti Jānaṃtapi,@} according to the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (viii. 23).

{@A-mūlā@}¦ (‘without root’) is the name in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> of a plant ({%Methonica superba%}), which was used for poisoning arrows. Bloomfield,<sup>2</sup> however, renders it as ‘movable property.’ <F>1) v. 314. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 18, 286; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 279, accepts ‘rootless (plant).’</F> <F>2) {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 457.</F>

{@Ambarīṣa@}¦ is mentioned as a Vārṣāgira in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> along with {@Ṛjrāśva, Sahadeva, Surādhas,@} and {@Bhayamāna.@} <F>1) i. 100, 17. {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 140.</F>
{@Ambaṣṭha.@}¦ See {@Āmbaṣṭhya.@}
{@Aya.@}¦ See {@Akṣa.@}

{@Ayas.@}¦ — The exact metal denoted by this word when used by itself, as always in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> is uncertain. As favouring the sense of ‘bronze’ rather than that of ‘iron’ may perhaps be cited with Zimmer<sup>2</sup> the fact that Agni is called {%ayo-daṃṣṭra,%} ‘with teeth of Ayas,’<sup>3</sup> with reference to the colour of his flames, and that the car-seat of Mitra and Varuṇa is called {%ayaḥ-sthūṇa,%}<sup>4</sup> ‘with pillars of Ayas’ at the setting of the sun.<sup>5</sup> Moreover, in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā,<sup>6</sup> Ayas is enumerated in a list of six metals: gold ({%hiraṇya%}), Ayas, Śyāma, Loha, lead ({%sīsa%}), tin ({%trapu%}). Here {%śyāma%} (‘swarthy’) and {%loha%} (‘red’) must mean ‘iron’ and ‘copper’ respectively; {%ayas%} would therefore seem to mean ‘bronze.’ In many passages in the Atharvaveda<sup>7</sup> and [Page1-032+ 48] other books, the Ayas is divided into two species — the {%śyāma%} (‘iron’) and the {%lohita%} (‘copper’ or ‘bronze’). In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>8</sup> a distinction is drawn between Ayas and {%lohāyasa,%} which may either be a distinction between iron and copper as understood by Eggeling,<sup>9</sup> or between copper and bronze as held by Schrader.<sup>10</sup> In one passage of the Atharvaveda,<sup>11</sup> the sense of iron seems certain. Possibly, too, the arrow of the Rigveda,<sup>12</sup> which had a tip of Ayas ({%yasyā ayo mukham%}), was pointed with iron. Copper, however, is conceivable, and bronze quite likely. <div n="P"/>Iron is called {%śyāma ayas%} or {%śyāma%} alone.<sup>13</sup> See also {@Kārṣṇāyasa.@} Copper is {@Lohāyasa@} or {@Lohitāyasa.@} <div n="P"/>The smelting ({%dhmā%} ‘to blow’) of the metal is frequently referred to. The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>14</sup> states that if ‘well smelted’ ({%bahu-dhmātam%}) it is like gold, referring evidently to bronze. A heater of Ayas is mentioned in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā,<sup>15</sup> and bowls of Ayas are also spoken of.<sup>16</sup> <F>1) Rv. i. 57, 3; 163, 9; iv. 2, 17; vi. 3, 5.</F> <F>2) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 52.</F> <F>3) Rv. i. 88, 5; x. 87, 2.</F> <F>4) Rv. v. 62, 8 ({%cf.%} 7).</F> <F>5) But this is not convincing, as in the same verse it is said to be ‘of golden appearance at the flush of dawn.’</F> <F>6) xviii. 13.</F> <F>7) xi. 3, 1. 7; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iv. 2, 9.</F> <F>8) v. 4, 1, 2.</F> <F>9) {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 41, 90</F> <F>10) {%Prehistoric Antiquities,%} 189.</F> <F>11) v. 28, 1.</F> <F>12) vi. 75, 15.</F> <F>13) Av. ix. 5, 4.</F> <F>14) vi. 1, 3, 5. {%Cf.%} vi. 1, 1, 13; v. 1, 2, 14; xii. 7, 1, 7; 2, 10, etc.</F> <F>15) xxx. 14; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 10, 1.</F> <F>16) Av. viii. 10, 22; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃ- hitā, iv. 2, 13.</F>

{@Aya-sthūṇa.@}¦ — He was Gṛhapati (‘householder,’ the sacrificer at sacrificial sessions) of those whose Adhvaryu was Śaulvā- yana, and taught the latter the proper mode of using certain spoons.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xi. 4, 2, 17 {%et seq.%}</F>

{@Ayāsya Āṅgirasa.@}¦ — This sage appears to be mentioned in two passages of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> and the Anukramaṇī ascribes to him several hymns of the Rigveda (ix. 44-46; x. 67; 68). In the Brāhmaṇa tradition he was Udgātṛ at the Rājasūya or Royal Inauguration Sacrifice, at which Śunaḥśepa was to have been slain, and his Udgītha (Sāmaveda chant) is referred to elsewhere.<sup>3</sup> He is also referred to several times as a ritual <div n="P"/>2) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vii. 16. [Page1-033+ 59] authority.<sup>4</sup> In the Vaṃśas, or Genealogies of the Bṛhadāraṇ- yaka Upaniṣad,<sup>5</sup> he is named as the pupil of Ābhūti Tvāṣṭra. <F>1) x. 67, 1; 108, 8. Perhaps x. 92. 15 also refers to him, but not i. 62, 7; x. 138, 4.</F> <F>3) Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa, ii. 7, 2. 6; 8, 3. {%Cf.%} Chāndogya Upaniṣad, i. 2, 12.</F> <F>4) Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xiv. 3, 22; xvi. 12, 4; xi. 8, 10; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, i. 3, 8. 19. 24; Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, xxx. 6.</F> <F>5) ii. 6, 3; iv. 6, 3 (in both recensions). <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rig- veda, 3, 136; Hillebrandt, {%Vedische%} {%Mythologie,%} 2, 159; Weber, {%Indische%} {%Studien,%} 1, 255, n.; Pischel, {%Vedische%} {%Studien,%} 3, 204.</F>

{@Ayogū@}¦ is a word of quite doubtful meaning, found in the list of victims in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā.<sup>1</sup> It may, like the late {%āyogava,%} denote a member of a mixed caste (theoretically a descendant of a Śūdra by a Vaiśya wife).<sup>2</sup> Weber<sup>3</sup> rendered it as ‘unchaste woman.’<sup>4</sup> Zimmer thinks it denotes a brotherless maiden who is exposed to the dangers of prostitution ({%cf.%} {%āyogava%}). <F>1) xxx. 5; Taithrīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 1, 1.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>3) {%Indische Streifen,%} 1, 76, n. b. In the {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen%} {%Gesellschaft,%} 18, 277, he thought it re- ferred to dicing ({%ayas%}). Risley, {%Peoples%} {%of India,%} 250, regards the Āyogavas as a functional caste of carpenters ({%cf.%} Manu, x. 48).</F> <F>4) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 328.</F>
{@Ara.@}¦ See {@Ratha.@}

{@Araṭu.@}¦ — A plant<sup>1</sup> ({%Colosanthes Indica%}) from the wood of which the axle of a chariot was sometimes made.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) Av. xx. 131, 17.</F> <F>2) Rv. viii. 46, 27. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 62, 247.</F>

{@Araṇya.@}¦ — This term denotes the uncultivated land — not necessarily forest land — beyond the village. It is contrasted with home ({%amā%}),<sup>1</sup> and with the plough land ({%kṛṣi%}),<sup>2</sup> being spoken of as apart ({%tiras%}) from men.<sup>3</sup> It is also contrasted with the {@Grāma,@}<sup>4</sup> and it is the place where thieves live.<sup>5</sup> The character of the forest is described in a hymn of the Rigveda<sup>6</sup> to the forest spirit (Araṇyānī). The dead are carried there for burial,<sup>7</sup> and hermits live there.<sup>8</sup> Forest fires were common.<sup>9</sup> <F>1) Rv. vi. 24, 10.</F> <F>2) Av. ii. 4, 5.</F> <F>3) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 6, 2, 20.</F> <F>4) Av. xii. 1, 56; Rv. i. 163, 11; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, iii. 45; xx. 17.</F> <F>5) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, v. 2, 3, 5; xiii. 2, 4, 4.</F> <F>6) x. 146.</F> <F>7) Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, v. 11.</F> <F>8) Chāndogya Upaniṣad, viii. 5, 3.</F> <F>9) Rv. i. 65, 4; 94, 10. 11; ii. 14, 2; x. 92, 1; 142, 4; Av. vii. 50, etc. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 48, 142.</F>

{@Aratni.@}¦ — This word, which primarily means ‘elbow,’ occurs frequently from the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> onwards as denoting a measure of length (‘ell’ or ‘cubit’), the distance from the elbow to the tip of the hand. The exact length nowhere appears from the early texts. <F>1) Rv. viii. 80, 8; Av. xix. 57, 6; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, viii. 5; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, vi. 3, 1, 33, etc. For Rv. viii. 80, 8, see also Āji.</F>

{@A-rājānaḥ,@}¦ ‘not princes,’ is a term used to describe persons in two passages of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> and in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> Weber<sup>3</sup> also finds them mentioned in the Atharvaveda,<sup>4</sup> and thinks that they — {@Sūtas@} (‘charioteers’) and {@Grāmaṇīs@} (‘troop-leaders’) there referred to — were called thus because, while not themselves princes, they assisted in the con- secration of princes. <F>1) iii. 4, 1, 7. 8; xiii. 4, 2, 17.</F> <F>2) viii. 23.</F> <F>3) {%Indische Studien,%} 17, 199.</F> <F>4) iii. 5, 7, where he emends {%rājānaḥ%} to {%a-rājānaḥ%} (see Whitney's note on the passage). {%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the%} {%Atharvaveḍa,%} 333; Weber, {%Über den%} {%Rājasūya,%} 22 {%et seq.%}</F>

{@Arāṭakī@}¦ is a plant mentioned once in the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> and apparently identical with the {@Ajaśṛṅgī.@} {%Cf.%} also {@Araṭu.@} <F>1) iv. 37, 6. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 68; Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 408.</F>
{@Arāḍa Dātreya Śaunaka.@}¦ — He is mentioned in the Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> as the pupil of {@Dṛti Aindrota Śaunaka.@} <F>1) {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 384.</F>

{@Aritra@}¦ denotes the ‘oar’ by which boats were propelled.
