The Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā<sup>2</sup> speak of a vessel with a hundred oars, and a boat ({%nau%}) is said to be ‘propelled by oars’ ({%aritra-paraṇa%}).<sup>3</sup> In two passages of the Rigveda<sup>4</sup> the term, according to the St. Petersburg Dictionary, denotes a part of a chariot. The rower of a boat is called {%aritṛ.%}<sup>5</sup> See {@Nau.@} <F>1) i. 116, 5.</F> <F>2) xxi. 7.</F> <F>3) Rv. x. 101, 2. {%Cf.%} Śatapatha Brāh- maṇa, iv. 2, 5, 10.</F> <F>4) i. 46, 8; {%daśāritra,%} ii. 18, 1.</F> <F>5) Rv. ii. 42, 1; ix. 95, 2. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 256.</F>
{@Ariṃ-dama Sana-śruta@}¦ is mentioned as a Mahārāja in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vii. 34.
{@Arim-ejaya@}¦ is mentioned as one who served as Adhvaryu at the snake feast celebrated in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) xxv. 15. See Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 35.</F>
{@Aruṇa Āṭa@}¦ was Achāvāka at the snake feast in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa (xxv. 15).

{@Aruṇa Aupaveśi Gautama@}¦ is the full style<sup>1</sup> of a teacher, who is repeatedly referred to in the later Saṃhitās<sup>2</sup> and Brāhmaṇas,<sup>3</sup> and whose son was the famous {@Uddālaka Āruṇi.@} He was a pupil of Upaveśa,<sup>4</sup> and a contemporary of the prince {@Aśvapati,@} by whom he was instructed. {%Cf.%} {@Āruṇa.@} <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vi. 1, 9, 2; 4, 5, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, i. 4, 10; iii. 6, 4. 6; 7, 4; 8, 6; 10, 5; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxvi. 10.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 1, 5, 11; Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 2, 2, 20; xi. 4, 1, 4; 5, 3, 2.</F> <F>3) Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, vi. 5, 3 (in both recensions).</F> <F>4) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, x. 6, 1, 2. {%Cf.%} Geldner, {%Vedische Studien,%} 3, 146, n.^4</F>

1. {@Arundhatī@}¦ is the name of a plant celebrated in several passages of the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> as possessing healing properties in case of wounds, as a febrifuge, and as inducing cows to give milk. The plant was a climber which attached itself to trees like the {@Plakṣa, Aśvattha, Nyagrodha,@} and {@Parṇa.@}<sup>2</sup> It was of golden colour ({%hiraṇya-varṇā%}), and had a hairy stem ({%lomaśa-%} {%vakṣaṇā%}).<sup>3</sup> It was also called Silācī, and the {@Lākṣā@} appears to have been a product of it.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) iv. 12, 1; v. 5, 5. 9; vi. 59, 1. 2; viii. 7, 6; xix. 38, 1.</F> <F>2) Av. v. 5, 5.</F> <F>3) Av. v. 5, 7; Pischel, {%Vedische%} {%Studien,%} 1, 174; Bloomfield, {%Zeitschrift%} {%der Deutschen Morgenländischen Gesell-%} {%schaft,%} 48, 574.</F> <F>4) {%Cf.%} Whitney's note on Av. iv. 12; Bloomfield, {%Atharvaveda,%} 61.</F>
2. {@Arundhatī,@}¦ as the name of a star, is often referred to in the Sūtra literature, but only once in a late Āraṇyaka.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, iii. 9, 2.</F>

{@Arka,@}¦ as the name of the tree {%Colotropis gigantea,%} is perhaps found in one obscure passage of the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) vi. 72, 1, where see Whitney's note. {%Cf.%} St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>

{@Argala.@}¦ — The word which is usual later to denote the wooden pin of a door is found in the Śāṇkhāyana Āraṇyaka (ii. 16) in the compound {%argaleṣīke%} to denote the pin and bar of the door of a cow-pen. {%Cf.%} {@Iṣīkā.@}

{@Argala-Kāhoḍi@}¦ is mentioned in the Kāṭhaka Samhitā (xxv. 7) as a teacher. The name may, however, be Aryala, as suggested in the St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.,%} and as read by v. Schroeder in his edition. The Kapiṣṭhala (xxxix. 5) has Ayala. See below.

{@Arcant@}¦ is possibly, as Ludwig<sup>1</sup> thinks, the name of the author of a hymn of the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> ; but the word may be merely the ordinary participle ‘praising.’ <F>1) Translation of the Ṛigveda, 3, 133.</F> <F>2) x. 149, 5.</F>

{@Arcanānas.@}¦ — In one passage of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> the gods Mitra- Varuṇa are besought to protect Arcanānas. He is also in- voked with {@Śyāvāśva@} and several other ancestors enumerated in the Atharvaveda.<sup>2</sup> He appears as father of Śyāvāśva in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>3</sup> The later tradition makes him play a part in the legend of his son's wedding, which Sieg<sup>4</sup> endeavours to show is known to the Rigveda. <F>1) v. 64, 7.</F> <F>2) xviii. 3, 15.</F> <F>3) viii. 5, 9.</F> <F>4) {%Die Sagenstoffe des Ṛgveda,%} 50 {%et seq.%} {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 127; Oldenberg, {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 354.</F>
{@Arcā.@}¦ See {@Brāhmaṇa.@}

{@Arjunī@}¦ is, in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> the name of the {@Nakṣatra@} (‘lunar mansion’), elsewhere<sup>2</sup> called Phalgunī. It occurs in the marriage hymn, with {@Aghā@} for {@Maghā,@} and, like that word, is apparently a deliberate modification. <F>1) x. 85, 13.</F> <F>2) Av. xiv. 1, 13. {%Cf.%} Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 1, 11, 2.</F>

{@Arbuda@}¦ is mentioned as Grāvastut priest at the snake festival described in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> He is ob- viously the same mythical figure as Arbuda Kādraveya, a seer spoken of in the Aitareya<sup>2</sup> and Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇas<sup>3</sup> as a maker of Mantras. <F>1) xxv. 15.</F> <F>2) vi. 1.</F> <F>3) xxix. 1. {%Cf.%} Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 4, 3, 9.</F>

{@Arya.@}¦ — This word is not common in the older literature, in places where the quantity of the first vowel is fixed as short, except in a mere adjectival sense. Geldner,<sup>1</sup> indeed, contends that no other sense is anywhere needed; but Roth<sup>2</sup> and Zimmer<sup>3</sup> agree in thinking that in several passages of the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā<sup>4</sup> the word has the same sense as {@Ārya,@} and this appears probable. Whether it is necessary to ascribe this sense to the word in the compound {%arya-patnī%}<sup>5</sup> applied to the waters set free by Indra, is more doubtful. The commentator, Mahīdhara,<sup>6</sup> suggests that the word means a {@Vaiśya,@} not an {@Ārya@} generally. This view is supported by the explanation in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>7</sup> of one of the passages of the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā.<sup>8</sup> But though the use of Arya to denote a Vaiśya became common later, it is not clear that it was original. <F>1) {%Vedische Studien,%} 3, 96.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>3) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 214, 215.</F> <F>4) xiv. 30; xx. 17; xxiii. 21; xxvi. 2. {%Cf.%} also Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxxviii. 5; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vii. 4, 19, 3. In Atharvaveda, xix. 32, 8, an analogous form occurs, as contrasted with {%brāh-%} {%maṇa, rājanya,%} and {%śūdra;%} but even there Whitney renders it as ‘Āryan.’ {%Cf.%} xix. 62, 1; Rv. viii. 94, 3; Pischel, {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen%} {%Gesellschaft,%} 40, 125.</F> <F>5) Rv. vii. 6, 5; x. 43, 8.</F> <F>6) On Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiii. 30.</F> <F>7) xiii. 2, 9, 8. Contrast Śāṅkhāyana Srauta Sūtra, xvi. 4, 4 {%et seq.,%} where Arya appears to be taken in the wider sense.</F> <F>8) xxiii. 30. {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 212; Weber, {%Indische%} {%Studien,%} x. 6; Oldenberg, {%Ṛgveda-%} {%Noten,%} 1, 126, 363.</F>

{@Aryamṇaḥ Panthā,@}¦ ‘Aryaman's Way,’ an expression which occurs in the Brāhmaṇas,<sup>1</sup> denotes, according to Weber,<sup>2</sup> ‘the milky way,’ but, according to Hillebrandt,<sup>3</sup> ‘the ecliptic.’ <F>1) Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 7, 6, 6; Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xxv. 12, 3; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, v. 3, 1, 2.</F> <F>2) {%Über den Rājasūya,%} 48, 2.</F> <F>3) {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 3, 79, 80.</F>
{@Aryala.@}¦ — Those at whose snake feast the Gṛhapati was Aryala, and the Hotṛ was {@Āruṇi@} are mentioned in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa (xxiii. 1, 5). See also {@Argala.@}
{@Arvant.@}¦ See {@Aśva.@}

{@Arśas@}¦ is the name of a disease mentioned in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> with consumption and other ailments. It appears to designate ‘hæmorrhoids,’ as in the later medical literature. <F>1) xii. 98. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 398; Roth, St. Petersburg Dic- tionary, {%s.v.%}</F>

{@Alaja@}¦ designates some kind of bird — one of the victims in the Aśvamedha,<sup>1</sup> or Horse Sacrifice. <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 4, 11, 1; 5, 20, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 18; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxi. 4; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 34.</F>

{@Alaji@}¦ is the name of a disease in the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> The later {%alajī%} denotes an eye-disease — a discharge at the junction of the cornea and the sclerotica. <F>1) ix. 8, 20. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 390; St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>
{@Alamma Pārijānata@}¦ is mentioned in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāh- maṇa (xiii. 4, 11; 10, 8) as a sage.
{@Alasālā.@}¦ — This word occurring only in one passage of the Atharvaveda (vi. 16, 4) is said to denote a grain-creeper.

{@Alāṇḍu.@}¦ — This is the reading in the text of the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> of the name of a species of worm. Bloomfield<sup>2</sup> shows reason to adopt the reading Algaṇḍu as the correct form of the word. <F>1) ii. 31, 2.</F> <F>2) {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 315.</F>

{@Alābu.@}¦ — The bottle-gourd ({%Lagenaria vulgaris%}). Vessels made of it are referred to in the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) viii. 10, 29. 30; xx. 132, 1. 2. {%Cf. alāpu%} in Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iv. 2, 13.</F>

{@Alāyya@}¦ is a word occurring in an obscure verse of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> and appearing to be a proper name. Hillebrandt,<sup>2</sup> however, amends the text so as to remove the name. The St. Petersburg Dictionary suggests that it refers to Indra. Pischel<sup>3</sup> holds that [Page1-039+ 51] it is the name of a person whose axe was stolen, and for whom the hymn was written as a spell for the recovery of the axe. <F>1) ix. 67, 20.</F> <F>2) {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgen-%} {%ländischen Gesellschaft,%} 48, 418.</F> <F>3) {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgen-%} {%ländischen Gesellschaft,%} 48, 701.</F>
{@Aliklava@}¦ is a kind of carrion bird mentioned in the Athar- vaveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) xi. 2, 2; 9, 9. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 88.</F>

{@Alina@}¦ is the name of a people mentioned once only in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> Roth<sup>2</sup> thought that the Alinas were allies — possibly a subdivision — of the {@Tṛtsus.@} Ludwig<sup>3</sup> more probably thinks that they were defeated by {@Sudās,@} together with the {@Pakthas,@} {@Bhalānas, Śivas,@} and {@Viṣāṇins,@} with whom they are mentioned, at the {@Paruṣṇī;@} and Zimmer<sup>4</sup> suggests that they lived to the north-east of Kafiristan. <F>1) vii. 18, 7.</F> <F>2) {%Zur Litteratur und Geschichte des%} {%Weda,%} 95; Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 126.</F> <F>3) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 207.</F> <F>4) {%Op. cit.,%} 431. The land is men- tioned by Hiouen Thsang.</F>
{@Alīkayu Vācas-patya@}¦ is twice mentioned as an authority in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa (xxvi. 5; xxviii. 4).

{@Alpa-śayu@}¦ is a kind of insect mentioned in the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) iv. 36, 9. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Athar-%} {%vaveda,%} 408; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 210.</F>

{@Avakā@}¦ is an aquatic plant ({%Blyxa octandra%}) frequently re- ferred to in the Atharvaveda as well as in the later Saṃhitās<sup>2</sup> and Brāhmaṇas.<sup>3</sup> The Gandharvas are said to eat it.<sup>4</sup> Its later name is {%śaivala,%} and it is identical with the {@Śīpāla.@} <div n="P"/>1) viii. 7, 9; 37, 8-10. <div n="P"/>5) With which it is glossed in Āśval- āyana Gṛhya Sūtra, ii. 8; iv. 4. {%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Proceedings of the American%} {%Oriental Society,%} October, 1890, xli.-xliii.; {%American Journal of Philology,%} 11, 349; Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 71. <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iv. 6, 1, 1; v. 4, 2, 1; 4, 3; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xvii. 4; xxv. 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 10, 1.</F> <F>3) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, vii. 5, 1, 11; viii. 3, 2, 5; ix. 1, 2, 20. 22; xiii. 8, 3, 13.</F> <F>4) Av. iv. 37, 8.</F>

{@Avata,@}¦ a word occurring several times in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> denotes a well, artificially made ({%khan%} ‘to dig’) in contrast with a spring [Page1-040+ 51] ({%utsa%}), though the latter expression is also applied to an artificial well. Such wells were covered by the makers,<sup>2</sup> and are described as unfailing ({%a-kṣita%}) and full of water.<sup>3</sup> The water was raised by a wheel ({%cakra%}) of stone, to which was fastened a strap ({%varatrā%}), with a pail ({%kośa%})<sup>4</sup> attached to it. When raised it was poured ({%siñc%}) into buckets ({%āhāva%}) of wood.<sup>5</sup> Sometimes those wells appear to have been used for irrigation purposes, the water being led off into broad channels ({%sārmī suṣirā%}).<sup>6</sup> <F>1) i. 55, 8; 85, 10. 11; 116, 9, 22; 130, 2; iv. 17, 16; 50, 3; viii. 49, 6; 62, 6; 72, 10, 12; x. 25, 4; 101, 5. 7. {%Cf.%} Nirukta, v. 26.</F> <F>2) Rv. i. 55, 8.</F> <F>3) Rv. x. 101, 6, etc.</F> <F>4) {%Aṃsatra-kośam,%} Rv. x. 101, 7, is best thus rendered. For the stone wheel ({%aśma-cakra%}) which was above ({%uccā-%} {%cakra%}), see Rv. x. 101, 7; viii. 72, 10. For the {%varatrā,%} see Rv. x. 101, 6. Perhaps {%kū-cakra%} in Rv. x. 102, 11, is another name for the wheel, but {%cf.%} St. Peters- burg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>5) Rv. x. 101, 6. 7.</F> <F>6) Rv. viii. 69, 12. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 156, 157; Geldner, {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 14.</F>

{@Avatsāra@}¦ is mentioned as a seer in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> as a priest in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa,<sup>2</sup> and as Prāsravaṇa (or Prāśravaṇa), son of Prasravaṇa, in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa.<sup>3</sup> A hymn of the Rigveda<sup>4</sup> is incorrectly ascribed to him in the Anukramaṇī. <F>1) v. 44. 10.</F> <F>2) ii. 24.</F> <F>3) xiii. 3.</F> <F>4) ix. 58. {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 138; Weber, {%Indische%} {%Studien,%} 1, 188; 2, 315; Sieg, {%Die%} {%Sagenstoffe des Ṛgveda,%} 62, {%et seq.%}</F>
{@A-vadhyatā.@}¦ See {@Brāhmaṇa.@}
{@Avasa@}¦ in the adjective {%an-avasa%} in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> may mean ‘drag.’ <F>1) vi. 66, 7. {%Cf.%} Max Müller, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 32, 372.</F>

{@Ava-skava.@}¦ — A kind of worm, mentioned along with others in the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) ii. 31, 4. {%Cf.%} Whitney, {%ad loc.;%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 13, 201; Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 90; Bloom- field, {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 316.</F>
{@Avāta.@}¦ See {@Vāta.@}

{@Avi.@}¦ — ‘Sheep’ are repeatedly mentioned in the Rigveda, and later, often in conjunction with goats ({%aja%}). The wolf ({%vṛka%}) was their great enemy,<sup>1</sup> and they were tended by shepherds.<sup>2</sup> [Page1-041+ 52] Sheep as well as kine were captured from the enemy.<sup>3</sup> The Soma sieve was made of sheep's wool, and is repeatedly referred to ({%avi, meṣī, avya, avyaya%}).<sup>4</sup> Considerable herds must have existed, as Ṛjrāśva is said<sup>5</sup> to have slain one hundred rams, and in a Dānastuti (‘Praise of Gifts’)<sup>6</sup> a hundred sheep are mentioned as a gift. The ({%meṣa,%}<sup>7</sup> {%vṛṣṇi%}<sup>8</sup> ) ram was sometimes castrated ({%petva%}).<sup>9</sup> The main use of sheep was their wool; hence the expression ‘woolly’ ({%ūrṇāvatī%})<sup>10</sup> is employed to designate a sheep. In the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā<sup>11</sup> the ram is described as ‘woolly,’ and as ‘the skin of beasts, quadruped and biped,’ with reference to the use of its wool as clothing for men and shelter for animals. Pūṣan is said<sup>12</sup> to weave raiment from the wool of sheep. Normally the sheep stayed out at pasture; in an obscure passage of the Rigveda<sup>13</sup> reference appears to be made to rams in stall. Gandhāra<sup>14</sup> ewes were famous for their wool. Pischel<sup>15</sup> considers that the {@Paruṣṇī@}<sup>16</sup> was named from its richness in sheep, {%parus%}<sup>17</sup> denoting the ‘flocks’ of wool. <F>1) Av. v. 8, 4; Rv. viii. 34, 3; 66, 8.</F> <F>2) {%Avi-pāla,%} Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxx. 11; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iv. 1, 5, 2; {%avi-pa,%} Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 9, 1.</F> <F>3) Rv. viii. 86, 2.</F> <F>4) Rv. ix. 109, 16; 36, 4, etc. See Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 203.</F> <F>5) Rv. i. 116, 17.</F> <F>6) Rv. viii. 67, 3.</F> <F>7) Rv. i. 43, 6; 116, 16, etc.</F> <F>8) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 3, 7, 4, etc.</F> <F>9) Rv. vii. 18, 17; Av. iv. 4, 8; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 22, 1; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xxix. 58; 59.</F> <F>10) Rv. viii. 67, 3. {%Cf.%} x. 75, 8; so {%urā,%} x. 95, 3.</F> <F>11) xiii. 50.</F> <F>12) Rv. x. 26, 6.</F> <F>13) x. 106, 5.</F> <F>14) Rv. i. 126, 7.</F> <F>15) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 210.</F> <F>16) Rv. iv. 22, 2; v. 52, 9.</F> <F>17) Rv. ix. 15, 6; {%parvan,%} iv. 22, 2. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 229, 230; Oldenberg, {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 348.</F>

{@Aśani.@}¦ — Zimmer<sup>1</sup> cites this word from the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> as denoting a sling stone, and compares a similar use of {@Adri.@}<sup>3</sup> In either case, however, the weapons are mythical, being used in descriptions of Indra's deeds. Schrader<sup>4</sup> also cites {%aśan%} in this sense, but no Vedic passage requires this sense. <F>1) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 301.</F> <F>2) vi. 6, 5. {%Cf.%} 1, 121, 9.</F> <F>3) i. 51, 3.</F> <F>4) {%Prehistoric Antiquities,%} 221.</F>

{@Aśma-gandhā@}¦ (‘rock-smell’) is a plant mentioned in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> probably identical with the late {%aśva-%} {%gandhā,%} ‘horse-smell’ ({%Physalis flexuosa%}). <F>1) xiii. 8, 1, 16, with Eggeling's note in the {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 44, 427.</F>

{@Aśva@}¦ is the commonest word for ‘horse’ in the Vedic literature. The horse is also called ‘the runner’ ({%atya%}), ‘the swift’ ({%arvant%}), ‘the strong,’ for pulling ({%vājin%}), ‘the runner’ ({%sapti%}), and ‘the speeding’ ({%haya%}). The mare is termed {%aśvā,%} {%atyā, arvatī, vaḍavā,%} etc. Horses of various colour were known, dun ({%harita, hari%}), ruddy ({%aruṇa, aruṣa, piśaṅga, rohita%}), dark brown ({%śyāva%}), white ({%śveta%}), etc. A white horse with black ears is mentioned in the Atharvaveda as of special value.<sup>1</sup> Horses were highly prized,<sup>2</sup> and were not rare, as Roth<sup>3</sup> thought, for as many as four hundred mares are mentioned in one Dānastuti (‘Praise of Gifts’).<sup>4</sup> They were on occasion ornamented with pearls and gold.<sup>5</sup> <div n="P"/>Mares were preferred for drawing chariots because of their swiftness and sureness.<sup>6</sup> They were also used for drawing carts, but were not ordinarily so employed.<sup>7</sup> No mention is made of riding in battle, but for other purposes it was not unknown.<sup>8</sup> <div n="P"/>Horses were often kept in stalls,<sup>9</sup> and fed there.<sup>10</sup> But they were also allowed to go out to grass,<sup>11</sup> and were then hobbled.<sup>12</sup> They were watered to cool them after racing.<sup>13</sup> Their attendants [Page1-043+ 59] are frequently referred to ({%aśva-pāla,%}<sup>14</sup> {%aśva-pa,%}<sup>15</sup> {%aśva-pati%}).<sup>16</sup> Stallions were frequently castrated ({%vadhri%}).<sup>17</sup> <div n="P"/>Besides reins ({%raśmayaḥ%}), reference is made to halters ({%aśvābhidhānī%}),<sup>18</sup> and whips ({%aśvājani%}).<sup>19</sup> See also {@Ratha.@} <div n="P"/>Horses from the Indus were of special value,<sup>20</sup> as also horses from the {@Sarasvatī.@} <F>1) Av. v. 17, 15.</F> <F>2) Rv. i. 83, 1; iv. 32, 17; v. 4, 11; viii. 78, 2, etc.</F> <F>3) {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgen-%} {%ländischen Gesellschaft,%} 35, 686.</F> <F>4) Rv. viii. 55, 3. {%Cf.%} v. 33, 8; vi. 47, 22-24; 63, 10; viii. 6, 47; 46, 22, and Hopkins, {%American Journal of Philology,%} 15, 157.</F> <F>5) Rv. x. 68, 11.</F> <F>6) Pischel, {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen%} {%Morgenländischen Gesellschaft,%} 35, 712- 714; {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 10, 305. {%Cf.%} {%ratho vadhūmān,%} Rv. i. 126, 3; vii. 18, 22, {%vājinīvān,%} vii. 69, 1.</F> <F>7) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, v. 5, 4, 35.</F> <F>8) The Aśvins ride, Rv. v. 61, 1-3. An {%aśva-sāda%} is referred to in Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxx. 13; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 7, 1; and riding is meant in Rv. i. 162, 17; 163, 9. Av. xi. 10, 24. is doubtful. {%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%Journal of the%} {%American Oriental Society,%} 13, 262; Lud- wig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 221. {@Aśva-tara, Aśva-tarī@}¦ are respectively the masculine and feminine name of ‘mule.’ These animals are mentioned frequently from the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> onwards. They were known not to be fruitful,<sup>2</sup> and were probably considered inferior to horses,<sup>3</sup> but a mule-car was quite common.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) iv. 4, 8; viii. 8, 22; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 47; iv. 9; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xii. 4, 1, 10, etc.; Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa, i. 4, 4.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vii. 1, 1, 2. 3. {%Cf.%} Adbhuta Brāhmaṇa in {%Indische%} {%Studien,%} 1, 40.</F> <F>3) As were asses, Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 1, 2, 2; Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, vi. 4, 4, 7.</F> <F>4) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, iv. 9; Chān- dogya Upaniṣad, iv. 2, 1 (in both pas- sages {%aśvatarī-ratha%}). {%Cf.%} Oertel, {%Trans-%} {%actions of the Connecticut Academy of Arts%} {%and Sciences,%} 15, 175.</F>

1. {@Aśva-ttha@}¦ (‘horse-stand’) is one of India's greatest trees, the {%Ficus religiosa,%} later called {%pippala%}<sup>1</sup> (now Peepal). Vessels made of the wood of the Aśvattha are mentioned in the Rigveda,<sup>2</sup> and the tree itself is constantly referred to later.<sup>3</sup> Its hard wood formed the upper of the two pieces of wood used for kindling fire, the lower being of {@Śamī.@}<sup>4</sup> It planted its roots in shoots of other trees, especially the {@Khadira,@} and destroyed them;<sup>5</sup> hence it is called ‘the destroyer’ ({%vaibādha%}). Its berries [Page1-044+ 37] are referred to as sweet, and as eaten by birds.<sup>6</sup> The gods are said to sit under it in the third heaven.<sup>7</sup> It and {@Nyagrodha@} are styled the ‘crested ones’ ({%śikhaṇḍin%}).<sup>8</sup> <F>1) The word {%pippala%} as a neuter occurs once in the Rv. (i. 164, 20) designating the berry of the Peepal-tree.</F> <F>2) i. 135, 8; x. 97, 5.</F> <F>3) Atharvaveda, iii. 6, 1; iv. 37, 4, etc.</F> <F>4) Av. vi. 11, 1; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xi. 5, 1, 13.</F> <F>5) Av. iii. 6.</F> <F>6) Rv. i. 164, 20. 22.</F> <F>7) Av. v. 4, 3. {%Cf.%} Chāndogya Upani- ṣad, viii. 5, 3; Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad, i. 3.</F> <F>8) Av. iv. 37, 4. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altin-%} {%disches Leben,%} 57, 58.</F>

2. {@Aśva-ttha.@}¦ — This prince is celebrated in a Dānastuti<sup>1</sup> as having given gifts to Pāyu. He is identified with {@Divodāsa@} by Griffith,<sup>2</sup> but it is impossible to be certain of this identifica- tion. <F>1) Rv. vi. 47, 24.</F> <F>2) {%Hymns of the Rigveda,%} 1, 611. The name is spelt Aśvatha in the text, but that is merely the usual shortened spelling of the group {%tth.%}</F>

{@Aśva-dāvan.@}¦ — Ludwig<sup>1</sup> finds a prince of this name in a passage of the Rigveda,<sup>2</sup> where a gift of fifty horses is mentioned, but the word appears to be an epithet of Indra (‘bestower of horses’). <F>1) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 274.</F> <F>2) v. 18, 3.</F>

{@Aśva-pati@}¦ (‘lord of horses’) is a name of a prince of the {@Kekayas,@} who instructed {@Prācīnaśāla@} and other Brahmins.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Chāndogya Upaniṣad, v. 11, 4; Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, x. 6, 1, 2.</F>

{@Aśva-medha@}¦ (‘offering a horse-sacrifice’) is a prince men- tioned in a hymn of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> which contains a Dānastuti (‘Praise of Gifts’) of {@Tryaruṇa,@} and to which three verses have been added in praise of Aśvamedha. See also {@Āśvamedha.@} <F>1) v. 27, 4-6. {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 275.</F>
{@Aśva-yujau.@}¦ See {@Nakṣatra.@}
{@Aśvala,@}¦ the Hotṛ priest of {@Janaka,@} King of {@Videha,@} appears as an authority in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (iii. 1, 2. 10).

{@Aśva-vāra, Aśva-vāla@}¦ (‘hair of a horse's tail’). — The former form occurs in the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā,<sup>1</sup> the latter in the [Page1-045+ 36] Kāṭhaka<sup>2</sup> and Kapiṣṭhala Saṃhitās<sup>3</sup> and Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>4</sup> denoting a species of reed ({%Saccharum spontaneum%}). <F>1) iii. 7, 9.</F> <F>2) xxiv. 8.</F> <F>3) xxxviii. 1.</F> <F>4) iii. 4, 1, 7. {%Cf.%} Von Schroeder's edition of the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, i., p. xv.</F>

{@Aśva-sūkti@}¦ is the name of a seer to whom the Rigveda Anukramaṇī ascribes two hymns of the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> The Pañca- viṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> knows a Sāman of Aśvasūkti. <F>1) viii. 14; 15.</F> <F>2) xix. 4, 10. {%Cf.%} Oldenberg, {%Zeit-%} {%schrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen%} {%Gesellschaft,%} 42, 230, n. 4.</F>
{@Aśvinī.@}¦ See {@Nakṣatra.@}

{@Aṣāḍha Kaiśin@}¦ is the name of a man referred to in a corrupt and obscure passage of the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> as connected with the defeat of the {@Pañcālas@} by the {@Kuntis.@} <F>1) xxvi. 9; Kapiṣṭhala, xli. 7. See Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 3, 471.</F>
{@Aṣāḍha Uttara Pārāśarya@}¦ is mentioned as a teacher in a Vaṃśa or Genealogy in the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa (iii. 41, 1).
{@Aṣāḍhā.@}¦ See {@Nakṣatra.@}

{@Aṣāḍhi Sauśromateya@}¦ was a man who is stated in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (vi. 2, 1, 37) to have died because the heads for the sacrifice in connection with the laying of the bricks of the fire-altar had been obtained in an improper manner.
{@Aṣṭaka@}¦ is mentioned in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> as one of the sons of {@Viśvāmitra.@} <F>1) vii. 17. Also in the Sāṅkhāyana Srauta Sūtra, xv. 26.</F>
{@Aṣṭakā.@}¦ See {@Māsa.@}

{@Aṣṭa-karṇī@}¦ is an expression which occurs in one passage of the Ṛigveda,<sup>1</sup> and which Roth<sup>2</sup> was at first inclined to interpret [Page1-046+ 46] as a proper name. There can, however, be no doubt that it means a cow, not a man, as suggested by Grassmann. The exact reason why a cow should be so described is uncertain. Roth<sup>3</sup> was later inclined to see in it the sense ‘having pierced ears,’ similar epithets being at a later period known to Pāṇini<sup>4</sup> ({%bhinna-karṇa, chinna-karṇa%}). Grassmann's more obvious rendering, ‘having the sign for (the number) 8 marked on the ear,’ is supported by the similar epithets, ‘having the mark of a lute on the ear’ ({%karkari-karṇyaḥ%}), ‘having the mark of a sickle on the ear’ ({%dātra-karṇyaḥ%}), ‘having the mark of a stake on the ear’ ({%sthūṇā-%} {%karṇyaḥ%}), ‘having the ears bored’ ({%chidra-karṇyaḥ%}), and {%viṣtya-%} {%karṇyaḥ,%} given in the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā.<sup>5</sup> The simple mean- ing, ‘with marked ears,’ is, however, supported by the same passage of the Maitrāyaṇī, where the verb {%akṣ%} occurs in the sense ‘to mark.’ In the Atharvaveda the mark used is the Mithuna, no doubt as a magical device to secure fertility. <div n="P"/>The marking of ears was apparently a regular practice. It is twice referred to in the Atharvaveda.<sup>6</sup> The mark is termed {%lakṣman,%}<sup>7</sup> and was made with a copper-knife<sup>8</sup> ({%lohita%}). The Maitrayaṇī Saṃhitā<sup>9</sup> forbids the use of an arrow-shaft ({%tejana%}), or of iron, but permits that of a stem of sugar-cane ({%ikṣu-kāṇḍa%}) or copper. <F>1) x. 62, 7.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>3) {%Cf.%} Böhtlingk, Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>4) vi. 3, 115.</F> <F>5) iv. 2, 9.</F> <F>6) vi. 141, 1. 2; xii. 4, 6.</F> <F>7) Av. vi. 141, 2; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, {%loc. cit.%}</F> <F>8) Av., {%loc. cit.%}</F> <F>9) {%Loc. cit.%} <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 234, 348; Delbrück, {%Gurupūjākaumudī,%} 48, 49; Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 13, 466; Whitney, Translation of the Atharva- veda, 387.</F>
{@Aṣṭā-daṃṣṭra Vairūpa.@}¦ — To him the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa (viii. 9, 21) ascribes two Sāmans.

{@Aṣṭrā@}¦ is the plougher's ‘goad,’ the badge of agriculture. It is mentioned several times in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) iv. 57, 4; vi. 53, 9; 58, 2; {%aṣṭrā-vin%} occurs in x. 102, 8. See also Kauśika Sūtra, 80. {%Cf.%} Roscher, {%Archiv für%} {%Religionswissenschaft,%} 1, 63; Hille- brandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 3, 364, n. 8.</F>

{@Asamāti Rātha-prauṣṭha.@}¦ — The story of the quarrel between Asamāti, the Ikṣvāku prince of the Rathaproṣṭha family, and [Page1-047+ 52] his priests, the Gaupāyanas, is found only in the later Brāhmaṇas.<sup>1</sup> It appears to be based on a misreading of the Rigveda,<sup>2</sup> where {%asamāti%} is merely an adjective. The later story is that the king was induced to abandon his family priests by two Asuras, Kirāta and Ākuli, who by their magic com- passed the death of Subandhu, one of the brother priests, and that the others revived him by the use of the hymns (Rigveda, x. 57-60). <F>1) Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 167 ({%Journal of the American Oriental Society,%} 18, 41 {%et seq.%}); Sāṭyāyanaka, cited in Sāyaṇa on Rv. x. 57, 1; 60, 7; Bṛhad- devatā, vii. 83 {%et seq.,%} with Macdonell's notes; Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 12, 5.</F> <F>2) x. 60, 2. 5; Av. vi. 79, 1. {%Cf.%} Bloom- field, {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 499; Max Müller, {%Journal of the Royal Asiatic%} {%Society,%} 1866, 426-465; Böhtlingk's Dictionary, {%s.v.;%} Hopkins, {%Transactions%} {%of the Connecticut Academy of Arts and%} {%Sciences,%} 15, 48, n. 1.</F>

{@Asi@}¦ usually denotes the sacrificial knife,<sup>1</sup> but occasionally appears to mean a knife used in war.<sup>2</sup> Mention is made of a sheath ({%vavri%})<sup>3</sup> to which a belt ({%vāla%})<sup>4</sup> was attached. The word {%asi-dhārā%}<sup>5</sup> also denotes ‘sheath.’ <F>1) Rv. i. 162, 20; x. 79, 6; 18; Av. ix. 3, 9; x. 1, 20, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. xi. 9, 1. The use of the ‘sword’ increases in the Epic period. See Hop- kins, {%Journal of the American Oriental%} {%Society,%} 13, 284.</F> <F>3) Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xv. 4.</F> <F>4) {%Ibid.;%} Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 6, 5.</F> <F>5) Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa, iii. 139.</F>

{@Asiknī@}¦ (‘black’) is the name in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> of the river known later as Candra-bhāgā, and to the Greeks as Akesines, now the Chenab in the Punjab. <F>1) viii. 20, 25; x. 75, 5; Nirukta, ix. 26. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 12.</F>

1. {@Asita@}¦ is a name of the ‘black snake,’ referred to in the later Saṃhitās.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Av. iii. 27, 1; v. 13, 5. 6; vi. 56, 2, etc.; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 10, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 18; perhaps Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 37.</F>

2. {@Asita.@}¦ — ({%a%}) A mythical sage of this name figures as a magician in the Atharvaveda in conjunction with {@Gaya@}<sup>1</sup> or with {@Jamadagni.@}<sup>2</sup> In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> he appears as [Page1-048+ 40] Asita Dhānva,<sup>4</sup> and as Daivala or Devala in the Pañcaviṃsa Brāhmaṇa<sup>5</sup> and Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā.<sup>6</sup> <div n="P"/>({%b%}) {@Asita Vārṣa-gaṇa@} is a pupil of {@Harita Kaśyapa@} according to the Vaṃśa or Genealogy in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Av. i. 14, 4.</F> <F>2) Av. vi. 137, 1.</F> <F>3) xiii. 4, 3, 11.</F> <F>4) Dhānvana in the Śāṅkhāyana Srauta Sūtra, xvi. 2, 19.</F> <F>5) xiv. 11, 18. 19, {%Cf.%} xv. 5, 27.</F> <F>6) xxii. 11. {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 132.</F> <F>1) vi. 5, 3 (Kāṇva = vi. 4, 33, Mādhyandina).</F>

{@Asita-mṛga@}¦ is the designation in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> of a family of the {@Kaśyapas@} who were excluded from a sacrifice by {@Janamejaya,@} but who took away the conduct of the offering from the {@Bhūtavīras,@} whom the king employed. In the Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> and the Ṣaḍviṃsa Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> the Asita- mṛgas are called ‘sons of the Kaśyapas,’ and one is mentioned as {@Kusurubindu@}<sup>4</sup> {@Auddālaki.@} <F>1) vii. 27. {%Cf.%} Eggeling, {%Sacred Books%} {%of the East,%} 43, 345.</F> <F>2) i. 75.</F> <F>3) i. 4.</F> <F>4) Variously read as Asurbinda, Kusurbinda, Kusurubinda.</F>

{@Asura-vidyā,@}¦ ‘the science of the Asuras,’ the term used in the Śāṅkhāyana and Āśvalāyana<sup>1</sup> Śrauta Sūtras as the equiva- lent of the term {%māyā%} employed in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>2</sup> clearly means ‘magic,’ as it is rendered by Professor Eggeling.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) x. 7.</F> <F>2) xiii. 4, 3, 11. {%Cf.%} Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, x. 61, 2. 21.</F> <F>3) {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 44, 368.</F>

{@Astṛ,@}¦ ‘shooter,’ is a term frequently used in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and Atharvaveda<sup>2</sup> for the archer who fought from the chariot. <F>1) i. 8, 4; 64, 10; ii. 42, 2, etc.</F> <F>2) vi. 93, 1. 2; xi. 2, 7. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 296.</F>

{@Ahan,@}¦ ‘day.’ Like other peoples, the Indians used night as a general expression of time as well as day, but by no means predominantly.<sup>1</sup> Night is also termed the dark ({%kṛṣṇa%}), as [Page1-049+ 56] opposed to the light ({%arjuna%}), day.<sup>2</sup> Aho-rātra<sup>3</sup> is a regular term for ‘day and night’ combined. <div n="P"/>The day itself is variously divided. In the Atharvaveda<sup>4</sup> a division into ‘the rising sun’ ({%udyan sūryaḥ%}), ‘the coming together of the cows’ ({%saṃ-gava%}), ‘midday’ ({%madhyaṃ-dina%}), ‘afternoon’ ({%aparāhṇa%}), and ‘sunset’ ({%astaṃ-yan%}) is found. In the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa<sup>5</sup> the same series appears with ‘early’ ({%prātar%}) and ‘evening’ ({%sāyāhna%}) substituted for the first and last members, while a shorter list gives {%prātar,%} {%saṃgava, sāyam.%} In the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā<sup>6</sup> there is the series ‘dawn’ {%(uṣas), saṃgava, madhyaṃdina,%} and {%aparāhṇa.%} <div n="P"/>The morning is also, according to Zimmer, called {%api-śarvara,%}<sup>7</sup> as the time when the dark is just past. It is named {%svasara,%}<sup>8</sup> as the time when the cows are feeding, before the first milking at the {%saṃgava,%} or when the birds are awakening.<sup>9</sup> It is also called {%pra-pitva,%}<sup>10</sup> according to Zimmer.<sup>11</sup> But Geldner<sup>12</sup> points out that that term refers to the late midday, which also is called {%api-śarvara,%} as bordering on the coming night, being the time when day is hastening to its close, as in a race. From another point of view, evening is called {%abhi-pitva,%}<sup>13</sup> the time when all come to rest. Or again, morning and evening are denoted as the dawning of the sun ({%uditā sūryasya%}), or its setting ({%ni-mruc%}). The midday is regularly {%madhyam ahnām,%}<sup>14</sup> {%madhye,%}<sup>15</sup> or {%madhyaṃdina. Saṃgava%}<sup>16</sup> is the forenoon, between the early morning ({%prātar%}) and midday ({%madhyaṃdina%}). <div n="P"/>The divisions of time less than the day are seldom precisely given. In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>17</sup> however, a day and [Page1-050+ 48] night make up 30 {%muhūrtas;%} 1 {%muhūrta%} = 15 {%kṣipra;%} 1 {%kṣipra%} = 15 {%etarhi;%} 1 {%etarhi%} = 15 {%idāni;%} 1 {%idāni%} = 15 breathings; 1 breath- ing = 1 spiration; 1 spiration = 1 twinkling ({%nimeṣa%}), etc. In the Sāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka<sup>18</sup> the series is {%dhvaṃsayo, nimeṣāḥ,%} {%kāṣṭhāḥ, kalāḥ, kṣanā, muhūrtā, ahorātrāḥ.%} A thirtyfold division of day as well as of night is seen in one passage of the Rigveda<sup>19</sup> by Zimmer, who compares the Babylonian sixty- fold division of the day and night. But the expression used —  thirty Yojanas — is too vague and obscure — Bergaigne<sup>20</sup> refers it to the firmament — to build any theory upon with safety. <div n="P"/>The longer divisions of time are regularly ‘half month’ ({%ardha-māsa%}), ‘month’ ({%māsa%}), ‘season’ ({%ṛtu%}), and ‘year’ ({%saṃvatsara%}), which often<sup>21</sup> occur in this sequence after {%ahorātrāṇi%} (‘days and nights’). <F>1) Rv. iv. 16, 19; viii. 26, 3; i. 70, 4. {%Cf.%} Av. x. 7, 42.</F> <F>2) Rv. vi. 9. 1.</F> <F>3) Rv. x. 190, 2; Av. xiii. 3, 8, etc.; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiii. 41, etc.</F> <F>4) ix. 6, 45.</F> <F>5) i. 5, 3, 1; 4, 9, 2.</F> <F>6) iv. 2, 11.</F> <F>7) Rv. iii. 9, 7; {%cf.%} Oldenberg, {%Ṛgveda-%} {%Noten,%} 1, 230.</F> <F>8) Rv. ii. 34, 8; ix. 94, 2.</F> <F>9) Rv. ii. 19, 2; 34, 5.</F> <F>10) Rv. vii. 41, 4; viii. 1, 29. Sieg. {%Die Sagenstoffe des Ṛgveda,%} 127 {%et seq.,%} interprets {%paritakmyāyām%} (Rv. i. 116, 15) similarly.</F> <F>11) {%Altindisches Leben.%} 362.</F> <F>12) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 155-179.</F> <F>13) Rv. i. 126, 3; iv. 34, 5.</F> <F>14) Rv. vii. 41, 4.</F> <F>15) Rv. viii. 27, 20.</F> <F>16) {%Cf.%} Rv. v. 76, 3 ({%saṃgave, prātar%} {%ahno, madhyaṃdine%}); Taittirīya Brāh- maṇa, ii. 1, 1, 3; Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa, i. 12, 4; Aitareya Brāh- maṇa, iii. 18, 14; Geldner, {%Vedische%} {%Studien,%} 3, 112, 113. Zimmer, {%op. cit.,%} 362, places it too early — before the cows are driven out.</F> <F>17) xii. 3, 2, 5. {%Cf.%} Taittirīya Brāh- maṇa, iii. 10, 1, 1 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>18) vii. 20. {%Cf.%} Śāṅkhāyana Srauta Sūtra, xiv. 78 {%et seq.;%} Weber, {%Indische%} {%Streifen,%} 1, 92-95.</F> <F>19) Rv. i. 123, 8.</F> <F>20) {%Religion Védique.%} 3, 283 {%et seq.%} {%Cf.%} Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v. kratu.%}</F> <F>21) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vii. 1, 15; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 12, 7; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xxii. 28; Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka, vii. 20; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad. iii. 8, 9, etc. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 361-363.</F>

{@Ahalyā Maitreyī@}¦ is practically a mythical name, the exist- ence of the lady whose story is alluded to in several Brāhmaṇas<sup>1</sup> being derived from the epithet of Indra, ‘lover of Ahalyā’ ({%ahalyāyai jāra%}). <F>1) Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 3, 4, 18; Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 79; Ṣaḍviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, i. 1.</F>

{@Ahi.@}¦ — This word occurs frequently from the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> onwards to denote ‘snake.’ Reference is several times<sup>2</sup> made to its casting its slough. Mention is also made of the serpent's peculiar movement,<sup>3</sup> which earns for it the designation<sup>4</sup> of ‘the toothed rope’ ({%datvatī rajjuḥ%}). The poisonous character [Page1-051+ 39] of its bite is spoken of,<sup>5</sup> as well as the torpidity of the reptile in winter, when it creeps into the earth.<sup>6</sup> The cast skin is used as an amulet against highwaymen.<sup>7</sup> Mention is made of a mythical horse, Paidva, which the Aśvins gave to Pedu as a protection against snakes,<sup>8</sup> and which is invoked as a destroyer of serpents.<sup>9</sup> The ichneumon ({%nakula%}) is regarded as their deadly enemy, and as immune against their poison through the use of a healing plant,<sup>10</sup> while men kill them with sticks<sup>11</sup> or strike off their heads.<sup>12</sup> <div n="P"/>Many species of snakes are mentioned: see {@Aghāśva,@} {@Ajagara, Asita, Kaṅkaparvan, Karikrata, Kalmāṣagrīva,@} {@Kasarṇīla, Kumbhīnasa, Tiraścarāji, Taimāta, Darvi, Daśo-@} {@nasi, Puṣkarasāda, Pṛdāku, Lohitāhi, Śarkoṭa, Śvitra, Sarpa.@} <F>1) vii. 104, 7, etc. The word {%sarpa,%} which is usual in the Atharvaveda, occurs only once (x. 16, 6) in the Rv.</F> <F>2) Rv. ix. 86, 44; Av. i. 27; Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, xi. 2, 6, 13; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, iv. 4, 10; Jaiminīya Brāh- maṇa, i. 9. ii. 139; Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad, ii. 6; 17.</F> <F>3) Aitareya Āraṇyaka, v. 1, 4.</F> <F>4) Av. iv. 3, 2.</F> <F>5) Rv. vii. 104. 7; Av. x. 4, 4 {%et seq.;%} 6, 56.</F> <F>6) Av. xii. 1, 46.</F> <F>7) Av. i. 27.</F> <F>8) Rv. i. 117-119</F> <F>9) Av. x. 4, 6. 10.</F> <F>10) Av. vi. 139, 5; viii. 7, 23.</F> <F>11) Av. x. 4, 9.</F> <F>12) Av. vi. 67, 2. See Zimmer, {%Altin-%} {%disches Leben,%} 94, 95.</F>

{@Ahīnā Āśvatthya@}¦ was a sage ({%muni%}) who achieved immor- tality by knowledge of a certain rite ({%sāvitram%}).<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 10, 9, 10. The form of the first name is remark- able. The second may be compared with {@Aśvattha.@}</F>
{@Ākuli.@}¦ — This mythical priest plays, together with {@Kirāta,@} a part in the later tale of {@Asamāti@} and the {@Gaupāyanas.@}

{@Āktākṣya@}¦ is mentioned as a teacher who had peculiar views on the fire ritual ({%agni-citi%}), which are rejected in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) vi. 1, 2, 24. {%Cf.%} Lévi, {%La Doctrine du Sacrifice,%} 140.</F>
{@Ā-kramaṇa.@}¦ — In the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa^1 (i. 3) this word is used with the specific sense of ‘steps to climb trees.’

{@Ākhu.@}¦ — The exact sense of this word is uncertain. Zimmer<sup>1</sup> renders it ‘mole,’ while Roth<sup>2</sup> prefers ‘mouse’ or ‘rat.’ It is frequently mentioned in the later Saṃhitās,<sup>3</sup> and is known to the Rigveda,<sup>4</sup> where, however, the word is regarded by Pischel<sup>5</sup> as having acquired the secondary sense of ‘thief.’ This is denied by Hillebrandt.<sup>6</sup> <F>1) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 84, 85, followed by Bloomfield. {%Hymns of the Athar-%} {%vaveda,%} 142.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.,%} followed by Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 317, 318.</F> <F>3) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 14, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14. 7; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, iii. 57; xxiv. 26; 28; Av. vi. 50, 1.</F> <F>4) ix. 67, 30.</F> <F>5) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 246; {%Zeitschrift%} {%der Deutschen Morgenländischen Gesell-%} {%schaft,%} 48, 701.</F> <F>6) {%Zeitschrift,%} 48, 418; {%Vedainterpreta-%} {%tion,%} 7.</F>

{@Ā-khyāna.@}¦ — In the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> we hear of the Śaunaḥśepa Ākhyāna, ‘the story of {@Śunaḥśepa,@}’ which is told by the Hotṛ priest at the Rājasūya (‘royal inauguration’). The series of stories<sup>2</sup> used at the Aśvamedha (‘horse sacrifice’) during the year while the sacrificial horse is allowed to wander at its will is called the ‘cyclic’ ({%pari-plavam%}). The Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> mentions also Ākhyāna-vids (‘men versed in tales’), who tell the Sauparṇa legend, elsewhere<sup>4</sup> known as a {@Vyākhyāna.@} Yāska, in the Nirukta,<sup>5</sup> frequently uses the term, sometimes in a pregnant sense as denoting the doctrine of the Aitihāsikas or traditional interpreters of the Rigveda.<sup>6</sup> <F>1) vii. 18, 10. {%Cf.%} Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xv. 27.</F> <F>2) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa. xiii. 4, 3, 2. 15.</F> <F>3) iii. 25, 1.</F> <F>4) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 6. 2. 7.</F> <F>5) v. 21; vii. 7.</F> <F>6) xi. 19; 25. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Sieg. {%Die Sagenstoffe des Ṛgveda.%} 16 {%et seq.%}</F>

{@Ā-khyāyikā.@}¦ — This word occurs apparently but once in the Vedic literature, in the late Taittirīya Āraṇyaka,<sup>1</sup> where its significance is doubtful. <F>1) i. 6. 3. {%Cf.%} Sieg. {%Die Sagenstoffe des Ṛgveda,%} 20, n.</F>
{@Āgastya@}¦ appears as a teacher in the Aitareya (iii. 1, 1) and Śāṅkhāyana (vii. 2) Āraṇyakas.

{@Āgni-veśi Śatri.@}¦ — A prince of this name appears to be referred to in a Dānastuti (‘Praise of Gifts’) in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) v. 34, 9. {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 155.</F>

In the Mādhyandina recension<sup>1</sup> Āgniveśya is a pupil of {@Saitava.@} In the Kāṇva recension he is a pupil of {@Śāṇḍilya@} and {@Ānabhimlāta@} in one Vaṃśa,<sup>2</sup> and of {@Gārgya@} in the second Vaṃśa.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) ii. 5, 21; iv. 5, 27.</F> <F>2) ii. 6, 2.</F> <F>3) iv. 6, 2.</F>

{@Ā-ghāṭi@}¦ is a musical instrument, the ‘cymbal,’ used to accompany dancing. It is known to the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and Atharvaveda.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) x. 146, 2.</F> <F>2) iv. 37, 4 ({%āgkāṭa%}). {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 289.</F>
{@Āṅgirasa@}¦ is a title denoting a claim to be of the family of {@Aṅgiras,@} borne by many sages and teachers, like {@Kṛṣṇa,@} {@Ājīgarti, Cyavana, Ayāsya, Saṃvarta, Sudhanvan,@} etc.
{@Āja-keśin@}¦ is the name of a family in which, according to the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa (i. 9, 3), {@Baka@} used violence against Indra.
{@Ājani.@}¦ — This word is used to denote a ‘goad’ in the Atharvaveda (iii. 25, 5).
{@Ājāta-śatrava.@}¦ See {@Bhadrasena.@}

{@Āji@}¦ is constantly used in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and the later literature to express the sense of ‘a race,’ and only seldom denotes ‘a battle.’ {@Horse@}-racing was one of the favourite amusements of the {@Vedic@} Indian,<sup>2</sup> the other being dicing [Page1-054+ 65] ({@Akṣa@}). The racecourse, called Kāṣṭhā<sup>3</sup> or Āji<sup>4</sup> itself, appears from the Atharvaveda<sup>5</sup> to have been a quasi-circular one to a mark ({%kārṣman%}<sup>6</sup> ) and back again. In the Rigveda the course is described as broad ({%urvī%}) and the distance as measured out ({%apāvṛktā aratnayaḥ%}).<sup>7</sup> Prizes ({%dhana%}) were offered ({%dhā%}),<sup>8</sup> and eagerly competed for. Other words for victory and the prize are {%kāra%}<sup>9</sup> and {%bhara;%}<sup>10</sup> and to ‘run a race’ is described by the expressions {%ājim aj, i, dhāv, sṛ.%}<sup>11</sup> The person who instituted a race is referred to as {%āji-sṛt,%}<sup>12</sup> and Indra is called {%āji-kṛt%}<sup>13</sup> (‘race-maker’), and {%āji-pati%}<sup>14</sup> (‘lord of the race’). <div n="P"/>The swift steeds ({%vājin, atya%}) used for the races were often washed and adorned.<sup>15</sup> According to Pischel<sup>16</sup> the name of one swift mare is preserved — viz., Viśpalā,<sup>17</sup> whose broken leg was replaced by the Aśvins in a race; but the interpretation is very doubtful. Geldner<sup>18</sup> has also found a comic picture of a horse-chariot race in the Mudgala hymn in the Rigveda, but Bloomfield<sup>19</sup> has shown that that interpretation is un- sound. Pischel<sup>20</sup> also seeks to show that races were run in honour of gods, but the evidence for the theory is inadequate.<sup>21</sup> [Page1-055+ 46] A formal race, however, is a feature of the ritual of the Rājasūya or royal consecration.<sup>22</sup> <F>1) v. 37, 7; vi. 24, 6, etc.</F> <F>2) Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 291; Geldner, {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 120; 2. 1 {%seq.%}</F> <F>3) Rv. viii. 80, 8; Av. ii. 14, 6.</F> <F>4) Rv. iv. 24, 8; Av. xiii. 2, 4.</F> <F>5) ii. 14, 6; xiii. 2, 4.</F> <F>6) Rv. ix. 36, 1; 74, 8.</F> <F>7) The sense is doubtful in Rv. viii. 80, 8. Zimmer suggests that it may mean ‘the course is straight,’ without twistings, for which idea {%cf.%} Geldner, {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 160, quoting the comparison of the courser's race with a bowstring (Rv. iii. 53, 24).
