{@Ājīgarti.@}¦ — See {@Śunaḥśepa,@} who bears this patronymic in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> He is called an Āṅgirasa in the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) vii. 17. {%Cf.%} Śāṅkhāyana Srauta Sūtra, xvi. 11, 2.</F> <F>2) xix. 11.</F>
{@Ājya.@}¦ See {@Ghṛta.@}

{@Āñjana.@}¦ — A salve frequently referred to in the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> which came from Mount {@Trikakubh@}<sup>2</sup> in the Himālaya, and was used to anoint the eyes.<sup>3</sup> The region of the {@Yamunā@}<sup>4</sup> is also given as a possible place of origin, and the ointment is declared as potent to remove jaundice, {@Yakṣma, Jāyānya,@} and other diseases.<sup>5</sup> A female ointment-maker is mentioned in the list of victims of the {@Puruṣamedha@} (‘human sacrifice’).<sup>6</sup> <F>1) iv. 9; vi. 102, 3; ix. 6, 11; xix. 44.</F> <F>2) Av. iv. 9, 9. 10; xix. 44, 6.</F> <F>3) {%Cf.%} Av. iv. 9, 1 ({%akṣyam%}); Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, i. 3. Hence the legend in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vi. 1, 1, 5; {%cf.%} i. 2, 1, 2; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, 6, 3; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 1, 3, 15; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, iv. 3.</F> <F>4) Av. iv. 9, 10.</F> <F>5) Av. xix. 44, 1 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>6) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxx. 14 ({%āñ-%} {%janī-kāri%}); Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 10, 1. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 5, 69; Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda%} 381 {%et seq.; American Journal of Philology,%} 17, 405, 406; Whitney Translation of the Atharvaveda, 159.</F>
{@Āṭikī@}¦ is the name of the wife of {@Uṣasti@} in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (i. 10, 1).
{@Aṭṇāra.@}¦ — Patronymic of {@Para.@}

{@Āḍambara@}¦ was a kind of ‘drum.’ A ‘drummer’ ({%āḍambarā-%} {%ghāta%}) is mentioned in the list of victims at the Puruṣa-medha (‘human sacrifice’) in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) xxx. 19. {%Cf.%} Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiv. 4, 8, 1.</F>

{@Āṇi.@}¦ — This word, which is found in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> but rarely later,<sup>2</sup> appears to be best taken with Roth<sup>3</sup> and Zimmer<sup>4</sup> as denoting the part of the axle of the chariot which is inserted into the nave of the wheel. Sāyaṇa renders it as lynch-pin, and this sense is accepted by Leumann,<sup>5</sup> being apparently also found in the Nirukta.<sup>6</sup> In one place in the Rigveda<sup>7</sup> the word appears by synecdoche to denote the whole chariot, but the passage is, according to Geldner,<sup>8</sup> completely obscure. <F>1) i. 35, 6; v. 43, 8.</F> <F>2) In a Mantra in the Aitareya Āraṇ- yaka, ii. 7. See Keith's edition, pp. 266, 267, and Vānī.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>4) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 247.</F> <F>5) {%Etymologisches Wörterbuch,%} 30.</F> <F>6) vi. 32.</F> <F>7) i. 63, 8. {%Cf.%} Pischel, {%Vedische%} {%Studien,%} 1, 96.</F> <F>8) Geldner, {%ibid.,%} 1, 141, n. 3.</F>

{@Āṇḍīka@}¦ (‘bearing eggs’) is a term found in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> denoting an edible plant, apparently with fruit or leaves of egg shape ({%āṇḍa%}), akin to the lotus. <F>1) iv. 34, 5; v. 17, 16. In the first passage the Paippalāda version has {%pauṇḍarīka%} in its place; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 207. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 70; Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 18, 138.</F>

{@Ātā.@}¦ — The framework of the door of a house appears to be denoted by the plural of this word in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> (though in all passages there it is used only by synecdoche of the doors of the sky), and in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā.<sup>2</sup> Zimmer<sup>3</sup> compares the Latin {%antae,%} to which the word etymologically corresponds.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) i. 56, 5; 113, 14; iii. 43, 6; ix. 5, 5 ({%ātaiḥ%}).</F> <F>2) xxix. 5 {%(ātaiḥ). Cf. ātābhiḥ%} in Durga on Nirukta, iv. 18.</F> <F>3) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 154.</F> <F>4) Brugmann, {%Grundriss,%} 1, 209; 2, 214.</F>

{@Āti,@}¦ an aquatic bird. The Apsarases in the legend of Purūravas and Urvaśī appear to him like Ātis, probably swans.<sup>1</sup> The birds appear also in the list of animals in the Aśvamedha (‘horse sacrifice’),<sup>2</sup> where Mahīdhara<sup>3</sup> renders them as the [Page1-057+ 40] later Āḍī ({%Turdus ginginianus%}), and Sāyaṇa<sup>4</sup> quotes a view, according to which the Āti was the Cāṣa, or blue jay ({%Coracias%} {%indica%}). <F>1) Rv. x. 95, 9. {%Cf.%} Satapatha Brāh- maṇa, xi. 5, 1, 4.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 13, 1; Maītrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 18; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 34.</F> <F>3) On Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, {%loc. cit.%}</F> <F>4) On Taittirīya Saṃhitā, {%loc. cit. Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben;%} 89.</F>
{@Ātithi-gva.@}¦ — Patronymic of {@Indrota.@}

{@Ātreya@}¦ is the patronymic of a pupil of Māṇṭi in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.<sup>1</sup> An Ātreya appears as a Purohita of {@Aṅga@} in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> An Ātreya was regularly the priest in certain rites,<sup>3</sup> and an Ātreyī occurs in an obscure passage in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) ii. 6, 3; iv. 6, 3 (in both ver- sions).</F> <F>2) viii. 22.</F> <F>3) {%Ibid.,%} vii. 7; Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, iv. 3, 4, 21; Kātyāyana Srauta Sūtra, x. 2, 21 ({%sadasaḥ purastāt%}).</F> <F>4) i. 4, 5, 13. {%Cf.%} Roth, St. Peters- burg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>
{@Ātreyī-putra@}¦ is mentioned as a pupil of {@Gautamīputra@} in a Vaṃśa, or Genealogy, in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (vi. 5, 2, in both versions).

{@Ātharvaṇa,@}¦ a patronymic formed from the name of the mythic Atharvan, is found normally in the plural neuter as a designation of the hymns of the Atharvans. This use appears in the late nineteenth book of the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> and in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> In the singular the expression Ātharvaṇa (Veda), though not occurring till the Chāndogya Upaniṣad,<sup>3</sup> is earlier than the term ‘Atharvaveda,’ which is first found in the Sūtras.<sup>4</sup> In the Nidāna Sūtra<sup>5</sup> Ātharvaṇikas, or ‘followers of the Atharvaveda,’ appear. <div n="P"/>Specific but mainly mythical Ātharvaṇas are {@Kabandha,@} {@Bṛhaddiva, Bhiṣaj, Dadhyaṅc,@} and {@Vicārin.@} <F>1) xix. 23, 1.</F> <F>2) xii. 9, 10.</F> <F>3) vii. 1, 2, 4; 2, 1; 7, 1.</F> <F>4) Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xvi. 2, 10, etc.</F> <F>5) ii. 12. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Athar-%} {%vaveda,%} xxv.; {%Atharvaveda,%} 8 {%et seq.%}</F>

{@Ā-darśa,@}¦ ‘mirror,’ is a term found only in the Upaniṣads<sup>1</sup> and Āraṇyakas.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, ii. 1, 9; iii. 9, 15; Chāndogya Upaniṣad, viii. 7. 4; Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad, iv. 2; 11.</F> <F>2) Aitareya Āraṇyaka, iii. 2, 4; Sāṅkh- āyana Āraṇyaka, viii. 7.</F>

{@Ādāra@}¦ was a kind of plant which was prescribed as a substitute for {@Soma.@}<sup>1</sup> It is identified in the Śatapatha Brāh- maṇa<sup>2</sup> with {@Pūtīka.@} <F>1) Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, iv. 5, 10, 4.</F> <F>2) xiv. 1, 2, 12. {%Cf.%} Kāthaka Saṃ- hitā, xxiv. 3; Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xxv. 12, 19. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 276.</F>
{@Ānanda-ja Cāndhanāyana@}¦ is mentioned as a pupil of {@Śāmba@} in the Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 372.</F>
{@Ānabhi-mlāta@}¦ is mentioned in a Vaṃśa, or Genealogy, in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad<sup>1</sup> as a pupil of Ānabhimlāta. <F>1) ii. 6, 2 (not in the Mādhyandina version).</F>
{@Ānava.@}¦ See {@Anu.@}

{@Ānūka.@}¦ — Geldner<sup>1</sup> thinks that in its solitary occurrence in the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> this word means an ornament. Roth<sup>3</sup> takes it adverbially, and so do Ludwig and Oldenberg. <F>1) {%Vedische Studien,%} 3, 94.</F> <F>2) v. 33, 9.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary. {%s.v.%}</F>

{@Āpayā@}¦ is the name of a river mentioned once only in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> when it occurs between the {@Dṛṣadvatī@} and the {@Sarasvatī.@} Ludwig<sup>2</sup> was inclined to identify it with the Āpagā as a name for the Ganges, but Zimmer<sup>3</sup> correctly places it near the Sarasvatī, either as the small tributary which flows past Thānesar or the modern Indramatī farther west, while Pischel<sup>4</sup> assigns it to {@Kurukṣetra,@} of which the Āpayā is mentioned as a famous river in the Mahābhārata.<sup>5</sup> <F>1) iii. 23, 4.</F> <F>2) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 200. But {%cf. ibid.,%} 4, 304.</F> <F>3) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 18.</F> <F>4) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 218.</F> <F>5) Mahābhārata, iii. 83, 68.</F>

{@Ābayu@}¦ is apparently the name of a plant in the Atharvaveda;<sup>1</sup> the mustard plant<sup>2</sup> may have been meant, but the sense is quite uncertain.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) vi. 16, 1.</F> <F>2) Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Atharva-%} {%veda,%} 465, following the indication of the use of the hymn in the Kauśika Sūtra.</F> <F>3) Whitney, Translation of the Athar- vaveda, 292; Zimmer. {%Altindisches Leben,%} 72.</F>
{@Ābhi-pratāriṇa.@}¦ — Patronymic of {@Vṛddhadyumna.@}

{@Ā bhūti Tvāṣṭra@}¦ is mentioned in two Vaṃśas, or Genealogies, of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad<sup>1</sup> as a pupil of {@Viśvarūpa@} {@Tvāṣṭra,@} both teachers being no doubt equally mythical. <F>1) ii. 6, 3; iv. 6, 3 (in both recensions).</F>
{@Āmalaka@}¦ (neuter), a common word later, is found in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (vii. 3, 1), denoting the Myrobalan fruit. {%Cf.%} {@Amalā.@}

{@Āmikṣā@}¦ designates a mess of clotted curds. It is not known to the Rigveda, but occurs in all the later Saṃhitās,<sup>1</sup> Brāh- maṇas,<sup>2</sup> etc., and is associated with the Vaiśya in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) Av. x. 9, 13; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 5, 5, 4; iii. 3, 9, 2; vi. 2, 5, 3; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 1, 9; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xix. 21; 23, etc.</F> <F>2) Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 8, 1, 7. 9; iii. 3, 3, 2, etc.; Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, ii. 8, 8; Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 438 ({%Journal of the American Oriental Society,%} 19, 99, 101); Chāndogya Upaniṣad, viii. 8, 5, etc.</F> <F>3) {%Loc. cit. Cf.%} Mānava Srauta Sūtra, ii. 2, 40.</F>

{@Āmba@}¦ denotes in the Taittirīya<sup>1</sup> and Kāṭhaka<sup>2</sup> Saṃhitās a grain, called {@Nāmba@} in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> <F>1) i. 8, 10, 1.</F> <F>2) xv. 5.</F> <F>3) v. 3, 3, 8.</F>

{@Āmbaṣṭhya@}¦ is mentioned in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (viii. 21) as a king, whose priest for the Rājasūya, or royal inauguration, was {@Nārada.@} Presumably the name is local, meaning ‘King of [Page1-060+ 43] the Ambaṣṭhas,’ as interpreted in the St. Petersburg Dictionary. Later the term Ambaṣṭha denotes ‘a man of mingled Brāhmaṇa and Vaiśya parentage by father and mother’ respectively.

{@Ā-yatana.@}¦ — The general sense of ‘abode’ or ‘home’ appears to be limited in one passage of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (vii. 24, 2) to the sense of ‘holy place,’ ‘sanctuary,’ which is found in the epic.

{@Āyavasa@}¦ is mentioned apparently as a king in a corrupt and unintelligible verse of the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) i. 122, 15. {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 206; Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>

{@Āyu@}¦ appears in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> with {@Kutsa@} and {@Atithigva@} as having been defeated, with Indra's aid, by {@Tūrvayāṇa,@} who is believed by Pischel<sup>2</sup> to have been King of the {@Pakthas.@} Possibly he is elsewhere<sup>3</sup> referred to as victorious, by Indra's aid, over {@Veśa.@} Elsewhere he is quite mythical.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) i. 53, 10; ii. 14, 7; vi. 18, 3; viii. 53, 2; Bergaigne, {%Religion Védique,%} 1, 60.</F> <F>2) {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 71-75.</F> <F>3) Rv. x. 49, 5; but the word is possibly not a proper name.</F> <F>4) {%Cf.%} Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} 100, 135, 140.</F>
{@Āyuta.@}¦ See {@Ghṛta.@}

{@Ā-yudha,@}¦ ‘weapon,’ in its widest sense covers the whole of a Kṣatriya's warlike equipment, which in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> is summed up as horse-chariot ({%aśva-ratha%}), bow and arrows ({%iṣu-dhanva%}), and corselet ({%kavaca%}). As the bow and arrow ({%iṣu, dhanvan%}) were essential as the main weapons of the Vedic fighter, they are probably meant when Āyudha is used specifically of weapons, as often from the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> onwards. The battle hymn in the Rigveda<sup>3</sup> confirms this view, as it presents to us the warrior armed with bow and arrow on his chariot, and clad in armour ({@Varman@}), with a guard ({@Hastaghna@}) on the left arm to avoid the friction of the bow-string. The corselet was not a single solid piece of metal, but consisted of many pieces fitted together ({%syūta%});<sup>4</sup> it may [Page1-061+ 41] have been made either of metal plates or, as is more likely, of some stiff material plated with metal. In addition the warrior wore a helmet ({@Śiprā@}). There is no trace of the use of a shield, nor is there any clear record of the employment of greaves or other guard for the feet.<sup>5</sup> Skill in the use of weapons is referred to in the Rigveda.<sup>6</sup> <div n="P"/>It is doubtful whether sling stones ({@Adri, Aśani@}) were in ordinary use. The hook ({%aṅkuśa%})<sup>7</sup> also is merely a divine weapon, and the axe ({%svadhiti,%}<sup>8</sup> {%vāśī, paraśu%}) does not occur in mortal combats. For the use of the spear see {@Ṛṣṭi, Rambhiṇī,@} {@Śakti, Śaru;@} of the sword, {@Asi, Kṛti.@} Neither weapon can be considered ordinary in warfare, nor was the club ({@Vajra@}) used. For the modes of warfare see {@Saṃgrāma.@} <F>1) vii. 19, 2.</F> <F>2) i. 39, 2; 61. 13; 92, 1; ii. 30, 9. etc.; Av. vi. 133, 2, etc.</F> <F>3) vi. 75.</F> <F>4) Rv. i. 31, 15.</F> <F>5) Grassmann saw greaves in {%vaṭūriṇā%} {%padā%} in Rv. i. 133, 2, but this is most improbable.</F> <F>6) i. 92, 1. {%Cf.%} Geldner, {%Vedische%} {%Studien,%} 3, 183; Hopkins, {%Journal of the%} {%American Oriental Society,%} 13, 295.</F> <F>7) Rv. viii. 17, 10; x. 44, 9; 134, 6; Av. vi. 83, 3. {%Cf.%} Muir, {%Sanskrit Texts.%} 5, 87.</F> <F>8) Rv. v. 32, 10; ix. 67, 30; x. 43, 9. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 298- 301; Muir, {%Sanskrit Texts.%} 5, 469-472; Hopkins, {%Journal of the American Oriental%} {%Society,%} 13, 281 {%et seq.%}</F>

{@Āyogava. — Marutta Āvi-kṣita,@}¦ the Āyogava king, is men- tioned as a sacrificer in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> where also a Gāthā (‘stanza’) celebrating his sacrifice is cited. {%Cf.%} {@Ayogū.@} <F>1) xiii. 5. 4, 6. {%Cf.%} Śāṅkhāyana Srauta Sūtra, xvi. 9, 14-16.</F>
{@Āraṅgara@}¦ is one of the names of the bee found in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> Other names are {@Sarah@} and {@Bhṛṅgā.@} <F>1) x. 106, 10. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 97.</F>

{@Ārā,@}¦ a word later<sup>1</sup> known as an ‘awl’ or ‘gimlet,’ occurs in the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> only to designate a weapon of Pūṣan, with whose pastoral character its later use for piercing leather is con- sistent. {%Cf.%} {@Vāśī.@} <F>1) Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 3, 365. n. 1.</F> <F>2) vi. 53. 8.</F>
{@Ārāḍhi.@}¦ — Patronymic of {@Saujāta.@} {%Cf.%} {@Arāḍa.@}
{@Āruṇa Aupa-veśi.@}¦ — So the manuscripts let us read the former word in the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, but this is doubtless an error for {@Aruṇa.@}

{@Āruṇi@}¦ is the patronymic normally referring to {@Uddālaka,@} son of {@Aruṇa Aupaveśi.@} Uddālaka is probably also meant by Āruṇi Yaśasvin, who occurs as a teacher of the Subrahmaṇyā (a kind of recitation) in the Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> Āruṇis are referred to both in the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> and in the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā,<sup>3</sup> as well as in the Aitareya Āraṇyaka.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) ii. 80.</F> <F>2) ii. 5, 1. {%Cf.%} Keith, {%Aitareya Āraṇ-%} {%yaka,%} 204.</F> <F>3) xiii. 12.</F> <F>4) ii. 4. 1.</F>

{@Āruṇeya.@}¦ — An epithet of {@Śvetaketu,@} indicating his descent from {@Uddālaka Āruṇi@} and {@Aruṇa Aupaveśi.@} It is apparently confined to the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> and Chāndogya Upani- ṣad,<sup>2</sup> in which Śvetaketu plays a great part. <F>1) x. 3, 4, 1; xi. 2, 7, 12; 5, 4, 18; 6, 2, 1; xii. 2, 1, 9; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, vi. 2, 1.</F> <F>2) v. 3, 1; vi. 1, 1.</F>
{@Ārkṣa.@}¦ — Patronymic of {@Śrutarvan@} and of {@Āśvamedha.@}

{@Ārjīka@}¦<sup>1</sup> and {@Ārjīkīya@}<sup>2</sup> (masc.), {@Ārjīkīyā@}<sup>3</sup> (fem.). — The two masculine forms probably denote the people or land, while the feminine word designates the river of the land. Hillebrandt<sup>4</sup> locates the country in or near Kaśmir, as Arrian<sup>5</sup> mentions Arsaces, brother of Abhisares, who presumably took his name from his people, and Abhisāra bordered on Kaśmir. Pischel<sup>6</sup> accepts Ārjīka as designating a country, which he, however, thinks cannot be identified. But neither Roth<sup>7</sup> nor Zimmer<sup>8</sup> recognizes the word as a proper name. On the other hand, all authorities agree in regarding Ārjīkīyā as the name of a [Page1-063+ 38] river. {@Roth@}<sup>9</sup> does so in one passage<sup>10</sup> only, elsewhere seeing references to Soma vessels; but it seems necessary to treat the word alike in all passages containing it. Zimmer does not locate the river, and Pischel denies the possibility of its identification. Hillebrandt thinks it may have been the Upper Indus, or the {@Vitastā@} (the Jhelum), or some other stream. Grassmann follows Yāska<sup>11</sup> in identifying it with the the {@Vipāś@} (Beäs), but this is rendered improbable by the position of the name in the hymn in praise of rivers ({%nadī-%} {%stuti%}).<sup>12</sup> Brunnhofer<sup>13</sup> identifies it with the Arghesan, a tributary of the Arghanab. <F>1) Singular: Rv. viii. 7, 29; ix. 113, 2. Plural: ix. 65, 23.</F> <F>2) Rv. viii. 64, 11.</F> <F>3) Rv. x. 75, 5.</F> <F>4) {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 126-137.</F> <F>5) Anabasis, v. 29, 4.</F> <F>6) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 209, 217.</F> <F>7) St. Petersburg Dictionary.</F> <F>8) {%Altindisches Leben.%} 12-14.</F> <F>9) {%Op. cit., s.v. suṣomā.%}</F> <F>10) Rv. x. 75, 5.</F> <F>11) Nirukta, ix. 26.</F> <F>12) Rv. x. 75.</F> <F>13) {%Iran und Turan,%} 52. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Max Mūller, {%Sacred Books of the%} {%East,%} 32, 398; 399.</F>
{@Ārjuneya.@}¦ — In the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> this name occurs as the patro- nymic of {@Kautsa.@} <F>1) i. 112, 23; iv. 26, 1; vii. 19, 2; viii. 1, 11.</F>

{@Ārtabhāgī-putra@}¦ is mentioned as a pupil of {@Śauṅgī-putra@} in a Vaṃśa or Genealogy in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.<sup>1</sup> Ārtabhāga is a patronymic of Jaratkārava in the same Upaniṣad.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) vi. 5, 2 (also in the Mādhyandina version).</F> <F>2) iii. 2, 1, 13.</F>

{@Ārtava.@}¦ — This expression denotes a portion of the year consisting of more seasons than one. But it does not bear the exact sense of ‘half-year,’ as suggested by Zimmer.<sup>1</sup> This is shown by the fact that it occurs regularly in the plural, not in the dual. In the Atharvaveda it occurs between seasons and years ({%hāyana%}),<sup>2</sup> but also in the combinations, ‘seasons, Ārtavas, months, years,;<sup>3</sup> ‘half-months, months, Ārtavas, seasons’;<sup>4</sup> [Page1-064+ 61] ‘seasons, Ārtavas, months, half-months, days and nights, day’;<sup>5</sup> and in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā ‘months, seasons, Ārtavas, the year,’<sup>6</sup> or simply with the seasons.<sup>7</sup> <F>1) {%Altindisches Leben.%} 374.</F> <F>2) iii. 10, 9.</F> <F>3) iii. 10, 10.</F> <F>4) xi. 7, 20. {%Cf.%} xv. 6, 6; 17, 6.</F> <F>5) xvi. 8, 18.</F> <F>6) xxii. 28.</F> <F>7) Av. v. 28, 2. 13; x. 6, 18; 7, 5; xi. 3, 17; 6, 17; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vii. 2, 6, 1, 3. Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad, i, 3. cited in this sense in the St. Petersburg Dictionary, is not so to be understood, as the word there is merely adjectival.</F>

{@Ārtnī@}¦ denotes the end of the bow to which the bow-string ({%jyā%}) was attached.<sup>1</sup> The string was not normally kept fastened to both ends of the bow, but when an arrow was to be shot it was strung taut.<sup>2</sup> On the other hand, the legend of the death of Viṣṇu, told in the later Saṃhitās<sup>3</sup> and Brāhmaṇas,<sup>4</sup> expressly contemplates his leaning on his strung bow, which cleaves his head by the sudden springing apart of the two ends when the bow-string is gnawed through. <F>1) Rv. vi. 75, 4; Av. i. 1, 3; Maitrā- yaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 9, 2; Kāṭhaka Saṃ- hitā, xvii. 11; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xvi. 9, etc.</F> <F>2) Rv. x. 166, 3. {%Cf.%} Av. vi. 42, 1.</F> <F>3) Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iv. 5. 9.</F> <F>4) Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, vii. 5. 6; Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiv. 1, 1, 7 {%et%} {%seq.%} <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 297, 298; Hopkins, {%Journal of the American%} {%Oriental Society,%} 13, 270.</F>

{@Ārya@}¦ is the normal designation in the Vedic literature from the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> onwards of an Āryan, a member of the three upper classes, {@Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya,@} or {@Vaiśya,@} as the formal division is given in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> The Ārya stands in opposition to the {@Dāsa,@}<sup>3</sup> but also to the {@Śūdra.@} Sometimes<sup>4</sup> the expression is restricted to the Vaiśya caste, [Page1-065+ 56] the Brāhmaṇa and the Kṣatriya receiving special designations; but this use is not common, and it is often uncertain also whether {@Arya@} is not meant. The phrase Śūdrāryau<sup>5</sup> is espe- cially ambiguous, but appears to have denoted originally the Śūdra and the Āryan, for in the Mahāvrata ceremony the fight between a Śūdra and an Ārya is represented in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa as one between a Brāhmaṇa and a Śūdra, though the Sūtra treats it as a fight between a Vaiśya and a Śūdra. <div n="P"/>The word Ārya (fem. Āryā or Ārī) also occurs frequently used as an adjective to describe the Āryan classes ({%viśaḥ%}),<sup>6</sup> or name ({%nāman%}),<sup>7</sup> or caste ({%varṇa%}),<sup>8</sup> or dwellings ({%dhāman%});<sup>9</sup> or again reference is made to the Āryan supremacy ({%vrata%})<sup>10</sup> being extended over the land. Āryan foes ({%vṛtra%})<sup>11</sup> are referred to beside Dāsa foes, and there are many<sup>12</sup> references to war of Āryan versus Āryan, as well as to war of Āryan against Dāsa. From this it can be fairly deduced that even by the time of the Rigveda the Āryan communities had advanced far beyond the stage of simple conquest of the aborigines. In the later Saṃhitās and Brāhmaṇas the wars alluded to seem mainly Āryan wars, no doubt in consequence of the fusion of Ārya and Dāsa into one community. <div n="P"/>Weber<sup>13</sup> considers that the five peoples known to the Rigveda were the Āryans and the four peoples of the quarters ({%diś%}) of the earth, but this is doubtful. Āryan speech ({%vāc%})<sup>14</sup> is specially referred to in the Aitareya and Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyakas. <F>1) Rv. i. 51, 8; 130, 8; 156, 5, etc.</F> <F>2) iv. 1, 6 (Kāṇva recension).</F> <F>3) Rv. i. 51, 8. 9; 103, 3; vi. 20, 10; 25, 2, 3, etc. (opposed to Dāsa); Av. iv. 20, 4. 8; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iv. 6, 6; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xiv. 30, etc. (opposed to Sūdra).</F> <F>4) Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 205, 215, finds this use — understanding Ārya as meant — in Atharvaveda, xix. 32, 8, and 62, 1, as well as in passages where Śūdrāryau is found. Lanman, in Whitney's Translation of the Athar- vaveda, 948, 1003, quotes his view with approval; but Whitney's version leaves no doubt that he read and understood the text as Ārya, the Āryan, not the Vaiśya. For Whitney's view, Av. iv. 20, 4. 8 may be cited; and so Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.,%} takes the passages. In Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iv. 3, 10, 8, Śūdrāryau must mean Sūdra and Vaiśya; but the Padapāṭha takes it as Arya, and so does Zimmer.</F> <F>5) See Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vii. 5, 9, 3, with Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xiii. 3, 7. 8; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxxiv. 5; Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, v. 5, 17; Tait- tirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 2, 6, 7; Lāṭyāyana Sūtra, iv. 2, 5; Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xvii. 6, 2; Anupada Sūtra, vii. 10.</F> <F>6) Rv. i. 77, 3; 96, 31; x. 11, 4; 43, 4, etc.</F> <F>7) Rv. x; 49, 3.</F> <F>8) Rv. iii. 34, 9. {%Cf.%} {@Varṇa.@}</F> <F>9) Rv. ix. 63, 14.</F> <F>10) Rv. x. 65, 11. So Agni and Indra are styled Āryan, as supporters of the Āryan people (Rv. vi. 60, 6).</F> <F>11) Rv. vi. 33, 3; vii. 83, 1; x. 69, 6.</F> <F>12) Rv. i. 102, 5; iii. 32, 14; vi. 22, 10; 25, 2. 3; viii. 2, 4. 27; x. 38, 3; 83, 1; 102, 3, etc.</F> <F>13) {%Indische Studien,%} 17, 288. {%Cf.%} Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v. kṛṣṭi,%} and {@Pañca Janāsaḥ.@}</F> <F>14) Aitareya Āraṇyaka, iii. 2, 5; Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka, viii. 9. {%Cf.%} Keith, {%Aitareya Āraṇyaka,%} 196, 255; and {@Vāc.@} <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rig- veda, 3, 207 {%et seq.;%} Zimmer, {%Altin-%} {%disches Leben,%} 214 {%et seq.%}</F>
{@Ārya.@}¦ See {@Mālya.@}
{@Arṣṭi-ṣeṇa.@}¦ — Patronymic of {@Devāpi.@}<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Rv. x. 98, 5. 6. 8; Nirukta, ii. 11; Bṛhaddevatā, vii. 155.</F>

{@Āla@}¦ appears to mean ‘weed’ in the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> and to form part of three other words,<sup>2</sup> denoting, according to Sāyaṇa, grass-creepers ({%sasya-vallī%}) — viz., Alasālā, Silañjālā,<sup>3</sup> and Nīlā- galasāla. Whitney,<sup>4</sup> however, does not think that the words can be given any determinate sense. <F>1) Av. vi. 16, 3. But Whitney takes the word as a verb, comparing v. 22, 6.</F> <F>2) Av. vi. 16, 4.</F> <F>3) Sāyaṇa reads Śalāñjālā, and the manuscripts of the Kauśika Sūtra (vi. 16), have Śilāñjālā. But {%cf.%} {@Silācī.@}</F> <F>4) Translation of the Atharvaveda, 292, 293. {%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Hymns of%} {%the Atharvaveda,%} 466.</F>

{@Ālambāyanī-putra@}¦ is mentioned in a Vaṃśa or Genealogy of the Kāṇva recension of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (vi. 5, 2) as a pupil of {@Ālambī-putra.@} In the Mādhyandina recension (vi. 4, 32) the relation is reversed, for there he is teacher of Ālambī-putra and pupil of {@Jāyantī-putra.@}

{@Ālambī-putra@}¦ is a pupil of {@Jāyantī-putra@} according to a Vaṃśa in the Kāṇva recension of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (vi. 5, 2), but of {@Ālambāyanī-putra@} according to the Mādhy- andina (vi. 4, 32).
{@Āligī@}¦ is the name of a kind of serpent in the Atharvaveda (v. 13, 7). {%Cf.%} {@Viligī.@}

{@Ā-vasatha@}¦ (‘dwelling’). — The precise sense<sup>1</sup> of this term appears to be a place for the reception of guests, especially Brāhmaṇas and others on the occasion of feasts and sacrifices (somewhat like the modern meaning of Dharma-śālā as a rest- house for pilgrims), a use derived from the more general sense of ‘abode.’<sup>2</sup> <F>1) Av. ix. 6, 5 (a hymn in praise of entertaining Brāhmaṇas); Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 1, 10, 6; iii. 7, 4, 6; Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, xii. 4, 4, 6 (where Eggeling renders the word as if meaning ‘house’ merely); Chāndogya Upaniṣad, iv. 1, 1, etc. Details are given in the Sūtras — {%e.g.,%} Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra, v. 9, 3; Dharma Sūtra, ii. 9, 25, 4.</F> <F>2) {%E.g.,%} Aitareya Upaniṣad, iii. 12. {%Cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 2, 120, n. 1.</F>
{@Āvika@}¦ (‘coming from the sheep,’ {%avi%}) is a term for ‘wool,’ which occurs first in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (ii. 3, 6). {%Cf.%} {@Avi.@}
{@Avi-kṣita.@}¦ — Patronymic of {@Marutta,@}<sup>1</sup> the {@Āyogava.@} <F>1) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, viii. 21; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 5, 4, 6.</F>

{@Ā-śarīka@}¦ appears to denote a disease in a hymn of the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> celebrating the powers of the {@Jaṅgida@} plant. Zimmer<sup>2</sup> thinks that it merely denotes the pain in the limbs accompanying fever. Whitney<sup>3</sup> suggests taking the word as merely an epithet. <F>1) xix. 34, 10.</F> <F>2) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 65, 391.</F> <F>3) Translation of the Atharvaveda, 953. {%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the%} {%Atharvaveda,%} 673.</F>

{@Ā-śir@}¦ (‘admixture’) denotes the mixing, and more especially the milk mixed with the juice, of the Soma before it was offered to the gods. In this sense it is not rare from the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> onwards. Not milk alone was employed for this purpose. The epithet ‘having three admixtures’ applied to Soma<sup>2</sup> is explained by the other epithets, ‘mixed with milk’ ({%gavāśir%}), ‘mixed with curds’ ({%dadhy-āśir%}), and ‘mixed with grain’ ({%yavāśir%}) — all referring to Soma. <F>1) i. 134, 6; iii. 53, 14; viii. 2, 10. 11, etc.; Av. ii. 29, 1, etc.; Nirukta, vi. 8; 32.</F> <F>2) Rv. v. 27, 5; {%cf.%} viii. 2, 7. {%Cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 209 {%et seq.%}</F>

{@Āśī-viṣa,@}¦ occurring only in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> is understood by Roth<sup>2</sup> as designating a particular kind of snake, and perhaps means ‘having poison ({%viṣa%}) in its fangs’ ({%āśī%}). <F>1) vi. 1.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} It is a common word in the Epic and later.</F>

{@Āśu,@}¦ the ‘swift,’ is frequently used without {@Aśva@} to denote the chariot steed from the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> onwards. <F>1) ii. 16, 3; 31, 2; 38, 3, etc.; Av. ii. 14, 6; iv. 27, 1; xiii. 2, 2; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, i. 8, 10; Satapatha Brāh- maṇa, v. 3, 3, 3, etc.</F>

{@Āśuṃ-ga@}¦ in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> seems to denote some sort of animal. It is qualified by the word ‘young’ ({%śiśuka%}), and Roth<sup>2</sup> suggests that it may mean a bird (‘swift-flying’), or that the expression denotes ‘a foal going to its dam’ ({%āśu-ga%}). Sāyaṇa, however, reads the accompanying word as {%śuśuka,%} which he assumes to denote an animal. Bloomfield<sup>3</sup> renders the two words ‘a swift ({%āśuṃga%}) foal ({%śiśuka%}),’ thus agreeing with one of Roth's suggestions in sense, though not in the explanation of Aśuṃga. <F>1) vi. 14, 3.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>3) {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 464. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Whitney, Translation of the Athar- vaveda, 291.</F>

{@Ā-śrama@}¦ (‘resting-place’) does not occur in any Upaniṣad which can be regarded as pre-Buddhistic. Its earliest use as denoting the stages of a Hindu's life is found in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad.<sup>1</sup> In one passage<sup>2</sup> of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad reference is made only to the {@Brahmacārin@} and householder, to whom, as a reward for study, the procreation of children, the practice of Yoga, abstention from injury to living creatures, and sacrifices, freedom from transmigration are promised. In another place<sup>3</sup> three states are contemplated, but not as con- secutive. The Brahmacārin may either become a householder or become an anchorite, or remain in his teacher's house all his life. Similarly, reference<sup>4</sup> is made to the death of the anchorite in the forest, or the sacrifice in the village. In contrast with all three<sup>5</sup> is the man who stands fast in Brahman (Brahma- saṃstha). In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad<sup>6</sup> the knower of the Ātman is contrasted with those who (1) study, or (2) sacrifice and give alms, or (3) are anchorites, and in another place<sup>7</sup> with those who sacrifice and make benefactions, and those who practice asceticism. This position of superiority to, and distinction from, the Āśramas became later a fourth<sup>8</sup> Āśrama, [Page1-069+ 35] the {@Gṛhastha,@} or householder, who was in the second stage, being required to pass not only into the stage of {@Vānaprastha,@} but also that of the Sannyāsin ({@Bhikṣu, Parivrājaka@}). The first stage, that of the {@Brahmacārin,@} was still obligatory, but was no longer allowed to remain a permanent one, as was originally possible. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Deussen, {%Philosophy of the Upanishads,%} 60, 367 {%et seq.%} <F>1) {%Atyāśramin,%} Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, vi. 21; Maitrāyaṇī Upaniṣad, iv. 3, etc.</F> <F>2) viii. 5.</F> <F>3) ii. 23, 1.</F> <F>4) v. 10.</F> <F>5) ii. 23, 1.</F> <F>6) iv. 2, 22. {%Cf.%} iii. 5.</F> <F>7) iii. 8, 10.</F> <F>8) Jābāla Upaniṣad, 4. {%Cf.%} Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad, ii. 1, 7.</F>
{@Ā-śreṣā, Ā-śleṣā.@}¦ See {@Nakṣatra.@}

{@Āśva-ghna.@}¦ — This name occurs in one passage of the Rig- veda,<sup>1</sup> in a very obscure hymn, where it appears to denote a prince who had made offerings to Indra, and who may, as Ludwig<sup>2</sup> thinks, have been called {@Vitaraṇa.@} <F>1) x. 61, 21.</F> <F>2) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 165.</F>

{@Aśvatara Āśvi,@}¦ or {@Āśvatarāśvi.@} — These two expressions are used<sup>1</sup> as patronymics of {@Buḍila,@} denoting, according to Sāyaṇa,<sup>2</sup> that he was son of Aśva, and descendant of Aśvatara. <F>1) The first is found in Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vi. 30; the second in Sata- patha Brāhmaṇa, iv. 6, 1, 9; x. 6, 1, 1; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, iv. 15, 8; Chāndogya Upaniṣad, v. 11, 1; 16, 1.</F> <F>2) On Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, {%loc. cit.%}</F>
{@Aśva-tthya.@}¦ — Patronymic of Ahīnā.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 10, 9, 10. Possibly to be read Āśvathya.</F>
{@Aśva-medha@}¦ is the patronymic of an unnamed prince, who occurs in a Dānastuti (‘Praise of Gifts’) in the Rigveda (viii. 68, 15. 16).

{@Āśva-vāla.@}¦ — From this adjective (‘made of horse-tail grass’), applied to a strew ({%prastara%}) in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (iii. 4, 1, 17; 6, 3, 10), follows the existence of the Aśvavāla grass ({%Saccharum spontaneum%}).
{@Āśva-sūkti@}¦ is mentioned in Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa (xix. 4, 2, {%et seq.%}) as an author of Sāmans (Soma chants) along with {@Gausūkti.@}

{@Āśvina,@}¦ or {@Āśvīna,@} designates, in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and two Brāhmaṇas,<sup>2</sup> the length of journey made in a day by a horseman ({%aśvin%}). The exact distance is not defined. In the Atharva it appears to exceed five leagues, being mentioned immediately after a distance of three or five {@Yojanas;@} in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa the heavenly world is placed at a distance of a thousand {@Āśvinas.@} <F>1) vi. 131, 3.</F> <F>2) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 17; Pañ- caviṃśa Brāhmaṇa in {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 34.</F>

{@Āṣādhi Sauśromateya.@}¦ — According to the Śatapatha Brāh- maṇa,<sup>1</sup> he was ruined because the heads were put on at the Agniciti in a certain manner, and not correctly. <F>1) vi. 2, 1, 37. Eggeling has Aṣāḍhi, but as it is a patronymic of Aṣāḍha, the form Āṣāḍhi seems correct.</F>
{@Āṣṭrā@}¦ seems in the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā (xxxvii. 1) to denote the ploughman's goad.

{@Āṣṭrī.@}¦ — In the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> the word seems to denote a fire- place. The evil bird is entreated not to settle there on the hearth. <F>1) x. 165, 3. {%Cf.%} Schrader, {%Prehistoric Antiquities,%} 347.</F>

{@Āsaṅga Plāyogi@}¦ is a king who appears in a Dānastuti (‘Praise of Gifts’) in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as a generous patron. Owing, however, to the addition of a curious phallic verse to the hymn, and its early misunderstanding,<sup>2</sup> a legend was invented that he lost his manhood and became a woman, but by the intercession of {@Medhyātithi@} was transformed into a man, much to the delight of his wife, {@Śaśvatī,@} whose existence is based on a misunderstanding of the phrase ‘every woman’ ({%śaśvatī nārī%}) in the added verse.<sup>3</sup> Another misunderstanding [Page1-071+ 50] of the Dānastuti<sup>4</sup> gives him a son Svanad-ratha, really a mere epithet, and makes him a descendant of Yadu. <F>1) viii. 1, 32. 33.</F> <F>2) viii. 1, 34. See Hopkins, {%Religions%} {%of India,%} 150, n. 1; Bṛhaddevatā, ii. 83; vi. 41, with Macdonell's notes. Dyā- dviveda gives the tale at length in Vedic words taken from the Nighaṇṭu, a curious {%jeu d'esprit.%} See the extract from the Nītimañjarī given by Sieg, {%Die Sagenstoffe des Ṛgveda,%} 40, 41.</F> <F>3) viii. 1, 34.</F> <F>4) viii. 1, 31. 32. {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Trans- lation of the Rigveda, 3, 159; Hopkins, {%Journal of the American Oriental Society,%} 17, 89; Griffith, {%Hymns of the Rigveda,%} 2, 106, 107; Oldenberg. {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 354.</F>

{@Ā-sandī.@}¦ — This is a generic term for a seat of some sort, occurring frequently in the later Saṃhitās<sup>1</sup> and Brāhmaṇas.<sup>2</sup> but not in the Rigveda. In the Atharvaveda<sup>3</sup> the settle brought for the {@Vrātya@} is described at length. It had two feet, lengths wise and cross-pieces, forward and cross-cords, showing that it was made of wood and also cording. It was also covered with a cushion ({@Āstaraṇa@}) and a pillow ({@Upabarhaṇa@}), had a seat ({@Āsāda@}) and a support ({@Upaśraya@}). Similar seats are described in the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad<sup>4</sup> and the Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa.<sup>5</sup> The seat for the king at the royal consecration is described in very similar terms in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa,<sup>6</sup> where the height of the feet is placed at a span, and the lengthwise and cross-pieces are each to be a cubit, while the interwoven part ({%vivayana%}) is to be of Muñja grass, and the seat of Udumbara wood. In another passage of the Atharvaveda<sup>7</sup> Lanman seems to take the seat meant as a ‘long reclining chair.’ There also a cushion ({@Upadhāna@}) and coverlet ({@Upavāsana@}) are mentioned. The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa repeatedly describes the Āsandī in terms showing that it was an elaborate seat. In one place<sup>8</sup> it is said to be made of Khadira wood, perforated ({%vi-tṛṇṇā%}), and joined with straps ({%vardhra-yutā%}) like that of the Bhāratas. At the Sautrāmaṇī rite<sup>9</sup> (an Indra sacrifice) the seat is of Udumbara wood, is knee-high, and of unlimited width and depth, and is covered with plaited reed-work. The [Page1-072+ 40] imperial seat<sup>10</sup> is to be shoulder-high, of Udumbara wood, and wound all over with cords of Balvaja grass ({%Eleusina indica%}). Elsewhere<sup>11</sup> the seat is a span high, a cubit in width and depth, of Udumbara wood, and covered with reed-grass cords, and daubed with clay. <F>1) Av. xiv. 2, 65; xv. 3, 2 {%et seq.;%} Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vii. 5, 8, 5; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, viii. 56; xix. 16; 86, etc.</F> <F>2) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, viii. 5; 6; 12; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 3, 4, 26; v. 2, 1, 22; 4, 4, 1, etc.</F> <F>3) xv. 3, 2 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>4) i. 5. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 397; Keith, {%Śāṅkhāyana Aran-%} {%yaka,%} 19.</F> <F>5) ii. 24.</F> <F>6) viii. 5; 6; 12.</F> <F>7) xiv. 2, 65. See his note in Whit- ney's Translation of the Atharvaveda, 765.</F> <F>8) v. 4, 4, 1.</F> <F>9) xii. 8, 3, 4 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>10) xiv. 1, 3, 8 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>11) vi. 7, 1, 12 {%et seq.%} <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 155.</F>

{@Āsandī-vant,@}¦ ‘possessing the throne,’ is the title of the royal city of {@Janamejaya Pārikṣita,@} in which the horse, for his famous Aśvamedha, was bound. The authorities both cite a Gāthā for the fact, but they differ as to the priest who celebrated the rite. In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> he is stated to have been Indrota Daivāpa Śaunaka, but in the Aitareya<sup>2</sup> {@Tura Kāvaṣeya.@} <F>1) xiii. 5, 4, 2.</F> <F>2) viii. 21. {%Cf.%} Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xvi. 9, 1. Pāṇini, viii. 2, 12, knows the name.</F>

{@Ā-sāda,@}¦ ‘seat,’ occurs in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> as a description of part of the settle ({@Āsandī@}) of the {@Vrātya.@} It seems best to regard it with Whitney<sup>2</sup> as the seat proper; Aufrecht,<sup>3</sup> Zimmer,<sup>4</sup> and Roth<sup>5</sup> render it as the ‘cushion for the seat,’ but that is sufficiently described by the word {@Āstaraṇa.@} <F>1) xv. 3, 8.</F> <F>2) Translation of the Atharvaveda, 771.</F> <F>3) {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 131.</F> <F>4) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 155.</F> <F>5) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>

{@Āsurāyaṇa@}¦ is mentioned as a pupil of {@Traivaṇi@} in the first two Vaṃśas<sup>1</sup> (lists of teachers) of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad in both recensions, but as a pupil of {@Āsuri@} in the third Vaṃśa.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) ii. 6, 3; iv. 6, 3.</F> <F>2) vi. 5, 2. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 434, n.</F>

{@Āsuri@}¦ occurs in the first two Vaṃśas<sup>1</sup> (lists of teachers) of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad as a pupil of {@Bhāradvāja@} and teacher of {@Aupajandhani,@} but in the third<sup>2</sup> as a pupil of {@Yājñavalkya@} and teacher of {@Āsurāyaṇa.@} He appears as a [Page1-073+ 42] ritual authority in the first four books of the Śatapatha Brāh- maṇa,<sup>3</sup> and as an authority on dogmatic, specially noted for his insistence on truth, in the last book.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) ii. 6, 3; iv. 6, 3.</F> <F>2) vi. 5, 2.</F> <F>3) i. 6, 3, 26; ii. 1, 4, 27; 3, 1, 9; 4, 1, 2; 6, 1, 25. 33; 3, 17; iv. 5, 8, 14.</F> <F>4) xiv. 1, 1, 33, and notes 1, 2. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 430 {%et seq.,%} whose suggestion of the identity of this teacher and the founder of the Sāṃkhya system is not, however, ac- ceptable. See Garbe, {%Sāṃkhya Philo-%} {%sophie,%} 29, 30.</F>
{@Āsuri-vāsin@}¦ is a name of {@Prāśnī-putra@} in a Vaṃśa (list of teachers) of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (vi. 5, 2, in both recensions).

{@Ā-secana@}¦ designates a vessel to hold liquids, such as meat juice ({%yūṣan%})<sup>1</sup> or ghee.<sup>2</sup> Of its shape and make we know nothing. <F>1) Rv. i. 162, 13.</F> <F>2) Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 1, 9, 5. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 271.</F>

{@Ā-staraṇa@}¦ denotes the coverlet of the settle ({@Āsandī@}) of the {@Vrātya.@}<sup>1</sup> A tiger's skin serves as the coverlet of the king's seat in the royal consecration (Rājasūya).<sup>2</sup> In the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad<sup>3</sup> the word used is {@Upastaraṇa.@} <F>1) Av. xv. 3, 7.</F> <F>2) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, viii. 5.</F> <F>3) i. 5. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 155.</F>

{@Āstra-budhna@}¦ is the name of a man whom Indra is said in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> to have assisted. It is not clear whether {@Venya,@} who is mentioned in the same line, was his friend<sup>2</sup> or his enemy,<sup>3</sup> whom Indra saved or defeated for him. <F>1) x. 171, 3.</F> <F>2) So Grassmann and Griffith in their translations.</F> <F>3) So Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 167.</F>

{@Ā-sthātṛ.@}¦ — The warrior in the chariot is once thus desig- nated (as ‘standing on the car’) in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> Normally he is named {@Rathin@} or {@Ratheṣṭhā.@} <F>1) vi. 47, 26. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 296.</F>

{@Ā-srāva@}¦ (‘discharge’) denotes a disease, thrice referred to in the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> the precise nature of which is uncertain. The Scholiast<sup>2</sup> in one place interprets it as painful urination ({%mūtrātisāra%}), while Lanman<sup>3</sup> suggests diabetes. Bloomfield<sup>4</sup> takes it to be diarrhœa, and Zimmer<sup>5</sup> argues that as the remedy is called ‘wound healer’ ({%arus-srāṇa%}), the sense is ‘the flux from unhealed wounds.’ Whitney<sup>6</sup> renders it ‘flux,’ and questions Bloomfield's rendering. Ludwig<sup>7</sup> translates it vaguely by ‘sick- ness’ and ‘cold.’ <F>1) i. 2, 4; ii. 3, 2; vi. 44, 2.</F> <F>2) On Av. i. 2, 4. {%Cf.%} on ii. 3, 2.</F> <F>3) In Whitney's Translation of the Atharvaveda, 3.</F> <F>4) {%American Journal of Philology,%} 7, 467; {%Journal of the American Oriental Society,%} 13, cxiii; {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 233, 234.</F> <F>5) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 392.</F> <F>6) {%Op. cit.,%} 3, 41.</F> <F>7) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 507, 509.</F>

{@Āhanasyā@}¦ (‘unchaste’). — This word in the plural (‘lascivious verses’) denotes a section (xx. 136) of the Kuntāpa hymns of the Atharvaveda, which are of an obscene character.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vi. 36; Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, xxx. 7. {%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Atharvaveda,%} 99.</F>
{@Ā-hāva@}¦ denotes a pail or bucket, especially in conjunction with a well ({@Avata@}).<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Rv. i. 34, 8; vi. 7, 2; x. 101, 5; 112, 6; Nirukta, v. 26.</F>
{@Āhneya.@}¦ — Patronymic of {@Sauca@} (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, ii. 12).

{@Ikṣu,@}¦ the generic name for the sugar-cane, is first found in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and the later Saṃhitās.<sup>2</sup> Whether it grew wild, or was cultivated, does not appear from the references. <F>1) i. 34, 5.</F> <F>2) Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 7, 9; iv. 2, 9 ({%ikṣu-kāṇḍa%}). In Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxv. 1; Taittirīya Saṃhiṭā, vii. 3, 16, 1; Kāṭhaka Aśvamedha, in. 8, ‘eyelash’ is meant. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches%} {%Leben,%} 72; Roth, St. Petersburg Dic- tionary, {%s.v.%}</F>

{@Ikṣvāku.@}¦ — In the Rigveda this name occurs but once,<sup>1</sup> and in a doubtful context. It is clear, however, that it denotes a prince; later interpretations make {@Asamāti,@} whose name is read into the hymn, an Ikṣvāku prince.<sup>2</sup> In the Atharvaveda<sup>3</sup> also the name is found in only one passage, where it is uncertain whether a descendant of Ikṣvāku, or Ikṣvāku himself, is referred to; in either case he seems to be regarded as an ancient hero. In the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>4</sup> mention is made of {@Tryaruṇa@} {@Traidhātva@} Aikṣvāka, who is identical with the {@Tryaruṇa@} {@Traivṛṣṇa@} of the Bṛhaddevatā,<sup>5</sup> and with {@Tryaruṇa Trasa-@} {@dasyu@} in the Rigveda.<sup>6</sup> The connection of Trasadasyu with the Ikṣvākus is confirmed by the fact that {@Purukutsa@} was an Aikṣvāka, according to the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.<sup>7</sup> Thus the Ikṣvāku line was originally a line of princes of the Pūrus. Zimmer<sup>8</sup> places them on the upper Indus, but they may well have been somewhat further east.<sup>9</sup> Later Ikṣvāku is connected with Ayodhyā <F>1) x. 60, 4.</F> <F>2) {%Cf.%} Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 167; Sāṭyāyanaka in Max Müller, Rigveda, 4, c-cvii, 167; {%Journal of the American%} {%Oriental Society,%} 18, 42; Bṛhaddevatā, vii. 85 {%et seq.,%} with Macdonell's notes.</F> <F>3) xiv. 39, 9. {%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Hymns%} {%of the Atharvaveda,%} 680; Whitney Translation of the Atharvaveda, 961.</F> <F>4) xiii. 3, 12.</F> <F>5) v. 14 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>6) v. 27, 3. {%Cf.%} Sieg, {%Die Sagenstoffe%} {%des Ṛgveda,%} 68-75; Macdonell, {%Bṛhad-%} {%devatā,%} 2, 170; Oldenberg, {%Vedic Hymns,%} 366 {%et seq.;%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 133, 138; 4, 324.</F> <F>7) xiii. 5, 4, 5.</F> <F>8) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 104, 130.</F> <F>9) {%Cf.%} Pischel, {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 218; Geldner, {%ibid.,%} 3, 152.</F>

1. {@Iṭa.@}¦ — This word occurs twice in the Atharvaveda. in the first passage<sup>1</sup> it seems to denote a bulrush of the sort that dies in a year; in the second<sup>2</sup> it refers to the reed work of the house. <F>1) vi. 14, 3. {%Cf.%} iv. 19, 1; Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 464.</F> <F>2) ix. 3, 18. {%Cf.%} Pischel, {%Zeitschrift%} {%der Deutschen Morgenlāndischen Gesell-%} {%schaft,%} 35, 718.</F>

2. {@Iṭa@}¦ appears as a Ṛṣi and a protégé of Indra in one hymn of the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> Roth,<sup>2</sup> however, thinks that the word is really part of a verb ({%iṭ%}) meaning ‘to err, wander’ (cp. {%aṭ%}), and [Page1-076+ 49] that the name is a mere misunderstanding. It is already so regarded in the Anukramaṇī, but not apparently in the Bṛhaddevatā.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) x. 171, 1.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>3) viii. 73. {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 133.</F>

{@Iṭant Kāvya@}¦ is the name of a sage, contemporary with {@Keśin Dārbhya,@} in the Kauṣitaki Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> He is also mentioned as Iḍhant in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) vii. 4. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 293; 2, 308.</F> <F>2) xiv. 9, 16.</F>

{@Itihāsa,@}¦ as a kind of literature, is repeatedly mentioned along with {@Purāṇa@} in the later texts of the Vedic period. The earliest reference to both occurs in the late fifteenth book of the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> Itihāsa then appears in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>2</sup> the Jaiminīya,<sup>3</sup> Bṛhadāraṇyaka,<sup>4</sup> and Chāndogya Upaniṣads.<sup>5</sup> In the latter it is expressly declared with Purāṇa to make up the fifth Veda, while the Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra<sup>6</sup> makes the Itihāsa a Veda and the Purāṇa a Veda. The Itihāsa-veda and the Purāṇa-veda appear also in the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>7</sup> while the Śatapatha<sup>8</sup> identifies the Itihāsa as well as the Purāṇa with the Veda. In one passage {@Anvākhyāna@} and Itihāsa are distinguished<sup>9</sup> as different classes of works, but the exact point of distinction is obscure; probably the former was supplementary. The Taittirīya Āraṇyaka<sup>10</sup> mentions Itihāsas and Purāṇas in the plural. <div n="P"/>There is nothing to show in the older literature what dis- tinction there was, if any, between Itihāsa and Purāṇa; and the late literature,<sup>11</sup> which has been elaborately examined by Sieg,<sup>12</sup> yields no consistent result. Geldner<sup>13</sup> has conjectured that there existed a single work, the Itihāsa-purāṇa, a collection [Page1-077+ 51] of the old legends of all sorts, heroic, cosmogonic, genealogical; but though a work called Itihāsa, and another called Purāṇa, were probably known to Patañjali,<sup>14</sup> the inaccuracy of Geldner's view is proved by the fact that Yāska shows no sign of having known any such work. To him the Itihāsa may be a part of the Mantra literature itself,<sup>15</sup> Aitihāsikas being merely people who interpret the Rigveda by seeing in it legends where others see myths.<sup>16</sup> The fact, however, that the use of the compound form is rare, and that Yāska regularly has Itihāsa,<sup>17</sup> not Itihāsa-purāṇa, is against the theory of there ever having been one work. <div n="P"/>The relation of Itihāsa to {@Ākhyāna@} is also uncertain. Sieg<sup>18</sup> considers that the words Itihāsa and Purāṇa referred to the great body of mythology, legendary history, and cosmogonic legend available to the Vedic poets, and roughly classed as a fifth Veda, though not definitely and finally fixed. Thus, Anvākhyānas, {@Anuvyākhyānas,@} and {@Vyākhyānas@} could arise, and separate Ākhyānas could still exist outside the cycle, while an Ākhyāna could also be a part of the Itihāsa-purāṇa. He also suggests that the word Ākhyāna has special reference to the form of the narrative. Oldenberg,<sup>19</sup> following Windisch,<sup>20</sup> and followed by Geldner,<sup>21</sup> Sieg, and others, has found in the Ākhyāna form a mixture of prose and verse, alternating as the narrative was concerned with the mere accessory parts of the tale, or with the chief points, at which the poetic form was naturally produced to correspond with the stress of the emotion. This theory has been severely criticized by Hertel<sup>22</sup> and von Schroeder.<sup>23</sup> These scholars, in accordance with older suggestions of Max Müller<sup>24</sup> and Lévi,<sup>25</sup> see in the [Page1-078+ 34] so-called Ākhyāna hymns of the Rigveda, in which Oldenberg finds actual specimens of the supposed literary genus, though the prose has been lost, actual remains of ritual dramas. Elsewhere<sup>26</sup> it has been suggested that the hymns in question are merely literary dialogues. <F>1) xv. 6, 4 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>2) xiii. 4, 3, 12. 13, and as com- pounded in xi. 5, 6, 8; 7, 9.</F> <F>3) i. 53.</F> <F>4) ii. 4, 10; iv. 1, 2; v. 11.</F> <F>5) iii. 4, 1. 2; vii. 1, 2. 4; 2, 1; 7, 1.</F> <F>6) xvi. 2, 21. 27.</F> <F>7) i. 10.</F> <F>8) xiii. 4, 3, 12. 13.</F> <F>9) xi. 1, 6, 9. {%Cf.%} p. 24.</F> <F>10) ii. 9.</F> <F>11) See Sāyaṇa's Introduction to the Rigveda, p. 12 (ed. {@Id-, Idā-, Idu- Vatsara.@}¦ See {@Saṃvatsara.@}
{@Indra-gopa@}¦ (‘protected by Indra’), masc., is a designation of the cochineal insect in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (ii. 3, 6).

{@Indra-dyumna Bhāllaveya Vaiyāghra-padya@}¦ is mentioned as a teacher who with others was unable to agree as to the nature of Agni Vaiśvānara, and who was instructed by {@Aśvapati Kaikeya.@}<sup>1</sup> As Bhāllaveya he is cited several times in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> on ritual points. <F>1) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, x. 6, 1, 1 {%et seq.;%} Chāndogya Upaniṣad, v. 11, 1 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>2) i. 6, 1, 19; xiii. 5, 3, 4. {%Cf.%} ii. 1, 4. 6.</F>
{@Indra-bhū Kāśyapa@}¦ is mentioned as a pupil of {@Mitrabhū@} {@Kāśyapa@} in the Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 374.</F>

1. {@Indrota@}¦ is twice mentioned in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> in a Dānastuti (‘Praise of Liberality’) as a giver of gifts. In the second passage he has the epithet Ātithigva, which shows conclusively that he was a son of Atithigva, as Ludwig<sup>2</sup> holds, and not of Ṛkṣa, as Roth<sup>3</sup> states. <F>1) viii. 68, 10 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>2) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 163.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>

2. {@Indrota Daivāpa Śaunaka@}¦ is mentioned in the Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> as the priest who officiated at the horse [Page1-079+ 56] sacrifice of {@Janamejaya,@} although this honour is attributed in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> to {@Tura Kāvaṣeya.@} He also appears in the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> as a pupil of {@Śruta,@} and is mentioned in the Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>4</sup> He cannot be connected in any way with {@Devāpi,@} who occurs in the Rigveda.<sup>5</sup> <F>1) xiii. 5, 3, 5; 4, 1; Sāṅkhāyana Srauta Sūtra, xvi. 7, 7; 8, 27.</F> <F>2) viii. 21.</F> <F>3) iii. 40, 1.</F> <F>4) {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 384, 385.</F> <F>5) x. 98. {%Cf.%} Oldenberg, {%Zeitschrift%} {%der Deutschen Morgenlāndischen Gesell-%} {%schaft,%} 42, 240.</F>

1. {@Ibha@}¦ is a word of somewhat doubtful sense and inter- pretation. It is found only in the Saṃhitās,<sup>1</sup> and especially in the Rigveda.<sup>2</sup> According to Roth<sup>3</sup> and Ludwig<sup>4</sup> the sense is ‘retainer,’ and Zimmer<sup>5</sup> thinks that it includes not only dependants and servants, but also the royal family and the youthful cadets of the chief families. In the opinion of Pischel and Geldner<sup>6</sup> it denotes ‘elephant.’ This view is supported by the authority of the commentators Sāyaṇa<sup>7</sup> and Mahīdhara;<sup>8</sup> the Nirukta,<sup>9</sup> too, gives ‘elephant’ as one of the senses of the word. Megasthenes<sup>10</sup> and Nearchos<sup>11</sup> tell us that elephants were a royal prerogative, and the derivative word {@Ibhya@} may thus be naturally explained as denoting merely ‘rich’ (lit., ‘possessor of elephants’).<sup>12</sup> <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, i. 2, 14, 1; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xiii. 9.</F> <F>2) i. 84, 17; iv. 4, 1; ix. 57, 3, and perhaps vi. 20, 8.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>4) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 246, 247.</F> <F>5) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 167.</F> <F>6) {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, xv, xvi.</F> <F>7) On Taittirīya Saṃhitā, {%loc. cit.%}</F> <F>8) On Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, {%loc. cit.%}</F> <F>9) vi. 12. It gives also the sense ‘retainer,’ and in Aśoka's Edicts, No. 5, Bühler, {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgen-%} {%ländischen Gesellschaft,%} 37, 279, finds a Vaiśya denoted by its Pāli form.</F> <F>10) {%Apud%} Strabo, 704.</F> <F>11) {%Ibid.,%} 705.</F> <F>12) But it may equally well be ex- plained as ‘rich’ from the other sense of the primary word: ‘possessor of (many) retainers.’</F>

2. {@Ibha@}¦ in one passage of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> appears certainly to be intended as an abbreviation of the proper name {@Smadibha.@} <F>1) vi. 20, 8. {%Cf.%} Pischel and Geldner, {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, xvi; Roth, St. Peters- burg Dictionary, {%s.v.;%} Oldenberg, {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 380. Zimmer, {%Altin-%} {%disches Leben,%} 167, treats it as ‘retinue,’ as does Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 246, 247.</F>

{@Ibhya@}¦ occurs once in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> in the plural, when a king is said to devour his Ibhyas as the fire the forest; and twice in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad,<sup>2</sup> in one passage as the first member of a compound, and in the other as either a proper name or an adjective. Roth,<sup>3</sup> Ludwig,<sup>4</sup> and Zimmer<sup>5</sup> interpret the word as ‘retainers’ in the Rigveda, but in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad Roth thinks it means ‘rich.’ Pischel and Geldner<sup>6</sup> accept the sense in all passages. Böhtlingk in his trans- lation of the Chāndogya treats the word as simply a proper name, ‘Ibhya's village’ ({%ibhya-grāma%}) and ‘Ibhya.’ <F>1) i. 65, 4.</F> <F>2) i. 10, 1. 2.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>4) Translation of the Rigveda 3, 247.</F> <F>5) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 168.</F> <F>6) {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, xvi. {%Cf.%} Sāyaṇa on Rigveda, {%loc. cit., dhaninaḥ,%} and Śaṃkara on Chāndogya Upaniṣad, {%loc. cit., īśvaro hastyāroho vā;%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 476. {%Cf.%} also Little, {%Grammatical Index,%} 35.</F>

{@Iriṇa@}¦ (neut.) occurs not rarely in the later Saṃhitās<sup>1</sup> and Brāhmaṇas<sup>2</sup> in the sense of ‘a cleft in the ground,’ usually natural ({%sva-kṛta%}). The same meaning is also, as Pischel<sup>3</sup> shows, to be ascribed to it in three passages of the Rigveda,<sup>4</sup> in one<sup>5</sup> of which the hole is referred to as ‘made by water’ ({%apā kṛtam%}). In another passage of the Rigveda<sup>6</sup> the word refers to the place on which the dice are thrown. Hence Pischel<sup>7</sup> concludes that the dicing-board must have been so called because it contained holes into which the dice had to be thrown if possible. Lüders,<sup>8</sup> however, points out that this assumption is not necessary; the dice ({@Akṣa@}) were merely thrown on a space dug out, which could be called {@Iriṇa,@} as being a hole in the ground, though not a natural one. This view is supported by the commentary of Sāyaṇa,<sup>9</sup> as well as by Durga in his note on the Nirukta.<sup>10</sup> <F>1) Av. iv. 15, 12; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 5, 1, 3; iii. 4, 8, 5; v. 2, 4, 3; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, ix. 16.</F> <F>2) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, v. 2, 3, 2; vii. 2, 1, 8.</F> <F>3) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 222-225.</F> <F>4) i. 186, 9; viii. 4, 3; 87, 1. 4.</F> <F>5) viii. 4, 3.</F> <F>6) x. 34, 1. 9.</F> <F>7) {%Op. cit.,%} 2, 225.</F> <F>8) {%Das Würfelspiel im alben Indian,%} 14.</F> <F>9) On Rv., {%loc. cit. (ā-sphūra).%}</F> <F>10) ix. 8 ({%āsphuraka-sthāna%}).</F>
{@Iṣa Śyāvāśvi@}¦ is mentioned in a Vaṃśa (‘list of teachers’) of the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa (iv. 16, 1) as a pupil of Agastya.

{@Iṣīkā,@}¦ ‘a stalk of reed grass,’ occurs frequently from the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> onwards, often as an emblem of fragility. In the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka<sup>2</sup> it seems to denote the pin fixed in the bar of a pen to keep cattle in ({%argaleṣīke,%} ‘bolt and pin’). A basket ({%śūrpa%}) of Iṣīkā is referred to in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) Av. vii. 56, 4; xii. 2, 54; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iv. 3, 4, 16, etc.; Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 9; ii. 134; Chāndogya Upaniṣad, v. 24, 3; Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad, ii. 6, 17, etc.; Nirukta, ix. 8.</F> <F>2) ii. 16 ({%v. l. ˚ike%}).</F> <F>3) i. 1, 4, 19. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 71; Oertel, {%Journal of the American Oriental%} {%Society,%} 19, 122, n. 3.</F>

{@Iṣu@}¦ is the usual name for ‘arrow’ from the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> onwards. Other names are {@Śarya, Śārī,@} and {@Bāṇa.@} In the hymn of the Rigveda,<sup>2</sup> which gives a catalogue of armour, two kinds of arrows are distinctly referred to: the one is poisoned ({%ālāktā%}), and has a head of horn ({%ruru-śīrṣṇī%}); the other is copper-, bronze-, or iron-headed ({%ayo-mukham%}). Poisoned ({%digdhā%}) arrows are also referred to in the Atharvaveda.<sup>3</sup> The arrows were feathered.<sup>4</sup> The parts of an arrow are enumerated in the Atharvaveda<sup>5</sup> as the shaft ({%śalya%}), the feather-socket ({%parṇa-dhi%}), the point ({%śṛṅga%}), the neck of the point in which the shaft is fixed ({%kulmala%}), and the {@Apaskambha@} and {@Apāṣṭha,@} which are of more doubtful significance. In the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>6</sup> the parts of an arrow are given as the point ({%anīka%}), the {%śalya, tejana,%} and the feathers ({%parṇāni%}), where {%śalya%} and {%tejana%} must apparently mean the upper and lower parts of the shaft, since it is reasonable to suppose that the arrow is described as a whole consecutively. So in the Atharvaveda<sup>7</sup> the arrow of Kāma is described as having feathers, a shaft [Page1-082+ 56] ({%śalya%}), and a firm fastening ({%kulmala%}).<sup>8</sup> The arrow was shot from the ear, and so is described in the Rigveda<sup>9</sup> as ‘having the ear for its place of birth.’ <div n="P"/>As a measure of length, the Iṣu was five spans, say three feet.<sup>10</sup> A regular profession of arrow-making existed ({%iṣu-kṛt,%}<sup>11</sup> {%iṣu-kāra%}).<sup>12</sup> <F>1) ii. 24, 8; viii. 7, 4, etc.; Av. i. 13, 4, etc.; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xvi. 3, etc.; Nirukta, ix. 18.</F> <F>2) vi. 75, 15.</F> <F>3) iv. 6, 7; v. 18, 8. 15; 31, 4.</F> <F>4) Rv. x. 18, 14; vi. 75, 11; Av. v. 25, 1.</F> <F>5) iv. 6.</F> <F>6) i. 25.</F> <F>7) Av. iii. 25, 2.</F> <F>8) See also Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 8, 1. 2; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxv. 1.</F> <F>9) Rv. vi. 75, 3; ii. 24, 8 ({%karṇa-%} {%yoni%}).</F> <F>10) Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, vi. 5, 2, 10.</F> <F>11) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xvi. 46, {%Cf.%} Rv. i. 184, 3.</F> <F>12) {%Ibid.,%} xxx. 7; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 3, 1. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 300; Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 18, 29, 286; Hopkins, {%Journal of the American Oriental%} {%Society,%} 13, 275 {%et seq.;%} 25, 337.</F>

{@Iṣu Tri-kāṇḍā@}¦ is the name given in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> to some constellation, perhaps Orion's girdle. It is mentioned with {@Mṛga, Mṛgavyādha,@} and {@Rohiṇī.@} <F>1) iii. 33. {%Cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 2, 205, n.</F>

{@Iṣu-dhi@}¦ (‘arrow-holder’) is the name of the quiver which was carried by every bowman. The word is common from the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> onwards. No trace is to be found in Vedic literature of the later practice of carrying two quivers.<sup>2</sup> According to Pischel,<sup>3</sup> the curious expression {%iṣu-kṛt%} in the Rigveda<sup>4</sup> means quiver. <F>1) i. 33, 3; vi. 75, 5; x. 95, 3; Av. ii. 33, 2; iv. 10, 6, etc.; Nirukta, ix. 13.</F> <F>2) Hopkins, {%Journal of the American%} {%Oriental Society,%} 13, 274. Each quiver held from ten to twenty arrows.</F> <F>3) {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 17. But see Oldenberg, {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 182.</F> <F>4) i. 184, 3. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 300.</F>

{@Īṣā@}¦ denotes the ‘pole of a chariot.’ Normally the chariot had one pole ({%ekeṣaḥ%}),<sup>1</sup> but sometimes two poles are referred to.<sup>2</sup> The word is often<sup>3</sup> compounded with {@Yuga,@} ‘yoke,’ into which it was fastened (see {@Kha@}), and tied with ropes.<sup>4</sup> Exactly how it was attached to the chariot we do not know.<sup>5</sup> See also {@Ratha.@} <F>1) Rv. x. 135, 3; iii. 53, 17; viii. 5, 29; Av. viii. 8, 23.</F> <F>2) {%Cf.%} Av. ii. 8, 4; Satapatha Brāh- maṇa, i. 1, 2, 12 ({%īṣā-yugāni,%} but in iii. 9, 4, 3 dual); Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, vii. 9, 14, etc.</F> <F>3) Av., {%loc. cit.,%} etc.</F> <F>4) Rv. x. 60, 8. {%Cf.%} iii. 6, 6.</F> <F>5) {%Vāṇī%} in Rv. i. 119, 5 is taken by Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 249, to refer to the front part of the chariot, but it seems simply to be ‘voice.’</F>
{@Ukṣan.@}¦ See {@Go.@}

{@Ukṣaṇyāyana@}¦ is mentioned in a Dānastuti (‘Praise of Gifts’) in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> along with {@Harayāṇa@} and {@Suṣāman.@} Ludwig<sup>2</sup> thinks that all three are identical. Roth<sup>3</sup> finds a reference to Ukṣan himself in the verb {%ukṣaṇyati%}<sup>4</sup> and in the adjective {%ukṣaṇyu.%}<sup>5</sup> <F>1) viii. 25, 22.</F> <F>2) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 162, 270.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>4) Rv. viii. 26, 9.</F> <F>5) Rv. viii. 23, 16.</F>
{@Ukṣṇo-randhra Kāvya@}¦ is mentioned as a seer in the Pañca- viṃśa Brāhmaṇa (xiii. 9, 19).<sup>1</sup> <F>1) {%Cf.%} Max Müller, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 32, 397.</F>

{@Ukhā@}¦ is the regular word or a ‘cooking pot,’ usually mentioned in connexion with sacrifice, from the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> onwards. It was made of clay ({%mṛṇ-mayī%}).<sup>2</sup> See also {@Sthālī.@} <F>1) i. 162, 13. 15; iii. 53, 22; Av. xii. 3, 23; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 1, 6, 3, etc.</F> <F>2) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xi. 59; Tait- drīya Saṃhitā, iv. 1, 5, 4. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 253, 271.</F>

{@Ugra@}¦ in one passage of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad<sup>1</sup> seems to have a technical force, denoting ‘man in authority,’ or according to Max Müller's rendering, ‘policeman.’ Roth<sup>2</sup> compares a passage in the Rigveda,<sup>3</sup> where, however, the word has simply the general sense of ‘mighty man.’ Böhtlingk,<sup>4</sup> in his rendering of the Upaniṣad, treats the word as merely adjectival. <F>1) iv. 3, 37. 38.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>3) vii. 38, 6.</F> <F>4) P. 66 (with {%pratyenasaḥ%}).</F>

{@Ugra-deva@}¦ is mentioned with {@Turvaśa@} and {@Yadu@} in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> apparently as a powerful protector. The name occurs also in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> and the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka,<sup>3</sup> where he is styled {@Rājani@} and called a leper ({%kilāsa%}). <F>1) i. 36, 18 (Ugrādeva).</F> <F>2) xiv. 3, 17; xxiii. 16, 11.</F> <F>3) v. 4, 12. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rig- veda, 3, 147; Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.,%} who suggests that in the Rv. passage the word should be taken adjectivally.</F>

{@Ugra-sena@}¦ is mentioned in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (xiii. 5, 4, 3), and in a Gāthā there cited as being, with {@Bhīmasena@} and {@Śrutasena,@} a Pārikṣitīya and a brother of {@Janamejaya.@} The brothers were cleansed by the horse sacrifice from sin.

{@Uccaiḥ-śravas Kaupayeya@}¦ appears in the Jaiminīya Upani- ṣad Brāhmaṇa (iii. 29, 1-3) as a king of the {@Kurus@} and as maternal uncle of {@Keśin.@} His connexion with the Kurus is borne out by the fact that {@Upamaśravas@} was son of {@Kuru-@} {@śravaṇa,@} the names being strikingly similar.

{@Uc-chīrṣaka.@}¦ — This word, occurring in the description of the couch ({%paryaṅka%}) in the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad<sup>1</sup> (i. 5), apparently denotes a cushion for the head. See also {@Āsandī.@} <F>1) {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 403; Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 155.</F>

{@Uttara Kuru.@}¦ — The Uttara Kurus, who play a mythical part in the Epic and later literature, are still a historical people in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> where they are located beyond the Himālaya ({%pareṇa Himavantam%}). In another passage,<sup>2</sup> how- ever, the country of the Uttara Kurus is stated by {@Vāsiṣṭha@} {@Sātyahavya@} to be a land of the gods ({%deva-kṣetra%}), but {@Jānaṃ-@} {@tapi Atyarāti@} was anxious to conquer it, so that it is still not wholly mythical. It is reasonable to accept Zimmer's view that the northern Kurus were settled in Kaśmīr, especially as {@Kurukṣetra@} is the region where tribes advancing from Kaśmīr might naturally be found. {%Cf.%} {@Udīcyas.@} <F>1) viii. 14.</F> <F>2) viii. 23. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 165; Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 101, 102; Hopkins, {%Journal of the American Oriental%} {%Society,%} 13, 75, n.</F>

{@Uttara Madra@}¦ is the name of a tribe mentioned with the {@Uttara Kurus@} in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> as living beyond the Himālaya. Zimmer<sup>2</sup> points out that in the Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> {@Kāmboja Aupamanyava@} is a pupil of {@Madragāra,@} and thence [Page1-085+ 40] infers that Kambojas and Madras were not far distant in space. This conclusion is perfectly reasonable in view of the probable position of the Kāmbojas.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) viii. 14.</F> <F>2) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 102.</F> <F>3) {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 371.</F> <F>4) See map in Pargiter, {%Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society,%} 1908, p. 332. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 165.</F>

{@Ut-tāna Āṅgirasa@}¦ is mentioned in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> as a quasi-mythical person who received all good things, and yet was not harmed, as he was really a form of the earth, according to Sāyaṇa's<sup>2</sup> explanation. His name occurs also in the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā,<sup>3</sup> the Pancaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa,<sup>4</sup> and the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka.<sup>5</sup> <F>1) ii. 3, 2, 5. {%Cf.%} ii. 2, 5, 3.</F> <F>2) On Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 3, 2, 5.</F> <F>3) ix. 9.</F> <F>4) i. 8, 11.</F> <F>5) iii. 10, 2. 3.</F>
{@Udag-ayana.@}¦ See {@Sūrya.@}

{@Ud-aṅka Śaulbāyana.@}¦ — His views on Brahman, which he identified with the vital airs ({%prāṇa%}), are mentioned in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (iv. 1, 3). He would thus have been a contemporary of {@Janaka@} of Videha. He is also mentioned in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (vii. 5, 4, 2) as holding that the Daśarātra ceremony was the prosperity or best part of the Sattra (‘sacrificial session’).

{@Ud-añcana.@}¦ — This word, occurring only metaphorically in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> means a ‘pail’ or ‘bucket’ in the Brāhmaṇas.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) v. 44, 13 ({%dhiyām udañcanaḥ,%} ‘a very well of prayers’).</F> <F>2) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vii. 32; Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, iv. 3, 5, 21.</F>
{@Udamaya Ātreya@}¦ is mentioned in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (viii. 22) as Purohita, or domestic priest, of {@Aṅga Vairocana.@}

{@Udara Śāṇḍilya@}¦ is mentioned as a teacher in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad,<sup>1</sup> and as a pupil of {@Atidhanvan Śaunaka@} in the {@Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa.@}<sup>2</sup> <F>1) i. 9, 3.</F> <F>2) {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 384.</F>
{@Udala,@}¦ a Vaiśvāmitra, is mentioned in the Pañcaviṃsa Brāhmaṇa (xiv. 11, 33) as the seer of a Sāman.

{@Ud-āja@}¦ is the word used in the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> to denote the share of the booty of war taken by the king after a victory ({%saṃgrāmaṃ jitvā%}). This interpretation, which is that of Delbrück,<sup>2</sup> is clearly correct, as against the older version, ‘march out,’ given by von Schroeder<sup>3</sup> and accepted by Böhtlingk.<sup>4</sup> The Udāja thus corresponds precisely with the Homeric <lang n="greek">γέρας</lang> This sense also suits Nirāja, the variant of both the Kāṭhaka<sup>5</sup> and the Kapiṣṭhala<sup>6</sup> Saṃhitās. <F>1) i. 10, 16; iv. 3, 1.</F> <F>2) {%Festgruss an Böhtlingk,%} 25.</F> <F>3) Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, 1, xv.</F> <F>4) Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>5) xxviii. 3.</F> <F>6) xliv. 3.</F>

{@Udāna@}¦ is usually the fifth of the vital breaths ({@Prāṇa@}) when five are enumerated.<sup>1</sup> Sometimes<sup>2</sup> it appears as the second, coming after Prāṇa, and followed by Vyāna or Samāna. Again,<sup>3</sup> it is found simply opposed to Prāṇa, or it simply follows Prāṇa and Apāna.<sup>4</sup> In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>5</sup> it is treated as the breath that consumes food, a notion traceable in the later Upaniṣads,<sup>6</sup> while it is also regarded as the wind that rises up by the throat,<sup>7</sup> and leads the spirit forth at death.<sup>8</sup> <F>1) {%E.g.,%} Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 12, 9; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, v. 4; 10; Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, ix. 2, 2, 5; xi. 8, 3, 6 (in the order Prāṇa, Vyāna, Apāna, Udāna, Samāna); Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, i. 5, 3; iii. 4, 1 (Samāna is omitted); iii. 9, 26; Chāndogya Upani- ṣad, iii. 13, 5; v. 23, 1. 2; Aitareya Āraṇyaka, ii. 3, 3, etc.</F> <F>2) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, i. 20; vii. 27; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, ix. 4, 2, 10, etc. (with Vyāna); Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, i. 7, 2 (with Samāna).</F> <F>3) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, vi. 20; Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, iv. 1, 2, 2; ix. 2, 4, 5, etc.</F> <F>4) Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka, viii. 8; xi. 1.</F> <F>5) xi. 2, 4, 5.</F> <F>6) Maitrāyaṇī Upaniṣad, ii. 6.</F> <F>7) Amṛtabindu Upaniṣad, 34.</F> <F>8) Praśna Upaniṣad, iii. 7. {%Cf.%} Deus- sen, {%Philosophy of the Upaniṣads,%} 280.</F>

{@Ud-īcyas.@}¦ — The Brāhmaṇas of the northern parts are referred to in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> as engaging, with {@Svaidāyana@} {@Śaunaka@} as their spokesman, in a dispute with the Kurupañcāla Brāhmaṇa {@Uddālaka Āruṇi,@} and as vanquishing him. Their relation to the Kurupañcālas appears also from the fact that in [Page1-087+ 47] the same Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> reference is made to the speech of the north being similar to that of the Kurupañcālas. The speech of the Northerners was also celebrated for purity; hence Brāhmaṇas used to go to the north for purposes of study, according to the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa,<sup>3</sup> while in the Buddhist texts the school of Takṣaśilā (in Gandhāra) is famous as a resort of students.<sup>4</sup> Possibly, too, Sanskrit was specially developed in Kaśmīr, as suggested by Franke.<sup>5</sup> See also {@Kuru.@} <F>1) xi. 4, 1, 1. {%Cf.%} Gopatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 3, 6.</F> <F>2) iii. 2, 3, 15. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische%} {%Studien,%} 1, 191; Lévi, {%La Doctrine du%} {%Sacrifice,%} 35.</F> <F>3) vii. 6. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%op. cit.,%} 1, 153; 2, 309.</F> <F>4) Rhys Davids, {%Buddhist India,%} 8, 28, 203.</F> <F>5) {%Cf. Pāli und Sanskrit%} (1902), 88, 89.</F>

{@Udumbara.@}¦ — This name of the {%Ficus glomerata%} does not occur in the Rigveda, but is often found from the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> onwards. For ritual purposes of all kinds its wood was constantly used. The sacrificial post ({%yūpa%})<sup>2</sup> and the sacrificial ladle<sup>3</sup> were made of it, and amulets of Udumbara are mentioned.<sup>4</sup> Its wood, like that of other kinds of figtree —  {@Aśvattha, Nyagrodha,@} and {@Plakṣa@} — was considered suitable for employment at the sacrifice.<sup>5</sup> The sweetness of its fruit is referred to in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa,<sup>6</sup> where it is put on the same level as {@Madhu.@} It is there also spoken of as ripening three times a year.<sup>7</sup> A forest of Udumbara trees is mentioned in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>8</sup> <F>1) xix. 31, 1; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 1, 1, 6, etc.; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 2, 1, 33; vii. 4, 1, 38, etc.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 1, 1, 6.</F> <F>3) {%Ibid.,%} v. 4, 7, 3.</F> <F>4) Atharvaveda, xix. 31, 1.</F> <F>5) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 4, 8, 4.</F> <F>6) vii. 15.</F> <F>7) v. 24.</F> <F>8) xvi. 6, 4. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 59.</F>

{@Uddālaka Āruṇi.@}¦ — Uddālaka, son of Aruṇa, is one of the most prominent teachers of the Vedic period. He was a Brāh- maṇa of the Kurupañcālas, according to the Śatapatha Brāh- maṇa.<sup>1</sup> This statement is confirmed by the fact that he was teacher of {@Proti Kausurubindi@} of Kauśāmbī,<sup>2</sup> and that his son [Page1-088+ 60] {@Svetaketu@} is found disputing among the Pañcālas.<sup>3</sup> He was a pupil of Aruṇa, his father,<sup>4</sup> as well as of Patañcala Kāpya,<sup>5</sup> of Madra, while he was the teacher of the famous Yājñavalkya<sup>6</sup> Vājasaneya and of Kauṣītaki,<sup>7</sup> although the former is represented elsewhere<sup>8</sup> as having silenced him. He overcame in argument Prācīnayogya Śauceya,<sup>9</sup> and apparently also Bhadrasena Ājāta- śatrava,<sup>10</sup> though the text here seems to read the name as Āraṇi. He was a Gautama,<sup>11</sup> and is often alluded to as such. As an authority on questions of ritual and philosophy, he is repeatedly referred to by his patronymic name Āruṇi in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>12</sup> the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad,<sup>13</sup> the Chāndogya Upaniṣad,<sup>14</sup> and occasionally in the Aitareya,<sup>15</sup> the Kauṣītaki,<sup>16</sup> and the Ṣaḍviṃśa<sup>17</sup> Brāhmaṇas, as well as the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad.<sup>18</sup> In the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā he is not mentioned, according to Geldner,<sup>19</sup> but only his father Aruṇa; his name does not occur, according to Weber,<sup>20</sup> in the Pañca- viṃśa Brāhmaṇa, but in the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā<sup>21</sup> he is, as Āruṇi, known as a contemporary of {@Divodāsa Bhaimaseni,@} and in the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa<sup>22</sup> he is mentioned as serving {@Vāsiṣṭha Caikitāneya.@} In the Taittirīya tradition he seldom appears. There is an allusion in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>23</sup> to Kusurubinda Auddālaki, and according to the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa,<sup>24</sup> Naciketas was a son of Vājaśravasa Gautama, who [Page1-089+ 47] is made out to be Uddālaka by Sāyaṇa.<sup>25</sup> But the episode of Naciketas, being somewhat unreal, cannot be regarded as of historical value in proving relationship. Aruṇa is known to the Taittirīya Saṃhitā. A real son of Uddālaka was the famous {@Śvetaketu,@} who is expressly reported by Āpastamba<sup>26</sup> to have been in his time an Avara or later authority, a statement of importance for the date of Āruṇi. <F>1) xi. 4, 1, 2. {%Cf.%} Gopatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 3, 6.</F> <F>2) xii. 2, 2, 13.</F> <F>3) Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, vi. 1, 1; Chāndogya Upaniṣad, v. 3, 1.</F> <F>4) Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, vi. 4, 33 (in both recensions).</F> <F>5) {%Ibid.,%} iii. 7, 1.</F> <F>6) {%Ibid.,%} vi. 3, 15; 4, 33.</F> <F>7) Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka, xv.</F> <F>8) Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, iii. 7, 31.</F> <F>9) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xi. 5, 3, 1 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>10) v. 5, 5, 14. Eggeling, {%Sacred Books%} {%of the East,%} 41, 141, has Āraṇi. There is a chronological difficulty in taking Āruṇi as meant, since Ājātaśatrava must presumably have been a descen- dant of Ajātaśatru, a contemporary of Janaka (see Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad, iv. 1), who again was a patron of Yājñavalkya, a pupil of Āruṇi. But this difficulty is not fatal.</F> <F>11) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xi. 5, 3, 2; Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad, i. 1.</F> <F>12) i. 1, 2, 11; ii. 2, 1, 34; iii. 3, 4, 19; iv. 4, 8, 9; xi. 2, 6, 12.</F> <F>13) iii. 5, 1.</F> <F>14) iii. 11, 4; v. 11, 2; 17, 1; vi. 8, 1.</F> <F>15) viii. 7.</F> <F>16) xxvi. 4.</F> <F>17) i. 6.</F> <F>18) i. 1 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>19) {%Vedische Studien,%} 3, 146.</F> <F>20) {%Indian Literature,%} 69. But {%cf.%} xxiii. 1, 5.</F> <F>21) vii. 8. {%Cf.%} viii. 6.</F> <F>22) i. 42, 1.</F> <F>23) vii. 2, 2, 1 (a late passage).</F> <F>24) iii. 11, 8, 1 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>25) On Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, {%loc. cit.%} {%Cf.%} Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad, i. 11.</F> <F>26) See Bühler, {%Sacred Books of the%} {%East,%} 2, xxxviii; Keith, {%Aitareya Āraṇ-%} {%yaka,%} 39. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 170, n.; 2, 201, 202; Oldenberg, {%Buddha,%} 396, n.; Eggeling, {%Sacred Books of the%} {%East,%} 12, xl., xli.</F>
{@Uddālakāyana@}¦ is mentioned as a pupil of Jābālāyana in the second Vaṃśa (list of teachers) contained in the Kāṇva recen- sion of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (iv. 6, 2).

{@Udra@}¦ is the name of an animal occurring only in the list of sacrificial victims at the Aśvamedha given in the Saṃhitās of the Yajurveda.<sup>1</sup> According to Mahīdhara<sup>2</sup> it was a crab; but as the commentary on the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>3</sup> calls it a water- cat, there can be no doubt that it was an otter. <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 20, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 18; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 37.</F> <F>2) On Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, {%loc. cit.%}</F> <F>3) {%Loc. cit.%} <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 95, 96; Schrader, {%Prehistoric Antiquities,%} 247. {%Udrin%} occurs in the Baudhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, ii. 5.</F>

{@Uddhi@}¦<sup>1</sup> denotes some part of a chariot, probably the seat,<sup>2</sup> but, according to Roth,<sup>3</sup> the frame resting on the axle. <F>1) Av. viii. 8, 22; Śatapatha Brāh- maṇa, xii. 2, 2, 2; Aitareya Āraṇyaka, ii. 3, 8.</F> <F>2) So Whitney's Translation of the Atharvaveda, 506; Eggeling, {%Sacred%} {%Books of the East,%} 44, 149.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>
{@Upa-ketu@}¦ is the name of a man mentioned in the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā (xiii. 1).
{@Upa-kosala Kāmalāyana@}¦ is mentioned as a teacher and a pupil of {@Satyakāma Jābāla@} in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (iv. 10, 1; 14, 1).

{@Upa-kvasa@}¦ is the name in the Atharvaveda (vi. 50, 2) of a noxious insect injurious to seed. Sāyaṇa, however, reads the word as a plural adjective ({%a-pakvasaḥ = a-dagdāḥ%}), but the Paippalāda recension supports the form {%upakvasaḥ.%} <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 237; Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 486; Whitney's Translation of the Atharvaveda, 318.

{@Upa-gu Sauśravasa@}¦ is mentioned in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāh- maṇa (xiv. 6, 8) as Purohita of {@Kutsa Aurava,@} by whom he was murdered because of his paying homage to Indra. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 3, 268; Hopkins, {%Transactions of the Con-%} {%necticut Academy of Arts and Sciences,%} 15, 57.
