{@Upa-cit@}¦ occurs in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> as the name of a disease, which Roth<sup>2</sup> renders as ‘swelling,’ and which Bloomfield<sup>3</sup> identifies with {@Apacit.@} <F>1) xii. 97.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>3) {%Proceedings of the American Oriental%} {%Society,%} October, 1887, xviii.</F>

{@Upa-jihvikā, Upa-jīkā, Upa-dīkā@}¦ are all forms of one word denoting a species of ant.<sup>1</sup> To these ants is attributed in the Atharvaveda<sup>2</sup> the power of penetrating to water which possesses curative properties. They were accordingly used in all sorts of spells against poisoning. The belief in their healing qualities was no doubt due to the well-known properties of the earth of ant-heaps which contains their water. <F>1) {%Upajihvikā%} is the form in Rv. viii. 102, 21; {%upajīkā%} in Av. ii. 3, 4; vi. 100, 2; but {%upacīkā%} in both passages in the Paippalāda recension; {%upadīkā%} in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 1, 3, 4; Tait- tirīya Āraṇyaka, v. 1, 4; 10, 9; Sata- patha Brāhmaṇa, xiv. 1, 1, 8.</F> <F>2) vi. 100, 2. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%American Journal of%} {%Philology,%} 7, 482 {%et seq.; Hymns of the%} {%Atharvaveda,%} 511; Whitney's Transla- tion of the Atharvaveda, 41, 354; Bergaigne and Henry, {%Manuel Védique,%} 153.</F>
{@Upa-dhāna@}¦ denotes the ‘cushion’ of a seat ({@Āsandī@}) in the Atharvaveda (xiv. 2, 65). It corresponds to the {@Upabarhaṇa@} of other texts.

{@Upa-dhi@}¦ occurs once each in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and the Athar- vaveda,<sup>2</sup> in conjunction with {@Pradhi,@} denoting part of the wheel of a chariot. It is impossible to decide exactly what part is meant. Roth,<sup>3</sup> Zimmer<sup>4</sup> and Bloomfield,<sup>5</sup> agree in thinking that the word denotes the spokes collectively. Whitney,<sup>6</sup> considering this improbable, prefers to see in it the designation of a solid wheel, Pradhi being presumably the rim and Upadhi the rest. Other possibilities<sup>7</sup> are that the Upadhi is a rim beneath the felly, or the felly itself as compared with the tire (ordinarily {@Pavi@}). <F>1) ii. 39, 4.</F> <F>2) vi. 70, 3.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>4) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 248 (ignoring the Atharvaveda passage).</F> <F>5) {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 493.</F> <F>6) Translation of the Atharvaveda, 334.</F> <F>7) Bloomfield, {%loc. cit.%}</F>

{@Upa-niṣad@}¦ in the Brāhmaṇas<sup>1</sup> normally denotes the ‘secret sense’ of some word or text, sometimes the ‘secret rule’ of the mendicant. But in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad<sup>2</sup> it is already used in the plural as the designation of a class of writings, no doubt actually existing and similar to the Upaniṣads in the nature of their subject-matter and its treatment. Similarly the sections of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad end with the words {%ity upaniṣad.%} The Aitareya Āraṇyaka<sup>3</sup> commences its third part with the title ‘The Upaniṣad of the Saṃhitā,’ and the title occurs also in the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka.<sup>4</sup> The exact primary sense of the expression is doubtful. The natural derivation, adopted by Max Müller<sup>5</sup> and usual ever since, makes the word mean firstly a session of pupils, hence secret doctrine, and secondly the title of a work on secret doctrine. Oldenberg,<sup>6</sup> however, traces the use of the word to the earlier [Page1-092+ 42] sense of ‘worship’ ({%cf. upāsana%}). Deussen<sup>7</sup> considers the original sense to have been ‘secret word,’ next ‘secret text,’ and then ‘secret import,’ but this order of meaning is im- probable. Hopkins<sup>8</sup> suggests that Upaniṣad denotes a sub- sidiary treatise, but this sense does not account naturally for the common use as ‘secret meaning,’ which is far more frequent than any other. <F>1) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, x. 3, 5, 12; 4, 5, 1; 5, 1, 1; xii. 2, 2, 23, etc.; Chāndogya Upaniṣad, i. 1, 10; 13, 4; viii. 8, 4. 5; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, ii. 1, 20; iv. 2, 1; v. 5, 3; Aitareya Āraṇyaka, iii. 1, 6; 2, 5; Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad, ii. 1, etc.</F> <F>2) ii. 4, 10; iv. 1, 2; 5, 11.</F> <F>3) iii. 1, 1.</F> <F>4) vii. 2. {%Cf.%} Taittirīya Upaniṣad, i. 3, 1.</F> <F>5) {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 1, xxxiii {%et seq. Cf.%} St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.;%} Macdonell, {%Sanskrit Literature,%} 204.</F> <F>6) {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgen-%} {%ländischen Gesellschaft,%} 50, 457; 54, 70; {%Die Literatur des alten Indien,%} 72.</F> <F>7) {%Philosophy of the Upaniṣads,%} 16 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>8) {%Religions of India,%} 218.</F>

{@Upa-pati,@}¦ ‘the gallant,’ is mentioned with the Jāra, ‘lover,’ in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> as a victim in the human sacrifice ({%puruṣamedha%}). <F>1) xxx. 9; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 4, 1.</F>

{@Upa-barhaṇa@}¦ denotes a ‘pillow’ or ‘cushion,’ especially of a seat ({%āsandī%}), occurring in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> the Atharvaveda,<sup>2</sup> and the Brāhmaṇas.<sup>3</sup> The feminine Upabarhaṇī is found in the Rigveda with the same sense, but used metaphorically of the earth. <F>1) x. 85, 7.</F> <F>2) ix. 5, 28; xii. 2, 19. 20; xv. 3, 7.</F> <F>3) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, viii. 12; Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 8, 4, 10; Kauṣī- taki Upaniṣad, i. 5; Taittirīya Brāh- maṇa, i. 1, 6, 10; 6, 8, 9; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxviii. 4, etc.</F>

{@Upa-manthanī@}¦ is used in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad<sup>1</sup> to denote ‘churning sticks.’ In the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā<sup>2</sup> the ‘churner’ ({%upamanthitṛ%}) is included in the list of victims at the human sacrifice ({%puruṣamedha%}), and the verb {%upa-manth%} is often used of churning or mixing fluids.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) vi. 3, 13.</F> <F>2) xxx. 12; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 8, 1.</F> <F>3) Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 6, 8, 4. 5; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 6, 1, 6; Chān- dogya Upaniṣad, v. 2, 4.</F>

{@Upa-manyu@}¦ is, according to Ludwig,<sup>1</sup> the name of a person in the Rigveda,<sup>2</sup> but is more probably explained by Roth<sup>3</sup> as a mere epithet. <F>1) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 113.</F> <F>2) i. 102. 9.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>

{@Upama-śravas@}¦ is mentioned in a hymn of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as a son of {@Kuruśravaṇa,@} and grandson of {@Medhātithi.@} The exact force of the reference to him in however, uncertain. According to the Bṛhaddevatā,<sup>2</sup> followed by Ludwig,<sup>3</sup> and by Lanman,<sup>4</sup> the poet in the hymn consoles Upamaśravas for the death of his grandfather, Medhātithi. Geldner,<sup>5</sup> on the other hand, thinks that the poet, who was {@Kavaṣa Ailūṣa,@} was ill-treated by his patron's son, Upamaśravas, and cast into a ditch or well, where he uttered his complaint and appeal for mercy. But of this there is no adequate evidence, and the tradition of the Bṛhaddevatā seems sound. <F>1) x. 33, 6. 7.</F> <F>2) vii. 35. 36, with Macdonell's notes.</F> <F>3) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 165.</F> <F>4) {%Sanskrit reader,%} 386, 389.</F> <F>5) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 150, n.</F>

{@Upa-mit@}¦ occurs twice in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> and once in the Atharvaveda,<sup>2</sup> as the designation of some part of a house. The passages in the Rigveda leave little doubt that the word means an upright pillar. As it is, in the Atharvaveda, coupled with {@Parimit@} and {@Pratimit,@} the conclusion is natural that the latter word denotes the beams supporting the Upamit, presumably by leaning against it at an angle, while {@Parimit@} denotes the beams connecting the Upamits horizontally. These interpretations, however, can only be conjectural. See also {@Gṛha.@} <F>1) i. 59, 1; iv. 5, 1.</F> <F>2) ix. 3, 1. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 153; Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 596; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 525.</F>

{@Upara,@}¦ which, according to Pischel,<sup>1</sup> means ‘stone’ in general, is the technical name of the stone on which the Soma plant was laid in order to be pounded for the extraction of the juice by other stones ({%adri, grāvan%}). The word is rare, occur- ring only thrice in the Rigveda,<sup>2</sup> and once in the Atharvaveda.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 109. This is the sense of the form {%upala%} (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxv. 8, etc.).</F> <F>2) i. 79, 3; x. 94, 5; 175, 3.</F> <F>3) vi. 49, 3. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 154; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 317; Von Schroeder, {%Mysterium und Mimus,%} 414.</F>

{@Upala-prakṣiṇī@}¦ occurs once in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> where it desig- nates the occupation of a woman, as opposed to that of her son, who is a poet ({%kāru%}), and to that of his father, who is a physician ({%bhiṣaj%}). Yāska<sup>2</sup> renders the word by ‘maker of groats’ ({%saktu-kārikā%}), and Roth,<sup>3</sup> Grassmann,<sup>4</sup> Zimmer,<sup>5</sup> as well as others, connect it with the operation of grinding corn. Pischel,<sup>6</sup> however, who points out that corn was not ground between two stones, but beaten on a stone with a pestle ({%dṛṣad%}), considers that Upala-prakṣiṇī denotes a woman that assisted at the crushing of Soma ({%cf.%} {@Upara@}). Von Schroeder,<sup>7</sup> who more correctly points out that there is no objection to regarding {%upala%} as the mortar in which the corn was placed and then beaten with the pestle, renders the word literally as ‘one who fills the (lower) stone (with corn).’ <F>1) ix. 112, 3.</F> <F>2) Nirukta, vi. 5.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>4) {%Ibid., s.v.,%} ‘fitting the upper (to the lower) millstone.’</F> <F>5) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 269. {%Cf.%} Hille- brandt, {%Vedaschrestomathie, s.v.,%} who, taking {%pṛc%} in the sense of ‘fill,’ explains the compound as ‘filling the upper mill- stone,’ an interpretation which as it stands is unintelligible.</F> <F>6) {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 308-310.</F> <F>7) {%Mysterium und Mimus,%} 412 {%et seq.%} Von Schroeder does not accept the view that the mother of the singer is alluded to; but it seems impossible to draw any other conclusion from the language of the passage, and his own explanation of the word as refer- ring to a corn-mother is very im- probable; {%cf.%} Keith, {%Journal of the Royal%} {%Asiatic Society,%} 1909, 204.</F>

{@Upalā@}¦ in the Brāhmaṇas<sup>1</sup> may denote the upper and smaller ‘stone,’ which was used as a pestle with the {@Dṛṣad@} as the mortar, whereas {@Upara@} in the Saṃhitās denotes rather the mortar, and Dṛṣad the pestle. But see {@Dṛṣad.@} <F>1) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 1, 1, 22; ii. 1, 14, 17; ii. 2, 2, 1, etc. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Von Schroeder, {%Mysterium und%} {%Mimus,%} 413, n. 3.</F>

{@Upa-vāka@}¦ occurs in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> and the Brāh- maṇas<sup>2</sup> as a description of a species of grain, the {%Wrightia%} {%antidysenterica,%} known later as Indra-yava. The commentator Mahīdhara<sup>3</sup> simply glosses it with the more general term {@Yava.@} [Page1-095+ 50] According to the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, it formed the essential element of gruel ({%karambha%}), and Upavāka groats ({%saktavaḥ%}) are mentioned in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) xix. 22; 90; xxi. 30 (as ‘heal- ing’).</F> <F>2) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xii. 7, 1, 3; 2, 9, etc.</F> <F>3) On Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xix. 22.</F> <F>4) xii. 9, 1, 5. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 240, 270.</F>
{@Upa-veśi@}¦ is mentioned as a pupil of {@Kuśri@} in a Vaṃśa (list of teachers) in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (vi. 5, 3, in both recensions). See also {@Aupaveśi.@}

{@Upa-śrī, Upa-śraya,@}¦ are two readings of the same term. The former is found in one recension of the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad,<sup>1</sup> while the latter is probably the reading of the other recension of the Upaniṣad,<sup>2</sup> and certainly the reading in one passage of the Atharvaveda,<sup>3</sup> though the text has {%apaśrayaḥ,%} which is accepted as possible by Roth.<sup>4</sup> In both cases the term clearly means something connected with a couch ({@Āsandī@} in the Atharvaveda, {@Paryaṅka@} in the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad). Aufrecht,<sup>5</sup> Roth,<sup>6</sup> and Max Müller<sup>7</sup> render it as ‘coverlet’ or ‘cushion,’ but Whitney<sup>8</sup> seems evidently right in holding that it must mean a ‘support’ or something similar. <F>1) i. 5.</F> <F>2) See Keith, {%Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka,%} 20, n. 3.</F> <F>3) xv. 3, 8. {%Cf.%} Whitney's note in his Translation.</F> <F>4) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.,%} and still followed by Böhtlingk, Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>5) {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 131.</F> <F>6) {%S.v. apaśraya.%}</F> <F>7) {%Sacred Books af the East,%} 1, 278.</F> <F>8) Translation of the Atharvaveda, 777. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 402; Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 155.</F>

{@Upa-staraṇa@}¦ denotes in the description of the couch ({@Par-@} {@yaṅka@}) in the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad<sup>1</sup> a ‘coverlet,’ and has this sense, used metaphorically, in the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> also. In the Atharvaveda<sup>3</sup> it seems to have the same meaning. Whitney,<sup>4</sup> however, renders it ‘couch,’ though he translates<sup>5</sup> the parallel word {@Āstaraṇa@} in another passage<sup>6</sup> by ‘cushion.’ <F>1) i. 5.</F> <F>2) ix. 69, 5.</F> <F>3) v. 19, 12.</F> <F>4) Translation of the Atharvaveda, 254.</F> <F>5) {%Ibid.,%} 776.</F> <F>6) xv. 3, 7. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 403; Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 155.</F>

{@Upa-sti@}¦ denotes both in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and the Atharvaveda<sup>2</sup> a ‘dependent,’ just as later in the Epic<sup>3</sup> the subordination of the Vaiśya to the two superior castes is expressed by the verb {%upa-sthā,%} ‘stand under,’ ‘support.’ The word also appears, with the same sense, in the form of Sti, but only in the Rigveda.<sup>4</sup> The exact nature of the dependence connoted by the term is quite uncertain. Zimmer<sup>5</sup> conjectures that the ‘dependents’ were the members of defeated Aryan tribes who became clients of the king, as among the Greeks, Romans, and Germans, the term possibly including persons who had lost their freedom through dicing.<sup>6</sup> The evidence of the Athar- vaveda<sup>7</sup> shows that among the Upastis were included the chariot-makers ({%ratha-kāra%}), the smiths ({%takṣan%}), and the charioteers ({%sūta%}), and troop-leaders ({%grāma-ṇī%}), while the Rigveda passages negative the possibility of the ‘subjects’ ({%sti%}) being the whole people. It is therefore fair to assume that they were the clients proper of the king, not servile, but attached in a special relation to him as opposed to the ordinary population. They may well have included among them not only the classes suggested by Zimmer, but also higher elements, such as refugees from other clans, as well as ambitious men who sought advancement in the royal service. Indeed, the Sūta and the Grāmaṇī were, as such, officers of the king's house- hold — kingmakers, not themselves kings, as they are described in the Atharvaveda.<sup>8</sup> The use of the word in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā,<sup>9</sup> the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa,<sup>10</sup> and the Kāṭhaka,<sup>11</sup> is purely metaphorical, as well as in the one passage of the Rigveda in which it occurs. In the Paippalāda recension of the Atharvaveda,<sup>12</sup> Vaiśya, Śūdra, and Ārya are referred to as Upastis, perhaps in the general sense of ‘subject.’ <F>1) x. 97, 23 (= Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xii. 101; Av. vi. 15, 1).</F> <F>2) iii. 5, 6.</F> <F>3) Hopkins, {%Journal of the American%} {%Oriental Society,%} 13, 92.</F> <F>4) vii. 19, 11; x. 148, 4; {%sti-pa,%} vii. 66, 3; x. 69, 4.</F> <F>5) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 184, 185.</F> <F>6) Rv. x. 34.</F> <F>7) Av. iii. 5, 6. 7.</F> <F>8) iii. 5, 7.</F> <F>9) vii. 2, 5, 4. {%Cf.%} vi. 5, 8, 2.</F> <F>10) iii. 3, 5, 4.</F> <F>11) xxxi. 9.</F> <F>12) iii. 5, 7. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rig- veda, 3, 246; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 92; Weber, {%Indische%} {%Studien,%} 17, 196 {%et seq.%}</F>

{@Upa-stuta@}¦ is mentioned several times in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> always as a sage of old, and usually in connexion with Kaṇva, who was aided or favoured by Agni, the Aśvins, and other gods. The Upastutas, sons of Vṛṣṭihavya,<sup>2</sup> are mentioned as singers<sup>3</sup> <F>1) i. 36, 10. 17; 112, 15; viii. 5, 25; x. 115, 8.</F> <F>2) x. 115, 9.</F> <F>3) viii. 103, 8; x. 115, 9. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rig- veda, 3, 108; Max Müller, {%Sacred Books%} {%of the East,%} 32, 152, 153.</F>
{@Upa-hvara@}¦ denotes, in one passage of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> according to Geldner,<sup>2</sup> the body of a chariot ({%upa-stha%}). <F>1) i. 87, 2.</F> <F>2) {%Vedische Studien,%} 3, 40.</F>

{@Upānasa@}¦ is in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> opposed to {@Akṣa,@} and must mean something like ‘the body of the wagon,’ though Sāyaṇa suggests that it signifies either a ‘granary’ or a ‘wagon full of grain.’ In the Rigveda,<sup>2</sup> where the word occurs only once, its sense is doubtful. Pischel<sup>3</sup> explains the form which occurs there not as an adjective, but as an infinitive. <F>1) ii. 14, 2.</F> <F>2) x. 105, 4.</F> <F>3) {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 197. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Athar-%} {%vaveda,%} 301; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 56.</F>

{@Upā-nah@}¦ is the regular word for a ‘sandal’ or ‘shoe’ from the later Saṃhitās<sup>1</sup> onwards. Boarskin is mentioned in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> as a material of which shoes were made. The combination ‘staff and sandals’ ({%daṇḍopānaha%}) occurs as early as the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 4, 4, 4; 6, 6, 1, etc.</F> <F>2) v. 4, 3, 19.</F> <F>3) iii. 3.</F>
{@Upāvi Jāna-śruteya@}¦ is mentioned in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (i. 25, 15) as an authority on the Upasads (a kind of Soma ceremony).
{@Upoditi Gaupāleya@}¦ is mentioned in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāh- maṇa (xii. 13, 11) as a seer of Sāmans.

{@Ubhayā-dant,@}¦ ‘having incisors in both jaws,’ is an expression employed to distinguish, among domestic animals, the horse, [Page1-098+ 47] the ass, etc., from the goat, the sheep, and cattle. The distinction occurs in a late hymn of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> and is several times alluded to in the later Saṃhitās<sup>2</sup> and the Brāhmaṇas.<sup>3</sup> In one passage of the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>4</sup> man is classed with the horse as {%ubhayā-dant.%} The opposite is {%anyato-dant,%} ‘having incisors in one jaw only,’ a term regularly applied to cattle,<sup>5</sup> the eight incisors of which are, in fact, limited to the lower jaw. The ass is styled {%ubhayā-dant%} in the Atharvaveda.<sup>6</sup> In one passage of the Atharvaveda,<sup>7</sup> however, the epithet is applied to a ram; but the sense here is that a marvel occurs, just as in the Rigveda<sup>8</sup> a ram destroys a lioness. Bloomfield<sup>9</sup> suggests in the Atharvaveda passage another reading which would mean ‘horse.’ A parallel division of animals is that of the Taittirīya<sup>10</sup> and Vājasaneyi Saṃhitās<sup>11</sup> into ‘whole-hoofed’ ({%eka-śapha%}) and ‘small’ ({%kṣudra%}). <div n="P"/>Zimmer<sup>12</sup> seeks to show from the Greek <lang n="greek">ἀμφώδοντα</lang><sup>13</sup> and the Latin {%ambidens%}<sup>14</sup> that the Indo-European was familiar with the division of the five sacrificial animals into the two classes of man and horse on the one hand, and cattle, sheep, and goats on the other. But this supposition is not necessary. <F>1) x. 90, 10.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 2, 6, 3; v. 1, 2, 6; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, i. 8, 1.</F> <F>3) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 6, 3, 30 ({%ubhayato-dant%}).</F> <F>4) ii. 2, 6, 3.</F> <F>5) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 1, 1, 5; v. 1, 2, 6; 5, 1, 3.</F> <F>6) v. 31, 3.</F> <F>7) v. 19, 2.</F> <F>8) viii. 18, 17.</F> <F>9) {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 434.</F> <F>10) iv. 3, 10, 2.</F> <F>11) xiv. 30.</F> <F>12) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 74-76.</F> <F>13) Aristotle, {%Hist. An.,%} ii. 1, 8.</F> <F>14) Festus {%apud%} Paulum Diaconum <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 10, 58.</F>

{@Urā@}¦ as a name for ‘sheep’ is confined to the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> It is curious that in one of its two occurrences the wolf should be referred to as terrifying sheep, and that the epithet of the wolf, {%urā-mathi,%} ‘killing sheep,’ should occur once in the Rigveda,<sup>2</sup> both references being in one book of the Saṃhitā, a fact which suggests a dialectical origin of the word {%urā.%} See also {@Avi.@} <F>1) viii. 34, 3.</F> <F>2) viii. 66, 8. {%Cf.%} Nirukta, v. 21.</F>

{@Uru-kakṣa@}¦ occurs in only one passage of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> where the sense of the word is much disputed. The reading of the text is {%uruḥ kakṣo na gāṅgyaḥ,%} which may refer to a man, Urukakṣa, ‘dwelling on the Ganges,’<sup>2</sup> or to a man, son of Gaṅgā, or to a wood so called,<sup>3</sup> or may simply denote the ‘broad thicket on the Ganges.’<sup>4</sup> <F>1) vi. 45, 31.</F> <F>2) Grassmann; St. Petersburg Dic- tionary. {%Cf.%} Macdonell, {%Vedic Grammar,%} 291.</F> <F>3) Ludwig's translation ({%der wald Uru-%} {%kakṣa,%} or {%das weite dickicht%}).</F> <F>4) Weber, {%Episches im vedischen Ritual,%} 28, n. 5; Oldenberg, {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 396.</F>
{@Uru-kṣaya.@}¦ — A family of Urukṣayas, singers and worshippers of Agni, is referred to in one hymn of the Rigveda (x. 118, 8. 9). <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 167.
{@Uruñjirā@}¦ is given in the Nirukta (ix. 26) as one of the names of the river {@Vipāś@} (now Beäs).

{@Urvarā@}¦ is with {@Kṣetra@} the regular expression, from the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> onwards, denoting a piece of ‘ploughland’ (<lang n="greek">ἄρουρα</lang>). Fertile ({%apnasvatī%}) fields<sup>2</sup> are spoken of as well as waste fields ({%ārtanā%}).<sup>3</sup> Intensive cultivation by means of irrigation is clearly referred to both in the Rigveda<sup>4</sup> and in the Atharva- veda,<sup>5</sup> while allusion is also made to the use of manure.<sup>6</sup> The fields ({%kṣetra%}) were carefully measured according to the Rigveda.<sup>7</sup> This fact points clearly to individual ownership in land for the plough, a conclusion supported by the reference of Apālā, in a hymn of the Rigveda,<sup>8</sup> to her father's field ({%urvarā%}), which is put on the same level as his head of hair as a personal possession. Consistent with this are the epithets ‘winning fields’ ({%urvarā-sā, urvarā-jit, kṣetra-sā%}),<sup>9</sup> while ‘lord of fields’ used of a god<sup>10</sup> is presumably a transfer of a human epithet ({%urvarā-pati%}). Moreover, fields are spoken of in the same [Page1-100+ 66] connexion as children,<sup>11</sup> and the conquest of fields ({%kṣetrāṇi%} {%saṃ-ji%}) is often referred to in the Saṃhitās.<sup>12</sup> Very probably, as suggested by Pischel,<sup>13</sup> the ploughland was bounded by grass land (perhaps denoted by {@Khila, Khilya@}) which in all likelihood would be joint property on the analogy of property elsewhere. There is no trace in Vedic literature of communal property in the sense of ownership by a community of any sort,<sup>14</sup> nor is there mention of communal cultivation. Individual property in land seems also presumed later on. In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad<sup>15</sup> the things given as examples of wealth include fields and houses ({%āyatanāni%}). The Greek evidence<sup>16</sup> also points to individual ownership. The precise nature of the ownership is of course not determined by the expression ‘individual ownership.’ The legal relationship of the head of a family and its members is nowhere explained, and can only be conjectured (see {@Pitṛ@}). Very often a family may have lived together with undivided shares in the land. The rules about the inheritance of landed property do not occur before the Sūtras.<sup>17</sup> In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>18</sup> the giving of land as a fee to priests is mentioned, but with reproof: land was no doubt even then a very special kind of property, not lightly to be given away or parted with.<sup>19</sup> [Page1-101+ 39] <div n="P"/>On the relation of the owners of land to the king and others see {@Grāma;@} on its cultivation see {@Kṛṣi.@} <F>1) i. 127, 6; iv. 41, 6; v. 33, 4; vi. 25, 4; x. 30, 3; 142, 3, etc.; Av. x. 6, 33; 10, 8; xiv. 2, 14, etc.</F> <F>2) Rv. i. 127, 6.</F> <F>3) {%Ibid.%}</F> <F>4) vii. 49, 2.</F> <F>5) i. 6, 4; xix. 2, 2.</F> <F>6) Av. iii. 14, 3, 4; xix. 31, 3.</F> <F>7) i. 110, 5.</F> <F>8) viii. 91, 5.</F> <F>9) Rv. iv. 38, 1, and vi. 20, 1; ii. 21, 1; iv. 38, 1.</F> <F>10) viii. 21, 3. {%Cf.%} {@Kṣetra.@}</F> <F>11) Rv. iv. 41, 6, etc.</F> <F>12) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 2, 8, 5; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, v. 2; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iv. 12, 3.</F> <F>13) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 204-207.</F> <F>14) {%Cf.%} Baden Powell, {%Indian Village%} {%Community%} (1899); Zimmer, {%Altin-%} {%disches Leben,%} 236; Mrs. Rhys Davids, {%Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society,%} 1901, 860.</F> <F>15) vii. 24, 2.</F> <F>16) {%Cf.%} Diodorus, ii. 40; Arrian, {%Indica,%} 11; Strabo, p. 703; Hopkins, {%Journal%} {%of the American Oriental Society,%} 13, 87 {%et seq. Cf. ibid.,%} 20, 22, 23.</F> <F>17) {%Cf.%} Gautama Dharma Sūtra, xviii. 5 {%et seq.;%} Baudhāyana Dharma Sūtra, ii. 2, 3; Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra, ii. 6, 14. Of course, the rules probably go back to the earlier period, but how far it is impossible to say. With the settlement of the country, however, inheritance of land and its partition must have become inevitable.</F> <F>18) xiii. 6, 2, 18; 7, 1, 13. 15.</F> <F>19) It is significant that in the famous episode (Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 1, 9, 4) of Manu's division of his property, from which Nābhānediṣṭha was ex- cluded, this exclusion is made good by the son's obtaining cattle ({%paśavaḥ%}). It is clear that cattle, not land, was the real foundation of wealth, just as in Ireland, Italy ({%cf. pecunia%}), Greece, etc. Cattle could be, and were, used indi- vidually, but land was not open to a man's free disposal; no doubt, at any rate, the consent of the family or the community might be required, but we are reduced to reliance on analogy in view of the silence of the texts. {%Cf.%} Schrader, {%Prehistoric Antiquities,%} 289; Jolly, {%Recht und Sitte,%} 94-96; Rhys Davids, {%Buddhist India,%} 48 {%et seq.%}</F>

{@Urvārū,@}¦ f., {@Urvāruka,@} n., ‘cucumber.’ The former<sup>1</sup> of these words denotes the plant, the latter<sup>2</sup> the fruit, but both are very rare. The passages all seem to refer to the fact that the stem of the plant becomes loosened when the fruit is ripe.<sup>3</sup> The fruit is also called Urvāru in a Brāhmaṇa.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) Av. vi. 14, 2.</F> <F>2) Rv. vii. 59, 12 = Av. xiv. 1, 17 = Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, i. 10, 4 = Taittirīya Saṃhitā, i. 8, 6, 2 = Vājasaneyi Saṃ- hitā, iii. 60.</F> <F>3) Sāyaṇa on Av. vi. 14, 2.</F> <F>4) Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, ix. 2. 19. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 242.</F>

{@Ula@}¦ is the name of some unknown wild animal, perhaps, as Whitney<sup>1</sup> suggests, the ‘jackal.’ It is mentioned in the Atharvaveda<sup>2</sup> and later Saṃhitās,<sup>3</sup> but not definitely identified by the commentators. <F>1) Translation of the Atharvaveda, 669.</F> <F>2) xii. 1, 49.</F> <F>3) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 12, 1 (as {%ūla%}); Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 13, 12; 14, 2; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 31. {%Cf.%} {%ulala%} in Baudhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, ii. 5. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 82.</F>
{@Ula Vārṣṇi-vṛddha@}¦ is mentioned as a teacher in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa (vii. 4).

{@Ulapa@}¦<sup>1</sup> is the name of a species of grass referred to in the Rigveda and the later Saṃhitās.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) x. 142, 3.</F> <F>2) Av. vii. 66, 1. Adjectives derived from the word are {%ulapya%} (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xvi. 45, etc.) and {%upolapa%} (Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, i. 7, 2).</F>
{@Ulukya Jāna-śruteya@}¦ is mentioned as a teacher in the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa (i. 6, 3).

{@Ulūka@}¦ is the ordinary word for ‘owl’ from the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> onwards. The bird was noted for its cry,<sup>2</sup> and was deemed the harbinger of ill-fortune ({%nairṛta%}).<sup>3</sup> Owls were offered at the horse sacrifice to the forest trees,<sup>4</sup> no doubt because they roosted there. <F>1) x. 165, 4.</F> <F>2) Rv. {%loc. cit.%}</F> <F>3) Av. vi. 19, 2: Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 18, 1; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 38.</F> <F>4) Vājasaneyi Samhitā, xxiv. 23; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14. 4.</F>

{@Ulūkhala@}¦ is the regular expression for ‘mortar’ from the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> onwards, occurring frequently also in the compound<sup>2</sup> Ulūkala-musala, ‘mortar and pestle.’ The exact construction of the vessel is quite unknown till we reach the Sūtra period. <F>1) i. 28, 6; Av. x. 9, 26; xi. 3, 3; xii. 3, 13: Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 2, 8, 7; vii. 2, 1, 3; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 1, 4, 6, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. ix. 6, 15; Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 1, 1, 22</F>

{@Ulkā@}¦ regularly denotes a meteor from the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> onwards. In the Brāhmaṇas<sup>2</sup> it also signifies a ‘firebrand.’ The much rarer form Ulkuṣī<sup>3</sup> has both senses. <F>1) iv. 4, 2; x. 68, 4; Av. xix. 9, 8, Ṣaḍviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, vi. 8, etc.</F> <F>2) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, v. 5, 4, 19.</F> <F>3) As ‘meteor,’ Av. v. 17, 4; Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, xi. 2, 7, 21; as ‘fire- brand,’ {%ibid.,%} iii. 9, 2, 9.</F>

{@Ulmuka@}¦ is the common word in the Brāhmaṇas<sup>1</sup> for ‘fire- brand,’ from which a coal ({%aṅgāra%})<sup>2</sup> could be taken. <F>1) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 11; Sata- patha Brāhmaṇa, i. 8, 2, 1; ii. 1, 4, 28, etc.; Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 76 ({%Journal of the American Oriental Society,%} 15, 239)</F> <F>2) Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, xii. 4, 3, 3; Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 61, 1 ({%Journal%} {%of the American Oriental Society,%} 23, 342).</F>

{@Ulmukavakṣayaṇa@}¦ is an expression that occurs several times in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> signifying a ‘means of extinguishing ({%ava-kṣayaṇa%}) a firebrand,’ or possibly more pre- cisely ‘tongs.’ Compare {@Aṅgārāvakṣayaṇa.@} <F>1) iv. 6. 8, 7; v. 2, 4, 15; xi. 6, 3, 3; Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 76. {%Cf.%} Böhtlingk, Dictionary, s.v.</F>

{@Uśanas Kāvya@}¦ is an ancient seer, already a half-mythical figure in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> where he is often mentioned, especially as associated with Kutsa and Indra. Later on<sup>2</sup> he becomes the Purohita of the Asuras in their contests with the gods. A variant of his name is Kavi Uśanas.<sup>3</sup> He appears in the Brāhmaṇas as a teacher also.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) i. 51, 10; 83. 5; 121, 12; iv. 16, 2; vi. 20, 11; viii. 23, 17; ix. 87, 3; 97, 7; x. 40, 7; probably also i. 130, 9; v. 31, 8; 34. 2; viii. 7, 26; x. 22, 6. Also in Av. iv. 29, 6.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 5, 8, 5: Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, vii. 5, 20; Śāṅkhāyana Srauta Sūtra, xiv. 27, 1.</F> <F>3) Rv. iv. 26, 1.</F> <F>4) Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xiv. 12, 5; Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa. ii. 7. 2, 6. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.;%} Geldner, {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 167 {%et%} {%seq.;%} Bergaingne, {%Religiou Vidique,%} 2, 339. {%et%} {%seq.;%} Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} p. 147.</F>
{@Uśanā@}¦ occurs in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (iii. 4, 3, 13; iv. 2, 5, 15) as the name of a plant from which Soma was prepared.

{@Uśīnara@}¦ — In the Aitareya Brāhmaṇā<sup>1</sup> the Kuru-Pañcālas are mentioned as dwelling together in the ‘Middle Country’ with the Vaśas and the Uśīnaras. In the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad<sup>2</sup> also the Uśīnaras are associated with the Kuru-Pañcālas and Vaśas, but in the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> the Uśīnaras and Vaśas are re- garded as northerners. In the Rigveda<sup>4</sup> the people is alluded to in one passage by reference to their queen, Uśīnarāṇī. Zimmer<sup>5</sup> thinks that the Uśīnaras earlier lived farther to the north-west, but for this there is no clear evidence. His theory is based merely on the fact that the Anukramaṇī (Index) of the Rigveda ascribes one hymn<sup>6</sup> to Śibi Auśīnara, and that the Śibis were known to Alexander's followers as <lang n="greek">Σίβοι</lang>,<sup>7</sup> living between the Indus and the Akesines (Chenab). But this is in no way conclusive, as the Śibis, at any rate in Epic times,<sup>8</sup> occupied the land to the north of Kurukṣetra, and there is no reason whatever to show that in the Vedic period the Uśīnaras were farther west than the ‘Middle Country.’ <F>1) viii. 14.</F> <F>2) iv. 1. See Keith {%Śāṅkhāyana%} {%Āranyaka,%} 36.</F> <F>3) ii 9.</F> <F>4) x. 59, 10.</F> <F>5) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 130.</F> <F>6) Rv. x. 179.</F> <F>7) Diodorus, xvii. 19.</F> <F>8) See Pargiter's map. {%Journal of the%} {%Royal Asiatic Society,%} 1908. p. 322. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 213, 419; Hultzsch {%Indian Antiquary,%} 34, 179.</F>
{@Uṣa,@}¦ ‘salt ground,’ occurs as a variant of Ūṣa in the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā (i. 6, 3).
{@Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa@}¦ is mentioned as a teacher in the Bṛhad- āraṇyaka (iii. 5, 1) and Chāndogya (i. 10, 1; 11, 1) Upaniṣads, the name in the latter work appearing as Uṣasti.

{@Uṣṭi, Uṣṭra.@}¦ — Both of these words, of which the former is quite rare,<sup>1</sup> must have the same sense. Roth<sup>2</sup> and Aufrecht<sup>3</sup> hold that in the Rigveda<sup>4</sup> and the Brāhmaṇas<sup>5</sup> the sense is ‘humped bull’ or ‘buffalo,’ but the former thinks that in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā<sup>6</sup> the sense is doubtful, and ‘camel’ may be meant. Hopkins<sup>7</sup> is decidedly of opinion that the sense in every case is ‘camel.’ The animal was used as a beast of burden yoked in fours.<sup>8</sup> <F>1) Perhaps in Rv. x. 106, 2; Tait- tirīya Saṃhitā, v. 6, 21, 1; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xv. 2.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>3) Cited in Muir, {%Sanskrit Texts,%} 5, 468. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 224.</F> <F>4) i. 138, 2; viii. 5, 37; 6, 48; 46, 22. 31; Av. xx. 127, 2; 132, 13; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xiii. 50.</F> <F>5) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, 1, 2, 3, 9, etc.; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 8.</F> <F>6) xxiv. 28. 39.</F> <F>7) {%Journal of the American Oriental%} {%Society,%} 17, 83.</F> <F>8) Av. xx. 127, 2; Rv. viii. 6, 48.</F>

{@Uṣṇīṣa@}¦ denotes the ‘turban’ worn by Vedic Indians, men and women<sup>1</sup> alike. The Vrātya's turban is expressly referred to in the Atharvaveda<sup>2</sup> and the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>3</sup> A turban was also worn at the Vājapeya<sup>4</sup> and the Rājasūya<sup>5</sup> ceremonies by the king as a token of his position. <F>1) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vi. 1; Sata- patha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 3, 2, 3; iv. 5, 2, 7 (used at the sacrifice to wrap the embryo in); xiv. 2, 1, 8 (Indrāṇī's Uṣṇīṣa), etc.; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xiii. 10.</F> <F>2) xv. 2, 1.</F> <F>3) xvii. 1, 14. {%Cf.%} xvi. 6, 13.</F> <F>4) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, v. 3, 5, 23.</F> <F>5) Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iv. 4, 3.</F>

{@Uṣyala@}¦ occurs once in the description of the couch or the bridal car in the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> where it seems to mean the four ‘frame-pieces.’ The form is doubtful: {%uṣpala%} is possible.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) xiv. 1, 60.</F> <F>2) Whitney, Translation of the Athar- vaveda, 385. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 155; Whitney, {%op. cit.,%} 752.</F>

{@Usra,@}¦ m.; {@Usrā,@} f.; {@Usrika,@} m.; {@Usriya,@} m.; {@Usriyā,@} f. All these words denote a ‘bull’ or a ‘cow,’ occurring frequently in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> and sometimes later,<sup>2</sup> but usually with some reference to the morning light. In some passages the sense is doubtful. See {@Go.@} <F>1) {%Usra,%} Rv. vi. 12, 4; {%usrā,%} i. 3, 8; viii. 75, 8; 96, 8; ix. 58, 2, etc.; {%usrika,%} i. 190, 5; {%usriya,%} v. 58, 6 (with {%vṛṣabhaḥ%}); ix. 74. 3; {%usriyā,%} i. 153, 4; 180, 3; ii. 40, 2, etc. In ix. 70, 6, {%usriya%} is applied to a calf; and in ix. 68, 1; 93, 2, {%usriyā%} means ‘milk.’</F> <F>2) {%Usrau dhūrṣāhau,%} Vājasaneyi Saṃ- hitā, iv. 33; {%usrā,%} Av. xii. 3, 37; {%usriya,%} Av. i. 12, 1; {%usriyā,%} Av. ix. 4, 1; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxxv. 2. 3. In Av. v. 20, 1; 28, 3, it means ‘cow- hide,’ or perhaps in v. 28, 3, ‘milk.’</F>
{@Ūrjayant Aupamanyava@}¦ is mentioned in the Vaṃśa Brāh- maṇa<sup>1</sup> as a pupil of {@Bhānumant Aupamanyava.@} <F>1) {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 372.</F>

{@Ūrjayantī@}¦ is regarded by Ludwig<sup>1</sup> in one passage of the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> as the name of a fort, the stronghold of {@Nārmara.@} The verse is, however, quite unintelligible.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 152.</F> <F>2) ii. 13, 8.</F> <F>3) Sāyaṇa makes Urjayantī a Piśācī; Grassmann, the sun; Roth, {%s.v. ūrjay,%} takes it adjectivally. {%Cf.%} Oldenberg, {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 199.</F>

{@Ūrjavya,@}¦ a word occurring only once in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> is taken by Ludwig<sup>2</sup> to be the name of a sacrificer. Roth,<sup>3</sup> how- ever, regards the word as an adjective meaning ‘rich in strength,’ and this is the more probable interpretation. <F>1) v. 41, 20.</F> <F>2) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 155.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>

{@Ūrṇa-nābhī,@}¦<sup>1</sup> {@Ūrṇa-vābhi, Ūrṇā-vant@} are all names of the spider in the later Saṃhitās and the Brāhmaṇas in allusion to the insect's spinning threads of wool, as it were. <F>1) {%Ūrṇa-nābhi%} (‘having wool in its navel’), Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 1, 2, 5; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, ii. 1, 23; {%ūrṇa-vābhī%} (‘wool-spinner’), Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, viii. 1; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiv. 5, 1, 23; {%ūrṇā-vant%} (‘possessing wool’), Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, xix. 3 (in a Mantra).</F>

{@Ūrṇā,@}¦ ‘wool,’ is very frequently mentioned from the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> onwards. The Paruṣṇī country was famous for its wool,<sup>2</sup> like Gandhāra<sup>3</sup> for its sheep. The term for the separate tufts was {%parvan%}<sup>4</sup> or {%parus.%}<sup>5</sup> ‘Soft as wool’ ({%ūrṇa-mradas%})<sup>6</sup> is not a rare epithet. The sheep is called ‘woolly’ ({%ūrṇāvatī%}).<sup>7</sup> ‘Woollen thread’ ({%ūrṇā-sūtra%}) is repeatedly referred to in the later Saṃhitās<sup>8</sup> and the Brāhmaṇas.<sup>9</sup> The word {%ūrṇā%} was not restricted to the sense of sheep's wool,<sup>10</sup> but might denote goat's hair also.<sup>11</sup> <F>1) iv. 22, 2; v. 52, 9; Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, xii. 5, 1, 13: 7, 2, 10, etc.; {%ūrṇāyu,%} ‘woolly,’ Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xiii. 50; Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xii. 11, 10.</F> <F>2) Rv., {%loc. cit.;%} Pischel, {%Vedische%} {%Studien,%} 2, 210. But {%cf.%} Max Müller, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 32, 315.</F> <F>3) Rv. i. 126, 7.</F> <F>4) Rv. iv. 22, 10.</F> <F>5) Rv. ix. 15, 6.</F> <F>6) Rv. v. 5, 4; x. 18, 10; Vājasa- neyi Saṃhitā, ii. 2: iv. 10; xxi. 33, etc.</F> <F>7) Rv. viii. 56, 3.</F> <F>8) Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 11, 9; Kāṭhaka Samhitā, xxxviii. 3; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xix. 80, etc. {%Cf.%} {%ūrṇā-stukā,%} Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, i. 28; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxv. 3.</F> <F>9) Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 6, 4; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xii. 7, 2, 11, etc.</F> <F>10) {%Cf. anaiḍakīr ūrṇāḥ%} (‘wool not coming from the {%eḍaha,%}’ a species of sheep) in Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 5 2, 15.</F> <F>11) {%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%Journal of the American%} {%Oriental Society,%} 17, 83, n.</F>

{@Ūrṇā-vatī.@}¦ — In the hymn of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> which celebrates the rivers Ludwig<sup>2</sup> finds a reference to an affluent of the Indus called Ūrṇāvatī. This interpretation, however, seems certainly wrong. Roth<sup>3</sup> renders the word merely as ‘woolly,’ and Zimmer<sup>4</sup> rejects Ludwig's explanation on the ground that it throws the structure of the hymn into confusion. Pischel<sup>5</sup> makes the word an epithet of the Indus, ‘rich in sheep.’ <F>1) x. 75. 8.</F> <F>2) Translation of the Rigveda, 3. 200.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>4) {%Altindisches Leben.%} 429.</F> <F>5) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 210.</F>

{@Ūrdara.@}¦ — This word occurs once in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> when reference is made to filling Indra with Soma as one fills an [Page1-107+ 42] Ūrdara with grain ({@Yava@}). Sāyaṇa renders it granāry, but Roth<sup>2</sup> and Zimmer<sup>3</sup> seem more correct in simply making it a measure for holding grain, or ‘garner.’ <F>1) ii. 14, 11.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>3) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 238.</F>
{@Ūla@}¦ is a variant of {@Ula.@}

{@Ūṣa@}¦ in the later Saṃhitās<sup>1</sup> and Brāhmaṇas<sup>2</sup> denotes salt ground suited for cattle. {%Cf.%} {@Uṣa.@} <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 2, 3, 2, etc.</F> <F>2) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, iv. 27; Sata- patha Brāhmaṇa, v. 2, 1, 16, etc.</F>

1. {@Ṛkṣa,@}¦ ‘bear,’ is found only once in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> and seldom later,<sup>2</sup> the animal having evidently been scarce in the regions occupied by the Vedic Indians. Not more frequent<sup>3</sup> is the use of the word in the plural to denote the ‘seven bears,’ later called the ‘seven Ṛṣis,’<sup>4</sup> the constellation of the ‘Great Bear’ (<lang n="greek">ἄρκτος</lang>, {%ursa%}). <F>1) v. 56, 3.</F> <F>2) Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 17; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 36; Jai- minīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 184. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 81.</F> <F>3) Rv. i. 24, 10; Satapatha Brāhmaṇa. ii. 1, 2, 4; Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, i. 11, 2. {%Cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 3, 422.</F> <F>4) {%Cf.%} Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} p. 144 (D).</F>

2. {@Ṛkṣa@}¦ is the name of a patron mentioned in one verse of a Dānastuti (‘Praise of Gifts’) in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> his son being referred to in the next verse as {@Ārkṣa.@} <F>1) viii. 68, 15. {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 163.</F>

{@Ṛkṣākā@}¦ is a word occurring once in an obscure passage of the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> The sense is quite unknown. Weber<sup>2</sup> thinks it refers to the ‘milky way,’ but his view rests on no evidence. Whitney<sup>3</sup> despairs of the passage. <F>1) xviii. 2, 31.</F> <F>2) {%Festgruss an Roth,%} 138, n. 2; Berlin Catalogue, 2, 59, 11.; {%Proccedings of the%} {%Berlin Academy,%} 1895, 856.</F> <F>3) Translation of the Atharvaveda, 840.</F>

{@Ṛkṣīkā,@}¦ a word found in the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā,<sup>2</sup> and the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>3</sup> appears to denote a demon. Harisvāmin, however, in his commentary on the Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, connects the word with {@Ṛkṣa,@} as meaning ‘bear.’ <F>1) xii. 1, 49.</F> <F>2) xxx. 8.</F> <F>3) xiii. 2, 4, 2. 4. {%Cf.%} Eggeling, {%Sacred%} {%Books of the East,%} 44, 307.</F>

{@Ṛg-veda,@}¦ the formal name of the collection of Ṛcs, first appears in the Brāhmaṇas,<sup>1</sup> and thereafter frequently in the Āraṇyakas<sup>2</sup> and Upaniṣads.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, i. 32, and implied in Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 12, 9, 1; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, vi. 5, 4, 6; 8, 3; xii. 3, 4, 9.</F> <F>2) Aitareya Āraṇyaka, iii. 2, 3. 5; Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka, viii. 3. 8.</F> <F>3) Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, i. 5, 12; ii. 4, 10; iv. 1, 6; 5, 11; Chāndogya Upaniṣad, i. 3, 7; iii. 1, 2. 3; 15, 7; vii. 1, 2. 4; 2, 1; 7, 1.</F>

{@Ṛjiśvan@}¦ is mentioned several times in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> but always in a vague manner, as if very ancient. He assists Indra in fights against demoniac figures like Pipru and the dusky brood ({%kṛṣṇa-garbhāḥ%}). According to Ludwig,<sup>2</sup> he was called Auśija's son,<sup>3</sup> but this is doubtful. He is twice<sup>4</sup> clearly called Vaidathina, or descendant of Vidathin. <F>1) i. 51, 5; 53, 8; 101, 1; vi. 20, 7; viii. 49, 10; x. 99, 11; 138, 3.</F> <F>2) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 143, 149.</F> <F>3) Rv. x. 99, 11. {%Cf.%} {@Auśija.@}</F> <F>4) Rv. iv. 16, 13; v. 29, 11. {%Cf.%} Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} p. 161 (C).</F>
{@Ṛjūnas@}¦ is mentioned once only in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> along with six other Soma sacrificers. <F>1) viii. 52, 2. {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 163.</F>

{@Ṛjrāśva@}¦ appears in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as one of the {@Vārṣāgiras,@} along with {@Ambarīṣa, Surādhas, Sahadeva,@} and {@Bhayamāna,@} and as apparently victorious in a race. Elsewhere<sup>2</sup> in the [Page1-109+ 55] Rigveda he is celebrated as having been blinded by his father for slaying one hundred rams for a she-wolf, and as having been restored to sight by the Aśvins, a legend of quite obscure meaning. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} p. 52. <F>1) i. 100, 16. 17.</F> <F>2) i. 116, 17; 117, 16. 17.</F>

{@Ṛṇa,@}¦ ‘debt,’ is repeatedly mentioned from the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> onwards, having apparently been a normal condition among the Vedic Indians. Reference is often made<sup>2</sup> to debts con- tracted at dicing. To pay off a debt was called {%ṛṇaṃ saṃ-nī.%}<sup>3</sup> Allusion is made to debt contracted without intention of payment.<sup>4</sup> <div n="P"/>The result of non-payment of a debt might be very serious: the dicer might fall into slavery.<sup>5</sup> Debtors, like other male- factors, such as thieves, were frequently bound by their creditors to posts ({%dru-pada%}),<sup>6</sup> presumably as a means of putting pressure on them or their friends to pay up the debt. <div n="P"/>The amount of interest payable is impossible to make out. In one passage of the Rigveda and Atharvaveda<sup>7</sup> an eighth ({%śapha%}) and a sixteenth ({%kalā%}) are mentioned as paid, but it is quite uncertain whether interest or an instalment of the principal is meant. Presumably the interest would be paid in kind. <div n="P"/>How far a debt was a heritable interest or obligation does not appear. The Kauśika Sūtra<sup>8</sup> regards three hymns of the [Page1-110+ 64] Atharvaveda<sup>9</sup> as applicable to the occasion of the payment of a debt after the creditor's decease. For the payment of a debt. by a relation of the debtor the evidence is still less clear.<sup>10</sup> <div n="P"/>Zimmer<sup>11</sup> thinks that payments of debt were made in the presence of witnesses who could be appealed to in case of dispute. This conclusion is, however, very uncertain, resting solely on a vague verse in the Atharvaveda.<sup>12</sup> <F>1) ii. 27, 4, etc., usually in a meta- phorical sense.</F> <F>2) Rv. x. 34, 10; Av. vi. 119, 1.</F> <F>3) Rv. viii. 47, 17 = Av. vi. 46, 3.</F> <F>4) Av. vi. 119, 1.</F> <F>5) Rv. x. 34. {%Cf.%} Lüders, {%Das Wūrfel-%} {%spiel im alten Indien,%} 61.</F> <F>6) Rv. x. 34, 4, seems to refer rather to the binding and taking away as a slave, though Pischel, {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 228, explains it as the binding of a debtor for non-payment, interpreting the obscure verse i. 169, 7, in the same way. But Av. vi. 115, 2, 3, may refer to debt, and if this is the meaning the allusion to binding to a post as a punish- ment is clear. See, however, Bloom- field, {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 528, n. 1; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 364, who interprets the hymn as referring only to sin. Rv. i. 24, 13. 15; Av. vi. 63, 3 = 84, 4; 121, 1 {%et seq.,%} are general; while Rv. vii. 86, 5; Av. xix. 47, 9; 50, 1, refer to the binding of thieves in the stocks. {%Cf.%} {@Taskara.@}</F> <F>7) Rv. viii. 47, 17 = Av. vi. 46, 3.</F> <F>8) xlvi. 36-40. See Caland, {%Altindisches%} {%Zauberritual,%} 154; Bloomfield, {%op. cit.,%} 528.</F> <F>9) vi. 117-119. The name for unpaid debt is in Av. vi. 117, 1, {%apamityam%} {%apratītam.%} In the Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 3, 8, 1, {%kusīdam apratīttam;%} in the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iv. 14, 17, and Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, ii. 3, 1, 8, {%kusīdam%} {%apratītam;%} in the Mantra Brāhmaṇa, ii. 3. 20, {%apradattam.%}</F> <F>10) {%Cf.%} Rv. iv. 3, 13 (a brother's sin or debt); Jolly, {%Recht und Sitte,%} 99, 100.</F> <F>11) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 181. This sug- gestion is ignored by Bloomfield, {%op. cit.,%} 375, and Whitney, {%op. cit.,%} 304.</F> <F>12) vi. 32, 3 = viii. 8, 21. {%Cf.%} Śāṅkh- āyana Āraṇyaka, xii. 14, and see Jñātṛ. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%op. cit.,%} 181, 182; 259.</F>

{@Ṛṇaṃ-caya,@}¦ a prince of the {@Ruśamas,@} is celebrated in a Dānastuti (‘Praise of Gifts’) of the Rigveda (v. 30, 12. 14) for his generosity to a poet named {@Babhru.@} <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 129; Bṛhadevatā, ed. Macdonell, 2, 169, 174.

{@Ṛtu,@}¦ ‘season,’ is a term repeatedly mentioned from the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> onwards, Three seasons of the year are often alluded to,<sup>2</sup> but the names are not usually specified. In one passage of the Rigveda<sup>3</sup> spring ({%vasanta%}), summer ({%grīṣma%}), and autumn ({%śarad%}) are given. The Rigveda knows also the rainy season ({%prā-vṛṣ%}) and the winter ({%himā, hemanta%}). A more usual<sup>4</sup> division (not found in the Rigveda) is into five seasons, [Page1-111+ 57] {%vasanta, grīṣma, varṣā, śarad, hemama-siśira,%} but occasionally the five are otherwise divided, {%varṣā-śarad%} being made one season.<sup>5</sup> Sometimes six<sup>6</sup> seasons are reckoned, {%hemanta%} and {%śiśira%} being divided, so that the six seasons can be made parallel to the twelve months of the year. A still more artificial arrangement<sup>7</sup> makes the seasons seven, possibly by reckoning the intercalary month as a season, as Weber and Zimmer<sup>8</sup> hold, or more probably because of the predilection for the number seven, as Roth<sup>9</sup> suggests. Occasionally the word {%ṛtu%} is applied to the months.<sup>10</sup> The last season, according to the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>11</sup> is {%hemanta.%} <div n="P"/>The growth of the division of the seasons from three to five is rightly explained by Zimmer<sup>12</sup> as indicating the advance of the Vedic Indians towards the east. It is not Rigvedic, but dominates the later Saṃhitās. Traces of an earlier division of the year into winter and summer do not appear clearly in the Rigveda, where the appropriate words {%himā%} and {%samā%} are merely general appellations of the year, and where {%śarad%}<sup>13</sup> is commoner than either as a designation of the year, because it denotes the harvest, a time of overwhelming importance to a young agricultural people. The division of the year in one passage of the Atharvaveda<sup>14</sup> into two periods of six months is merely formal, and in no way an indication of old tradition. <F>1) i. 49, 3; 84, 18, etc.</F> <F>2) {%Cf.%} Rv. i. 164, 2 ({%tri-nābhi%}), 48 ({%trīṇi%} {%nabhyāni%}); also perhaps the Ṛbhus as the genii of the three seasons and the three dawns. {%Cf.%} Macdonell, {%Vedic%} {%Mythology,%} p. 133; Hillebrandt, {%Vedische%} {%Mythologie,%} 2, 33 {%et seq.:%} Śatapatha Brāh- maṇa, xiv. 1, 1, 28, and the {%cāturmāsyāni,%} or four-monthly sacrifices performed at the beginning of the seasons in the ritual (Weber, {%Naxatra,%} 2, 329 {%et seq.%}).</F> <F>3) x. 90, 6. Hillebrandt, {%op. cit.,%} 2, 35, finds in Rv. v. 14, 4: ix. 91, 6, reference to three seasons in the triad {%gāvaḥ%} (? spring), {%āpaḥ%} (rains), {%svar%} {%(= gharma),%} and in the ritual literature (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra, viii. 4, 2) in the threefold division into {%ṛta, gharma,%} and {%oṣadhi.%}</F> <F>4) Av. viii. 2, 22; 9, 15; xiii. 1, 18; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, i. 6, 2, 3; iv. 3, 3, 1. 2; v. 1, 10, 3; 3, 1, 2; 4. 12, 2; 6. 10, 1; 7, 2, 4; vii. 1, 18, 1. 2; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, i. 7, 3; iii. 4, 8; 13, 1; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, iv. 14; ix. 16; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, x. 10-14; Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, i. 3, 5, 11; vi. 2, 2, 3. etc.; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 10, 4, 1; 11, 10, 4, etc. {%Cf.%} Rv. i, 164, 13. {@Ṛtu-parṇa@}¦ appears in a Brāhmaṇa-like passage of the Baudh- āyana Śrauta Sūtra<sup>1</sup> as son of Bhaṅgāśvina and king of Śaphāla. {@Ṛtv-ij@}¦ is the regular term for ‘sacrificial priest,’ covering all the different kinds of priests employed at the sacrifice. It appears certain that all the priests were Brāhmaṇas.<sup>1</sup> The number of priests officiating at a sacrifice with different functions was almost certainly seven. The oldest list, occurring in one passage of the Rigveda,<sup>2</sup> enumerates their names as Hotṛ, Potṛ, Neṣṭṛ, Agnīdh, Praśāstṛ, Adhvaryu, Brahman, besides the institutor of the sacrifice. The number of seven probably explains the phrase ‘seven Hotṛs’ occurring so frequently in the Rigveda, and is most likely connected with that of the mythical ‘seven Ṛṣis.’ It may be compared with the eight of Iran.<sup>3</sup> The chief of the seven priests was the Hotṛ, who was the singer of the hymns, and in the early times their composer also. The Adhvaryu performed the practical work of the sacrifice, and accompanied his performance with muttered formulas of prayer and deprecation of evil. His chief assist- ance was derived from the Agnīdh, the two performing the smaller sacrifices without other help in practical matters. The Praśāstṛ, Upavaktṛ, or Maitrāvaruṇa, as he was variously called, appeared only in the greater sacrifices as giving in- structions to the Hotṛ, and as entrusted with certain litanies. The Potṛ, Neṣṭṛ, and Brahman belonged to the ritual of the Soma sacrifice, the latter being later styled Brāhmaṇāc- chaṃsin to distinguish him from the priest who in the later [Page1-113+ 60] ritual acted as supervisor. Other priests referred to in the Rigveda<sup>4</sup> are the singers of Sāmans or chants, the Udgātṛ and his assistant the Prastotṛ, while the Pratihartṛ, another assistant, though not mentioned, may quite well have been known. Their functions undoubtedly represent a later stage of the ritual, the development of the elaborate series of sacrificial calls on the one hand, and on the other the use of long hymns addressed to the Soma plant. Other priests, such as the Achāvāka,<sup>5</sup> the Grāvastut, the Unnetṛ, and the Subrahmaṇya, were known later in the developed ritual of the Brāhmaṇas, making in all sixteen priests, who were technically and artificially classed in four groups<sup>6</sup> Hotṛ, Maitrāvaruṇa, Achāvāka, and Grāvastut; Udgātṛ, Prastotṛ, Pratihartṛ, and Subrahmaṇya; Adhvaryu, Pratisthātṛ, Neṣṭṛ, and Unnetṛ; Brahman, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, Agnīdhra, and Petṛ. <div n="P"/>Apart from all these priests was the {@Purohita,@} who was the spiritual adviser of the king in all his religious duties. Geldner<sup>7</sup> holds that, as a rule, when the Purohita actually took part in one of the great sacrifices he played the part of the Brahman, in the sense of the priest who superintended the whole conduct of the ritual. He sees evidence for this view in a considerable number of passages of the Rigveda<sup>8</sup> and the later literature,<sup>9</sup> where Purohita and Brahman were combined or identified. Oldenberg,<sup>10</sup> however, more correctly points out [Page1-114+ 49] that in the earlier period this was not the case: the Purohita was then normally the Hotṛ, the singer of the most important of the songs; it was only later that the Brahman, who in the capacity of overseer of the rite is not known to the Rigveda, acquired the function of general supervision hitherto exercised by the Purohita, who was {%ex officio%} skilled in the use of magic and in guarding the king by spells which could also be applied to guarding the sacrifice from evil demons. With this agrees the fact that Agni, pre-eminently<sup>11</sup> the Purohita of men, is also a Hotṛ, and that the two divine Hotṛs of the Āprī hymns are called<sup>12</sup> the divine Purohitas. On the other hand, the rule is explicitly recognized in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>13</sup> that a Kṣatriya should have a Brahman as a Purohita; and in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>14</sup> the Vasiṣṭha family have a special claim to the office of Brahman-Purohita, perhaps an indi- cation that it was they who first as Purohitas exchanged the function of Hotṛs for that of Brahmans in the sacrificial ritual. <div n="P"/>The sacrifices were performed for an individual in the great majority of cases. The Sattra,<sup>15</sup> or prolonged sacrificial session, was, however, performed for the common benefit of the priests taking part in it, though its advantageous results could only be secured if all the members actually engaged were consecrated ({%dīkṣita%}). Sacrifices for a people as such were unknown. The sacrifice for the king was, it is true, intended to bring about the prosperity of his people also; but it is characteristic that the prayer<sup>16</sup> for welfare includes by name only the priest and the king, referring to the people indirectly in connexion with the prosperity of their cattle and agriculture. <F>1) This is assumed throughout the Vedic texts, and is accompanied by the rule that no Kṣatriya can eat of the sacrificial offering ({%Cf.%} Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vii. 26): no doubt because only the Brāhmaṇas were sufficiently holy to receive the divine essence of the sacrifice into which, by partaking of it, the deity has entered in part.</F> <F>2) ii. 1, 2. {%Cf.%} Oldenberg. {%Rdigion%} {%des Veda,%} 383.</F> <F>3) Darmesteter, {%Le Zend-Avesta,%} 1, lxx {%et seq.%}</F> <F>4) Rv. viii. 81. 5.</F> <F>5) {%Cf.,%} for the Achāvāka, Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, xxviii. 4; Aitareya Brāh- maṇa, vi. 14, 8, etc.; Bergaigne, {%Recherches sur l'histoire de la liturgie%} {%védique,%} 47; Oldenberg. {%Religion des%} {%Veda,%} 397, n. 2. {@Ṛṣi,@}¦ ‘seer,’ is primarily a composer of hymns to the gods. In the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> reference is often made to previous singers and to contemporary poets. Old poems were inherited and refurbished by members of the composer's family,<sup>2</sup> but the great aim of the singers was to produce new and approved hymns.<sup>3</sup> It is not till the time of the Brāhmaṇas that the [Page1-116+ 62] composition of hymns appears to have fallen into disuse,<sup>4</sup> though poetry was still produced, for example, in the form of {@Gāthās,@} which the priests were required to compose them- selves<sup>5</sup> and sing to the accompaniment of the lute at the sacrifice. The Ṛṣi was the most exalted of Brāhmaṇas,<sup>6</sup> and his skill, which is often compared with that of a carpenter,<sup>7</sup> was regarded as heaven-sent.<sup>8</sup> The Purohita, whether as Hotṛ or as Brahman (see {@Ṛtvij@}), was a singer.<sup>9</sup> No doubt the Ṛṣis were normally<sup>10</sup> attached to the houses of the great, the petty kings of Vedic times, or the nobles of the royal household. Nor need it be doubted that occasionally<sup>11</sup> the princes them- selves essayed poetry: a Rājanyarṣi, the prototype of the later Rājarṣi or ‘royal seer,’ who appears in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa,<sup>12</sup> though he must be mythical as Oldenberg<sup>13</sup> points out, indicates that kings cultivated poetry<sup>14</sup> just as later they engaged in philosophic disputations.<sup>15</sup> Normally, how- ever, the poetical function is Brahminical, Viśāmitra and others not being kings, but merely Brāhmaṇas, in the Rigveda. <div n="P"/>In the later literature the Ṛṣis are the poets of the hymns preserved in the Saṃhitās. a Ṛṣi being regularly<sup>16</sup> cited when a Vedic Saṃhitā is quoted. Moreover, the Ṛṣis become the representatives of a sacred past, and are regarded as holy sages, [Page1-117+ 56] whose deeds are narrated as if they were the deeds of gods or Asuras.<sup>17</sup> They are typified by a particular group of seven,<sup>18</sup> mentioned four times in the Rigveda,<sup>19</sup> several times in the later Saṃhitās,<sup>20</sup> and enumerated in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad<sup>21</sup> as Gotama, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, and Atri. In the Rigveda itself Kutsa,<sup>22</sup> Atri,<sup>23</sup> Rebha,<sup>24</sup> Agastya,<sup>25</sup> the Kuśikas,<sup>26</sup> Vasiṣṭha,<sup>27</sup> Vyaśva,<sup>28</sup> and others appear as Ṛṣis; and the Atharvaveda<sup>29</sup> contains a long list, including Aṅgiras, Agastī, Jamadagni, Atri, Kaśyapa, Vasiṣṭha, Bharadvāja, Gaviṣṭhira, Viśvāmitra, Kutsa, Kakṣīvant, Kaṇva, Medhātithi, Triśoka, Uśanā Kāvya, Gotama, and Mudgala. <div n="P"/>Competition among the bards appears to have been known. This is one of the sides of the riddle poetry ({@Brahmodya@}) that forms a distinctive feature<sup>30</sup> of the Vedic ritual of the Aśva- medha, or horse sacrifice. In the Upaniṣad period such competitions were quite frequent. The most famous was that of Yājñavalkya, which was held at the court of Janaka of Videha, as detailed in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad,<sup>31</sup> and which was a source of annoyance to {@Ajātaśatru@} of {@Kāśī.@}<sup>32</sup> According to an analogous practice, a Brāhmaṇa, like {@Uddālaka@} {@Aruṇi,@} would go about disputing with all he came across, and compete with them for a prize of money.<sup>33</sup> <F>1) i. 1, 2; 45, 3; viii. 43, 13, etc.</F> <F>2) i. 89, 3; 96, 2; iii. 39, 2; viii. 6. 11. 43; 76, 6, etc.</F> <F>3) i. 109, 2; ii. 18, 3; iii. 62, 7; vi. 50, 6; vii. 14, 4; 93, 1; viii. 23, 14, etc.</F> <F>4) Geldner, {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 151.</F> <F>5) Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 4, 2, 8; 3, 5.</F> <F>6) Rv. ix. 96, 6, etc. {%Cf.%} Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, xii. 4, 4, 6, where pre- eminence is assigned to a Brāhmaṇa descended from a Ṛṣi.</F> <F>7) Rv. i. 130, 6; v. 2, 11; 29, 15; 73, 10; x. 39, 14.
