{@Ekāyana@}¦ denotes some object of study in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.<sup>1</sup> The St. Petersburg Dictionary renders it ‘doctrine ({%ayana%}) of unity’ ({%eka%}), ‘monotheism,’ while Max Müller prefers ‘ethics,’ and Monier-Williams in his Dicitionary ‘worldly wisdom.’<sup>2</sup> <F>1) vii. 1, 2. 4; 2, 1; 7, 1.</F> <F>2) Max Müller and Monier-Williams thus follow Śaṅkara's interpretation as {%nīti-śāstra,%} ‘moral teaching.’ {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 267, 484; Little, {%Grammatical Index,%} 43.</F>

{@Ekāṣṭakā.@}¦ — That Aṣṭakā is the eighth day after the full moon appears clearly from the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> Ekāṣṭakā, or ‘sole Aṣṭakā,’ must denote not merely any Aṣṭakā, but some particular one. Sāyaṇa, in his commentary on the Atharva- veda,<sup>2</sup> in which a whole hymn celebrates the Ekāṣṭakā, fixes the date meant by the term as the eighth day in the dark half of the month of Māgha (January — February). The Ekāṣṭakā, is declared in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>3</sup> to be the time for the consecration ({%dīkṣā%}) of those who are going to perform a year long sacrifice. See also {@Māsa.@} <F>1) xv. 16, 2. {%Cf.%} Satapatha Brāh- maṇa, vi. 2, 2, 23; 4, 2, 10.</F> <F>2) iii. 10.</F> <F>3) vii. 4, 8 1. {%Cf.%} iii. 3, 8, 4; iv. 3, 11, 1; v. 7, 2, 2; Pañcaviṃśa Brāl maṇa, v. 9, 4. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 305; Weber, {%Naxatra,%} 2, 341, 342.</F>
{@Ejatka@}¦ is the name of an insect in the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) v. 23, 7. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindiches Leben,%} 98; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 262.</F>

{@Eḍaka@}¦ appears to denote a ‘vicious ram’ in the Śatapatha<sup>1</sup> and Jaiminīya<sup>2</sup> Brāhmaṇas. <F>1) xii. 4, 1, 4; {%cf.%} ii. 5, 2, 15.</F> <F>2) i. 51, 4 ({%Journal of the American%} {%Oriental Society,%} 23, 332). {%Cf.%} Eggeling, {%Sacrea Books of the East,%} 44, 178.</F>

{@Eṇī@}¦ denotes the ‘female antelope’ in the later Saṃhitās,<sup>1</sup> perhaps as the feminine of {@Eta.@} <F>1) Av. v. 14, 11; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 15, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 17; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 36; {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 82.</F>

{@Eta@}¦ in the plural ({%etāḥ%}) denotes the steeds of the Maruts, being a swift species of deer, which are mentioned several times in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> and the skins of which are also said to be worn by the Maruts on their shoulders.<sup>2</sup> The epithet {%pṛthu-%} {%budhna,%} once applied to them in the Rigveda,<sup>3</sup> and variously interpreted as ‘broad-hoofed,’<sup>4</sup> ‘broad-chested,’<sup>5</sup> and ‘broad in the hinder part,’<sup>6</sup> seems to indicate that they were not gazelles.<sup>7</sup> <F>1) i. 165. 2; 169, 6, 7; v. 54, 5; x. 77. 2.</F> <F>2) Rv. i. 166, 10. {%Cf.%} Roth, St. Peters- burg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>3) i. 169. 6.</F> <F>4) By Grassman and Zimmer.</F> <F>5) Griffith, {%Hymns of the Rigveda,%} 1, 235.</F> <F>6) Monier-Williams, Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>7) {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 83.</F>

1. {@Etaśa@}¦ is in several passages of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> according to Roth<sup>2</sup> the name of a protégé whom Indra helped against the sun-god Sūrya. But in all these passages Etaśa seems merely to designate the horse of the sun.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) i. 62, 15; iv. 30. 6; v. 29. 5.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>3) Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} pp. 149. 150.</F>

2. {@Etaśa@}¦ is in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> the name of a sage who is said to have cursed his children because they interrupted him in the midst of a rite; hence the Aitaśāyanas (descendants of Etaśa) are declared to be the worst of the Bhṛgus. The same story appears in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇā<sup>2</sup> where, how- ever, the sage's name is Aitaśa, and the Aitaśāyanas are described as the worst of the Aurvas. <F>1) xxx. 5.</F> <F>2) vi. 33. {%Cf.%} Hillebrandt. {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 2, 173.</F>

{@Edidhiṣuḥ-pati@}¦ is a term occurring only in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā,<sup>1</sup> where the commentator Mahīdhara interprets it as [Page1-121+ 34] meaning the ‘husband of a younger sister married before the elder sister.’ Though this sense is probably correct, the form is doubtless, as Delbrück<sup>2</sup> points out, corrupt. See {@Didhiṣūpati.@} <F>1) xxx. 9.</F> <F>2) {%Die indogermanischen Verwandschaftsnamen,%} 569. n. 1.</F>
{@Eraṇḍa,@}¦ the castor-oil plant ({%Ricinus communis%}), is first mentioned in the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka (xii. 8).

{@Evāvada@}¦ is regarded by Ludwig<sup>1</sup> in a very obscure passage of the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> as the name of a singer beside {@Kṣatra, Manasa,@} and {@Yajata.@} The commentator Sāyaṇa also interprets the word as a proper name. Roth,<sup>3</sup> however, considers it to be an adjective meaning ‘truthful.’ <F>1) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 138.</F> <F>2) v. 44, 10.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>

{@Aikādaśākṣa Mānu-tantavya@}¦ appears in the Aitareya Brāh- maṇa<sup>1</sup> as a king who observed the rule of sacrificing when the sun had risen ({%udita-homin%}), and as a contemporary of {@Nagarin@} {@Jāna-śruteya.@} <F>1) v. 30. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 223.</F>

{@Aikṣvāka,@}¦ ‘descendant of Ikṣvāku,’ is the patronymic borne by {@Purukutsa@} in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> Another Aikṣvāka is Vārṣṇi, a teacher mentioned in the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> A king {@Hariścandra Vaidhasa@} Aikṣvāka is known to the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa,<sup>3</sup> and {@Tryaruṇa@} is an Aikṣvāka in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) xiii. 5, 4, 5.</F> <F>2) i. 5, 4.</F> <F>3) vii. 13, 16.</F> <F>4) xiii. 3, 12.</F>

{@Aitareya,@}¦ perhaps a patronymic from Itara, though the commentator Sāyaṇa<sup>1</sup> regards the word as a metronymic from [Page1-122+ 38] Itarā, is an epithet of {@Mahidāsa@} in the Aitareya Āraṇyaka<sup>2</sup> and the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) Cited by Aufrecht, {%Aitareya Brāhmaṇa,%} 3.</F> <F>2) ii. 1, 8; 3. 7.</F> <F>3) iii. 16, 7. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische%} {%Studien,%} 1, 389. The form Aitareyin occurs in the Anupada Sūtra, viii. 1; Āśvalāyana Srauta Sūtra, i. 3, etc.; and a Mahaitareya in Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra, iii. 4, 4, etc.</F>

{@Aitaśa, Aitaśāyana.@}¦ See {@Etaśa, Etaśāyana.@} The Aitaśa- pralāpa, or ‘Discourse of Aitaśa,’ is a part of the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) xx. 129-132. {%Cf.%} Bṛhaddevatā, viii. 101, with Macdonell's note.</F>

{@Aiti-hāsika.@}¦ — This term was applied to the people who explained the Vedic hymns by treating them as legendary history ({@Itihāsa@}), as Sieg<sup>1</sup> shows by the passages of the Nirukta,<sup>2</sup> where their views are opposed to those of the {@Nairuktas,@} who relied rather on etymology. Sieg<sup>3</sup> also seems right in finding them in the Naidānas of the Nirukta:<sup>4</sup> it is possible that their textbook was called the Nidāna. <F>1) {%Die Sagenstoffe des Ṛgveda,%} 13 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>2) ii. 16; xii. 1, etc.</F> <F>3) {%Op. cit.,%} 29.</F> <F>4) vi. 9; vii. 6.</F>
{@Aibhāvata,@}¦ ‘descendant of Ibhāvant,’ is the patronymic of {@Pratīdarśa.@}<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, xii. 8, 2, 3.</F>

{@Airāvata,@}¦ ‘son of Irāvant,’ is the patronymic of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, as a snake demon,<sup>1</sup> in the Atharvaveda<sup>2</sup> and the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) In the later literature Airāvata is the elephant of Indra: perhaps con- nected with this Vedic snake demon. as {%nāga%} means both ‘serpent’ and ‘elephant.’</F> <F>2) viii. 10, 29.</F> <F>3) xxv. 15, 3.</F>
{@Ailūṣa,@}¦ ‘descendant of Ilūṣa,’ is the patronymic of {@Kavaṣa.@}
{@Aiṣa-kṛta.@}¦ See {@Śitibāhu.@}

{@Aiṣā-vīra.@}¦ — The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa once<sup>1</sup> refers to the Aiṣā-vīras as officiating at a sacrifice, with the implication that they were bad sacrificers. Sāyaṇa regards the word as a proper name (‘descendants of Eṣavīra’), denoting the members of a despised family. But Roth may be right in explaining the word both in the passage mentioned above and elsewhere as meaning ‘weak’<sup>2</sup> or ‘insignificant man.’<sup>3</sup> <F>1) xi. 2, 7, 32.</F> <F>2) In the St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>3) In Böhtlingk's Dictionary, {%s.v.%} (‘one who wishes to be a man, but is not’). {%Cf.%} Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, ix. 5, 1, 16; Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, i. 1, where, however, Lindner's edition reads {%saiṣā%} {%vīra iva. Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 228; Eggeling, {%Sacred Books of the%} {%East,%} 44, 45.</F>
{@Aiṣumata,@}¦ ‘descendant of Iṣumant,’ is the patronymic of {@Trāta@} in the Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 372.</F>

{@Ogaṇa@}¦ is a word occurring only once, as a plural, in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> where it appears to indicate persons hostile to the seer of the hymn, and apparently opposed to the Āryan religion. Ludwig<sup>2</sup> regards the terms as the proper name of a people, but Pischel<sup>3</sup> thinks that it is merely an adjective meaning ‘weak’ ({%ogaṇa = ava-gaṇa%}), as in Pāli. <F>1) x. 89, 15</F> <F>2) Translation of the Rigveda, 5, 209.</F> <F>3) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 191, 192.</F>

{@Otu@}¦ in Vedic literature<sup>1</sup> denotes the ‘woof’ in weaving and corresponds to {@Tantu,@} ‘the warp,’ the roots {%vā,%}<sup>2</sup> ‘to weave,’ and {%tan,%}<sup>3</sup> to stretch,’ from which these two terms are derived, being used in parallel senses. In the process of weaving a shuttle ({@Tasara@}) was used. The ‘weaver’ is termed {%vāya,%}<sup>4</sup> and the ‘loom’ {%veman.%}<sup>5</sup> A wooden peg ({@Mayūkha@}) was used to [Page1-124+ 56] stretch the web on, while lead was employed as a weight to extend it.<sup>6</sup> <div n="P"/>The work of weaving was probably the special care of women.<sup>7</sup> A metaphor in the Atharvaveda<sup>8</sup> personifies Night and Day as two sisters weaving the web of the year, the nights serving as warp, the days as woof. <F>1) Rv. vi. 9, 2. 3; Av. xiv. 2, 51; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vi. 1, 1, 4, etc.</F> <F>2) Rv. vi. 9, 2. etc.</F> <F>3) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xix. 80; Rv. x. 130, 2; Av. x. 7, 43, etc.</F> <F>4) Rv. x. 26, 6, etc.</F> <F>5) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xix. 83.</F> <F>6) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xix. 80.</F> <F>7) Av. x. 7, 42; xiv. 2, 51. {%Cf.%} Rv. i. 92. 3.</F> <F>8) x. 7, 42; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 5, 5, 3. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 254, 255; Muir, {%Sanskrit Texts,%} 5, 465.</F>

{@Odana@}¦ is a common expression<sup>1</sup> denoting a mess, usually of grain cooked with milk ({%kṣīra-pākam odanam%}).<sup>2</sup> Special varieties are mentioned, such as the ‘milk-mess’ ({%kṣīraudana%}),<sup>3</sup> the ‘curd-mess’ ({%dadhy-odana%}),<sup>4</sup> the ‘bean-mess’ ({%mudgaudana%}),<sup>5</sup> the ‘sesame-mess’ ({%tilaudana%}),<sup>6</sup> the ‘water-mess’ ({%udaudana%}),<sup>7</sup> the ‘meat-mess’ ({%māṃsaudana%}),<sup>8</sup> the ‘ghee-mess’ ({%ghṛtaudana%}),<sup>9</sup> etc. <F>1) Rv. viii. 69, 14, etc.; Av. iv. 14, 7, etc.</F> <F>2) Rv. viii. 77, 10.</F> <F>3) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 5, 3, 4; xi. 5, 7, 5; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, vi. 4, 13.</F> <F>4) Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, vi. 4, 14.</F> <F>5) Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka, xii. 8.</F> <F>6) {%Ibid.;%} Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, vi. 4, 15.</F> <F>7) {%Ibid.,%} vi. 4, 15.</F> <F>8) {%Ibid.,%} vi. 4, 16; Satapatha Brāh- maṇa, xi. 5, 7, 5; Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇ- yaka, xii. 8.</F> <F>9) Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka, xii. 8.</F>

{@Opaśa@}¦ is a word of somewhat doubtful sense, occurring in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> the Atharvaveda,<sup>2</sup> and occasionally later.<sup>3</sup> It probably means a ‘plait’ as used in dressing the hair, especially of women,<sup>4</sup> but apparently, in earlier times,<sup>5</sup> of men also. The goddess Sinīvālī is called {%svaupaśā,%}<sup>6</sup> an epithet of doubtful sense, from which Zimmer<sup>7</sup> conjectures that the wearing of [Page1-125+ 50] false plaits of hair was not unknown in Vedic times. What was the difference between {{the braic->the braids||20210704|Dr. Sampada Savardekar|https://github.com/sanskrit-lexicon/csl-corrections/issues/67|}} referred to in the epithets {%pṛthu ṣṭuka,%}<sup>8</sup> ‘having broad braids,’ and {%viṣita-ṣṭuka,%}<sup>9</sup> ‘having loosened braids,’ and the Opaśa cannot be made out from the evidence available. Geldner<sup>10</sup> thinks that the original sense was ‘horn,’ and that when the word applies to Indra<sup>11</sup> it means ‘diadem.’ <F>1) x. 85. 8, {%Cf.%} i. 173, 6; viii. 14, 5; ix. 71. 1.</F> <F>2) vi. 138, 1. 2; ix. 3, 8, where it is applied metaphorically in describing the roof of a house.</F> <F>3) Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, iv. 1, 1.</F> <F>4) Av. vi. 138. 1, 2.</F> <F>5) Rv. i. 173, 6; viii. 14, 5.</F> <F>6) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iv. 1, 5, 3; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 7, 5; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xi. 56. The reading is uncertain. Bloomfield (see below) assumes {%sv-opaśā%} to be the correct form (‘having a fair {%opaśa%}’).</F> <F>7) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 264.</F> <F>8) Rv. x. 86, 8.</F> <F>9) Rv. i. 167, 5 (of Rodasī).</F> <F>10) {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 131, quoting Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 4, 3, where {%dvy-epaśāḥ%} is used of cattle; but the sense may be figurative.</F> <F>11) Rv. viii. 14, 5. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Athar-%} {%vaveda,%} 538, 539; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 348.</F>

{@Oṣadhi.@}¦ — Roughly speaking, the vegetable world is divided in Vedic literature<sup>1</sup> between Oṣadhi or {@Vīrudh@} ‘plants’ and {@Vana@} or {@Vṛkṣa@} ‘trees.’ Oṣadhi is employed in opposition to Vīrudh to denote plants as possessing a healing power or some other quality useful to men, while Vīrudh is rather a generic term for minor vegetable growths, but sometimes,<sup>2</sup> when occur- ring beside Oṣadhi, signifies those plants which do not possess medicinal properties. <div n="P"/>A list of the minor parts of which a plant is made up is given in the later Saṃhitās.<sup>3</sup> It comprises the root ({%mūla%}), the panicle ({%tūla%}), the stem ({%kāṇḍa%}), the twig ({%valśa%}), the flower ({%puṣpa%}), and the fruit ({%phala%}), while trees<sup>4</sup> have, in addition, a corona ({%skandha%}), branches ({%śākhā%}), and leaves ({%parṇa%}). The Atharvaveda<sup>5</sup> gives an elaborate, though not very intelligible, division of plants into those which expand ({%pra-stṛṇatīḥ%}), are bushy ({%stambinīḥ%}), have only one sheath ({%eka-śuṅgāḥ%}), are creepers ({%pra-tanvatīḥ%}), have many stalks ({%aṃśumatīḥ%}), are [Page1-126+ 35] jointed ({%kāṇḍinīḥ%}), or have spreading branches ({%vi-śākhāḥ%}). In the Rigveda<sup>6</sup> plants are termed ‘fruitful’ ({%phalinīḥ%}), ‘blossom- ing’ ({%puṣpavatīḥ%}), and ‘having flowers’ ({%pra-sūvarīḥ%}). <F>1) Rv. x. 97 and {%passim. Oṣadhi-%} {%vanaspati%} is a frequent compound, from the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (vi. 1, 1, 12) onwards. The medicinal properties of plants account for the epithet ‘of manifold powers’ ({%nānā-vīryā%}) applied to them in Av. xii. 1, 2.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 5, 3, 2.</F> <F>3) {%Ibid.,%} vii. 3, 19, 1; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxii. 28.</F> <F>4) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vii. 3, 20, 1. {%Cf.%} Rv. i. 32, 5; Av. x. 7, 38.</F> <F>5) viii. 7, 4, with Whitney's notes. {%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Atharva-%} {%veda,%} 579; Henry, {%Les livres VIII. et%} {%IX. de l' Atharvavéda,%} 58 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>6) x. 97. 3. 15. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben.%} 57.</F>

{@Aukṣa-gandhi@}¦ (‘having the smell of bull's grease’) appears in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> as the name of an Apsaras, beside other names, of which {@Guggulū@} and {@Naladī@} clearly indicate plants. This name, therefore, presumably also denotes some sort of fragrant plant. Aukṣa in the same Saṃhitā<sup>2</sup> means ‘bull's grease’ (from {%akṣan,%} ‘bull’). <F>1) iv. 37. 3.</F> <F>2) ii. 36. 7. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 69; Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 324; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 211, 212, and on Aukṣa, {%ibid.,%} 82, 83.</F>
{@Augra-sainya,@}¦ ‘descendant of Ugrasena,’ is the patronymic of King {@Yuddhāmśrauṣṭi@} in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (viii. 21).

{@Audanya,@}¦ ‘descendant of Udanya or Odana,’ is the patro- nymic in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> of Muṇḍibha, who is credited with inventing an expiation for the crime of slaying a Brahmin. In the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> the name appears in the form of Audanyava. <F>1) xiii. 3, 5, 4.</F> <F>2) iii. 9, 15, 3. {%Cf.%} St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} Odana; Eggeling, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 44, 341, n. 1.</F>

{@Audamaya@}¦ is Weber's<sup>1</sup> reading of the name of the Ātreya, who was Purohita of {@Aṅga Vairocana,@} according to the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> Aufrecht, however, in his edition more probably takes the correct form of the name to be {@Udamaya.@} <F>1) {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 228.</F> <F>2) viii. 22. {%Cf.%} St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} Udamaya.</F>

{@Auda-vāhi,@}¦ ‘descendant of Udavāha,’ appears in the first two Vaṃśas (lists of teachers) of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad<sup>1</sup> as a teacher of Bhāradvāja. <F>1) ii. 5, 20; iv. 5, 26 (in the Mādhyaṃdina recension).</F>
{@Aud-umbarāyaṇa,@}¦ ‘descendant of Udumbara,’ is the patro- nymic of a grammarian in the Nirukta (i. 1).

{@Aud-dālaki,@}¦ ‘descendant of Uddālaka,’ is the patronymic of the teacher variously called {@Asurbinda@}<sup>1</sup> or {@Kusurubinda,@}<sup>2</sup> and of {@Śvetaketu.@}<sup>3</sup> <F>1) Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 75 ({%Journal%} {%of the American Oriental Society,%} 23, 327).</F> <F>2) Ṣaḍviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, i. 16; Pañca- viṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xxii. 15, 10.</F> <F>3) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 3, 13; iv. 2, 5, 15. He is perhaps also meant in Katha Upaniṣad, i. 11.</F>
{@Aud-bhāri,@}¦ ‘descendant of Udbhāra,’ is the patronymic in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (xi. 8, 4. 6) of {@Khaṇḍika,@} teacher of {@Keśin.@}

{@Aupa-jandhani,@}¦ ‘descendant of Upajandhana,’ is the patro- nymic of a teacher mentioned in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad<sup>1</sup> as a pupil of {@Āsuri,@} and also<sup>2</sup> as a pupil of {@Sāyakāyana.@} <F>1) ii. 6, 3; iv. 6, 3 (in Vaṃśas).</F> <F>2) iv. 5, 27 (in the Mādhyaṃdina recension)</F>
{@Aupa-tasvini,@}¦ ‘descendant of Upatasvina,’ is the patronymic of {@Rāma@} in the Śatapatha {@Brāhmaṇa@} (iv. 6, 1. 7).

{@Aupa-manyava,@}¦ ‘descendant of Upamanyu,’ is the patro- nymic of various persons: see {@Kāmboja, Prācīnaśāla, Mahā-@} {@śāla.@} The best known bearer of the name is the grammarian who disagreed with the onomatopoetic theory of the derivation of names, and who is mentioned by Yāska.<sup>1</sup> An Aupamanyavī- putra occurs in the Baudhāyana Śrauta Sūtra<sup>2</sup> as a teacher. <F>1) i. 1; ii. 2. 6. 11, etc.</F> <F>2) xxii. 1 {%et seq%}</F>
{@Aupara,@}¦ ‘descendant of Upara,’ is the patronymic of {@Daṇḍa@} in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (vi. 2, 9, 4).
{@Aupa-veśi,@}¦ ‘descendant of Upaveśa,’ is the patronymic borne by {@Aruṇa,@} father of Uddālaka.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) See Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxvi. 10, and {@Aruṇa.@}</F>

{@Aupasvatī-putra,@}¦ ‘son of a female descendant of Upa- svant’(?), is mentioned as a pupil of {@Pārāśarīputra@} in a Vaṃśa (list of teachers) of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) vi. 5, 1 (only in the Kāṇva recension).</F>

{@Aupāvi@}¦ (‘descendant of Upāva’) {@Jāna-śruteya@} (‘descendant of Janaśruti’), appears in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> and the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā<sup>2</sup> as a sacrificer who used to offer the Vājapeya sacrifice and ascend to the other world. <F>1) v. 1, 1, 5. 7.</F> <F>2) i. 4, 5. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 222, 223.</F>

{@Aupoditi,@}¦ ‘descendant of Upodita,’ is the patronymic applied in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> to {@Tumiñja,@} and in the Baudhāyana Śrauta Sūtra<sup>2</sup> to {@Gaupālāyana,@} son of {@Vyāghrapad,@} Sthapati (‘general’) of the Kurus. In the form of Aupoditeya, a metro- nymic from Upoditā, the name is found in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>3</sup> where the Kāṇva text calls him Tumiñja Aupo- diteya Vaiyāghrapadya. <F>1) i. 7, 2, 1.</F> <F>2) xx. 25.</F> <F>3) i. 9, 3. 16. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Eggeling, {%Sacred Books of the East.%} 12, 271, n. 2.</F>

{@Aurṇa-vābha,@}¦ ‘descendant of Ūrṇavābhi.’ (1) This is the name of a pupil of {@Kauṇḍinya@} mentioned in a Vaṃśa (list of teachers) of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.<sup>1</sup> (2) A teacher of this name is frequently referred to in the Nirukta. His explanations in two passages<sup>2</sup> agree with those of the Nairuktas [Page1-129+ 41] or etymological school of interpreters of the Rigveda. In other passages<sup>3</sup> he appears rather to belong to the school of the Aitihāsikas, who relied on traditional legends. He was thus probably, as Sieg<sup>4</sup> suggests, an eclectic. <F>1) iv. 5, 26 (Mādhyaṃdina recension).</F> <F>2) vii. 15; xii. 19.</F> <F>3) vi. 13; xii. 1.</F> <F>4) {%Die Sagenstoffe des Ṛgveda,%} 13, n. 1.</F>

{@Aurva,@}¦ ‘descendant of Uru or Urva,’ appears in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> in close connexion with {@Bhṛgu,@} being probably a Bhṛgu himself. As in one passage of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa,<sup>2</sup> the descendants of Aitaśa are called the worst of the Aurvas, while the parallel version of the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> calls them the worst of the Bhṛgus, the Aurvas must have been a branch of the larger family of the Bhṛgus. Aurva himself is said in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>4</sup> to have received offspring from Atri. In the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>5</sup> two Aurvas are referred to as authorities. See also {@Kutsa.@} <F>1) viii. 102, 4.</F> <F>2) vi. 33.</F> <F>3) xxx. 5.</F> <F>4) vii. 1, 8, 1.</F> <F>5) xxi. 10, 6. Hopkins, {%Transactions%} {%of the Connecticut Academy of Arts and%} {%Sciences,%} 15, 54, reads {%ūrvau.%} <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 2, 173, n. 1.</F>

{@Aulāna@}¦ is a word occurring in a single passage of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> where it may possibly be a patronymic of {@Śaṃtanu@} as a ‘descendant of Ula.’ Ludwig,<sup>2</sup> however, conjectures that the reading should be ‘Kaulāna.’ Sieg<sup>3</sup> regards Aulāna as a later descendant<sup>4</sup> of Śaṃtanu, who utilized the story of Devāpi's rain-making as an introduction to his rain hymn. <F>1) x. 98, 11.</F> <F>2) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 166.</F> <F>3) {%Die Sagenstoffe des Ṛgveda,%} 141.</F> <F>4) {%Cf.%} Sāyaṇa on Rv. x, 98, 11; {%Kuru%} {%kula-jātaḥ Śāṃtaṇavaḥ,%} ‘a descendant of Śaṃtanu, born in the family of the Kurus</F>
{@Auluṇḍya,@}¦ ‘descendant of Uluṇḍa,’ is the patronymic of {@Supratīta@} in the Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 372.</F>

{@Auśija,@}¦ ‘descendant of Uśij,’ is a patronymic clearly applied to {@Kakṣīvant@} in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> It is also applied to {@Ṛjiśvan,@}<sup>2</sup> but Ludwig<sup>3</sup> thinks that the correct reading of the passage in question is {%auśijasyarjiśvā,%} ‘Ṛjiśvan, son of Auśija.’ In one verse<sup>4</sup> Auśija and Kakṣīvant are both mentioned, but in such a way that two different persons must apparently be meant. In other passages where the patronymic occurs alone, it is doubtful who is meant, or whether a proper name at all is intended.<sup>5</sup> Kakṣīvant Auśija appears also in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>6</sup> and elsewhere. <F>1) i. 18, 1.</F> <F>2) x. 99, 11.</F> <F>3) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 143, 149.</F> <F>4) Rv. i. 112, 11.</F> <F>5) Rv. i. 119, 9; 122, 4; iv. 21, 6, 7; v. 41, 5; vi. 4, 6. {%Cf.%} St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>6) xiv. 11, 16. See Hopkins, {%Transac-%} {%tions of the Connecticut Academy of Arts%} {%and Sciences,%} xv. 56, n., and {@Kakṣīvant,@} n. 15.</F>
{@Auṣṭrākṣi,@}¦ ‘descendant of Uṣṭrākṣa,’ occurs as the patro- nymic of {@Sāti@} in the Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 372. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indian Literature,%} 75.</F>

{@Kaṃsa,@}¦ a word denoting a ‘pot or vessel of metal,’ occurs in the Atharvaveda and elsewhere.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Av. x. 10, 5; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, viii. 10; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, vi. 3, 1, etc.; Nirukta, vii. 23; Śāṅkhā- yana Āraṇyaka, xii. 8.</F>

{@Kakara@}¦ occurs in the Yajurveda Saṃhitās<sup>1</sup> as the name of a victim at the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha). It probably denotes some ‘sort of bird,’ as rendered by the commentator Mahī- dhara.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 1; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xx. 24.</F> <F>2) On Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, {%loc. cit.%} {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 94.</F>

{@Kakuṭha,@}¦ a word occurring in the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā,<sup>1</sup> presumably denotes some kind of animal. According to Böhtlingk,<sup>2</sup> it is identical with {@Kakkaṭa.@} <F>1) iii. 14, 13.</F> <F>2) Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>

{@Kakuha,@}¦ a word occurring several times in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> is understood by Roth<sup>2</sup> to designate part of a chariot, perhaps the seat. Ludwig,<sup>3</sup> again, regards it in one passage<sup>4</sup> as the proper name of a Yādava prince who took spoil from {@Tirindira,@} the {@Parśu,@} but this view is hardly probable.<sup>5</sup> It is, on the whole, most likely that the word always means ‘chief,’ ‘pre-eminent,’ being applied as an epithet to horses, chariots, princes, etc.<sup>6</sup> This is the only sense given by Grassmann,<sup>7</sup> and later adopted by Roth.<sup>8</sup> <F>1) i. 46, 3; 181 5; 184, 3; ii. 34, 11; iii. 54, 14; v. 73, 7; 75, 4; viii. 6, 48.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>3) Translation of the Rigveda, 2, 182; 3, 160, 161; 5, 142.</F> <F>4) viii. 6, 48.</F> <F>5) Weber, {%Episches im vedischen Ritual,%} 36, 37.</F> <F>6) So certainly in Rv. viii. 45, 14; ix. 67, 8; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 3, 3, 1. 2, and often in the older form {%kakubha.%}</F> <F>7) In his Lexicon, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>8) In Böhtlingk's Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>

{@Kakkaṭa@}¦ denotes the ‘crab’ in the Yajurveda Saṃhitās,<sup>1</sup> being a Prākritized form of Karkaṭa, which is common in the later literature.<sup>2</sup> Roth,<sup>3</sup> however, takes the word to mean a bird, and compares {@Kakara.@} See also {@Kakuṭha.@} <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 15, 1 (where Weber has {%katkaṭa%}); Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 32.</F> <F>2) Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 95.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>

{@Kakṣa@}¦ is the name of two men mentioned as teachers in a Vaṃśa (list of teachers) of the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa. One is Kakṣa Vārakya, pupil of {@Proṣṭhapada Vārakya,@}<sup>1</sup> and the other Kakṣa Vārāki<sup>2</sup> or Vārakyā,<sup>3</sup> pupil of {@Dakṣa Kātyā-@} {@yani Ātreya.@} See also {@Urukakṣa.@} <F>1) iii. 41, 1.</F> <F>2) iii. 41, 1.</F> <F>3) iv. 17, 1.</F>

{@Kakṣīvant@}¦ is the name of a Ṛṣi mentioned frequently in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> and occasionally elsewhere.<sup>2</sup> He appears to have been a descendant of a female slave named Uśij.<sup>3</sup> He must have been a {@Pajra@} by family, as he bears the epithet Pajriya,<sup>4</sup> [Page1-132+ 55] and his descendants are called Pajras.<sup>5</sup> In a hymn of the Rigveda<sup>6</sup> he celebrates the prince {@Svanaya Bhāvya,@} who dwelt on the {@Sindhu@} (Indus), as having bestowed magnificent gifts on him; and the list of Nārāśaṃsas (‘Praises of Heroes’) in the Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra<sup>7</sup> mentions one by Kakṣīvant Auśija in honour of Svanaya Bhāvayavya. In his old age he obtained as a wife the maiden {@Vṛcayā.@}<sup>8</sup> He appears to have lived to be a hundred,<sup>9</sup> the typical length of life in the Vedas. He seems always to be thought of as belonging to the past, and in a hymn of the fourth book of the Rigveda<sup>10</sup> he is mentioned with the semi-mythical {@Kutsa@} and {@Kavi Uśanas.@} Later, also, he is a teacher of bygone days.<sup>11</sup> <div n="P"/>In Vedic literature he is not connected with {@Dīrghatamas@} beyond being once mentioned along with him in a hymn of the Rigveda.<sup>12</sup> But in the Bṛhaddevatā<sup>13</sup> he appears as a son of Dīrghatamas by a slave woman, Uśij. <div n="P"/>Weber<sup>14</sup> considers that Kakṣīvant was originally a Kṣatriya, not a Brāhmaṇa, quoting in favour of this view the fact that he is mentioned beside kings like {@Para Āṭṇāra, Vītahavya@} {@Śrāyasa,@} and {@Trasadasyu Paurukutsya.@}<sup>15</sup> But that these are all kings is an unnecessary assumption: these persons are mentioned in the passages in question undoubtedly only as famous men of old, to whom are ascribed mythical sacrificial performances, and who thus gained numerous sons. <F>1) i. 18, 1; 51, 13; 112, 11; 116, 7; 117, 6; 126, 3; iv. 26, 1; viii. 9, 10; ix. 74, 8; x. 25, 10; 61, 16.</F> <F>2) Av. iv. 29, 5, and passage noted below.</F> <F>3) Rv. i. 18, 1; perhaps also i, 112, 11, but Auśija may there be a separate name (see Auśija). {%Cf.%} Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xiv. 11, 16.</F> <F>4) Rv. i. 116, 7; 117, 6.</F> <F>5) Rv. i. 126, 4.</F> <F>6) i. 126.</F> <F>7) xvi. 4, 5.</F> <F>8) Rv. i. 51, 13.</F> <F>9) Rv. ix. 74, 8.</F> <F>10) iv. 26, 1.</F> <F>11) Av. iv. 29, 5; xviii. 3, 15; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, i. 21, 6. 7; Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa, ii. 6, 11.</F> <F>12) viii. 9, 10</F> <F>13) iv. 11 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>14) {%Episches im vedischen Ritual,%} 22-25.</F> <F>15) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 6, 5, 3; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxii. 3; Pancaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xxv. 16, 3, {%Cf.%} xiv. 11, 16. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Oldenberg, {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen%} {%Morgenländischen Gesellschaft,%} 42, 221, 236, n. 1; Ludwig Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 102; Geldner, {%Rigveda,%} {%Kommentar,%} 23, 24.</F>

{@Kaṅka@}¦ is the name of a bird, usually taken to mean ‘heron,’<sup>1</sup> but, at any rate in some passages, rather denoting some bird of prey.<sup>2</sup> It first appears in the Yajurveda Saṃhitās.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 92.</F> <F>2) Roth. St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v. Cf.%} Sāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka, xii. 13.</F> <F>3) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 4, 11, 1 ({%kaṅka-cit,%} an altar ‘piled in the form of a heron’); Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 31; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 12; Sāma- veda, ii. 9, 3, 6, 1</F>

{@Kaṅkata@}¦ is the name of an animal mentioned once in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> According to Sāyaṇa it is a destructive beast; perhaps, as Grassmann renders it, a ‘scorpion.’ <F>1) i. 191, 1. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 98.</F>

{@Kaṅkatīya@}¦ is the name of a family said in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> to have learned from {@Śāṇḍilya@} the piling up of the sacrificial fire ({%agni-cayana.%}) In the Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra<sup>2</sup> a Kaṅkati Brāhmaṇa, no doubt the textbook of the school, is referred to. It may have been identical with the Chāgaleya Brāhmaṇa, cited in the Baudhāyana Śrauta Sūtra.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) ix. 4, 4, 17.</F> <F>2) xiv. 20, 4.</F> <F>3) xxv. 5. {%Cf.%} Caland, {%Über das vituclle%} {%Sūtra des Baudhāyana,%} 40.</F>

{@Kaṅka-parvan@}¦ (‘heron-jointed’?), a term occurring once in the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> is applied to a snake, meaning perhaps ‘scorpion.’ As the Paippalāda recension has a different reading ({%aṅga-parvaṇaḥ%}), the passage may be corrupt. <F>1) vii. 56, 1. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches%} {%Leben,%} 94; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 426; Bloomfield, {%Hymns%} {%of the Atharvaveda,%} 553; Böhtlingk, Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>

{@Kaṭa@}¦ denotes a ‘mat,’ which was ‘made of reeds’ ({%vaitasa%}). The maker of mats from reeds ({%bidala-kārī%}) is mentioned in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā,<sup>2</sup> and the process of splitting reeds for the purpose is referred to in the Atharvaveda.<sup>3</sup> <div n="P"/>^1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā. v. 3, 12, 2. {%Cf.%} Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 3, 1, 3. <F>2) xxx. 8, with Mahīdhara's Com- mentary. {%Bidala-kāra%} is read in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 5, 1.</F> <F>3) vi. 138, 5. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 255.</F>

{@Kaṇṭakī-kārī,@}¦ ‘worker in thorns,’ is one of the victims at the human sacrifice (Puruṣamedha) in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā,<sup>1</sup> No doubt the thorns were cut up and used to plait mats ({@Kaṭa@}) or to stuff cushions. <F>1) xxx. 8. The Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 5, 1, has {%kaṇṭaka-kāra. Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 255.</F>

{@Kaṇva@}¦ is the name of an ancient Ṛṣi repeatedly referred to in the Rigveda and later.<sup>1</sup> His sons and descendants,<sup>2</sup> the Kaṇvas, are also often mentioned, especially in the eighth book of the Rigveda, the authorship of that book, as well as of part of the first, being attributed to this family. A descendant of Kaṇva is also denoted by the name in the singular, either alone<sup>3</sup> or accompanied by a patronymic, as Kaṇva Nārṣada<sup>4</sup> and Kaṇva Śrāyasa,<sup>5</sup> besides in the plural the Kaṇvas Sauśra- vasas.<sup>6</sup> The Kaṇva family appears to have been connected with the Atri family,<sup>7</sup> but not to have been of great importance.<sup>8</sup> In one passage of the Atharvaveda<sup>9</sup> they seem to be definitely regarded with hostility. <F>1) Rv. i. 36, 8. 10. 11. 17. 19; 39, 7. 9; 47, 5; 112, 5; 117, 18; 118, 7; 139, 9; v. 41, 4; viii. 5, 23. 25; 7, 18; 8, 20; 49, 10; 50, 10; x. 71, 11; 115, 5; 150, 5; Av. iv. 37, 1; vii. 15, 1; xviii. 3, 15; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xvii. 74; Pañca- viṃśa Brāhmaṇa, viii. 2, 2; ix. 2, 6; Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, xxviii. 8, Kaṇva- vat occurs in Rv. viii. 6, 11; 52, 8; Av. ii. 32, 3; Kaṇva-mant in Rv. viii. 2, 22.</F> <F>2) As {%Kaṇvāḥ%} (in the plural), Rv. i. 14, 2. 5; 37, 1. 14; 44, 8; 46, 9; 47. 2. 4-10; 49, 4; viii. 2, 16; 3, 16; 4, 2. 3; 5, 4; 6, 3. 18. 21. 31. 34. 47; 7, 32; 8, 3; 9, 14; 32, 1; 33, 3; 34, 4; as {%Kaṇvasya sūnavaḥ,%} Rv. i, 45, 5; as {%putrāḥ,%} viii. 8, 4. 8; as {%Kāṇvāyanāḥ,%} viii. 55, 4. {%Kāṇva%} is found in viii. 1, 8; 2, 40; 4, 20; 7, 19; 9, 3, 9; 10, 2.</F> <F>3) {%Eg.,%} Rv. i. 48, 4; viii. 34, 1, and probably elsewhere.</F> <F>4) Rv. i. 117, 8; Av. iv. 19, 2; Lud- wig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 150.</F> <F>5) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 4, 7, 5; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxi. 8; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 3, 9.</F> <F>6) Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xiii. 12. There is also Vatsa Kāṇva in Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xvi. 11, 20.</F> <F>7) Oldenberg, {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen%} {%Morgenländischen Gesellschaft,%} 42, 214.</F> <F>8) Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 3, 285. {%Cf.%} 1, 207, 438.</F> <F>9) Av. ii. 25. {%Cf.%} Vārttika on Pāṇini, iii. 1, 14; Bergaigne, {%Religion Védique,%} 2, 465; Hillebrandt, {%op. cit.,%} 1, 207; Oldenberg, {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 110. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Oldenberg, {%op. cit.,%} 216 {%et seq.;%} Ludwig, {%op. cit.,%} 3, 105.</F>

{@Kathā.@}¦ — The later use of this word<sup>1</sup> in the sense of a ‘philo- sophical discussion’ appears in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) Colebrooke, {%Miscellaneous Essays,%} 1, 293.</F> <F>2) i. 8, 1: {%hantodgīthe kathāṃ vadāma,%} ‘let us begin a discussion regarding the Udgītha.’</F>

{@Kadrū,@}¦ a word occurring only once in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> is interpreted by Ludwig<sup>2</sup> as the name of a priest, but it more probably means a Soma vessel.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) viii. 45, 26.</F> <F>2) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 162.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>

{@Kanaknaka,@}¦ a word occurring once in the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> either denotes a poison or is an adjective qualifying {%kāṇḍā-viṣa,%} a species of poison. <F>1) x. 4, 22. {%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Hymns%} {%of the Atharvaveda,%} 604; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 578.</F>

{@Kanā, Kanyā.@}¦ — Both these words, of which the former is very rare,<sup>1</sup> while the latter is the normal term from the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> onwards, denote ‘maiden’ or ‘young woman.’ It is doubtful whether Kanīnakā (accented on the final syllable) has this meaning,<sup>3</sup> or only denotes the pupil of the eye,<sup>4</sup> which is the sense of {%kanīnakā%} or {%kanīnikā%} (both accented on the ante- penultimate) in the later Saṃhitās and the Brāhmaṇas. See also {@Strī.@} <F>1) Rv. x. 61, 5, etc.</F> <F>2) i. 123, 10; 161, 5; iii. 23, 10, etc.; Av. i. 14, 2; xi. 5, 18; xii, 1, 25, etc.</F> <F>3) Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.,%} cites in this sense Rv. iv. 32, 23; x. 40, 9; Nirukta, iv. 15; but neither of the Rv. passages is at all clear.</F> <F>4) See Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Athar-%} {%vaveda,%} 401; Keith, {%Aitareya Āraṇyāka,%} 207. Other rare forms are {%kanyanā,%} Rv. viii. 35, 5; {%kauyalā,%} Av. v. 5, 3; xiv. 2, 52.</F>

{@Kapanā,@}¦ from its solitary occurrence in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> appears to mean a ‘worm’ that destroys the leaves of trees, and is so interpreted in the Nirukta.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) v. 54, 6.</F> <F>2) vi. 4. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches%} {%Leben,%} 97; Max Müller, {%Sacred Books of%} {%the East,%} 32, 330.</F>

{@Kaparda,@}¦ ‘braid,’ {@Kapardin,@} ‘wearing braids.’ These words refer to the Vedic custom of wearing the hair in braids or plaits. Thus a maiden is said to have her hair in four plaits ({%catuṣ-kapardā%}),<sup>1</sup> and the goddess Sinīvālī is described as ‘wear- ing fair braids’ ({%su-kapardā%}).<sup>2</sup> Men also wore their hair in this style, for both Rudra<sup>3</sup> and Pūṣan<sup>4</sup> are said to have done so, while the {@Vasiṣṭhas@}<sup>5</sup> were distinguished by wearing their hair in a plait on the right ({%dakṣiṇatas-kaparda%}). The opposite was to wear one's hair ‘plain’ ({%pulasti%}).<sup>6</sup> See also {@Opaśa.@} <F>1) Rv. x. 114, 3.</F> <F>2) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xi. 56.</F> <F>3) Rv. i. 114, 1. 5; Vājasaneyi Saṃ- hitā, xvi. 10. 29. 43. 48. 59.</F> <F>4) Rv. vi. 55, 2; ix. 67. 11.</F> <F>5) Rv. vii. 33, 1. {%Cf.%} 83, 8.</F> <F>6) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xvi. 43. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 264, 265; Muir, {%Sanskrit Texts,%} v. 462; Max Müller, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 32, 424.</F>

1. {@Kapi,@}¦ ‘monkey,’ occurs only once in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> with reference to Vṛṣā-kapi, the ‘Man-ape,’ in the dialogue of Indra and Indrāṇī in the presence of Vṛṣākapi. There the ape is termed the ‘tawny’ ({%harita%}). In the Atharvaveda<sup>2</sup> the monkey is mentioned several times as hairy, and an enemy of dogs. That the ape was tamed appears from its position in the Vṛṣākapi hymn, and from the mention, in the Taittirīya Saṃ- hitā,<sup>3</sup> of a {@Mayu@} as belonging to the forest. See also {@Mayu,@} {@Markaṭa,@} and {@Puruṣa Hastin.@} <F>1) x. 86. 5. {%Cf.%} Oldenberg, {%Religion%} {%des Veda,%} 174; Geldner, {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 22 {%et seq.;%} von Schroeder, {%Mysterium%} {%und Mimus,%} 304 {%et seq.;%} Schirmeisen, {%Die Arischen Göttergestalten,%} 218 {%et seq.;%} Tilak, {%Orion,%} 170-197.</F> <F>2) iii. 9, 4; iv. 32, 11; vi. 49, 1. {%Cf.%} also Chāndogya Upaniṣad, i. 6, 7 ({%kapy-āsa,%} ‘seat of an ape’).</F> <F>3) iv. 2, 10, 1. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altin-%} {%disches Leben,%} 85, 86.</F>
2. {@Kapi@}¦ is, according to the St. Petersburg Dictionary, another name for Luśa Khārgali in the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā (xxx. 2), but the name appears rather to be {@Luśākapi.@}

{@Kapiñjala,@}¦ the name of the ‘francoline partridge’ or ‘hazel- cock,’ is found in all the Yajurveda Saṃhitās,<sup>1</sup> and occasionally later.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 5, 1, 1; v. 5, 16, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 1; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xii. 10; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 20. 38.</F> <F>2) Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 6, 3, 3; v. 5, 4, 4; xiii. 5, 1, 13; Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 154, 2 ({%Transactions of the%} {%Connecticut Academy of Arts and Sciences,%} 15, 181). <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 91.</F>

{@Kapila@}¦ appears in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad<sup>1</sup> as a teacher, according to Weber<sup>2</sup> and Garbe,<sup>3</sup> who think that the expres- sion {%kapila ṛṣiḥ%} there refers to the founder of the Sāṅkhya philosophy. But this is doubtful.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) v. 2.</F> <F>2) {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 24 {%et seq.;%} 5, 412; {%Indian Literature,%} 236.</F> <F>3) {%Sāṅkhya Philosophie,%} 27 {%et seq.;%} Translation of the Śāṅkhyatattvakau- mudī, 531.</F> <F>4) Max Müller, {%Sacred Books of the%} {%East,%} 2, xli, and Deussen, in his trans- lation ({%Sechzig Upanishads,%} 304), do not take the word as a teacher's name. The latter renders {%kapila ṛṣiḥ,%} by ‘the red sage,’ as referring to Hiraṇya- garbha.</F>

{@Kapi-vana Bhauvāyana@}¦ is mentioned as a teacher in the Yajurveda Saṃhitās<sup>1</sup> and the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> A rite called Kapivana's Dvyaha (‘ceremony lasting two days’) is also referred to in the Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, i. 4, 5; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxxii. 2.</F> <F>2) xx. 13, 4.</F> <F>3) xxv. 2, 3. {%Cf.%} Āśvalāyana Srauta Sūtra, x. 2. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 24, 3, 473; Hopkins, {%Transactions of the%} {%Connecticut Academy of Arts and Sciences,%} 15, 55, n. 2; Hillebrandt, {%Vedische%} {%Mythologie,%} 2, 157.</F>

{@Kapota@}¦ is the name of a bird, probably the ‘pigeon’ (its sense in the later language), occurring from the Rigveda onwards.<sup>1</sup> It is associated in some passages<sup>2</sup> with the owl ({@Ulūka@}) as a messenger of Nirṛti (‘dissolution,’ ‘misfortune’). This aspect of the pigeon as a bird of evil omen is probably based on an ancient belief which is also found beyond the confines of India.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) Rv. i. 30, 4; Av. xx. 135, 12; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 4; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 23. 38.</F> <F>2) Rv. x. 165, 1-5; Av. vi. 29, 2.</F> <F>3) {%Cf.%} Schrader, {%Prchistoric Antiquities,%} 253. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 89; St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>

{@Kabandha Ātharvaṇa@}¦ is mentioned in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad<sup>1</sup> along with {@Sudhanvan Āṅgirasa,@} as a teacher, but is semi-mythical. His son was {@Vicārin Kābandhi.@} <F>1) vi. 7, 1. {%Cf.%} also Gopatha Brāh- maṇa, i. 2, 9. 18; Hillebrandt, {%Vedische%} {%Mythologie,%} 2, 176, n. 4; Weber, {%Indian%} {%Literature,%} 149.</F>

{@Kama-dyū@}¦ appears once in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as the wife of {@Vimada.@} She is probably identical with the ‘maiden’ ({%yoṣā%}) of {@Purumitra,@} no doubt his daughter. She is elsewhere<sup>2</sup> referred to in connexion with Vimada, who appears to have taken her for his bride against the will of her father. <F>1) x. 65, 12.</F> <F>2) i. 117, 20; x. 39, 7. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 310.</F>
{@Kambala@}¦ denotes in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> a ‘woollen coverlet’ or ‘blanket.’ <F>1) xiv. 2, 66. 67. {%Cf.%} Nirukta, ii. 2.</F>

{@Kamboja. — Yāska,@}¦ in the Nirukta,<sup>1</sup> refers to the speech of the Kambojas as differing from that of the other Āryas. The Kambojas were later settled to the north-west of the Indus, and are known as Kambujiya in the old Persian inscriptions. A teacher, {@Kāmboja Aupamanyava,@} pupil of {@Madragāra,@} is mentioned in the Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> This points to a possible connexion of the Madras, or more probably the {@Uttara Madras,@} with the Kambojas, who probably had Iranian as well as Indian affinities. <F>1) ii. 2.</F> <F>2) {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 372. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 102; Weber, {%Indische Streifen,%} 2, 493; 3, 384; {%Indische Studien,%} 10, 7; {%Episches im%} {%vedischen Ritual,%} 45; Max Müller, {%Zeit-%} {%schrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen%} {%Gesellschaft,%} 7, 373. On the relation of Indian and Iranian, see also Jacobi, {%Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society,%} 1909, 721 {%et seq.;%} 1910, 457 {%et seq.;%} Oldenberg, {%ibid.,%} 1095 {%et seq.;%} Keith, {%ibid.,%} 1100 {%et%} {%seq.;%} Kennedy, {%ibid.,%} 1107 {%et seq.;%} and see {@Parśu.@}</F>

{@Karañja,@}¦ a word which in the Sūtras and later denotes the tree {%Pongamia glabra,%} occurs only twice in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as the name of a foe of Indra, but whether a demon or a man<sup>2</sup> is intended remains uncertain. <F>1) i. 53, 8; x. 48, 8.</F> <F>2) Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 63; Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 149; Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 3, 292.</F>

{@Karambha@}¦ is the name, from the Rigveda onwards,<sup>1</sup> of a kind of porridge made of grain ({@Yava@}), which was unhusked, parched slightly, and kneaded.<sup>2</sup> It was the especial sacrificial portion of Pūṣan, no doubt in his capacity of an agricultural deity. Karmabha was also made of barley ({@Upavāka@})<sup>3</sup> or of sesame ({@Tirya@}).<sup>4</sup> <F>1) Rv. i. 187, 16; iii. 52, 7; vi. 56, 1; 57, 2; viii. 102, 2; Av. iv. 7, 2. 3; vi. 16, 1; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 1, 10, 2; vi. 5, 11, 4, etc.</F> <F>2) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 5, 2, 14; iv. 2, 4, 18. {%Cf.%} Schrader, {%Prehistoric%} {%Antiquities,%} 317; Eggeling, {%Sacred Books%} {%of the East,%} 12, 395, n. 1.</F> <F>3) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xix. 22.</F> <F>4) Av. iv. 7, 3, but see Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 377; Whit- ney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 155. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 270.</F>
{@Karikrata@}¦ denotes, according to Zimmer,<sup>1</sup> a snake in the Atharvaveda.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 95</F> <F>2) x. 4, 13. The Paippalāda version has Kanikrada.</F>

{@Karīra,@}¦ the name of a leafless shrub, {%Capparis aphylla,%} or its fruit, first appears in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) ii. 4, 9, 2; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xi. 11; xxxvi. 7; Śatapatha Brahmaṇa, ii. 5, 2, 11.</F>

{@Karīṣa@}¦ denotes ‘dry cow dung’ in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> The Atharvaveda<sup>2</sup> shows that the value of the natural manure of animals in the fields was appreciated. <F>1) ii. 1, 1, 7.</F> <F>2) Av. iii. 14, 3. 4; xix. 31, 3. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 236.</F>

1. {@Karkandhu@}¦ is the ordinary word for ‘jujube,’ the tree ({%Zizyphus jujuba%}) and the fruit, from the Yajurveda Saṃhitās onwards.<sup>1</sup> The berry is red ({%rohita%}).<sup>2</sup> Compare {@Kuvala@} and {@Badara,@} which denote the fruit. <F>1) Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xii. 10; Maitrā- yaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 11, 2; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xix. 23. 91; xxi. 32; xxiv. 2; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, v. 5, 4, 10; xii. 7, 2, 9; 9, 1, 5, etc.; Jaiminīya Brāh- maṇa, ii. 156. 5.</F> <F>2) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 2. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 242.</F>

2. {@Karkandhu@}¦ is only the name borne by a protégé of the Aśvins in the Rigveda (i. 112, 6). Its identity with the word for jujube indicates that the latter, though not otherwise mentioned there, was known at the time of the Rigveda.

{@Karkari,@}¦ a musical instrument, probably the ‘lute,’ occurs from the Rigveda onwards.<sup>1</sup> The Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā<sup>2</sup> mentions cattle branded on the ears with a mark resembling a lute ({%karkari-karṇyaḥ%}). <F>1) Rv. ii. 43, 3; Av. iv. 37. 4. {%Cf.%} xx. 132. 3. 8.</F> <F>2) iv. 2, 9. {%Cf.%} Delbrück, {%Gurupūjā-%} {%kaumudī,%} 48, 49. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 289.</F>

{@Karkī@}¦ may denote in one passage of the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> a white cow,’ according to the suggestion of Roth.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) iv. 38, 6. 7. {%Cf.%} Bloomfield {%Hymns%} {%of the Atharvaveda,%} 414.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary and Böhtlingk's Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>

{@Karṇa-śobhana@}¦ denotes an ‘ornament for the ear’ in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> apparently for the use of men. Some deity is called ‘gold-eared’ in another passage of the Rigveda.<sup>2</sup> Hopkins<sup>3</sup> considers the use of ear-rings later than that of necklets and wristlets. <F>1) viii. 78, 3.</F> <F>2) i. 122, 14. See also i. 64, 10.</F> <F>3) {%Journal of the American Oriental%} {%Society,%} 17, 35. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 262.</F>
{@Karṇa-śravas Āṅgirasa@}¦ is mentioned in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa (xiii. 11, 14) as a seer of Sāmans or chants, the same tale being told of him as of {@Dāvasu.@}

{@Karmāra,@}¦ the ‘smith,’ is several times mentioned with approval in the Vedic Saṃhitās.<sup>1</sup> In the Atharvaveda<sup>2</sup> smiths appear with fishermen ({%dhīvānaḥ%}) and chariot-builders ({%ratha-%} {%kārāḥ%}), all being classified as clever workers ({%manīṣiṇaḥ%}): possibly a quasi-caste of smiths was already developing from the guild organization that probably existed.<sup>3</sup> <div n="P"/>Little is known of the smith's methods of work and of his tools. No doubt he smelted ({%dhmā%}) the ore in the fire; hence he is called {%dhmātṛ,%} the ‘smelter.’<sup>4</sup> Mention is also made of [Page1-141+ 50] his bellows of birds' feathers.<sup>5</sup> He made metal vessels ({%gharma%} {%ayasmaya%})<sup>6</sup> to be put on the fire: even the Soma cup could occasionally be made of hammered metal ({%ayo-hata%}).<sup>7</sup> <F>1) Rv. x. 72, 2; Av. iii. 5, 6; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xvii. 13; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 9, 5; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xvi. 27; xxx. 7. {%Cf. karmāra,%} Rv. ix. 112, 2; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 3, 1.</F> <F>2) iii. 5, 6. The exact sense of the passage is doubtful. Zimmer, {%Altin-%} {%disches Leben,%} 252; Bloomfield, {%Hymns%} {%of the Atharvaveda,%} 144; and Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 92, take the reference to be to ‘skilled chariot-makers’ ({%dhīvāno ratha-kārāḥ%}) and ‘clever smiths,’ but this is perhaps less likely. The commentator interprets {%dhīvānaḥ%} as ‘fishermen’ (in the later language {%dhīvara%} means both a ‘clever man’ and a ‘fisherman’).</F> <F>3) {%Cf.%} Fick, {%Die sociale Gliederung,%} 182.</F> <F>4) Rv. v. 9. 5.</F> <F>5) Rv. ix. 112, 2.</F> <F>6) Rv. v. 30, 15.</F> <F>7) Rv. ix. 1, 2. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%op. cit.,%} 252, 253; Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 17, 196 {%et seq.; Über%} {%den Rājasūya,%} 19 {%et seq.%}</F>

{@Karvara,@}¦ a word found in one passage of the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> seems to mean some kind of fish<sup>2</sup> caught by a fisherman ({%pauñjiṣṭha%}). <F>1) x. 4, 19.</F> <F>2) Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 96; Whitney, Translation of the Atharva- veda, 578.</F>
{@Karṣū,@}¦ a rare word found in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> denotes a ‘furrow’ or ‘trench.’ <F>1) i. 8, 1, 3; xiii. 8, 3, 10. {%Cf.%} Schrader, {%Prehistoric Antiquities,%} 283.</F>

{@Kalaviṅka,@}¦ a name of the ‘sparrow,’ is found in the Yajurveda Saṃhitās,<sup>1</sup> and occasionally later.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 5, 1, 2; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 1; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xii. 10; Vājasaneyi Samhitā, xxiv. 20. 31.</F> <F>2) Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 6, 3, 4; v. 5, 4, 5; Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 154, 3 ({%Transactions of the Connecticut Academy%} {%of Arts and Sciences,%} 15, 181). {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 91.</F>

{@Kalaśa@}¦ is, from the Rigveda onwards,<sup>1</sup> a common word for ‘pot’ or ‘jar,’ probably either formed of a gourd or made of clay (unburnt or baked), as we know that both kinds of pot were in use.<sup>2</sup> The wooden Soma tub ({%droṇa-kalaśa%}) is frequently referred to in the ritual. See also {@Kośa.@} <F>1) Rv. i. 117, 12; iii. 32, 15; iv. 27, 5; 32, 19, etc.; Av. iii. 12, 7; ix. 1, 6; 4, 15; xviii. 4, 13, etc. In Rv. x. 32, 9, the word, according to the Śt. Peters- burg Dictionary, is used as a proper name, but the passage is very doubtful.</F> <F>2) Av. iv. 17, 4; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, i. 1, 8, 1; iv. 1, 5, 4; v. 1, 7, 2; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, i. 22; xi. 59. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 253; Eggel- ing, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 26, 257; Oertel, {%Transactions of the Connecticut%} {%Academy of Arts and Sciences,%} 15, 185, n. 3; Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 183 {%et seq.%}</F>

{@Kalā@}¦ denotes a fractional part, normally ‘one-sixteenth,’ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> It is often mentioned in connexion with {@Śapha,@} ‘one-eighth.’ <F>1) viii. 47, 17.</F> <F>2) Av. vi. 96, 3; xix. 57, 1; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vi. 1, 10, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 7, 7; Śatapatha Brāh- maṇa, iii. 3, 3, 1; xii. 8, 3, 13, etc.; Nirukta, xi. 12. {%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%Journal%} {%of the American Oriental Society,%} 16, 278; Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 259.</F>
1. {@Kali.@}¦ See {@Akṣa.@}

2. {@Kali@}¦ occurs in the Rigveda, twice in the singular<sup>1</sup> as the name of a protégé of the Aśvins, and once in the plural.<sup>2</sup> The persons meant in the latter passage seem to be different from the former one. The Kalis are once mentioned in the Atharvaveda<sup>3</sup> beside the Gandharvas.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) i. 112, 15; x. 39, 8.</F> <F>2) viii. 66, 15.</F> <F>3) x. 10, 13.</F> <F>4) These Kalis may be connected with dicing, as in the Atharvaveda the Apsarases, the wives of the Gandharvas, are fond of dice, and bestow luck at play. See Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} p. 135. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%Journal of the American%} {%Oriental Society,%} 17, 89; Ludwig, Trans- lation of the Rigveda, 3, 163.</F>
{@Kalpa@}¦ in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka (ii. 10) seems to denote Kalpa Sūtra.

{@Kalmāṣa-grīva@}¦ (‘speckled-neck’) is the name of a snake in the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) iii. 27, 5 (where the Paippalāda recension has {%kulmāṣa-%}); xii. 3, 59. {%Cf.%} Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 10, 2. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 94, 95.</F>

{@Kalyāṇa@}¦ is the name, in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> of an Āṅgirasa who saw the Aurṇāyava Sāman. <F>1) xii. 11, 10. {%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%Transactions of the Connecticut Academy of Arts and%} {%Sciences,%} 15, 68, n. 2.</F>

{@Kavaca@}¦ denotes a ‘corselet’ or ‘breastplate’ in the Atharva- veda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> There is nothing to show whether it was made of metal, but that it was so is quite possible (see {@Varman@}). The Atharvaveda<sup>3</sup> refers to a ‘corselet-strap’ ({%kavaca-pāśa%}), which may point to a linen corselet such as those known to Herodotus.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) Av. xi. 10, 22 ({%kavacin%}).</F> <F>2) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 2, 2, 7; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vii. 19, 2; Nirukta, v. 25 ({%kavaca%}); Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 1, 6, 3; 4, 1, 5; Aitareya Brāh- maṇa, iii. 48; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xvi. 45 ({%kavacin%}).</F> <F>3) xi. 10, 22.</F> <F>4) Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Atharva-%} {%veda,%} 129, and Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 659, seem to recognize coats of mail only.</F>

{@Kavaṣa@}¦ is mentioned in a hymn of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as one of those whom, together with the {@Druhyu@} king, Indra overthrew for the {@Tṛtsus.@} The Anukramaṇī (Index) also attributes to him the authorship of several hymns of the Rigveda, including two (x. 32. 33) that deal with a prince {@Kuruśravaṇa@} and his descendant {@Upamaśravas.@} There seems no reason to doubt this attribution, which is accepted by both Zimmer<sup>2</sup> and Geldner.<sup>3</sup> The former holds that Kavaṣa was the Purohita of the joint tribes named {@Vaikarṇa,@} in whom he sees the Kuru- Krivi (Pañcāla) peoples, and that Kavaṣa in that capacity is mentioned in the Rigveda as representative of those peoples. He also suggests that the language of Rigveda x. 33, 4 is best explained by the reduced position in which the Kuru-Krivis found themselves on their defeat by the Tṛtsus. Ludwig,<sup>4</sup> on the other hand, thinks that Kavaṣa was the priest of the five peoples. Geldner<sup>5</sup> holds that Kavaṣa was the Purohita of Kuruśravaṇa, by whose son, Upamaśravas, he was ill-treated, and that he composed Rigveda x. 33 to deprecate the anger of his royal master. Hopkins<sup>6</sup> thinks that he was a king. <div n="P"/>In the Brāhmaṇas of the Rigveda<sup>7</sup> mention is made of [Page1-144+ 45] Kavaṣa Ailūṣa, who was a Brāhmaṇa born of a female slave, and was reproached on this ground by the other Ṛṣis. He is possibly identical with the Kavaṣa of the Rigveda. <F>1) vii. 18, 12.</F> <F>2) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 127.</F> <F>3) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 150.</F> <F>4) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 139.</F> <F>5) {%Loc. cit.%}</F> <F>6) {%Journal of the American Oriental%} {%Society,%} 15, 261, 263.</F> <F>7) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 19; Kauṣī- taki Brāhmaṇa, xii. 1, 3. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 3, 459; Lanman, {%Sanskrit Reader,%} 386, 387; Pargiter, {%Journal of the Royal Asiatic%} {%Society,%} 1910, 50.</F>

{@Kaśa@}¦ is the name of an unknown animal mentioned as a victim at the horse sacrifice in the Yajurveda Saṃhitās.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 17, 1; 18, 1; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 26; 38. {%Cf.%} Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 7. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 84.</F>

{@Kaśipu@}¦ denotes a ‘mat’ or ‘cushion’ made, according to the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> by women from reeds ({%naḍa%}), which they crushed for the purpose by means of stones. {@Kaśyapa,@}¦ a word denoting ‘tortoise,’ occurs in the Atharva- veda<sup>1</sup> and often later.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) iv. 20. 7.</F> <F>2) Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 18; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 37; Sata- patha Brāhmaṇa, vii. 5, 1, 5; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 6. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 18, 86; Bloomfield, {%American Journal of Phil-%} {%ology,%} 17, 403.</F>

{@Kaśyapa@}¦ is the name of a sage who is mentioned only once in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> but is a common figure in the later Saṃhitās.<sup>2</sup> He is always of a mythical character, as belonging to the distant past. According to the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa,<sup>3</sup> he anointed King {@Viśvakarman Bhauvana,@} and in the Upaniṣads<sup>4</sup> he is mentioned as a Ṛṣi. The Kaśyapas appear in connexion with {@Janam-@} {@ejaya@} in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.<sup>5</sup> <F>1) ix. 114, 2.</F> <F>2) Sāmaveda, i. 1, 2, 4, 10; 4, 2, 3, 2 (but in these passages the St. Peters- burg Dictionary, {%s.v.,%} accepts the sense of a divine being, identical with Prajā- pati); Av. i. 14, 4; ii. 33, 7; iv. 20, 7; 29, 3; 37, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iv. 2, 9, Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, iii. 62.</F> <F>3) viii. 21; Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 7, 1, 15.</F> <F>4) Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, ii. 2, 6; Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa, iv. 3, 1 (in a quotation).</F> <F>5) vii. 27. {%Cf.%} Oldenberg, {%Zeitschrift%} {%der Deutschen Morgenländischen Gesell-%} {%schaft,%} 42, 235, n. 1.</F>

{@Kaśyapa Naidhruvi@}¦ is mentioned as a teacher in the last Vaṃśa (list of teachers) of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, vi. 4, 33 (Mādhyaṃdina = vi. 5, 3, Kāṇva).</F>
{@Kaṣkaṣa@}¦ designates a kind of worm in the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) v. 23, 7. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 98.</F>

{@Ka-stambhī@}¦ denotes in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> a piece of wood used as a prop for the end of a wagon-pole to rest on. <F>1) i. 1, 2, 9. {%Cf.%} Caland and Henry, {%L'Agniṣṭoma,%} 49; Eggeling, {%Sacred Books of%} {%the East,%} 12, 14, n. 1.</F>

{@Kahoḍa Kauṣītaki@}¦<sup>1</sup> or {@Kauṣītakeya@}<sup>2</sup> is mentioned in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad,<sup>2</sup> and the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka,<sup>1</sup> as a teacher, contemporary with Yājña- valkya. {%Cf.%} {@Kāhoḍi.@} <F>1) Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 4, 3, 1; Sāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka, xv.</F> <F>2) Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, iii. 5, 1.</F> <F>1) Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 4, 3, 1; Sāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka, xv.</F> <F>2) Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, iii. 5, 1.</F> <F>1) Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 4, 3, 1; Sāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka, xv.</F>
{@Kākambīra@}¦ is the name in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> of a useful tree of some kind. <F>1) vi. 48, 17. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 62.</F>
{@Kākṣa-seni@}¦ is the patronymic (‘son of {@Kakṣasena’@}) of {@Abhipratārin@} in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa (xiv. 1, 12).

{@Kāṇṭhe-viddhi@}¦ (‘descendant of Kaṇṭheviddha’) is mentioned as a teacher in the Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 382.</F>

{@Kānīna@}¦ in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> apparently denotes the ‘son of a maiden.’ See {@Pati.@} <F>1) v. 5, 8. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 334.</F>
{@Kāṇḍā-viṣa@}¦ in the Atharvaveda (x. 4, 22) denotes some kind of poison. {%Cf.%} {@Kanaknaka.@}

{@Kābandhi@}¦ (‘descendant of Kabandha’) is the patronymic of {@Vicārin@} in the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa (i. 2, 9. 18).

{@Kāmpīla.@}¦ — In one passage of the Yajurveda Saṃhitās<sup>1</sup> the epithet Kāmpīla-vāsinī is applied to a woman, perhaps the king's Mahiṣī or chief wife, whose duty it was to sleep beside the slaughtered animal at the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha). So also Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 204; von Schroeder, Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, 1, xxi; {%Indiens Literatur und%} {%Cultur,%} 164; Eggeling, {%Sacred Books of%} {%the East,%} 44, 321, 322.</F>

{@Kāmboja@}¦ (‘native of {@Kamboja@}’) {@Aupamanyava@} (‘descendant of Upamanyu’) is mentioned as a teacher in the Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 372; {%Episches im vedischen Ritual,%} 45: Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 102.</F>

{@Kārapacava@}¦ is the name in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> of a place on the {@Yamunā.@} <F>1) xxv. 10, 23. {%Cf.%} Āśvalāyana Srauta Sūtra, xii. 6; Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xiii. 29, 25; Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xxiv. 6, 10; Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 34.</F>

{@Kāraskara@}¦ is the name of a people mentioned in the Baudhā- yana Śrauta Sūtra<sup>1</sup> and the Āpastamba<sup>2</sup> and Hiraṇyakeśi<sup>3</sup> Sūtras. <F>1) xx. 13. (14). {%Cf.%} Baudhāyana Dharma Sūtra, i. 2, 14.</F> <F>2) xxii. 6, 18.</F> <F>3) xvii. 6, {%Cf.%} Bühler, {%Sacred Books%} {%of the East,%} 14, 148; Caland, {%Zcitschrift%} {%der Deutschen Morgenländischen Gesell-%} {%schaft,%} 56, 553.</F>

{@Kāri@}¦ is the name of one of the victims of the human sacrifice (Puruṣamedha) in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā,<sup>1</sup> and is there dedi- cated to ‘laughter.’ The commentator Mahīdhara<sup>2</sup> interprets the word as ‘worker’ ({%karaṇa-śīla%}), but the St. Petersburg Dictionary suggests that it means a ‘jubilant’ person (as derived from the root {%kṛ,%} ‘to praise’). <F>1) xxx. 6. 20; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 2, 1.</F> <F>2) On Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, {%loc. cit.%}</F>
{@Kārīradi@}¦ is the name of persons mentioned in the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa (ii. 4, 4) as holding a special view of the Udgītha (Sāmaveda Chant).

{@Kāru,@}¦ ‘poet,’ is a word almost confined to the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> There is evidence that the poet was regarded as a professional man, just as much as the physician ({@Bhiṣaj@}).<sup>2</sup> The poets, no doubt, mainly lived at the courts of princes amid their re- tainers,<sup>3</sup> though they would probably also sing the praises of rich merchants. There was probably no essential connexion between the priest and the poet. Though the priest was often a poet, yet poetry can hardly have been restricted to the priestly caste. Indeed, at the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha) the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>4</sup> expressly requires that one of the singers of pane- gyrics should be a Rājanya, while the other was a Brāhmaṇa, both singing verses of their own composition. The Anukra- maṇī (Index) in several cases<sup>5</sup> attributes hymns of the Rigveda to princes; and even though this may often be merely the same sort of procedure<sup>6</sup> as has made Śūdraka the author of the Mṛcchakaṭikā, or Harṣa of the Ratnāvalī, and has given us royal teachers of the Brahman doctrine,<sup>7</sup> still the Indian tradition evidently saw nothing odd in the idea of non- Brāhmaṇas as poets. Most of the non-sacred poetry has, [Page1-151+ 37] however, disappeared, for the epic is a product, as it stands, of a later period. See also {@Ṛṣi.@} <F>1) i. 148, 2; 165, 12; 177, 5; 178, 3; ii. 43, 1; iii. 33, 8; 39, 7; v. 33, 7; vii. 27; 68, 9; 72, 4, etc.: Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, i. 8, 7; Gopatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 2, 21.</F> <F>2) ix. 112. 3.</F> <F>3) vii. 73. 1.</F> <F>4) xiii. 1, 5, 1; 4, 3, 5.</F> <F>5) {%E.g.,%} x. 92 is attributed to Śāryāta Mānava.</F> <F>6) See Pischel, {%Vedische Studien,%} 3, 202.</F> <F>7) Weber, {%Episches im vedischen Ritual,%} 20, n. 4, sees in Av. xx. a recension of Kṣatriya character. He also finds Kṣatriyas in {@Viśvāmitra@} and {@Kakṣīvant,@} but hardly with reason. {%Cf.%} {@Varṇa.@}</F>

{@Kārotara@}¦ appears to denote in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> and occasionally later,<sup>2</sup> a ‘filter’ or ‘sieve’ for purifying the liquor called {@Surā.@} <F>1) i. 116, 7.</F> <F>2) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xix. 16, 82; Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, xii. 9, 1, 2; Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, ii. 7. {%Cf.%} Zim- mer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 280.</F>

{@Kārṣmarya@}¦ is the name of a tree ({%Gmelina arborea%}) which is often alluded to in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā,<sup>1</sup> the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā,<sup>2</sup> and the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) v. 2, 7, 3. 4; vi. 2, 1, 5.</F> <F>2) iii. 2, 6; 7, 9.</F> <F>3) iii. 4, 1, 6; 8, 2, 17; iv. 3, 3, 6; vii. 4, 1, 37. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches%} {%Leben,%} 62.</F>

{@Kāla,@}¦ the generic expression for ‘time,’ first occurs in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> where, however, it is used only once, in the late tenth book. It is known to the Atharvaveda,<sup>2</sup> where Kāla has already developed the sense of time as fate. The word is frequent in the Brāhmaṇas,<sup>3</sup> superseding the earlier use of {@Ṛtu.@} The more general division of time is into ‘past’ ({%bhūta%}), ‘present’ ({%bhavat%}), and ‘future’ ({%bhaviṣyat%}).<sup>4</sup> For other divisions see {@Ahan, Māsa, Saṃvatsara.@} <F>1) x. 42, 9.</F> <F>2) xix. 53. 54.</F> <F>3) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 7, 3, 3; ii. 4, 2, 4; iii. 8, 3, 36; vii. 2, 2, 21, etc.</F> <F>4) {%E.g.,%} Sāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka, vii. 20.</F>

{@Kālakā@}¦ is the name of one of the victims at the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha) in the Yajurveda Saṃhitās,<sup>1</sup> variously identified with a bird<sup>2</sup> or a chameleon.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 15, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 16; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 35.</F> <F>2) Mahīdhara on Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, {%loc. cit.%}</F> <F>3) Sāyaṇa on Taittirīya Saṃhitā, {%loc.%} {%cit. Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 99.</F>

{@Kāla-kāñja.@}¦ — In the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> mention is made of the Kālakāñjas as being in the sky. Both Roth<sup>2</sup> and Zimmer<sup>3</sup> hold that some constellation is meant. But as the defeat of the Kālakāñjas is one of Indra's exploits,<sup>4</sup> it is doubtful whether any stress can be laid on that interpretation of the passage in the Atharvaveda. Whitney<sup>5</sup> suggests that the three stars of Orion are meant, Bloomfield<sup>6</sup> that the galaxy or the stars in general are intended. <F>1) vi. 80, 2.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>3) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 353.</F> <F>4) Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, viii. 1, {%Cf.%} also Maitrāyanī Saṃhitā, i. 6, 9; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 1, 2, 4-6; Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad, iii, 1.</F> <F>5) Translation of the Atharvaveda, 341.</F> <F>6) {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 500; {%Journal of the American Oriental Society,%} 15, 163-169. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 410, 414 {%et seq.;%} 3, 465; Oertel, {%Journal%} {%of the American Oriental Society,%} 19, 121.</F>

{@Kāvaṣeya@}¦ (‘descendant of Kavaṣa’) is the constant patro- nymic of {@Tura.@} The Kāvaṣeyas are also mentioned as teachers of philosophical points in the Rigveda Āraṇyakas.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Aitareya Āraṇyaka, iii. 2, 6; Sāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka, viii. 11. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 391, n.; 2, 418; Keith, {%Aitareya Āraṇyaka,%} 257.</F>

{@Kāvya@}¦ (‘descendant of Kavi’) is the constant<sup>1</sup> patronymic of {@Uśanas.@} In the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa it is also applied to {@Iḍhat@}<sup>2</sup> and {@Ukṣṇorandhra.@}<sup>3</sup> <F>1) Rv. i. 51, 11; 83, 5; 121, 12; vi. 20. 11; viii. 23, 17; Av. iv. 29, 6; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 5, 8, 5, etc.</F> <F>2) xiv. 9, 16.</F> <F>3) xiii. 9, 19. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%Transactions of the Con-%} {%necticut Academy of Arts and Sciences,%} 15, 48, 49.</F>

{@Kāśa.@}¦ — Roth<sup>1</sup> finds this word, which denotes a species of grass ({%Saccharum spontaneum%}) used for mats, etc., in one passage of the Rigveda,<sup>2</sup> but the reading is uncertain. The word has this sense in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>2) x. 100, 10.</F> <F>3) vi. 9, 1.</F>

{@Kāśi, Kāśya.@}¦ — The name Kāśi denotes (in the plural<sup>1</sup>) the people of Kāśi (Benares), and Kāśya, the king of Kāśi. The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> tells of {@Dhṛtarāṣṭra,@} king of Kāśi, who was defeated by {@Śatānīka Sātrājita,@} with the result that the Kāśis, down to the time of the Brāhmaṇa, gave up the kindling of the sacred fire. Sātrājita was a {@Bharata.@} We hear also of {@Ajātaśatru@} as a king of Kāśi;<sup>3</sup> and no doubt {@Bhadrasena@} {@Ajātaśatrava,@} a contemporary of {@Uddālaka,@} was also a king of Kāśi. <div n="P"/>The Kāśis and {@Videhas@} were closely connected, as was natural in view of their geographical position. The compound name Kāśi-Videha occurs in the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad;<sup>4</sup> in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad<sup>5</sup> {@Gārgī@} describes Ajātaśatru as either a Kāśi or a Videha king. The Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra<sup>6</sup> [Page1-154+ 49] mentions one Purohita as acting for the kings of Kāśi, Kosala, and Videha; and the Baudhāyana Śrauta Sūtra<sup>7</sup> mentions Kāśi and Videha in close proximity. Weber,<sup>8</sup> indeed, throws out the suggestion that the Kāśis and the Videhas together con- stitute the {@Uśīnaras,@} whose name is very rare in Vedic literature. <div n="P"/>As Kosala and Videha were in close connexion, Kāśi and Kosala are found combined in the compound name Kāśi- Kauśalyas of the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa.<sup>9</sup> <div n="P"/>Though Kāśi is a late word, it is quite possible that the town is older, as the river {@Varaṇāvatī@} referred to in the Athar- vaveda<sup>10</sup> may be connected with the later Vārāṇasī (Benares). <div n="P"/>It is significant that while the Kāśis, Kosalas, and Videhas were united, any relations which the Kuru-Pañcala peoples may have had with them were hostile. It is a fair conclusion that between these two great groups of peoples there did exist some political conflict as well as probably a difference of culture in some degree. The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>11</sup> in the story of the advance of Āryan civilization over Kosala and Videha, preserves a clear tradition of this time, and a piece of evidence that in the Kuru-Pañcāla country lay the real centre of the Brāhmaṇa culture (see also {@Kuru-Pañcāla@}). That the Kosala-Videhas were originally settlers of older date than the Kuru-Pañcālas is reasonably obvious from their geographical position, but the true Brāhmaṇa culture appears to have been brought to them from the Kuru-Pañcala country. It is very probable that the East was less Āryan than the West, and that it was less completely reduced under Brahmin spiritual supremacy, as the movement of Buddhism was Eastern, and the Buddhist texts<sup>12</sup> reveal a position in which the Kṣatriyas rank above Brāhmaṇas. With this agrees the fact that the later Vedic texts<sup>13</sup> display [Page1-155+ 43] towards the people of Magadha a marked antipathy, which may be reasonably explained by that people's lack of orthodoxy, and which may perhaps be traced as far back as the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā.<sup>14</sup> It is, of course, possible that the Kosala-Videhas and Kāśis actually were merely offshoots of the tribes later known as the Kuru-Pañcālas, and that they by reason of distance and less complete subjugation of the aborigines lost their Brahminical culture. This hypothesis, however, appears less likely, though it might be supported by a literal inter- pretation of the legend of the Aryan migration in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.<sup>15</sup> <F>1) Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 5, 4, 19. 21. The plural occurs also in the Paippalāda recension of the Athar- vaveda, v. 22, 14.</F> <F>2) xiii. 5, 4, 19.</F> <F>3) Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, ii. 1, 1; iii. 8, 2; Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad, iv. 1.</F> <F>4) Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad, {%loc. cit.%}</F> <F>5) iii. 8, 2.</F> <F>6) xvi. 29, 5.</F> <F>7) xxi. 13.</F> <F>8) {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 212, 213.</F> <F>9) i. 2, 9.</F> <F>10) iv. 7. 1. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches%} {%Leben,%} 20; Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the%} {%Atharvaveda,%} 376.</F> <F>11) i. 4, 1, 10 {%et seq.
