Weber, {%Indian Literature,%} 45; {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 191.</F> <F>40) xvii. 1, 1. See also Av. xv. with Whitney's and Lanman notes; Weber, {%Ind the Studien,%} 1, 33 {%et seq.; Indian%} {%Literature,%} 67, 78, 80.</F> <F>41) vii. 13. {%Cf.%} Oldenberg, {%Buddha,%} 400, note*; Weber, {%Indian Literature,%} 112, n. 126.</F> <F>42) See {%e.g.%} Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xi. 4, 1, 2, and note 6.</F> <F>43) This is recognized, {%e.g.,%} by Olden- berg, {%Buddha,%} 9, 391, 398, 399; Lanman, {%Sanskrit Keader,%} 297, etc. The narra- tive of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 4, 1, 10 {%et seq.%} (Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 170), rather implies that the Kosala- Videhas are offshoots of the Kuru- Pañcālas, but Oldenberg and Mac- donell ({%Sanskrit Literature,%} 214 interpret this as referring to the spread of Vedic tradition and culture, not of nationality.</F> <F>44) {%Cf.%} Grierson, {%Languages of India,%} 52 {%et seq.; Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society,%} 1908, 837 {%et seq.%} On the other hand, it is probably an error to assume that the Bharatas were originally situated far west of Kurukṣetra, and that the main action of the Rigveda was confined to the Panjab. When Vasiṣṭha celebrates the crossing of the Vipāś and Śutudrī (Rv. iii. 33), he probably came from the east, as Pischel, {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 218, points out, and not from the west. Adopting the ordinary view, Hopkins, {%India, Old and New,%} 52, finds it necessary to suggest that Yamunā is only another name in the Rv. for the Paruṣṇī. But the necessity for this suggestion, which is not in itself plausible, disappears when it is realized that the Bharatas held a territory roughly corresponding to Kurukṣetra, and bounded on the east by the Yamunā. On the other hand, Hille- brandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 142, 143. places the Kurus near the Ārjīkīyā in Kaśmīr, which puts them too far north. So also Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 103, and Eggeling, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 12, xlii. It seems probable that the Kurus were at a very early period widely scattered to the north of the Himālaya, in Kurukṣetra, and about the Sindhu and Asiknī. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Oldenberg, {%Buddha,%} 400 {%et seq.;%} Macdonell, {%Sanskrit Literature,%} 152-157; von Schroeder, {%Indiens Literature und%} {%Cultur,%} 164 {%et seq.;%} Weber, {%Indische%} {%Studien,%} 1, 187 {%et seq.; Indian Literature,%} 114, 135, 136; Rhys Davids, {%Buddhist%} {%India,%} 27; Pargiter, {%Journal of the Royal%} {%Asiatic Society,%} 1908, 333 {%et seq.;%} Hopkins, {%Journal of the American Oriental Society,%} 13, 205, n.</F>

{@Kuru-kṣetra@}¦ (‘land of the Kurus’) is always regarded in the Brāhmaṇa texts<sup>1</sup> as a particularly sacred country. Within its boundaries flowed the rivers {@Dṛṣadvatī@} and {@Sarasvatī,@} as well as the {@Āpayā.@}<sup>2</sup> Here, too, was situated {@Śaryaṇāvant,@}<sup>3</sup> which [Page1-170+ 46] appears to have been a lake, like that known to the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa by the name of {@Anyataḥ-plakṣā.@}<sup>4</sup> According to Pischel, there was also in Kurukṣetra a stream called {@Pastyā,@}<sup>5</sup> which he sees in certain passages of the Rigveda. The boun- daries of Kurukṣetra are given in a passage of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka<sup>6</sup> as being Khāṇḍava on the south, the Tūrghna on the north, and the Parīṇah on the west. Roughly speaking, it corresponded to the modern Sirhind. <F>1) Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xxv. 10; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iv. 1, 5, 13; xi. 5, 1, 4; xiv. 1, 1, 2; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vii. 30; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃ- hitā, ii. 1, 4; iv. 5, 9; Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 126 ({%Journal of the%} {%American Oriental Society,%} 11, cxlvi); Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xv. 16, 11, etc.</F> <F>2) {%Cf.%} Rv. iii. 23; Pischel, {%Vedische%} {%Studien,%} 2, 218.</F> <F>3) See Pischel, {%loc. cit.,%} and {%cf.%} {@Ārjī-@} {@kīyā.@}</F> <F>4) Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, xi. 5, 1, 4.</F> <F>5) Pischel, {%loc. cit.,%} 219.</F> <F>6) v. 1, 1. These places cannot be further identified. See also {@Mara.@} <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} von Schroeder, {%Indiens Literatur%} {%und Cultur,%} 164, 165; Max Mūller, {%Sacred%} {%Books of the East,%} 32, 398, 399; Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 78, 79; Macdonell, {%Sanskrit Literature,%} 174. Eggeling, {%Sacred%} {%Books of the East,%} 12, xli., seems to place Kurukṣetra, as lying between the Yamunā and Gaṅgā, too far east.</F>

{@Kuruṅga@}¦ is mentioned in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as a prince and a patron. Ludwig<sup>2</sup> suggests that he was a king of the {@Anus,@} but for this theory there seems no good ground. As the {@Turvaśas@} are mentioned in the same verse, he may possibly have been one of their kings. The name suggests a connexion with the {@Kurus,@} and it may be noted that in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> the Turvaśas are connected with the {@Pañcālas@} {@(Krivis).@} <F>1) viii. 4, 19; Nirukta, vi. 22.</F> <F>2) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 160.</F> <F>3) xi. 5, 4, 16. See Oldenberg, {%Buddha,%} 404.</F>

{@Kuru@}¦-śravaṇa {@Trāsadasyava@} is alluded to as dead in a hymn of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> which refers also to his son {@Upamaśravas,@} and his father {@Mitrātithi.@} In another hymn<sup>2</sup> he is mentioned as still alive. His name connects him on the one hand with the {@Kurus,@} and on the other with {@Trasadasyu@} and the {@Pūrus.@} <F>1) x. 33, 4. {%Cf.%} Bṛhaddevatā, vii. 35, 36.</F> <F>2) x. 32, 9. {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 165: Geldner, {%Vediscke Studien,%} 2, 150, 184; Lanman, {%Sanskrit Reader,%} 386.</F>
{@Kurūru,@}¦ apparently the name of a species of worm, is mentioned twice in the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) ii. 31, 2; ix. 2, 22. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 98.</F>
{@Kurkura@}¦ is an onomatopoetic name for the dog in the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> See also {@Śvan.@} <F>1) vii. 95, 2. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 233.</F>

{@Kula, Kula-pā.@}¦ — As an uncompounded word, Kula does not occur before the period of the Brāhmaṇas.<sup>1</sup> It denotes the ‘home’ or ‘house of the family,’ and by metonymy the family itself, as connected with the home. The Kula-pā (lit. ‘house protector’), or chief of the family, is mentioned in the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> as inferior to and attendant on the {@Vrājapati@} in war, the latter being perhaps the leader of the village contingent of the clan. In the Atharvaveda<sup>3</sup> a girl is ironically called Kulapā, because she is left without a husband in the world, and has only Yama (the god of death) for a spouse. <div n="P"/>The use of the term Kula points clearly to a system of individual families, each no doubt consisting of several members under the headship of the father or eldest brother, whose Kula the dwelling is. As distinct from {@Gotra,@} Kula seems to mean the family in the narrower sense of the members who still live in one house, the undivided family. {%Cf.%} {@Gṛha, Grāma,@} {@Jana, Viś.@} <F>1) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 1, 2, 22; ii. 1, 4, 4; 4, 1, 14; xi. 5, 3, 11; 8, 1, 3; xiii. 4, 2, 17; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, i. 5, 32; Chāndogya Upaniṣad, iii., 13, 6, etc.</F> <F>2) x. 179, 2.</F> <F>3) i. 14, 3. {%Cf.%} Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 15; Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Athcrvaveda,%} 252, correcting Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 314. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%op. cit.,%} 162.</F>

{@Kulāla,@}¦ the word denoting a ‘potter,’ occurs in the Śata- rudriya, or litany to Rudra in the Yajurveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xvi. 27. {%Cf.%} {%kulāla-kṛta,%} ‘made by a potter,’ Maitrāyaṇi Saṃhitā, i. 8. 3, and {@Kaulāla.@}</F>

{@Kuliśa,@}¦ ‘axe,’ is mentioned in the Rigveda as used for the making of chariots,<sup>1</sup> and also in warfare,<sup>2</sup> while the Atharvaveda refers to its employment in cutting down trees.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) iii. 2, 1.</F> <F>2) i. 32. 5.</F> <F>3) ii. 12, 3. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 252.</F>

{@Kulīkaya@}¦ is the form in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> of the name of an animal, apparently a kind of fish, as explained by Mahī- dhara in his commentary, which is called Kulīpaya in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā,<sup>2</sup> and Purīkaya in the Atharvaveda,<sup>3</sup> variants probably due to the faulty tradition of an unfamiliar. name. <F>1) v. 5, 13, 1.</F> <F>2) xxiv. 21. 35.</F> <F>3) xi. 2, 25. The commentator reads Pulīkaya, as in the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃ- hitā, iii. 14, 2. See Whitney, Transla- tion of the Atharvaveda, 624. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 96.</F>

{@Kulīkā@}¦ is the name of a bird mentioned in the list of victims at the horse sacrifice in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā.<sup>1</sup> The Maitrā- yaṇī Saṃhitā<sup>2</sup> has Pulīkā instead. <F>1) xxiv. 24.</F> <F>2) iii. 14, 5. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 94.</F>

{@Kuluṅga@}¦ is the name of an animal, perhaps a gazelle, men- tioned in the list of victims at the horse sacrifice in the Yajur- veda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 11, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 9, 13 (with the variant Kulaṅga); Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 27. 32. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 83.</F>

{@Kulmala@}¦ seems, in the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā,<sup>2</sup> and the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>3</sup> to denote the neck of an arrow in which the shaft is fixed. <F>1) iv. 6, 5; v. 18, 15.</F> <F>2) iii. 8, 1. 2.</F> <F>3) iii. 4, 4, 14.</F>
{@Kumala-barhis@}¦ is mentioned in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa (xv. 3, 21) as the seer of a Sāman or Chant.
{@Kumāra Hārita@}¦ is mentioned in the first Vaṃśa (list of teachers) in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad<sup>1</sup> as a pupil of {@Gālava.@} <F>1) ii. 5, 22 (Mādhyaṃdina = ii. 6, 3, Kāṇva).</F>

{@Kulmāṣa,@}¦ a word mentioned by the Chāndogya Upaniṣad<sup>1</sup> in the plural, is interpreted by the commentator as ‘bad beans’ ({%kutsitā māṣāḥ%}), a version adopted by Böhtlingk in his [Page1-173+ 42] Dictionary.<sup>2</sup> Little<sup>3</sup> renders it ‘sour gruel’ in accordance with the Nirukta.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) i. 10, 2. 7.</F> <F>2) {%Cf.%} Bhāgavata Purāṇa, v. 9. 12. where it is glossed ‘worm-eaten beans.’</F> <F>3) {%Grammatical Index,%} 52.</F> <F>4) i. 4.</F>

{@Kulyā@}¦ in two passages of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> according to Muir,<sup>2</sup> possibly refers to artificial watercourses flowing into a reservoir ({%hrada%}). See {@Avata.@} <F>1) iii. 45, 3; x. 43, 7.</F> <F>2) {%Sanskrit Texts,%} 5, 465, 466.</F>
{@Kuvaya.@}¦ See {@Kvayi.@}

{@Kuvala@}¦ is a name of the jujube fruit ({%Zizyphus jujuba%}) occurring frequently in the Yajurveda Saṃhitās<sup>1</sup> and Brāh- maṇas<sup>2</sup> in connexion with {@Karkandhu@} and {@Badara.@} See also {@Kola.@} <F>1) Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 11, 2; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xix. 22, 89; xxi. 29; Kāthaka Saṃhitā, xii. 10.</F> <F>2) Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, v. 5, 4, 10; xii. 7, 1, 2; 2, 9; 9, 1, 5, etc. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 242.</F>

{@Kuśa,@}¦ a word later denoting the ‘sacred grass’ ({%Poa cyno-%} {%suroides%}), is taken by the St. Petersburg Dictionary to mean simply ‘grass’ in the passages of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa in which it occurs. <div n="P"/>^1) ii. 5, 2, 15; iii. 1, 2, 16; v. 3, 2, 7, etc. Kuśā and Kuśī occur in Maitrā- yaṇī Saṃhitā, iv. 5, 7; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 6, 2, 9; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 5, 10, 1. 2, 7, apparently denoting pins of wood or metal, used as a mark in a special mode of recita- tion.

{@Ku-sara@}¦ is mentioned with {@Śara@} and other grasses in one hymn of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as affording lurking places for serpents. <F>1) i. 191, 3. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 72.</F>

{@Kuśika@}¦ is the probably mythical forefather<sup>1</sup> of the Kuśikas, and especially the father of the most important member of that family, {@Viśvāmitra.@}<sup>2</sup> The Kuśikas are repeatedly referred [Page1-174+ 52] to in the third Maṇḍala of the Rigveda,<sup>3</sup> and figure in the legend of Śunaḥśepa in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.<sup>4</sup> They were clearly a family of priests who attached themselves to the service of the princes of the {@Bharatas.@} They were especially devoted to the worship of Indra; hence he is styled Kauśika even in the Rigveda.<sup>5</sup> <F>1) Nirukta, ii. 25.</F> <F>2) Rv. iii. 33, 5.</F> <F>3) iii. 26, 1; 29, 15; 30, 20; 33, 5; 42, 9; 50, 4; 53, 9. 10.</F> <F>4) vii. 18; Sāṅkhāyana Srauta Sūtra, xv. 27.</F> <F>5) i. 10, 11, with Sāyaṇa's note. {%Cf.%} Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iv. 5, 7; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 3, 4, 19; Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, i. 12, 4; Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} pp. 62, 63. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} i, 38; Muir, {%Sanskrit Texts,%} 1^2, 342 {%et seq.;%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 101, 121; Macdonell, {%Sanskrit Litera-%} {%ture,%} 155; Oldenberg. {%Zeitschrift der%} {%Deutschen Morgenländischen Gesellschaft,%} 42, 209.</F>

{@Kuśri Vāja-śravasa@}¦ appears as a teacher concerned with the lore of the sacred fire in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> and in the last Vaṃśa (list of teachers) of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad<sup>2</sup> he is mentioned as a pupil of {@Vājaśravas.@} It is not clear whether he is identical with the Kuśri of the last Vaṃśa of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka<sup>3</sup> in the Kāṇva recension, and of the Vaṃśa in the tenth book of the Śatapatha,<sup>4</sup> who is mentioned as a pupil of {@Yajñavacas Rājastambāyana.@} <F>1) x. 5, 5. 1.</F> <F>2) vi. 4, 33 (Mādhyaṃdina = vi. 5, 3, Kāṇva).</F> <F>3) vi. 5, 4 (Kāṇva only).</F> <F>4) x. 6, 5, 9. In the Vaṃśas the name is accented Kúśri, but in x. 5, 5, 1, as Kuśrī; no stress can, however, be laid on this. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 70; Eggeling, {%Sacred Books of the%} {%East,%} 12, xxxiii.</F>

{@Ku-ṣaṇḍa@}¦ is mentioned with {@Ṣaṇḍa@} as a priest at the snake festival described in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) xxv. 15, 3. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 34; Lāṭyāyana Śranta Sūtra, x. 20, 10.</F>

1. {@Kuṣītaka@}¦ denotes, according to the commentary on the one passage of the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> in which it is found, the sea crow ({%samudra-kāka%}) <F>1) v. 5, 13. 1. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 72.</F>

2. {@Kuṣītaka Sāma-śravasa@}¦ is mentioned in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> as the Gṛhapati, or householder at a sacrificial session, of the Kauṣītakis. <F>1) xvii. 4. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 34.</F>

{@Kuṣumbhaka@}¦ seems in one passage of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> to mean a poisonous insect, Kuṣumbha in th Atharvaveda<sup>2</sup> clearly having the sense of a poison bag. Sāyaṇa renders it as ‘ichneumon’ ({%nakula%}). <F>1) i. 191, 16. The sense of ‘poison- bag’ is possible in i. 191, 15, and is accepted there by Böhtlingk in his Dictionary.</F> <F>2) ii. 32, 6. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches%} {%Leben,%} 99; Griffith, {%Hymns of the Rigveda,%} 1, 257.</F>

1. {@Kuṣṭha@}¦ is the name of a plant ({%Costus speciosus%} or {%arabicus%})<sup>1</sup> which is prominent in the Atharvaveda.<sup>2</sup> It grew especially on the mountains, along with the Soma, on the high peaks of the Himālaya ({%Himavant%}) where the eagles nest, and was thence brought east to men.<sup>3</sup> Like Soma, it is said to have grown in the third heaven under the famous {@Aśvattha@} tree, where the gods were wont to assemble, and thence it was brought in a golden ship.<sup>4</sup> As a remedy, it held the highest place among herbs, being called by the auspicious names Nagha-māra and Naghā-riṣa, and styled the offspring of Jīvala and Jīvalā, the ‘lively’ ones.<sup>5</sup> It cured headache ({%śīrṣāmaya%}), diseases of the eyes, bodily affliction,<sup>6</sup> but especially fever — hence called ‘fever- destroyer’ ({%takma-nāśana%}) — and consumption ({@Yakṣma@}). From its general properties it was also named ‘all-healing’ ({%viśva-%} {%bheṣaja%}).<sup>7</sup> Its aromatic qualities were apparently known, as it is classed with ‘salve’ ({@Āñjana@}) and ‘nard’ ({@Nalada@}).<sup>8</sup> <F>1) Or {%Saussurea auriculata,%} Hillebreandt. {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 65.</F> <F>2) v. 4; vi. 102; xix. 139.</F> <F>3) v. 4, 1. 2. 8; xix. 39, 1.</F> <F>4) v. 4, 3-6; vi. 75, 1. 2; xix. 39, 6-8.</F> <F>5) v. 4, 1; xix. 39, 4.</F> <F>6) v. 4, 10.</F> <F>7) xix. 39, 9.</F> <F>8) vi. 102, 3. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Grohmann, {%Indische, Studien,%} 9, 420 {%et seq.;%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 63, 64; Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Athar-%} {%vaveda,%} 415, 680; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 227, 228.</F>

2. {@Kuṣṭha.@}¦ — In one passage of the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> there is a series of fractions, {@Kalā, Kuṣṭha, Śapha, Pad,@} which appear to denote one-sixteenth, one-twelfth, one-eighth, and one-fourth respectively. <F>1) iii. 7, 7. {%Cf.%} Böhtlingk, Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>

{@Kusīdin@}¦ is a designation of the ‘usurer’ found in the Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> and the Nirukta,<sup>2</sup> and often in the Sūtras. Jolly,<sup>3</sup> referring doubtless to the expression {%kusīda apratītta,%}<sup>4</sup> ‘a loan not yet repaid,’ occurring in connexion with {%an-ṛṇa,%} ‘free from debt,’ appears to be right in taking Kusīda to have the sense of ‘loan’ in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā. The rate of interest on loans is not specified before the Sūtra period.<sup>5</sup> {%Cf.%} {@Ṛṇa.@} <F>1) xiii. 4, 3, 11.</F> <F>2) vi. 32.</F> <F>3) {%Recht und Sitle,%} 98, 99.</F> <F>4) iii. 3, 8, 1. 2.</F> <F>5) {%E.g.,%} Gautama Sūtra, xii. 29 {%et seq.%} {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 259.</F>

{@Kusurubinda Auddālaki@}¦ appears as an authority on ritual matters in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> the Taittirīya Saṃhitā,<sup>2</sup> the Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa,<sup>3</sup> and the Ṣaḍviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>4</sup> He may have been the brother of {@Śvetaketu,@} as suggested by Weber.<sup>5</sup> <F>1) xxii. 15, 1. 10.</F> <F>2) vii. 2, 2, 1.</F> <F>3) i. 75 ({%Journal of the American Oriental%} {%Society,%} 23, 327), where the reading seems to be Asurbinda.</F> <F>4) i. 16. See Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 39. The name is there read as Ku- surubindu; in the Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xvi. 22, 14 it is Kusurabindu.</F> <F>5) {%Indische Studien,%} 5, 61, n.</F>
{@Kuhū.@}¦ See {@Māsa.@}

{@Kūcakra@}¦ is a word occurring only once in an obscure verse of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> where Zimmer<sup>2</sup> suggests that it has the sense of the wheel by which water is raised from a well. Much more probable is the interpretation of Roth,<sup>3</sup> who understands it to mean the female breast. <F>1) x. 102, 11.</F> <F>2) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 157. {%Cf.%} Geldner, {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 14.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>

{@Kūṭa,@}¦ a word found in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> the Atharvaveda,<sup>2</sup> and the Brāhmaṇas,<sup>3</sup> is of doubtful signification. On the whole, [Page1-177+ 50] the most probable sense is hammer,<sup>4</sup> which suits every passage adequately. The St. Petersburg Dictionary renders it ‘horn,’ which is the sense accepted by Whitney<sup>5</sup> for the Atharvaveda passage where it occurs. Geldner<sup>6</sup> thinks that it means ‘trap.’ <F>1) x. 102, 4.</F> <F>2) viii. 8, 16.</F> <F>3) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vi. 24; Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 8, 1, 15; Jai- minīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 49, 9; 50, 2 ({%Journal of the American Oriental Society,%} 19, 114).</F> <F>4) So Bloomfield, {%Zeitschrift der%} {%Deutschen Morgenländischen Gesellschaft,%} 48, 546; {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 585.</F> <F>5) Translation of the Atharvaveda, 505.</F> <F>6) {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 138; 2, 7. {%Cf.%} von Bradke, {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen%} {%Morgenländischen Gesellschaft,%} 46, 458; Kuhn's {%Zeitschrift,%} 34, 156; Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 9, 222.</F>

{@Kūdī,@}¦ written also Kūṭī in the manuscripts, occurs in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and the Kauśika Sūtra<sup>2</sup> denoting a twig — identi- fied by the scholiast with {@Badarī,@} the jujube — which was tied to the bodies of the dead to efface their traces, presumably in order to render the return of the spirit to the old home difficult. <F>1) v. 19, 12.</F> <F>2) Bloomfield's edition, xliv. {%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%American Journal of Philology,%} 11, 355; 12, 416; Roth, {%Festgrnss an%} {%Böhtlingk,%} 98; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 254; Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} p. 165.</F>

{@Kūpa@}¦ occurs in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later literature<sup>2</sup> denoting an artificial hollow in the earth, or pit. In some cases they must have been deep, as Trita in the myth is said to have fallen into one from which he could not escape unaided.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) i. 105, 17.</F> <F>2) Av. v. 31, 8; Satapatha Brah- maṇa, iii. 5, 4, 1; iv. 4, 5, 3; vi. 3, 3. 26, etc.; Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 184. etc. The adjective {%kūpya,%} ‘being in a hole,’ occurs frequently in the later Saṃhitās.</F> <F>3) Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} p. 67.</F>
{@Kūbara@}¦ in the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā (ii. 1, 11) and {@Kūbarī@} in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (iv. 6, 9, 11. 12) and the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa (xxvii. 6) denote the pole of a cart.

{@Kūrca@}¦ is found in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> de- noting a bundle of grass used as a seat. In one passage of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> a golden Kūrca is referred to. <F>1) vii. 5, 8, 5.</F> <F>2) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xi. 5, 3, 4. 7; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, ii. 11, 1; Aitareya Āraṇyaka, v, 1, 4.</F> <F>3) xiii. 4, 3, 1.</F>

{@Kūrma,@}¦ the ‘tortoise,’ is mentioned frequently in the later Saṃhitās<sup>1</sup> and Brāhmaṇas,<sup>2</sup> but nothing is said of its charac- teristics. See also {@Kaśyapa.@} <F>1) Av. ix. 4, 16; Taittirīya Saṃ- hitā, ii. 6, 3, 3; v. 2, 8, 4. 5; 7, 13, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 15, 3; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 34, etc.</F> <F>2) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 6, 2, 3; vi. 1, 1, 12, etc. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 95; Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} p. 153.</F>

{@Kūśāmba Svāyava Lātavya@}¦ is mentioned in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> as a priest. His name apparently means<sup>2</sup> Kūśāmba,<sup>3</sup> of the Lātavya clan, son of Svāyu. <F>1) viii. 6, 8.</F> <F>2) The form is peculiar, as Kuśāmba would be expected.</F> <F>3) Hopkins, {%Transactions of the Con-%} {%necticut Academy of Arts and Sciences,%} 15, 55, n. 2.</F>

{@Kṛkalāsa@}¦ denotes the ‘chameleon’ mentioned in the list of sacrificial victims at the horse sacrifice in the Yajurveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> The female chameleon, Kṛkalāsī, is also referred to in the Brāhmaṇas.<sup>3</sup> See {@Godhā@} and {@Śayaṇḍaka.@} <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 19, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 21; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 40.</F> <F>2) Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, i. 5, 22.</F> <F>3) Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 221 ({%Journal%} {%of the American Oriental Society,%} 18, 29), Sāṭyāyanaka in Sāyaṇa on Rv. viii. 91. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 95.</F>

{@Kṛka-vāku,@}¦ the ‘cock,’ being named in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> with sheep, goats, and other domesticated animals, was pre- sumably tamed.<sup>2</sup> In the list of victims at the horse sacrifice in the Yajurveda,<sup>3</sup> it appears as dedicated to Savitṛ: Yāska<sup>4</sup> explains this by the fact that it declares the time of day ({%kālānuvāda%}). The commentator Mahīdhara<sup>5</sup> explains the name by {%tāmra-cūḍa,%} ‘red-crested.’ It is of course onomato- poetic (‘calling kṛka’).<sup>6</sup> See also {@Kukkuṭa.@} <F>1) v. 31, 2. {%Cf.%} x. 136, 10.</F> <F>2) {%Cf.,%} however, Sāyaṇa on Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 18, 1, who says that it is a ‘forest’ Kukkuṭa.</F> <F>3) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, {%loc. cit.;%} Maitrā- yaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 15; Vājasaneyi; Saṃhitā, xxiv. 35.</F> <F>4) Nirukta, xii. 3.</F> <F>5) On Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, {%loc. cit.%}</F> <F>6) Schrader, {%Prehistoric Antiquities,%} 251; Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 18. 285. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 91.</F>
{@Kṛta.@}¦ See 2. {@Akṣa@} and 2. {@Yuga.@}

{@Kṛti.@}¦ — From one passage in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> where the Maruts are described as having Kṛtis, Zimmer<sup>2</sup> concludes that the word means a dagger used in war. But there is no evidence that Kṛti was ever a human weapon. See {@Asi.@} <F>1) i. 168, 3.</F> <F>2) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 301. {%Cf.%} Schrader, {%Prehistoric Antiquities,%} 221.</F>
{@Kṛttikās.@}¦ See {@Nakṣatra.@}

{@Kṛtvan.@}¦ — In one passage of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> the word Kṛtvan in the plural is mentioned with the {@Ārjīkas@} and the five peoples. Pischel<sup>2</sup> thinks that it means a people, and Sāyaṇa expressly says that the Kṛtvans designate a country.<sup>3</sup> The name in that case would point to some connexion with the {@Kurus@} or {@Krivis.@} Hillebrandt,<sup>4</sup> however, thinks that the word is an adjective which qualifies Ārjīkas and designates this people as magicians, being applied to them by an opponent. In favour of this view, he quotes Hiouen Thsang's statement<sup>5</sup> that the neighbouring kings held the base Kaśmīrians in such scorn as to refuse all alliance with them, and to give them the name of Ki-li-to, or Kṛtyas. He suggests that the Ārjīkas settled in Kasmīr in ancient times already had the same evil reputation as their successors in later days. <F>1) ix. 65, 23.</F> <F>2) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 209.</F> <F>3) {%Kṛtvāna iti deśābhidhānam.%}</F> <F>4) {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 136, 137</F> <F>5) Cunningham, {%Aneient Gevgraphy of%} {%India,%} 93. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Roth, St. Petersburg Dic- tionary, {%s.v.%}</F>
{@Kṛpa@}¦ is mentioned in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> along with Ruśama and {@Śyāvaka,@} as a protégé of Indra. <F>1) viii. 3, 12; 4, 2. {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 163.</F>

{@Kṛmi,@}¦ ‘worm.’ In the later Saṃhitās,<sup>1</sup> and especially in the Atharvaveda,<sup>2</sup> worms play a considerable part. They are [Page1-180+ 47] regarded as poisonous, and are spoken of as found in the mountains, in forests, in waters, in plants, and in the human body. In accordance with widespread primitive ideas, they are considered to be the causes of disease in men and animals. The Atharvaveda contains three hymns<sup>2</sup> as charms directed against them. The first of these hymns is of a general character, the second is meant to destroy worms in cattle, and the third is intended to cure children of worms. When found in men, worms are said to have their place in the head and ribs,<sup>3</sup> and to creep into the eyes, nose, and teeth.<sup>4</sup> They are described as dark brown, but white in the fore part of the body, with black ears, and as having three heads.<sup>5</sup> They are given many specific names: {@Alāṇḍu, Ejatka, Kaṣkaṣa, Kīṭa, Kurūru, Nīlaṅgu,@} {@Yevāṣa, Vaghā, Vṛkṣasarpī, Śaluna, Śavarta, Śipavitnuka,@} {@Stega.@} <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 11, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 11; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 30; Mantra Brāh- maṇa, ii. 7; Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, iv. 36; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, v. 4, 1, 2; and {%of.%} Rv. i. 191.</F> <F>2) ii. 31. 32; v. 23.</F> <F>2) ii. 31, 32; v. 23.</F> <F>3) Av. ii. 31, 4.</F> <F>4) Av. v. 23, 3.</F> <F>5) Av. v. 23, 4 {%et seq.%} <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 98, 393; Kuhn, {%Zeitschrift für vergleichende%} {%Sprachforschung,%} 13, 49 {%et seq.;%} 113 {%et seq.;%} Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the%} {%Atharvaveda,%} 313 {%et seq.;%} Weber, {%Indische%} {%Studien,%} 13, 199; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 73.</F>

{@Kṛmuka@}¦ is the name in the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā.<sup>1</sup> and the Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> of a species of wood used for fuel.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) xix. 10.</F> <F>2) vi. 6, 2, 11.</F> <F>3) {%Ibid.%} ({%Krāmuha%} as applied to {%samidh%}).</F>

{@Kṛśa@}¦ is mentioned with {@Saṃvarta@} as a pious sacrificer to Indra in one of the Vālakhilya hymns of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and in another<sup>2</sup> as a speaker of truth, while a third is traditionally<sup>3</sup> ascribed to his authorship. He seems also to be mentioned with {@Śayu@} as a protégé of the Aśvins in another hymn of the Rigveda,<sup>4</sup> but here the word may merely denote the ‘feeble man.’<sup>5</sup> <F>1) viii. 54, 2.</F> <F>2) viii. 59, 3.</F> <F>3) {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 293, n.</F> <F>4) x. 40, 8.</F> <F>5) Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 132, 164.</F>

{@Kṛśana,@}¦ ‘pearl.’ In the Rigveda pearls are mentioned as adorning the car of Savitṛ<sup>1</sup> as well as being used for the adorn- ment of a horse.<sup>2</sup> Hence the horse is spoken of as the ‘pearled one’ ({%kṛśanāvant%}).<sup>3</sup> The Atharvaveda<sup>4</sup> also refers to pearls, and mentions that ‘pearl shell’ ({%śañkhaḥ kṛśanaḥ%}) won from the sea was used as an amulet.<sup>5</sup> The Nighaṇṭu<sup>6</sup> renders the word as ‘gold.’ <F>1) i. 35, 4.</F> <F>2) x. 68, 1.</F> <F>3) i. 126, 4. {%Cf. kṛśanin,%} vii. 18, 23.</F> <F>4) x. 1, 7.</F> <F>5) iv. 10, 1. 3.</F> <F>6) i. 2. {%Cf.%} Sāma Mantra Brāhmaṇa, 1, 6, 22. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%}, 53, 54; Lanman in Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 161.</F>

{@Kṛśānu@}¦ appears in the Rigveda as a mythological personage.<sup>1</sup> In one verse,<sup>2</sup> however, Roth<sup>3</sup> sees in this word the name of a bowman, but there seems no reason to dissociate this passage from the rest. <F>1) Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} pp. 74, 112, 137; Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mytho-%} {%logie,%} 1, 448.</F> <F>2) i. 112, 21.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.,%} 4.</F>

{@Kṛṣi,@}¦ ‘ploughing.’ The cultivation of the soil was no doubt known to the Indians before they separated from the Iranians, as is indicated by the identity of the expressions {%yavaṃ kṛṣ%} and {%sasya%} in the Rigveda with {%yao karesh%} and {%hahya%} in the Avesta, referring to the ploughing in of the seed and to the grain which resulted.<sup>1</sup> But it is not without significance that the expressions for ploughing occur mainly in the first<sup>2</sup> and tenth<sup>3</sup> books of the Rigveda, and only rarely in the so-called ‘family’ books (ii.-vii.).<sup>4</sup> In the Atharvaveda {@Pṛthī Vainya@} is credited with the origination of ploughing,<sup>5</sup> and even in the Rigveda the Aśvins are spoken of as concerned with the sowing of grain by means of the plough.<sup>6</sup> In the later Saṃhitās and the Brāhmaṇas ploughing is repeatedly referred to.<sup>7</sup> [Page1-182+ 51] <div n="P"/>Even in the Rigveda<sup>8</sup> there is clear proof of the importance attached to agriculture. In the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>9</sup> the {@Vrātyas,@} Hindus without the pale of Brahminism, are de- scribed as not cultivating the soil. <div n="P"/>The plough land was called {@Urvarā@} or {@Kṣetra;@} manure ({@Śakan, Karīṣa@}) was used, and irrigation was practised ({@Khani-@} {@tra@}). The plough ({@Lāṅgala, Sīra@}) was drawn by oxen, teams of six, eight, or even twelve being employed.<sup>10</sup> The operations of agriculture are neatly summed up in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>11</sup> as ‘ploughing, sowing, reaping, and threshing’ ({%kṛṣantaḥ,%} {%vapantaḥ, lunantaḥ, mṛṇantaḥ%}). The ripe grain was cut with a sickle ({@Dātra, Sṛṇi@}), bound into bundles<sup>12</sup> ({@Parṣa@}), and beaten out on the floor of the granary ({@Khala@}).<sup>13</sup> The grain was then separated from the straw and refuse either by a sieve ({@Titau@}) or a winnowing fan ({@Śūrpa@}).<sup>14</sup> The winnower was called {@Dhānyākṛt,@}<sup>15</sup> and the grain was measured in a vessel called {@Urdara.@}<sup>16</sup> <div n="P"/>The Rigveda leaves us in doubt as to the kind of grain grown, for {@Yava@} is a word of doubtful signification, and {@Dhānā@} is also vague. In the later Saṃhitās<sup>17</sup> things are different. Rice ({@Vrīhi@}) appears, Yava means barley, with a species styled {@Upavāka.@} Beans ({@Mudga, Māṣa@}), sesamum ({@Tila@}), and other grains ({@Aṇu, Khalva, Godhūma, Nīvāra, Priyaṅgu,@} {@Masūra, Śyāmāka@}) are mentioned, while cucumbers ({@Urvārū,@} {@Uryārūka@}) were known. It is uncertain whether fruit trees ({@Vṛkṣa@}) were cultivated, or merely grew wild;<sup>18</sup> but frequent mention is made of the jujube ({@Karkandhu, Kuvala, Badara.@}). <div n="P"/>The seasons for agriculture are briefly summed up in a passage of the Taittirīya Saṃhitā:<sup>19</sup> barley ripened in summer, being no doubt sown, as in modern India, in winter; rice [Page1-183+ 52] ripened in autumn, being sown in the beginning of the rains; beans and sesamum, planted at the time of the summer rains, ripened in the winter and the cool season. There were two harvests ({@Sasya@}) a year according to the Taittirīya Saṃhitā;<sup>20</sup> the winter crop was ripe by the month of Caitra (March-April) according to the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa.<sup>21</sup> <div n="P"/>The farmer had plenty of trouble of his own: moles destroyed the seed, birds and various kinds of reptiles ({@Upakvasa, Jabhya,@} {@Tarda, Pataṅga@}) injured the young shoots, excessive rain or drought might damage the crops. The Atharvaveda contains spells to prevent these evils.<sup>22</sup> <F>1) Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 235; Hopkins, {%Journal of the American Oriental%} {%Society,%} 17, 85.</F> <F>2) Forms of the root {%kṛṣ,%} ‘to plough,’ occur in Rv. i. 23, 15; 176, 2.</F> <F>3) Rv. x. 34, 13; 117, 7. In x. 146, 6, {%akṛṣīvala,%} ‘not agricultural,’ occurs. {%Cf.%} x. 101, 4.</F> <F>4) {%Kṛṣ%} is also found in viii. 20, 19; 22, 6; in the family books only in iv. 57, 4, and as {%vi-kṛṣ%} in iv. 57, 8.</F> <F>5) viii. 10, 24.</F> <F>6) i. 117, 21.</F> <F>7) {%Kṛṣi%} is found, {%e.g.,%} in Av. ii. 4, 5; viii. 2, 19; 10, 24; x. 6, 12; xii. 2, 27, etc.; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vii. 1, 11; 1, etc.; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, i. 2, 2; iii. 6, 8; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, iv. 10; ix. 27; xiv. 19. 21, etc.; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, vii. 2, 2, 7; viii. 6, 2, 2; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 1, 2, 5, etc. In Av. vi. 116, 1, {%kārṣīvaṇa%} denotes a ‘plougher.’ See also Kārṣman.</F> <F>8) x. 34, 13; 117, 7. {%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%India, Old and New,%} 208.</F> <F>9) xvii. 1.</F> <F>10) Av. vi. 91, 1; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xv. 2. {%Cf.%} Rv. viii. 6, 48; x. 101, 4.</F> <F>11) i. 6, 1, 3.</F> <F>12) viii. 78, 10; x. 101, 3; 131, 2.</F> <F>13) Rv. x. 48, 7.</F> <F>14) Rv. x. 71, 2; Av. xii. 3, 19. The technical terms are {%tuṣair vi-vic,%} Av. xi. 1, 12; {%palāvān apa-vic,%} xii. 3, 19.</F> <F>15) Rv. x. 94, 13.</F> <F>16) Rv. ii. 14, 11. See also {@Sthivi.@}</F> <F>17) See Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xviii. 12, for a list.</F> <F>18) The pulling of ripe fruit is referred to in Rv. iii. 45, 4. {%Cf. pakvā śākhā,%} Rv. i. 8, 8; {%vṛkṣa pakva,%} Rv. iv. 20, 5; Av. xx. 127, 4. But that does not prove arboriculture.</F> <F>19) vii. 2, 10, 2.</F> <F>20) v. 1, 7, 3.</F> <F>21) xix. 3. {%Cf.%} Keith, {%Śāṅkhāyana%} {%Āraṇyaka,%} 81, n. 1.</F> <F>22) See Av. vi. 50. 142; vii. 11. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 235- 243.</F>

{@Kṛṣṭi@}¦ denotes ‘people’ in general from the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> onwards. Its common and regular use in this sense appears to show that the Āryans, when they invaded India, were already agricul- turists, though the employment of the words referring to ploughing mentioned under {@Kṛṣi@} indicates that not all of the people devoted themselves equally to that occupation. Indra and Agni are {%par excellence%} the lords of men (Kṛṣṭi).<sup>2</sup> Some- times the word is further defined by the addition of an adjective meaning ‘belonging to mankind,’ ‘of men’ ({%mānuṣīḥ,%}<sup>3</sup> {%mānavīḥ%}).<sup>4</sup> <div n="P"/>Special mention is frequently<sup>5</sup> made of the ‘five peoples’ ({%pañca kṛṣṭayaḥ%}). The exact sense of this expression is doubtful. See {@Panca Janāsaḥ.@} <F>1) i. 52, 11; 100, 10; 160, 5; 189, 3; iii. 49, 1; iv. 21, 2, etc.; Av. xii. 1, 3. 4.</F> <F>2) i. 177, 1; iv. 17, 5; vii. 26, 5; viii. 13, 9 (Indra); i. 59, 5; vi. 18, 2; vii. 5, 5 (Agni).</F> <F>3) Rv. i. 59, 5; vi. 18, 2.</F> <F>4) Av. iii. 24, 3.</F> <F>5) Rv. ii. 2, 10; iii. 53, 16; iv. 38, 10; x. 60, 4; 119, 6; 178, 3; Av. iii. 24, 2; xii. 1, 42. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 141.</F>

1. {@Kṛṣṇa@}¦ (‘black’) denotes a dark-coloured animal or bird. In some passages,<sup>1</sup> as the context shows, an antelope is certainly [Page1-184+ 51] meant. In a few others<sup>2</sup> a bird of prey seems indicated. See also {@Kṛṣṇājina.@} <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 2, 6, 5; vi. 1, 3, 1; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 1, 4, 1; iii. 2, 1, 28. So {%kṛṣṇa-viṣāṇā,%} ‘horn of the black antelope,’ {%ibid.,%} iii. 2, 1, 18, 28; 2, 20; iv. 4, 5, 2; v. 4, 2, 5; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vi. 1, 3, 7. See also the Aśvamedha passages, Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 17; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 36 ({%cf.%} ii. 1).</F> <F>2) Rv. x. 94, 5; Av. xi. 2, 2; Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka, xii. 27.</F>

2. {@Kṛṣṇa@}¦ appears as the name of a seer in one hymn of the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> Tradition assigns to him or to Viśvaka, son of Kṛṣṇa ({%Kārṣṇi%}), the authorship of the following hymn.<sup>2</sup> The word Kṛṣṇiya may be a patronymic<sup>3</sup> formed from the same name in two other hymns of the Rigveda,<sup>4</sup> where the Aśvins are said to have restored {@Viṣṇāpū@} to Viśvaka Kṛṣṇya. In that case Kṛṣṇa would seem to be the grandfather of Viṣṇāpū. This Kṛṣṇa may be identical with Kṛṣṇa Āṅgirasa mentioned in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa.<sup>5</sup> <F>1) viii. 85, 3. 4.</F> <F>2) viii. 86.</F> <F>3) i. 116, 23; 117, 7.</F> <F>4) As a patronymic, it would be an isolated formation ({%cf.%} however {%Pajriya%}), instead of {%Kārṣṇya. Cf.%} Macdonell, {%Vedic%} {%Grammar,%} 228{%a%} and 200.</F> <F>5) xxx. 9. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rig- veda, 3, 108; Macdonell, {%Vedia Myth-%} {%ology,%} p. 52.</F>

3. {@Kṛṣṇa Devakī-putra@}¦ is mentioned in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad<sup>1</sup> as a pupil of the mythical {@Ghora Āṅgirasa.@} Tradition,<sup>2</sup> and several modern writers like Grierson, Garbe, and von Schroeder, recognize in him the hero Kṛṣṇa, who later is deified. In their view he is a Kṣatriya teacher of morals, as opposed to Brahminism.<sup>3</sup> This is extremely doubtful. It appears better either to regard the coincidence of name as accidental, or to suppose that the reference is a piece of Euhemerism. To identify this Kṛṣṇa with the preceding, as does the St. Petersburg Dictionary, seems to be quite groundless. <F>1) iii. 17, 6.</F> <F>2) {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indian Literature,%} 169.</F> <F>3) Von Schroeder, {%Vienna Oriental%} {%Journal,%} 19, 414, 415; Grierson, {%Encyclo-%} {%padia of Religions,%} article ‘Bhakti’; Garbe, {%Bhagavadgītā.%} <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%op. cit.,%} 71; 148; Hopkins, {%Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society,%} 1905, 386.</F>

4. {@Kṛṣṇa Hārīta@}¦ is mentioned as a teacher in the Aitareya Āraṇyaka.<sup>1</sup> The Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka<sup>2</sup> has Kṛtsna in the parallel passage. <F>1) iii. 2. 6.</F> <F>2) viii. 10. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 391, n.; {%Indian Literature,%} 50.</F>
{@Kṛṣṇa-datta Lauhitaya@}¦ (‘descendant of Lohita’) is mentioned in a Vaṃśa (list of teachers) of the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāh- maṇa (iii. 42, 1) as a pupil of {@Śyāmasujayanta Lauhitya.@}
{@Kṛṣṇa-dhṛti Sātyaki@}¦ (‘descendant of Satyaka’) is mentioned in a Vaṃśa (list of teachers) of the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāh- maṇa (iii. 42, 1) as a pupil of {@Satyaśravas.@}
{@Kṛṣṇa-rāta Lauhitya@}¦ (‘descendant of Lohita’) is mentioned in a Vaṃśa (list of teachers) of the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāh- maṇa (iii. 42, 1) as a pupil of {@Śyāmaiajayanta Lauhitya.@}

{@Kṛṣṇala@}¦ denotes the berry of the {%Abrus precatorius,%} used as a weight according to the later authorities, one Māṣa (‘bean’) being equated to four Kṛṣṇalas.<sup>1</sup> In the sense of a weight it occurs in the Taittirīva<sup>2</sup> and other Saṃhitās,<sup>3</sup> and later.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) Manu, viii. 134.</F> <F>2) ii. 3, 2, 1 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>3) Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 2, 2; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xi. 4 ({%hiraṇya%} {%kṛṣṇala%}).</F> <F>4) Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 3, 6, 7; Anupada Sūtra, ix. 6. In the later language it is also called {%raktikā%} or {%guñjā%} (being a smooth red berry with a black spot at one end). <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber's edition of the Jyotiṣa, 82 {%et seq.; Indische Strcifen,%} 1, 102, 103.</F>

{@Kṛṣṇājina@}¦ is the skin ({%ajina%}) of the black antelope ({@Kṛṣṇa.@}) It is repeatedly referred to in the later Saṃhitās and Brāh- maṇas<sup>1</sup> with regard to its ritual use. <F>1) Av. ix. 6, 17; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 4, 9, 2; v. 4, 4, 4: Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 1, 1, 22; 4, 1; 9, 2, 35, etc.</F>
{@Kṛṣṇāyasa@}¦ (‘black metal’), ‘iron,’ is referred to in the Chān- dogya Upaniṣad (vi. 1, 6). See also {@Ayas@} and {@Kārṣṇāyasa.@}

{@Kṛsara,@}¦ a term denoting a mess of rice and sesamum, often mentioned in the Sūtras, occurs in the Ṣaḍviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) v. 2. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Omina und Portenta,%} 315 {%et seq.%}</F>

{@Kekaya@}¦ is the name of a tribe which in later days, and probably also in Vedic times, was settled in the north-west, [Page1-186+ 48] {{oetween->between||20210704|Dr. Sampada Savardekar|https://github.com/sanskrit-lexicon/csl-corrections/issues/67|}} the {@Sindhu@} (Indus) and {@Vitastā.@}<sup>1</sup> In the Vedic texts the Kekayas are mentioned indirectly only in the name of their prince {@Aśvapati Kaikeya.@}<sup>2</sup> <F>1) Pargiter, {%Journal of the Royal Asiatic%} {%Society,%} 1908, 317, 332.</F> <F>2) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, x. 6, 1, 2. {%et seq.;%} Chāndogya Upaniṣad, v. 11, 4. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indian Litenature,%} 120; {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 126.</F>

1. {@Ketu@}¦ is a term which Weber<sup>1</sup> understands in the sense of ‘meteor’ or ‘comet’ in the late Adbhuta Brāhmaṇa. <F>1) {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 41. The {%aruṇāḥ%} {%ketavaḥ%} (Av. xi. 10, 1. 2. 7), referred to in this sense in the St. Petersburg Dictionary, are not so treated by Böhtlingk in his Dictionary.</F>
2. {@Ketu Vājya@}¦ (‘descendant of Vāja’) is mentioned as a teacher in the Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 372.</F>

{@Kevarta, Kaivarta@}¦ are two variant forms denoting ‘fisher- man’ in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> and Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> lists of victims at the Puruṣamedha, or human sacrifice. <F>1) xxx. 16, with Mahīdhara's note.</F> <F>2) iii. 4, 12, 1, with Sāyaṇa's note.</F>

{@Keśa,@}¦ ‘hair of the head,’ is repeatedly mentioned in the later Saṃhitās and Brāhmaṇas.<sup>1</sup> The hair was a matter of great care to the Vedic Indian, and several hymns of the Atharva- veda<sup>2</sup> are directed to securing its plentiful growth. Cutting or shaving ({%vap%}) the hair is often referred to.<sup>3</sup> For a man to wear long hair was considered effeminate.<sup>4</sup> As to modes of dressing the hair see {@Opaśa@} and {@Kaparda;@} as to the beard see {@Śmaśru.@} <F>1) Av. v. 19, 3; vi. 136, 3, etc.; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xix. 22; xx. 5; xxv. 3; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 5, 2, 48, etc.</F> <F>2) vi. 136. 137. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altin-%} {%disches Leben,%} 68; Bloomfield, {%Hymns of%} {%the Atharvaveda,%} 536, 537.</F> <F>3) Av. viii. 2, 17; Satapatha Brāh- maṇa, v. 5, 3, 1, etc. {%Cf.%} Oldenberg, {%Religion des Veda,%} 425 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>4) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, v. 1, 2, 14. But {%cf.%} Vincent Smith, {%Indian%} {%Antiquary,%} 34, 203.</F>

1. {@Keśin@}¦ is the name of a people occurring in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> where their king is mentioned as learning from {@Khaṇḍika@} the atonement for a bad omen at the sacrifice. <F>1) xi. 8, 4, 6. {%Cf.%} Pānini, vi. 4, 165; Eggeling, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 44, 131, 134.</F>

2. {@Keśin Dārbhya@}¦<sup>1</sup> or {@Dālbhya@}<sup>2</sup> (‘descendant of Darbha’) is a somewhat enigmatic figure. According to the Śatapatha Brāh- maṇa<sup>3</sup> and the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmana<sup>4</sup> he was a king, sister's son of {@Uccaiḥśravas,@} according to the latter authority. His people were the {@Pañcālas,@} of whom the Keśins must there- fore have been a branch, and who are said to have been threefold ({%tryanīka%}).<sup>5</sup> A story is told of his having a ritual dispute with {@Ṣaṇḍika@} in the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā<sup>6</sup> this appears in another form in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.<sup>3</sup> He was a contemporary of a fellow sage, {@Keśin Sātyakāmi,@} according to the Maitrā- yaṇī<sup>7</sup> and Taittirīya<sup>8</sup> Saṃhitās. The Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>9</sup> attributes to him a Sāman or chant, and the Kauṣītaki Brāh- maṇa<sup>10</sup> tells how he was taught by a golden bird. <div n="P"/>In view of the fact that the early literature always refers to Dārbhya as a sage, it seems doubtful whether the commentator is right in thinking that the Śatapatha refers to a king and a people, when a sage alone may well be meant, while the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa is of no great authority. The latter work may have assumed that the reference in the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā<sup>11</sup> to the Keśin people signifies kingship, but this is hardly necessary. <F>1) This is the form of the name in the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa, the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, the Taittirīya Saṃhitā, and the Kauṣītaki Brāh- maṇa; also later in the Bṛhaddevatā.</F> <F>2) This is the form in the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā and the Pañcaviṃśa Brāh- maṇa. It also appears later in the Rigveda Anukramaṇī.</F> <F>3) xi. 8, 4, 1 {%et seq.,%} as explained by Sāyaṇa.</F> <F>4) iii. 29, 1 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>5) Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxx. 2 (Weber {%Indische Studien,%} 3, 471); Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa, {%loc. cit.;%} Baudh- āyana Śrauta Sūtra, xx. 25.</F> <F>6) i. 4, 12 (von Schroeder gives no variant reading; but {%ṣ%} and {%kh%} are con- stantly confused in manuscripts).</F> <F>3) xi. 8, 4, 1 {%et seq.,%} as explained by Sāyaṇa.</F> <F>7) i. 6, 5.</F> <F>8) ii. 6, 2, 3.</F> <F>9) xiii. 10, 8.</F> <F>10) vii. 4.</F> <F>11) xxx. 2. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 193, 209; 2, 308; Hopkins, {%Transactions of%} {%the Connecticut Academy of Arts and%} {%Sciences,%} 15, 58, 59; Sieg, {%Die Sagenstoffe%} {%des Ṛgveda,%} 62, n. 2.</F>
3. {@Keśin Sātya-kāmi@}¦ (‘descendant of Satyakāma’) is men- tioned as a teacher and contemporary of {@Keśin Dārbhya@} in the Taittirīya (ii. 6, 2, 3) and Maitrāyaṇī (i. 6, 5) Saṃhitās.

{@Kesara-prābandhā.@}¦ — In the list of the crimes of the {@Vaita-@} {@havyas@} narrated in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> is the cooking of the last she-goat ({%caramājām%}) of Kesaraprābandhā, who may presum- ably be deemed to have been a woman, ‘having braided hair.’<sup>2</sup> Ludwig,<sup>3</sup> followed by Whitney,<sup>4</sup> appears to amend the passage ({%carama-jām%}) as meaning ‘the last-born calf’ of Kesaraprā- bandhā, a cow. But this interpretation does not suit the name so well. <F>1) v. 18, 11.</F> <F>2) Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Athar-%} {%vaveda,%} 432, 433.</F> <F>3) Translation of the Rigveda, 2, 447.</F> <F>4) Translation of the Atharvaveda, 252.</F>
{@Kaikeya,@}¦ ‘king of the Kekayas,’ is an epithet of {@Aśvapati.@}<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, x. 6, 1, 2; Chāndogya Upaniṣad, v. 11, 4.</F>
{@Kairāta@}¦ is the name of a snake in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> — possibly, but not probably, the modern Karait. <F>1) v. 13, 5. {%Cf.%} Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 243</F>
{@Kairātikā,@}¦ a ‘maiden of the {@Kirāta@} people,’ is mentioned in the Atharvaveda (x. 4, 14) as digging up roots for medicinal use.
{@Kairiśi,@}¦ ‘descendant of Kiriśa,’ is the patronymic of {@Sutvan@} in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (viii. 28).
{@Kaivarta.@}¦ See {@Kevarta.@}

{@Kaiśinī.@}¦ — The {%Kaiśinyaḥ prajāḥ,%} ‘offspring or people<sup>1</sup> of Keśin,’ are mentioned in an obscure passage of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> either as still existing at the date of the Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> or as extinct. <F>1) So Sāyaṇa.</F> <F>2) xi. 8, 4, 6.</F> <F>3) {%Cf.%} Eggeling, {%Sacred Books of the%} {%East,%} 44, 134. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 208.</F>

{@Kaiśorya,@}¦ ‘descendant of Kaiśori,’ is the patronymic of {@Kāpya@} in the first two Vaṃśas (lists of teachers) in the Bṛhad- āraṇyaka Upaniṣad.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) ii. 5, 22; iv. 5, 28 (Mādhyaṃdina = ii. 6, 3; iv. 6, 3 Kāṇva).</F>

1. {@Koka,@}¦ a word occurring in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and the Atharva- veda,<sup>2</sup> seems to denote the ‘cuckoo.’ In all the three passages in which it is found, Sāyaṇa explains it as the {@Cakravāka.@} Roth<sup>3</sup> renders it in the Atharvaveda passages as a certain destructive parasitic animal. {%Cf.%} {@Anyavāpa.@} <F>1) vii. 104, 22 ({%koka-yātu,%} a ghost in the shape of a cuckoo).</F> <F>2) v. 23, 4; viii. 6, 2.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.,%} 6. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Athar-%} {%vaveda,%} 454; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 262; Geldner, {%Rig-%} {%veda, Glossar,%} 49; Zimmer, {%Altindisches%} {%Leben,%} 92.</F>
2. {@Koka@}¦ is mentioned in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (xiii. 5, 4, 17) as a son of the Pañcāla king, {@Sātrāsāha.@}

{@Kokila,@}¦ a very frequent word in the Epic and later, denoting the cuckoo, is only inferred for the Vedic period from its being the name of a Rājaputra in the Kāṭhaka Anukramaṇī.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 3, 460.</F>
{@Koṇeya, Kauṇeya.@}¦ See {@Rajana.@}
{@Kola,@}¦ another form of {@Kuvala,@} the {%Zizyphus jujuba,%} is mentioned in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (vii. 3, 1).

1. {@Kośa@}¦ is the name in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> for the ‘bucket’ used in drawing water by means of a rope from a well ({@Avata@}). In the ritual<sup>2</sup> it denotes a large vessel to hold Soma, as opposed to {@Kalaśa.@} <F>1) i. 130, 2; iii. 32, 15; iv. 17, 6. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 156.</F> <F>2) Rv. ix. 75. 3; Av. xviii. 4. 30, etc. {%Cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 183 {%et seq.%}</F>

2. {{{@Kosa@}->{@Kośa@}||20160315|Marcis Gasuns||print missing diacritic over s}}¦ denotes the body of a chariot.<sup>1</sup> Presumably it was fastened to the axles, but it was probably not very secure, as the body of Pūṣan's chariot is said not to fall.<sup>2</sup> The ropes<sup>3</sup> used to fasten the Kośa are perhaps referred to in the word {%akṣā-nah.%}<sup>4</sup> By synecdoche this word also denotes the whole chariot.<sup>5</sup> See also {@Vandhura, Ratha.@} <F>1) Rv. i. 87, 2; x. 85, 7, etc.</F> <F>2) Rv. vi. 54, 3.</F> <F>3) {%Gāvaḥ,%} Rv. viii. 48, 5.</F> <F>4) See under 1. {@Akṣa.@}</F> <F>5) Rv. viii. 20, 8; 22, 9. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%op. cit.,%} 246.</F>

3. {@Kośa.@}¦ — The exact sense of this word in {@Kośa-kārī,@} the designation of a female victim at the Puruṣamedha, or human sacrifice,<sup>1</sup> is uncertain. It may be ‘sheath.’ <F>1) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxx. 14; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 10, 1.</F>
{@Koṣa.@}¦ — The Koṣas appear as a priestly family in the Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, where one of them, {@Suśravas,@} is mentioned by name.<sup>2</sup> <div n="P"/>^1 x. 5, 5, 8. <F>2) x. 5, 5, 1.</F>

{@Kosala@}¦ is the name of a people not occurring in the earliest Vedic literature. In the story of the spread of Āryan culture told in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> the Kosala-Videhas, as the offspring of {@Videgha Māthava,@} appear as falling later than the Kuru-Pañcālas under the influence of Brahminism. The same passage gives the {@Sadānīrā@} as the boundary of the two peoples  — Kosala and Videha. Elsewhere<sup>2</sup> the Kausalya, or Kosala king, {@Para Āṭṇāra Hairaṇyanābha,@} is described as having performed the great Aśvamedha, or horse sacrifice. Connexion with {@Kāśi@} and {@Videha@} appears also from a passage of the Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra.<sup>3</sup> Weber<sup>4</sup> points out that Āśvalāyana, who was very probably a descendant of {@Aśvala,@} the Hotṛ priest of Videha, is called a Kosala in the Praśna Upaniṣad.<sup>5</sup> The later distinction of North and South Kosala is unknown to both Vedic and Buddhist literature.<sup>6</sup> <div n="P"/>Kosala lay to the north-east of the Ganges, and corresponded roughly to the modern Oudh. <F>1) i. 4, 1, 1 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>2) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 5, 4, 4. {%Cf.%} Hiraṇya-nābha, a Rājaputra, in Praśna Upaniṣad, iii. 2, and Śāṅkhā- yana Śrauta Sūtra, xvi. 9, 13, as a Kausalya, while {%ibid.,%} 11, Para is styled Vaideha.</F> <F>3) xvi. 29, 5.</F> <F>4) {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 182, 441.</F> <F>5) vi. 1.</F> <F>6) Oldenberg, {%Buddha,%} 393, n. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} von Schroeder, {%Indiens Literatur%} {%und Cultur,%} 167; Eggeling, {%Sacred Books%} {%of the East,%} 12, xlii; Weber, {%Indian%} {%Literature,%} 39, 132 {%et seq.;%} Macdonell, {%Sanskrit Literature,%} 213-215; Rhys Davids, {%Buddhist India,%} 25.</F>

{@Kaukūsta@}¦ is mentioned in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> as a giver of a Daksiṇā, or gift to the priests officiating at a sacrifice. The Kāṇva recension reads the name {@Kaükthasta.@}<sup>2</sup> <F>1) iv. 6, 1, 13.</F> <F>2) Eggeling, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 26, 426, n. 1. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indian Literature,%} 134.</F>
{@Kauṇeya.@}¦ See {@Rajana.@}

{@Kauṇṭha-ravya@}¦ is mentioned as a teacher in the Aitareya<sup>1</sup> and Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyakas.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) iii. 2, 2.</F> <F>2) vii. 14; viii. 2. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Keith, {%Aitareya Āraṇyaka,%} 249.</F>
{@Kauṇḍinī.@}¦ See {@Pārāśarīkauṇḍinīputra.@}

{@Kauṇḍinya@}¦ is mentioned as a pupil of {@Śāṇḍilya@} in the first two Vaṃśas (lists of teachers) in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.<sup>1</sup> See also {@Vidarbhīkauṇḍinya,@} and the following. <F>1) ii. 5, 20; iv. 5, 26 (Mādhyaṃdina = ii. 6, 1; iv. 6, 1, Kāṇva).</F>

{@Kauṇḍinyāyana@}¦ is mentioned in the first Vaṃśa (list of teachers) of the Mādhyaṃdina recension of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad<sup>1</sup> as a pupil of Kauṇḍinya, pupil of Kauṇḍinya and Āgniveśya; in the second<sup>2</sup> as a pupil of the two Kauṇḍinyas, pupil of Kauṇḍinya and Āgniveśya. Neither Vaṃśa is of much value.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) ii. 5, 20.</F> <F>2) iv. 5, 26.</F> <F>3) Eggeling, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 12, xxxiv.</F>

{@Kautasta,@}¦ a word occurring once in the dual, is apparently a patronymic of {@Arimejaya@} and {@Janamejaya,@} two Adhvaryu priests at the snake sacrifice described in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) xxv. 15, 3. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 35.</F>

{@Kautsa@}¦ (‘descendant of Kutsa’) is mentioned in the Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> as a pupil of {@Māhitthi.@} A Kautsa is also attacked in the Nirukta<sup>2</sup> as denying the value of the Vedas, and there is a strong ritual tradition of hostility to the Kautsas.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) x. 6, 5, 9; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upani- ṣad, vi. 5, 4 (Kāṇva recension only).</F> <F>2) i. 15.</F> <F>3) {%E.g.,%} Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra, x. 20, 12; Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Myth-%} {%ologie,%} 3, 285. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indian%} {%Literature,%} 77, 140.</F>

{@Kautsī-putra@}¦ (‘son of a female descendant of {@Kutsa@}’) is mentioned as a pupil of {@Baudhīputra@} in the last Vaṃśa (list of teachers) of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad in the Mādhyaṃdina recension (vi. 4, 31).
{@Kaupayeya@}¦ is the patronymic of {@Uccaiḥśravas.@}
{@Kaumbhya@}¦ (‘descendant of Kumbhya’) is the patronymic of {@Babhru@}
{@Kaurama.@}¦ See {@Kaurava.@}

{@Kaurayāṇa@}¦ is apparently a patronymic of {@Pākasthāman@} in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> Hopkins<sup>2</sup> suggests that Kaurāyaṇa may be meant. <F>1) viii. 3, 21. {%Cf.%} Nirukta, v. 25.</F> <F>2) {%Journal of the American Oriental Society,%} 17, 90, n. 2.</F>

{@Kaurava@}¦ is the reading of the text of the Khilas<sup>1</sup> and of some manuscripts of the Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra<sup>2</sup> for the Kaurama of the Atharvaveda,<sup>3</sup> who appears in a Dānastuti (‘Praise of Gifts’) as a generous donor among the {@Ruśamas.@} <F>1) v. 8, 1 (Scheftelowitz, {%Die Apo-%} {%kryphen des Ṛgveda,%} 155).</F> <F>2) xii. 14, 1.</F> <F>3) xx. 127, 1. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Athar-%} {%vaveda,%} 689.</F>

{@Kauravya@}¦ (‘belonging to the {@Kurus’@}). A man of the Kuru people, is described in the Atharvaveda as enjoying prosperity with his wife under the rule of King {@Parikṣit.@}<sup>1</sup> Mention is also made of the Kauravya king {@Balhika Prātipīya@} in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>2</sup> and in the later legend {@Ārṣṭiṣeṇa@} and {@Devāpi@} are alleged to have been Kauravyas.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) xx. 127, 8; Khila, v. 10, 2; Śāṅkh- āyana Śrauta Sūtra, xii. 17, 2. {%Cf.%} a Mantra in the Vaitāna Sūtra, xxxiv. 9.</F> <F>2) xii. 9, 3, 3.</F> <F>3) Nirukta, ii. 10.</F>
{@Kauravyāyaṇī-putra@}¦ (‘son of a female descendant of {@Kuru@}’) is mentioned as a teacher in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (v. 1, 1).

{@Kauru-pañcāla,@}¦ ‘belonging to the Kuru-Pañcālas,’ is an epithet of {@Āruṇi@} in the Śatapatha Brāhmana (xi. 4, 1, 2), and a practice of those tribes is designated by this word in the same work (i. 7, 2, 8).
{@Kaulakāvatī@}¦ are two persons mentioned in the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā (ii. 1, 3) as having given advice, in the capacity of priests, to {@Rathaprota Dārbhya.@}

{@Kaulāla@}¦ is a word denoting a hereditary potter (‘son of a {%kulāla%} or potter’) according to the commentator Mahīdhara on the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā.<sup>1</sup> The other Samhitās<sup>2</sup> have {@Kulāla.@} <F>1) xxx. 7.</F> <F>2) Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 9, 5; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xvii. 13, and {%cf.%} Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xvi. 27.</F>

{@Kaulitara@}¦ is mentioned in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as a {@Dāsa.@} Appar- ently the name is an epithet of {@Śambara,@} meaning ‘son of Kulitara’: this points to Śambara having been a terrestrial foe, and not a mere demon.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) iv. 30. 14.</F> <F>2) {%Cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 3, 273; Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} pp. 64, 161.</F>

{@Kaulīka,@}¦ like {@Kulīkā,@} is the name of some sort of bird in the list of victims at the Aśvamedha, or horse sacrifice, in the Yajurveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 24; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 5.</F>

{@Kauśāmbeya@}¦ is the patronymic (‘descendant of Kuśāmba’) of a teacher {@Proti@} in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> according to the St. Petersburg Dictionary: a view supported by the fact that {@Kūśāmba@} actually occurs as the name of a man in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> It is, however, possible that the word means a ‘native of the town Kauśāmbī’ as understood by Harisvāmin in his commentary on the Śatapatha Brāhmana.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) xii. 2, 2, 13; Gopatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 2, 24.</F> <F>2) viii. 6, 8. The name is also found later (in the Epic) in the form of Kuśāmba.</F> <F>3) Eggeling, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 44, 153, n. 5. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische%} {%Studien,%} 1, 193; Rhys Davids, {%Buddhist%} {%India,%} 3, 36; Oldenberg, {%Buddha,%} 397.</F>

{@Kauśika@}¦ is an epithet of Indra as ‘connected with the Kuśikas,’ and also of {@Viśvāmitra@} as ‘son of Kuśika.’<sup>1</sup> A teacher named Kauśika is mentioned as a pupil of {@Kauṇḍinya@} in the first two Vaṃśias (lists of teachers) of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) In a late Khila, Scheftelowitz, {%Die%} {%Apokryphen des Ṛgveda,%} 104.</F> <F>2) ii. 6, 1; iv. 6, 1 (Kāṇva recension).</F>

{@Kauśikāyani@}¦ (‘descendant of Kauśika’) is mentioned as a teacher and a pupil of {@Ghṛtakauśika@} in the first two Vaṃśas (lists of teachers) of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) ii. 5, 21; iv. 5, 27 (Mādhyaṃdina = ii. 6, 3; iv. 6, 3, Kāṇva).</F>

{@Kauśikī-putra@}¦ (‘son of a female descendant of Kuśika’) is mentioned in a Vaṃśa (list of teachers) in the Kāṇva recension of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (vi. 5, 1) as a pupil of {@Ālam-@} {@bīputra@} and {@Vaiyāghrapadīputra.@}
{@Kauśreya@}¦ (‘descendant of Kuśri’) is the patronymic of {@Somadakṣa@} in the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā (xx. 8; xxi. 9).
{@Kauṣārava@}¦ (‘descendant of Kuṣāru’) is the patronymic of {@Maitreya@} in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (viii. 28).

{@Kauṣītaki@}¦ (‘descendant of Kuṣītaka’) is the patronymic of a teacher, or series of teachers, to whom the doctrines set forth in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> and in the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka,<sup>2</sup> and the Śrauta and Gṛhya Sūtras,<sup>3</sup> are referred. He is rarely mentioned elsewhere.<sup>4</sup> The doctrine of Kauṣītaki is called the Kauṣītaka.<sup>5</sup> The pupils of Kauṣītaki are known as the Kauṣī- takis in the Nidāna Sūtra,<sup>6</sup> and in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>7</sup> [Page1-195+ 43] they with Kuṣītaka are stated to have been cursed by {@Luśākapi.@} Elsewhere<sup>8</sup> they are called Kauṣītakins. If the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka<sup>9</sup> can be trusted, there were among them at least two leading teachers, {@Kahoḍa@} and {@Sarvajit,@} the former of whom is mentioned elsewhere.<sup>10</sup> <F>1) ii. 9; vii. 4, 10; viii. 8; xi. 5. 7; xiv. 3. 4; xv. 2; xvi. 9; xviii. 5; xxii. 1. 2; xxiii. 1. 4; xxiv. 8. 9; xxv. 8. 10. 14. 15, etc.</F> <F>2) ii. 17: xv. 1; Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad, ii. 1. 7.</F> <F>3) Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, iv. 15, 11; vii. 21, 6; ix. 20, 33; xi. 11, 3. 6, etc.</F> <F>4) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 4, 3, 1; Chāndogya Upaniṣad, i. 5, 2.</F> <F>5) Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, iii. 1; xix. 3; Sāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, iv. 2, 13; xi. 14, 26; Anupada Sūtra, ii. 7: vii. 11 viii. 5, etc.</F> <F>6) vi. 12.</F> <F>7) xvii. 4, 3.</F> <F>8) Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra, x. 1. 10; Āśvalāvana Grhya Sūtra, i. 23.</F> <F>9) {%Cf%} Kelth, {%Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka,%} 14, 24, 71</F> <F>10) Sarapatna Brāhmaṇa, ii. 4, 3, 1; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, iii. 4, 1; Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra, iii. 4. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 259; 2, 289 {%et seq.; Indian Literature,%} 44 {%et seq.;%} Lindner, {%Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa,%} ix.</F>
{@Kauṣya,@}¦ ‘descendant of Koṣa,’ is the patronymic of {@Suśravas.@}

{@Kausalya,@}¦ ‘prince of Kosala,’ is the designation of {@Para Āṭṇāra@} in the Satapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> and of {@Hiraṇyanābha@} in the Sāṅkhāvana Śrauta Sūtra.<sup>2</sup> Āśvalāyana is styled Kausalya, as ‘belonging to the Kosala country,’ in the Praśna Upaniṣad,<sup>3</sup> and the Kaśī-Kausalyāḥ, or the ‘Kāśis and people of Kosala,’ are mentioned in the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) xiii 5, 4, 4.</F> <F>2) xvi. 9, 13. {%Cf.%} xvi. 29, 5.</F> <F>3) i. 1.</F> <F>4) i. 2, 9 (spelt {%Kauśalyāḥ%}).</F>
{@Kausita@}¦ appears in the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā (ii. 1, 11) in connexion with the demon Kusitāyin as the name of a lake. The Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā (x. 5) has Kausida instead.
{@Kausurubindi,@}¦ ‘descendant of {@Kusurubinda,@}’ is the patro- nymic of {@Proti Kauśāmbeya@} in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (xii. 2, 2, 13). In the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa (i. 4, 24) the form is Kausuravindu.

{@Kauhaḍa,@}¦ ‘descendant of Kohaḍa,’ is the patronymic of a teacher, {@Mitravinda,@} mentioned in the Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> as well as of {@Śravaṇadatta.@} <F>1) Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 372, 382 {%et seq.%} A school of Kauhaḍīyas is known in the Gobhila Gṛhya Sūtra, iii. 4, 34.</F>

{@Kratu-jit Jānaki@}¦ (‘descendant of {@Janaka@}’) is mentioned in the Yajurveda<sup>1</sup> as the priest of {@Rajana Kauṇeya.@} See also {@Kratuvid.@} <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 3, 8, 1; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xi. 1. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 3, 474.</F>
{@Kratu-vid Jānaki@}¦ (‘descendant of {@Janaka@}’) is mentioned in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (vii. 34) as having learned a certain doctrine regarding Soma from Agni.

{@Kraya,@}¦ ‘sale,’ is a word which does not actually occur in the Rigveda, though the verb {%krī,%} from which this noun is derived, is found there.<sup>1</sup> Both noun and verb are common in the later Saṃhitās.<sup>2</sup> Sale appears to have regularly consisted in barter in the Rigveda:<sup>3</sup> ten cows are regarded as a possible price for an (image of) Indra to be used as a fetish, while elsewhere not a hundred, nor a thousand, nor a myriad are considered as an adequate price ({%śulka%}) for the purchase of Indra.<sup>4</sup> The Athar- vaveda<sup>5</sup> mentions, as possible objects of commerce, garments ({%dūrśa%}), coverlets ({%pavasta%}), and goatskins ({%ajina%}). The haggling of the market was already familiar in the days of the Rigveda,<sup>6</sup> and a characteristic hymn of the Atharvaveda<sup>7</sup> is directed to procuring success in trade. The ‘price’ was called {@Vasna,@} and the ‘merchant’ {@Vaṇij.@} his greed being well known.<sup>8</sup> <div n="P"/>There is little evidence of a standard of value in currency having been adopted. When no specific mention is made of the standard, the unit was probably the cow.<sup>9</sup> In a consider- able number of passages of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>10</sup> and elsewhere,<sup>11</sup> however, the expression {%hiraṇyaṃ śata-mānam%} suggests that there must have been some standard other than [Page1-197+ 48] cows, though it might in all these passages be rendered as ‘gold worth a hundred cows.’ But the use of the {@Kṛṣṇala@} as a measure of weight<sup>12</sup> suggests that the meaning is ‘gold weighing a hundred Kṛṣṇalas,’ and this seems the more probable explana- tion. This unit seems not to be known in the Rigveda, where the meaning of the term {@Manā,@} which occurs once, is mysterious, and where necklets ({@Niṣka@}) seem to have been one of the more portable forms of wealth, like jewellery in modern India, and may perhaps have served as a means of exchange. <F>1) iv. 24, 10.</F> <F>2) {%Kraya:%} Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 1, 2, 1; vi. 1, 3, 3; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, viii. 55; xix. 13; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 3, 2, 10, etc.; {%krī:%} Av. iii. 15, 2; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vi. 1, 10, 3; vii. 1, 6, 2, etc.; {%apa-krī:%} Av. viii. 7, 11; {%pari-krī:%} Av. iv. 7, 6, etc.; {%vi-krī:%} Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, iii. 49, etc.</F> <F>3) iv. 24, 10.</F> <F>4) Rv. viii. 1, 5.</F> <F>5) iv. 7, 6.</F> <F>6) iv. 24, 9. See Oldenberg, {%Ṛgveda-%} {%Noten,%} 1, 419, 420, correcting Sieg, {%Die%} {%Sagenstoffe des Ṛgveda,%} 91, and Geldner's {%Kommentar%} on iv. 24.</F> <F>7) iii. 15. See Bloomfield, {%Hymns of%} {%the Atharvaveda,%} 352; Whitney, Trans- lation of the Atharvaveda, 111, 112.</F> <F>8) Rv. i. 33, 3, and See {@Paṇi.@}</F> <F>9) {%Cf.%} Harisvāmin on Satapatha Brāh- maṇa, xiii. 4, 2, 1, where he renders {%sahasrārha%} as equal to ‘worth a thousand cows,’ in which Eggeling follows him; Saṃkṣiptasāra on Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xxii. 10, 33.</F> <F>10) xii. 7, 2, 13; 9, 1, 4; xiii. 1, 1, 4; 2, 3, 2; 4, 1, 13; xiv. 3, 1, 32. {%Cf.%} v. 5, 5, 16; xiii. 4, 1, 6.</F> <F>11) Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xviii. 3, 2, where a long series of compounds of numerals with {%-māna%} occurs; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, viii. 5; xiv. 8; xxii. 8.</F> <F>12) {%Cf.%} Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xi. 4; Tait- tirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 3, 6, 7; Anupada Sūtra, ix. 6: Weber, {%Indische Streifen,%} 1, 99-103. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 255- 260. Barter had for the most part passed away by the time of the Jātakas, an illustration of the modern character of the society they represent. See Mrs. Rhys Davids, {%Journal of the Royal Asiatic%} {%Society,%} 1901, 874 {%et seq.%}</F>

{@Kravaṇa,@}¦ a word occurring only once in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> is understood by Ludwig<sup>2</sup> as the name of the Hotṛ priest or the sacrificer. Roth considered it an adjective without at first<sup>3</sup> assigning a sense, but afterwards<sup>4</sup> as meaning ‘timid.’ Sāyaṇa interprets it as ‘worshipping.’ Oldenberg<sup>5</sup> considers the meaning uncertain, suggesting as possible ‘the slayer of the victim.’ <F>1) v. 44. 9.</F> <F>2) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 138.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>4) Böhtlingk's Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>5) {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 342.</F>

{@Kravya,@}¦ ‘raw flesh,’ is never mentioned in Vedic literature as eaten by men. Demons alone are spoken of as consuming it,<sup>1</sup> apart from Agni being called {%kravyād,%} ‘eating raw flesh,’ as consumer of the bodies of the dead.<sup>2</sup> The man who in the Rigveda is compelled by starvation to eat dog's flesh, never- theless cooks it.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) Rv. vii. 104, 2; x. 87, 2. 19; 162, 2; Av. iii. 28, 2; iv. 36, 3: v. 29 10, etc.</F> <F>2) Rv. x. 16, 9. 10. See Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} pp. 97, 165.</F> <F>3) iv. 18, 13. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 270, 271.</F>
{@Krātu-jāteya@}¦ is a patronymic of {@Rāma Krātujāteya Vaiyā-@} {@ghrapadya@} in the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa (iii. 40, 2; iv. 16, 1).
{@Krimi.@}¦ See {@Kṛmi.@}

{@Krivi@}¦ is asserted in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> to have been the older name of the {@Pañcālas.@} This statement is supported by the name of the king there mentioned, {@Kraivya Pāñcāla,@} The Krivis appear in the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> as settled on the {@Sindhu@} and the {@Asiknī.@} It is a plausible conjecture of Zimmer's<sup>3</sup> that with the {@Kurus@} they made up the {@Vaikarṇa@} people.<sup>4</sup> The importance of the Pañcālas, and the insignificance of the Krivis, may be explained in part by the fact that the later Kuru-Pañcāla alliance included the {@Bharatas.@} It is also probable, as Oldenberg<sup>5</sup> suggests, from the Śatapatha Brāh- maṇa,<sup>6</sup> that the {@Turvaśas@} were included in the Pañcālas, and as the latter name indicates, probably other tribes also. Or, if Hopkins' view<sup>7</sup> is accepted that Turvaśa was king of the Yadus, the latter may in part have been allied with the Krivis to form the Pañcālas. <F>1) xiii. 5, 4, 7.</F> <F>2) viii. 20, 24; 22, 12. Elsewhere- Krivi is doubtful in sense. In several passages (i. 30, 1; viii. 87, 1; ix. 9, 6, and perhaps i. 166, 6, where {%krivir-datī%} is an epithet of lightning) Oldenberg, {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} i. 166, 341, understands the word to mean ‘horse.’ Elsewhere (ii. 17, 6; 22, 2; viii. 51, 8) he takes it to be a proper name, while in v. 44, 4, he is doubtful. In the passages last cited this view may very well be correct.</F> <F>3) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 103.</F> <F>4) {%Cf.%} {@Kavaṣa.@}</F> <F>5) {%Buddha,%} 404.</F> <F>6) xiii. 5, 4, 16.</F> <F>7) {%Journal of the American Oriental%} {%Society,%} 15, 258 {%et seq.%} This view is hardly convincing, while the disappear- ance of the Turvaśas is easily to be accounted for by their being merged, along with the Krivis, in the Pañcālas. The name of Krivi is lost in the Epic as completely as that of Turvaśa (Pargiter, {%Journal of the Royal Asiatic%} {%Society,%} 1910, 48, notes 4, 5). <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Macdonell, {%Sanskrit Literature,%} 155, 157; Grierson, {%Journal of the Royal%} {%Astatic Society,%} 1908, 602-607; Keith, {%ibid.,%} 831 {%et seq.;%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 152, 153; Eggeling, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 12, xli.; Max Müller, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 32, 407.</F>
{@Krīta Vaita-hotra@}¦ (‘descendant of Vītahotra’) is mentioned in the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā (iv. 2, 6) in connexion with the {@Kurus.@}

1. {@Kruñc,@}¦<sup>1</sup> {@Kruñca,@}<sup>2</sup> {@Krauñca,@}<sup>3</sup> are variant forms denoting the ‘curlew’ or ‘snipe.’ To it is attributed in the Yajurveda<sup>1</sup> [Page1-199+ 49] the faculty, later assigned to the {@Haṃsa,@} of extracting milk from water when the two fluids are mixed.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 11, 6; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxxviii. 1; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xix. 73 {%et seq.;%} Tait- tirīya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 6, 2, 1-3.</F> <F>2) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 22. 31 (in xxv. 6 the sense is quite uncertain); Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 3.</F> <F>3) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 12, 1.</F> <F>1) Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 11, 6; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxxviii. 1; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xix. 73 {%et seq.;%} Tait- tirīya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 6, 2, 1-3.</F> <F>4) Lanman, {%Journal of the American%} {%Oriental Society,%} 19, 151-158; Macdonell, {%Sanskrit Literature,%} 150. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 91, 92.</F>

2. {@Krunc Āṅgirasa@}¦ is in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> the name of the seer of a Sāman or Chant called the Krauñca. It is doubtless invented to explain the name of the Chant on the ordinary principle that Sāmans are called after their authors, though this rule has many exceptions.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) xiii. 9, 11; 11, 20.</F> <F>2) Hopkins, {%Transactions of the Con-%} {%necticut Academy of Arts and Sciences,%} 15, 68. {%Cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mytho-%} {%logie,%} 2, 160.</F>

{@Krumu@}¦ is the name of a stream mentioned twice in the Rigveda — once in the fifth book<sup>1</sup> and once in the last, in the Nadī-stuti, or ‘praise of rivers.’<sup>2</sup> There can be little doubt that this river is identical with the modern Kurum, a western tributary of the Indus.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) v. 53, 9.</F> <F>2) x. 75, 6.</F> <F>3) Roth, {%Nirukta, Erläuterungen,%} 43; Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 14: Lud- wig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 200.</F>
{@Krumuka@}¦ as the name of ‘wood’ appears to be a variant form of Kṛmuka. <div n="P"/>^1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 1, 9, 3; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 4, 7, 3.

{@Kraivya. Pāñcāla,@}¦ the king of the {@Krivis,@}<sup>1</sup> is mentioned in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> as having performed the Aśvamedha, or horse sacrifice, on the {@Parivakrā.@} Eggeling,<sup>3</sup> however, takes the word as a proper name, ‘Kraivya, the Pāñcāla king.’ <F>1) So the St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.;%} Weber, {%Indian Literature,%} 125, n.; Oldenberg, {%Buddha,%} 409, n.</F> <F>2) xiii. 5, 4, 7.</F> <F>3) {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 44, 397 (but {%cf.%} p. 398, top).</F>

{@Krośa,@}¦ as a measure of distance (lit. ‘a shout,’ as expressing the range of the voice), is found in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) xvi. 13, 12. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische%} {%Studien,%} 8, 432 {%et seq.%} In the later literature it is equivalent to about two miles. The word still survives in the vernacular form of Kos as the most popular measure of distance in India.</F>

{@Kroṣṭṛ@}¦ (lit. ‘howler’), the ‘jackal,’ is mentioned in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as by nature cowardly compared with the wild boar ({@Varāha@}). In the Atharvaveda<sup>2</sup> it is spoken of as devouring corpses. The word also occurs in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā,<sup>3</sup> where the commentator glosses it with Sṛgāla, another name of the jackal. See also {@Lopāśa.@} <F>1) x. 28, 1.</F> <F>2) xi. 2, 2.</F> <F>3) xxiv. 32. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 84.</F>
1. {@Krauñca.@}¦ See {@Kruñc.@}

2. {@Krauñca,@}¦ as the name of a mountain, occurs only in the latest Vedic literature.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, i. 31, 2. See Weber, {%Indian Literature,%} 93; {%Indische%} {%Studien,%} 1, 78.</F>

{@Krauñcikī-putra,@}¦ ‘son of a female descendant of Krauñca,’ is mentioned as a pupil of {@Vaiṭṭabhatīputra@}<sup>1</sup> in the last Vaṃśa (list of teachers) in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) Vaidabhṛtī-putra in the Mādhyaṃ- dina recension, vi. 4, 32.</F> <F>2) vi. 5, 2 (Kāṇva).</F>

Indische Studien,%} 1, 105.</F> <F>3) 5.</F> <F>4) Weber, Berlin Catalogue of San- skrit MSS., 1, 94.
