{@Kṣatriya.@}¦ — As the origin of caste, the relation of the castes, intermarriage, and cognate matters may most conveniently be discussed under {@Varṇa,@} this article will be confined to deter- mining, as far as possible, the real character of the class called Kṣatriyas, or collectively {@Kṣatra.@} <div n="P"/>The evidence of the Jātakas<sup>1</sup> points to the word Khattiya [Page1-203+ 47] denoting the members of the old Āryan nobility who had led the tribes to conquest, {@as well@} as those families of the aborigines who had managed to maintain their princely status in spite of the conquest. In the epic<sup>2</sup> also the term Kṣatriya seems to include these persons, but it has probably a wider signification than Khattiya, and would cover all the royal military vassals and feudal chiefs, expressing, in fact, pretty much the same as the {%barones%} of early English history. Neither in the Jātakas<sup>3</sup> nor in the epic<sup>4</sup> is the term co-extensive with all warriors; the army contains many besides the Kṣatriyas, who are the leaders or officers, rather than the rank and file. <div n="P"/>In the later Saṃhitās<sup>5</sup> and the Brāhmaṇas<sup>6</sup> the Kṣatriya stands as a definite member of the social body, distinct from the priest, the subject people, and the slaves, {@Brāhmaṇa,@} {@Vaiśya,@} and {@Śūdra.@} It is significant that Rājanya is a variant to Kṣatriya, and an earlier one. Hence it is reasonable to suppose that the Kṣatriya and Rājanya are both of similar origin, being princely or connected with royalty. Moreover, the early use of Kṣatriya in the Rigveda<sup>7</sup> is exclusively con- nected with royal authority or divine authority. <div n="P"/>It is impossible to say exactly what persons would be in- cluded in the term Kṣatriya. That it covered the royal house and the various branches of the royal family may be regarded as certain. It, no doubt, also included the nobles and their families: this would explain the occasional opposition of Rājanya and Kṣatriya, as in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa,<sup>8</sup> where a Rājanya asks a Kṣatriya for a place for sacrifice ({%deva-yajana%}). Thus, when strictly applied, Kṣatriya would have a wider denotation than Rājanya. As a rule, however, the two expressions are identical, and both are used as evidence in what follows. That Kṣatriya ever included the mere fighting [Page1-204+ 72] man has not been proved: in the Rigveda<sup>9</sup> and later<sup>10</sup> others than Kṣatriyas regularly fought; but possibly if the nobles had retinues as the kings had, Kṣatriya would embrace those retainers who had military functions. The term did not apply to all members of the royal entourage; for example, the {@Grāmaṇī@} was usually a Vaiśya. <div n="P"/>The connexion of the Kṣatriyas with the Brahmins was very close. The prosperity of the two is repeatedly asserted<sup>11</sup> to be indissolubly associated, especially in the relation of king ({@Rājan@}) and domestic priest ({@Purohita@}). Sometimes there was feud between Kṣatriya and Brahmin.<sup>12</sup> His management of the sacrifice then gave the Brahmin power to ruin the Kṣatriya by embroiling him with the people<sup>13</sup> or with other Kṣatriyas.<sup>14</sup> <div n="P"/>Towards the common people, on the other hand, the Kṣa- triya stood in a relation of well-nigh unquestioned superiority.<sup>15</sup> There are, however, references to occasional feuds between [Page1-205+ 60] the people and the nobles,<sup>16</sup> in which no doubt the inferior numbers of the latter were compensated by their superior arms and prowess. In the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>17</sup> the Vaiśya is described as tributary to another ({%anyasya bali-kṛt%}), to be devoured by another ({%anyasyādya%}), and to be oppressed at will ({%yathākāma-jyeya%}). Probably these epithets apply most strictly to the relation of the king and his people, but the passage shows that the people were greatly at the mercy of the nobles. No doubt the king granted to them the right, which may have been hereditary, to be supported by the common people, whose feudal superiors they thus became. In return for these privileges the Kṣatriyas had probably duties of protection to perform, as well as some judicial functions, to judge from an obscure passage of the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā.<sup>18</sup> <div n="P"/>The main duty of the Kṣatriya in the small states<sup>19</sup> of the Vedic period was readiness for war. The bow is thus his special attribute,<sup>20</sup> just as the goad is that of the agriculturist; for the bow is the main weapon of the Veda. Whether the Kṣatriyas paid much attention to mental occupations is uncertain. In the latest stratum of the Brāhmaṇa literature there are references to learned princes like {@Janaka@} of {@Videha,@} who is said to have become a Brahmin ({%brahmā%}), apparently in the sense that he had the full knowledge which a Brahmin possessed.<sup>21</sup> Other learned Kṣatriyas of this period were [Page1-206+ 62] {@Pravāhaṇa Jaivali,@}<sup>22</sup> {@Aśvapati Kaikeya,@}<sup>23</sup> and Ajātaśatru.<sup>24</sup> Garbe,<sup>25</sup> Grierson,<sup>26</sup> and others believe they are justified in holding the view that the Ksatriyas developed a special philosophy of their own as opposed to Brahminism, which appears later as Bhakti, or Faith. On the other hand, there is clear evidence<sup>27</sup> that the opinion of Ksatriyas on such topics were held in little respect, and it must be remembered that to attribute wisdom to a king was a delicate and effective piece of flattery. There are earlier references to royal sages ({%rājan-%} {%yarṣi%}),<sup>28</sup> but it is very doubtful if much stress can be laid on them, and none can be laid on the later tradition of Sāyaṇa.<sup>29</sup> Again, the Nirukta<sup>30</sup> gives a tradition relating how {@Devāpi,@} a king's son, became the Purohita of his younger brother {@Śaṃtanu;@} but it is very doubtful if the story can really be traced with Sieg<sup>31</sup> in the Rigveda<sup>32</sup> itself. In any case, the stories refer only to a few selected Kṣatriyas of high rank, while there is no evidence that the average Kṣatriya was concerned with intellectual pursuits. Nor is there any reference to Kṣatriyas engaging in agriculture or in trade or commerce. It may be assumed that the duties of administration and war were adequate to absorb his atten- tion. On the other hand, we do hear of a Rājanya [Page1-207+ 54] as a lute player and singer at the Aśvamedha or horse sacrifice.<sup>33</sup> <div n="P"/>Of the training and education of a Kṣatriya we have no record; presumably, as in fact if not in theory later on, he was mainly instructed in the art of war, the science of the bow, and the rudimentary administrative functions which would devolve on him. At this early state of the development of the nobility which appears to be represented in the Rigveda, it was probably not unusual or impossible for a Vaiśya to become a Kṣatriya; at least, this assumption best explains the phrase<sup>34</sup> ‘claiming falsely a Kṣatriya's rank’ ({%kṣatriyaṃ mithuyā dhārayantam%}). <div n="P"/>The king and the Kṣatriyas must have stood in a particularly close relation. The former being the Kṣatriya {%par excellence,%} it is to him rather than to the ordinary Kṣatriya that we must refer passages like that in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>35</sup> where it is said that the Kṣatriya, with the consent of the clansmen, gives a settlement to a man: clearly a parallel to the rule found among many peoples that the chief, but only with the consent of the people, can make a grant of unoccupied land. In the same Brāhmaṇa<sup>36</sup> it is said that a Kṣatriya consecrates a Kṣatriya, a clear reference, as the commentator explains, to the practice of the old king consecrating the prince ({%kumāra%}) who is to succeed him; and again,<sup>37</sup> the Kṣatriya and the Purohita are regarded as alone complete in contrast with other people, the parallel with the Purohita here suggesting that the Kṣatriya {%par excellence%} is meant. See under {@Varṇa.@}</F> <F>33) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 4, 3, 5. This mention is proof of the existence of a class of Kṣatriya bards (as opposed to priestly reciters), from whose pro- ductions the Epic naturally grew up. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%Journal of the American%} {%Oriental Society,%} 15, 258.</F> <F>34) vii. 104, 13. {%Cf.%} for a similarly false claim to be a Brahmin, x. 71, 8.</F> <F>35) vii. 1, 1, 8.</F> <F>36) xii. 8, 3, 19; Eggeling, {%Sacred Books%} {%of the East,%} 44, 254, n. 1.</F> <F>37) {%Cf.%} Eggeling, {%ibid.,%} 41, 259.</F> <F>38) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 4, 2, 17, and see {@Rājanya.@}</F> <F>39) See references in Bühler, {%Sacred%} {%Books of the East,%} 14, 395, 396. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 212 {%et seq.;%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 231 {%et seq.;%} von Schroeder, {%Indiens Literatur und Cultur,%} 151 {%et seq.;%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 10, 4 {%et seq.%} (where practically every passage on the subject is cited or referred to); Hopkins, {%Journal of the American Oriental Society,%} 13, 98 {%et seq.%} (for the Epic parallels).</F>

{@Kṣa-pāvan,@}¦ ‘protector of the earth,’<sup>1</sup> is an epithet of a king,<sup>2</sup> or denotes a king<sup>3</sup> in the Rigveda. The word is significant, as showing the function of the king as the protector of the tribal territory. <F>1) The word occurs only in the nominative singular as {%kṣapāvān,%} which would be the regular form from a stem {%kṣapāvant;%} but it is probably an irregu- larity for {%kṣapāvā. Cf.%} Oldenberg. {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 72.</F> <F>2) iii. 55, 17.</F> <F>3) i. 70, 5; vii. 10, 5; viii. 71, 2; x. 29, 1. {%Cf. kṣiti-pa,%} ‘guardian of earth,’ ‘king,’ in later Sanskrit.</F>

{@Kṣiti@}¦ is in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> a regular word for ‘dwelling,’ and in particular the {%kṣitir dhruvā,%} ‘the secure dwelling,’ is mentioned<sup>2</sup> in a context that shows it, to be equivalent to the {@Vṛjana@} or {@Grāma@} regarded as a stronghold. From this sense is developed that of the peoples occupying the settlements,<sup>3</sup> and in particular the five peoples<sup>4</sup> (for whom see {@Pañca Janāsaḥ@}). <F>1) i. 65, 3; iii. 13, 4; v. 37. 4, etc.</F> <F>2) i. 73, 4 ({%cf.%} 2); vii. 88, 7. See Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 142.</F> <F>3) Rv. iii. 38, 1; iv. 24, 4; 38, 5; v. 1, 10, etc.</F> <F>4) i. 7, 9; 176, 3; v. 35, 2; vi. 46, 7; vii. 75, 4; 79, 1.</F>

{@Kṣipta,@}¦ ‘a wound’ (caused by shooting), or ‘bruise’ (caused by throwing), is mentioned in the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> together with a remedy for it, the {@Pippalī.@} <F>1) vi. 109, 1. 3. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 389.</F>
{@Kṣipra-śyena,@}¦ ‘swift falcon,’ is the name of a bird in the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā (iii. 14, 11) and the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa x. 5, 2, 10).

{@Kṣīra,@}¦ ‘milk,’ also called {@Go@} or {@Payas,@} played a large part in the economy of the Vedic Indians.<sup>1</sup> It was taken warm ({%pakva%} [Page1-209+ 46] as it came from the cow,<sup>2</sup> or was used with grain to make a ‘mess cooked with milk’ ({%kṣīra-pākam odanam%}).<sup>3</sup> It was also used for mixing with Soma ({@Abhiśrī, Āśir@}). From it butter ({@Ghṛta@}) was made. Milk was also curdled, the {@Pūtīkā@} and {@Kvala@} plants, among others, being used for the purpose.<sup>4</sup> The curdled milk ({@Dadhi@}) was undoubtedly used for food; and a kind of cheese is perhaps referred to in one passage of the Rigveda.<sup>5</sup> Goat's milk ({%aja-kṣīra%}) is also mentioned.<sup>6</sup> <F>1) The word {%kṣīra%} does not occur in Rv. ii. vii. It is found in i. 109, 3; 164, 7; viii. 2, 9; ix. 67, 32; x. 87, 16 (= Av. viii. 3, 15). See Hopkins, {%Journal of the American Oriental Society,%} 17, 64, 73 {%et seq.%} See also Av. ii. 26, 4; v. 19, 5; x. 9, 12, etc.; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 4, 8, 7, etc.</F> <F>2)i. 62, 9; 180, 3; iii. 30, 4.</F> <F>3)Rv. viii. 77, 10; Av. xiii. 2, 20. {%Cf. kṣīra-śrī,%} ‘milk-mixed,’ Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iv. 4, 0, 1; Vājasaneyi Saṃ- hitā, viii. 57, etc.</F> <F>4) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 5, 3, 5.</F> <F>5) vi. 48, 18.</F> <F>6) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiv. 1, 2, 13; see {@Aja.@} <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 63, 226, 226, 268.</F>
{@Kṣīraudana,@}¦ ‘rice cooked with milk,’ is mentioned frequently in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (ii. 5, 3, 4; xi. 5, 7, 5, etc.).

{@Kṣudra-sūktas,@}¦ ‘makers of short hymns,’ is the name given in the Aitareya Āraṇyaka<sup>1</sup> to the authors of certain hymns of the Rigveda. {%Cf.%} {@Mahāsūkta.@} <F>1) ii. 2, 2. {%Cf.%} Keith, {%Aitareya Āraṇyaka,%} 212, and Macdonell, {%Bṛhaddevatā.%} notes on iii. 116.</F>

{@Kṣumpa@}¦ is a word occurring only in one passage of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> where it seems to mean a ‘bush.’ The Nirukta<sup>2</sup> identifies it with the Ahichatraka, a ‘mushroom.’ <F>1) i. 84, 8.</F> <F>2) v. 16. {%Cf.%} Benfey, {%Sāmaveda, Glossar,%} 53.</F>

{@Kṣura@}¦ occurs three times in the Rigveda. The word appears to have the general sense of ‘blade’<sup>1</sup> in one passage,<sup>2</sup> possibly also in another,<sup>3</sup> where it is said that the hare swallowed a [Page1-210+ 57] Kṣura, and where the sense ‘blade’ is adequate. In the third passage<sup>4</sup> there seems to be a reference to the sharpening of a razor on a grindstone<sup>5</sup> ({%bhurijos,%} the dual denoting precisely, as Pischel<sup>6</sup> points out, the two sides of the apparatus, between which the stone revolved like the modern grindstone). But Muir,<sup>7</sup> following another view of Roth,<sup>8</sup> adopts the sense ‘the edge of scissors,’ which, however, hardly suits the other passage, one in the Atharvaveda,<sup>9</sup> where a Kṣura is described as moving about on the {%bhurijos,%}<sup>10</sup> as the tongue on the lip. The meaning ‘razor’ is perfectly clear in the Atharvaveda,<sup>11</sup> where shaving by means of it is mentioned; in many other passages<sup>12</sup> either sense is adequate. A {%kṣuro bhṛjvān%} occurs in the Yajur- veda:<sup>13</sup> it seems to denote, as Bloomfield<sup>14</sup> suggests, a razor with a strop (in the shape of a small grinding apparatus). Kṣura-dhārā<sup>15</sup> denotes ‘the edge of a razor,’ like {%kṣurasya%} {%dhārā.%}<sup>16</sup> In the Upaniṣads<sup>17</sup> a razor-case (Kṣura-dhāna) is mentioned. See also {@Śmaśru.@} <F>1) Hopkins, {%Journal of the American%} {%Oriental Society,%} 17, 61, 69. {%Cf.%} 13, 292 (as ‘knife’ in the Epic).</F> <F>2) i. 166, 10 ({%paviṣu kṣurāḥ%} on the fellies of the Maruts' car; possibly ‘razors’ may be meant, as Max Müller says in his note on this passage, {%Sacred%} {%Books of the East,%} 32, 235, n. 4).</F> <F>3) x. 28, 9, where Sāyaṇa renders it as meaning ‘having claws.’ The later tradition ascribes the swallowing to a goat.</F> <F>4) viii. 4, 16 ({%saṃ naḥ śiśīhi bhurijor%} {%iva kṣuram,%} ‘sharpen us like a razor on a grindstone or stropping apparatus’).</F> <F>5) Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>6) {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 243.</F> <F>7) {%Sanskrit Texts,%} 5, 466.</F> <F>8) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} {%bhurij.%}</F> <F>9) xx. 127, 4.</F> <F>10) Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Athar-%} {%vaveda,%} 197, translates {%bhurijos%} by ‘on a strop.’</F> <F>11) vi. 68, 1. 3; viii. 2, 7.</F> <F>12) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 6, 4, 5; iii. 1, 2, 7; {%kṣura-pavi,%} Av. xii. 5, 20. 55; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 1, 5, 7; 5, 5, 6; v. 6, 6, 1; Śatapatha Brāh- maṇa, iii. 6, 2, 9. etc.; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, i. 10, 14; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxxvi. 8; Nirukta, v. 5.</F> <F>13) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iv. 3, 12, 3. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 8, 7; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xv. 4; Śatapatha Brāh- maṇa, viii. 5, 2, 4.</F> <F>14) {%American Journal of Philology,%} 17, 418.</F> <F>15) Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa, iii. 13, 9.</F> <F>16) Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, iii. 3, 2.</F> <F>17) Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad, iv. 20. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 266; Pischel, {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 239-243; Schrader, {%Prehistoric Antiquities,%} 38 {%et seq.%}</F>

{@Kṣetra,@}¦ ‘field.’ The use of this word in the Rigveda points clearly to the existence of separate fields<sup>1</sup> carefully measured off,<sup>2</sup> though in some passages the meaning is less definite, [Page1-211+ 64] indicating cultivated land generally.<sup>3</sup> In the Atharvaveda<sup>4</sup> and later the sense of a separate field is clearly marked, though the more general use is also found.<sup>5</sup> The deity Kṣetrasya Pati,<sup>6</sup> ‘Lord of the Field,’ should probably be understood as the god presiding over each field, just as Vāstoṣ Pati presides over each dwelling.<sup>7</sup> It is a fair conclusion from the evidence that the system of separate holdings already existed in early Vedic times.^8 See also {@Urvarā, Khilya.@} <F>1) x. 33, 6. {%Cf.%} iii. 31, 15; v. 62, 7.</F> <F>2) i. 110, 5.</F> <F>3) i. 100, 18; ix. 85, 4; 91, 6; {%Kṣetra-%} {%jeṣa,%} i. 33, 15, ‘acquisition of land’; {%kṣetrā-sā,%} iv. 38, 1, ‘gaining land’; {%kṣetraṃ-jaya,%} ‘conquering cultivated land,’ Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 2, 11. The wider sense of ‘place’ also occurs, v. 2, 3; 45, 9; vi. 47, 20, etc., and often later.</F> <F>4) iv. 18, 5; v. 31, 4; x. 1, 18; xi. 1, 22; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 2, 1, 2; Chāndogya Upaniṣad, vii. 24, 2, etc.</F> <F>5) Av. ii. 29, 3; xiv. 2, 7; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 4, 1, 15. 16, etc.</F> <F>6) Rv. iv. 37, 1, 2; vii. 35, 10; x. 66, 13; Av. ii. 8, 5; {%kṣetrasya patnī,%} ‘Mis- tress of the Field,’ 12, 1; {%kṣetrāṇāṃ%} {%patiḥ,%} ‘Lord of Fields,’ Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xvi. 18.</F> <F>7) Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} p. 138. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 236; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, vii. 1, 1, 8, where the Kṣatriya, with the consent of the people, gives a settlement to a man: that is, presumably assigns to him a definite Kṣetra for his own, probably measured out as recorded in Rv. i. 110, 5.</F>

{@Kṣetriya@}¦ is a disease which is mentioned several times in the Atharvaveda, and against which three hymns are specially directed.<sup>1</sup> It is also mentioned in the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā<sup>2</sup> and the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa.<sup>3</sup> The commentators on the Athar- vaveda agree in taking it to be a hereditary disease. The word may mean ‘organic,’<sup>4</sup> or possibly ‘produced in the field,’ as a theory of its origin. What disease is really intended is quite uncertain. Weber<sup>5</sup> considered that the aim of the Atharvan hymns was to drive away injury threatening the fields, but this is improbable. Bloomfield<sup>6</sup> suggests ‘scrofula’ or ‘syphilis.’ The remedies mentioned throw no light on the symptoms. <F>1) ii. 8. 10; iii. 7. {%Cf.%} ii. 14, 5; iv. 18, 7.</F> <F>2) xv. 1.</F> <F>3) ii. 5, 6, 1-3, where the form is Kṣetrī, explained as a demon causing illness, merely an incorrect version of Av. iii. 10.</F> <F>4) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>5) {%Indische Studien,%} 5, 145; 13, 150 {%et seq.:%} 17, 208; {%Naxatra,%} 2, 292.</F> <F>6) {%Atharvaveda,%} 60. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Athar-%} {%vaveda,%} 286 {%et seq.;%} Whitney, Transia- tion of the Atharvaveda, 48, 49; Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 391, 392; Speijer, {%De ceremonia apud Indos quœ%} {%jātakarma vocatur,%} 76-83; Pāṇini, v. 2, 92, with the Kāśikā Vṛtti.</F>

{@Kṣema-dhṛtvan Pauṇḍarīka@}¦ (‘descendant of Puṇḍarīka’) is mentioned in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> as having sacrificed on the bank of the river {@Sudāman.@} <F>1) xxii. 18, 7. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 32. Later, the name is Kṣema-dhanvan, Harivaṃśa, 824, etc.</F>
{@Kṣaimi,@}¦ ‘descendant of Kṣema,’ is the patronymic of {@Suda-@} {@kṣiṇa@} in the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa (iii. 6, 3; 7, 1, etc.; 8, 6).

{@Kṣoṇī.@}¦ — This word, when used in the plural, denotes, according to the St. Petersburg Dictionary and Ludwig,<sup>1</sup> in several passages of the Rigveda,<sup>2</sup> the free retainers of the king. Geldner<sup>3</sup> at one time thought it referred to the wives of the king, pointing to polygamy; but later<sup>4</sup> he concluded that it means certain divine wives. <F>1)Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 247.</F> <F>2) i. 57, 4; 173, 7; viii. 3, 10; 13, 17; x. 95. 19. In ii. 34, 13; x. 22, 9, the sense is doubtful.</F> <F>3) Bezzenberger, {%Beiträge,%} 11, 327.</F> <F>4) {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 279, 283.</F>
{@Kṣauma,@}¦ ‘a linen garment,’ is mentioned in the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā (iii. 6, 7, etc.) and in the Sūtras.

{@Kṣviṅkā@}¦ is mentioned once in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as a bird of {@prey.@} The word also occurs in the list of victims at the Aśvamedha, or horse sacrifice, in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā,<sup>2</sup> where the com- mentary absurdly explains it as ‘a red-mouthed female ape’ ({%rakta-mukhī vānarī%}). <F>1) x. 87, 7.</F> <F>2) v. 5, 15, 1. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 93.</F>

{@Kha@}¦ denotes in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> the hole in the nave of the wheel in which the axle is inserted. There was a difference, it seems, in the size of the hole in the wheel of a cart ({@Anas@}) and of a chariot ({@Ratha@}).<sup>3</sup> See also 1. {@Yuga.@} <F>1) Rv. viii. 77, 3; 91, 7; x. 156, 3, where only the Kha is referred to. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} the adjective {%su-kha,%} ‘having a good axle-hole,’ ‘running easily’; later, ‘agreeable.’</F> <F>2) Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, v. 12, 1 (Mādhyaṃdina; v. 10, 1 Kāṇva).</F> <F>3) Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa, 1, 3, 6; Geldner, {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 333. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 247.</F>
{@Khaṅga.@}¦ See {@Khaḍga.@}

{@Khaḍga@}¦ is the reading in the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> of the name of an animal which, in the text of the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā,<sup>2</sup> variously appears as Khaṅga and Khaḍga. The rhinoceros seems clearly to be meant.<sup>3</sup> In the Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra<sup>4</sup> a rhinoceros hide is mentioned as the covering of a chariot. <F>1) iii. 14, 21.</F> <F>2) xxiv. 40.</F> <F>3) Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 86.</F> <F>4) xiv. 33, 26 ({%khāḍga-kavaca aśvaratha%})</F>

{@Khaṇḍika Audbhāri@}¦ (‘descendant of Udbhāra’) is mentioned in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> as a teacher of {@Keśin,@} and in the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā<sup>2</sup> as having been defeated by Keśin as a sacrificer. A Khāṇḍika appears in the Baudhāyana Śrauta Sūtra<sup>3</sup> as an enemy of Keśin. <F>1) xi. 8, 4, 1.</F> <F>2) i. 4, 12, where Ṣaṇḍika is the read- ing of the MSS.</F> <F>3) Caland, {%Über das rituelle Sūtra des%} {%Baudhāyana,%} 20.</F>

{@Khadira@}¦ is mentioned frequently from the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> onwards<sup>2</sup> as a tree with hard wood<sup>3</sup> — the {%Acacia catechu.%} The {@Aśvattha@} is referred to as engrafting itself upon it in the Atharvaveda,<sup>4</sup> [Page1-214+ 42] and from it the climbing plant {@Arundhatī@} is said to have sprung.<sup>5</sup> The {%sruva%} or sacrificial ladle is spoken of as having been made from it,<sup>6</sup> no doubt because of its hardness. It is in the same passage also said to have sprung from the sap ({%rasa%}) of the Gāyatrī. There is no clear reference to Catechu having been prepared from its core,<sup>7</sup> as it was later. The core ({%sāra%}) was used for making amulets.<sup>8</sup> <F>1) iii. 53, 19.</F> <F>2) Av. iii. 6, 1; v. 5, 5; viii. 8, 3; x. 6, 6; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 9, 3, etc. So {%khādira,%} ‘made of Khadira wood,’ Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 5, 7, 1; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 1; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 3, 3, 20; iii. 6, 2, 12 etc.</F> <F>3) Av. x. 6, 6.</F> <F>4) iii. 6, 1. {%Cf.%} viii. 8, 3.</F> <F>5) Av. v. 5. 5.</F> <F>6) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 5, 7, 1.</F> <F>7) It is called {%bahu-sāra,%} ‘of great strength,’ in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 4, 4, 9.</F> <F>8) Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka, xii. 8. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 58, 58.</F>
{@Kha-dyota@}¦ (‘sky-illuminator’), ‘the firefly,’ is mentioned in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (vi. 7, 3. 5).

{@Khanitra,@}¦ a ‘shovel’ or ‘spade’ for digging, is mentioned in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) i. 179, 6 (possibly metaphorical: see Oldenberg. {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 172; the passage is obscure).</F> <F>2) Lāṭyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, viii. 2, 4, etc.</F>

{@Khanitrima,@}¦ ‘produced by digging,’ as an epithet of {%āpaḥ,%} ‘waters,’ clearly refers to artificial water channels used for irrigation, as practised in the times of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and the Atharvaveda.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) vii. 49, 2.</F> <F>2) i. 6, 4; xix. 2, 2. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 236; Muir, {%Sanskrit Texts,%} 5, 466.</F>

{@Khara,@}¦ ‘ass,’ is mentioned in the Aitareya Āraṇyaka,<sup>1</sup> where a team of asses is alluded to. Probably the passages in the Satapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>2</sup> where the word is used to denote an earth mound on which the sacrificial vessels were placed, pre- suppose the sense of ‘ass,’ the mound being shaped in this form.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) iii. 2, 4.</F> <F>2) v. 1, 2, 15; xiv. 1, 2, 17; 2, 2, 30.</F> <F>3) {%Cf.%} St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>
{@Khargalā@}¦ is an ‘owl’ or other nocturnal bird mentioned in one passage of the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) vii. 104, 17. {%Cf.%} Kauśika Sūtra, 107; Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 93.</F>

{@Kharjūra@}¦ is the name of a tree ({%Phœnix silvestris%}) which is mentioned in the Yajurveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 4, 9, 2; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xi. 10; xxxvi. 7. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 63.</F>

{@Khala,@}¦ the ‘threshing-floor,’ is mentioned in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and the Atharvaveda.<sup>2</sup> See {@Kṛṣi.@} <F>1) x. 48, 7; Nirukta, iii. 10.</F> <F>2) xi. 3, 9; {%khala-ja,%} ‘produced on a threshing-floor,’ viii. 6, 15; {%khalya,%} ‘being on a threshing-floor,’ Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 9, 6. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 238.</F>

{@Khala-kula@}¦ is a word occurring in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad,<sup>1</sup> where Sāyaṇa glosses it by Kulattha, a kind of pulse ({%Dolichos uniflorus%}). <F>1) vi. 3. 22 (Mādhyaṃdina = vi. 3, 13 Kāṇva). {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien%} 1, 355.</F>

{@Khalva@}¦ is some sort of grain or leguminous plant, perhaps, as Weber<sup>1</sup> thinks, the {%Phaselus radiatus.%} It is mentioned with other grains of all sorts in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā,<sup>2</sup> and as being crushed with the {@Dṛṣad@} in the Atharvaveda.<sup>3</sup> It occurs also in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad,<sup>4</sup> where Śaṅkara glosses it with {%niṣpāva.%} <F>1) {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 355.</F> <F>2) xviii. 12, where Mahīdhara glosses it by {%caṇaka,%} ‘chick-pea.’</F> <F>3) ii. 31. 1; v. 23, 8.</F> <F>4) vi. 3. 22 (Mādhyaṃdina = vi. 3, 13 Kāṇva). <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 241.</F>

{@Khāṇḍava@}¦ is mentioned in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka<sup>1</sup> as one of the boundaries of {@Kurukṣetra.@} There seems no reason to doubt its identity with the famous Khāṇḍava forest of the Mahābhārata. The name occurs also in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> and the Śāṭyāyanaka.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) v. 1, 1.</F> <F>2) xxv. 3, 6.</F> <F>3) Max Müller, {%Ṛgveda,%} ^2 iv. ci. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 78.</F>

{@Khādi@}¦ occurs frequently in the Rigveda denoting either anklets<sup>1</sup> or armlets,<sup>2</sup> or sometimes rings on the hands.<sup>3</sup> Max Müller<sup>4</sup> considers that the word means quoits, the later Cakra.<sup>5</sup> The rings were sometimes of gold.<sup>6</sup> <F>1) v. 54, 11, and perhaps 53, 4.</F> <F>2) This is what Khādis on the shoulders must mean, i. 166, 9; vii. 56, 13.</F> <F>3) i. 168, 3; {%khādi-hasta,%} ‘with rings on the hands,’ 5, 58, 2. So Roth takes Khādin in vi. 16, 40; St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} Khādin occurs also in ii. 34, 2; x. 38, 1.</F> <F>4) {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 32, 120, 230.</F> <F>5) {%Cf. vṛṣa-khādi,%} Rv. i. 64, 10.</F> <F>6) {%Hiraṇya-khādi,%} Śāṅkhāyana Śranta Sūtra, iii. 5, 12; viii. 23, 6. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 262; Muir, {%Sanskrit Texts,%} 5, 149.</F>
{@Khārī@}¦ designates a measure of Soma in one passage of the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) iv. 32, 17. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 280.</F>
{@Khārgali,@}¦ ‘descendant of Khargalā or Khṛgala,’ is the metronymic or patronymic of Luśākapi.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxx. 2; Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xvii. 4, 3.</F>

1. {@Khila,@}¦<sup>1</sup> {@Khilya@}<sup>2</sup> appear to have the same meaning. According to Roth,<sup>3</sup> these terms denote the waste land lying between cultivated fields; but he admits that this sense does not suit the passage of the Rigveda<sup>4</sup> in which it is said that the god places the worshipper on an unbroken Khilya ({%abhinne%} {%khilye%}), and he accordingly conjectures the reading {%akhilya-%} {%bhinne,%} ‘land unbroken by barren strips.’ Pischel<sup>5</sup> thinks that the meaning intended is broad lands, which were used for the pasturing of the cattle of the community, and were not broken up by cultivated fields. Oldenberg,<sup>6</sup> however, points out that the sense is rather the land which lay between cultivated fields, but which need not be deemed to have been unfertile, as Roth thought. This agrees with the fact that in Vedic times separate fields were already known: see {@Kṣetra.@} <F>1) Av. vii. 115, 4; Śatapatha Brāh- maṇa, viii. 3, 4, 1.</F> <F>2) Rv. vi. 28, 2; x. 142, 3.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} So Whitney on Av., {%loc. cit.%}</F> <F>4) vi. 28, 2.</F> <F>5) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 205.</F> <F>6) {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 385, 386. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 236; Ludwig. Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 499; Keith, {%Journal of the Royal Asiutic%} {%Society,%} 1910, 228.</F>

2. {@Khila@}¦ as a designation of certain hymns appended to the received text of the Rigveda occurs only in the Sūtra period.<sup>1</sup> The term is a metaphorical application of the preceding word, ‘a space not filled up,’ ‘a supplement.’ <F>1) See Scheftelowitz, {%Die Apokryphen des Ṛgveda,%} 16 {%et seq.%}</F>

{@Khṛgala,@}¦ or, as the Paippalāda recension of the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> has it, Khugila, is an obscure expression found in two passages only — once in the Rigveda,<sup>2</sup> and once in the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> In the former the meaning ‘crutch’ seems required; in the latter Sāyaṇa glosses it by ‘armour’ ({%tanu-trāṇa%}), but the sense is quite uncertain. <F>1) iii. 9. 3.</F> <F>2) ii. 39, 4. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Athar-%} {%vaveda,%} 340; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 98.</F> <F>1) iii. 9. 3.</F>

{@Khela@}¦ occurs in one passage of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> where Pischel<sup>2</sup> considers that a god, Vivasvant, is meant, and that races were run in his honour, explaining thus the phrase {%ājā khelasya,%} as ‘in the race of Khela.’ Roth<sup>3</sup> thinks that a man is meant, and Sieg,<sup>4</sup> following Sāyaṇa, sees in him a king whose Purohita was Agastya. See also {@Aṃśu.@} <F>1) i. 116, 15.</F> <F>2) {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 171-173.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>4) {%Die Sagenstoffe des Ṛgveda,%} 127, 128. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rig- veda, 4. 28.</F>

{@Gaṅgā,@}¦ the modern Ganges, is mentioned directly in the Rigveda only once, in the Nadī-stuti or ‘Praise of Rivers.’<sup>1</sup> But it is also referred to in the derivative form {%gāṅgyaḥ%} as an epithet of {@Urukakṣa.@}<sup>3</sup> The name of this river does not occur <div n="P"/><sup>2</sup> [Page1-218+ 43] in the other Saṃhitā, but appears in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>4</sup> where victories of {@Bharata Dauḥṣanti@} on both Gaṅgā and {@Yamunā@} are referred to, and in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka<sup>5</sup> especial honour is assigned to those who dwell between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, this being. To doubt, the region in which that text originated. The identification of the Gaṅgā with the Apayā<sup>6</sup> made by Ludwig<sup>7</sup> must be rejected: see {@Āpayā.@} <F>1) x. 75, 5.</F> <F>3) The reference to the Gaṅgā re- mains, even if with Oldenberg ({%Ṛgveda-%} {%Noten,%} 1, 396) we assume that a thicket i meant, and not a proper name ({%cf.%} Wackernagel, {%Altindische Grammatik,%} 2, 288). See also Weber, Proceed- ings of the Berlin Academy, 1898, 563, n. 1.</F> <F>2) vi. 45, 31.</F> <F>4) xiii. 5, 4, 11. The victory on the Gaṅgā represents the farthest extent of Bharata or Kuru rule. {%Cf.%} Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, viii. 23, and a verse in the Vaitāna Sūtra, xxxiv. 9, where the Sarasvatī is also referred to.</F> <F>5) ii. 20.</F> <F>6) Rv. iii. 23, 4.</F> <F>7) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 200. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 4. 5.</F>

{@Gaja,@}¦ the common name of the elephant in Epic<sup>1</sup> and later Sanskrit, is only found in the late Adbhuta Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> See {@Hastin.@} <F>1) Hopkins, {%Journal of the American%} {%Oriental Society,%} 13, 265, 269.</F> <F>2) {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 39.</F>

{@Gaṇaka,@}¦ ‘an astrologer,’ occurs in the list of victims at the Puruṣamedha, or human sacrifice, in the Yajurveda.<sup>1</sup> See also Nakṣatradarśa. <F>1) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxx. 20; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 15, 1. {%Cf.%} Weber. {%Indische Streifen,%} 1, 78.</F>
{@Gandharvāyaṇa Bāleya@}¦ (‘descendant of Bali’) {@Āgniveśya@} is mentioned as a Pañcāla in the Baudhāyana Śrauta Sūtra (xx. 25).

{@Gandhāra@}¦ is a later form of the name of the people called {@Gandhāri@} in the Rigveda and Atharvaveda. In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad<sup>1</sup> the Gandhāras are referred to as being distant from the writer. See also {@Gāndhāra.@} <F>1) vi. 14, 1. 2. See Oldenberg, {%Buddha,%} 399, n.; Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 219, n. On the other hand, Max Müller, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 15. 106, thought the passage meant that the Gandhāras were near the writer.</F>

{@Gandhāri@}¦ is the name of a people in the north-west of India. In the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> the good wool of the sheep of the Gandhāris is referred to. The Gandhāris are also mentioned with the {@Mūjavants, Angas,@} and {@Magadhas@} in the Atharvaveda.<sup>2</sup> Gandhāris<sup>3</sup> or Gāndhāris<sup>4</sup> are also spoken of in the Śrauta Sūtras.<sup>5</sup> Zimmer<sup>6</sup> considers that they were settled in Vedic times on the south bank of the {@Kubhā@} up to its mouth in the Indus, and for some distance down the east side of the Indus itself. They later formed a portion of the Persian empire, and detachments of Gandarians accompanied Xerxes in his expedition against Greece.<sup>7</sup> <F>1) i. 126, 7.</F> <F>2) v. 22, 14. The latter two tribes are apparently the Eastern limit of the poet's knowledge, the two former the Northern.</F> <F>3) Hiraṇyakeśi Śrauta Sūtra, xvii. 6; Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra, xxii. 6, 18.</F> <F>4) Baudhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xxi. 13.</F> <F>5) See Caland, {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen%} {%Morgenländischen Gesellschaft,%} 56, 553.</F> <F>6) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 30, 31.</F> <F>7) Keith, {%Aitareya Āraṇyaka,%} 23. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rig- veda, 3, 206.</F>

{@Gabhasti@}¦ denotes, according to Roth,<sup>1</sup> the pole of a chariot in the epithet {%syūma-gabhasti,%} ‘having reins as a pole,’ used of the car of the gods in the Rigveda,<sup>2</sup> and independently in the plural in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa.<sup>3</sup> The meaning is, however, doubtful.<sup>4</sup> Roth<sup>5</sup> himself suggests that {%syūma-gabhasti%} may refer to a sort of double reins. <F>1) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>2) i. 122, 5; vii. 71, 3.</F> <F>3) ii. 7, 13, 4.</F> <F>4) See Oldenberg, {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 55.</F> <F>5) {%Op. cit., s.v.%}</F>

1. {@Gaya,@}¦ ‘house,’ is a common word in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> and sometimes occurs later.<sup>2</sup> As its sense includes the inmates as well as their belongings, it is equivalent to ‘household.’ <F>1) i. 74, 2; v. 10, 3; 44, 7; vi. 2, 8, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. vi. 3, 3; 84, 1; {@Vājasaneyi@} Saṃhitā, xxvii. 3.</F>

2. {@Gaya Plāta@}¦ (‘son of Plati’) is referred to in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> two hymns of which he clearly claims to have composed, and which are attributed to him in the Sarvānukramaṇī and the [Page1-220+ 52] Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> In the Atharvaveda<sup>3</sup> he appears with Asita and Kaśyapa as a half-mythical magician.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) x. 63, 17; 64, 17 (as son of Plati).</F> <F>2) v. 2.</F> <F>3) i. 14, 4. {%Cf.%} also the Khila after Rv. v. 51, 15; {%Indische Studien,%} 3, 214.</F> <F>4) Bloomfield, {%American Journal of%} {%Philology,%} 17, 403. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rig- veda, 3, 133; Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 3, 460.</F>

1. {@Gara,@}¦ ‘poison,’ is referred to in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> in the compound {%gara-gīrṇa,%} ‘poisoned.’ In the Śatapatha Brāh- maṇa<sup>2</sup> it means simply a ‘fluid.’ <F>1) v. 18, 13. {%Cf. gara%} alone, Pañca- viṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xix. 4, 2 (see {%Indische%} {%Studien,%} 1, 33); Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, i. 9, 10; {%gara-gir,%} ‘poisoned,’ Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xvii. 1, 9; xix. 4, 2. 10.</F> <F>2) xi. 5, 8, 6.</F>

2. {@Gara@}¦ is mentioned in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> as the author of a Sāman or Chant, and as a friend of Indra. <F>1) ix. 2, 16. {%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%Transactions of the Connecticut Academy of Arts and%} {%Sciences,%} 15, 52.</F>

{@Garga@}¦ is the name of a sage who is not mentioned in any of the Saṃhitās,<sup>1</sup> but his descendants, the {%Gargāḥ Prāvareyāḥ,%} are referred to in the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā.<sup>2</sup> Garga himself does not occur till the Sūtra period.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) The authorship of Rv. vi. 47 is attributed to Garga Bhāradvāja in the Anukramaṇī.</F> <F>2) xiii. 12. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 3, 374.</F> <F>3) Garga-trirātra, Garga-tryaha, a three-night or three-day feast of Garga. See Āśvalāyana Srauta Sūtra, x. 2; Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xvi. 22. 2; Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xxiii. 2, 8.</F>

{@Gargara,@}¦ apparently the designation of a musical instrument, is mentioned once in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) viii. 69, 9. {%Cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 144, n. 1; Zimmer, {%Altin-%} {%disches Leben,%} 289.</F>

{@Garta@}¦ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> primarily denotes the seat of the chariot on which the archer sat. It seems to have been of considerable [Page1-221+ 54] size, being described as {%bṛhant,%}<sup>2</sup> ‘large.’ The word then comes to denote the chariot<sup>3</sup> itself, either really or metaphorically.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) vi. 20, 9. Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 246, 247. Zimmer wrongly takes this passage to refer to standing in the car. See Hopkins. {%Journal of the American%} {%Oriental Society,%} 13, 238, 239; Geldner, {%Vedische Studien,%} 3, 48, and {%cf. garta-sad,%} ‘sitting on the car seat,’ in Rv. ii. 33. 11.</F> <F>2) v. 62, 8; 68, 5.</F> <F>3) So probably in v. 62, 5; {%gartā-ruh,%} ‘mounting the chariot,’ in Rv. i. 124, 7; Nirukta, iii. 5, may refer merely to mounting the seat. The passage is obscure; see Geldner, {%Rigveda, Kom-%} {%mentar,%} 22.</F> <F>4) vii. 64, 4 (of the hymn).</F>

{@Gardabha,@}¦ ‘the ass,’ is mentioned in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as inferior to the horse. In the Taittirīya Saṃhitā he again appears as inferior to the horse,<sup>2</sup> but at the same time as the best bearer of burdens ({%bhāra-bhāritama%}) among animals.<sup>3</sup> The same authority styles the ass {%dvi-retas,%} ‘having double seed,’<sup>4</sup> in allusion to his breeding with the mare as well as the she-ass. The smallness of the young of the ass, and his capacity for eating, are both referred to.<sup>5</sup> The disagreeable cry of the animal is mentioned in the Atharvaveda,<sup>6</sup> and in allusion to this the term ‘ass’ is applied opprobriously to a singer in the Rigveda.<sup>7</sup> A hundred asses are spoken of as a gift to a singer in a Vālakhilya hymn.<sup>8</sup> The mule ({%aśvatara%}) is the offspring of an ass and a mare, the latter, like the ass, being called {%dvi-%} {%retas,%}<sup>9</sup> ‘receiving double seed,’ for similar reasons. The male ass is often also termed {@Rāsabha.@} The female ass, Gardabhī, is mentioned in the Atharvaveda<sup>10</sup> and the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.<sup>11</sup> <F>1) iii. 53, 23. A car drawn by asses is referred to in the Aitareya Brāh- maṇa, iv. 9; see also {@Khara.@}</F> <F>2) v. 1, 2, 1. 2.</F> <F>3) v. 1, 5, 5.</F> <F>4) v. 1, 5, 5; vii. 1, 1, 2; Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 57, 4 (Oertel, {%Transactions%} {%of the Connecticut Academy of Arts and%} {%Sciences,%} 15, 177-180): of the Rāsabha, Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, vi. 3, 1, 23.</F> <F>5) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 1, 5, 5.</F> <F>6) viii. 6, 10.</F> <F>7) i. 29, 5.</F> <F>8) viii. 56, 3.</F> <F>9) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vii. 1, 1, 2. 3; Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, vi. 1, 6; Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 57, 4.</F> <F>10) x. 1, 4.</F> <F>11) i. 4, 8. For other references to the ass as Gardabha, see Av. v. 31, 3; Aita- reya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 34; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iv. 5, 1, 9; xii. 7, 1, 5. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 232, 233.</F>
{@Gardabhī-mukha@}¦ is mentioned as a teacher in the Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 384.</F>

{@Gardabhī-vipīta,@}¦ or {@Gardabhī-vibhīta,@} is the name of a teacher who was a Bhāradvāja and a contemporary of {@Janaka,@} mentioned in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad. <div n="P"/>1) iv. 1, 11 (Mādhyaṃdina = iv. 1, 5 Kāṇva).

{@Garmut@}¦ is the name of a kind of wild bean mentioned in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā.<sup>1</sup> The Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā<sup>2</sup> has the form Ganmut, which is probably a false reading. The adjective {%gārmuta,%} ‘made from the Garmut bean,’ is found in the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) ii. 4, 4, 1. 2.</F> <F>2) x. 11.</F> <F>3) ii. 2, 4. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.;%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 71.</F>

{@Galunta@}¦ is a word occurring only once in the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> apparently in the sense of ‘swelling,’<sup>2</sup> but Whitney<sup>3</sup> translates it by ‘neck.’ <F>1) vi. 83, 3.</F> <F>2) Bloomfield, {%Proceedings of the%} {%American Oriental Society,%} October, 1887, xvi; {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 505.</F> <F>3) Translation of the Atharvaveda, 343.</F>
{@Galūnasa Ārkṣākāyaṇa@}¦ (‘descendant of Ṛkṣāka’) is mentioned as a teacher in the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa (i. 38, 4).

{@Gavaya,@}¦ the name of a species of ox ({%Bos gavacus%}) occurs frequently from the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> onwards.<sup>2</sup> It is mentioned with {@Gaura@} and {@Mahiṣa@} in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā,<sup>3</sup> where also a wild Gavaya is spoken of.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) iv. 21, 8.</F> <F>2) Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 10; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xvi. 17; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 28; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 8; iii. 34; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 2, 3, 9; Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xvi. 3, 14, etc.</F> <F>3) xxiv. 28.</F> <F>4) xiii. 49; Taittirīya Samhitā, iv. 2, 10, 3; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 7, 17; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xvi. 17. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 83, 84.</F>

{@Gavāśir,@}¦ ‘mixed with milk,’ is a frequent epithet of {@Soma@} in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) i. 137, 1; 187, 9; ii. 41, 3; iii. 32, 2; 42, 1. 7; viii. 52, 10; 101, 10. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 279.</F>

{@Gav-iṣṭi@}¦ (lit. ‘desire of cows’) in several passages of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> denotes ‘conflict’ or ‘battle,’ evidently with reference to cattle raids. Gavyā<sup>2</sup> is similarly used. <F>1) i. 91, 23; iii. 47, 4; v. 63, 5; vi. 31, 3; 47, 20; 59, 7; viii. 24, 2; ix. 76, 2. So Av. iv. 24, 5.</F> <F>2) Rv. vii. 18, 7.</F>

{@Gavi-ṣṭhira Ātreya@}¦ (‘descendant of {@Atri@}’) is mentioned as a {@Ṛṣi,@} or seer, in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and the Atharvaveda.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) v. 1, 12; x. 150, 5.</F> <F>2) iv. 29, 5. See also Āśvalāyana Srauta Sūtra, xii. 14. 1. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rig- veda, 3, 126.</F>

{@Gavīdhukā,@}¦<sup>1</sup> {@Gavedhukā,@}<sup>2</sup> is the name of a species of grass ({%Coix barbata%}). It is also referred to in the adjectival forms {%gāvīdhuka%}<sup>3</sup> and {%gāvedhuka.%}<sup>4</sup> It was boiled with rice<sup>5</sup> ({%gavīdhukā-%} {%yavāgā%}) or barley<sup>6</sup> ({%gavedhukā-saktavaḥ%}) in preparing gruel. <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 4, 3, 2.</F> <F>2) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, v. 2, 4, 13; 3, 1, 10; xiv. 1, 2, 19.</F> <F>3) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, i. 8, 7, 1; 9, 2; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 7, 3, 6; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 6, 5; iv. 3, 8; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xv. 5.</F> <F>4) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, v. 2, 4, 11. 13; 3, 1, 10; 3, 7.</F> <F>5) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 4, 3, 2.</F> <F>6) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, ix. 1, 1, 8.</F>
{@Gavya.@}¦ See {@Gavyūti.@}
{@Gavyā.@}¦ See {@Gaviṣṭi.@}

{@Gavyūti@}¦ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> means, according to Roth,<sup>2</sup> grass land for the pasturing of cattle, in which sense Gavya is also found.<sup>3</sup> Thence it derives the sense of a measure of distance found in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>4</sup> Geldner, on the other hand, takes the original meaning to be ‘road,’ real<sup>6</sup> or meta- phorical,<sup>7</sup> thence a measure of distance,<sup>8</sup> and finally ‘land.’<sup>9</sup> <div n="P"/>5) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 290, 291. <F>1) i. 25, 16; iii. 62, 16; v. 66, 3; vii. 77, 4, etc.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>3) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, iv. 28; St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} 3b.</F> <F>4) Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xvi. 13, 12.</F> <F>6) Rv. i. 25, 16.</F> <F>7) Rv. vi. 47, 20; x. 14, 2.</F> <F>8) Rv. viii. 60, 20, and n. 4.</F> <F>9) Rv. iii. 62, 16; vii. 62, 5; 65, 4; viii. 5, 6.</F>

{@Gāṅgya,@}¦ ‘being on the Ganges,’ is the epithet of {@Urukakṣa@}<sup>1</sup> or of a thicket<sup>2</sup> in the Rigveda.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v. Cf.%} Wackernagel, {%Altindische Gram-%} {%matik,%} 2, 288; Weber, {%Episches im vedischen%} {%Ritual,%} 28.</F> <F>2) Oldenberg, {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 398.</F> <F>3) vi. 45, 31. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 2, 291, n.</F>

{@Gāṅgyāyani,@}¦ ‘descendant of Gāṅgya,’ occurs as the patro- nymic of {@Citra@} in the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) i. 1. There is a {%v.l.%} Gārgyāyaṇi. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 395.</F>
{@Gātu.@}¦ See {@Gāthā.@}

{@Gāthā@}¦ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> usually means only ‘song,’ ‘verse,’ like Gātu.<sup>2</sup> In one passage,<sup>3</sup> however, it already has a more special sense, as it is classed with {@Nārāśaṃsī@} and {@Raibhī,@} a collocation repeatedly found later.<sup>4</sup> The commentators identify the three terms with certain verses of the Atharvaveda,<sup>5</sup> but Oldenberg<sup>6</sup> has shown that this identification is incorrect for the Rigveda. Gāthās are often mentioned elsewhere,<sup>7</sup> and are referred to as metrical in the Aitareya Āraṇyaka,<sup>8</sup> where the {@Ṛc, Kumbyā,@} and Gāthā are classed as forms of verse. The Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>9</sup> distinguishes between Ṛc and Gāthā as divine and human respectively. According to the usage of the [Page1-225+ 51] Brāhmaṇas and the liturgical literature, as stated by the St. Petersburg Dictionary, the Gāthās are, though religious in content, distinguished from Ṛc, Yajus, and Sāman as non- Vedic — that is, are not Mantras. This view is consistent with the fact that the phrase {@Yajña-gāthā,@} meaning a verse summarizing a sacrificial usage, is not rare. The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>10</sup> preserves several Gāthās, which generally accord with this description as epitomizing the sacrifices of famous kings, and the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā<sup>11</sup> states that a Gāthā is sung at a wedding. Sometimes<sup>12</sup> Gāthā is qualified as Nārāśaṃsī, where it must be a eulogy of a generous donor. <F>1) viii. 32, 1; 71, 14; 98, 9; ix. 99, 4; {%gātha,%} i. 167, 6; ix. 11, 4; {%gātha-pati,%} ‘lord of song,’ i. 43, 4; {%gāthā-nī,%} ‘lead- ing a song,’ i. 190, 1; viii. 92, 2; {%ṛju-%} {%gātha,%} ‘singing correctly,’ v. 44, 5; {%gāthin,%} ‘singer,’ i. 7, 1. {%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%Journal of the American Oriental Society,%} 17, 65.</F> <F>2) i. 151, 2; ii. 20, 5; iii. 4, 4; iv. 4, 6; v. 87, 8; x. 20, 4; 122, 2.</F> <F>3) x. 85, 6.</F> <F>4) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vii. 5, 11, 2; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, Aśvamedha, v. 2; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vi. 32; Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, xxx. 5; Śatapatha Brāh- maṇa, xi. 5, 6, 8, where Raibhī does not occur; Gopatha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 6, 12.</F> <F>5) Viz., Gāthā = Av. xx. 127, 12 {%et seq.;%} Nārāśaṃsī = Av. xx. 127, 1-3; Raibhī = Av. xx. 127, 4-6; while {%ibid.,%} 7-10, are known as Pārikṣityaḥ ({%scil., ṛcaḥ%}).</F> <F>6) {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgen-%} {%ländischen Gesellschaft,%} 42, 238. Bloom- field, {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 689 {%et seq.,%} seems to accept the identification even for the Rigveda.</F> <F>7) Av. x. 10, 20; xv. 6, 4 (distinct from Nārāśaṃsī); Śatapatha Brāh- maṇa, iii. 2, 4, 16; xi. 5, 7, 10; xiii. 1, 5, 6; 4, 2, 8; 5, 4, 2; Taittirīya Āraṇ- yaka, ii. 10 (distinct from Nārāśaṃsī); Chāndogya Upaniṣad, iv. 17, 9, etc.</F> <F>8) ii. 3, 6, with Keith's note; Sata- patha Brāhmaṇa, xi. 5, 7, 10.</F> <F>9) vii. 18. The story of Śunaḥśepa is described as {%śata-gātham,%} ‘told in a hundred Gāthās.’</F> <F>10) xiii. 5, 4, etc., and see xiii. 4, 2, 8, where the Gāthās are plainly Dānas- tutis, or ‘praises of gifts,’ just as the Nārāśaṃsī verses are declared to be in the Bṛhaddevatā, iii. 154.</F> <F>11) iii. 7, 3.</F> <F>12) Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 3, 2, 6. So Eggeling, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 44, 98, takes Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xi. 5, 6, 8, where Sāyaṇa hesitates between identifying the two and distinguishing them. It seems reasonable to regard Gāthā as the wider term which covers, but is not coextensive with, Nārāśaṃsī. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Sāyaṇa's example of a Gāthā in his commentary on Aitareya Āraṇyaka, ii. 3, 6: {%prātaḥ prātar anṛtaṃ te vadanti,%} ‘they every morning tell an untruth,’ which is clearly not a Nārāśaṃsī. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Athar-%} {%vaveda,%} 689 {%et seq.;%} Weber, {%Episches im%} {%Vedischen Ritual,%} 4 {%et seq.;%} Max Müller, {%Ancient Sanskrit Literature,%} 493.</F>

{@Gāthin@}¦ is mentioned as the son of {@Kuśika@} and father of {@Viśvāmitra@} in the Sarvānukramaṇī. It is difficult to say whether this tradition is correct; it derives some support from the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (vii. 18), where reference is made to the divine lore ({%daiva veda%}) of the Gāthins, which is said to be shared by {@Śunaḥśepa@} as a result of his adoption by {@Viśvāmitra.@} See {@Gāthina.@}

{@Gāthina.@}¦ — The sons of Viśvāmitra are described in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> as Gāthinas, or descendants of Gāthin, who, according to tradition, was their grandfather;<sup>2</sup> and {@Viśvāmitra@} himself is styled Gāthina in the Sarvānukramaṇī. <F>1) vii. 18. {%Cf.%} Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra, vii. 18; Weber, {%Episches im%} {%Vedischen Ritual,%} 16, n. 3.</F> <F>2) {%Cf.%} Muir, {%Sanskrit Texts,%} 1^2, 348 {%et seq.;%} Pargiter, {%Journal of the Royal%} {%Asiatic Society,%} 1910, 32 {%et seq.%}</F>

{@Gāṃ-dama@}¦ is the form in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> of the name of {@Ekayāvan,@} which in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> is read as Kāṃdama. <F>1) xxi. 14, 20.</F> <F>2) ii. 7, 11, 2. {%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%Transac%} {%tions of the Connecticut Academy of Arts%} {%and Sciences,%} 15, 69.</F>

{@Gāndhāra,@}¦ ‘a king of Gandhāra’ named {@Nagnajit,@} is mentioned in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> he or some descendant figures as {@Svarjit Nāgnajita@} or Nagnajit, and as giving an opinion on the ritual, which is rejected with the observation that the author was merely a princely person ({%rājanya-bandhu%}). <F>1) vii. 34. in the list of teachers who handed down the knowledge of the substitute for Soma.</F> <F>2) viii. 1, 4, 10.</F>

{@Gārgī Vācaknavī@}¦ is referred to in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad<sup>1</sup> as a female contemporary and rival of {@Yājñavalkya.@} <F>1) iii. 6, 1; 8, 1. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 10, 118.</F>

{@Gārgī-putra,@}¦ ‘son of Gargī,’ occurs as the name of three teachers in the last Vaṃśa (list of teachers) in the Mādhyaṃdina recension of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (vi. 4, 30). The earliest of these three was the pupil of {@Bāḍeyīputra@} and the teacher of the second Gārgīputra. The latter was the teacher of {@Pārāśarīkauṇḍinīputra,@} the teacher of the third Gārgīputra.

{@Gārgya,@}¦ ‘descendant of Garga,’ is the patronymic of {@Bālāki@} in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka<sup>1</sup> and the Kauṣītaki<sup>2</sup> Upaniṣads. Two Gārgyas are mentioned in the second Vaṃśa (list of teachers) in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad:<sup>3</sup> one of them is the pupil of Gārgya, who again is the pupil of Gautama. Others occur in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka<sup>4</sup> and in the Nirukta,<sup>5</sup> as well as later in the ritual Sūtras. Thus the family was evidently long connected with the development of liturgy and grammar. <F>1) ii. 1, 1.</F> <F>2) iv. 1.</F> <F>3) iv. 6, 2 (Kāṇva)</F> <F>4) i. 7, 3.</F> <F>5) i. 3. 12; iii. 13.</F>
{@Gārgyāyaṇa,@}¦ ‘descendant of Gārgya,’ is mentioned as a pupil of {@Uddālakāyana@} in the second Vaṃśa (list of teachers) in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (iv. 6, 2 Kāṇva).
{@Gārgyāyaṇi,@}¦ ‘descendant of Gārgya,’ is a variant reading for {@Gāṅgyāyani@} as the patronymic of {@Citra@} in the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad (i. 1).

{@Gālava@}¦ is mentioned as a pupil of {@Vidarbhīkauṇḍinya@} in the first two Vaṃśas (lists of teachers) in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.<sup>1</sup> It is possibly the same man that is referred to regarding a point of ritual in the Aitareya Āraṇyaka.<sup>2</sup> A grammarian of this name is mentioned in the Nirukta.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) ii. 5, 22; iv. 5, 28 (Mādhyaṃdina = ii. 6, 3; iv. 6, 3 Kāṇva).</F> <F>2) v. 3, 3.</F> <F>3) iv. 3. {%Cf.%} Pāṇini, vi. 3, 61; vii. 1, 74; 3, 99; viii. 4, 67.</F>

{@Giri,@}¦ ‘mountain’ or ‘height,’ is a word that occurs repeatedly in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> Thus reference is made to the trees on the hills, hence called ‘tree-haired’ ({%vṛkṣa-keśāḥ%}),<sup>2</sup> and to the streams proceeding from the hills to the sea ({%samudra%}).<sup>3</sup> The term is frequently coupled with the adjectival {%parvata.%}<sup>4</sup> The Rigveda mentions the waters from the hills,<sup>5</sup> and the Athar- vaveda<sup>6</sup> refers to the snowy mountains. Actual names of mountains, as {@Mūjavant, Trikakud, Himavant,@} are very rare. References to {@Krauñca, Mahāmeru,@} and {@Maināga,@} are confined to the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, while {@Nāvaprabhraṃśana@} can no longer be considered a proper name.<sup>7</sup> <F>1) i. 56, 3; 61, 14; 63, 1; iv. 20, 6; vi. 24, 8, etc.</F> <F>2) Rv. v. 41, 11.</F> <F>3) Rv. vii. 95, 2.</F> <F>4) Rv. i. 56, 4; viii. 64, 5; Av. iv. 7, 8; vi. 12, 3; 17, 3; ix. 1, 18, etc.</F> <F>5) Rv. vi. 66, 11, on which passage, see Oldenberg, {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 411; viii. 32, 4; x. 68, 1, etc.</F> <F>6) xii. 1, 11. See {@Himavant.@}</F> <F>7) Av. xix. 37, 8, with Whitney's note in his Translation; Macdonell, {%Journal%} {%of the Royal Asiatic Society,%} 1909, 1107. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 47.</F>
{@Giri-kṣit Auccā-manyava,@}¦ ‘descendant of Uccāmanyu,’ is mentioned in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa (x. 5, 7) as a con- temporary of {@Abhipratārin Kākṣaseṇi@}

{@Giri-ja Bābhravya,@}¦ ‘descendant of Babhru,’ is mentioned in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (vii. 1) as having been taught by {@Śrauta@} the method of dividing the sacrificial animal ({%paśor%} {%vibhakti%}).

{@Guggulu,@}¦ ‘bdellium,’ is referred to in one passage of the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> as produced by the Sindhu<sup>2</sup> and by the sea. The latter source presumably alludes, as Zimmer<sup>3</sup> assumes, to sea- borne trade, bdellium being the gum of a tree, not a product of the sea. It is, however, possible that in this passage some other substance may be meant. The word in this form also occurs elsewhere in the Atharvaveda<sup>4</sup> and later;<sup>5</sup> it is often<sup>6</sup> mentioned in the older form of {@Gulgulu,@} between which and Guggulu the manuscripts constantly vary <F>1) xix. 38, 2.</F> <F>2) Or ‘from streams’ ({%saindhava%}), as Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} {%guggulu,%} suggests.</F> <F>3) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 28.</F> <F>4) ii. 36, 7.</F> <F>5) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, i. 28.</F> <F>6) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vi. 2, 8, 6; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 8, 5; Pañca- viṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xxiv. 13; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 5, 2, 16. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Athar-%} {%vaveda,%} 675; Lassen, {%Indische Alterthums-%} {%kunde,%} 12, 339; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 957, 958.</F>

{@Guṅgu.@}¦ — The descendants of Guṅgu are referred to as Guṅgus in a hymn of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> apparently as friends of {@Atithigva.@} Possibly a people may be meant. <F>1) x. 48, 8. {%Cf.%} Ludwig. Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 165.</F>

{@Gupta@}¦ is the name in the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa (iii. 42) of {@Vaipaścita Dārḍhajayanti Gupta Lauhitya.@} All the three other names being patronymics show that he was descended from the families of Vipaścit, Dṛḍhajayanta, and Lohita.
{@Gulgulu.@}¦ See {@Guggulu.@}

{@Gṛtsa-mada@}¦ is the name of a seer to whom the Sarvānu- kramaṇī attributes the authorship of the second Maṇḍala of the Rigveda. This tradition is supported by the Aitareya Brāh- [Page1-229+ 57] maṇa<sup>1</sup> and the Aitareya Araṇyaka.<sup>2</sup> The Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> speaks of him as a {@Bhārgava,@} ‘descendant of Bhṛgu,’ with a variant {@Bābhrava,@} ‘descendant of Babhru,’ but the later tradition keeps to the former patronymic.<sup>4</sup> The Gṛtsamadas are often mentioned in the second Maṇḍala of the Rigveda,<sup>5</sup> and are also called Śunahotras,<sup>6</sup> but never Gārtsamadas or Śaunahotras, and Gṛtsamada himself never occurs there.<sup>7</sup> <F>1) v. 2, 4.</F> <F>2) ii. 2, 1.</F> <F>3) xxii. 4. {%Cf.%} Gārtsamadī, xxviii. 2.</F> <F>4) Muir, {%Sanskrit Texts,%} 12, 226 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>5) ii. 4, 9; 19, 8; 39, 8; 41, 18.</F> <F>6) ii. 18, 6; 41, 14. 17.</F> <F>7) Oldenberg, {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen%} {%Morgenländischen Gesellschaft,%} 42, 200, 201. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rig- veda, 3, 118; Hillebrandt, {%Vedische%} {%Mythologie,%} 3, 287.</F>

{@Gṛdhra,@}¦ ‘the vulture,’ is often mentioned from the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> downwards.<sup>2</sup> The swiftness of its flight<sup>3</sup> and its fondness for devouring carrion are especially noticed.<sup>4</sup> More generally the word is used to designate any bird of prey, the eagle ({@Śyena@}) being classed as the chief of the Gṛdhras.<sup>5</sup> <F>1) i. 118, 4; ii. 39, 1; vii. 104, 22; x. 123, 8.</F> <F>2) Av. vii. 95, 1; xi. 2, 2; 9, 9; 10. 8. 24; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iv. 4, 7, 1; v. 5, 20, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iv. 9, 19; Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, iv. 29; Adbhuta Brāhmaṇa in {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 40; etc.</F> <F>3) Rv. ii. 39, 1.</F> <F>4) Av. xi. 10, 8. 24; Maitrāyaṃ Saṃ- hitā, {%loc. cit.%}</F> <F>5) Rv. ix. 96, 6. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 88; Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 225.</F>

{@Gṛṣṭi,@}¦ ‘a young cow,’ which has only calved once, occurs in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and the Atharvaveda,<sup>2</sup> as well as in the later Sūtra literature.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) iv. 18, 10.</F> <F>2) ii. 13, 3; viii. 9, 24; xix. 24, 5.</F> <F>3) Kauśika Sūtra, 19. 24, etc.</F>

{@Gṛha@}¦ is used in the singular,<sup>1</sup> or oftener in the plural,<sup>2</sup> to denote the ‘house’ of the Vedic Indian. {@Dama@} or {@Dam@} has [Page1-230+ 62] the same sense, while {@Pastyā@} and {@Harmya@} denote more especially the home with its surroundings, the family settle- ment. The house held not only the family, which might be of considerable size, but also the cattle<sup>3</sup> and the sheep<sup>4</sup> at night. It was composed of several rooms, as the use of the plural indicates, and it could be securely shut up.<sup>5</sup> The door ({@Dvār,@} {@Dvāra@}) is often referred to, and from it the house is called {@Duroṇa.@} In every house the fire was kept burning.<sup>6</sup> <div n="P"/>Very little is known of the structure of the house. Presum- ably stone was not used,<sup>7</sup> and houses were, as in Megasthenes' time,<sup>8</sup> built of wood. The hymns of the Atharvaveda<sup>9</sup> give some information about the construction of a house, but the details are extremely obscure, for most of the expressions used do not recur in any context in which their sense is clear. According to Zimmer,<sup>10</sup> four pillars ({@Upamit@}) were set up on a good site, and against them beams were leant at an angle as props ({@Pratimit@}). The upright pillars were connected by cross beams ({@Parimit@}) resting upon them. The roof was formed of ribs of bamboo cane ({%vaṃśa%}),<sup>11</sup> a ridge called {@Viṣūvant,@} and a net ({@Akṣu@}), which may mean a thatched covering<sup>12</sup> over the bamboo ribs. The walls were filled up with grass in bundles ({%palada%}), and the whole structure was held together with ties of [Page1-231+ 53] various sorts ({%nahana, prāṇāha, saṃdaṃśa, pariṣvañjalya%}).<sup>13</sup> In connexion with the house, mention is made of four terms which, though primarily sacrificial in meaning, seem to designate parts of the building: Havirdhāna, ‘oblation-holder’; Agniśāla,<sup>14</sup> ‘fire- place’; Patnīnāṃ Sadana, ‘wives’ room’; and Sadas, ‘sitting room.’ Slings or hanging vessels ({@Śikya@}) are also mentioned.<sup>15</sup> Reedwork ({%iṭa%}) is spoken of, no doubt as part of the finishing of the walls of the house.<sup>16</sup> The sides are called {@Pakṣa.@} The door with its framework was named {@Ātā.@} <F>1) Rv. iii. 53, 6; iv. 49, 6; viii. 10. 1, etc.; Av. vii. 83, 1; x. 6, 4; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, viii. 21.</F> <F>2) Rv. ii. 42, 3; v. 76, 4; x. 18, 12; 85, 26; 142, 4; 165, 2; Av. i. 27, 4; iii. 10, 11; vi. 137, 1; Aitareya Brāh- maṇa, ii. 31; viii. 26; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, ii. 32; iv. 33; xviii. 44; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 1, 2, 22; 6, 1, 19, etc.</F> <F>3) Rv. vii. 56, 16; Av. i. 3, 4; ix. 3, 13.</F> <F>4) Rv. x. 106, 5; Av. iii. 3.</F> <F>5) Rv. vii. 85, 6.</F> <F>6) Rv. i. 69, 2. {%Cf.%} the Gārhapatya Agni, Av. v. 31, 5; vi. 120, 1; 121, 2; viii. 102; ix. 6, 30; xii. 2, 34; xviii. 4, 8; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā. iii. 39; xix. 18; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vii. 6. 12; Kauṣīt taki Brāhmaṇa, ii. 1; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 6, 1, 28; vii. 1, 1, 6, etc.</F> <F>7) Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 153. Muir's view, {%Sanskrit Texts,%} 5, 461, that clay was used can only apply to the minor finishing of the walls of a house.</F> <F>8) Arrian, {%Indica,%} x. 2.</F> <F>9) iii. 12; ix. 3. See Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 343 {%et seq.;%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 17, 234 {%et seq.;%} Whitney, Translation of the Athar- vaveda, 525 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>10) {%Op. cit.,%} 153. No certainty can attach to the rendering of the words.</F> <F>11) It seems likely that, as the ribs were of bamboo and were probably fixed in the ridge, the roof was wagon headed, like the huts of the Todas at the present day (see illustrations in Rivers, {%The Todas,%} pp. 25, 27, 28, 51), and the rock-cut Chaityas, or Assembly Halls, of the Buddhists in Western India, in some of the earliest of which the wooden ribs of the arched roof are still pre- served. See Fergusson, {%History of%} {%Indian Architecture,%} 22, 135, {%cf.%} 126.</F> <F>12) Av. ix. 3, 8, where Bloomfield, {%op. cit.,%} 598, thinks of a wickerwork roof; Geldner, {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 136, of a pole with countless holes.</F> <F>13) Av. ix. 3, 4. 5.</F> <F>14) Zimmer conjecturally identifies the Agniśāla with the central room, the Havirdhāna with a place for keep- ing the grain, etc. ({%e.g.,%} Av. iii. 3, 4), the Patnīnāṃ Sadana with the women's apartments, and the Sadas with the subsidiary buildings.</F> <F>15) Av. ix. 3, 6. {@Gṛha-pa@}¦<sup>1</sup> or {@Gṛha-pati@}<sup>2</sup> is the regular name, from the Rigveda onwards, of the householder as master of the house. 1. {@Go@}¦ ({%a%}), ‘ox’ or ‘cow.’<sup>1</sup> These were among the chief sources of wealth to the Vedic Indian, and are repeatedly [Page1-232+ 62] referred to from the Rigveda onwards.<sup>2</sup> The milk ({@Kṣīra@}) was either drunk fresh or made into butter ({@Ghṛta@}) or curds ({@Dadhi@}), or was mixed with {@Soma@} or used for cooking with grain ({@Kṣīraudana@}). The cows were milked thrice a day, early ({%prātar-doha%}), in the forenoon ({@Saṃgava@}), and in the evening ({%sāyaṃ-doha%}).<sup>3</sup> Thrice a day they were driven out to graze, according to the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa<sup>4</sup> ({%prātaḥ, saṃgave, sāyam%}). The first milking was productive, the last two scanty.<sup>3</sup> According to the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa,<sup>5</sup> among the Bharatas the herds in the evening are in the {@Goṣṭha,@} at midday in the {@Saṃgavīnī.@} This passage Sāyaṇa expands by saying that the herds go home to the Śālā, or house for animals, at night so far as they consist of animals giving milk, while the others stayed out in the Goṣṭha, or open pasturage; but both were together in the cattle-shed during the heat of the day. The time before the Saṃgava, when the cows were grazing freely on the pastureland, was called {@Svasara.@}<sup>6</sup> When the cows were out feeding they were separated from the calves, which were, how- ever, allowed to join them at the Saṃgava,<sup>7</sup> and sometimes in the evening.<sup>8</sup> <div n="P"/>While grazing the cattle were under the care of a herdsman ({@Gopā, Gopāla@}) armed with a goad,<sup>9</sup> but they were liable to all sorts of dangers, such as being lost, falling into pits, breaking limbs,<sup>10</sup> [Page1-233+ 60] and being stolen. The marking of the ears of cattle was repeatedly adopted, no doubt, to indicate ownership.<sup>11</sup> <div n="P"/>Large herds of cattle were well-known, as is shown by the Dānastutis, or ‘praises of gifts,’ in the Rigveda,<sup>12</sup> even when allowances are made for the exaggeration of priestly gratitude. The importance attached to the possession of cattle is shown<sup>13</sup> by the numerous passages in which the gods are asked to prosper them, and by the repeated prayers<sup>14</sup> for wealth in kine. Hence, too, forays for cattle ({@Gaviṣṭi@}) were well known; the Bharata host is called the ‘horde desiring cows’ ({%gavyan grāmaḥ%}) in the Rigveda;<sup>15</sup> and a verbal root {%gup,%}<sup>16</sup> ‘to protect,’ was evolved as early as the Rigveda from the denominative {%go-pāya,%} ‘to guard cows.’ The Vedic poets<sup>17</sup> do not hesitate to compare their songs with the lowing of cows, or to liken the choir of the singing Apsarases to cows.<sup>18</sup> <div n="P"/>The cattle of the Vedic period were of many colours: red ({%rohita%}), light ({%śukra%}), dappled ({%pṛśni%}), even black ({%kṛṣṇa%}).<sup>19</sup> Zimmer<sup>20</sup> sees a reference to cows with blazes on the face in one passage of the Rigveda,<sup>21</sup> but this is uncertain. <div n="P"/>Oxen were regularly used for ploughing or for drawing wagons ({%anaḍvāh%}), in which case they were, it seems, usually castrated.<sup>22</sup> Cows were not properly used for drawing carts, {{hough->though||20210704|Dr. Sampada Savardekar|https://github.com/sanskrit-lexicon/csl-corrections/issues/67|}} they at times did so.<sup>23</sup> The flesh of both cows and bulls was sometimes eaten ({@Māmsa@}). Cattle were certainly the [Page1-234+ 44] objects of individual ownership, and they formed one of the standards of exchange and valuation (see {@Kraya@}). <div n="P"/>({%b%}) The term {@Go@} is often applied to express the products of the cow. It frequently means the milk,<sup>1</sup> but rarely the flesh<sup>2</sup> of the animal. In many passages it designates leather used as the material of various objects, as a bowstring,<sup>3</sup> or a sling,<sup>4</sup> or thongs to fasten part of the chariot,<sup>5</sup> or reins,<sup>6</sup> or the lash of a whip.<sup>7</sup> See also {@Carman,@} with which Go is sometimes synonymous.<sup>8</sup> <div n="P"/>({%c%}) {@Gāvaḥ@} means the stars of heaven in two passages of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> according to Roth.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) i. 83, 1; 135, 8; ii. 23, 18, etc.; {%gāva ukṣaṇaḥ,%} i. 168, 2; Av. iii. 11, 8; {@Vājasaṇeyi@} Saṃhitā, xxi. 20; {%gāvo%} {%dhenavaḥ,%} Rv. i. 173. 1; vi. 45. 28; x. 95, 6; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxi. 19. etc.</F> <F>2) The five sacrificial animals are man, goat, sheep, ox, horse, Sāṅkh- āyana Śrauta Sūtra, ix. 23, 4; Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 4, 3, 13; iii. 1, 2, 13; iv. 5, 5, 10; xiv. 1, 1, 32.</F> <F>3) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vii. 5, 3, 1.</F> <F>4) i. 4, 9, 2. The exact sense of this notice is obscure. Strictly speaking the cows were driven out from the cattle- shed in the morning, spent the heat of the day in the Saṃgavinī, were then driven out during the evening to graze, and finally came or were driven home, as is often mentioned: Rv. i. 66, 5; 149, 4; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xv. 41.</F> <F>3) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vii. 5, 3, 1.</F> <F>5) iii. 18, 14.</F> <F>6) Rv. ii. 2, 2; 34, 8; v. 62, 2; viii. 88, 1; ix. 94, 2. 2. {@Go Āṅgirasa@}¦ (‘descendant of {@Aṅgiras@}’) is the reputed author of a Sāman or Chant in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> There is little doubt that he is mythical.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) xvi. 7, 7. {%Cf.%} Lāṭyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, vi. 11, 3.</F> <F>2) Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 2, 160; Hopkins, {%Transactions of the Con-%} {%necticut Academy of Arts and Sciences,%} 15, 68.</F>

{@Go-ghāta,@}¦ ‘a cow-killer,’ is enumerated in the list of victims at the Puruṣamedha, or human sacrifice, in the Yajurveda.<sup>1</sup> See {@Māṃsa.@} <F>1) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxx. 18; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 16, 1.</F>

{@Gotama@}¦ is mentioned several times in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> but never in such a way as to denote personal authorship of any hymn.<sup>2</sup> It seems clear that he was closely connected with the [Page1-235+ 60] Aṅgirases, for the Gotamas frequently refer to {@Aṅgiras.@}<sup>3</sup> That he bore the patronymic Rāhūgaṇa is rendered probable by one hymn of the Rigveda,<sup>4</sup> and is assumed in the Śatapatha Brāh- maṇa,<sup>5</sup> where he appears as the Purohita, or domestic priest, of {@Māthava Videgha,@} and as a bearer of Vedic civilization. He is also mentioned in the same Brāhmaṇa<sup>6</sup> as a contemporary of {@Janaka@} of {@Videha,@} and {@Yājñavalkya,@} and as the author of a Stoma.<sup>7</sup> He occurs, moreover, in two passages of the Atharvaveda.<sup>8</sup> <div n="P"/>The Gotamas are mentioned in several passages of the Rigveda,<sup>9</sup> {@Vāmadeva@} and {@Nodhas@} being specified as sons of Gotama. {@Gotamī-putra,@}¦ ‘son of Gotamī,’ is mentioned as a pupil of {@Bhāradvājī-putra@} in the Kāṇva recension of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (vi. 5, 1). See also {@Gautamī-putra.@}

{@Gotra@}¦ occurs several times in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> in the account of the mythic exploits of Indra. Roth<sup>2</sup> interprets the word as ‘cowstall,’ while Geldner<sup>3</sup> thinks ‘herd’ is meant. The latter sense seems to explain best the employment which the term shows in the later literature as denoting the ‘family’ or ‘clan,’ and which is found in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.<sup>4</sup> <div n="P"/>In the Gṛhya Sūtras<sup>5</sup> stress is laid on the prohibition of [Page1-236+ 55] marriage within a Gotra, or with a Sapiṇḍa of the mother of the bridegroom — that is to say, roughly, with agnates and cognates. Senart<sup>6</sup> has emphasized this fact as a basis of caste, on the ground that marriage within a {%curia, phratria,%} or caste ({@Varṇa@}) was Indo-European, as was marriage outside the circle of agnates and cognates. But there is no evidence at all<sup>7</sup> to prove that this practice was Indo-European, while in India the Śatapatha<sup>8</sup> expressly recognizes marriage within the third or fourth degree on either side. According to Sāyaṇa, the Kāṇvas accepted marriage in the third degree, the Saurāṣṭras only in the fourth, while the scholiast on the Vajrasūcī<sup>9</sup> adḍs to the Kāṇvas the Andhras and the Dākṣiṇātyas, and remarks that the Vājasaneyins forbade marriage with the daughter of the mother's brother. All apparently allowed marriage with the daughter of a paternal uncle, which later was quite excluded. Change of Gotra was quite possible, as in the case of {@Śunaḥ-@} {@śepa@} and {@Gṛtsamada,@} who, once an Aṅgirasa, became a Bhārgava.<sup>10</sup> <F>1) i. 51, 3; ii. 17, 1; 23, 18; iii. 39, 4; 43, 7; viii. 74, 5; x. 48, 2; 103, 7.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>3) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 275, 276, where he divides the passages according as real or mythical herds are meant.</F> <F>4) iv. 4, 1. So Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra; i. 4, 16, etc.; Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra, iv. 4, etc.; Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, xxv. 15.</F> <F>5) Gobhila Gṛhya Sūtra, iii. 4, 4; Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra, ii. 5, 11, 15. 16, in Max Müller, {%Ancient Sanskrit%} {%Literature,%} 387. {@Go-dāna@}¦ appears to mean ‘the whiskers’ in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> where the person, being consecrated, first shaves off the right and then the left ‘whisker.’ Later on the Godāna- vidhi, or ceremony of shaving the head, is a regular part of the initiation of a youth on the attainment of manhood and on marriage;<sup>2</sup> but though the ceremony is recognized in the Atharvaveda,<sup>3</sup> the name<sup>4</sup> does not occur there. <F>1) iii. 1, 2, 5, 6.</F> <F>2) Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra, i. 19; Śāṅkhāyana Gṛhya Sūtra, i. 28, etc.</F> <F>3) vi. 68. See Whitney, Translation of the Atharva- veda, 56, 57, correcting Weber, {%Indische%} {%Studien,%} 13, 173, and Zimmer, {%Altin-%} {%disches Leben,%} 322, 323. {%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 306, 574, 665.</F> <F>4) The meaning ‘whisker’ is a secon- dary one, derived, doubtless, from the ‘gift of a cow’ ({%go-dāna%}), accompanying the ceremony of shaving the whiskers or hair.</F>

{@Go-pā@}¦ and {@Go-pāla,@} ‘protector of cows,’ occur in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later, but the former is usually metaphorical in sense, applying to any protector, while the latter has the literal force of ‘cow-herd.’ <F>1) {%Gopā:%} Rv. i. 164, 21; ii. 23, 6; iii. 10, 2; v. 12, 4, etc.; {%Gopāla:%} Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xxx. 11; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iv. 1, 5, 4. {%Gopā,%} in the sense of ‘guardian,’ occurs in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xxiv. 18, in a compound. {%Gopītha,%} in the sense of ‘protection,’ occurs in Rv. v. 65, 6; x. 35, 14, etc. {%Goptṛ,%} ‘protector,’ first occurs in Av. x. 10, 5, and is thereafter common.</F>
{@Go-bala@}¦ (‘ox-strength’) {@Vārṣṇa@} (‘descendant of Vṛṣṇi’) is mentioned as a teacher in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (iii. 11, 9, 3) and the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa (i. 6, 1).

{@Go-matī,@}¦ ‘possessing cows,’ is mentioned as a river in the Nadī-stuti, or ‘Praise of Rivers,’ in the tenth Maṇḍala of the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> In that hymn a river flowing into the Indus must be meant, and its identification<sup>2</sup> with the Gomal, a western tributary of the Indus, cannot be doubted. In one other passage of the Rigveda<sup>3</sup> the accentuation of Gomati shows that a river is meant. It is possible that in a third passage<sup>4</sup> the reading should be changed to {%gomatír%} from {%gómatīr.%} Geldner<sup>5</sup> suggests that in the two last passages the Gumti, or rather its four upper arms (hence the use of the plural) is meant: this accords well with the later use of the name and with the general probability of the river here intended being in {@Kurukṣetra,@} as the centre of Vedic civilization.<sup>6</sup> <F>1) x. 75, 6.</F> <F>2) Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 14; Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 200.</F> <F>3) viii. 24. 30.</F> <F>4) v. 61, 19. See Oldenberg, {%Ṛgveda-%} {%Noten.%} 1, 355, 356.</F> <F>5) {%Vedische Studien,%} 3, 152, n. 2.</F> <F>6) Pischel, {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 218; Hopkins, {%Journal of the American Oriental%} {%Society,%} 19, 19 {%et seq.;%} Macdonell, {%Sanskrit Literature,%} 174; Keith, {%Journal%} {%of the Royal Asiatic Society,%} 1908, 1141.</F>
{@Go-māyu,@}¦ ‘lowing like a cow,’ does not occur as the name of the ‘jackal’ till the late Adbhuta Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 40.</F>

{@Go-mṛga,@}¦ a species of ox, now called Gayal ({%Bos gavaeus%}), is mentioned in the list of victims at the Aśvamedha, or horse sacrifice, in the Yajurveda Saṃhitās<sup>1</sup> and Brāhmaṇas.<sup>2</sup> In the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>3</sup> it is declared to be neither a wild nor a tame animal; this presumably means that it was semi- domesticated, or perhaps that it was both tamed and found wild. With the name of this animal may be compared the Mṛga Mahiṣa, which is clearly mentioned as wild in the Rigveda.<sup>4</sup> See also {@Gayava.@} <F>1) Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 11; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 1. 30.</F> <F>2) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 3, 4, 3; 5, 2, 10; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 8, 20, 5.</F> <F>3) ii. 1, 10, 2</F> <F>4) ix. 92, 6. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 83, 84; Eggeling, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 44, 338, n. 1.</F>

{@Golattikā@}¦ is the name of some unknown animal in the list of victims at the Aśvamedha, or horse sacrifice, in the Yajurveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 16, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 18; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 37. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 99.</F>

{@Go-vikartana@}¦ (‘cow-butcher’) designates the ‘huntsman’ in the Satapatha Brāhmaṇa (v. 3, 1, 10).<sup>1</sup> See {@Goghāta.@} <F>1) {%Cf.%} Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 16, 1; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxx. 18; Weber, {%Indische Streifen,%} 1, 82.</F>

{@Gośarya@}¦ is the name of a protégé of the Aśvins in the Rigveda (viii. 8, 20; 49, 1; 50, 10).

The Mādhyaṃdina, ii. 5, 20; iv. 5, 26, knows a Gautama, pupil of {@Vaijavāpā-@} {@yana@} and {@Vaiṣṭhapureya.@}</F>

{@Gautamī-putra@}¦ (‘son of a female descendant of Gotama’) is mentioned in the Kāṇva recension of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (vi. 5, 2) as a pupil of {@Bhāradvājīputra.@} In the Mādhyaṃdina (vi. 4, 31) a Gautamīputra is a pupil of {@Ātreyī-@} {@putra,@} pupil of a Gautamīputra, pupil of {@Vātsīputra.@} See also {@Gotamīputra.@}

{@Gaupa-vana@}¦ (‘descendant of {@Gopavana@}’) is mentioned as a pupil of {@Pautimāṣya@} in the first two Vaṃśas (lists of teachers) in the Kāṇva recension of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (ii. 6, 1; iv. 6, 1).

{@Gaupāyana@}¦ (‘descendant of Gopa’). The Gaupāyanas appear in the legend of {@Asamāti, Kirāta,@} and {@Ākuli,@} which is first met with in the Brāhmaṇas.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 12, 5; Jaiminīva Brāhmaṇa, iii. 167 ({%Journal%} {%of the American Oriental Society,%} 18, 41); Sāṭyāyanaka in Sāyaṇa on Rv. x. 57 (Max Müller's edition, 4^2, c {%et seq.%}); Bṛhaddevatā, vii. 83 {%et seq.,%} with Mac- donell's notes.</F>

{@Gauśra@}¦ (‘descendant of Guśri’) is the name of a teacher mentioned in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa (xvi. 9; xxiii. 5). See {@Gauśla.@}
{@Gauśrāyaṇi@}¦ (‘descendant of Gauśra’) is the patronymic of a teacher, {@Citra,@} in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa (xxiii. 5).
