{@Jambhaka,@}¦ as the name of a demon, presumably identical with the demon causing {@Jambha,@} is mentioned in the Vāja saneyi Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> and the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) xxx. 16.</F> <F>2) xii. 25. {%Cf.%} Keith, {%Śāṅkhāyana Āranyaka,%} 67, n. 7.</F>
{@Jayaka Lauhitya@}¦ (‘descendant of Lohita’) is mentioned in a Vaṃśa (list of teachers) of the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa (iii. 42, 1) as a pupil of {@Yaśasvin Jayanta Lauhitya.@}

{@Jayanta@}¦ is the name of several teachers in the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa: <div n="P"/>({%a%}) Jayanta Pārāśarya (‘descendant of {@Parāśara@}’) is mentioned as a pupil of {@Vipaścit@} in a Vaṃśa (list of teachers).<sup>1</sup> <div n="P"/>({%b%}) Jayanta Vārakya (‘descendant of Varaka’) appears in the same Vaṃśa<sup>1</sup> as a pupil of {@Kubera Vārakya.@} His {{grandtather->grandfather||20210704|Dr. Sampada Savardekar|https://github.com/sanskrit-lexicon/csl-corrections/issues/67|}} is also mentioned there as a pupil of {@Kaṃsa Vārakya.@} <div n="P"/>({%c%}) A Jayanta Vārakya, pupil of {@Suyajña Śāṇḍilya,@} perhaps identical with the preceding, is found in another Vaṃśa.<sup>2</sup> <div n="P"/>({%d%}) Jayanta is a name of {@Yaśasvin Lauhitya.@}<sup>3</sup> <div n="P"/>See also {@Dakṣa Jayanta@} Lauhitya. <F>1) iii. 41, 1.</F> <F>1) iii. 41, 1.</F> <F>2) iv. 17, 1.</F> <F>3) iii. 42, 1. Not only is the forma- tion of the name a late one ({%cf.%} Whitney, {%Sanskrit Grammar,%} 1209d, and Mac- donell, {%Vedic Grammar%} 191{%a%}), but the Upaniṣad in which it occurs is also a late one.</F>

{@Jarā-bodha,@}¦ a word occurring only once in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> is of doubtful meaning. It is held by Ludwig<sup>2</sup> to be the name of [Page1-278+ 47] a seer. Roth<sup>3</sup> regards it as a mere adjective meaning ‘attending to the invocation,’ which is perhaps the most probable inter- pretation. Oldenburg,<sup>4</sup> however, thinks that the word is a proper name, the literal sense being ‘alert in old age.’ <F>1) i. 27, 10.</F> <F>2) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 103.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} {%Cf.%} Nirukta, x. 8.</F> <F>4) {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 23. He compares the {%ṛṣī bodha-pratibodhau%} of Av. v. 30, 10.</F>

{@Jarāyu@}¦ is found once in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> in the sense of a ‘serpent's skin.’ Usually<sup>2</sup> it denotes the outer covering (chorion) of the embryo, as opposed to the {%ulva,%} the inner covering (amnion). <div n="P"/>Living things are occasionally classified according to their mode of origin. In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad<sup>3</sup> they are divided into {%(a) āṇḍa-ja,%} ‘egg-born’; {%(b) jīva-ja,%} ‘born alive,’ or born from the womb; {%(c) udbhij-ja,%} ‘propagated by sprouts.’ In the Aitareya Āraṇyaka<sup>4</sup> the division is fourfold: {%(a) āṇḍa-ja;%} {%(b) jāru-ja,%} that is, {%jarāyu-ja%} (found in the Atharvaveda,<sup>5</sup> and needlessly read here by Böhtlingk);<sup>6</sup> {%(c) udbhij-ja;%} and {%(d)%} {%svcda-ja,%} ‘sweat-born,’ explained as ‘insects.’ <F>1) i. 27, 1.</F> <F>2) Rv. v. 78, 8; Av. i. 11, 4; vi. 49, 1; ix. 4, 4; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vi. 5, 6, 3; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, x. 8; xix. 76; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, i. 3; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 2, 1, 11, etc; Chān- dogya Upanisad, iii. 10. 2, etc.</F> <F>3) vi. 3, 1.</F> <F>4) ii. 6.</F> <F>5) i. 12, 1.</F> <F>6) See {%jāru%} in Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 430, 6. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Deussen, {%Philosophy of the Upani-%} {%shads,%} 196, 292; Keith, {%Aitareya Āraṇ-%} {%yaka,%} 235.</F>

1. {@Jaritṛ@}¦ is the regular term in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> and occasion- ally later,<sup>2</sup> for a singer of hymns of praise or worshipper. <F>1) i. 2, 2; 165, 14; ii. 33, 11; iii. 60, 7, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. v. 11, 8; xx. 135, 1, etc.</F>

2. {@Jaritṛ.@}¦ According to Sieg,<sup>1</sup> mention is made in one hymn of the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> of Jaritṛ, one of the Śārṅgas. That hymn he seeks to bring into connexion with the epic<sup>3</sup> tradition [Page1-279+ 35] of the Ṛṣi Mandapāla, who wedded Jaritā, a female Śārṅga bird — apparently a hen sparrow ({%caṭakā%}) — and had four sons. These being abandoned by him and exposed to the danger of being consumed by a forest fire, prayed to Agni with the hymn Rigveda x. 142. This interpretation is very doubtful, though Sāyaṇa<sup>4</sup> appears to have adopted it. <F>1) {%Die Sagenstoffe des Ṛgveda,%} 44 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>2) x. 142.</F> <F>3) Mahābhārata, i. 222, 1 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>4) On Rv. x. 142, 7. 8.</F>

{@Jarūtha,@}¦ mentioned in three passages of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> appears to denote a {@demon@} defeated by Agni.<sup>2</sup> Ludwig, how- ever, followed by Griffith,<sup>3</sup> sees in him a foe slain in a battle in which {@Vasiṣṭha,@} the traditional author of the seventh Maṇḍala of the Rigveda, was Purohita, or domestic priest. <F>1) vii. 1, 7; 9, 6; x. 80. 3.</F> <F>2) Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.;%} Nirukta, vi. 17.</F> <F>3) {%Hymns of the Rigveda,%} 2, 11, n.</F>

{@Jartila,@}¦ ‘wild sesamum,’ is mentioned in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (v. 4, 3, 2) as an unsuitable sacrificial offering. In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (ix. 1, 1, 3) sesamum seeds are regarded as combining the qualities of cultivation (viz., edibility) with those of wild growth (because they are produced on unploughed land).
{@Jarvara@}¦ was Gṛhapati or ‘householder’ at the snake festival described in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) xxv. 15, 3. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 35.</F>

{@Jala Jātūkarṇya@}¦ (‘descendant of Jātūkarṇa’), is mentioned in the Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra (xvi. 29, 6) as having obtained the position of Purohita, or domestic priest, of the three peoples or kings of {@Kāśi, Videha,@} and {@Kosala.@}

{@Jalāṣa-bheṣaja,@}¦ ‘whose remedy is Jalāṣa,’ is an epithet of Rudra in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and the Atharvaveda.<sup>2</sup> The word [Page1-280+ 54] {@Jālāṣa@} occurs in a hymn of the Atharvaveda,<sup>3</sup> where it denotes a remedy, perhaps, for a tumour or boil.<sup>4</sup> The commentator on this passage and the Kauśika Sūtra<sup>5</sup> regard Jālāṣa as meaning ‘urine,’ which seems a probable interpretation.<sup>6</sup> But Geldner<sup>7</sup> thinks that rain-water, conceived as urine, is meant; and the Naighaṇṭuka<sup>8</sup> identifies {%jalāṣa%} and {%udaka%} ‘water.’ <F>1) i. 43, 4; viii. 29, 5.</F> <F>2) ii. 27, 6. It also occurs in the Nīlarudra Upaniṣad (a very late work), 3, and {%jalāṣa%} as an adjective is found in Rv. ii. 33, 7; viii. 33, 6.</F> <F>3) vi. 57.</F> <F>4) Bloomfield, {%American Journal of%} {%Philology,%} 11, 321 {%et seq.;%} {%Hymns of the%} {%Atharvaveda,%} 489.</F> <F>5) xxxi. 11.</F> <F>6) Bloomfield, {%American Journal of%} {%Philology,%} 12, 425 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>7) {%Vedische Studien,%} 3, 139, n. 2.</F> <F>8) i. 12. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 323, 324; Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} pp. 76, 77; Hopkins, {%Proceedings of the American Oriental Society,%} 1894, cl.</F>

{@Jaṣa@}¦ is the name of some aquatic animal or fish in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and the Taittirīya Saṃhitā.<sup>2</sup> The commentary on the latter text explains it by {%makara,%} probably meaning ‘dolphin.’ The word also occurs in the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa.<sup>3</sup> <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} {@Jhaṣa.@} <F>1) xi. 2, 25. There are various read- ings: {%jhaṣa, jakha, jagha.%}</F> <F>2) v. 5, 13, 1.</F> <F>3) ii. 2, 5. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 96; Whitney, Translation of the Atharva- veda, 624</F>

{@Jahakā,@}¦ the ‘polecat,’ is mentioned as a victim at the Aśvamedha, or horse sacrifice, in the Yajurveda.<sup>1</sup> Sāyaṇa<sup>2</sup> thinks it means a jackal living in holes ({%vila-vāsī kroṣṭā%}). <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 18, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 17; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 36. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 86.</F> <F>2) On Taittirīya Saṃhitā, {%loc. cit.%}</F>

{@Jahnu@}¦ occurs only in the plural in the legend of {@Śunaḥśepa,@} who is said to have obtained, as Devarāta, both the lordship of the Jahnus and the divine lore of the Gāthins.<sup>1</sup> A {@Jāhnava,@} or descendant of Jahnu, was, according to the Pañcaviṃśa [Page1-281+ 45] Brāhmaṇa,<sup>2</sup> {@Viśvāmitra,@} who is said, by means of a certain {%catū-rātra%} or ‘four-night’ ritual, to have secured the kingdom for the Jahnus in their conflict with the {@Vṛcīvants.@} He is here described as a king. Again, in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa,<sup>3</sup> Viśvāmitra is addressed as a {%rāja-putra,%} ‘prince,’ and {%Bharata-%} {%rṣabha,%} ‘bull of the Bharatas.’ It is therefore clear that the Brāhmaṇas, though not the Saṃhitās, saw in him at once a priest and a prince by origin, though there is no trace whatever of their seeing in him a prince who won Brahmanhood as in the version of the later texts.<sup>4</sup> <div n="P"/>A Jahnāvī is mentioned twice in the Rigveda,<sup>5</sup> being either the wife of Jahnu, or, as Sāyaṇa thinks, the race of Jahnu. The family must clearly once have been a great one, later merged in the Bharatas. <F>1) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vii. 18 ({%Jah-%} {%nūnām cādhipatye daive vede ca Gāthinām%}); Asvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xii. 14; Sāṅkhāyana Srauta Sūtra, xv. 27 (p. 195, 1. 21, ed. Hillebrandt, where the read- ing is different and the sense altered: {%Jahnūnāṃ cādhitasthire daive vede ca%} {%Gāthinaḥ.%} The two {%ca%}'s cannot be justified, and the text must be in- correct).</F> <F>2) xxi. 12. {%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%Transactions%} {%of the Connecticut Academy of Arts and%} {%Sciences,%} 15, 54, who correctly explains the passage which Sāyaṇa misunder- stands.</F> <F>3) vii. 17, 6, 7.</F> <F>4) Muir, {%Sanskrit Texts,%} 1, 337 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>5) i. 116, 19; iii. 58, 6. {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 153.</F>
{@Jāta Śākāyanya@}¦ (‘descendant of Śāka’) is mentioned as a ritual authority and contemporary of {@Śaṅkha@} in the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā (xxii. 7).

{@Jāta-rūpa,@}¦ ‘possessing native beauty,’ is the name of ‘gold’ in the later Brāhmaṇas<sup>1</sup> and the Sūtras.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, viii. 13 ({%jāta-%} {%rūpa-maya,%} ‘composed of gold’); Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, vi. 4, 25; Naighaṇṭuka, i. 2.</F> <F>2) {%Rajata-jātarūpe,%} ‘silver and gold,’ Lāṭyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, i. 6, 24. {%Cf.%} viii. 1, 3; Kauśika Sūtra, x. 16; xiii. 3, etc.; Sāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, iii. 19, 9.</F>

{@Jāti,@}¦ which in the Pāli<sup>1</sup> texts is the word denoting ‘caste,’ does not occur at all in the early Vedic literature; when it is found, as in the Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra,<sup>2</sup> it has only the sense of ‘family’ (for which {%cf.%} {@Kula, Gotra,@} and {@Viś@}). For the influence of the family system on the growth of caste, see {@Varṇa.@} To assume that it was the basis of caste, as does [Page1-282+ 48] Senart,<sup>3</sup> is difficult in face of the late appearance of words for family and of stress on family.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) Fick, {%Die sociale Gliederung,%} 22, n. 4.</F> <F>2) xv. 4, 14. So {%jātīya,%} xx. 2, 11, etc.</F> <F>3) {%Les Castes dans l'Inde%} (1896).</F> <F>4) Fick, {%op. cit.,%} 3; Oldenberg, {%Zeit-%} {%schrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen%} {%Gesellschaft,%} 51, 267 {%et seq.%}</F>

{@Jātū-karṇya,@}¦ ‘descendant of {@Jātūkarṇa,@}’ is the patronymic of several persons. <div n="P"/>({%a%}) A pupil of {@Āsurāyaṇa@} and {@Yāska@} bears this name in a Vaṃśa (list of teachers) of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad in the Kāṇva recension.<sup>1</sup> In the Mādhyaṃdina<sup>2</sup> he is a pupil of {@Bhāradvāja.@} <div n="P"/>({%b%}) A Kātyāyanī-putra, ‘son of Kātyāyanī,’ bears this name in the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka.<sup>3</sup> <div n="P"/>({%c%}) A Jātūkarṇya is mentioned in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa<sup>4</sup> as a contemporary of {@Alīkayu Vācaspatya@} and other sages. <div n="P"/>({%d%}) Jātūkarṇya is in the Sūtras<sup>5</sup> frequently a patronymic of teachers whose identity cannot be determined. The same person or different persons may here be meant. <F>1) ii. 6, 3; iv. 6, 3.</F> <F>2) ii. 5, 21; iv. 5, 27.</F> <F>3) viii. 10.</F> <F>4) xxvi. 5 (Jātukarṇya in Lindner's index, 159, is a misprint).</F> <F>5) Aitareya Āraṇyaka, v. 3, 3; Śāṅkh- āyana Srauta Sūtra, i. 2, 17; iii. 16, 14; 20, 19; xvi. 29, 6 ({@Jala@}); Kātyāyana Srauta Sūtra, iv. 1, 27; xx. 3, 17; xxv. 7, 34, etc. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indian Literature,%} 138- 140.</F>

{@Jātū-ṣṭhira@}¦ occurs in one verse of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> where Sāyaṇa and Ludwig<sup>2</sup> interpret the word as a proper name. Roth<sup>3</sup> renders it as an adjective meaning ‘naturally powerful.’<sup>4</sup> <F>1) ii. 13, 11.</F> <F>2) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 152.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} (with a wrong reference, ii. 23, 11).</F> <F>4) {%Urkräftig.%} Grassmann, {%Wörterbuch,%} similarly explains the word as ‘power- ful by nature or birth’ ({%jātū%}).</F>

{@Jāna,@}¦ ‘descendant of Jana,’ is the patronymic of {@Vṛśa@} in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> and apparently in the Śāṭyāyanaka.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) xiii. 3, 12.</F> <F>2) In Sāyaṇa on Rv. v. 5. {%Cf.%} Bṛhad- devatā, v. 14 {%et seq.,%} with Macdonell's notes; Sieg, {%Die Sagenstoffe des Ṛgveda,%} 64 {%et seq.%}</F>

{@Jānaka,@}¦ ‘descendant of Janaka,’ is the patronymic of {@Kratuvid@} in some MSS. of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> In the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>2</sup> the name appears instead as {@Kratujit@} {@Jānaki.@} Jānaka is also, according to some manuscripts of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad,<sup>3</sup> the patronymic of {@Āyasthūṇa,@} but is here no doubt a misreading of {@Jānaki.@} <F>1) vii. 34.</F> <F>2) ii. 3, 8, 1; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xi. 1.</F> <F>3) vi. 3, 10 (Kāṇva).</F>

{@Jānaki,@}¦ ‘descendant of Janaka,’ is the patronymic of {@Kratujit@} in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā,<sup>1</sup> of {@Kratuvid@} in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa,<sup>2</sup> and of {@Āyasthūṇa@} in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad,<sup>3</sup> where he is mentioned as a pupil of {@Cūḍa Bhāgavitti,@} and as teacher of {@Satyakāma Jābāla.@} <F>1) ii. 3, 8, 1; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xi. 1.</F> <F>2) vii. 34.</F> <F>3) vi. 3, 10 (Kāṇva = vi. 3, 18. 19, Mādhyaṃdina).</F>
{@Jānaṃ-tapi,@}¦ ‘descendant of Janaṃtapa,’ is the patronymic of {@Atyarāti@} in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (viii. 23).
{@Jāna-pada.@}¦ See {@Janapada.@}
{@Jāna-śruti,@}¦ ‘descendant of Jānaśruta,’ is the patronymic of {@Pautrāyaṇa@} in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (iv. 1, 1; 2, 1).

{@Jāna-śruteya,@}¦ ‘descendant of Jānaśruti’ or of ‘Janaśrutā.’ is the patronymic or metronymic of several persons — {@Upāvi@}<sup>1</sup> or {@Aupāvi,@}<sup>2</sup> {@Ulukya,@}<sup>3</sup> {@Nagarin,@}<sup>4</sup> and {@Sāyaka.@}<sup>5</sup> <F>1) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, i. 25, 115.</F> <F>2) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, v. 1, 1, 5. 7; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, i. 4, 5.</F> <F>3) Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa, i. 6, 3.</F> <F>4) {%Ibid.,%} iii. 40, 2.</F> <F>5) {%Ibid.%}</F>

{@Jābāla,@}¦ ‘descendant of {@Jabāla,@}’ is the metronymic of {@Mahā-@} {@śāla@}<sup>1</sup> and {@Satyakāma.@}<sup>2</sup> Jābāla is also mentioned as a teacher in the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa,<sup>3</sup> which refers to the [Page1-284+ 44] Jābālas<sup>4</sup> as well. The Jābāla Gṛhapatis are spoken of in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa.<sup>5</sup> <F>1) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, x. 3, 3, 1; 6, 1, 1.</F> <F>2) {%Ibid.,%} xiii. 5, 3, 1; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, iv. 1, 14; vi. 3, 19; Chān- dogya Upaniṣad, iv. 4, 1, etc.; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, viii. 7.</F> <F>3) iii. 9, 9.</F> <F>4) iii. 7, 2.</F> <F>5) xxiii. 5. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 395.</F>

{@Jābālāyana,@}¦ ‘descendant of Jābāla,’ is the patronymic of a teacher, a pupil of {@Mādhyaṃdināyana,@} who is mentioned in the second Vaṃśa (list of teachers) of the Kāṇva recension of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (iv. 6, 2).

{@Jāmadagniya@}¦ is the patronymic of two ‘descendants of Jamadagni’ in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā.<sup>1</sup> It appears from the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> that the {@Aurvas@} are meant, and that Jamadagni's descendants were ever prosperous. <F>1) vii. 1, 9, 1.</F> <F>2) xxi. 10, 6. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 12, 251, n.; Hopkins, {%Transactions of the Connecticut%} {%Academy of Arts and Sciences,%} 15, 54.</F>

{@Jāmātṛ@}¦ is a rare word denoting ‘son-in-law’ in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> where also occurs the word {@Vijāmātṛ,@} denoting an ‘unsatis- factory son-in-law,’ as one who does not pay a sufficient price, or one who, having other defects, must purchase a bride. Friendly relations between son-in-law and father-in-law are referred to in the Rigveda.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) viii. 2, 20. Vāyu is called the {%jāmātṛ%} of Tvaṣṭṛ in viii. 26, 21. 22. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Delbrück, {%Die indogermanischen Ver-%} {%wandtschaftsnamen,%} 517; Pischel, {%Vedische%} {%Studien,%} 2, 78, 79.</F> <F>2) x. 28, 1. {%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Journal%} {%of the American Oriental Society,%} 15, 255.</F>

{@Jāmi,@}¦ a word which appears originally to have meant ‘related in blood,’ is not rarely used as an epithet of ‘sister’ ({@Svasṛ@}), and sometimes even denotes ‘sister’ itself, the emphasis being on the blood-relationship.<sup>1</sup> So it appears in a passage of the Atharvaveda,<sup>2</sup> where ‘brotherless sisters’ [Page1-285+ 39] ({%abhrātara iva jāmayaḥ%}) are referred to. The word is similarly used in the dispute occurring in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> as to the precedence of Rākā, or of the wives of the gods, in a certain rite. One party is there described as holding that the sister should be preferred ({%jāmyai vai pūrva-peyam%}) — apparently at a ceremonial family meal — to the wife, presumably as being of one blood with the husband, while the wife is not (being {%anyo-%} {%daryā,%} ‘of another womb’).<sup>4</sup> In the neuter<sup>5</sup> the word means ‘relationship,’ like {%jāmi-tva,%} which also occurs in the Rigveda.<sup>6</sup> <F>1) {%Cf.%} Delbrück, {%Dic indogermanischen%} {%Verwandtschaftsnamen,%} 463, 464. As ‘rela- tion,’ it occurs, {%e.g.,%} Rv. i. 31, 10; 75, 3. 4; 100, 11; 124, 6, etc.; as ‘sister,’ Rv. i. 65, 7; x. 10, 10, etc.; with {%svasā,%} i. 123, 5; 185, 5; iii. 1, 11; ix. 65, 1; 89, 4, etc.</F> <F>2) i. 17, 1.</F> <F>3) iii. 37.</F> <F>4) Delbrück, {%loc. cit.%}</F> <F>5) Rv. iii. 54, 9; x. 10, 4; {%jāmi-kṛt,%} ‘making relationship,’ Av. iv. 19, 1. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Altareya Brāhmaṇa, {%loc. cit.%}</F> <F>6) i. 105, 9; 166, 13; x. 55, 4; 64, 13.</F>

{@Jāmi-śaṃsa,@}¦ the ‘imprecation by a sister’ or ‘relation,’ is mentioned in the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> showing that family disputes were not rare. This is also indicated by the word {@Bhrātṛvya,@} which, while properly meaning ‘father's brother's son,’ regularly denotes simply ‘enemy.’ <F>1) ii. 10, 1 (= Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 5, 6, 3), and personified in ix. 4, 15. <div n="P"/>{%Cf. jāmyāḥ śapathaḥ,%} Av. ii. 7, 2; Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 362.</F>

{@Jāmbila,@}¦ ‘hollow of the knee,’<sup>1</sup> occurs once in the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā<sup>2</sup> The word also occurs in the form of Jāmbīla in the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā<sup>3</sup> and the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā.<sup>4</sup> Mahīdhara, in his commentary on the latter text, interprets the word as ‘knee-pan,’ which he says is so named because of its resemblance to the citron, {%jāmbīra.%} <F>1) Perhaps for {%jānu-bila. Cf.%} Mac- donell, {%Vedic Grammar,%} p. 11, n. 4.</F> <F>2) iii. 15, 3.</F> <F>3) v. 13, 1.</F> <F>4) xxv. 3.</F>

{@Jāyantī-putra,@}¦ ‘son of Jāyantī,’ is mentioned in the last Vaṃśa (list of teachers) in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad<sup>1</sup> as a pupil of {@Māṇḍūkāyanīputra.@} <F>1) vi. 5, 2 (Kāṇva = vi. 4, 32 Mādhyaṃdina).</F>

{@Jāyā@}¦ regularly denotes ‘wife,’ and, as opposed to {@Patnī,@} wife as an object of marital affection, the source of the continuance [Page1-286+ 57] of the race.<sup>1</sup> So it is used of the wife of the gambler, and of the wife of the Brāhmaṇa in the Rigveda;<sup>2</sup> it is also frequently combined with {@Pati,@} ‘husband,’<sup>3</sup> both there and in the later literature.<sup>4</sup> Patnī, on the other hand, is used to denote the wife as partner in the sacrifice;<sup>5</sup> when no share in it is assigned to her, she is called Jāyā.<sup>6</sup> The distinction is, of course, merely relative; hence one text<sup>7</sup> calls Manu's wife Jāyā, another<sup>8</sup> Patnī. Later on Jāyā is superseded by Dāra. <F>1) Delbrück, {%Die indogermanischen Ver-%} {%wandtschaftsnamen,%} 411, 412. {%Cf.%} Rv. i. 105, 2; 124, 7; iii. 53, 4; iv. 3, 2; 18, 3; ix. 82, 4; x. 10, 7; 17, 1; 71, 4, etc.; Av. iii. 30, 2; vi. 60, 1, etc.</F> <F>2) x. 34, 2. 3. 13, and x. 109.</F> <F>3) Rv. iv. 3, 2; x. 149, 4.</F> <F>4) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 23, 1. {%Cf.%} vii. 13, 10; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iv. 6, 7, 9. {%Cf.%} Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, i. 6, 12.</F> <F>5) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 9, 2, 14.</F> <F>6) i. 1, 4, 13.</F> <F>7) {%Ibid.,%} i. 1, 4, 16.</F> <F>8) Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iv. 8, 1.</F>

{@Jāyānya,@}¦<sup>1</sup> {@Jāyenya,@}<sup>2</sup> are variant forms of the name of a disease mentioned in the Atharvaveda and the Taittirīya Saṃ- hitā. In one passage of the former text<sup>3</sup> it is mentioned with jaundice ({%harimā%}) and pains in the limbs ({%aṅga-bhedo visalpakaḥ%}). Zimmer<sup>4</sup> thinks these are its symptoms, and identifies it with a kind of Yakṣma, or disease of the lungs. Bloomfield<sup>5</sup> prefers to identify it with syphilis, in accordance with certain indica- tions in the ritual of the Kauśika Sūtra.<sup>6</sup> Roth conjectures ‘gout,’ but Whitney<sup>7</sup> leaves the nature of the disease doubtful. <F>1) Av. vii. 76, 3-5; xix. 44, 2.</F> <F>2) ii. 3, 5, 2; 5, 6, 5.</F> <F>3) xix. 44, 2.</F> <F>4) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 377, following Wise, {%Hindu System of Medicint,%} 321, describing Akṣata.</F> <F>5) {%American Journal of Philology,%} 11, 320 {%et seq.; Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 559-561.</F> <F>6) xxxii. 11. {%Cf.%} also the commentary on Av. vii. 76, and Taittirīya Saṃhitā, {%loc. cit.%}</F> <F>7) Translation of the Atharvaveda, 442. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Henry, {%Lelivre vii de l' Atharvavéda,%} 98.</F>

{@Jāra,@}¦ ‘lover,’ has no sinister sense in the early texts<sup>1</sup> generally, where the word applies to any lover. But it seems probable that the Jāra at the Puruṣamedha, or human sacrifice,<sup>2</sup> [Page1-287+ 33] must be regarded as an illegitimate lover; this sense also appears in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad,<sup>3</sup> and Indra is styled the lover of {@Ahalyā,@} wife of {@Gautama@}<sup>4</sup> <F>1) Rv. i. 66, 8; 117, 18; 134, 3; 152, 4; ix. 32, 5, etc. The word is often used mythologically, as, {%e.g., jāra%} {%uṣasām,%} ‘lover of the dawns,’ vii. 9, 1. {%Cf%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 308.</F> <F>2) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxx. 9; Tait- tirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 4. 1.</F> <F>3) vi. 4, 11.</F> <F>4) Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} p. 65.</F>

{@Jārat-kārava@}¦ (‘descendant of Jaratkāru’) {@Ārtabhāga@} (‘de- scendant of Ṛtabhāga’) is the name of a teacher mentioned in the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka (vii. 20) and the Bṛhadāranyaka Upaniṣad (iii. 2, 1, in both recensions).
{@Jāru.@}¦ See {@Jarāyu.@}

{@Jāla@}¦ occurs in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and the Sūtras<sup>2</sup> in the sense of ‘net.’ Jālaka is used in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad<sup>3</sup> of a reticulated membrane resembling a woven covering. <F>1) viii. 8. 5. 3 (as used against foes); x. 1, 30.</F> <F>2) Kātyāyana Srauta Sūtra, vii. 4, 7. etc.</F> <F>3) iv. 2, 3.</F>
{@Jālāṣa.@}¦ See {@Jalāṣa,@} which is read by Sāyaṇa in the Athar- vaveda (vi. 57, 2) for Jālāṣa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) {%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%American Journal of Philology,%} 11, 320.</F>
{@Jāṣkamada@}¦ is the name of an unknown animal in the Athar- vaveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) xi. 9, 9. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 88.</F>

{@Jās-pati@}¦ occurs once in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> in the sense of the ‘head of the family.’ The abstract formed from this word, Jās-patya, apparently denoting ‘lordship of children,’ is also found there.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) i. 135. 8.</F> <F>2) Rv. v. 28, 3; x. 85, 23.</F>
{@Jāhuṣa@}¦ is the name in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> of a protégé of the Aśvins. <F>1) i. 116, 10; vii. 71, 5 {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 159.</F>

{@Jāhnava,@}¦ ‘descendant of {@Jahnu,@}’ is the patronymic of {@Viśvā-@} {@mitra@} in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> This fact is of some importance as disproving Aufrecht's theory<sup>2</sup> that the Jahnus were the clan of {@Ajīgarta@} the father of {@Śunaḥśepa.@} <F>1) xxi. 12. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 32; Hopkins, {%Transactions of the Con-%} {%necticut Academy of Arts and Sciences,%} 15, 54.</F> <F>2) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, 424.</F>

{@Jitvan Śailini@}¦ is the name of a teacher in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad,<sup>1</sup> a contemporary of {@Janaka@} and {@Yājñavalkya.@} He held that speech ({%vāc%}) was Brahman. <F>1) iv. 1, 2 (Kāṇva = iv. 1, 5 Mādhyaṃdina, which has Śailina as the patronymic).</F>

{@Jihvāvant Bādhyoga@}¦ is the name, in the last Vaṃśa (list of teachers) of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad,<sup>1</sup> of a teacher, pupil of {@Asita Vārṣāgaṇa.@} <F>1) vi. 5, 3 (Kāṇva = vi. 4, 33 Mādhyaṃdina).</F>

{@Jīva-gṛbh,@}¦ ‘seizing alive,’ is, according to Roth,<sup>1</sup> the term for a police official in the Rigveda.<sup>2</sup> But although this sense is rendered possible by the mention of {@Madhyamaśī,@} perhaps ‘arbitrator,’ in the same passage,<sup>3</sup> it is neither necessary nor probable.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) St Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.;%} {%Siebenzig Lieder,%} 174.</F> <F>2) x. 97, 11.</F> <F>3) Rv. x. 97, 12.</F> <F>4) Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 180.</F>
{@Jīva-ja.@}¦ See {@Jarāyu.@}

{@Jīvant@}¦ appears to denote a certain plant in one passage of the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> where the edition of Roth and Whitney has the unjustified emendation {@Jīvala.@}<sup>2</sup> <F>1) xix. 39, 3. {%Cf.%} Whitney, Transla- tion of the Atharvaveda, 960.</F> <F>2) With this conjectural form, {%cf.%} Jīvalā, an epithet of a plant in Av. vi. 59, 3; viii. 2, 6; 7, 6; xix. 39. 3.</F>
{@Jīvala Callaki,@}¦ ‘descendant of Celaka,’ is mentioned in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> as reproving {@Takṣan.@} <F>1) ii. 3, 1, 31-35. {%Cf.%} Lévi, {%La Doctrine du Sacrifice,%} 140.</F>
{@Juhū@}¦ is the regular name in the Rigveda and later for the tongue-shaped ladle in which butter was offered to the gods. <div n="P"/>1) Rv. viii. 44, 5; x. 21, 3; Av. xviii. 4, 5. 6, etc.

{@Jūrṇi,@}¦ ‘firebrand,’ is regarded by Zimmer<sup>1</sup> as one of the weapons of the Vedic Indians. But since it is only mentioned in the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> as a weapon used by demons, its employment in normal war cannot be safely assumed. <F>1) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 301.</F> <F>2) i. 129, 8. {%Cf.%} Nirukta, vi. 4.</F>
{@Jūrṇī@}¦ is one of the names given to serpents in a hymn of the Atharvaveda (ii. 24, 5), perhaps from their habit of casting their slough. See {@Ahi.@}
{@Jetṛ.@}¦ See {@Sṛṇi.@}

{@Jaitrāyaṇa Saho-jit@}¦ is apparently in the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> the name of a prince who celebrated the Rājasūya, or ‘royal consecration.’ Von Schroeder<sup>2</sup> quotes in support of Jaitrā- yaṇa as a proper name the derivative Jaitrāyaṇi, ‘descendant of Jaitra,’ formed according to the Gaṇa {%karṇādi,%} which is referred to by Pāṇini;<sup>3</sup> but it should be noted that in the parallel passage of the Kapiṣṭhala Saṃhitā<sup>4</sup> the reading is different, and no proper personal name appears, the subject being Indra, the god. This reading seems much more probable, for the verse should be general, and suit every king performing the rite. <F>1) xviii. 5.</F> <F>2) {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgen-%} {%lāndischen Gesellschaft,%} 49, 168.</F> <F>3) iv. 2, 80.</F> <F>4) xxviii. 5, cited by von Schroeder {%Kāṭhaka,%} 1, p. 269.</F>

{@Jaimini@}¦ does not appear till the Sūtra period.<sup>1</sup> But a Jaiminīya Saṃhitā of the Sāmaveda is extant, and has been edited and discussed by Caland;<sup>2</sup> and a Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa, of which a special section is the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāh- maṇa,<sup>3</sup> is known and has formed the subject of several articles by Oertel.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra, iii. 4; Śāṅkhāyana Gṛhya Sūtra, iv. 10; vi. 6, etc. He appears also as a pupil of Vyāsa, Sāmavidhāna Brāhmaṇa, {%ad fin.;%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 377. {%Cf.%} his {%Indian Literature,%} 56.</F> <F>2) As part ii. of Hillebrandt's {%Indische%} {%Forschungen, Breslau,%} 1907. See Olden- berg, {%Göttingische Gelehrte Anzeigen,%} 1908, 712 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>3) Edited by Oertel, {%Journal of the%} {%American Oriental Society,%} 16, 79-260.</F> <F>4){%Journal of the American Oriental%} {%Society,%} 18, 15 {%et seq.;%} 19, 97; 23, 325, 26, 176, 306; 28, 81; {%Actes du onzieme%} {%Congres International des Orientalistes,%} 1, 225; {%Transactions of the Connectieut%} {%Academy of Arts and Sciences,%} 15, 155 {%et seq.%}</F>

{@Jaivantāyana,@}¦ ‘descendant of Jīvanta,’ is mentioned in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad<sup>1</sup> as a teacher, with {@Śaunaka@} and {@Raibhya,@} of {@Rauhiṇāyana.@} <F>1) iv. 5, 26 (Mādhyaṃdina). The name is recognised by Pāṇini, iv. 1, 103.</F>

{@Jaivala@}¦ or {@Jaivali,@} ‘descendant of Jīvala,’ is the patronymic of {@Pravāhaṇa@} in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka<sup>1</sup> and Chāndogya Upani- ṣads.<sup>2</sup> Jaivali, the king, in the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> is the same person. <F>1) vi. 2, 1 (Kāṇva = vi. 1, 1 Mādhyaṃ- dina), where the form is Jaivala.</F> <F>2) i. 8, 1. 2. 8; v. 3, 1.</F> <F>3) i. 38, 4.</F>

{@Jñātṛ@}¦ occurs in two passages of the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and one of the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka<sup>2</sup> with a somewhat obscure sense. Zimmer<sup>3</sup> conjectures not unnaturally that the word is a technical term taken from law, meaning ‘witness.’ The reference is, perhaps, to a custom of carrying on transactions of business before witnesses as practised in other primitive societies.<sup>4</sup> Roth<sup>5</sup> suggests that the word has the sense of [Page1-291+ 61] ‘surety.’ But Bloomfield<sup>6</sup> and Whitney<sup>7</sup> ignore these inter- pretations. <F>1) vi. 32, 3; viii. 8, 21.</F> <F>2) xii. 14. {%Cf.%} Keith, {%Śāṅkhāyana%} {%Āraṇyaka,%} 66, n. 4.</F> <F>3) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 181.</F> <F>4) In Manu, viii. 57, the word is a various reading for {%sākṣin,%} ‘witness.’ <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Jolly, {%Recht und Sitte,%} 140.</F> <F>5) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>6) {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 475.</F> <F>7) Translation of the Atharvaveda, 306.</F>

{@Jñāti@}¦ (masc.), a word which originally seems to have meant ‘acquaintance,’<sup>1</sup> denotes in the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> and later<sup>3</sup> a ‘relation,’ apparently one who was connected by blood on the father's side, though the passages do not necessarily require the limitation. But this sense follows naturally enough from the patriarchal basis of Vedic society.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) Being in all probability derived from {%jñā,%} ‘know,’ not from {%jan,%} ‘beget,’ as would at first sight seem more likely on account of the sense. {%Cf.%} the St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>2) vii. 55, 5, seems to refer to the members of the joint family sleeping in the paternal house; x. 66, 14; 85, 28 (the kinsmen of the bride are meant); 117, 9 (perhaps ‘brother and sister’ are meant by {%jñātī%} here, but ‘kinsfolk’ will do; {%of.%} Muir, {%Sanskrit%} {%Texts,%} 5, 432).</F> <F>3) Av. xii. 5, 44 (where Whitney in his Translation renders the word by ‘acquaintances,’ which seems too vague and feeble); Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 6, 5, 2; Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 6, 4, 3 ({%jñātibhyāṃ vā sakhibhyāṃ, vā,%} ‘where ‘relations’ are contrasted with ‘friends’ or ‘companions’); ii. 2, 2, 20; 5, 2, 20; xi. 3, 3, 7, etc.</F> <F>4) For the transition from the etymo- logical meaning, {%cf.%} <lang n="greek">γνωτός, γνωτή</lang>, which in Homer designate ‘brother’ and ‘sister’; St. Petersburg Dic- tionary, {%s.v.%}</F>

{@Jyā@}¦ is the regular word for ‘bowstring’ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> The making of bowstrings was a special craft, as is shown by the occurrence of the Jyā-kāra, or ‘maker of bow- strings,’ among the victims at the Puruṣamedha, or human sacrifice, in the Yajurveda.<sup>3</sup> The bowstring consisted of a thong of ox-hide.<sup>4</sup> It was not usually kept taut,<sup>5</sup> but was specially tightened when the bow was to be used.<sup>6</sup> The sound of the bowstring ({%jyā-ghoṣa%}) is referred to in the Atharvaveda.<sup>7</sup> <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} {@Ārtnī.@} <F>1) iv. 27, 3; vi. 75, 3; x. 51, 6, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. i. 1, 3; v. 13, 6; vi. 42, 1; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xvi. 9; xxix. 51, etc.</F> <F>3) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxx. 7; Tait- tirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 3, 1.</F> <F>4) Rv. vi. 75, 3; Av. i. 1, 3. In the Epic the bowstring is made of hemp ({%maurvī%}); Hopkins, {%Journal of the%} {%American Oriental Society,%} 13, 271.</F> <F>5) Av. vi. 42, 1.</F> <F>6) Rv. x. 166, 3.</F> <F>7) v. 21, 9. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 298 299.</F>

{@Jyākā@}¦ means ‘bowstring,’ with a contemptuous sense, in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> and in the simple sense in the Atharvaveda.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) x. 133, 1, where {%anyakeṣāṃ jyākāḥ%} is unmistakably contemptuous. {%Cf.%} Macdonell, {%Vedic Grammar,%} p. 137.</F> <F>2) i. 2, 2.</F>
{@Jyā-pāśa@}¦ means ‘bowstring’ in the Atharvaveda (xi. 10, 22).

{@Jyā-hroḍa@}¦ occurs in the description of the arms of the {@Vrātya@} in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> and is also mentioned in the Sūtras.<sup>2</sup> The sense is somewhat obscure, for one Sūtra describes it as a ‘bow not meant for use’ ({%ayogyaṃ dhanus%}),<sup>3</sup> while the other speaks of it as a ‘bow without an arrow’ ({%dhanuṣka aniṣu%}).<sup>4</sup> Some sort of a bow, therefore, seems to be meant. <F>1) xvii. 1, 14 (spelt {%-hṇoḍa%} in text, {%-hnoḍa%} in comm.).</F> <F>2) Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xxii. 4, 11 (spelt {%-hroḍa%}); Lāṭyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, viii. 6, 8 (spelt {%-hnoḍa:%} the editor notes that the Drāhyāyaṇa Sūtra has the same reading).</F> <F>3) Kātyāyana, {%loc. cit.%}</F> <F>4) Lāṭyāyana, {%loc. cit.%} <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 38; Hopkins, {%Transactions of the Connecticut%} {%Acad my of Arts and Sciences,%} 15, 32; Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 33, 52.</F>

{@Jyeṣṭha,@}¦ ordinarily meaning ‘greatest,’ has further the specific sense of ‘eldest’<sup>1</sup> brother in the Rigveda.<sup>2</sup> It also means the eldest among sons, which is another side of the same sense.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) With changed accent, {%jyeṣṭhá. Cf.%} Macdonell, {%Vedic Grammar,%} p. 83, 14.</F> <F>2) iv. 33, 5; x. 11, 2.</F> <F>3) Av. xii. 2, 35; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vii. 17; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xi. 5, 3, 8, {%and cf.%} Jyaiṣthineya.</F>

{@Jyeṣṭha-ghnī,@}¦ ‘slaying the eldest,’ is the name of a {@Nakṣatra,@} or lunar mansion, usually called {@Jyeṣṭhā,@} in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> It is Antares or {%Cor Scipionis.%} <F>1) vi. 110, 2. {%Cf.%} vi. 112, 1.</F> <F>2) i. 5, 2, 8. {%Cf.%} Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 361.</F>
{@Jyeṣṭhā.@}¦ See {@Nakṣatra.@}

{@Jyaiṣṭhineya@}¦ denotes, in combination with {@Jyeṣṭha,@} the eldest,’ a ‘son of the father's first wife’ ({%jyeṣṭhā%}), in the Brāh- maṇas.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 1, 8, 1 (opposed to {%haniṣṭha%} and {%hāniṣṭhineya%}); Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, ii. 1, 2; xx. 5, 2.</F>

{@Jyotiṣa,@}¦ ‘astronomy.’ It is important to note that no refer- ence to any work on astronomy occurs in the Saṃhitās or Brāhmaṇas. The text which claims to represent the astro- nomical science of the Veda has been edited by Weber,<sup>1</sup> and has frequently been discussed since.<sup>2</sup> Its date is unknown, but is undoubtedly late, as is shown alike by the contents and form of the work. <F>1) {%Ueber den Vedakalender namens%} {%Jyotiṣam%} (1862).</F> <F>2) See references in Thibaut, {%Astren-%} {%omie, Astrologie und Mathematik,%} 20, 29.</F>
{@Jvālāyana,@}¦ ‘descendant of Jvāla,’ is the name of a man, a pupil of {@Gauṣūkti,@} mentioned in the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa (iv. 16, 1), in a list of teachers.

{@Jhaṣa@}¦ is mentioned in the story of Manu told in the Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> where it means a ‘great fish’ ({%mahā-matsya%}) according to the commentator. Eggeling<sup>2</sup> suggests that a horned fish is meant, because in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>3</sup> the Iḍā, or personified libation, is represented as a cow, and this may have brought in the idea of a horned fish in the later form of an old legend. But {%cf.%} {@Jaṣa.@} <F>1) i. 8, 1, 4.</F> <F>2) {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 12, 217, n. 3; 26, xxxi.</F> <F>3) i. 7, 1; ii. 6, 7.</F>

{@Takavāna@}¦ appears to be a patronymic from Taku,<sup>1</sup> and to be the name of a seer in the Rigveda,<sup>2</sup> presumably a descendant of Taku Kakṣīvant, for his name occurs in a group of hymns composed by the Kākṣīvatas.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) {%Cf.%} Bhṛgavāṇa, from Bhṛgu; Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v. Taku,%} as an adjective(?), occurs in Rigveda, ix. 97, 52.</F> <F>2) i. 120, 6.</F> <F>3) Oldenberg, {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen%} {%Morgenlāndischen Gesellschaft,%} 42, 221. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Pischel, {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 92; Ludwig, {%Über Methode bei Interpretation%} {%des Ṛgveda,%} 47.</F>

{@Takman@}¦ is a disease repeatedly mentioned in the Athar- vaveda, but later not known under this name. It is the subject of five hymns<sup>1</sup> of the Atharvaveda, and is often mentioned else- where.<sup>2</sup> Weber<sup>3</sup> first identified it with ‘fever,’ and Grohmann<sup>4</sup> showed that all the symptoms pointed to that ailment.<sup>5</sup> Refer- ence is made to the alternate hot and shivering fits of the patient,<sup>6</sup> to the yellow colour of the jaundice which accompanies the fever,<sup>7</sup> and to its peculiar periodicity. The words used to describe its varieties are {%anye-dyuḥ,%}<sup>8</sup> {%ubhaya-dyuḥ,%}<sup>9</sup> {%tṛtīyaka,%}<sup>10</sup> {%vi-tṛtīya,%}<sup>11</sup> and {%sadaṃ-di,%}<sup>12</sup> the exact sense of most of which terms is somewhat uncertain. It is agreed<sup>13</sup> that the first epithet designates the fever known as {%quotidianus,%} which recurs each day at the same hour, though the word is curious (lit. [Page1-295+ 54] ‘on the other — {%i.e.,%} next, day’). The {%ubhaya-dyuḥ%} (‘on both days’) variety appears to mean a disease recurring for two suc- cessive days, the third being free; this corresponds to the {%rhythmus%} {%quartanus complicatus.%}<sup>14</sup> But Sāyaṇa considers that it means a fever recurring on the third day, the ‘tertian.’ The {%tṛtīyaka,%} however, must be the ‘tertian’ fever,<sup>15</sup> though Zimmer<sup>16</sup> suggests that it may mean a fever which is fatal at the third paroxysm. Grohmann<sup>17</sup> regards the {%vi-tṛtīyaka%} as equivalent to the {%tertiana%} {%duplicata,%} a common form in southern countries, in which the fever occurs daily, but with a correspondence in point of time or severity of attack on alternate days. Bloomfield<sup>18</sup> suggests that it is identical with the {%ubhaya-dyuḥ%} variety. The {%sadaṃ-di%}<sup>19</sup> type appears to be the kind later known as {%saṃtata-jvara%} (‘continuous fever’), in which there are attacks of several days’ duration, with an interval followed by a fresh period of attack. Fever occurred at different seasons, in the autumn ({%śārada%}), in the hot weather ({%graiṣma%}), in the rains ({%vārṣika%}),<sup>20</sup> but was especially prevalent in the first, as is indicated by the epithet {%viśva-śārada,%} ‘occurring every autumn.’<sup>21</sup> <div n="P"/>The disease is said to arise when Agni enters the waters.<sup>22</sup> From this Weber<sup>23</sup> deduced that it was considered to be the result of a chill supervening on heat, or the influence of heat on marshy land. Grohmann<sup>24</sup> preferred to see in this connexion of the origin of the disease with Agni's entering the waters<sup>25</sup> an allusion to the fact that fever arises in the rainy season, the time when Agni, as lightning, descends to earth with the rain. Zimmer.<sup>26</sup> who accepts this view, further refers to the prevalence [Page1-296+ 41] of fever in the Terai, and interprets {%vanya,%} an epithet of fever found in the Atharvaveda,<sup>27</sup> as meaning ‘sprung from the forest,’ pointing out that fever is mentioned as prevalent among the {@Mūjavants@} and {@Mahāvṛṣas,@} two mountain tribes of the western Himālaya.<sup>28</sup> There is no trace of fever having been observed to be caused by the bite of the {%anopheles%} mosquito, which breeds in stagnant water: this theory has without reason been held to be known to classical Indian medicine.<sup>29</sup> <div n="P"/>Among the symptoms of Takman, or among complications accompanying it, are mentioned ‘itch’ ({@Pāman@}), ‘headache’ ({%śīrṣa-śoka%}),<sup>30</sup> ‘cough’ ({@Kāsikā@}), and ‘consumption,’ or perhaps some form of itch ({@Balāsa@}). <div n="P"/>It is perhaps significant that the Takman does not appear until the Atharvaveda. It is quite possible that the Vedic Āryans, when first settled in India, did not know the disease, which would take some generations to become endemic and recognized as dangerous. What remedies they used against it is quite uncertain, for the Atharvaveda mentions only spells and the {@Kuṣṭha,@} which can hardly have been an effective remedy, though still used in later times. Fever must, even in the Atharvan period, have claimed many victims, or it would not be mentioned so prominently. <F>1) i. 25; v. 22; vi. 20; vii. 116; xix. 39 ({%cf.%} v. 4).</F> <F>2) Av. iv. 9, 8; v. 4. 1. 9; 30, 16; ix. 8, 6; xi. 2, 22. 26, etc.</F> <F>3) {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 119; Roth, {%Zur%} {%Litteratur und Geschishte des Weda,%} 39, had, from the use of Kuṣṭha as a remedy, regarded it as denoting ‘leprosy,’ and was followed by Pictet, Kuhn's {%Zeitschrift%} 5, 337. Muir, {%Sanskrit%} {%Texts,%} 4, 280, thought ‘consumption’ was meant.</F> <F>4) {%Indische Studien,%} 9, 381 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>5) See also Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the%} {%Atharvaveda,%} 451 {%et seq.;%} Zimmer, {%Altin-%} {%disches Leben,%} 379-385, and compare the {%jvara%} (a non-Vedic word) of the classical medicine, Wise, {%Hindu System of%} {%Medicine,%} 219 {%et seq.;%} Jolly, {%Medicin,%} 70-72. {@Takvan,@}¦<sup>1</sup> {@Takvarī,@}<sup>2</sup> seem in the Rigveda to denote a ‘swift- flying bird.’ Sāyaṇa<sup>3</sup> explains Takvan as a swift steed. <F>1) Rv. i. 66, 2. {%Cf.%} i. 134, 5, and {@Tsārin.@}</F> <F>2) {%Ibid.,%} i. 151, 5; x. 91, 2. {@Takṣaka Vaiśāleya@}¦ (‘descendant of Viśālā’) is a mythical figure, mentioned as the son of Virāj in the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> and as Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin priest at the snake sacrifice in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) vii. 10, 29.</F> <F>2) xxv. 15, 3. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 35.</F>

1. {@Takṣan,@}¦ ‘carpenter,’ is mentioned in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and often later.<sup>2</sup> He was employed to do all sorts of work in wood, such as the making of chariots ({@Ratha@}) and wagons ({@Anas@}). Carved work of a finer type seems also to have fallen to his lot.<sup>3</sup> The axe ({%kuliśa,%}<sup>4</sup> {%paraśu%})<sup>5</sup> is mentioned as one of his tools, and perhaps the {@Bhurij,@} a word which is, however, uncertain in sense. In one passage of the Rigveda<sup>6</sup> reference seems to be made to the pains of the carpenter in bending over his work. That the carpenters were a low caste, or formed a separate class of the people, is certainly not true of Vedic times.<sup>7</sup> <F>1) ix. 112, 1.</F> <F>2) Av. x. 6, 3; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xii. 10; xviii. 13; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 9, 5; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xvi. 27; xxx. 6; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 2, 1; Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 1, 3, 12; iii. 6, 4, 4, etc.</F> <F>3) Rv. x. 86, 5; Av. xix. 49, 8. {%Cf.%} Rv. i. 161, 9; iii. 60. 2.</F> <F>4) Rv. iii. 2, 1.</F> <F>5) Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xii. 10.</F> <F>6) Rv. i. 105, 18. {%Cf.%} Roth, {%Nirukta,%} {%Erläuterungen,%} 67; Oldenberg. {%Ṛgveda-%} {%Noten,%} 1, 100.</F> <F>7) Fick, {%Die sociale Gliederung,%} 210, n. 1. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 245, 253.</F>

2. {@Takṣan@}¦ is mentioned in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> as a teacher whose view of a certain formula was not accepted by {@Jīvala Cailaki.@} <F>1) ii. 3, 1, 31-35. {%Cf.%} Lévi, {%La Doctrine du Sacrifice,%} 140.</F>

{@Taṇḍula,@}¦ ‘grain,’ especially ‘rice grain,’ is mentioned very often in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and later,<sup>2</sup> but not in the Rigveda. This accords with the fact that rice cultivation seems hardly known in the Rigveda.<sup>3</sup> Husked ({%karṇa%}) and unhusked ({%akarṇa%}) rice is referred to in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) x. 9, 26; xi. 1, 18; xii. 3, 18. 29. 30.</F> <F>2) Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 6, 6; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, x. 1, etc.; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, i. 1; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 1, 4, 3; ii. 5, 3, 4; v. 2, 3, 2; vi. 6, 1, 8, etc.; {%śyāmāka-taṇḍula,%} ‘millet grain,’ {%ibid.,%} x. 6, 3, 2; Chāndogya Upaniṣad, iii. 14, 3; {%apāmārga-taṇḍula,%} ‘grain of the {%Achyranthes aspera,%}’ v. 2, 4, 15, etc.</F> <F>3) Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 239. {@Tanaya,@}¦ n., denotes ‘offspring,’ ‘descendants’ in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> where also it is often used adjectivally with {@Toka.@}<sup>2</sup> There seems no ground for the view<sup>3</sup> that {%toka%} means ‘sons,’ ‘children,’ and {%tanaya%} ‘grandchildren.’ <F>1) i. 96, 4; 183, 3; 184, 5; ii. 23, 19; vii. 1, 21, etc.; {%tokaṃ ca tanayaṃ ca,%} i. 92, 13; ix. 74, 5. {%Cf.%} vi. 25, 4; 31, 1; 66, 8; and i. 31, 12, as explained by Pischel, {%Vedische Studien,%} 3, 193.</F> <F>2) Rv. i. 64, 14; 114, 6; 147, 1; 189, 2; ii. 30, 5, etc.; Aitareya Brāh- maṇa, ii. 7.</F> <F>3) Nirukta, x. 7; xii. 6. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} {%Tan, tana,%} and {%tanas,%} have the same sense as Tanaya. {@Tanti@}¦ occurs in one passage of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> where Roth<sup>2</sup> renders the plural of the word by ‘files’ of calves. {@Tantu@}¦ appears properly to mean ‘thread,’ and in particular the ‘warp’ of a piece of weaving, as opposed to {@Otu,@} the ‘woof.’ Both senses are found in the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> the ‘warp’ is called {%anuchāda,%} the ‘woof’ {%paryāsa,%} the {%tantavaḥ%} being the ‘threads.’ In the Taittirīya Saṃhitā,<sup>3</sup> [Page1-299+ 38] on the other hand, the ‘warp’ is {%prācīna-tāna,%} the ‘woof’ {%otu.%} The threads or cords of the throne ({@Pary ṅka@}) are referred to in the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad.<sup>4</sup> <div n="P"/>In the Rigveda the word is used only metaphorically, and this is its most frequent use even in the Brāhmanas.<sup>5</sup> See also {@Vāṇa.@} <F>1) xiv. 2, 51 (opposed to {%otu%}); xv. 3, 6 (the {%prāñcaḥ%} and {%tiryañcaḥ%} threads or cords of the throne of the Vrātya [{@Āsandī@}]).</F> <F>2) iii. 1, 2, 18; Eggeling, {%Sacred Books%} {%of the East,%} 26, 8, 9.</F> <F>3) vi. 1, 1, 4.</F> <F>4) i. 5; Keith, {%Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka,%} 20, n. 2.</F> <F>5) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} It is applied to the filaments of plants in Rv. x. 134, 5; to the spider's web in Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upanisad. ii. 1, 23.</F>

{@Tantra@}¦ means, like {@Tantu,@} the ‘warp’ of a piece of weaving, or more generally the ‘web’ itself. It is found in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) x. 71, 9.</F> <F>2) Av. x. 7, 42; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 5, 5, 3; Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, x. 5; Śatapa ha Brāhmaṇa, xiv. 2, 2, 22. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 254.</F>

This is merely a misunderstanding of the Rv. {%Cf.%} Oertel, {%Journal of the%} {%American Oriental Society,%} 18, 39; Sieg, {%Die Sagenstoffe des Ṛgveda,%} 50 {%et seq.;%} 62, 63; Oldenberg, {%Zeitschrift der%} {%Deutschen Morgenländischen Gesellschaft,%} 42, 232, n. 1; {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 353, 354, where he points out that the Brāhmaṇa tradition, and that of the Bṛhaddevatā (v. 50-81, with Macdonell's notes), are not to be accepted as real explanations of the Rigveda.</F>
