{@Taskara@}¦ occurs in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and frequently later,<sup>2</sup> denoting ‘thief’ or ‘robber.’ It appears to be practically synonymous with {@Stena,@} in connexion with which it is often mentioned.<sup>3</sup> The Stena and the Taskara are contrasted in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā<sup>4</sup> with the {@Malimlu,@} who is a burglar or house-breaker, while they are highwaymen, or, as the Rigveda<sup>5</sup> puts it, ‘men who haunt the woods and risk their lives’ ({%tanū-tyajā vanar-gū%}). In another passage of the Rigveda,<sup>6</sup> however, the dog is told to bark at the Taskara or the Stena, which clearly points to an attempt at house-breaking. The thief goes about at night,<sup>7</sup> and knows the paths<sup>8</sup> on which he attacks his victim. In one passage of the Rigveda<sup>9</sup> the use of cords is mentioned, but whether to bind the thieves when captured, or to bind the [Page1-303+ 53] victim, is not clear.<sup>10</sup> The Atharvaveda<sup>11</sup> refers to the Stena and the Taskara as cattle and horse thieves.<sup>12</sup> <F>1) i. 191, 5; vi. 27, 3; vii. 55, 3; viii. 29, 6.</F> <F>2) Av. iv. 3, 2; xix. 47, 7; 50, 5; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xi. 77-78; xii. 62; xvi. 21, etc; Nirukta, iii. 14.</F> <F>3) Rv. vii. 55. 3; Av. xix. 47, 7; 50, 5; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xi. 79; xvi. 21, etc.</F> <F>4) xi. 79 (the Malimlu is {%janeṣu,%} ‘among men’; the others {%vane,%} ‘in the forest’). {%Cf.%} for the Malimlu, Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vi. 3, 2, 6; Atharvaveda, xix. 49, 10.</F> <F>5) x. 4, 6.</F> <F>6) vii. 55, 3.</F> <F>7) Rv. i. 191, 5.</F> <F>8) Rv. viii. 29, 6.</F> <F>9) x. 4, 6.</F> <F>10) Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 178, n.</F> <F>11) xix. 50, 5. {%Cf.%} Rv. x. 97, 10 ({%stena%}).</F> <F>12) Whitney, Translation of the Athar- vaveda, 984.</F>

{@Tāyu@}¦ was another name for thief, perhaps of a less distinguished and more domestic character than the highway- man, for though he is referred to as a cattle-thief,<sup>13</sup> he is also alluded to as a stealer of clothes ({%vastra-mathi%})<sup>14</sup> and as a debtor.<sup>15</sup> In one passage the Tāyus are said to disappear at the coming of dawn (which is elsewhere called {%yāvayad-dveṣas,%} ‘driving away hostile beings,’ and {%ṛta-pā,%} ‘guardian of order’), like the stars of heaven ({%nakṣatra%}).<sup>16</sup> <div n="P"/>In the Śatarudriya litany of the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā<sup>17</sup> Rudra is called lord of assailers ({%ā-vyādhin%}), thieves ({%stena%}), robbers ({%taskara%}), pickpockets ({%stāyu%}), stealers ({%muṣṇant%}), and cutters ({%vi-kṛnta%}); and designations of sharpers ({%gṛtsa%}) and bands ({%gaṇa, vrāta%}), apparently of robbers, are mentioned.<sup>18</sup> It is therefore not surprising that the Rigveda<sup>19</sup> should contain many prayers for safety at home or on the way, or that the Atharvaveda should devote several hymns to night<sup>20</sup> chiefly for protection against the evil doings of thieves and robbers. <div n="P"/>Pischel<sup>21</sup> suggests that in one passage of the Rigveda<sup>22</sup> {@Vasiṣṭha@} is represented as a burglar, but the admits that, since Vasiṣṭha was attacking the house of his father Varuṇa, he was only seeking to obtain what he may have regarded as his own. But the interpretation of the hymn is not certain.<sup>23</sup> <div n="P"/>Sāyaṇa's explanation of one passage of the Rigveda,<sup>24</sup> as [Page1-304+ 60] referring to professional cattle-trackers, like the Khojis of the Panjab, seems quite probable.<sup>25</sup> <div n="P"/>The punishment of thieves appears primarily to have been left to the action of the robbed. The practice of binding them in stocks<sup>26</sup> seems clearly referred to. But later, at any rate —  and in all probability earlier also, as in other countries — a more severe penalty could be exacted, and death inflicted by the king.<sup>27</sup> There is no hint in Vedic literature of the mode of conviction; a fire ordeal is not known to the Atharvaveda,<sup>28</sup> and the ordeal known to the Chāndogya Upaniṣad<sup>29</sup> is not said to be used in the case of theft. No doubt the stolen property was recovered by the person robbed if he could obtain it. Nothing is known as to what happened if the property had passed from the actual thief into the possession of another person. <F>13) Rv. i. 65, 1; vii. 86, 5.</F> <F>14) Rv. iv. 38, 5.</F> <F>15) Rv. vi. 12, 5. No doubt this theft is the result of despair at being in debt, which might lead to loss of liberty (Ṛṇa).</F> <F>16) Rv. i. 50, 2. {%Cf.%} Macdonell, {%Vedic%} {%Mythology,%} p. 47.</F> <F>17) xvi. 20, 21. {%Cf.%} Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iv. 5, 4, 1; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xvii. 13; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 9, 4.</F> <F>18) xvi. 25.</F> <F>19) i. 129, 9; ii. 23, 16; vi. 24, 10; 41, 5; 51, 15; x. 63, 16.</F> <F>20) Av. xix. 47-50.</F> <F>21) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 55, 56. Con- trast 1, 106.</F> <F>22) Rv. vii. 55.</F> <F>23) {%Cf.%} Aufrecht, {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 337 {%et seq.;%} Lanman, {%Sanskrit Reader,%} 370; Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 308; Bṛhaddevatā, vii. 11 {%et seq.,%} with Mac- donell's notes.</F> <F>24) vi. 54, 1.</F> <F>25) Zimmer, {%op. cit.,%} 182, 183, citing Elliot, {%Memoirs,%} 1, 276; Jolly, {%Recht%} {%und Sitte,%} 123.</F> <F>26) {%Cf.%} Rv. i. 24, 13, 15; vii. 86, 5; Av. vi. 63, 3 = 84, 4; 115, 2. 3; 121; xix. 47, 9; 50, 1, all of which passages are cited by Zimmer, 181, 182, to prove this practice. But it must be noted that Rv. vii. 86, 5, alone is not at all con- clusive evidence, though Av. xix. 47, 9; 50, 1 ({%drupade āhan%}), probably mean the same thing. Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 976, 983, renders the passages as referring to casting a thief into a snare, and Pischel, {%Vedische%} {%Studien,%} 1, 106, makes Rv. vii. 86, 5, refer to the cattle-thief ({%paśu-tṛp%}) taking away the rope from the calf he means to steal. For Rv. x. 4, 6, see above, n. 10. The German and Slavonic parallels cited by Zimmer, 182, n., support his view. See also for a similar punishment in case of debt, {@Ṛṇa.@}</F> <F>27) Gautama Dharma Sūtra, xii. 43- 45; Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra, i. 9, 25, 4. 5; Jolly, {%op. cit.,%} 124.</F> <F>28) Av. ii. 12 was so interpreted by Schlagintweit, {%Die Gottesurtheile der%} {%Inder,%} 9 {%et seq.%} (1866); Weber, {%Indische%} {%Studien,%} 13, 164 {%et seq.;%} Ludwig, Trans- lation of the Rigveda, 3, 445; Zimmer, 183 {%et seq.;%} but see Bloomfield, {%American%} {%Journal of Philology,%} 11, 330 {%et seq.;%} {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 294-296; Whitney, Translation of the Atharva- veda, 54; Grill, {%Hundert Lieder,%}^2 47, 85; Jolly, {%op cit.,%} 146.</F> <F>29) vi. 16; Jolly, {%loc. cit.%}</F>

{@Tastuva,@}¦ or {@Tasruva,@} as the Paippalāda recension has it, is the name of a remedy against snake poison, and is mentioned along with {@Tābuva@} in the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) v. 13, 10, 11. {%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 428; Whit- ney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 244.</F>

{@Tājad-bhaṅga@}¦ (‘easily broken’) is apparently the name of a tree or plant in the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> The Kauśika Sūtra<sup>2</sup> treats it as a compound word, and its commentator makes it out to be the castor-oil plant ({%eraṇḍa%}). Whitney,<sup>3</sup> however, treats the expression as two separate words, and thinks that the passage means ‘may they be broken suddenly ({%tājat%}) like hemp ({%bhañga%}).’ <F>1) viii. 8, 3 (a battle hymn).</F> <F>2) xvi 14. {%Cf.%} Bloomfield's edition, xliv; {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 583, 584; Caland, {%Altindisches Zauberritual,%} 35; Lanman in Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 502; Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 72.</F> <F>3) {%Op. cit.,%} 504.</F>

{@Tāṇḍa@}¦ seems to be the name of a sage to whose school belonged the Tāṇḍa Brāhmaṇa mentioned in the Lāṭyāyana Śrauta Sūtra.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) vii. 10, 17. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 49.</F>
{@Tāṇḍa-vinda,@}¦ or {@Tāṇḍa-vindava,@} is the name of a teacher mentioned in the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) viii. 10. The manuscripts differ as to the form of the name.</F>
{@Tāṇḍi@}¦ occurs as the name of a pupil of {@Bādarāyaṇa@} in the Vaṃśa (list of teachers) at the end of the Sāmavidhāna Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) See Konow's Translation, 80, n. 2.</F>

{@Tāṇḍya@}¦ is the name of a teacher in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> quoted on a point bearing on the Agniciti, or piling of the sacred fire. He is also mentioned in the Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> The Tāṇḍya Mahābrāhmaṇa or Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> of the Sāmaveda represents the school of the Tāṇḍins. <F>1) vi. 1, 2, 25. {%Cf.%} Lévi, {%La Doctrine%} {%du Sacrifice,%} 140.</F> <F>2) Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 373, 384.</F> <F>3) Edited in the {%Bibliotheca Indica%} Series, 1869-74. See Weber, {%Indian%} {%Literature,%} 66 {%et seq.,%} 74, 133; Macdonell, {%Sanskrit Literature,%} 203, 210; Hopkins, {%Transactions of the Connecticut Academy%} {%of Arts and Sciences,%} 15, 23 {%et seq.%}</F>

{@Tāta,@}¦ apparently ‘dada's boy,’ an affectionate term of address by a father ({%cf.%} {@Tata@}) to a son, is found in the Brāhmaṇas,<sup>1</sup> occurring in the vocative only. But in the sense of ‘father,’ through confusion with Tata, it occurs also as early as the Aitareya Āraṇyaka.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vii. 14, 4; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, vi. 1, 6; Chāndogya Upaniṣad, iv. 4, 2.</F> <F>2) i. 3, 3, where Tata and Tāta are given as variant forms of the address of the child to the father. Little, {%Grammatical Index,%} 75, takes Tāta to mean ‘father’ primarily, but this seems unlikely. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Delbrück, {%Die indogermanischen%} {%Verwandtschaftsnamen,%} 449, 454.</F>

{@Tādurī@}¦ is mentioned in a verse of the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> together with the female frog ({@Maṇḍūkī@}). Some similar animal must be meant,<sup>2</sup> but Roth,<sup>3</sup> with the commentator Durga on the Nirukta,<sup>4</sup> regards the word as an adjective describing the frog. <F>1) iv. 15, 14.</F> <F>2) Whitney, Translation of the Athar- vaveda, 175.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.,%} where he suggests {%tāḍurī,%} from the root {%taḍ,%} ‘beat,’ with the sense of ‘splashing.’</F> <F>4) ix. 7.</F>

1. {@Tānva@}¦ in an obscure passage of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> seems to mean a ‘legitimate son,’ who is said not to leave the heritage ({%riktha%}) of his father to his sister ({%jāmi%}). The exact meaning is probably unascertainable,<sup>2</sup> but the passage may convey a statement of what was no doubt the fact, that the daughter had no share in the paternal inheritance; her brother had to provide for her during her life if she remained unmarried, but she had no independent portion.<sup>3</sup> (See {@Dāya.@}) <F>1) iii. 31, 2.</F> <F>2) {%Cf.%} Griffith, {%Hymns of the Rigveda,%} 1, 348; Oldenberg, {%Ṛgveda Noten,%} 1, 240; Geldner, {%Vedische Studien,%} 3, 34.</F> <F>3) {%Cf.%} Jolly, {%Recht und Sitte,%} 87, for the modern law of the Panjab.</F>

2. {@Tānva@}¦ appears to be a patronymic, ‘descendant of Tanva,’ in a verse of the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> Ludwig<sup>2</sup> thinks that it is the patronymic of {@Duḥśīma,@} who is mentioned in the preceding verse, but this is uncertain. <F>1) x. 93, 15.</F> <F>2) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 166.</F>
1. {@Tāpasa,@}¦ ‘ascetic,’ is not found in Vedic literature till the Upaniṣads.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, iv. 3, 22. {%Cf.%} Fick, {%Die sociale Gliederung,%} 40.</F>
2. {@Tāpasa@}¦ is a name of {@Datta@} who was Hotṛ priest at the snake festival described in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa (xxv. 15).

{@Tābuva@}¦ is the name in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> of a remedy against snake poison. The Paippalāda recension has Tāvuca instead. Weber<sup>2</sup> thinks that the original form was Tāthuva, from the root {%sthā,%} ‘stand,’ and that it meant ‘stopping’; but this is hardly probable.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) v. 13, 10.</F> <F>2) Proceedings of the Berlin Academy, 1896, 681.</F> <F>3) Barth. {%Revne del'Histoire des Religions,%} 39, 26. {%Cf.%} Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 244; Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 428.</F>
{@Tāyādara,@}¦ ‘belonging to the {@Tayādara@}’ (Av. vi. 72, 2).

{@Tāyu,@}¦ ‘thief,’ is mentioned several times in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> See {@Taskara.@} <F>1) i. 50, 2; 65, 1; iv. 38, 5; v. 15, 5; 52, 12; vi. 12, 5; vii. 86, 5 ({%paśu-tṛṭ,%} ‘cattle-thief,’ see Pischel, {%Vedische%} {%Studien,%} 1, 106).</F>

{@Tārakā@}¦ is found several times in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> denoting a star. The masculine form Tāraka occurs in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) ii. 8, 1; iii. 7, 4; vi. 121, 3; xix. 49, 8.</F> <F>2) i. 5, 2, 5.</F>

{@Tārukṣya@}¦ is the name of a teacher in the Aitareya<sup>1</sup> and Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyakas.<sup>2</sup> In the former passage Tārkṣya is a variant reading, and in the latter Tārkṣya is read, but this is probably only due to confusion with Tārkṣya, the reputed author of a Rigvedic hymn.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) iii. 1, 6.</F> <F>2) vii. 19.</F> <F>3) Aitareya Āraṇyaka, i. 5, 2, with Keith's note; Sāṅkhāyana Srauta Sūtra xi. 14, 28; xii. 11, 12, Āśvalāyana Srauta Sūtra, ix. 1.</F>

{@Tārkṣya@}¦ is mentioned in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as a divine steed, apparently the sun conceived as a horse.<sup>2</sup> But Foy,<sup>3</sup> judging by the name, apparently a patronymic of {@Tṛkṣi,@} who is known from the Rigveda<sup>4</sup> onwards as a descendant of {@Trasadasyu,@} thinks that a real steed, the property of Tṛkṣi, is meant; but this is not very probable.<sup>5</sup> See also {@Tārukṣya.@} <F>1) i. 89, 6; x. 178.</F> <F>2) Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} p. 149.</F> <F>3) Kuhn's {%Zeitschrift,%} 11, 366, 367.</F> <F>4) viii. 22, 7.</F> <F>5) In Khila, ii. 4, 1, Tārkṣya is repre- sented as a bird ({%vāyasa%}), also a symbol of the sun. In the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xv. 18, he is mentioned with Ariṣṭanemi, originally an epithet of his (Rv. i. 89, 6; x. 178, 1), as a person, and in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 4, 3, 13, he appears as Vaipaśyata (Vaipaścita in Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra, x. 7), king of the birds ({%cf.%} Eggeling, {%Sacred Books%} {%of the East,%} 44, 369).</F>

{@Tārpya@}¦ denotes, in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and later,<sup>2</sup> a garment made of some material, the nature of which is uncertain. The commentators on the Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra and the Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> suggest that a linen garment, or one thrice soaked in ghee, or one made of the {%tṛpā%} or of the {%triparṇa%} plant, is meant: it is doubtful whether the sense was known even to the author of the Brāhmaṇa himself. Goldstücker's<sup>4</sup> rendering of the word is ‘silken garment,’ which Eggeling<sup>5</sup> is inclined to accept.^6 <F>1) xviii. 4, 31.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 4, 11, 6; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 3, 7, 1; 7, 6, 4; Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xxi. 1; Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, v. 3, 5, 20; Kātyāyana Śranta Sūtra, xv. 5, 7 {%et seq.;%} Śāṅkh- āyana Śrauta Sūtra, xvi. 12, 19.</F> <F>3) v. 3, 5, 20. {%Cf.%} Kātyāyana, {%loc. cit.;%} Sāyaṇa on Av., {%loc. cit.;%} Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 879.</F> <F>4) Dictionary, {%s.v. abhiṣecanīya.%}</F> <F>5) {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 41, 85, n. 1.</F>

{@Tārṣṭāgha,@}¦ a species of tree, is mentioned in the Kauśika Sūtra,<sup>1</sup> while the adjective formed from it, {%tārṣṭāghī,%} ‘derived from the Tārṣṭāgha tree,’ is found in the Atharvaveda.<sup>2</sup> Weber<sup>3</sup> thinks that the {%sarṣapa,%} or mustard plant, is meant. <F>1) xxv. 23.</F> <F>2) v. 29, 15. {%Cf.%} Whitney's note in his Translation of the Atharvaveda.</F> <F>3) {%Indische Studien,%} 18, 280. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 62.</F>

{@Titaü@}¦<sup>1</sup> is found once in the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> denoting a ‘sieve,’ or perhaps ‘winnowing fan,’ which was used for purifying corn ({%saktu%}). <F>1) On the peculiar form of this word, {%of.%} Macdonell, {%Vedic Grammar,%} 20, 3.</F> <F>2) x. 71, 2. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 238.</F>

{@Tittira, Tittiri,@}¦ is the name of the partridge in the later Saṃhitās<sup>1</sup> and the Brāhmaṇas,<sup>2</sup> being presumably an onomato- poetic formation. The bird is described as having variegated plumage ({%bahu-rūpa%}). It is usually associated with the {@Kapiñ-@} {@jala@} and {@Kalaviṅka.@} <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 5, 1, 2; v. 5, 16, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 4, 1; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xii. 10; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 30, 36. The form Tittira occurs in the Maitrāyaṇī Samhitā, iii. 14, 1.</F> <F>2) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 6, 3, 5; v. 5, 4, 6; Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 154, 6 (Oertel, {%Transactions of the%} {%Connecticut Academy of Arts and Sciences,%} 15, 181). <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 91; Schrader, {%Prehistoric Antiquities,%} 251.</F>

{@Tithi,@}¦ as the name of a lunar day, the thirtieth part of a lunar month of rather over twenty-seven days, is only found in the later Sūtras,<sup>1</sup> being completely unknown to the Brāhmaṇas, in which the only day is the natural one.<sup>2</sup> See {@Māsa.@} <F>1) Gobhila Gṛhya Sūtra, i. 1, 13; ii. 8, 12, 20; Śāṅkhāyana Gṛhya Sūtra, i. 25; v. 2, etc.</F> <F>2) Thibaut, {%Astronomie, Astrologie und%} {%Mathematik,%} 7, 8.</F>

{@Timirgha Daure-śruta@}¦ (‘descendant of Dūreśruta’) is men- tioned as Agnīdh (‘fire-kindling’) priest at the snake sacrifice described in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) xxv. 15. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 35.</F>

{@Tiraśca@}¦ is read in some manuscripts of the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> in the description of the Vrātya's throne ({@Āsandī@}), meaning ‘the cross-pieces.’ But the reading should be {%tiraścye,%} which is adjectival, and is used in the same sense. <F>1) xv. 3, 5. {%Cf.%} Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 776; Keith, {%Śāṅkh-%} {%āyana Araṇyaka,%} 19, n. 3.</F>

{@Tiraśca-rāji,@}¦<sup>1</sup> {@Tiraści-rāji,@}<sup>2</sup> {@Tiraścīna-rāji,@}<sup>3</sup> are variant forms of a name for ‘snake’ (lit., ‘striped across’), found in the later Saṃhitās. <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 10, 2; Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 94, 95, reports this form from the Av., but the text and Roth (St. Petersburg Dic- tionary, {%s.v.%}) read {%tiraści-rāji%} there.</F> <F>2) Av. iii. 27, 2; vi. 56, 2; vii. 56, 1; x. 4, 13; xii. 3, 56.</F> <F>3) Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 13, 21; Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka, xii. 27. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Athar-%} {%vaveda,%} 488, 553; Keith, {%Śāṅkhāyana%} {%Āraṇyaka,%} 68, n. 2; Weber, {%Indische%} {%Studien,%} 17, 295-297.</F>

{@Tiraścī@}¦ is, according to the Anukramaṇī, the author of a Rigvedic hymn<sup>1</sup> in which he appeals to Indra to hear his call. The Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> adopts this view of the name, and mentions a Tiraścī Āṅgirasa. But Roth<sup>3</sup> thinks that the word is not a proper name at all. <F>1) viii. 95, 4.</F> <F>2) xii. 6, 12.</F> <F>3) {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgen-%} {%ländischen Gesellschaft,%} 48, 115. {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 5, 187; Hopkins, {%Journal of the American%} {%Oriental Society,%} 17, 90; Macdonell, {%Vedic Grammar,%} p. 273.</F>
{@Tiraścīna-vaṃśa,@}¦ ‘cross-beam,’ is used to denote a ‘bee- hive’ in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.<sup>1</sup> See also {@Vaṃśa.@} <F>1) iii. 1, 1. {%Cf.%} Little, {%Grammatical Index,%} 75.</F>

{@Tirindira@}¦ is mentioned in a Dānastuti, or ‘Praise of Gifts,’ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as having, along with {@Parśu,@} bestowed gifts on the singer. In the Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra<sup>2</sup> this state- ment is represented by a tale that the Kaṇva Vatsa obtained a gift from Tirindira Pāraśavya, Tirindira and Parśu being in this version thus treated as one and the same man. Ludwig<sup>3</sup> sees in the Rigvedic passage a proof that the Yadus had gained a victory over Tirindira, and gave a part of the booty to the singers; but there is no proof whatever of the correctness of this interpretation, which Zimmer<sup>4</sup> shows to be most unlikely. Yadu princes must be meant by Tirindira and [Page1-311+ 57] Parśu, though Weber<sup>5</sup> thinks that the singers were Yadus, not the princes. The latter he holds to have been Iranian ({%cf.%} <lang n="greek">Τιρίβαζος</lang>, and see {@Parśu@}), and he thinks that in this there is evidence of continual close relations between India and Iran. This is perfectly possible, but the evidence for it is rather slight. <div n="P"/>6 For the recent controversy as to Iranian names found at Boghaz-kiöi, {%cf.%} Jacobi, {%Journal of the Royal Asiatic%} {%Society,%} 1909, 721 {%et seq.;%} Oldenberg, {%ibid.,%} 1095-1100; Keith, {%ibid.,%} 1100-1106; Sayce, {%ibid.,%} 1106, 1107; Kennedy, {%ibid.,%} 1107-1119. Hillebrandt, {%Vedische%} {%Mythologie,%} 1, 94 {%et seq.,%} argues in favour of an early connexion of Iranians and Indians in Arachosia, where he places part of the action of the Rigveda. Hopkins, {%Journal of the American Oriental%} {%Society,%} 17, 16, 277, holds that traces of Iranian connexion are signs of late date; Arnold, {%ibid.,%} 18, 205 {%et seq.,%} opposes this view. <F>1) viii. 6, 46-48.</F> <F>2) xvi. 11. 20.</F> <F>3) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 160, 161; 5, 142.</F> <F>4) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 136, 137.</F> <F>5) {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 356, n.; {%Indian%} {%Literature,%} 3, 4; {%Episches im vedischen%} {%Ritual,%} 37, 38.</F>

{@Tirīṭa@}¦<sup>1</sup> is found in the Atharvaveda<sup>2</sup> in the adjectival derivative {%tirīṭin%} used of a demon, and presumably meaning ‘adorned with a tiara.’ <F>1) Meaning, according to later native lexicographers, ‘head-dress’ or ‘dia- dem.’</F> <F>2) viii. 6, 7. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches%} {%Leben,%} 265; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 495.</F>

{@Tirya@}¦ occurs in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> as an epithet of {@Karambha,@} ‘gruel.’ It is probably equivalent to {%tilya,%} ‘made of sesamum,’ as rendered by Roth<sup>2</sup> and Whitney,<sup>3</sup> but {%tiriya%} is read by Roth<sup>4</sup> in the Rāja-nighaṇṭu as a kind of rice. <F>1) iv. 7, 3.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>3) Translation of the Atharvaveda, 155.</F> <F>4) See Whitney, {%loc. cit.,%} with Lan- man's additional note. Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 377, construes the adjective with {%viṣam,%} and renders ‘the poison which comes in a horizontal direction’ ({%cf. tiryañc%}). Grill, {%Hundert%} {%Lieder,%}^2 121, amends to {%atiriya,%} ‘over- flowing.’ <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 270; Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 201.</F>

{@Tiryañc Āṅgirasa@}¦ is mentioned as a seer of Sāmans, or Chants, in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> The name is doubtless feigned. <F>1) xii. 6, 12. {%Cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 2, 160.</F>

{@Tila@}¦ denotes in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> the sesamum plant, and particularly its grains, from which a rich oil ({@Taila@}) was extracted. It is often<sup>3</sup> mentioned in connexion with {@Māṣa,@} ‘kidney bean.’ The Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>4</sup> attributes the bean and the sesamum to the winter ({%hemanta%}) and the cool ({%śiśira%}) seasons. The stalk of the sesamum plant ({%tila-piñjī,%}<sup>5</sup> {%til-piñja%}<sup>6</sup>) was used for fuel, and the seed was boiled in the form of porridge ({%tilaudana%}<sup>7</sup>) for food. <F>1) ii. 8, 3; vi. 140, 2; xviii. 3, 69; 4, 32.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vii. 2, 10, 2; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iv. 3, 2; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xviii. 12; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, ix. 1, 1, 3, etc.</F> <F>3) Av. vi. 140, 2; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, {%loc. cit.;%} Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, vi. 3, 22; Chāndogva Upaniṣad, v. 10, 6, etc.</F> <F>4) {%Loc. cit.%}</F> <F>5) Av. ii. 8, 3.</F> <F>6) Av. xii. 2, 54.</F> <F>7) Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, vi. 4, 16; Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka, xii. 8. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 240.</F>

{@Tilvaka@}¦ is mentioned in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> as a tree ({%Symplocos racemosa%}), near which it is inauspicious to construct a grave. The adjectival derivative {%tailvaka,%} ‘made of the wood of the Tilvaka,’ is found in the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā,<sup>2</sup> and is employed to describe the {%yūpa,%} or sacrificial post, in the Ṣaḍviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) xiii. 8, 1, 16.</F> <F>2) iii. 1, 9.</F> <F>3) iii. 8.</F>

{@Tiṣya@}¦ occurs twice in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> apparently as the name of a star,<sup>2</sup> though Sāyaṇa takes it to mean the sun. It is doubtless identical with the Avestan Tistrya. Later it is the name of a lunar mansion: see {@Nakṣatra.@} <F>1) v. 54, 13; x. 64, 8 (with Kṛśānu as in archer).</F> <F>2) Weber, {%Naxatra,%} 2, 290; Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 355; Max Müller, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 32, 331; Keith, {%Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka,%} 77, n. 1.</F>

{@Tisṛ-dhanva,@}¦ ‘a bow with three (arrows),’ is mentioned as a gift to the priest at the sacrifice in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> and in the Brāhmaṇas.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) i. 8, 19, 1.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 8, 3, 4; ii. 7, 9, 2; Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, xi. 1, 5, 10; xiv. 1, 1, 7.</F>

{@Tugra@}¦ appears in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as the name of the father of {@Bhujyu,@} a protégé of the Aśvins, who is accordingly called Tugrya<sup>2</sup> or Taugrya.<sup>3</sup> A different Tugra seems to be referred to in other passages of the Rigveda<sup>4</sup> as an enemy of Indra. <F>1) i. 116, 3; 117, 14; vi. 62, 6.</F> <F>2) Rv. viii. 3, 23; 74, 14.</F> <F>3) Rv. i. 117, 15; 118, 6; 182, 5. 6; viii. 5, 22; x. 39, 4.</F> <F>4) vi. 20, 8; 26, 4; x. 49, 4. {%Cf.%} Oldenberg, {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen%} {%Morgenländischen Gesellschaft,%} 55, 328, 329; Ludwig, Translation of the Rig- veda, 3, 157.</F>

{@Tugrya@}¦ occurs in the Rigveda as a patronymic of {@Bhujyu,@}<sup>1</sup> but also in a passage<sup>2</sup> in which no reference to Bhujyu appears to be meant, and in which it may mean ‘a man of the house of Tugra.’ A similar sense seems to occur in the locative plural feminine in the Rigveda,<sup>3</sup> where (supplying {%vikṣu%}) the meaning must be ‘among the Tugrians.’ This explanation may also apply to the epithet of Indra<sup>4</sup> or Soma,<sup>5</sup> {%tugryā-vṛdh,%} ‘rejoicing among the Tugrians.’ <F>1) Who is also called {%Tugrasya sūnu,%} Rv. vi. 62, 6. {%Cf.%} the use of {%Pajriya%} and perhaps {%Kṛṣṇiya%} in the patronymic sense without Vṛddhi.</F> <F>2) viii. 32, 20.</F> <F>3) i. 33, 15. {%Cf.%} Griffith, {%Hymns of%} {%the Rigveda,%} 1, 47.</F> <F>4) viii. 45, 29; 99, 7.</F> <F>5) viii. 1, 15, where, however, Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.,%} sug- gests an alteration to make it refer to Indra. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 128.</F>

{@Tuc@}¦ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> occasionally occurs denoting ‘children.’ Tuj occurs rather more often in the same sense.<sup>2</sup> {%Cf.%} {@Tanaya@} and {@Toka.@} <F>1) viii. 18, 18; 27, 14; vi. 48, 9.</F> <F>2) iii. 45, 4; iv. 1, 3; v. 41, 9; viii. 4, 15.</F>

{@Tuji@}¦ is the name in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> of a protégé of Indra, who in another hymn<sup>2</sup> appears to be called Tūtuji. <F>1) vi. 26, 4; x. 49, 4.</F> <F>2) vi. 20, 8. {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 156; Oldenberg, {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen%} {%Gesellschaft,%} 55, 328.</F>
{@Tumiñja Aupoditi@}¦ is mentioned in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (i. 7, 2, 1) as a Hotṛ priest at a Sattra, or ‘sacrificial session,’ and as having been engaged in a discussion with {@Suśravas.@}

{@Tura Kāvaṣeya@}¦ is mentioned in the Vaṃśa (list of teachers) at the end of the tenth book of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> as the source of the doctrine set forth in that book, and as separated, in the succession of teachers, from {@Śāṇḍilya@} by {@Yajñavacas@} and {@Kuśri.@} In the same Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> he is quoted by Śāṇḍilya as having erected a fire-altar on the {@Kārotī.@} In the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> he appears as a Purohita, or ‘domestic priest,’ of {@Janamejaya Pārikṣita,@} whom he consecrated king. In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad<sup>4</sup> and a Khila<sup>5</sup> he appears as an ancient sage. Oldenberg,<sup>6</sup> no doubt rightly, assigns him to the end of the Vedic period. He is probably<sup>7</sup> identical with Tura, the {%deva-muni,%} ‘saint of the gods,’ who is mentioned in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>8</sup> <F>1) x. 6, 5, 9.</F> <F>2) ix. 5, 2, 15.</F> <F>3) iv. 27; vii. 34; viii. 21.</F> <F>4) vi. 5, 4 (Kāṇva, not in Mādhyaṃ- dina).</F> <F>5) i. 9, 6; Scheftelowitz, {%Die Apokryphen%} {%des Ṛgveda,%} 65, 190.</F> <F>6) {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgen-%} {%ländischen Gesellschaft,%} 42, 239.</F> <F>7) So the St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>8) xxv. 14, 5. See Hopkins, {%Transac-%} {%tions of the Connecticut Academy of Arts%} {%and Sciences,%} 15, 68. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 203, n.; {%Indian Literature,%} 120, 131; Eggeling, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 43, xviii.</F>

{@Tura-śravas@}¦ is the name of a seer mentioned in the Pañca- viṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> as having pleased Indra by two Sāmans (Chants) of his composition. Indra in return appears to have given him the oblation of the {@Pārāvatas@} on the {@Yamunā.@} <F>1) ix. 4, 10. {%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%Transactions%} {%of the Connecticut Academy of Arts and%} {%Sciences,%} 15, 53; Max Müller, {%Sacred%} {%Books of the East,%} 32, 316.</F>

{@Turya-vāh,@}¦ masc.; {@Turyauhī,@} fem., ‘a four-year-old ox or cow,’ is mentioned in the later Saṃhitās.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iv. 3, 3, 2; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 11, 11; 13, 17; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xiv. 10; xviii. 26, etc.</F>
{@Turva@}¦ occurs only once in the Rigveda (x. 62, 10), doubtless as a name of the {@Turvaśa@} people or king.

{@Turvaśa@}¦ occurs frequently in the Rigveda as the name of a man or of a people, usually in connexion with {@Yadu.@} The two words usually occur in the singular without any connecting particle, {%Turvaśa Yadu%} or {%Yadu Turvaśa.%}<sup>2</sup> In a plural form the name Turvaśa occurs once with the Yadus,<sup>3</sup> and once alone<sup>4</sup> in a hymn in which the singular has already been used. In one passage<sup>5</sup> the dual {%Turvaśā-Yadū%} actually occurs, and in another<sup>6</sup> {%Yadus Turvaś ca,%} ‘Yadu and Turva.’ In other passages<sup>7</sup> Turvaśa appears alone, while in one<sup>8</sup> Turvaśa and Yādva occur. <div n="P"/>From these facts Hopkins<sup>9</sup> deduces the erroneousness of the ordinary view,<sup>10</sup> according to which Turvaśa is the name of a tribe, the singular denoting the king, and regards Turvaśa as the name of the Yadu king. But the evidence for this is not conclusive. Without laying any stress on the argument based on the theory<sup>11</sup> that the ‘five peoples’ of the Rigveda are the {@Anus, Druhyus,@} Turvaśas, Yadus, and {@Pūrus,@} it is perfectly reasonable to hold that the Turvaśas and Yadus were two distinct though closely allied tribes. Such they evidently were to the seers of the hymns which mention in the dual the {%Turvaśā-Yadū%} and speak of {%Yadus Turvaś ca.%} This explanation also suits best the use of the plural of Turvaśa in two Rigvedic hymns. <div n="P"/>In the Rigveda the chief exploit of Turvaśa was his partici- pation in the war against {@Sudās,@} by whom he was defeated.<sup>12</sup> Hopkins<sup>13</sup> suggests that he may have been named Turvaśa because of his fleet ({%tura%}) escape from the battle. His escape <div n="P"/>1 i. 36, 18; 54, 6; 174, 9; vi. 20, 12; 45, 1; viii. 4, 7; 7, 18; 9, 14; 45, 27; x. 49, 8. In vii. 18, 6, Turvaśa is joined with Yakṣu, apparently a con- temptuous variant of Yadu (Hopkins, {%Journal of the American Oriental Society,%} 15, 261). {%Cf.%} {@Tṛtsu.@} [Page1-316+ 54] may have been assisted by Indra, for in some passages<sup>14</sup> Indra's aid to Turvaśa (and) Yadu is referred to; it is also significant that the Anu, and apparently the Druhyu, kings are mentioned as having been drowned in the defeat, but not the Turvaśa and Yadu kings, and that Turvaśa appears in the eighth book of the Rigveda as a worshipper of Indra with the Anu prince, the successor, presumably, of the one who was drowned.<sup>15</sup> Griffith,<sup>16</sup> however, proposes to refer these passages to a defeat by Turvaśa and Yadu of Arṇa and Citraratha on the {@Sarayu;@}<sup>17</sup> but the evidence for this is quite inadequate. <div n="P"/>Two passages of the Rigveda<sup>18</sup> seem to refer to an attack by Turvaśa and Yadu on {@Divodāsa,@} the father of Sudās. It is reasonable to suppose that this was an attack of the two peoples on Divodāsa, for there is some improbability of the references being to the Turvaśa, who was concerned in the attack on Sudās, the son. <div n="P"/>Zimmer<sup>19</sup> considers that the Turvaśas were also called {@Vṛcī-@} {@vants.@} This view is based on a hymn<sup>20</sup> in which reference is made to the defeat of the Vṛcīvants on the {@Yavyāvatī@} and {@Hariyūpīyā@} in aid of Daivarāta, and of Turvaśa in aid of {@Sṛñjaya,@} the latter being elsewhere<sup>21</sup> clearly the son of Deva- rāta. But as this evidence for the identification of the Turvaśas with the Vṛcīvants is not clear, it seems sufficient<sup>22</sup> to assume that they were allies. <div n="P"/>Later, in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>23</sup> the Turvaśas appear as allies of the Pañcālas, Taurvaśa horses, thirty-three in number, and armed men, to the number of 6,000, being mentioned.<sup>24</sup> But otherwise the name disappears: this lends [Page1-317+ 47] probability to Oldenberge's conjecture<sup>25</sup> that the Turvaśas became merged in the {@Pañcāla@} people. Hopkins<sup>26</sup> considers that in the Śatapatha passage the horses were merely named from the family of Turvaśa; but this view is less likely, since it ignores the difficulty involved in the reference to the men. <div n="P"/>It is impossible to be certain regarding the home of the Turvaśas at the time of their conflict with Sudās. They apparently crossed the {@Paruṣṇī,@}<sup>27</sup> but from which side is dis- puted. The view of Pischel<sup>28</sup> and Geldner,<sup>29</sup> that they advanced from the west towards the east, where the {@Bharatas@} were (see {@Kuru@}), is the more probable. <F>2) v. 31, 8.</F> <F>3) i. 108, 8.</F> <F>4) viii. 4, 18; singular with Ānava in viii. 4, 1.</F> <F>5) iv. 30, 17.</F> <F>6) x. 62, 10. {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 166; Oldenberg, {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen%} {%Gesellschaft,%} 42, 220, n. 1.</F> <F>7) i. 4, 77; vi. 27, 7. {%Cf.%} viii. 4, 1.</F> <F>8) vii. 19, 8.</F> <F>9) {%Op. cit.,%} 258 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>10) Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 122, 124; Oldenberg, {%Buddha,%} 404; Ludwig, {%op. cit.,%} 153; Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} p. 64; {%Sanskrit Literature,%} 153 {%et seq.,%} etc.</F> <F>11) Zimmer, 122, 124; Macdonell, 153, 154.</F> <F>12) vii. 18, 6.</F> <F>13) {%Op. cit.,%} 264.</F> <F>14) Rv. i. 174, 9; iv. 30, 17; v. 31, 8; viii. 4, 7.</F> <F>15) Hopkins, 265.</F> <F>16) {%Hymns of the Rigveda,%} 1, 433, n.</F> <F>17) The hymn is a late one, and the connexion of verse 18, where Arṇa and Citraratha are mentioned, is obscure. {%Cf.%} Hopkins. 259.</F> <F>18) vi. 45, 1; ix. 61, 2 (where Divo- dāsa is mentioned); vii. 19, 8 (where he appears as Atithigva).</F> <F>19) {%Op. cit.,%} 124.</F> <F>20) vi. 27, 5-7.</F> <F>21) iv. 15, 4.</F> <F>22) Oldenberg, {%Buddha,%} 404, n. {%Cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 105.</F> <F>23) xiii. 5, 4, 16.</F> <F>24) The sense is obscure. The St. Petersburg Dictionary takes it appar- ently as 6,033 horses (of armed warriors); Eggeling, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 44, 400, prefers to understand it as 33 horses and 6,000 men; Oldenberg, {%loc. cit.,%} takes it as 6,033 warriors. Harisvāmin's Commentary, cited by Eggeling, is obscure.</F> <F>25) {%Buddha,%} 404.</F> <F>26) {%Op. cit.,%} 258, n. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische%} {%Studien,%} 1, 220.</F> <F>27) Rv. vii. 18.</F> <F>28) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 218, {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 126.</F> <F>29) {%Vedische Studien,%} 3, 152. If in Rv. viii. 20, 24, 1 {%rvaśa%} is read with Ludwig for {%tūrvath%} hey are connected with the {@Sindhu.@} <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Oldenberg, {%Religion des Veda,%} 167; Muir, {%Sanskrit Text,%} 5, 286; Bergaigne, {%Religion Védique,%} 2, 354 {%et seq.%}</F>

{@Turvīti@}¦ is mentioned several times in the Rigveda, both in association with Vayya<sup>1</sup> and alone.<sup>2</sup> In three passages<sup>3</sup> reference is made to Indra aiding him over a flood. Ludwig<sup>4</sup> has conjectured that he was king of the Turvaśas and Yadus. But there is no sufficient evidence for this view, though presumably he was of the Turvaśa tribe. <F>1) i. 54, 6; ii. 13, 12; iv. 19, 6.</F> <F>2) Rv. i. 36, 18; 61, 11; 112, 23.</F> <F>3) i. 61, 11; ii. 13, 12; iv. 19, 6.</F> <F>4) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 147; 4, 254. {%Cf.%} {@Turvaśa,@} and Bergaigne, {%Religion Védique,%} 2, 358; Oldenberg, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 42, 36.</F>

{@Tulā,@}¦ ‘scales,’ is mentioned in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā.<sup>1</sup> The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> also speaks of the balance in con- nexion with the weighing of a man's good and evil deeds in the next and in this world. This differs very considerably from the later balance<sup>3</sup> ordeal, in which a man was weighed twice, and was pronounced guilty or innocent according as, on the second occasion, he was more or less heavy than on the [Page1-318+ 45] first. It is not possible to read the later practice into the earlier.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) xxx. 17.</F> <F>2) xi. 2, 7, 33.</F> <F>3) Jolly, {%Recht und Sitte,%} 145.</F> <F>4) Weber, {%Indische Streifen,%} 1, 21; 2, 363, quotes Schlagintweit as giving this passage as an example of the balance ordeal. {%Cf.%} Eggeling, {%Sacred%} {%Books of the East,%} 44, 45, n. 4.</F>

{@Tuṣa,@}¦ in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and later,<sup>2</sup> regularly denotes the ‘husk’ of grain, often used for a fire.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) ix. 6, 16; xi. 1, 12, 29; 3, 5; xii. 3, 19.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 6, 5, 5; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 7, 9, etc.</F> <F>3) {%Tuṣa-pakva,%} Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 2, 4, 2; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 2, 4; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, vii. 2, 1, 7.</F>

{@Tūṇava@}¦ denotes in the later Saṃhitās<sup>1</sup> and the Brāhmaṇas<sup>2</sup> a musical instrument of wood, probably the ‘flute.’ A ‘flute- blower’ is enumerated among the victims of the Puruṣamedha, or ‘human sacrifice.’<sup>3</sup> <F>1) Taittirīya Samhitā, vi. 1, 4, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 6, 8; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxiii. 4; xxxiv. 5 ({%Indische%} {%Studien,%} 3, 477).</F> <F>2) Pañcavimśa Brāhmaṇa, vi. 5, 13; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 13, 1; 15, 1; Nirukta, xiii. 9.</F> <F>3) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxx. 19, 20; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, {%loc. cit.%} <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 289.</F>
{@Tūtuji.@}¦ See {@Tuji.@}

{@Tūpara,@}¦ ‘hornless,’ is a frequent description of animals intended for the sacrifice, especially of the goat, in the Atharvaveda and later.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Av. xi. 9, 22; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 1, 1, 4, etc.; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 1, 15; xxix. 59, etc.; Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, v. 1, 3, 7, etc.</F>

{@Tūrghna@}¦ is mentioned in the Taittirīya Āraṇyak (v. 1) as the northern part of Kurukṣetra.<sup>1</sup> Its exact position, however, cannot be ascertained. <F>1) {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 78.</F>
{@Tūrṇāśa,@}¦ in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> seems to denote a ‘mountain torrent.’ <F>1) viii. 32, 4. {%Cf.%} Nirukta, v. 16.</F>

{@Tūrvayāṇa@}¦ is the name of a prince mentioned in the Rigveda. He appears by name in two passages,<sup>1</sup> and is clearly alluded to in a third,<sup>2</sup> as an enemy of {@Atithigva, Āyu,@} and {@Kutsa.@} With this accords the fact that the {@Pakthas@} were opposed in the battle of the ten kings to the Tṛtsus,<sup>3</sup> and that Tūrvayāṇa  is shown by another passage of the Rigveda<sup>4</sup> to have been a prince of the Pakthas. He is there represented as having been a protégé of Indra, who aided him against {@Cyavāna@} and his guardians, the Maruts. It is not probable that he is identical with {@Suśravas.@}<sup>5</sup> <F>1) i. 53, 10; vi. 18, 13.</F> <F>2) ii. 14, 7 (as a comparison of the two preceding passages shows); per- haps also viii. 53, 2. In i. 174, 3, Tūrvayāṇa seems also to be a proper name, though Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.,%} here regards the word as an adjective.</F> <F>3) vii. 18.</F> <F>4) x. 61, 1 {%et seq.;%} Pischel, {%Vedische%} {%Studien,%} 1, 71-77.</F> <F>5) Mentioned in i. 53, 9. 10. {%Cf.%} Griffith, {%Hymns of the Rigveda,%} 1, 75, n.</F>

{@Tūṣa@}¦ is found in the later Saṃhitās and the Brāhmaṇas<sup>1</sup> denoting the ‘fringe’ or ‘trimming’ of a garment. <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, i. 8, 1, 1; ii. 4, 9, 1; vi. 1, 1, 3; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxiii. 1; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 6, 1, 8; Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xvii. 1, etc. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 262.</F>

{@Tṛkṣi@}¦ is, in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> the name of a prince who was a Trāsadasyava, ‘descendant of {@Trasadasyu.@}’ He also appears with the Druhyu and the Pūru peoples in another hymn.<sup>2</sup> It has been conjectured, but it is not probable, that the steed {@Tārkṣya@} (as ‘belonging to Tṛkṣi’) was his.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) viii. 22, 7.</F> <F>2) vi. 46, 8. It is not certain that the two persons are identical ({%cf.%} Hille- brandt, {%Vedische Mythologic,%} 1, 113, notes 3, 4), but it is probable.</F> <F>3) Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} p. 149.</F>

{@Tṛṇa,@}¦ ‘grass,’ is often mentioned in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> It was used as straw to roof in a house or hut.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) i. 161, 1; 162, 8, 11; x. 102, 10, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. ii. 30, 1; vi. 54, 1, etc.; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 22; viii. 24, etc.</F> <F>3) Av. iii. 12, 5; ix. 3, 4, 7.</F>
{@Tṛṇa-jalāyuka,@}¦ ‘caterpillar,’ is mentioned in the Bṛhad- āraṇyaka Upaniṣad (iv. 2, 4).

{@Tṛṇa-skanda@}¦ occurs once in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as the name of a prince, his subjects ({%viśaḥ%}) being referred to.<sup>2</sup> The word may originally have meant ‘grasshopper.’<sup>3</sup> <F>1) i. 172, 3.</F> <F>2) Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 159, takes {%viśaḥ%} as ‘cantons,’ but see Viś.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>
{@Tṛtīyaka,@}¦ ‘the tertian (fever),’ is mentioned in the Athar- vaveda (i. 25, 4; v. 22, 13; xix. 39, 10). See {@Takman.@}

{@Tṛtsu@}¦ occurs in the Rigveda, once in the singular<sup>1</sup> and several times in the plural,<sup>2</sup> as a proper name. The Tṛtsus were clearly helpers of {@Sudās@} in the great battle against the ten kings, {@Śimyu,@} the {@Turvaśa,@} the {@Druhyu, Kavaṣa,@} the {@Pūru,@} the {@Anu, Bheda, Śambara,@} the two {@Vaikarṇas,@} and perhaps the {@Yadu,@} who led with them as allies<sup>3</sup> the {@Matsyas, Pakthas,@} {@Bhalānas, Alinas, Viṣāṇins, Śivas, Ajas, Śigrus,@} and perhaps Yakṣus.<sup>4</sup> The defeat of the ten kings is celebrated in one [Page1-321+ 56] hymn of the Rigveda,<sup>5</sup> and is evidently alluded to in two others.<sup>6</sup> The great battle took place on the {@Paruṣṇī,@} but there was also a fight on the {@Yamunā@} with Bheda, the Ajas, Śigrus, and Yakṣus. As the Yamunā and the Parusṇī represent opposite ends of the territory of the Tṛtsus (for we cannot with Hopkins<sup>7</sup> safely identify the streams), it is difficult to see exactly how the ten kings could be confederated, but it should be noted that the references to the ten kings occur in the two later hymns,<sup>6</sup> and not in the hymn<sup>5</sup> describing the battle itself; besides, absolute numerical accuracy cannot be insisted upon. <div n="P"/>It is difficult exactly to determine the character of the Tṛtsus; especially in their relation to the Bharatas, who under Viśvāmitra's guidance are represented as prospering and as advancing to the {@Vipāś@} and {@Śutudrī.@}<sup>8</sup> Roth ingeniously brought this into connexion with the defeat of his enemies by Sudās, which is celebrated in the seventh book of the Rigveda — a book attributed to the Vasiṣṭha family — and thought that there was a reference in one verse<sup>9</sup> to the defeat of the Bharatas by Sudās. But it seems certain that the verse is mistranslated, and that the Bharatas are really represented as victors with Sudās.<sup>10</sup> Ludwig<sup>11</sup> accordingly identifies the Tṛtsus and the Bharatas. Oldenberg,<sup>12</sup> after accepting this view at first,<sup>13</sup> later expressed the opinion that the Tṛtsus were the priests of the Bharata people, and therefore identical with the Vasiṣṭhas. This view is supported by the fact that in one passage<sup>14</sup> the Tṛtsus are clearly described as wearing their hair in the peculiar manner affected by the Vasiṣṭhas,<sup>15</sup> and would in that passage thus seem to represent the Vasiṣṭhas. [Page1-322+ 59] But Geldner<sup>16</sup> has suggested with great probability that Tṛtsu, who is once mentioned in the singular,<sup>17</sup> means the Tṛtsu king — that is, Sudās.<sup>18</sup> This explanation alone justifies the description<sup>19</sup> of the Bharatas as {%Tṛtsūnāṃ viśaḥ,%}<sup>20</sup> ‘subjects of the Tṛtsus,’ meaning the Tṛtsu Gotra or family, for the people could not be said to be subjects of a body of priests. The Vasiṣṭhas might be called Tṛtsus because of their close con- nexion with the royal house of that people. The reverse process is also quite possible, but is rendered improbable by the fact that the {@Pratṛdaḥ@} are referred to as receiving Vasiṣṭha.<sup>21</sup> This name of the Tṛtsu dynasty is probably older than its connexion with Vasiṣṭha in the time of Sudās, a conclusion supported by the name of {@Pratardana,@} who is mentioned later as a descendant of Divodāsa,<sup>22</sup> an ancestor of Sudās. The Tṛtsu dynasty could therefore hardly have been referred to as Vasiṣṭhas. For the further history of the dynasty and its relation with Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra, see {@Sudās.@} <div n="P"/>If the Tṛtsus and their subjects, the Bharatas, were in the Rigvedic period at war with the tribes on either side of the territory between the Paruṣṇī and the Yamunā, it is clear<sup>23</sup> that later on they coalesced with the Pūrus and probably others of those tribes to form the {@Kuru@} people. Already in the Rigveda<sup>24</sup> the Tṛtsus are allied with the {@Sṛñjayas,@} and in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>25</sup> one Purohita serves both Kurus and Sṛñjayas. [Page1-323+ 50] <div n="P"/>Hillebrandt<sup>26</sup> considers that the Tṛtsus cannot be identified with the Bharatas, but that Sudās and the Bharatas represent an invading body, which, however, became allied with the Tṛtsus and the Vasiṣṭha priests. He also thinks that the Rigveda reveals a time when {@Divodāsa,@} the grandfather or ancestor of Sudās, was living in Arachosia, on the {@Sarasvatī,@} and warring against the {@Paṇis,@} whom he identifies with the Parnians. But this conjecture<sup>27</sup> cannot be regarded as probable. In the Sarasvatī<sup>28</sup> it is not necessary to see any other river than the later Sarasvatī, in the middle country, which flowed within the boundaries of the Tṛtsus: it is also significant that there are references<sup>29</sup> to contests between {@Turvaśa Yadu@} and Atithigva or Divodāsa. Thus there is no reason to doubt that Divodāsa and the Bharatas were in the middle country, and not in Iran. <F>1) vii. 18, 13.</F> <F>2) vii. 18, 7. 15. 19; 33, 5. 6; 83, 4. 6. 8.</F> <F>3) They were regarded as enemies of the kings by Roth, {%Zur Litteratur und%} {%Geschichte des Weda,%} 95, and by Zimmer, {%op. cit.,%} 126, The latter, however, altered his view (see pp. 430, 431, which Hopkins, {%op. cit.,%} 260, has over- looked), and there is no doubt that the later opinion is correct. {%Cf.%} also Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 173; Hopkins, 260, 261. Of these tribes the Pakthas, Alinas, Bhalānas, Viṣāṇins, and Śivas, were probably settled in the north-west, to the west of the Indus, and around the Kabul River. The Anus, Pūrus, Turvaśas, Yadus, and Druhyus, were probably tribes of the Panjab; the Ajas, Śigrus, and Yakṣus, tribes of the east, under Bheda; Śambara may also have been a native of the east; Śimyu and Kavaṣa are doubtful; and the Vaikarṇau prob- ably belonged to the north-west.</F> <F>4) This is uncertain; the text of the Rigveda, vii. 18, 6, has Yakṣu, and the same word recurs in verse 19. On the other hand, the word Yadu would naturally be expected in verse 6, as Tur- vaśa is mentioned. Zimmer, {%Altindisches%} {%Leben,%} 122, says that Yadu occurs in vii. 18, but on p. 126 he cites Yakṣu in both places, evidently by oversight. Hopkins, {%Journal of the American Oriental%} {%Society,%} 15, 261, n., considers that Tur- vaśa, the Yakṣu, is a sarcastic expres- sion, instead of Turvaśa, the Yadu, making Turvaśa, whom he regards as king of the Yadus, ridiculous as a member of an insignificant people, and alluding to him also as a sacrificial victim (as it were, {%yaṣṭavya,%} ‘to be offered’; {%of puroḍāś,%} ‘cake of sacrifice,’ in verse 6, as a pun on {%purogās,%} ‘leader’). Whether Yakṣu is used contemptuously for Yadu or not, it seems hard not to believe that the Yadus are referred to.</F> <F>5) vii. 18.</F> <F>6) vii. 33 and 83.</F> <F>7) {%India, Old and New,%} 52.
