({%śvityañco dakṣiṇatas-%} {%kaparainaḥ%}).</F> <F>16) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 136; {%Ṛgveda-%} {%Glossar,%} 74.</F> <F>17) Rv. vii. 18, 13.</F> <F>18) {%Cf.%} Rv. vii. 18, 24. The parallelism of verses 13 and 24 is quite beyond question. Moreover, the praise of Sudās and of the Bharatas is found coupled in Rv. iii. 53, 9. 12. 24, and in Rv. vi. 16, 4, 5, Divodāsa is coupled with the Bharatas in such a way as to suggest irresistibly that Divodāsa was a Bharata.</F> <F>19) Rv. vii. 33, 6.</F> <F>20) That this is the sense of {%viśaḥ%} is almost certain. See Geldner, {%Vedische%} {%Studien, loc. cit.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches%} {%Leben,%} 159, and Hillebrandt, {%Vedische%} {%Mythologie,%} 1, 111, render it ‘cantons,’ but see Vīś.</F> <F>21) Rv. vii. 33, 14. Geldner ({%op. cit.,%} 138, 139) ingeniously suggests that Vasiṣṭha, being miraculously born, needed a Gotra, and so became a Tṛtsu.</F> <F>22) Pratardana is mentioned in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, xxvi. 5, as Daivo- dāsi, ‘descendant of Divodāsa.’</F> <F>23) {%Cf.%} Oldenberg, {%Buddha,%} 406 {%et seq.,%} and see {@Kuru.@}</F> <F>24) See Rv. vi. 47, where Divodāsa and Sārñjaya are both praised. In vi. 27, 5, the Turvaśas are opposed to the Sṛñjayas, and in vii. 18, 6; 19, 8, the Tṛtsus are opposed to the Turvaśas.</F> <F>25) ii. 4, 4, 5.</F> <F>26) {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 98 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>27) {%Cf.%} also Grierson, {%Journal of the%} {%Royal Asiatic Society,%} 1908, 837 {%et%} {%seq.%}</F> <F>28) Rv. vi. 61, 3. Brunnhofer, {%Iran%} {%und Turan,%} 127, identifies this river with the Oxus, but Hillebrandt identifies it with the Haraqaiti.</F> <F>29) Rv. ix. 61, 2. {%Cf.%} vi. 45, 1; Zimmer, {%op. cit.,%} 124. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Max Müller, {%Sacred Books of the%} {%East,%} 32, 424.</F>

{@Tṛṣṭa@}¦ is mentioned in the Maitrāyaṇī<sup>1</sup> and Kāṭhaka Saṃhitās<sup>2</sup> as being along with {@Varutri@} the priest of the Asuras. <F>1) iv. 8, 1. The reading is uncer- tain; it may be {%Tṛṣṭhā-varutrī.%} See von Schroeder's edition, p. 106, n.</F> <F>2) xxx. 1, where again the reading is uncertain. The Kapiṣṭhala Saṃhitā, xlvi. 4, has {%Tvaṣṭā-varutrī%} (von Schroeder's edition of the Kāṭhaka, 2, 181, n.). <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Muir, {%Sanskrit Texts,%} 12, 190, 191; Lévi, {%La Doctrine du Sacrifice,%} 119.</F>

{@Tṛṣṭāmā@}¦ is mentioned as a stream in the Nadī-stuti, or ‘praise of rivers,’ in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> There seems to be no means of identifying it. <F>1) x. 75, 6. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 14.</F>

{@Tejana@}¦ denotes in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> a rod or staff of reed used for measuring a field. In the Atharvaveda the sense of ‘bamboo’ is found twice,<sup>2</sup> the bamboo being specified in the [Page1-324+ 53] second passage as ‘of the spring’ ({%vāsantika%}); more particularly it denotes the shaft of an arrow,<sup>3</sup> a sense often found in later Vedic texts.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) i. 110, 5.</F> <F>2) i. 2, 4; xx. 136, 3 (= Khila, v. 22, 3). {%Cf. taijana%} as an adjective in Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxi. 10.</F> <F>3) Av. vi. 49, 1 (Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 317); {%iṣu eka-tejanā,%} ‘an arrow with one shaft,’ vi. 57, 1.</F> <F>4) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, i. 25; iii. 26; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxv. 1 (with {%śṛṅga%} and {%śalya%} as the three parts of an arrow; in Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 8, 1, {%kulmala%} takes the place of {%tejana; cf.%} {%ibid.,%} 2). The Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vi. 3, 3, 1, has {%anīka, śalya,%} and {%tejana.%} {%Cf.%} {@Iṣu.@}</F>

{@Tejanī@}¦ denotes in the later Saṃhitās and Brāhmaṇas a bundle of reeds,<sup>1</sup> and in some cases such a bundle twisted into a rope,<sup>2</sup> for the two ends of the Tejanī are mentioned. <F>1) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 8, 3, 12; perhaps Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxiii. 9.</F> <F>2) Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxii. 13; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, i. 11, as rendered by Sāyaṇa.</F>

{@Tejas@}¦ is regarded by Schrader<sup>1</sup> as having in the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> the specific sense of ‘axe.’ But in all the passages the sense of the ‘bolt’ of the god is adequate. <F>1) {%Prehistoric Antiquities,%} 221.</F> <F>2) {%Cf.%} vi. 3, 5; 8, 5; 15, 19.</F>

{@Taittirīya@}¦ is the name of one of the divisions of the Black Yajurveda, which is, however, not found thus described until the Sūtra period.<sup>1</sup> The school is represented by a Saṃhitā,<sup>2</sup> a Brāhmaṇa,<sup>3</sup> and an Āraṇyaka,<sup>4</sup> besides an Upaniṣad,<sup>5</sup> which forms a part of the Āraṇyaka. <F>1) Anupada Sūtra, ii. 6; vii. 7. 10, etc. See Weber {%Indian Literature,%} 87 {%et seq.;%} Macdonell, {%Sanskrit Literature,%} 175 {%et seq.;%} von Schroeder, Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, 1, x {%et seq.%}</F> <F>2) Edited by Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} xi, xii, and in the {%Bibliotheca Indica,%} 1854-1899.</F> <F>3) Edited in the {%Bibliotheca Indica,%} 1855-1870, and in the Ānandāśrama Series, 1898.</F> <F>4) Edited in the {%Bibliotheca Indica,%} 1864- 1872, and in the Ānandāśrama Series, 1898.</F> <F>5) Edited by Roer, 1850, and in the Ānandāśrama Series, 1889.</F>

{@Taimāta@}¦ is twice mentioned as a species of snake in the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) v. 13, 6; 18, 4. {%Cf.%} Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 243; Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 425; Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 95.</F>

{@Taila,@}¦ ‘sesamum oil,’ is mentioned in the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> where<sup>2</sup> reference is made to keeping such oil in jars. In the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka,<sup>3</sup> reference is made to anointing with sesamum oil. <F>1) i. 7, 2 (all the manuscripts have {%taula,%} which must be wrong; the Paip- palāda MS has {%tūla:%} see Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 7).</F> <F>2) xx. 136, 16.</F> <F>3) xi. 4. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben.%} 240, 241.</F>

{@Toka@}¦ denotes ‘children’ or ‘descendants’ generally in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> The word is often joined with {@Tanaya.@}<sup>3</sup> <F>1) i. 43, 2; ii. 2, 11; 9, 2; vii. 62, 6; viii. 5, 20; 67, 11, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. i. 13, 2; 28, 3; v. 19, 2; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxxvi. 7 ({%Indische%} {%Studien,%} 3, 466); Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, vii. 5, 2, 39, etc.</F> <F>3) Rv. i. 31, 12; 64, 14; 114, 6; 147, 1; ii. 33, 14; v. 53, 13; vi. 1, 12, etc.; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 7.</F>

{@Tokman,@}¦ neut., denotes in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> the green shoots of any kind of grain. In the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> reference is made to the shoots of rice ({%vrīhi%}), large rice ({%mahā-%} {%vrīhi%}), panic seed ({%priyaṅgu%}), and barley ({%yava%}). <F>1) x. 62, 8.</F> <F>2) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xix. 13, 81; xxi. 30. 42; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xii. 11; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 11, 9; Tait- tirīya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 6, 4; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, viii. 5, etc.</F> <F>3) viii. 16. {%Cf.%} for its use at the Sautrāmaṇī, Hillebrandt, {%Rituallitte-%} {%ratur,%} 160.</F>
{@Tottra,@}¦ a ‘goad’ for driving cattle, is mentioned in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (xii. 4, 1, 10).

{@Toda@}¦ appears once to denote a ‘goad’ in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> but more often<sup>2</sup> it is an agent noun meaning ‘impeller.’ Geldner<sup>3</sup> considers that in one passage<sup>4</sup> the sense is ‘wielder of the rod of punishment’ (later {%daṇḍa-dhara%}) — that is, ‘prince.’ <F>1) iv. 16, 11; Mantra in Kauśika Sūtra, 107.</F> <F>2) Rv. vi. 6, 6; 12, 1, 3, are probably so to be understood.</F> <F>3) {%Vedische Studien,%} 3, 74.</F> <F>4) Rv. i. 150, 1.</F>
{@Taugrya,@}¦ ‘descendant of {@Tugra,@}’ is the patronymic of {@Bhujyu@} in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) i. 117, 16; 118, 6; 182, 5. 6; viii. 5, 22; x. 39, 4.</F>

{@Taudī@}¦ in one passage of the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> appears to denote a plant. <F>1) x. 4, 24. {%Cf.%} St. Petersburg Dic- tionary, {%s.v.%} Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 578, leaves the word untranslated. Bloomfield, {%Hymns of%} {%the Atharvaveda,%} 608, suggests that it is a fanciful name, ‘the piercer,’ since it is associated with {%ghṛtācī,%} ‘dripping with ghee,’ which is clearly such a word.</F>
{@Taurvaśa.@}¦ See {@Turvaśa.@}
{@Taula,@}¦ the reading of the text of the Atharvaveda (i. 7, 2), and a form which is otherwise unknown and cannot be satis- factorily explained, must doubtless be meant for {@Taila.@}

{@Tauvilikā,@}¦ occurring once in a hymn of the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> is a word of quite uncertain sense. Roth<sup>2</sup> thinks it means some kind of beast; Zimmer<sup>3</sup> and Whitney<sup>4</sup> regard it as a sort of plant; Sāyaṇa explains it as a disease-causing demon, while Bloomfield<sup>5</sup> leaves the sense doubtful. <F>1) vi. 16, 3.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>3) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 72.</F> <F>4) Translation of the Atharvaveda, 292.</F> <F>5) {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 30, 466.</F>

{@Trapu@}¦ denotes ‘tin’ in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> Its quality of being easily smelted, which Roth<sup>3</sup> thinks is indicated by the name (as derived from the root {%trap,%} ‘be ashamed’), is clearly alluded to in the Atharvaveda passage. <F>1) xi. 3, 8.</F> <F>2) Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xviii. 10; Maitrā- yaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 11, 5; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xviii. 13 (all in enumerations of metals); Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 12, 6, 5; Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa, iii. 17, 3; Chāndogya Upaniṣad, iv. 17, 7. In Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iv. 7, 5, 1, the form is {%trapus.%}</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 53.</F>

{@Trasa-dasyu,@}¦ son of {@Purukutsa,@}<sup>1</sup> is mentioned in the Rigveda as king of the Pūrus.<sup>2</sup> He was born to Purukutsa by his wife, {@Purukutsānī,@} at a time of great distress;<sup>3</sup> this, according to Sāyaṇa, refers to Purukutsa's captivity: possibly his death is really meant. Trasadasyu was also a descendant of Girikṣit,<sup>4</sup> and Purukutsa was a descendant of Durgaha. The genealogy, therefore, appears to be: Durgaha, Girikṣit, Purukutsa, Trasa- dasyu. Trasadasyu was the ancestor of {@Tṛkṣi,@}<sup>5</sup> and, according to Ludwig,<sup>6</sup> had a son Hiraṇin. Trasadasyu's chronological position is determined by the fact that his father, Purukutsa, was a contemporary of Sudās, either as an opponent<sup>7</sup> or as a friend.<sup>8</sup> That Purukutsa was an enemy of Sudās is more probable, because the latter's predecessor, Divodāsa, was apparently<sup>9</sup> at enmity with the Pūrus, and in the battle of the ten kings Pūrus were ranged against Sudās and the Tṛtsus. Trasadasyu himself seems to have been an energetic king. His people, the Pūrus, were settled on the {@Sarasvatī,@}<sup>10</sup> which was, no doubt, the stream in the middle country, that locality according well with the later union of the Pūrus with the {@Kuru@} people, who inhabited that country. This union is exemplified in the person of {@Kuruśravaṇa,@} who is called Trāsadasyava, ‘descendant of Trasadasyu,’ in the Rigveda,<sup>11</sup> whose father was {@Mitrātithi,@} and whose son was {@Upamaśravas.@} The relation of Mitrātithi to Tṛkṣi does not appear. <div n="P"/>Another descendant of Trasadasyu was {@Tryaruṇa Traivṛṣṇa,@} who is simply called Trasadasyu in a hymn of the Rigveda.<sup>12</sup> [Page1-328+ 50] He was not only a ‘descendant of Trivṛṣan,’ but, according to the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa,<sup>13</sup> he was also Traidhātva, ‘descendant of Tridhātu.’ The order of these two predecessors of Tryaruṇa cannot be determined in any way from Vedic literature. According to the later tradition,<sup>14</sup> a prince named Tridhanvan preceded Tryaruṇa in the succession. Vedic tradi- tion further fails to show in what precise relation Trasadasyu stood to Trivṛṣan or Tryaruṇa. <div n="P"/>Trasdasyu Paurukutsa appears in several Brāhmaṇas<sup>15</sup> as a famous sacrificer of ancient times, together with {@Para Āṭṇāra,@} {@Vītahavya Śrāyasa,@} and {@Kakṣīvant Auśija,@} who in the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa<sup>16</sup> are called ‘ancient great kings’ ({%pūrve mahārājāḥ%}). <F>1) Rv. v. 33, 8; vii. 19, 3; viii. 19, 36; iv. 42, 8 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>2) Rv. iv. 38, 1 {%et seq.;%} vii. 19, 3. He is merely alluded to in i. 63, 7; 112, 4; viii. 8, 21; 36, 7; 37, 7; 49, 10.</F> <F>3) Rv. iv. 42, 8 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>4) Rv. v. 33, 8.</F> <F>5) Rv. viii. 22, 7. He was a Pūru king. See vi. 46, 8.</F> <F>6) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 155, with reference to Rv. v. 33, 7 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>7) So Ludwig, 3, 174, who alters {%Sudāsam%} to {%Sudāse,%} in support of this view, in Rv. i. 63, 7. {%Cf.%} Oldenberg, {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen%} {%Gesellschaft,%} 42, 204, 205, 219, {%Ṛgveda-%} {%Noten,%} 1, 63; Geldner, {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 153; Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 112, n. 1. Foy, Kuhn's {%Zeitschrift,%} 34, 242, denies that the word in this passage is a proper name at all.</F> <F>8) {%Cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%loc. cit.%}</F> <F>9) Rv. i. 130, 7; Ludwig, 3, 114; but see Hillebrandt, 1, 113, 114.</F> <F>10) Rv. vii. 95, 96; Ludwig, 3, 175; Hillebrandt, 1, 115.</F> <F>11) x. 33, 4. {%Cf.%} Lanman, {%Sanskrit%} {%Reader,%} 386 {%et seq.;%} Geldner, {%Vedische%} {%Studien,%} 2, 150, 184.</F> <F>12) v. 27.</F> <F>13) xiii. 3, 12. The Tāṇḍaka, cited by Sāyaṇa (Sieg, {%Die Sagenstoffe des%} {%Ṛgveda,%} 67), has Trasadasyu, like the Rv.</F> <F>14) Harivaṃśa, 714 {%et seq.,%} where the name (716) is also misread as Tridhar- man. Traidhātva cannot reasonably be taken as representing a patronymic from Tridhanvan, as Sieg, {%op. cit.,%} 74- 76, seems to do. Trivṛṣan has entirely disappeared from the Epic tradition; there is thus no way of assigning a relative priority to either Trivṛṣan or Tridhanvan.</F> <F>15) Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xxv. 16; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxii. 3 ({%Indische%} {%Studien,%} 3, 473); Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 6, 5, 3.</F> <F>16) ii. 6, 11. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Oldenberg, {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen%} {%Morgenländischen Gesellschaft,%} 42, 217 {%et seq.;%} Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 111-116; 2, 165, n. 4; Weber, {%Indische%} {%Studien,%} 10, 25; Lanman, {%Sanskrit Reader,%} 386.</F>
{@Trāta Aiṣumata@}¦ (‘descendant of Iṣumant’) is mentioned in the Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> as a pupil of {@Nigaḍa Pārṇavalki.@} <F>1) i. 3. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 372.</F>

{@Trāyamāṇā@}¦ denotes in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> a plant of an unknown species. The word is possibly only an epithet, retaining its participial sense of ‘preserving,’ though this interpretation is not favoured by the accent.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) viii. 2, 6.</F> <F>2) {%Trāyamāṇā. Cf.%} Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 477.</F>

{@Trāsadasyava,@}¦ ‘descendant of {@Trasadasyu,@}’ is the patro- nymic in the Rigveda of {@Tṛkṣi@}<sup>1</sup> and of {@Kuruśravaṇa.@}<sup>2</sup> The [Page1-329+ 45] word is also applied to Agni as ‘protector of, or worshipped by, Trasadasyu’ and his line.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) viii. 22, 7.</F> <F>2) x. 33, 4.</F> <F>3) viii. 19, 32; Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} p. 96.</F>

{@Tri-kakud@}¦<sup>1</sup> or {@Tri-kakubh,@}<sup>2</sup> ‘having three peaks,’ occurs in the Atharvaveda and later as the name of a mountain in the Himālaya, the modern Trikota. From it came the salve (Āñjana),<sup>3</sup> which tradition made out to be derived from Vṛtra's eye.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) Av. iv. 9, 8; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 1, 3, 12.</F> <F>2) Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 6, 3; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxiii. 1; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xv. 4; Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xxii. 14.</F> <F>3) Hence called {%Traikakuda,%} Av. iv. 9, 9, 10; xix. 44, 6, etc.</F> <F>4) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, {%loc. cit.;%} Maitrāyaṇī and Kāṭhaka Saṃhitās, {%loc. cit.%} <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rig- veda, 3, 198; Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 5, 29, 30; Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Myth-%} {%ologie,%} 3, 239, n. 4; Bloomfield, {%Hymns%} {%of the Atharvaveda,%} 381.</F>
{@Tri-kadruka,@}¦ a term used in the plural only, appears to denote three vessels of some kind for holding Soma. <div n="P"/>^1 i. 32, 3; ii. 11, 17; 15, 1; 22, 1; x. 14, 16.
{@Tri-kharva@}¦ is the name of a school of priests mentioned in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa (ii. 8, 3) as practising a special rite with success.

{@Trita@}¦ is clearly a god<sup>1</sup> in Vedic literature, but Yāska in one passage of the Nirukta<sup>2</sup> already explains the name as that of a Ṛṣi or seer. <F>1) Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} pp. 67-69.</F> <F>2) iv. 6.</F>

{@Tri-pura,@}¦ ‘a threefold stronghold,’ is alluded to in the Brāhmaṇas<sup>1</sup> as a secure protection. But as the passages are mythical no stress can be laid on them as evidence for the existence of forts with three concentric walls. <F>1) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, vi. 3, 3, 25; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 11; Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa in {%Indische Studien,%} 2, 310. See also Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vi. 2, 3; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxiv. 10, etc., and Lévi, {%La Doctrine du Sacrifice,%} 46, n 1.</F>

{@Tri-plakṣa,@}¦ masc. plur., ‘the three fig-trees,’ is the name of the place where the {@Dṛṣadvatī@} disappeared, near the {@Yamunā,@} according to the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) xxv. 13, 4. {%Cf.%} Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xiii. 29, 33; Lāṭyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, x. 19, 9; Kātyāyana Srauta Sūtra, xxiv. 6, 39.</F>
{@Triy-avi.@}¦ See {@Tryavi.@}

{@Tri-yuga,@}¦ neut., is an expression occurring in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> where it is said that the plants ({%oṣadhi%}) were born ‘three ages’ before the gods ({%devebhyas triyugaṃ purā%}). The commentator on the Nirukta<sup>2</sup> thinks that the ages here meant are the Yugas of the later Indian chronology, the sense of the passage being that the plants were born in the first Yuga. The author of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> understands three seasons — spring, the rains, and autumn — to be meant in the verse, taking the two words {%triyugaṃ purā%} separately as ‘formerly, in the three seasons.’ The vague sense ‘three ages’ is quite adequate: the use of ‘three’ in such cases is a favourite feature in folklore. {%Cf.%} {@Yuga.@} <F>1) x. 97, 1 = Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iv. 2, 6, 1, and Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā; xii. 75.</F> <F>2) ix. 28.</F> <F>3) vii. 2, 4, 26. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Eggeling, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 41, 340.</F>

{@Tri-vatsa,@}¦ ‘three years old,’<sup>1</sup> is an expression applied to cattle in the later Saṃhitās and the Brāhmaṇas.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) As regards the form and meaning of this compound, {%cf.%} {@Tryavi.@}</F> <F>2) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xiv. 10; xviii. 26; xxviii. 27; Pañcaviṃśa Brāh- maṇa, xvi. 13; xviii. 9; xxi. 14, etc. {%Cf.%} Lāṭyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, viii. 3, 9 {%et seq.,%} where one explanation of the word is {%tri-varṣa.%}</F>
{@Tri-vṛt,@}¦ ‘threefold,’ is the designation of an amulet in the Atharvaveda (v. 28, 2. 4).

{@Tri-veda Kṛṣṇa-rāta Lauhitya@}¦ (‘descendant of Lohita’) is the name of a teacher, a pupil of {@Śyāmajayanta Lauhitya,@} according to a Vaṃśa (list of teachers) in the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa (iii. 42, 1).

{@Tri-śaṅku@}¦ is in Vedic literature the name of a sage men- tioned as a teacher in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad.<sup>1</sup> There is no trace of the later legend by which he becomes the victim of {@Vasiṣṭha's@} curse and the object of {@Viśvāmitra's@} solicitude, being eventually fixed in the sky as a constellation.<sup>2</sup> The confusion of the chronology in the tales of Triśaṅku is a good example of the worthlessness of the supposed epic tradition. <F>1) i. 10, 1.</F> <F>2) See Muir, {%Sanskrit Texts,%} 1^2, 362, 375 {%et seq.%}</F>

{@Tri-śoka@}¦ is the name of an ancient mythical seer who is mentioned both in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and the Atharvaveda.<sup>2</sup> A Sāman, or chant, named after him is referred to in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) i. 112, 13; viii. 45, 30. In x. 29, 2, the word seems merely to be an adjec- tive, meaning ‘with triple splendour.’</F> <F>2) iv. 29, 6.</F> <F>3) viii. 1. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rig- veda, 3, 107, 162; Hopkins, {%Transac-%} {%tions of the Connecticut Academy of Arts%} {%and Sciences,%} 15, 33.</F>
{@Trai-kakuda.@}¦ See {@Trikakud.@}

{@Traitana@}¦ appears in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as a {@Dāsa,@} an enemy of {@Dīrghatamas,@} who seems to have engaged him in single combat and defeated him. The St. Petersburg Dictionary suggests that he is rather a supernatural being allied to Trita ({%cf.%} the Avestan Thrita and Thraetaona).<sup>2</sup> <F>1) i. 158, 5.</F> <F>2) Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} p. 68. {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rig- veda, 3, 151; Oldenberg, {%Religion des%} {%Veda,%} 144.</F>
{@Trai-dhātva@}¦ (‘descendant of Tridhātu,’) is the patronymic of {@Tryaruṇa@} in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa (xiii. 3, 12).

{@Trai-pada,@}¦ neut., occurs as a measure of distance, ‘three- quarters’ of a {@Yojana,@} in the Pañcāviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, where half a Yojana is termed {@Gavyūti@} and a quarter {@Krośa.@}<sup>1</sup> <F>1) xvi. 13. {%Cf.%} Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xiv. 41, 12.</F>

{@Traivaṇi@}¦ is mentioned as a pupil of {@Aupacandhani@} or {@Aupa-@} {@jandhani@} in the first two Vaṃśas (lists of teachers) in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.<sup>1</sup> In the Mādhyaṃdina recension<sup>2</sup> his name occurs twice in the second Vaṃśa, in both cases as a pupil of Aupajandhani. <F>1) ii. 6, 3 (Kāṇva = ii. 5, 21 Mādhyaṃ- dina); iv. 6, 3 (= iv. 5, 27).</F> <F>2) iv. 5, 27.</F>
{@Trai-vṛṣṇa,@}¦ ‘descendant of Trivṛṣan,’ is the patronymic of {@Trayaruṇa@} in the Rigveda (v. 27, 1).

{@Try-aruṇa Trai-vṛṣṇa Trasadasyu@}¦ is the name of a prince whose generosity to a singer is celebrated in a hymn of the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> In the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> he appears as {@Tryaruṇa Traidhātva Aikṣvāka,@} and is the hero of the following story. He was out in his chariot with his Purohita, or domestic priest, {@Vṛśa Jāna,@} and by excessive speed in driving killed a Brahmin boy. This sin was atoned for by the Puro- hita's using his Vārśa Sāman (chant). The Śāṭyāyana Brāh- maṇa, cited by Sāyaṇa,<sup>3</sup> elaborates the tale. As Vṛśa had held the reins, king and priest accused each other of the murder. The Ikṣvākus being consulted threw the responsibility for the crime on Vṛśa, who thereupon revived the boy by the Vārśa Sāman. In consequence of this unfairness of theirs — being Kṣatriyas they were partial to a Kṣatriya — Agni's glow ceased to burn in their houses. In response to their appeal to restore it, Vṛśa came to them, saw the Piśācī (demoness), who, in the form of Trasadasyu's wife, had stolen the glow, and succeeded in restoring it to Agni. This version with some variations occurs also in the Bṛhaddevatā,<sup>4</sup> which connects the story with a hymn of the Rigveda.<sup>5</sup> Sieg's attempt<sup>6</sup> to show that the hymn really refers to this tale is not at all successful.<sup>7</sup> [Page1-333+ 44] <div n="P"/>It is clear that Trasadasyu must here mean ‘descendant of Trasadasyu,’ and not King Trasadasyu himself. The difference of the patronymics, Traivṛṣṇa and Traidhātva, by which he is referred to can best be explained by assuming that there were two kings, Trivṛṣan and Tridhātu (or possibly Tridhanvan), from whom Tryaruṇa was descended.<sup>8</sup> The connexion with the Ikṣvākus is important (see {@Ikṣvāku@}). <F>1) v. 27, 1-3.</F> <F>2) xiii. 3, 12. {%Cf.%} the Tāṇḍaka recen- sion, cited in Sāyaṇa, on Rv. v. 2, where Trasadasyu is given as the king's name.</F> <F>3) On Rv., {%loc. cit.%} See also the Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa version in Oertel, {%Journal of the American Oriental Society,%} 18, 20.</F> <F>4) v. 14 {%et seq.,%} with Macdonell's notes.</F> <F>5) v. 2.</F> <F>6) {%Die Sagenstoffe des Ṛgveda,%} 64-76. {%Cf.%} Geldner, {%Festtgruss an Roth,%} 192.</F> <F>7) See Oldenberg, {%Sacred Books of the%} {%East,%} 46, 366 {%et seq.; Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 312; Hillebrandt, {%Göttingische Gelehrte%} {%Anzeigen,%} 1903, 240 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>8) See Sieg, {%op. cit.,%} 74-76, and {@Trasadasyu.@}</F>

{@Try-avi@}¦ designates a calf eighteen months old<sup>1</sup> in the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> and later Saṃhitās.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) The etymological meaning is ap- parently ‘having three sheep (periods)’ -that is, ‘having periods of thrice six months,’ just as the adjective {%pañcāvi%} means ‘having five periods of six months,’ or ‘thirty months old.’</F> <F>2) iii. 55, 14.</F> <F>3) Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xvii. 2; xviii. 12, etc. (in the form {%triyavi%}); Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xiv. 10; xviii. 26, etc.</F>

{@Try-āśir,@}¦ ‘with three admixtures,’ is an epithet of Soma in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> According to Sāyaṇa this means mixed with curds ({@Dadhi@}), meal ({@Saktu@}), and milk ({@Payas@}). More accurately it would seem<sup>2</sup> to denote the milk ({%gavāśir%}), the barley ({%yavāśir%}), and the curds ({%dadhyāśir%}), which were used to mix with the Soma. <F>1) v. 27, 5. {%Cf.%} perhaps viii. 2, 7 ({%traya Indrasya somāḥ sutāsaḥ,%} ‘three kinds of Soma pressed for Indra’).</F> <F>2) Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologic,%} 1, 209; Oldenberg, {%Sacred Books of the%} {%East,%} 46, 422.</F>

{@Tvac,@}¦ ‘skin,’ ‘hide,’ ({%a%}) denotes specially in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> the hide used in the process of extracting the {@Soma@} juice from the plant. The Soma was pounded with stones ({%adri%}) upon the skin laid on the pressing boards ({%adhiṣavaṇe phalake%}),<sup>2</sup> which, however, are not mentioned in the Rigveda. Or if a pestle and mortar were used, the skin was still placed underneath them to catch the drops of juice, not above, as Pischel<sup>3</sup> thought. [Page1-334+ 51] <div n="P"/>({%b%}) Tvac also denotes the rind of the Soma plant that remains after the juice has been extracted.<sup>4</sup> <div n="P"/>({%c%}) Metaphorically the term {%kṛṣṇā tvac,%} ‘the black skins,’ is applied to the aboriginal enemies of the invading Āryans.<sup>5</sup> <F>1) i. 79, 3; iii. 21, 5; ix. 65, 25; 66, 29; 70, 7; 79, 4; 101, 11, 16, etc.</F> <F>2) Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologic,%} 1, 181-183, and {@Adhisavaṇa.@}</F> <F>3) {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 110.</F> <F>4) Rv. ix. 86, 44; Taittirīya Brāh- maṇa, iii. 7, 13, 1; Hillebrandt, {%op. cit.,%} 52.</F> <F>5) Rv. i. 130, 8, and probably ix. 41, 1, for which, however, {%cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%op. cit.,%} 51, n. 2, and see {@Dāsa.@}</F>

{@Tvaṣṭṛ@}¦ is employed once in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> to denote a ‘carpenter,’ with a deliberate play on the name of the god Tvaṣṭṛ. He is there mentioned as using an axe ({%svadhiti%}) to fashion (from wood) ‘a well-made form’ ({%rūpaṃ sukṛtam%}). See {@Taṣṭṛ.@} <F>1) xii. 3, 33. {%Cf.%} Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 688; Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 651.</F>

{@Tvāṣṭra,@}¦ ‘descendant of Tvaṣṭṛ,’ is the patronymic, in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad,<sup>1</sup> of the mythical teacher {@Ābhūti.@} <F>1) ii. 6, 3 (Kāṇva = ii. 5, 22 Mādhyaṃdina); iv. 6, 3 (= iv. 5, 28).</F>

{@Tsaru,@}¦ — ({%a%}) This word seems to denote some sort of crawling animal in one passage of the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> <div n="P"/>({%b%}) In the later literature the word means a ‘handle,’ as of a beaker ({@Camasa@}).<sup>1</sup> In this sense also it seems to occur in the description of the plough ({@Lāṅgala@}) in the Atharvaveda<sup>2</sup> and the later Saṃhitās.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) vii. 50, 1. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 99.</F> <F>1) Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xxv. 4. {%Cf.%} Lāṭyāyana Srauta Sūtra, x. 12, 12, etc.</F> <F>2) iii. 17, 3, where the ordinary text has {%soma-satsaru%} (so the Pada text), and the Paippalāda recension has {%soma-%} {%pitsalam.%}</F> <F>3) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iv. 2, 5, 6, has {%sumati-tsaru;%} Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 7, 12; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xvi. 12; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xii. 71; Vasiṣṭha Dharma Sūtra, ii. 34, have {%somapitsaru,%} which Vasiṣṭha renders as ‘provided with a handle for the drinker of Soma’ ({%i.e., somapi-tsaru%}). Weber, {%Indische%} {%Studien,%} 17, 255, suggests {%soma-sa-tsaru,%} ‘with ({%sa-%}) strap ({%uman,%} a conjectural word) and handle’ ({%tsaru%}). Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 116, prefers to read throughout {%sumati-tsaru,%} ‘with well-smoothed handle,’ from the root seen in {%matī-kṛ,%} etc. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 236; Bühler, {%Sacred%} {%Books of the East,%} 14, 13.</F>

{@Tsārin@}¦ denotes, in one passage of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> a ‘hunter’ engaged in the chase of the {%takva%} (an unknown beast), according to Ludwig and Max Müller.<sup>2</sup> But this explanation is quite conjectural. <F>1) i. 134, 5.</F> <F>2) {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 32, 448.</F>
{@Daṃśa@}¦ (lit., ‘biter’), ‘gad-fly,’ is mentioned in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (vi. 9, 3; 10, 2).

{@Daṃṣṭra,@}¦ denoting a prominent tooth, ‘tusk,’ or ‘fang’ of an animal, occurs often from the Rigveda onwards.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Rv. ii. 13, 4; x. 87, 3; Av. iv. 36, 2; x. 5, 43; xvi. 7, 3, etc.</F>
{@Dakṣa Kātyāyani Ātreya@}¦ (‘descendant of Atri’) is mentioned in the Vaṃśas (lists of teachers) of the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa (iii. 41, 1; iv. 17, 1) as a pupil of {@Śaṅkha Bābhravya.@}
{@Dakṣa Jayanta Lauhitya@}¦ (‘descendant of Lohita’) is men- tioned in a Vaṃśa (list of teachers) of the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa (iii. 42, 1) as a pupil of {@Kṛṣṇarāta Lauhitya.@}

{@Dakṣa Pārvati@}¦ (‘descendant of {@Parvata@}’) is mentioned in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> as having performed a certain rite which his descendants, the Dākṣāyaṇas, still maintained, thus enjoying royal dignity down to the time of the Brāhmaṇa itself. He appears in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> also. <F>1) ii. 4, 4, 6.</F> <F>2) iv. 4. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 223; 4, 358; Eggeling, {%Sacred Books of the%} {%East,%} 12, 374 {%et seq.;%} Lévi, {%La Doctrine%} {%du Sacrifice,%} 138.</F>
{@Dakṣiṇatas-kaparda@}¦ is an epithet of the {@Vasiṣṭhas@} in the Rigveda (vii. 33, 1) referring to their mode of ‘wearing the hair in a braid on the right side.’ See {@Kaparda.@}

{@Dakṣiṇā@}¦ appears repeatedly in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> as the designation of the gift presented to priests at the sacrifice, apparently because a cow — a prolific ({%dakṣiṇā%}) one — was the usual ‘fee’<sup>3</sup> on such an occasion.<sup>4</sup> The later Dāna-stutis, or ‘Praises of Gifts,’ in the Rigveda immensely exaggerate these donations, and the exaggeration grows in the Brāhmaṇas. It is important to notice that these enumerations of gifts in the main include nothing but articles of personal property, such as kine, horses, buffaloes, or camels ({%uṣṭra%}), ornaments, and so forth, but not land.<sup>5</sup> Reference is, however, made in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>6</sup> to land as a Dakṣiṇā, but with dis- approval, probably because the land came to be regarded as inalienable without the consent of the clansmen.<sup>7</sup> <F>1) A whole hymn, Rv. x. 107, is devoted to its praise. {%Cf.%} i. 168, 7; vi. 27, 8; viii. 24, 29; 39, 5; x. 62, 1, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. iv. 11, 4; v. 7, 11; xi. 7, 9; 8, 22; xiii. 1, 52; xviii. 4, 8, etc.; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, i. 7, 3, 1; 8, 1, 1; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, iv. 19, 23; xix. 30; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 7, 3, 3 {%et seq.;%} Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 9, 3, 1 {%et seq.%} The verses ({%gāthā nārāśaṃsī,%} either as a single expression or as two separate terms) used to win these Dakṣiṇās were notoriously false. See Kāṭhaka Saṃ- hitā, xiv. 5; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 3, 2, 6. 7; Nirukta, i. 7; xi. 2.</F> <F>3) The transition of meaning is similar in the use of the English word ‘fee’; ‘cattle,’ ‘money,’ ‘payment for service’ (see Murray's English Dictionary, {%s.v.%} ‘fee’). {%Cf.%} also {@Go-dāna,@} n. 4.</F> <F>4) {%Cf.%} the rule that when nothing is specified a cow is the Dakṣiṇā, Kāty- āyana Śrauta Sūtra, xv. 2, 13; Lāṭy- āyana Śrauta Sūtra, viii. 1, 2.</F> <F>5) So, {%e.g.,%} Rv. i. 126, 1-4; v. 30, 12-15; viii. 1, 32. 33; 3, 21 {%et seq.;%} 4, 19-21; 5, 37-39; 6, 46-48; 55; 56; vii. 18, 21-24, and the full list in Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 273-277. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 10, 49 {%et seq.%} Clothes ({%vāsas%}) and gold are mentioned as a Dakṣiṇā in Av. ix. 5, 14. The four Dakṣiṇās, according to the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iv. 3, 4, 7, are gold, a cow, clothes, and a horse. This is practically exhaustive if the trappings of the horse and ornaments are included.</F> <F>6) xiii. 7, 1, 13, with which compare xiii. 6, 2, 18, where the Brahmin's land is excluded; and see xiii. 7, 1, 15, where the gift of land is disapproved.</F> <F>7) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, vii. 1, 1, 4. {%Cf.%} above, pp. 100, n. 19, 246; below, pp. 351, 352. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 169- 171; Jolly, {%Recht und Sitte,%} 104, 105; Weber, {%Indische Streifen,%} 1, 96-98; Bloomfield, {%Religion of the Veda,%} 69-74; {%Atharvaveda,%} 76 {%et seq.,%} 100, 121.</F>

{@Dakṣiṇā-patha@}¦ (lit., ‘the road to the south’), ‘the south country,’ is found, probably as a designation of the Deccan, as early as the Baudhāyana Dharma Sūtra,<sup>1</sup> coupled with [Page1-337+ 45] Surāṣṭra. A similar expression is {%dakṣiṇā padā,%} ‘with south- ward foot,’ in the Rigveda,<sup>2</sup> referring to the place where the exile ({%parā-vṛj%}) goes on being expelled. This no doubt simply means ‘the south’ beyond the limits of the recognized Āryan world, which even as late as the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad<sup>3</sup> appears as bounded by the Vindhyas on the south. <F>1) i. 1, 2, 13. {%Cf.%} Oldenberg, {%Buddha,%} 394, n., and Baudhāyana Gṛhya Sūtra, v. 13.</F> <F>2) x. 61, 8.</F> <F>3) ii. 13. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 185; Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 408; Rhys Davids, Buddhist India, 30; Keith {%Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka,%} 28, n. 1; {%Aitareya%} {%Āraṇyaka,%} 200.</F>

{@Dakṣiṇā-praṣṭi@}¦ denotes ‘the side horse on the right.’ It appears from two passages of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> that there were at times four horses yoked to the chariot, the right and the left yoke horse ({%dakṣiṇā-yugya, savyā-yugya%}) in the middle, flanked by one on each side, the two latter of course not being fastened to the yoke at all, but presumably by traces alongside of the yoke horses. See {@Ratha.@} <F>1) v. 1, 4, 9; ix. 4, 2, 11 (this passage appears to speak of three horses only, but {%of.%} v. 4, 3, 17). {%Cf.%} also Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xvi. 13, 12.</F>
{@Dakṣiṇāyana.@}¦ See {@Sūrya.@}
{@Dakṣiṇā-yugya,@}¦ ‘the yoke horse on the right,’ is mentioned in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (v. 1, 4, 6; 4, 3, 8; ix. 4, 2, 11). See {@Ratha.@}

{@Daṇḍa,@}¦ ‘staff.’ ({%a%}) This word is often mentioned in the ordinary sense; for example, when used for driving cattle<sup>1</sup> ({%go-ajanāsaḥ%}), or as a weapon.<sup>2</sup> A staff was given to a man on consecration for driving away demons, according to the Satapatha Brāhmaṇa.<sup>3</sup> The staff also played a part in the initiation ({%upanayana%}) of a youth on attaining manhood.<sup>4</sup> In a modified sense the word is used to denote the handle of a ladle or similar implement.<sup>5</sup> [Page1-338+ 49] <div n="P"/>({%b%}) The ‘staff’ as the symbol of temporal power, implying punishment, is applied by the king ({%rāja-preṣito daṇḍaḥ%}).<sup>1</sup> The king, in modern phraseology, was the source of criminal law; and he clearly retained this branch of law in his own hands even in later times.<sup>2</sup> The punishment of the non-guilty ({%a-daṇḍya%}) is given as one of the characteristics of the non- Brahminical {@Vrātyas@} in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>3</sup> See also {@Dharma.@} <F>1) Rv. vii. 33, 6.</F> <F>2) Av. v. 5, 4. {%Cf.%} Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 35; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 5, 4, 6, etc.</F> <F>3) iii. 2, 1, 32.</F> <F>4) Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra, i. 19; 22; Sāṅkhāyana Gṛhya Sūtra, ii. 1, 6, 11, etc.</F> <F>5) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vii. 5; Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, vii. 4, 1, 36. Of a musical instrument, Sāṅkhāyana Āraṇ- yaka, viii. 9; Śrauta Sūtra, xvii. 3, 1 {%et%} {%seq.%}</F> <F>1) Pāraskara Gṛhya Sūtra, iii. 15. {%Cf.%} Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, v. 4, 4, 7, where the king, being himself ‘exempt from punishment’ ({%a-daṇḍya%}), inflicts judicial punishment ({%daṇḍa-vadha%}).</F> <F>2) Foy, {%Die königliche Gewalt,%} 21 {%et%} {%seq.%}</F> <F>3) xvii. 1, 9; Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 33.</F>
{@Daṇḍa Aupara@}¦ (‘descendant of Upara’) is mentioned in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (vi. 2, 9, 4) and the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā (iii. 8, 7) as having performed a certain rite.
{@Daṇḍana@}¦ occurs in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> among other names of ‘reed’ or ‘cane.’ <F>1) xii. 2, 54. {%Cf.%} Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 682.</F>
{@Datta Tāpasa@}¦ was Hotṛ priest at the snake festival described in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) xxv. 15, 3. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 35.</F>

{@Dadhi,@}¦ ‘sour milk,’ is repeatedly mentioned in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> mentions in order {@Ghrta@} (‘clarified butter’), Dadhi, {@Mastu,@} which Eggeling<sup>4</sup> renders ‘whey,’ and {@Āmikṣā,@} ‘curds.’ Dadhi often has the meaning of ‘curds’ also. It was used for mixing with {@Soma.@}<sup>5</sup> <F>1) viii. 2, 9; ix. 87, 1, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. iii. 12, 7; iv. 34, 6; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 5, 3, 4, etc.; Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xviii. 5, 12, etc.</F> <F>3) i. 8, 1, 7. {%Cf.%} Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 348.</F> <F>4) {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 12, 218.</F> <F>5) {%Dadhyāśir,%} ‘mixed with sour milk,’ is an epithet of Soma in Rv. i. 5, 5; 137, 2; v. 51, 7; vii. 32, 4. {%Cf.%} Hille- brandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 219 {%et seq.%} <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 227.</F>

{@Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa@}¦ is a purely mythical sage. In the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> he is clearly a divinity of some kind, but in the later [Page1-339+ 55] Saṃhitās<sup>2</sup> and the Brāhmaṇas<sup>3</sup> he is metamorphosed into a teacher. In the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmana<sup>4</sup> he is by oversight called an Āṅgirasa. <F>1) i. 80, 16; 84, 13, 14; 116, 12; 117, 22; 119, 9, etc. See Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} pp. 141, 142; Hille- brandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 176.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 1, 4, 4; 6, 6, 3; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xix. 4.</F> <F>3) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iv. 1, 5, 18; vi. 4, 2, 3; xiv. 1, 1, 18. 20. 25; 4, 13; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, ii. 5, 22; iv. 5, 28, etc.</F> <F>4) xii. 8, 6. So also Gopatha Brāh- maṇa, i. 5, 21. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Athar-%} {%vaveda,%} xxxv; {%Atharvaveda,%} 23, 116, 118, St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>
{@Dadhy-āśir.@}¦ See {@Dadhi@} and {@Soma.@}

{@Dant, Danta,@}¦ ‘tooth,’ is frequently mentioned from the Rigveda onwards.<sup>1</sup> Cleansing ({%dhāv%}) the teeth was an ordinary act, especially in preparation for a sacrifice, and accompanied bathing, shaving of the hair and beard ({%keśa-śmaśru%}), and the cutting of the nails.<sup>2</sup> A hymn of the Atharvaveda<sup>3</sup> celebrates the appearance of the first two teeth of a child, though its exact interpretation is doubtful.<sup>4</sup> In the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>5</sup> there is a reference to a child's first teeth falling out. The word seems in the Rigveda<sup>6</sup> once to denote an elephant's tusk. Whether dentistry was practised is doubtful. The occurrence in the Aitareya Āraṇyaka<sup>7</sup> of {@Hiraṇya-dant,@} ‘gold-toothed,’ as the name of a man, is perhaps significant, especially as it is certain that the stopping of teeth with gold was known at Rome as early as the legislation of the Twelve Tables.<sup>8</sup> <F>1) Rv. vii. 55, 2; x. 68, 6; Av. v. 23, 3; 29, 4; vi. 56, 3, etc. The more usual form is Danta, Rv. iv. 6, 8; vi. 75, 11; Av. iv. 3, 6, etc.</F> <F>2) Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 6, 2 (not exactly paralleled in Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vi. 1, 1, 2 {%et seq.%}).</F> <F>3) vi. 140.</F> <F>4) Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 321; Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 5, 224; Grill, {%Hundert Lieder,%}^2 176; Bloomfield, {%Hymns%} {%of the Atharvaveda,%} 540, 541; {%Atharva-%} {%veda,%} 71; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 386.</F> <F>5) vii. 14; Śāṅkhāyana Srauta Sūtra, xv. 18.</F> <F>6) iv. 6, 8; Pischel, {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 99; Oldenberg, {%Sacred Books of the%} {%East,%} 46, 341, 342.</F> <F>7) ii. 1, 5.</F> <F>8) Keith, {%Aitareya Āraṇyaka,%} 206. See Wordsworth, {%Fragments and Specimens%} {%of Early Latin,%} 537.</F>

{@Dabhīti@}¦ appears several times in the Rigveda as a hero or sage. Indra overcomes on his behalf {@Cumuri@} and {@Dhuni;@}<sup>1</sup> [Page1-340+ 58] he pressed Soma for Indra,<sup>2</sup> who rewarded him.<sup>3</sup> For him 30,000 {@Dāsas@} were sent to sleep,<sup>4</sup> and for him the {@Dasyus@} were bound without cords.<sup>5</sup> Dabhīti also appears, with {@Turvīti,@} as a protégé of the Aśvins.<sup>6</sup> There seems no reason to deny that he was a real person.<sup>7</sup> <F>1) x. 113, 9; ii. 15, 9; vii. 19, 4.</F> <F>2) vi. 20, 13.</F> <F>3) vi. 26, 6.</F> <F>4) iv. 30, 21.</F> <F>5) ii. 13, 9.</F> <F>6) i. 112, 23.</F> <F>7) Oldenberg, {%Religion des Veda,%} 155, 157, 158. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} p. 162.</F>

{@Dama,@}¦ ‘house,’ is a word that occurs several times in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> It denotes, according to Roth,<sup>2</sup> the place in which a man wields uncontrolled power (from the root {%dam,%} ‘control’). <F>1) i. 1, 8; 61, 9; 75, 5; 143, 4; ii. 1, 2, etc.; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, viii. 24.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} But this seems very doubtful in view of the apparent connexion of <lang n="greek">δόμος</lang> and <lang n="greek">δέμω</lang>, ‘build,’ in Greek.</F>

{@Dam-pati@}¦ denotes ‘the master of the house’<sup>1</sup> in the Rigveda,<sup>2</sup> but is more often used in the dual to designate ‘the master and the mistress,’<sup>3</sup> an expression that may legitimately be deemed to show the high status of women at the time of the Rigveda. See {@Strī.@} <F>1) For the form, {%cf.%} Macdonell, {%Vedic%} {%Grammar,%} p. 37, n. 9. Pischel, {%Vedische%} {%Studien,%} 2. 307 {%et seq.,%} argues in favour of the spelling {%daṃpati%} (adopted by Geldner in his {%Ṛgveda, Glossar%}). {%Cf.%} {%patir dan.%} Rv. i. 149, 2; Oldenberg, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 46, 176, 177.</F> <F>2) i. 127, 8; ii. 39, 2; v. 22, 4; viii. 69. 16; 84, 7.</F> <F>3) Rv. v. 3, 2; viii. 31, 5; x. 10, 5; 68, 2; 85, 32; 95, 12, etc.; Av. vi. 123, 3; xii. 3, 14; xiv. 2, 9, etc. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Delbrück, {%Die indogermanischen%} {%Verwandtschaftsnamen,%} 418, 420.</F>

{@Darbha@}¦ is the name of a grass in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> In the Atharvaveda it is used for the calming of anger ({%manyu-%} {%śamana%}),<sup>3</sup> and as an amulet for protection against the scattering of one's hair or the striking of one's breast.<sup>4</sup> It is also said to be ‘rich in roots’ ({%bhūri-mūla%}),<sup>5</sup> to possess a thousand leaves ({%sahasra-parṇa%}) and a hundred stalks ({%śata-kāṇḍa%}).<sup>6</sup> <F>1) i. 191, 3 (with {@Śara@} and {@Kuśara,@} varieties of grass).</F> <F>2) Av. vi. 43, 2; viii. 7, 20; x. 4, 13; xi. 6, 15; xix. 28, 1. etc.; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, i. 5, 1, 4, etc.</F> <F>3) Av. vi. 43.</F> <F>4) xix. 32, 2. {%Cf.%} xix. 30.</F> <F>5) Av. vi. 43, 2.</F> <F>6) Av. xix. 32, 1. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 70.</F>

{@Darvi,@}¦ or {@Darvī,@} properly denotes a ‘ladle,’ in which sense it is found in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> But the word also means a serpent's ‘hood’ in the Atharvaveda,<sup>3</sup> though Zimmer regards it as the name of a serpent. <div n="P"/>^4 {%Altindisches Leben,%} 95, where he takes {@Karikrata@} also as the name of a snake. <F>1) v. 6, 9; x. 105, 10.</F> <F>2) Av. iii. 10, 7; iv. 14, 7; ix. 6, 17, etc.</F> <F>3) x. 1, 13. See Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 577. Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 153.</F>

{@Darvidā,@}¦ the ‘woodpecker,’ is mentioned as a victim at the Aśvamedha or horse sacrifice, in the Yajurveda.<sup>1</sup> {%Cf.%} {@Dārvā-@} {@ghāta.@} <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 13, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 15, Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 3. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 93. The St. Peters- burg Dictionary, {%s.v.,%} suggests ‘wood- piercer’ ({%dāru-vidha%}) as the literal sense. On the etymology, {%cf.%} F. W. Thomas's article. ‘The D.Suffix,’ p. 121, in {%Transactions of the Cambridge Philological%} {%Society,%} 5, part ii.</F>

{@Darśa@}¦ (‘appearance’) denotes the new moon day,<sup>1</sup> usually in opposition to the day of full moon ({%pūrṇa-māsa%}).<sup>2</sup> Most frequently the word occurs in the compound<sup>3</sup> {%darśa-pūrṇa-%} {%māsau,%} ‘new and full moon,’ the days of special ritual impor- tance.<sup>4</sup> The order of the first two words here is worthy of note, for it distinctly suggests, though it does not conclusively prove, that the month was reckoned from new moon to new moon, not from full moon to full moon. See {@Māsa.@} <F>1) Av. vii. 81, 3, 4; Taittirīya Brāh- maṇa, i. 2, 1, 14; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xi. 2, 2, 1.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 4, 4, 1, etc.</F> <F>3) {%Ibid.,%} i. 6, 7, 1; 9, 3; ii. 5, 6, 1; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 2, 2, 1; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, i. 1; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 3, 5, 11, etc.</F> <F>4) Hillebrandt, {%Das altindische Neu-%} {%und Vollmondsopfer,%} Jena, 1880; {%Ritual-%} {%litteratur,%} 111-114; Oldenberg, {%Religion%} {%des Veda,%} 439.</F>

{@Daśa-gva@}¦ appears in one hymn of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as the name of a person who was assisted by Indra. The other references in that work,<sup>2</sup> however, clearly show the mythical character of the Daśagvas, and of any individual among them. <F>1) viii. 12, 2</F> <F>2) They are mentioned with the Navagvas in i. 62, 4; iii. 39, 5; iv. 51, 4; v. 29, 12; x. 62, 6, and alone in ii. 34, 12. See Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} p. 144 (C).</F>
{@Daśatayī@}¦ in the Nirukta<sup>1</sup> frequently denotes the text of the Rigveda as divided into ten Maṇḍalas. <F>1) vii. 8. 20; xi. 16; xii. 40.</F>

{@Daśa-dyu@}¦ appears twice in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as the name of a hero, but nothing can be made out regarding him or his relation to {@Vetasu,@} who is mentioned in one passage along with him. <F>1) i. 33, 14; vi. 26, 4. {%Cf.%} Oldenberg, {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen%} {%Gesellschaft,%} 55, 328.</F>

{@Daśan,@}¦ ‘ten,’ forms the basis of the numerical system of the Vedic Indians, as it does of the Āryan people generally. But it is characteristic of India<sup>1</sup> that there should be found at a very early period long series of names for very high numerals, whereas the Āryan knowledge did not go beyond 1,000. In the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā<sup>2</sup> the list is 1; 10; 100; 1,000; 10,000 ({%ayuta%}); 100,000 ({%niyuta%}); 1,000,000 ({%prayuta%}); 10,000,000 ({%arbuda%}); 100,000,000 ({%nyarbuda%}); 1,000,000,000 ({%samudra%}); 10,000,000,000 ({%madhya%}); 100,000,000,000 ({%anta%}); 1,000,000,000,000 ({%parārdha%}). In the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā<sup>3</sup> the list is the same, but {%niyuta%} and {%prayuta%} exchange places, and after {%nyarbuda%} a new figure ({%badva%}) intervenes, thus increasing {%samudra%} to 10,000,000,000, and so on. The Taittirīya Saṃhitā has in two places<sup>4</sup> exactly the same list as the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā. The Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā<sup>5</sup> has the list {%ayuta, prayuta,%} then {%ayuta%} again, {%arbuda,%} {%nyarbuda, samudra, madhya, anta, parārdha.%} The Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>6</sup> has the Vājasaneyi list up to {%nyarbuda%} inclusive, then follow {%nikharvaka, badva, akṣita,%} and apparently {%go%} = 1,000,000,000,000. The Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa<sup>7</sup> list [Page1-343+ 58] replaces {%nikharvaka%} by {%nikharva, badva%} by {%padma,%} and ends with {%akṣitir vyomāntaḥ.%} The Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra<sup>8</sup> con- tinues the series after {%nyarbuda%} with {%nikharvāda, samudra,%} {%salila, antya, ananta%} (= 10 billions). <div n="P"/>But beyond {%ayuta%}<sup>9</sup> none of these numbers has any vitality. {%Badva,%} indeed, occurs in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa,<sup>10</sup> but it cannot there have any precise numerical sense;<sup>11</sup> and later on the names of these high numerals are very much confused. <div n="P"/>An arithmetical progression of some interest is found in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa,<sup>12</sup> where occurs a list of sacrificial gifts in which each successive figure doubles the amount of the preceding one. It begins with {%dvādaśa-mānaṃ hiraṇyam,%} ‘gold to the value of 12’ (the unit being uncertain, but probably the {@Kṛṣṇala@}),<sup>13</sup> followed by ‘to the value of 24, 48, 96, 192, 384, 768, 1,536, 3072,’ then {%dve aṣṭāviṃśati-śata-māne,%} which must mean 2×128×24 (the last unit being not a single {%māna,%} but a number of 24 {%mānas%}) = 6,144, then 12,288, 24,576, 49,152, 98,304, 196,608, 393, 216. {@Dasyu,@}¦ a word of somewhat doubtful origin, is in many passages of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> clearly applied to superhuman enemies. On the other hand, there are several passages in which human foes, probably the aborigines, are thus designated. This may be regarded as certain in those passages where the Dasyu is opposed to the Āryan, who defeats him with the aid of the gods.<sup>2</sup> The great difference between the Dasyus and the Āryans was their religion: the former are styled ‘not sacrificing,’ ‘devoid of rites,’ ‘addicted to strange vows,’ ‘god- hating,’ and so forth.<sup>3</sup> As compared with the {@Dāsa,@} they are less distinctively a people: no clans ({%viśaḥ%}) of the Dasyus are mentioned, and while Indra's {%dasyu-hatya,%} ‘slaughter of the Dasyus,’ is often spoken of, there is no corresponding use of {%dāsa-hatya.%} That the Dasyus were real people is, however, shown by the epithet {%anās%} applied to them in one passage of the Rigveda.<sup>5</sup> The sense of this word is not absolutely certain: the Pada text and Sāyaṇa both take it to mean ‘without face’ ({%an-ās%}),<sup>6</sup> but the other rendering, ‘noseles’ ({%a-nās%}), is quite possible,<sup>7</sup> <div n="P"/>4 Rv. i. 51, 5, 6; 103, 4; x. 95, 7; 99, 7; 105, 11. {%Cf. dasyu-han.%} ‘Dasyu- slaying,’ i. 100, 12; vi. 45, 24; viii. 76, 11; 77, 3; x. 47, 4 (all of Indra); vi. 16, 15; viii. 39, 8 (of Agni), etc. [Page1-348+ 68] and would accord well with the flat-nosed aborigines of the Dravidian<sup>8</sup> type, whose language still persists among the Brahuis, who are found in the north-west. This interpretation would receive some support from Vṛtra's being called ‘broken-nosed’ if this were a correct explanation of the obscure word {%rujānās.%}<sup>9</sup> <div n="P"/>The other epithet of the Dasyus is {%mṛdhra-vāc,%} which occurs with {%anās,%}<sup>10</sup> and which has been rendered<sup>11</sup> ‘of stam- mering, or unintelligible speech.’ This version is by no means certain, and since the epithet is elsewhere<sup>12</sup> applied to Āryans, its correct meaning is more probably ‘of hostile speech.’ <div n="P"/>Dasyu corresponds with the Iranian {%daṅhu, daqyu,%} which denotes a ‘province.’ Zimmer<sup>13</sup> thinks that the original meaning was ‘enemy,’ whence the Iranians developed the sense of ‘hostile country,’ ‘conquered country,’ ‘province,’ while the Indians, retaining the signification of ‘enemy,’ ex- tended it to include demon foes. Roth<sup>14</sup> considers that the meaning of human enemy is a transfer from the strife of gods [Page1-349+ 59] and demons. Lassen<sup>15</sup> attempted to {{onnect->connect||20210704|Dr. Sampada Savardekar|https://github.com/sanskrit-lexicon/csl-corrections/issues/67|}} the contrast {%daqyu: dasyu%} with that of {%daeva: deva,%} and to see in it a result of the religious differences which, according to Haug's theory, had separated the Iranians and the Indians. 2. {@Dāna@}¦ (‘distribution’)<sup>1</sup> seems in several passages of the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> to be a designation of the sacrificial feast to which [Page1-351+ 46] the god is invited ({%cf.%} <lang n="greek">δαίς, δαίτη</lang>). In one passage<sup>3</sup> Sāyaṇa thinks that it denotes the {%mada-jalāni,%} ‘drops of water falling from the temples of a rutting elephant,’<sup>4</sup> but this is doubtful. In another passage<sup>5</sup> Roth thinks that ‘pasture land’ is meant. <F>1) From {%dā,%} ‘divide.’</F> <F>2) i. 55, 7; 48, 4; 180, 5; viii. 46, 26; 60, 8; 99, 4, etc. {%Cf.,%} however, Pischel {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 100.</F> <F>3) Rv. viii. 33, 8; Ludwig, Transla- tion of the Rigveda, 5, 157.</F> <F>4) Dāna in this sense, so common in the post-Vedic language, is probably derived from {%dā,%} ‘divide,’ meaning originally ‘secretion.’</F> <F>5) ii. 13, 7.</F>

3. {@Dāna@}¦ is in three passages of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> held by Roth to designate a chariot horse. <F>1) v. 27, 5; vii. 18, 23; viii. 46, 24. But in all these cases ‘gifts’ seems an adequate version, ‘horses’ being under- stood.</F>

{@Dāman,@}¦ a ‘rope’ or ‘girdle,’<sup>1</sup> is often mentioned in the Rigveda and later.<sup>2</sup> Reference is made to the rope of the sacrificial horse,<sup>3</sup> as well as to the practice of tying calves with ropes.<sup>4</sup> The word occurs in the sense of a ‘band’ of horse hair in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.<sup>5</sup> <F>1) Originally ‘bond,’ from {%dā,%} ‘bind.’</F> <F>2) Rv. i. 56, 3, etc.; Av. vi. 63, 1; 103, 2; vii. 103, 1. 2; Taittirīya Saṃ- hitā, ii. 4, 13, 1, etc.</F> <F>3) Rv. i. 162, 8.</F> <F>4) Rv. ii. 28, 7.</F> <F>5) v. 3, 1, 10. {%Cf.%} Eggeling, {%Sacred%} {%Books of the East,%} 41, 62, n. 2.</F>

{@Dāya@}¦ occurs in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> only in the sense of ‘reward’ of exertion ({%śrama%}), but later it means ‘inheritance’ — that is, a father's property which is to be divided among his sons either during his lifetime or after his death. The passages all negative the idea that the property of the family was legally family property: it is clear that it was the property of the head of the house, usually the father, and that the other members of the family only had moral claims upon it which the father could ignore, though he might be coerced by his sons if they were physically stronger. <div n="P"/>Thus {@Manu@} is said in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>2</sup> to have divided his property among his sons. He omitted {@Nābhānediṣṭha,@} [Page1-352+ 66] whom he afterwards taught how to appease the Aṅgirases, and to procure cows. This is a significant indication that the property he divided was movable property, rather than land ({@Urvarā@}). In the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> the division is said to have been made during Manu's lifetime by his sons, who left only their aged father to Nābhānediṣṭha. According to the Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa,<sup>4</sup> again, four sons divided the inheritance while their old father, Abhipratārin, was still alive. It is, of course, possible to regard Dāya as denoting the heritable property of the family, but the developed {%patria potestas%} of the father, which was early very marked, as shown by the legend of {@Śunaḥśepa,@} is inconsistent with the view that the sons were legally owners with their father, unless and until. they actually insisted on a division of the property.<sup>5</sup> Probably —  there is no evidence of any decisive character — land was not divided at first, but no doubt its disposal began to follow the analogy of cattle and other movable property as soon as the available supply of arable land became limited. <div n="P"/>As for the method of division, it is clear from the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>6</sup> that the elder son was usually preferred; perhaps [Page1-353+ 50] this was always the case after death. During the father's life- time another might be preferred, as appears from a passage of the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>7</sup> Women were excluded from partition or inheritance, according to the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>8</sup> and the Nirukta.<sup>9</sup> They were, no doubt, supported by their brothers; but if they had none they might be reduced to prosti- tution.<sup>10</sup> Detailed rules of inheritance appear in the Sūtras.<sup>11</sup> <div n="P"/>The heir is called Dayada,<sup>12</sup> ‘receiver ({%ā-da%}) of inheritance.’ <F>1) x. 114, 10.</F> <F>2) iii. 1, 9, 4 {%et seq. Cf.%} Muir, {%Sanskrit%} {%Texts,%} 1^2, 191-194; Lévi, {%La Doctrine du%} {%Sacrifice,%} 67, 68.</F> <F>3) v. 14.</F> <F>4) iii. 156 ({%Journal of the American%} {%Oriental Society,%} 26, 61, 62).</F> <F>5) The same question has been raised as to the origin of English or Teutonic property in land generally. Against any idea even of family ownership in a strict sense of the word, see Fustel de Coulanges, {%Recherches sur quelques%} {%Problèmes d'Histoire,%} 322 {%et seq.;%} Ashley, in Fustel de Coulanges, {%Origin of Pro-%} {%perty in Land,%} xvi-xxi; Pollock and Maitland, {%History of English Law,%} 2, 237 {%et seq.%} The older view, which accepted family and communal ownership, repre- sented in different forms by Maine ({%Vil-%} {%lage Communities in the East and West%}), Stubbs, Green, and others, is defended in a new form by Vinogradoff, {%Villanage%} {%in England.%} See also Keith, {%Journal%} {%of the African Society,%} 6, 201 {%et seq.%} Jolly, {%Recht und Sitte,%} 93-96, does not accept the communal ownership of land, but, {%ibid.,%} 80, is inclined to believe in the joint ownership of a family. He admits that this is inconsistent with the strict rule of {%patria potestas,%} which still exists in Bengal; Baden Powell, {%Village%} {%Communities in India,%} 133 {%et seq.,%} doubts the existence in early India of such a {%patria potestas.%} But the facts seem clearly to show that there was such a power, and that the father owned the property. His sons, as they grew up, came to claim the property, and he might have to divide it; hence the idea naturally developed that every child on birth had a legal share in the property. No doubt also from the first the right to part with land was one which grown-up sons and the rest of the community could object to, once the village had acquired a fixed existence. This would account ade- quately for the later system. {%Cf.%} also pp. 100, n. 19; 336, n. 7, and {@Rājanya.@}</F> <F>6) ii. 5, 2, 7.</F> <F>7) xvi. 4, 4.</F> <F>8) iv. 4, 2, 13.</F> <F>9) iii. 4.</F> <F>10) {%Cf.%} {@Ztrī.@}</F> <F>11) Inheritance is also alluded to in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vii. 17; Śāṅkh- āyana Śrauta Sūtra, xv. 27, 3; Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, i. 7, 2, 22; iii. 2, 1, 18. For the Sūtra rules, see Jolly, {%Recht%} {%und Sitte,%} 80 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>12) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xii. 4, 3, 9; Nirukta, iii. 4; metaphorically, Av. v. 18, 6, 14.</F>

{@Dāra,@}¦ ‘wife,’ is found in the Sūtras (usually as a plural masculine), and once (as a singular) in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) vi. 4, 12 (where {%dvāreṇa%} is a {%varia%} {%lectio;%} see St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}). {%Cf.%} Delbrück, {%Die indogermanischen%} {%Verwandtschaftsnamen,%} 415, 416, who {{igneres->ignores||20210704|Dr. Sampada Savardekar|https://github.com/sanskrit-lexicon/csl-corrections/issues/67|}} the Bṛhadāraṇyaka passage.</F>

{@Dārḍha-jayanti,@}¦ ‘descendant of {@Dṛḍhajayanta,@}’ is the patro- nymic of {@Vaipaścita Gupta Lauhitya@} and of {@Vaipaścita@} {@Dṛḍhajayanta Lauhitya@} in the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa (iii. 42, 1).

{@Dārteya,@}¦ ‘descendant of {@Dṛti.@}’ The Dārteyas are mentioned as authorities on sacrificial matters in the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> and the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) xxxi. 2 ({%Indische Studien,%} 3, 473).</F> <F>2) xxv. 3, 6.</F>

{@Dārv-āghāta,@}¦ the ‘woodpecker,’ is included in the list of sacrificial victims at the Aśvamedha, or ‘horse sacrifice,’ in the Yajurveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 15, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 16; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 35. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 92.</F>

Macdonell, 118). The St. Peters- burg Dictionary quotes the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, vii. 4, for Dālbhya (but also for Dārbhya, which is the reading of Lindner's edition).</F> <F>2) i. 8, 1.</F> <F>3) i. 38, 1; 56, 3.</F> <F>4) i. 2, 13; 12, 1, 3.</F> <F>5) xxx. 2, where Dālbhya is read, not Dālbhi, as stated in the St. Peters- burg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} The Kapiṣṭhala Saṃhitā, xlvi. 5, has {%Darbhasya.%} Dālbhi is found, however, in Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, x. 6.</F>

{@Dāva,@}¦ ‘forest fire,’ is mentioned in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> In the latter work such fires are referred to as occurring in spring. According to Sieg,<sup>3</sup> a hymn of the Rigveda<sup>4</sup> describes a forest fire. Watchers were employed to guard against surprise from such conflagrations ({%dāva-pa%}).<sup>5</sup> <F>1) vii. 45, 2.</F> <F>2) xi. 2, 7, 32.</F> <F>3) {%Die Sagenstoffe des Ṛgveda,%} 44 {%et%} {%seq.%}</F> <F>4) x. 142. Sieg's interpretation of this hymn is not at all probable.</F> <F>5) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxx. 16; Tait- tirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 11, 1.</F>
{@Dāva-su Āṅgirasa,@}¦ a seer of Sāmans, or chants, is mentioned in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) xxv. 5, 12, 14. {%Cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 2, 160.</F>

{@Dāśa,@}¦ ‘fisherman,’ is mentioned in the list of victims at the Puruṣamedha, or ‘human sacrifice,’ in the Yajurveda.<sup>1</sup> {%Cf.%} {@Dhaivara.@} <F>1) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxx. 16; Tait- tirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 12, 1. Weber, {%Indische Streifen%} 1, 81, renders the word by {%Fischerknecht,%} perhaps regarding it as equivalent to {%dāsa,%} ‘servant.’ {%Cf.%} Manu, x. 34; St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} Dāśa, 2. 3.</F>

{@Dāśataya,@}¦ ‘belonging to the (Rigveda text) divided into ten (books),’ is an epithet of Adhyāya, ‘section,’ in the Nidāna Sūtra.<sup>1</sup> The feminine form of the word is also found in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> and later<sup>3</sup> <F>1) ii. 11 ({%Indische Studien,%} 1, 45)</F> <F>2) viii. 7.</F> <F>3) Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya, xvi. 54; xvii. 30; Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xii. 2, 16, 22, etc.; Baudhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xxvi. 13; xxvii. 4, etc.</F>

{@Dāśa-rājña@}¦ is the name in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and the Athar- vaveda<sup>2</sup> of {@Sudās'@} famous ‘battle with the ten kings.’ It is somewhat difficult to make out exactly who the kings were (see {@Turvaśa@}), but the number is probably a round one, and cannot be pressed. The actual battle hymn<sup>3</sup> does not contain [Page1-356+ 62] the word, and the passages in which it is found may reasonably be considered late.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) vii. 33, 2, 5; 83, 8.</F> <F>2) x. 128, 12.</F> <F>3) 8, 18</F> <F>4) {%Cf.%} for the late date of vii. 33, Bergaigne, {%L'histoire de la Saṃhita,%} 38, 72; Oldenberg, {%Prolegomena,%} 198, 200, 265, n. 1; Arnold, {%Vedic Metre,%} 309; Geldner, {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 130, opposes this view, but not convincingly.</F>
{@Dāśarma@}¦ appears in the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> as a teacher and a contemporary of {@Āruṇi.@} <F>1) vii. 6. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 3, 472.</F>

{@Dāsa,@}¦ like {@Dasyu,@} sometimes denotes enemies of a demoniac character in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> but in many passages<sup>2</sup> the word refers to human foes of the Āryans. The Dāsas are described as having forts ({%puraḥ%}),<sup>3</sup> and their clans ({%viśaḥ%}) are mentioned.<sup>4</sup> It is possible that the forts, which are called ‘autumnal’ ({%śaradīḥ%}),<sup>5</sup> may be mythical, but it is not essential, for the epithet may allude to their being resorted to in the autumn season. The Dāsa colour ({@Varṇa@})<sup>6</sup> is probably an allusion to the black skin of the aborigines, which is also directly men- tioned.<sup>7</sup> The aborigines (as Dasyus) are called {%anās,%} ‘nose- less’(?),<sup>8</sup> and {%mṛdhra-vāc,%} ‘of hostile speech,’<sup>9</sup> and are probably meant by the phallus-worshippers ({%śiśna-devāḥ,%} ‘whose deity is a phallus’) of the Rigveda.<sup>10</sup> It is significant that constant [Page1-357+ 67] reference is made to the differences in religion between Ārva and Dāsa or Dasyu.<sup>11</sup> <div n="P"/>Since the Dāsas were in many cases reduced to slavery, the word Dāsa has the sense of ‘slave’ in several passages of the Rigveda.<sup>12</sup> Dāsī, the feminine, always has this sense from the Atharvaveda<sup>13</sup> onwards. Aboriginal women were, no doubt, the usual slaves, for on their husbands being slain in battle they would naturally have been taken as servants. They would sometimes also become concubines; thus {@Kavaṣa@} was taunted with being the son of a female slave ({%dāsyāḥ putraḥ%}) in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.<sup>14</sup> <div n="P"/>Ludwig<sup>15</sup> considers that in some passages<sup>16</sup> Dāsa is applied, in the sense of ‘enemy,’ to Āryan foes, but this is uncertain. Zimmer<sup>17</sup> and Meyer<sup>18</sup> think that Dāsa<sup>19</sup> originally meant ‘enemy’ in general, later developing in Iran into the name of the Dahae<sup>20</sup> of the Caspian steppes, and in India into a desig- nation of the aborigines. On the other hand, Hillebrandt<sup>21</sup> argues that, as the Dāsas and the Paṇis are mentioned together,<sup>22</sup> they must be deemed to be closely related tribes, identifying [Page1-358+ 51] the Paṇis with the Parnians and the Dāsas of the Rigveda with the Dahae. This view, of course, necessitates a transfer of the scenes of the Rigveda, where Dāsas are prominent, and especially those in which Divodāsa — ‘the heavenly Dāsa’ — plays an important part,<sup>23</sup> to the far west. Hillebrandt justifies this by regarding the scene of the sixth book of the Rigveda as quite different from that of the seventh and third, in which Sudās, the Bharatas, Vasiṣṭha, and Viśvāmitra appear. The Sarasvatī of the sixth book he locates in Arachosia, that of the seventh in the ‘Middle Country.’ It is, however, extremely doubtful whether this theory can be upheld. That Divodāsa should have been a Dāsa, and yet have fought against other Dāsas, is not in itself likely, especially when his son Sudās appears as a protagonist of Āryan civilization. It also seems unreasonable to seek in Arachosia for the river {@Sarasvati,@} which it is natural to locate in the ‘Middle Country.’ <div n="P"/>The wealth of the Dāsas was no doubt considerable,<sup>24</sup> but in civilization there is no reason to suppose that they were ever equal to the invaders.<sup>25</sup> Leading Dāsas were {@Ilībiśa, Cumuri@} and {@Dhuni, Pipru, Varcin, Śambara.@} For names of aboriginal tribes, see {@Kirāta, Kīkaṭa, Caṇḍāla, Parṇaka, Śiṃyu.@} <F>1) {%Cf.%} Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} p. 157.</F> <F>2) {%Cf.%} Rv. v. 34, 6; vi. 22, 10; 33, 3; 50, 6; vii. 83, 1; x. 38, 3; 69, 6; 3, 1; Av. v. 11, 3.</F> <F>3) ii. 20, 8 (called {%āyasīḥ,%} ‘made of iron’); i. 103, 3; iii. 12, 6; iv. 32, 10. They are called {%śāradīḥ,%} ‘autumnal,’ in 1. 131, 4; 174, 2; vi. 20, 10. {%Cf.%} also {%dehyaḥ,%} ‘ramparts,’ in vi. 47, 2.</F> <F>4) ii. 11, 4; iv. 28, 4; vi. 25, 2.</F> <F>5) {%Cf.%} Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} p. 60.</F> <F>6) ii. 12, 4; Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, viii. 25, 6. {%Cf.%} Rv. i. 101, 1; 130, 8; ii. 20, 7; iv. 16, 13; vi. 47, 21; vii. 5, 3. The Ārya colour is mentioned in iii. 34, 9, and the Dāsa is contrasted with the Varṇa (of the singers) in i. 104, 2. The ‘white-hued ({%śvitnya%}) friends’ who, in i. 100, 18, aid in the conquest of the Dasyu and Siṃyu are doubtless Āryans. In the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 30, the day and night ({%ahorātre%}) are paralleled with the Śūdrāryau — that is, probably with the Āryan and Śūdra (the compound is not to be taken as giving the words in the correct order; {%cf.%} Macdonell, {%Vedic Grammar,%} 268). See also Muir, {%Sanskrit Texts,%} 1^2, 140; Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 10, 10, 11.</F> <F>7) {%kṛṣṇā tvac,%} ‘black skin,’ i. 130, 8; ix. 41, 1.</F> <F>8) {%Cf.%} {@Dasyu,@} notes 6, 7.</F> <F>9) v. 29, 10. See {@Dasyu;@} Geldner, {%Rigveda, Glossar,%} 138.</F> <F>10) vii. 21, 5; x. 99, 3. {%Cf.%} Mac- donell, {%op. cit.,%} p. 155.</F> <F>11) Rv. i. 33, 4. 5; iv. 16, 9; v. 7, 10; 42, 9; vi. 14, 3; viii. 70, 10; x. 22, 7. 8, etc.</F> <F>12) vii. 86, 7; viii. 56, 3; x. 62, 10. Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.,%} 2, suggests that in viii. 46, 32, the word {%dāsān,%} ‘slaves,’ should be read in place of {%dāse,%} qualifying {@Balbūtha.@} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 117, quotes the passage to indicate the admixture of Āryan and Dāsa blood. See also Av. iv. 9, 8; Chāndogya Upaniṣad, vii. 24, 2. {@Didhiṣu@}¦ in the Rigveda denotes a ‘wooer.’ It is applied<sup>1</sup> to the relative, probably brother-in-law,<sup>2</sup> who takes the place of the husband at the funeral rite, and who, as in the Hebraic levirate, is to beget a child by the brother's wife if there is no son.<sup>3</sup> Hillebrandt<sup>4</sup> and Lanman<sup>5</sup> consider that the word originally meant only ‘wooer,’ and applied to the king who, after the chief queen had lain beside the dead victim in the Puruṣamedha or ‘human sacrifice,’ claimed her again; but this view is hardly plausible.<sup>6</sup> The term is also applied to the god Pūṣan<sup>7</sup> as the wooer of his mother, apparently Sūryā.<sup>8</sup> <F>1) x. 18, 18 = Av. xviii. 3, 2 (where {%didhiṣus%} is merely a bad reading) = Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, vi. 1, 3.</F> <F>2) Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra, iv. 2, 18, where are mentioned the brother-in-law ({%devṛ%}), a representative of the husband (there is nothing to show whether he is identical with the preceding or not), a pupil, or an aged servant ({%jarad-dāsa%}).</F> <F>3) {%Cf.%} Rv. x. 40, 2; Kaegi, {%Der Rigveda,%} n. 51.</F> <F>4) {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgen-%} {%ländischen Gesellschaft,%} 40, 708 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>5) {%Sanskrit Reader,%} 385.</F> <F>6) See Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 848, 849; Keith, {%Journal%} {%of the Royal Asiatic Society,%} 1907, 946.</F> <F>7) vi. 55, 5.</F> <F>8) {%Cf.%} Pischel, {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 21; Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} p. 35. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Geldner, {%Rigveda, Kommentar,%} 154.</F>

{@Didhiṣū-pati@}¦ occurs in the Kāṭhaka<sup>1</sup> and Kapiṣṭhala Saṃ- hitās,<sup>2</sup> as well as in the Āpastamba,<sup>3</sup> Gautama,<sup>4</sup> and Vasiṣṭha [Page1-360+ 55] Dharma Sūtras,<sup>5</sup> in lists of people who have committed sin ({%enas%}). The traditional rendering<sup>6</sup> is ‘husband of a woman married a second time’; Manu<sup>7</sup> seems to apply the term to the brother-in-law who is ‘married’ to his sister-in-law after his brother's death for the purpose of begetting a child, if he displays conjugal affection to her ({%anurajyate kāmataḥ%}).<sup>8</sup> This sense would be possible, since {@Didhiṣu@} denotes a ‘wooer,’ and a widow could be regarded as a ‘wooer’ when able to control her own choice of a spouse. But another tradition<sup>9</sup> holds that Didhiṣū means the elder sister whose younger sister has married before her. This view is supported by a passage in the Vasiṣṭha Dharma Sūtra,<sup>10</sup> and by the use of the word {%agre-%} {%didhiṣū-pati,%}<sup>11</sup> which must mean the ‘husband of a younger sister married before the elder.’ In this case also Didhiṣū would mean ‘wooer,’ the elder sister being so called because, if her parents do not arrange a marriage for her, she is, according to Viṣṇu,<sup>12</sup> to make her own choice of a husband ({%kuryāt svayaṃvaram%}). {@Div,@}¦ ‘sky.’ The world as a whole is regarded as divided into the three domains of ‘earth,’ ‘air’ or ‘atmosphere,’ and ‘heaven’ or ‘sky’ ({%div%}),<sup>1</sup> or alternatively into ‘heaven and earth’ ({%dyāvā-pṛthivī%}),<sup>2</sup> which two are then considered as com- prising the universe, the atmosphere being included in the sky. Lightning, wind, and rain belong to the atmosphere, solar and [Page1-361+ 56] similar phenomena to the sky. In some passages<sup>3</sup> the vault ({%nāka%}) of the sky is added after the usual triad, and before the celestial light ({%svar, jyotis%}). <div n="P"/>The threefold division of the universe is reflected in a three- fold division of the three elements — earth, air, and sky. Thus a highest ({%uttama,%}<sup>4</sup> {%uttara,%}<sup>5</sup> {%pārya%}<sup>6</sup> ), a middle, and a lowest heaven are specified.<sup>4</sup> In the Atharvaveda<sup>7</sup> the three heavens are distinguished as ‘rich in water’ ({%udanvatī%}), as {%pīlumatī%} (of uncertain meaning), and as the {%pradyaus,%} where the Fathers sit. Heaven is frequently called {%vyoman%} as well as {%rocana%}<sup>8</sup> (properly the ‘luminous space’ of heaven), and the dividing firmament which separates the visible upper world from the highest heaven is called, besides {%nāka,%} ‘vault,’ {%sānu,%} ‘summit,’ {%viṣṭap,%} ‘surface,’ and {%pṛṣṭha,%} ‘ridge,’ and even ‘ridge of the vault,’<sup>9</sup> or ‘summit of the vault.’<sup>10</sup> <div n="P"/>Similarly three atmospheres ({%rajas%}), or oftener two, are alluded to,<sup>11</sup> but the division here is merely artificial. In one passage<sup>12</sup> six {%rajāṃsi,%} ‘regions,’ are referred to, the heavens and the earths no doubt being meant. The usual name for the atmosphere is {%antarikṣa.%} <div n="P"/>The three earths are equally artificial, the origin of the triad being probably the use of {%pṛthivī%} in the plural<sup>13</sup> to denote the three divisions of the universe (just as {%pitarau,%} ‘two fathers,’ denotes ‘father and mother’).<sup>14</sup> The earth is called {%kṣam, kṣā,%} {%gmā,%} or designated by the epithets {%mahī,%} ‘the great,’ {%pṛthivī%} or {%urvī,%} ‘the broad,’ {%uttānā,%} ‘the extended,’ and is regularly con- trasted as {%idam,%} ‘this world here,’ with the upper sphere.<sup>15</sup> [Page1-362+ 59] The shape of the earth is compared with a wheel in the Rigveda,<sup>16</sup> and is expressly called ‘circular’ ({%pari-maṇḍala%}) in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.<sup>17</sup> When earth is conjoined with heaven, the two are conceived as great bowls ({%camvā%}) turned towards each other.<sup>18</sup> In the Aitareya Āraṇyaka<sup>19</sup> the two are regarded as halves of an egg. The distance of heaven from the earth is given by the Atharvaveda<sup>20</sup> as a thousand days' journey for the sun-bird, by the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>21</sup> as a thousand days' journey for a horse, while the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>22</sup> whimsically estimates the distance as equivalent to a thousand cows standing one on the top of the other. <div n="P"/>According to Zimmer,<sup>23</sup> the Vedic poets conceived the atmosphere to be above the earth in its upper division only, but below it in its lower stratum. The evidence,<sup>24</sup> however, for the latter assumption is quite insufficient.<sup>25</sup> The theory of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>26</sup> is that the sun merely reverses its bright side at night, turning its light on the stars and the moon while it retraverses its course to the east; and it has been shown<sup>25</sup> that this is probably the doctrine of the Rigveda also.<sup>27</sup> literature. The Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa See also {@Sūrya@} and {@Candramās.@} For the Vedic knowledge of the planets, see {@Graha.@} <div n="P"/>There is no geographical division of the earth in Vedic literature. The Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa<sup>28</sup> states that the centre of the earth is a span north of the {@Plakṣa Prāsravaṇā,@} and that the centre of the sky is the constellation of the seven Ṛṣis, the Great Bear. {@Divodāsa Atithigva@}¦ is one of the leading princes of the early Vedic age. He was a son of Vadhryaśva,<sup>1</sup> and father, or more probably grandfather, of {@Sudās,@} the famous king of the {@Tṛtsu@} family, among the {@Bharatas.@} Probably Pijavana was the son and Sudās the grandson. Divodāsa was naturally a {@Bharata,@}<sup>2</sup> and, like Sudās, was an opponent of the {@Turvaśas@} and {@Yadus.@}<sup>3</sup> His great enemy was {@Śambara,@} the {@Dāsa,@} who was apparently chief of a mountain people,<sup>4</sup> and whom he repeatedly defeated.<sup>5</sup> He was also, it seems, like his father Vadhryaśva,<sup>6</sup> an energetic supporter of the fire ritual, for Agni is once called by his name in the Rigveda.<sup>7</sup> On the other hand, he was defeated, with {@Āyu@} and {@Kutsa,@} by Indra's aid. In several passages he seems closely connected with the singer family, the {@Bharadvājas.@}<sup>8</sup> <div n="P"/>From one passage,<sup>9</sup> where Divodāsa is said to have fought against the {@Paṇis,@} the {@Pārāvatas,@} and {@Bṛsaya,@} Hillebrandt<sup>10</sup> has inferred that he was engaged in conflicts with the tribes of Arachosia, and interpreting the name as the ‘heavenly Dāsa’<sup>11</sup> conjectures that he was himself a Dāsa. {@Divya,@}¦ ‘ordeal,’ is a term not found until the later literature, but several references to the practice of ordeals have been seen in Vedic literature. The fire ordeal seen in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> by Schlagintweit,<sup>2</sup> Weber,<sup>3</sup> Ludwig,<sup>4</sup> Zimmer,<sup>5</sup> and others, has been disproved by Grill,<sup>6</sup> Bloomfield,<sup>7</sup> and Whitney.<sup>8</sup> But such an ordeal appears in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa,<sup>9</sup> and an ordeal with a glowing axe<sup>10</sup> occurs in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad as applied in an accusation of theft. Geldner<sup>11</sup> suggests that this usage is referred to even in the Rigveda,<sup>12</sup> but this is most improbable.<sup>13</sup> Ludwig<sup>14</sup> and Griffith<sup>15</sup> discover in another [Page1-365+ 55] passage of the Rigveda<sup>16</sup> references to {@Dīrghatamas'@} having been subjected to the fire and water ordeals, but this view cannot be supported.
