{@Divya Śvan,@}¦ the ‘divine dog,’ in one passage of the Athar- vaveda<sup>1</sup> appears to denote Canis major or Sirius. But Bloom- field<sup>2</sup> thinks that the two divine dogs referred to in the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā<sup>3</sup> and the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa<sup>4</sup> are the sun and moon, and that the sun is meant in the Atharvaveda. <F>1) vi. 80, 1.</F> <F>2) {%Journal of the American Oriental%} {%Society,%} 15, 163; {%Hymns of the Athar-%} {%vaveda,%} 500, 501.</F> <F>3) i. 6, 9.</F> <F>4) i. 1, 2, 4-6. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 353; Whitney, Translation of the Atharva- veda, 341.</F>

{@Diś,@}¦ ‘direction,’ is a word very frequently used in the Rigveda and later<sup>1</sup> to denote a quarter of the sky. As a general rule, four quarters are mentioned — east, south, west, north.<sup>2</sup> But the number of the ‘directions’ is sometimes increased up to ten by the addition to these four of various others. The five points include the zenith ({%ūrdhvā%});<sup>3</sup> the six, the zenith and the nadir ({%ūrdhvā%} and {%avācī%});<sup>4</sup> the seven, the zenith, the ground on which one stands ({%dhruvā%}), and the air ({%antarikṣa%}) between these two ({%vyadhvā%});<sup>5</sup> the eight include the inter- mediate quarters (S.E., S.W., N.E., N.W.);<sup>6</sup> the nine add to these the zenith;<sup>7</sup> the ten, zenith and nadir.<sup>8</sup> The number [Page1-366+ 56] five is sometimes made up by the ground beneath the observer's feet ({%dhruvā%}),<sup>9</sup> and the number six by that point ({%dhruvā%}) and the zenith ({%ūrdhvā%});<sup>10</sup> the ‘lofty’ ({%bṛhatī%})<sup>11</sup> sometimes taking the place of the ‘vertical’ ({%ūrdhvā%}). <F>1) Rv. i. 124, 3; 183, 5; iii. 30, 12; Av. iii. 31, 4; xi. 2, 12, etc.</F> <F>2) Rv. vii. 72, 5; x. 36, 14; 42, 11; Av. xv. 2, 1 {%et seq.,%} etc.</F> <F>3) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vii. 1, 15; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 8, 9.</F> <F>4) Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 12, 8; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxii. 24; Bṛhad- āraṇyaka Upaniṣad, iv. 2, 4.</F> <F>5) Rv. ix. 114, 3; Av. iv. 40, 1; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, vii. 4, 1, 20; ix. 5, 2, 8; Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, i. 7.</F> <F>6) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vii. 1, 15; Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 8, 1, 40, etc.</F> <F>7) Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xvi. 28, 2.</F> <F>8) Rv. i. 164, 14; viii. 101, 13; Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, vi. 2, 2, 34; viii. 4, 2, 13, etc.</F> <F>9) Av. viii. 9, 15; xiii. 3, 6; xv. 14, 1-5; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, ix. 32; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, ix. 4, 3, 10, and {%cf.%} {@Dhruvā.@}</F> <F>10) Av. iii. 27, 1; iv. 14, 8; xii. 3, 55; xv. 4, 1 {%et seq.;%} xviii. 3, 34; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, viii. 14, etc. {%Cf.%} Rv. x. 14, 16.</F> <F>11) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xiv. 13, Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xvii. 8. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 359; Weber, {%Proceedings of the Berlin Academy,%} 1895, 846; {%Indische Studien,%} 17, 293. 294; 18, 153; St. Petersburg Dic- tionary, {%s.v.%}</F>

{@Dīrgha-tamas@}¦ (‘long darkness’) {@Māmateya@} (‘son of Mamatā’) {@Aucathya@} (‘son of Ucatha’) is mentioned as a singer in one hymn of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> and is referred to in several passages<sup>2</sup> by his metronymic, Māmateya, alone. He is said, both in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and in the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka,<sup>3</sup> to have attained the tenth decade of life. In the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>4</sup> he appears as the priest of {@Bharata.@} The Bṛhaddevatā<sup>5</sup> contains a preposterous legend made up of fragments of the Rigveda,<sup>6</sup> according to which Dīrghatamas was born blind, but recovered his sight; in old age he was thrown into a river by his servants, one of whom, {@Traitana,@} attacked him, but killed himself instead. Carried down by the stream, he was cast up in the Aṅga country, where he married Uśij, a slave girl, and begot {@Kakṣīvant.@} The two legends here combined are not even con- sistent, for the second ignores Dīrghatamas' recovery of sight. To attach any historical importance to them, as does Pargiter,<sup>7</sup> would seem to be unwise. <F>1) i. 158, 1. 6.</F> <F>2) i. 147, 3; 152, 6; iv. 4, 13. In viii. 9, 10, Dīrghatamas is mentioned with Kakṣīvant, but not as a relative.</F> <F>1) i. 158, 1. 6.</F> <F>3) ii. 17; Keith, {%Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaha,%} 14.</F> <F>4) viii. 23.</F> <F>5) iv. 11-15; 21-25, with Macdonell's notes.</F> <F>6) From i. 140-164, which hymns are traditionally attributed to Dīrghatamas. But see Oldenberg, {%Zeitschrift der%} {%Deutschen Morgenländischn Gesellschaft,%} 42, 221.</F> <F>7) {%Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society.%} 1910, 44. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rig veda, 3, 164, 165; Muir, {%Sanskrit Texts,%} 1^2, 226, 232, 247, 268, 279.</F>

{@Dīrgha-nītha@}¦ appears to be the proper name of a sacrificer in one hymn of the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) viii. 50, 10. {%Cf.%} Roth, St. Peters- burg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} Ludwig under- stands the word as an adjective, mean- ing ‘of long duration.’</F>

{@Dīrgha-śravas@}¦ (‘far-famed’) is the name of a royal seer who, according to the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> having been banished from his kingdom, and suffering from actual hunger, ‘saw’ a certain Sāman (chant), and thus obtained food. In one passage of the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> an Auśija,<sup>3</sup> a merchant ({%vaṇij%}), is mentioned as {%dīrgha-śravas,%} which may be a proper name, as Sāyaṇa holds, or an adjective, as it is understood by Roth.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) xv. 3, 25.</F> <F>2) i. 112, 11.</F> <F>3) A metronymic, ‘descendant of Uśij,’ according to Sāyaṇa; but an adjective, meaning ‘desirous,’ accord- ing to Roth, St. Petersburg Dic- tionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>4) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rig- veda, 3, 114.</F>

{@Dīrghāpsas,@}¦ used in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as an epithet of a chariot, means, according to Roth,<sup>2</sup> ‘having a long front part.’ <F>1) i. 122, 15.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} {%Cf.%} Pischel, {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 312.</F>

{@Dīrghāyutva,@}¦ ‘longevity,’ is a constant object of the prayers of the Vedic Indians,<sup>1</sup> and length of life is never deprecated in the Saṃhitās and Brāhmaṇas, while the Atharvaveda<sup>2</sup> is full of spells intended to prolong existence ({%āyuṣyāṇi%}). <F>1) Rv. x. 62, 2; Av. i. 22, 2, etc.; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xviii. 6; Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, i. 9, 1, 13, etc. So the adjective {%dīrghāyus,%} Rv. iv. 15, 9. 10; x. 85, 39; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xii. 100, etc. The Brāhmaṇas regularly express the reward for ritual actions by the phrase {%sarvam āyur eti,%} ‘he lives all his days.’ The ideal of life is 100 years. See Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 17, 193; {%Festgruss an Roth,%} 137; Lanman, {%Sanskrit Reader,%} 384.</F> <F>2) ii. 13; 28; 29; vii. 32, and many other hymns. See Bloomfield, {%Hymns%} {%of the Atharvaveda,%} 49 {%et seq.; Atharva-%} {%veda,%} 63-65.</F>

{@Dīrghāraṇya,@}¦ ‘wide tract of forest,’ in the Aitareya<sup>1</sup> and Śatapatha<sup>2</sup> Brāhmanas refers to the extensive jungles which [Page1-368+ 43] must clearly then have covered Northern India. In one of the Aitareya passages<sup>3</sup> it is said that in the east the villages are close together and frequent, while in the west there are forests. <F>1) iii. 44; vi. 23.</F> <F>2) xiii. 3, 7, 10.</F> <F>3) iii. 44.</F>
{@Dīv@}¦ (fem.) in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and the Atharvaveda<sup>2</sup> denotes the ‘game of dice.’ See {@Akṣa.@} <F>1) x. 27, 17.</F> <F>2) vii. 50, 9; 109, 5.</F>
{@Dughā,@}¦ ‘yielding milk,’ denotes ‘cow’ in a few passages in the Saṃhitās.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Rv. viii. 50, 3; x. 67, 1; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxviii. 16, 39, etc.</F>

{@Dundubhi,@}¦ apparently an onomatopoetic word, means ‘drum,’ as used in both war and peace. It is often mentioned from the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> onwards.<sup>2</sup> A special sort of drum was the ‘earth drum,’ made by digging a hole in the ground and covering it with a hide. This was employed in the Mahāvrata, a rite performed at the winter solstice, for the purpose of driving away influences hostile to the return of the sun.<sup>3</sup> A ‘drum- beater’ is included in the list of sacrificial victims at the Puruṣamedha or ‘human sacrifice.’<sup>4</sup> <F>1) i. 28, 5; vi. 47, 29. 31.</F> <F>2) Av. v. 20, 1 {%et seq.;%} 21, 7; 31, 7; vi. 38, 4; xii. 1, 41; Taittirīya Brāh- maṇa, i. 3, 6, 2; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, v. 1, 5, 6; {%dundubhya,%} ‘connected with the drum,’ Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xvi. 35.</F> <F>3) Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxxiv. 5 ({%Indische%} {%Studien,%} 3, 477); Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xvii. 14, 11; Aitareya Āraṇyaka, v. 1, 5, with Keith's notes; Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 148, n. 2; Fried- laender, {%Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka,%} 29, 45.</F> <F>4) Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 13, 1 (not in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā). {%Cf.%} Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, ii. 4, 6. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 289; and for the epic drum in battle, Hopkins, {%Journal of the American Oriental%} {%Society,%} 13, 318.</F>
{@Dur@}¦ is used several times in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> to denote ‘door,’ both literally and metaphorically. <F>1) i. 68, 10; 113, 4; 121, 4; 188, 5; ii. 2, 7, etc.</F>

{@Duroṇa@}¦ is used in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> and sometimes later,<sup>2</sup> to denote ‘home,’ both literally and metaphorically. See {@Gṛha.@} <F>1) iii. 1, 18; 25, 5; iv. 13, 1; v. 76, 4, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. vii. 17, 3; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxxiii. 71, etc.</F>
{@Dur-ga,@}¦ ‘hard to approach,’ occurs in the Rigveda as a neuter substantive only, sometimes in the sense of ‘fort,’ ‘stronghold.’<sup>1</sup> {%Cf.%} {@Pur.@} <F>1) v. 34, 7; vii. 25, 2.</F>

{@Dur-gaha@}¦ is mentioned in a hymn of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> where his grandsons are lauded for their generosity, though Sāyaṇa renders the word adjectivally.<sup>2</sup> In another passage of the Rigveda,<sup>3</sup> however, Sāyaṇa sees in the epithet Daurgaha a description of {@Purukutsa@} as Durgaha's son, who was either captured by the enemy or slain, and whose wife, {@Purukutsānī,@} then obtained a son, {@Trasadasyu,@} to restore the line; he also quotes a story, not found in the Bṛhaddevatā,<sup>4</sup> to support this interpretation. On the other hand, the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>5</sup> seems to take Daurgaha as meaning a horse. Sieg<sup>6</sup> thinks that the same sense should be adopted in the Rigveda passage, which he interprets as referring to the sacrifice of a horse, Daurgaha, by King Purukutsa to gain a son; he also sees in Dadhikrāvan, with Pischel<sup>7</sup> and Ludwig,<sup>8</sup> a real horse, the charger of Trasadasyu. The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa's inter- pretation of Daurgaha is, however, doubtful, and cannot be regarded as receiving support from the case of Dadhikrāvan, who was probably a divinity, and not a real horse at all.<sup>9</sup> <F>1) viii. 65, 12.</F> <F>2) ‘Plunged in distress’ ({%duḥkhaṃ%} {%gāhamāna%}).</F> <F>3) iv. 42, 8.</F> <F>4) As Roth. St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.,%} says it is.</F> <F>5) xiii. 5, 4, 5. According to the Naighaṇṭuka (i. 14), Daurgaha is a synonym of ‘horse.’</F> <F>6) {%Die Sagenstoffe des Ṛgveda,%} 96-102.</F> <F>7) {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 124.</F> <F>8) Translation of the Rigveda, 4, 79. {%Cf.%} Oldenberg, {%Religion des Veda,%} 71.</F> <F>9) Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} pp. 148, 149. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Ludwig, {%op. cit.,%} 3, 163, 174; Oldenberg, {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 301, 302.</F>

{@Dur-ṇāman,@}¦ ‘of evil name,’ is the designation in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and the Atharvaveda<sup>2</sup> of a demon causing disease, or the disease itself. The Nirukta<sup>3</sup> explains the words as meaning a ‘worm,’ an interpretation which accords with the wide- spread belief in disease-causing worms.<sup>4</sup> Later Durnāman denotes ‘hæmorrhoids.’<sup>5</sup> <F>1) x. 162, 2.</F> <F>2) ii. 25, 2; viii. 6, 1 {%et seq.;%} xvi. 6, 7; xix. 36, 1 {%et seq.%} So also the feminine Durṇāmnī, iv. 17, 5; xix. 36, 6.</F> <F>3) vi. 12.</F> <F>4) Bloomfield, {%Atharvaveda,%} 61; {%Hymns%} {%of the Atharvaveda,%} 314 {%et seq.,%} 351.</F> <F>5) Suśruta, 1, 177, 10, etc.</F>

{@Dur-mukha,@}¦ ‘ugly-faced,’ is the name, in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> of a Pāñcāla, that is, Pañcāla king, who conquered the world, and whose priest was {@Bṛhaduktha.@} <F>1) viii. 23. The reading may be {%a-rājā,%} ‘not a king,’ but this is not necessary.</F>

{@Durya,@}¦ ‘belonging to the door or house,’ appears in several passages of the Saṃhitās<sup>1</sup> as a plural substantive denoting the ‘door-posts,’ or more generally ‘dwelling.’ <F>1) Masculine plural, Rv. i. 91, 19; x. 40, 12; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, i. 6, 3, 1; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, i. 11; feminine plural, Rv. iv. 1, 9. 18; 2, 12; vii. 1, 11.</F>
{@Duryoṇa@}¦ occurs a few times in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> in the sense of ‘house.’ <F>1) i. 174, 7; v. 29, 10; 32, 8.</F>

{@Dur-varāha@}¦ probably denotes a ‘wild boar.’ It is mentioned in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> and the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) xii. 4, 1, 4.</F> <F>2) i. 51, 4 ({%Journal of the American Oriental Society,%} 23, 332).</F>
{@Dulā.@}¦ See {@Nakṣatra (Kṛttikās).@}

{@Duś-carman,@}¦ ‘afflicted with a skin disease,’ occurs in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> and Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> The disease meant is probably leprosy, the usual name of which is {@Kilāsa.@}<sup>3</sup> <F>1) ii. 1, 4, 3; 5, 1, 7.</F> <F>2) i. 7, 8, 3.</F> <F>3) Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xiv. 3, 17; xxiii. 16, 11; Taittirīya Āraṇyaka v. 4, 12.</F>

{@Duḥ-śāsu@}¦ is possibly a proper name in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> and would then denote an enemy of {@Kuruśravaṇa.@} Ludwig<sup>2</sup> thinks that he was a {@Parśu@} or Persian, but this is most improbable, and the word may simply be an adjective meaning ‘malignant.’ <F>1) x. 33, 1.</F> <F>2) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 165.</F>

{@Duḥ-śīma@}¦ is mentioned in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as a generous donor, his patronymic perhaps being {@Tānva.@}<sup>2</sup> <F>1) x. 93, 14.</F> <F>2) x. 93, 15. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rig- veda, 3, 166.</F>

{@Duṣ-ṭarītu,@}¦ ‘hard to defeat,’ is the name of a king of the {@Sṛñjayas,@} who was deposed from a principality that had existed for ten generations, but was re-instated by {@Cākra@} {@Sthapati@} in spite of the resistance of {@Balhika Prātipīya,@} according to the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) xii. 9, 3, 1 {%et seq. Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 205-207.</F>
{@Duḥ-ṣanta.@}¦ See {@Dauḥṣanti.@}

{@Duhitṛ@}¦ is the regular designation of ‘daughter’ from the Rigveda onwards.<sup>1</sup> The word appears to be derived from {%duh,%} ‘milk,’ in the sense of one who nourishes a child, rather than as the ‘milker’ of the primitive family or the suckling.<sup>2</sup> See also {@Strī, Pati, Pitṛ, Bhrātṛ.@} <F>1) Rv. viii. 101, 15; x. 17, 1; 40, 5; 61, 5, 7; Av. ii. 14, 2; vi. 100, 3; vii. 12, 1; x. 1, 25; Śatapatha Brāh- maṇa, i. 7, 4, 1; 8, 1, 8, etc.</F> <F>2) Delbrück, {%Dic indogermanischen Ver-%} {%wandtschaftsnamen,%} 454.</F>

{@Dūta,@}¦ ‘messenger’ or envoy,' is found several times in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later,<sup>2</sup> used metaphorically. The {@Sūta@} seems to have performed the duties later assigned to the Dūta. <F>1) iii. 3, 2; vi. 8, 4; vii. 3, 3; x. 14, 12.</F> <F>2) Av. viii. 8, 10, etc.; Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 5, 1, 6; Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad, ii. 1, etc. The feminine form Dūtī is found in Rv. x. 108, 2, 3, in the story of Saramā's mission to the Paṇis. Dūtya, ‘mission,’ occurs in Rv. 1, 12, 4; 161, 1; iv. 7, 8; 8, 4, etc.</F>

{@Dūrvā,@}¦ a species of grass ({%Panicum dactylon%}), is mentioned frequently from the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> onwards.<sup>2</sup> It grew in damp ground.<sup>3</sup> A simile occurring in the Rigveda<sup>4</sup> seems to indicate that the ears lay horizontal with the stem. {%Cf.%} {@Pākadūrvā.@} <F>1) x. 16, 13; 134, 5; 142, 8.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iv. 2, 9, 2; v. 2, 8, 3; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xiii. 20; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, viii. 5. 8; Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, iv. 5, 10, 5; vii. 4, 2, 10, 12, etc.</F> <F>3) Rv. x. 16, 13; 142, 8.</F> <F>4) x. 134, 5. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 70.</F>

{@Dūrśa,@}¦ denoting some kind of garment, is mentioned twice in the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> Weber<sup>2</sup> thinks that it was worn by the aborigines. <F>1) iv. 7, 6; viii. 6, 11.</F> <F>2) {%Indische Studien,%} 18, 29.</F>

{@Dūṣīkā,@}¦ ‘rheum of the eyes,’ is mentioned as a disease in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) xvi. 6, 8.</F> <F>2) Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxxiv. 12; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xxv. 9; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 1, 3, 10.</F>

{@Dṛḍha-cyut Āgasti@}¦ (‘descendant of Agastya’) is mentioned in the Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> as having been Udgātṛ priest at the Sattra (‘sacrificial session’) of the Vibhindukīyas. <F>1) iii. 233 ({%Journal of the American%} {%Oriental Society,%} 18, 38). He is given in the Anukramaṇī (where the form of the patronymic is Āgastya) as the author of Rv. ix. 25. {%Cf. Indische%} {%Studien,%} 3, 219.</F>
{@Dṛḍha-jayanta.@}¦ See {@Vipaścit@} and {@Vaipaścita.@}

1. {@Dṛti,@}¦ a ‘leather bag to hold fluids,’ is frequently mentioned in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> In one passage<sup>3</sup> it is called {%dhmāta,%} ‘inflated,’ the man afflicted with dropsy being compared with such a bag. Milk ({@Kṣīra@}) and intoxicating liquor ({@Surā@}) are mentioned as kept in bags.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) i. 191, 10; iv. 51, 1, 3; v. 83, 7; vi. 48, 18; 103, 2; viii. 5, 19; 9, 18.</F> <F>2) Av. vii. 18, 1; Taittirīya Saṃ- hitā, i. 8, 19, 1; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxvi. 18, 19; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 8, 3, 4; Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, v. 10, 2, etc.</F> <F>3) Rv. vii. 89, 2. {%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%Journal%} {%of the American Oriental Society,%} 20, 30.</F> <F>4) Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xiv. 11, 26; xvi. 13, 13.</F>

2. {@Dṛti Aindrota@}¦ (‘descendant of {@Indrota@}’) is mentioned in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇā<sup>1</sup> as a contemporary of {@Abhipratārin@} {@Kākṣaseni@} and as a pupil of {@Indrota Daivāpa@} in a Vaṃśa (list of teachers) in the Jaīminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> Possibly the same Dṛti is meant in the compound Dṛti-Vātavantau, which is found in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>3</sup> The former is here said to have continued, after the Mahāvrata was over, the sacrificial session in which both had been engaged, with the result that his descendants prospered more than the Vātavatas. <F>1) xiv. 1, 12. 15.</F> <F>2) iii. 40, 2.</F> <F>3) xxv. 3, 6. So a Sattra of a year's duration is later called {%Dṛti-vātavator%} {%ayana,%} Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xxiv. 4, 16; 6, 25; Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xii. 3; Śāṅkhāyana Srauta Sūtra, xiii. 23, 1; Lāṭyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, x. 10, 7. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%Transactions of the Con-%} {%necticut Academy of Arts and Sciences,%} 15, 52, 53.</F>
{@Dṛpta-bālāki Gārgya@}¦ (‘descendant of {@Garga@}’) is the name of a teacher who is mentioned in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (ii. 1, 1) as a contemporary of {@Ajātaśatru@} of {@Kāśi.@}

{@Dṛbhīka@}¦ is the name of a man<sup>1</sup> or a demon,<sup>2</sup> who, according to the Rigveda,<sup>3</sup> was slain by Indra. <F>1) Ludwig, Translation of the Rig- veda, 3, 152, 207, who compares the Derbikes; Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} p. 162.</F> <F>2) Grassmann, {%Wörterbuch, s.v.;%} Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.;%} Geldner, {%Rigveda, Glossar,%} 85.</F> <F>3) ii. 14, 3.</F>
{@Dṛśāna Bhārgava@}¦ (‘descendant of {@Bhṛgu@}’) is mentioned as a seer in the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) xvi. 8. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 3, 459.</F>

{@Dṛṣad@}¦ appears in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and Atharvaveda<sup>2</sup> to denote not a millstone,<sup>3</sup> but merely a stone used to pound grain, which was placed on another stone as a support. When used later<sup>4</sup> [Page1-374+ 44] in connexion with {@Upalā,@} the lower and the upper millstone, or mortar and pestle may be meant; but this is not certain. Eggeling<sup>5</sup> renders them as the large and small millstones. See also {@Upara@} and {@Upalā.@} <F>1) vii. 104, 22; viii. 72, 4.</F> <F>2) ii. 31, 1; v. 23, 8.</F> <F>3) Roth. St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.;%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 269.</F> <F>4) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, i. 6, 8, 3; 9, 3; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 1, 1, 22; ii. 6, 1, 9, etc.</F> <F>5) {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 12, 11 ({%dṛṣad-upale,%} which are here distin- guished from ‘mortar and pestle,’ {%ulūkhala-musale%}). <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Pischel, {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 108, 109.</F>

{@Dṛṣadvatī,@}¦ ‘stony,’ is the name of a river which flows into the {@Sarasvatī@} after running for a time parallel to it. It is mentioned in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> along with the Sarasvatī and the {@Āpayā,@} as the scene of action of the Bharata princes. In the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> and later<sup>3</sup> the Dṛṣadvatī and the Sarasvatī are the scene of special sacrifices. In Manu<sup>4</sup> these two rivers form the western boundary of the Middle Country. <F>1) iii. 23, 4.</F> <F>2) xxv. 10, 13.</F> <F>3) Kātyāyana Srauta Sūtra, xxiv. 6, 6, 38; Lāṭyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, x. 19, 4.</F> <F>4) ii. 17. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 18; Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 34; {%Indian%} {%Literature,%} 67, 102; Macdonell, {%Vedic%} {%Mythology,%} p. 87.</F>
{@Dṛṣṭa.@}¦ See {@Adṛṣṭa.@}

{@Devaka Mānyamāna@}¦ (‘descendant of Manyamāna’) appears in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as an opponent of the Tṛtsus, and as connected with Śambara. Possibly, however, as Grassmann suggests, the words should be understood as denoting Śambara, ‘who deemed himself a god,’ {%devaka%} being used contemptuously.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) vii. 18, 20 ({%devakaṃ cin mānya-%} {%mānam%}).</F> <F>2) {%Cf.%} Rv. ii. 11. 2 ({%amartyaṃ cid dāsam%} {%manyamānam%}). <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 173.</F>

{@Devakī-putra,@}¦ ‘son of Devakī,’ is the metronymic of {@Kṛṣṇa@} in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.<sup>1</sup> According to the Epic,<sup>2</sup> a Devaka was father of Devakī, Kṛṣṇa's mother; the St. Peters- burg Dictionary suggests that he was the ‘king of the Gandh- arvas’, also referred to in the Epic.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) iii. 17, 6.</F> <F>2) Mahābhārata, i. 4480; v. 80, etc.</F> <F>3) {%Ibid.,%} i. 2704.</F>

{@Deva-jana-vidyā,@}¦ ‘knowledge of divine beings,’ is one of the sciences enumerated in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> and the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) xiii. 4, 3, 10. {%Cf.%} x. 5, 2, 20.</F> <F>2) vii. 1, 2. 4; 2, 1; 7, 1.</F>

{@Deva-taras Śyāvasāyana Kāśyapa@}¦ (‘descendant of Kaśyapa’) is mentioned in the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> as a pupil of {@Rsyasṛṅga.@} In the Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa,<sup>2</sup> as Śāvasāyana, he is a pupil of his father Śavas, who again was a pupil of Kāśyapa. <F>1) iii. 40, 2.</F> <F>2) {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 373.</F>

{@Devatyā@}¦ occurs in the text of the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> where it must, if the reading is correct, denote some animal.<sup>2</sup> But the reading should no doubt be {%rohiṇī-devatyās,%} ‘having the red one as deity.’<sup>3</sup> <F>1) i. 22, 3.</F> <F>2) Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>3) Whitney, Translation of the Athar- vaveda, 23.</F>

{@Devana@}¦ is mentioned once in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> in connexion with dicing. The word must designate the place on which the dice are thrown (elsewhere called {@Adhidevana@}), and it is so explained by Durga in his commentary on the Nirukta.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) x. 43, 5.</F> <F>2) v. 22. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Lüders, {%Das Würfelspiel im alten%} {%Indien,%} 14.</F>

{@Deva-nakṣatra,@}¦ ‘asterism of the gods,’ is the name applied in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> to the first fourteen lunar mansions, which are said to be south, while the others are called Yama- nakṣatra, ‘asterisms of Yama,’ and are said to be north. See {@Nakṣatra.@} <F>1) i. 5, 2, 6, 7. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Naxatra,%} 2, 309, 310.</F>

{@Deva-bhāga Śrautarṣa@}¦ is mentioned in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> as the Purohita, or ‘domestic priest,’ of both the [Page1-376+ 35] {@Sṛñjayas@} and the {@Kurus.@} In the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> he is said to have taught {@Girija Bābhravya@} the science of the dissection of the sacrificial animal ({%pasor vibhakti%}). In the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> he is an authority on the Sāvitra Agni. <F>1) ii. 4, 4, 5. This passage is mis- quoted by Sāyaṇa on Rv. i. 81, 3. See Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 2, 9. n.; Geldner, {%Vedische Studien,%} 3, 152.</F> <F>2) vii. x.</F> <F>3) iii. 10, 9, 11.</F>

{@Deva-malimluc,@}¦ ‘robber of the gods,’ is the epithet of Rahasya,<sup>1</sup> who is said in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> to have slain the pious {@Vaikhānasas@} at {@Munimaraṇa@} (‘saint's death’). He was apparently an Asura, but may have been a real person. <F>1) Or Rahasyu.</F> <F>2) xiv. 4, 7. {%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%Transactions%} {%of the Connecticut Academy of Arts and%} {%Sciences,%} 15, 51, 52.</F>
{@Deva-muni,@}¦ ‘divine saint,’ is the epithet of {@Tura@} in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa (xxv. 14, 5). The name is given in the Anukramaṇī to the author of a hymn of the Rigveda (x. 146).
{@Deva-rājan@}¦ apparently denotes a king of Brahminical descent in the phrase ‘Sāmans of Devarājans’ in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa (xviii. 10, 5). {%Cf.%} {@Rājanyarṣi@} and {@Varṇa.@}

{@Deva-rāta@}¦ (‘god-given’) {@Vaiśvāmitra@} (‘descendant of {@Viśvā-@} {@mitra@}’) is the name given to Śunaḥśepa after his adoption by Viśvāmitra in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) vii. 17. {%Cf.%} Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xv. 27.</F>
{@Devala@}¦ is mentioned as a Ṛṣi in the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā (xxii. 11). See also {@Daivala.@}

{@Devavant@}¦ is mentioned in a Dānastuti (‘Praise of Gifts’) in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as the ancestor of {@Sudās,@} apparently his grand- father; or if {@Pijavana@} be accepted as Sudās' father, and {@Divodāsa@} as his grandfather, then his great-great-grandfather, and father of {@Vadhryaśva.@} The succession in the latter case would then be Devavant, Vadhryaśva, Divodāsa, Pijavana, Sudās. <F>1) vii. 18, 22. {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 171; Geldner, {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 138.</F>

{@Deva-vāta@}¦ (‘desired of the gods’) is the name of a {@Bharata@} prince in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> where he is mentioned as sacrificing on the {@Dṛṣadvatī, Sarasvatī,@} and {@Āpayā.@} <F>1) iii. 23, 2. {%Cf.%} Oldenberg, {%Buddha,%} 409; Pischel, {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 218.</F>
{@Deva-vidyā,@}¦ ‘knowledge of the gods,’ is one of the sciences enumerated in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (vii. 1, 2, 4; 2, 1; 7, 1).

{@Deva-śravas@}¦ is the name of a {@Bharata@} prince who with {@Devavāta@} appears as a sacrificer on the {@Dṛṣadvatī, Sarasvatī,@} and {@Āpayā@} in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) iii. 23, 2. 3. In the Anukramaṇī he is called a son of Yama, and has a hymn, x. 17, ascribed to him.</F>

{@Devātithi Kāṇva@}¦ (‘descendant of {@Kaṇva@}’) is mentioned in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> as the seer of a Sāman (chant) by which he turned pumpkins into cows for himself and his son when they were starving in the desert, whither they had been driven by rivals. He is also the reputed author of a hymn of the Rigveda.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) ix. 2, 19.</F> <F>2) viii. 4. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%Transactions of the Con-%} {%necticut Academy of Arts and Sciences,%} 15, 61.</F>

{@Devāpi Ārṣṭiṣeṇa@}¦ (‘descendant of Ṛṣṭiṣeṇa’) is mentioned in a hymn of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and in the Nirukta.<sup>2</sup> According to the latter source there were two brothers, {@Devāpi@} and {@Śantanu,@} princes of the Kurus. The elder was Devāpi, but Śantanu got himself anointed king, whereupon no rain fell for twelve years. The drought being attributed by the Brahmins to his having superseded his elder brother, Śantanu offered the kingdom to Devāpi. The latter, however, refused, but acting as Purohita, or domestic priest, for his brother, obtained rain. The Bṛhad- devatā<sup>3</sup> tells much the same tale, but adds that the reason for Devāpi's exclusion from the throne was the fact that he suffered from a skin disease. The Epic and later legends further [Page1-378+ 54] develop the story, presenting two somewhat discrepant accounts. According to the one version,<sup>4</sup> the ground of Devāpi's being passed over was leprosy, while in the other his devoting himself to asceticism in his youth was the cause of his brother's taking his place. The Epic,<sup>5</sup> moreover, treats him as a son of Pratīpa, and names as his brothers Bāhlīka<sup>6</sup> and Āṛṣṭiṣeṇa,<sup>7</sup> who is a new figure developed from the patronymic of Devāpi Possibly Sieg<sup>8</sup> is right in holding that two stories, those of Devāpi, Pratīpa's son, and of Devāpi, Ṛṣṭiṣeṇa's son, have been confused; but in any case it is impossible to extract history from them.<sup>9</sup> <div n="P"/>The Rigvedic hymn certainly appears to represent Devāpi as sacrificing for Śantanu, who seems to be called {@Aulāna.@}<sup>10</sup> But there is no trace in it of the brotherhood of the two men, nor is there anything to show that Devāpi was not a Brahmin, but a Kṣatriya. Sieg,<sup>11</sup> who interprets the hymn by the Nirukta, thinks that he was a Kṣatriya, but on this occasion was enabled by the favour of Bṛhaspati to officiate as priest, and that the hymn shows clear recognition of the unusual character of his action; but this view seems very improbable. <F>1) x. 98.</F> <F>2) ii. 10.</F> <F>3) vii. 148 {%et seq.,%} with Macdonell's notes.</F> <F>4) Mahābhārata, v. 5054 {%et seq.%} (= 149, 15 {%et seq.%}), where Śāntanu is (as also in the Agni, cclxxvii. 34, the Brahma, xiii. 114, 118, and the Viṣṇu Purāṇas) the form of the name; Matsya Purāṇa, l, 39 {%et seq.,%} in which, as well as in the Bhāgavata, ix. 22, 12, 13, and the Vāyu Purāṇa, xcix. 234, 237, the form is Śantanu.</F> <F>5) Mahābhārata, i. 3751 (= 94, 62); ix. 2285 (= 40, 1); Vāyu Purāṇa, ii. 37, 230, etc.</F> <F>6) Mahābhārata, cited in n. 4; Hari- vaṃśa, 1819.</F> <F>7) {%Ibid.,%} cited in n. 5.</F> <F>8) {%Die Sagenstoffe des Ṛgveda,%} 136.</F> <F>9) As does Pargiter, {%Journal of the%} {%Royal Asiatic Society,%} 1910, 52, 53.</F> <F>10) Rv. x. 98, 11.</F> <F>11) {%Op. cit.,%} 129-142. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Muir, {%Sanskrit Texts,%} 1^2, 272 {%et seq.;%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 203; Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 192 {%et seq.;%} Macdonell, {%Bṛhaddevatā,%} 1, xxix; Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 131, 132.</F>

{@Devṛ@}¦ is a rare word denoting the wife's ‘brother-in-law’ (that is, the husband's brother). He is included with the sisters of the husband among those over whom the wife of the husband — his elder brother — rules;<sup>1</sup> at the same time the wife is to be devoted to him,<sup>2</sup> and friendly to him.<sup>3</sup> After the death [Page1-379+ 50] of the husband the Devṛ could perform the duty of begetting a son for him.<sup>4</sup> No word occurs for the wife's brother corresponding to Devṛ. <F>1) Rv. x. 85, 46. {%Cf.%} {@Pati.@}</F> <F>2) Rv. x. 85, 44.</F> <F>3) Av. xiv. 2, 18. {%Cf.%} xiv. 1, 39.</F> <F>4) Rv. x. 40, 2. {%Cf.%} x. 18, 8; Kaegi, {%Der Rigveda,%} n. 51; Lanman, {%Sanskrit%} {%Reader,%} 385; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 948. {%Cf.%} Delbrück, {%Die indogermanischen Verwandtschafts-%} {%namen,%} 516.</F>

{@Deśa,@}¦ ‘land,’ is a word that does not come into use till the time of the Upaniṣads and Sūtras,<sup>1</sup> excepting one occurrence in the latest period of the Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> literature, and one in a much-discussed passage of the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā,<sup>3</sup> where the {@Sarasvatī@} is mentioned as having five tributaries. This passage militates against the view that Sarasvatī was a name of the Indus, because the use of Deśa here seems to indicate<sup>4</sup> that the seer of the verse placed the Sarasvatī in the Madhya- deśa or ‘Middle Country,’ to which all the geographical data of the Yajurvedas point.<sup>5</sup> <F>1) Where its use becomes common; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, iv. 1, 16; 2, 3; Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, iv. 14, 6; Kātyāyana Srauta Sūtra, xv. 4, 17, etc. So the adjective {%deśīya,%} ‘belong- ing to a land,’ Kātyāyana, xxii. 4, 22; Lāṭyāyana Srauta Sūtra, viii. 6, 28.</F> <F>2) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, viii. 10 (a late passage).</F> <F>3) xxxiv. 11.</F> <F>4) {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 10, who thinks that the word crept into the text, where the Sarasvatī originally meant the Indus, with the five tribu- taries of the Panjab.</F> <F>5) Macdonell, {%Sanskrit Literature,%} 174.</F>

{@Dehī@}¦ in two passages of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> refers to defences thrown up against an enemy, apparently earthworks or dikes. {%Cf.%} {@Pur.@} <F>1) vi. 47, 2; vii. 6, 5. {%Cf.%} Schrader, {%Prehistoric Antiquities,%} 344; Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 143.</F>

{@Daidhiṣavya@}¦ is mentioned in a Mantra of the Taittirīya Saṃhitā.<sup>1</sup> Apparently the word (as derived from {@Didhiṣū@}) denotes the son of a younger sister married before the elder sister,<sup>2</sup> rather than the son of a woman twice married, the explanation of the St. Petersburg Dictionary. <F>1) iii. 2, 4, 4; Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, ii. 1, 22; Kauśika Sūtra, 3, 5; 137, 37.</F> <F>2) {%American Journal of Philology,%} 17, 431, n.</F>

{@Daiyāṃpāti,@}¦ ‘descendant of Dayāṃpāta,’ is the name of a teacher of the east, who was instructed by {@Śāṇḍilyāyana,@} according to the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (ix. 5, 1, 14), in the lore of the construction of the fire-altar. The same patronymic is given, in the form of Dayyāṃpāti, to {@Plakṣa,@} the contemporary of {@Atyaṃhas@} in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa (iii. 10, 9, 3-5).

1. {@Daiva@}¦ (masc.) appears in the list of sciences in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad,<sup>1</sup> where Śaṅkara explains it as {%utpāta-%} {%jñāna,%} apparently the ‘knowledge of portents.’ The St. Peters- burg Dictionary suggests that the word is here used adjectivally, and this view is followed by Little<sup>2</sup> and by Böhtlingk in his translation.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) vii. 1, 2, 4; 2, 1; 7, 1.</F> <F>2) {%Grammatical Index,%} 83.</F> <F>3) Though he does not render it ({%Daiva Nidhi%}).</F>
2. {@Daiva@}¦ is the patronymic of the mythical Atharvan in the first two Vaṃśas (lists of teachers) of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) ii. 5, 22; iv. 5, 28 (Mādhyaṃdina).</F>
{@Daivala,@}¦ ‘descendant of Devala,’ is the patronymic of {@Asita@} in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa (xiv. 11, 18).

{@Daiva-vāta,@}¦ ‘descendant of {@Devavāta,@}’ is the patronymic of {@Sṛñjaya,@} probably the Sṛñjaya king, in the Rigveda. He is mentioned<sup>1</sup> as a devotee of the fire cult, and as victorious over the {@Turvaśa@} king and the {@Vṛcīvants.@}<sup>2</sup> According to Zimmer,<sup>3</sup> his name was {@Abhyāvartin Cāyamāna Pārthava@} (‘descendant of Pṛthu’), but Hillebrandt<sup>4</sup> recognizes this as doubtful, though he none the less places the Sṛñjayas to the west of the Indus with {@Divodāsa.@} What is more important is to note that the name suggests connexion with the Bharata {@Devavāta,@} and as {@Kurus@} and Sṛñjayas were closely connected<sup>5</sup> this is not immaterial. <F>1) Rv. iv. 15, 4.</F> <F>2) Rv. vi. 27, 7.</F> <F>3) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 133, 134.</F> <F>4) {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 105, 106.</F> <F>5) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 4, 4, 5. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Oldenberg, {%Buddha,%} 402, 405; Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 153.</F>

{@Daivāpa,@}¦ ‘descendant of {@Devāpi,@}’ is the patronymic of {@Indrota@} in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> and the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> No connexion can be traced with the Devāpi of the Rigveda.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) xiii. 5, 4, 1.</F> <F>2) iii. 40, 1.</F> <F>3) x. 98. See Oldenberg, {%Zeitschrift%} {%der Deutschen Morgenlāndischen Gesell-%} {%schaft,%} 42, 240.</F>
{@Daivāvṛdha,@}¦ ‘descendant of Devāvṛdha,’ is the patronymic of {@Babhru@} in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (vii. 34).

{@Daivo-dāsi,@}¦ ‘descendant of {@Divodāsa,@}’ is the patronymic of {@Pratardana@} in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> and the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad.<sup>2</sup> It is impossible to ascertain whether the famous Divodāsa is meant. <F>1) xxvi. 5.</F> <F>2) iii. 1. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 214.</F>

{@Doṣā,@}¦ ‘evening,’ is frequently referred to from the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> onwards,<sup>2</sup> usually as contrasted with {%uṣas,%} ‘dawn.’ In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad<sup>3</sup> the word is contrasted with {%prātar,%} ‘early.’ See also {@Ahan.@} <F>1) i. 34, 3; 179, 1; ii. 8, 3; iv. 2, 8; v. 5, 6; 32, 11; vi. 5, 2, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. vi. 1, 1; Nirukta, iv. 17.</F> <F>3) vi. 13, 1.</F>

{@Doha,@}¦ ‘milking,’ is a common word in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> Reference is made in the Sūtras<sup>3</sup> to the {%sāyaṃ-doha,%} ‘evening milking,’ and the {%prātar-doha,%} ‘morning milking.’ Dohana has the same sense.<sup>4</sup> See also {@Go.@} <F>1) iv. 11, 4. 9. 12; v. 17, 17; viii. 9, 15 (where five milkings are referred to metaphorically). In Rv. x. 42, 2, the literal sense is found.</F> <F>2) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, viii. 62; Tait- tirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 1, 10, 2; ii. 2, 9, 9, etc.</F> <F>3) Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, iv. 2, 38, etc.</F> <F>4) Rv. viii. 12, 32; Satapatha Brāh- maṇa, ix. 2, 3, 30; Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, iv. 2, 37, etc.</F>
{@Daure-śravas,@}¦ ‘descendant of Dūreśravas,’ is the patronymic of the priest {@Pṛthuśravas,@} who officiated at the snake sacrifice described in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa (xxv. 15, 3).
{@Daure-śruta,@}¦ ‘descendant of Dūreśruta,’ is the patronymic of the priest {@Timirgha,@} who officiated at the snake sacrifice described in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa (xxv. 15, 3).
{@Daur-gaha.@}¦ See {@Durgaha.@}
{@Dauḥ-ṣanti@}¦ (‘descendant of Duḥṣanta’) is the patronymic of Bharata in the Aitareya (viii. 23) and Śatapatha (xiii. 5, 4, 11) Brāhmaṇas.

{@Dyutāna Māruta@}¦ (‘descendant of the Maruts’) is the name of a divine being invoked in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> and the Taittirīya Saṃhitā,<sup>2</sup> and also mentioned in the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā.<sup>3</sup> In the Śatapatha<sup>4</sup> Brāhmaṇa the name is explained to mean Vāyu, while in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>5</sup> he seems to be regarded as the author of a Sāman (chant). He is treated as a Ṛṣi by the Anukramaṇī, which credits him with the authorship of a hymn of the Rigveda (viii. 96). <F>1) v. 27.</F> <F>2) v. 5, 9, 4. {%Cf.%} vi. 2, 10, 4.</F> <F>3) xv. 7.</F> <F>4) iii. 6, 1, 16.</F> <F>5) xvii. 1, 7. {%Cf.%} vi. 4, 2. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 3, 311; {%Indische Studien,%} 3, 220.</F>

{@Dyumna,@}¦ according to Pischel,<sup>1</sup> denotes ‘raft’ in one passage of the Rigveda.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgen-%} {%ländischen Gesellschaft,%} 35, 720 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>2) viii. 19, 14.</F>

{@Dyūta,@}¦ ‘dicing,’ is mentioned in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and the Sūtras.<sup>2</sup> See {@Akṣa.@} <F>1) xii. 3, 46.</F> <F>2) Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xv. 6, 2; Lāṭyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, iv. 10, 23, etc.</F>

{@Dyotana@}¦ is, according to Sāyaṇa, the name of a prince in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> This is probably correct, though the word may also<sup>2</sup> be interpreted as denoting ‘glorification’ but it is not clear what relation existed between Dyotana and the other persons mentioned in the same passage, {@Vetasu, Daśoṇi,@} {@Tūtuji,@} and {@Tugra.@} <F>1) vi. 20, 8.</F> <F>2) As by Griffith, {%Hymns of the Rigveda,%} 1, 380. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Oldenberg, {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen%} {%Morgenländischen Gesellschaft,%} 55, 328.</F>

{@Drapsa@}¦ is a common word from the Rigveda onwards<sup>1</sup> for a ‘drop’: according to Sāyaṇa,<sup>2</sup> a ‘thick drop’ as opposed to {%stoka,%} a ‘small drop.’ Hence there frequently occurs the ex- pression {%dadḥi-drapsa,%}’ ‘drop of curds.’<sup>3</sup> In the Rigveda<sup>4</sup> the word normally denotes the thick drops of Soma or the Soma itself. <div n="P"/>In two passages<sup>5</sup> Roth<sup>6</sup> sees the sense of ‘banner,’ which is adopted by Oldenberg.<sup>7</sup> Geldner,<sup>8</sup> on the other hand, con- siders that ‘dust’ is meant, but this interpretation is not very probable. Max Müller<sup>9</sup> renders the word ‘rain-drop’ in one of the passages. <F>1) Rv. i. 94, 11 (perhaps a ‘drop’ of fire); v. 63, 4 (‘rain-drop’); vii. 33, 11 (= {%retas%}); Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, vi. 1, 2, 6; {%drapsin%} (‘thick-flowing’), xi. 4, 1, 15.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, 1, p. 70, 7. {%Cf.%} the epithet {%uru-drapsa,%} Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 3, 10, 2; Sāyaṇa, on Av. xviii. 4, 18, takes {%drapsa%} to mean ‘drops of curd’; so Agnisvāmin on Lāṭyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, iii. 2, 4.</F> <F>3) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, ix. 2, 3, 40.</F> <F>4) ix. 78, 4; 85, 10; 89, 2; 97, 56; 108, 8; x. 11, 4; 17, 11. 12. {%Cf.%} Tait- tirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 3, 9. 1.</F> <F>5) iv. 13, 2, and {%drapsin%} in i. 64, 2.</F> <F>6) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} {%satvan;%} Böhtlingk, Dictionary, {%s.v.%} {%drapsa, drapsin.%}</F> <F>7) {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 46, 357: {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 64, 65.</F> <F>8) {%Vedische Studien,%} 3, 57, 58; {%Rigveda,%} {%Glossar,%} 88.</F> <F>9) {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 32, 104. {%Cf.%} Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} p. 80, with reference to Rv. i. 64, 2. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Macdonell, {%op. cit.,%} pp. 105, 113.</F>

{@Drāpi@}¦ occurs several times in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> in the sense of ‘mantle’ or ‘cloak.’<sup>2</sup> Sāyaṇa, however, renders the word by ‘coat of mail’<sup>3</sup> ({%kavaca%}). This seems needless, but none of the passages are very decisive one way or the other. <F>1) i. 25, 13; 116, 10; iv. 33, 2; ix. 86, 14; 100, 9; Av. iii. 13, 1.</F> <F>2) Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.;%} Muir, {%Sanskrit Texts,%} 5, 472; Schrader, {%Prehistoric Antiquities,%} 333.</F> <F>3) {%Cf.%} Max Müller, {%Ancient Sanskrit%} {%Literature,%} 536; Pischel, {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 201, 202.</F>

{@Dru@}¦ denotes a vessel made of wood,<sup>1</sup> and in particular the vessel used at the Soma sacrifice,<sup>2</sup> perhaps, as Hillebrandt<sup>3</sup> sug- gests, to catch the Soma juice when running through the sieve. In the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa<sup>4</sup> the word simply means ‘wood.’ <F>1) Rv. i. 161, 1; v. 86, 3; viii. 66, 11; in x. 101, 10, the mortar seems meant. In v. 86, 3, Böhtlingk takes it to denote a ‘wooden handle.’</F> <F>2) ix. 1, 2; 65, 6; 98, 2.</F> <F>3) {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 191, 192.</F> <F>4) i. 3, 9, 1. So often in compounds, {%e.g.,%} Rv. ii. 7, 6; vi. 12, 4, etc.</F>

{@Dru-ghaṇa@}¦ is found in the Mudgala hymn of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and in the Atharvaveda.<sup>2</sup> The sense is uncertain. Yāska<sup>3</sup> renders it as a ‘{%ghana%} made of wood,’ probably, as Roth<sup>4</sup> takes it, meaning a ‘club of wood.’ Geldner<sup>5</sup> thinks that it was a wooden bull used by Mudgala as a substitute for a second bull when he wanted to join in a race. But this interpretation of the legend is very improbable.<sup>6</sup> Whitney<sup>7</sup> translates the word as ‘tree-smiter’ in the Atharvaveda, quoting Sāyaṇa, who explains it as a ‘cutting instrument,’ so called because trees are struck with it. <F>1) x. 101, 9.</F> <F>2) vii. 28, 1.</F> <F>3) Nirukta, ix. 23.</F> <F>4) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>5) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 3, 4.</F> <F>6) {%Cf.%} von Bradke, {%Zeitschrift der%} {%Deutschen Morgenländischen Gesellschaft,%} 46, 462; Bloomfield, {%ibid.,%} 48, 456; Franke, {%Vienna Oriental Journal,%} 8, 342.</F> <F>7) Translation of the Atharvaveda, 407.</F>

{@Dru-pada,@}¦ a ‘wooden pillar’ or ‘post,’ is several times referred to in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> Śunaḥśepa was bound to three posts for sacrifice.<sup>3</sup> Thieves, there is some evidence to show, were tied to posts as a penalty for stealing.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) i. 24, 13; iv. 32, 23.</F> <F>2) Av. vi. 63, 3; 115, 2; xix. 47, 9; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xx. 20.</F> <F>3) Rv. i. 24, 13.</F> <F>4) Av. xix. 47, 9; 50, 1. {%Cf.%} vi. 63, 3 = 84, 4. See Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 181, 182, and Taskara. n. 26.</F>
{@Druma,@}¦ ‘tree,’ is not found until the later period in the Ṣaḍviṃśa Brāhmaṇa (v. 11) and the Nirukta (iv. 19; v. 26; ix. 23).

{@Druvaya,@}¦ ‘wooden,’ is used in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> as an epithet of the drum. <F>1) v. 20, 2. {%Cf.%} xi. 1, 12, where it is an epithet of {%upaśvasa,%} ‘blower,’ pos- sibly ‘bellows’; but the manuscripts in part read {%dhruvaye,%} and the Paip- palāda has {%druye.%}</F>

{@Dru-han,@}¦ ‘wood-cutter,’ seems to be meant by the word {%druhantara%} in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> where it is usually taken as {%druhaṃ-%} {%tara,%} ‘fiend-overpowering.’ But as an epithet of {%paraśu,%} ‘axe,’ the other sense (‘mighty wood-cutter’)<sup>2</sup> is more probable.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) i. 127, 2.</F> <F>2) But if this explanation is correct, the word should have the accentuation of the comparative. See Oldenberg, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 46, 132.</F> <F>3) {%Cf.%} Oldenberg, {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 130.</F>

{@Druhyu@}¦ is the name of a people mentioned several times in the Rigveda. In one passage<sup>1</sup> it occurs, in the plural, with the {@Yadus, Turvaśas, Anus,@} and {@Pūrus,@} suggesting that these are the famous five peoples of the Rigveda.<sup>2</sup> Again, the Druhyu king shared in the defeat of his allies by {@Sudās,@} and appears to have perished in the waters.<sup>3</sup> In a second passage Druhyu, Anu, Turvaśa, and Yadu are all mentioned in the singular,<sup>4</sup> while in another Pūru and Druhyu occur.<sup>5</sup> From the tribal grouping it is probable that the Druhyus were a north-western people,<sup>6</sup> and the later tradition of the Epic connects Gāndhāra and Druhyu.<sup>7</sup> <F>1) i. 108, 8.</F> <F>2) {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 122, 125; Hopkins, {%Journal of the American%} {%Oriental Society,%} 15, 258 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>3) vii. 18.</F> <F>4) viii. 10, 5.</F> <F>5) vi. 46, 8.</F> <F>6) Roth, {%Zur Litteratur und Geschichte%} {%des Weda,%} 131-133.</F> <F>7) Pargiter, {%Journal of the Royal Asiatic%} {%Society,%} 1910, 49. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rig- veda, 3, 205; Macdonell, {%Vedic Myth-%} {%ology,%} p. 140.</F>

{@Droṇa@}¦ denotes in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> a ‘wooden trough,’ and more specifically it designates in the plural vessels used for holding Soma.<sup>2</sup> The great wooden reservoir for Soma is called a Droṇa-kalaśa.<sup>3</sup> The altar was sometimes made in the form of a Droṇa.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) vi. 2, 8; 37, 2; 44, 20; ix. 93, 1; Nirukta, v. 26.</F> <F>2) ix. 3, 1; 15, 7; 28, 4; 30, 4; 67, 14, etc. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 280.</F> <F>3) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 2, 1, 2; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xviii. 21; xix. 27; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vii. 17, 32. Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, i. 6, 3, 17, etc.</F> <F>4) Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 4, 7; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxi. 4; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, vi. 7, 2, 8.</F>

{@Droṇāhāva@}¦ is used as an epithet of {@Avata,@} ‘well,’ in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> apparently in the sense of ‘having wooden buckets’ with reference to the drawing up of water. <F>1) x. 101, 7. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 157.</F>

{@Dvādaśa,@}¦ ‘consisting of twelve,’<sup>1</sup> is used of the year in the Rigveda (vii. 103, 9). See {@Nakṣatra.@} <F>1) {%Cf.%} Oldenberg, {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen Gesellschaft,%} 48, 645 {%et seq.%}</F>
{@Dvāpara.@}¦ See {@Akṣa@} and {@Yuga.@}

{@Dvār@}¦ is frequently used from the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> onwards<sup>2</sup> to denote the ‘door’ of a house. The later form, Dvāra, has the same sense.<sup>3</sup> {%Cf.%} {@Gṛha.@} The ‘door-fastener’ is called Dvāra- pidhāna in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) i. 13, 6.</F> <F>2) Av. viii. 3, 22; xiv. 1, 63; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xxx. 10; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xi. 1, 1, 2; xiv. 3, 1, 13, etc.</F> <F>3) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 6, 1, 19; iv. 3, 5, 9; 6, 7, 9; xi. 4, 4, 2, etc. Av. x. 8, 43, has {%nava-dvāra,%} ‘having nine openings,’ of the body.</F> <F>4) xi. 1, 1, 1. {%Cf. dvāra-bāhū,%} ‘door- posts,’ in Lāṭyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, i. 3, 1; ii. 3, 9.</F>
{@Dvāra-pa,@}¦ ‘door-keeper,’ is only found in a metaphorical sense in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (i. 30), where Viṣṇu is called the ‘doorkeeper’ of the gods, and in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (iii. 13, 6).
{@Dvi-gat Bhārgava@}¦ (‘descendant of {@Bhṛgu@}’) is mentioned in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa (xiv. 9) as the seer of a Sāman or Chant, by means of which he twice went to the heavenly world.

{@Dvi-ja,@}¦ ‘twice-born,’ as an epithet of the Āryans generally, or of the Brahmins in particular, is not found in Vedic litera- ture except in a quite obscure verse of the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) xix. 71, 1. {%Cf.%} Whitney, Transla- tion of the Atharvaveda, 1008; Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 204. Neither {%dvi-%} {%janman%} nor {%dvi-jāti%} occurs early, and the idea is not in this form an early one.</F>

{@Dvi-pād,@}¦ ‘two-footed,’ ‘biped,’ denotes man, as opposed to quadrupeds, from the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> onwards.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) i. 49, 3; iii. 62, 14; viii. 27, 12; x. 97, 20; 117, 8.</F> <F>2) Av. ii. 34, 1; x. 1, 24; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, viii. 30; ix. 31; xiii. 17; xiv. 8, etc.</F>

{@Dvi-bandhu@}¦ is in an obscure hymn of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> according to Roth<sup>2</sup> and Grassmann,<sup>3</sup> the name of a man, while Ludwig<sup>4</sup> renders it as a simple adjective meaning ‘of double kinship.’ <F>1) x. 61, 17.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary.</F> <F>3) {%Wörterbuch, s.v.,%} and Translation of the Rigveda, 2, 475.</F> <F>4) Translation of the Rigveda, 2, 643, and 5, 526.</F>
{@Dvi-rāja@}¦ (neut,), ‘conflict between two kings,’ or ‘battle,’ is mentioned in the Atharvaveda (v. 20, 9). {%Cf.%} {@Dāśarājña.@}

{@Dvi-retas,@}¦ ‘having double seed,’ is an epithet of both the ass<sup>1</sup> and the mare.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, iv. 9; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, vi. 3, 1, 23. {%Cf.%} {@Gardabha.@}</F> <F>2) Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, vi. 1, 4.</F>

{@Dvīpa,@}¦ ‘island,’ is mentioned in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> But there is no reason to imagine that the islands referred to were other than sandbanks in the great rivers, Indus or Ganges.<sup>3</sup> Vedic literature knows nothing of the system of geography according to which the earth consists of four, seven, or thirteen Dvīpas grouped round Mount Meru. <F>1) i. 169, 3.</F> <F>2) Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xiii. 2; Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, xii. 2, 1, 3; Lāṭyā- yana Śrauta Sütra, i. 6, 10.</F> <F>3) Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 256.</F>

{@Dvīpin,@}¦<sup>1</sup> ‘panther’ or ‘leopard,’ is mentioned in the Athar- vaveda<sup>2</sup> and the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) Lit., ‘insulated’ — {%i.e.,%} ‘spotted.’</F> <F>2) iv. 8, 7; vi. 38, 2; xix. 49, 4, in every case associated with the tiger.</F> <F>3) ii. 1. 9. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 80.</F>

{@Dvaita-vana,@}¦ ‘descendant of Dvitavana,’ is the patronymic of {@Dhvasan,@} the king of the {@Matsyas,@} whose Aśvamedha, or ‘horse sacrifice,’ is mentioned in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (xiii. 5, 4, 9).
{@Dvy-opaśa.@}¦ See {@Opaśa.@}

{@Dhana,@}¦ ‘prize,’ is often found in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> probably the prize in racing rather than the ‘booty’ in battle. It also denotes<sup>2</sup> the ‘stake’ at dicing. In some passages it possibly means the ‘contest’ itself.<sup>3</sup> More generally it denotes ‘wealth’ or ‘gift.’<sup>4</sup> But it sometimes expresses ‘booty,’<sup>5</sup> probably from the notion of ‘wealth’ rather than of ‘prize.’ <F>1) Rv. i. 81, 3; vi. 45, 2; viii. 80, 8; ix. 53, 2; 109, 10. {%Cf.%} Geldner, {%Ve-%} {%dische Studien,%} 1, 120; Pischel, {%ibid.,%} 1, 171.</F> <F>2) Rv. x. 34, 10; Av. iv. 38, 3.</F> <F>3) Rv. i. 31, 6; v. 35, 7; vii. 38, 8; viii. 5, 26; 8, 21; 49, 9; 50, 9; x. 48, 5, etc.</F> <F>4) Rv. i. 42, 6; x. 18, 2; 84, 7; Av. i. 15, 3; ii. 7, 4; iii. 15, 2; v. 19, 9; vi. 81, 1; vii. 81, 4; viii. 5, 16, etc.</F> <F>5) Rv. i. 74, 3; 157, 2, etc.</F>
{@Dhana-dhānī,@}¦ a ‘treasure house,’ is mentioned in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka (x. 67).
{@Dhaniṣṭhā@}¦ (‘very rich’), used in the plural, is the later name<sup>1</sup> of the lunar mansion {@(Nakṣatra) Śraviṣṭhā.@} <F>1) Sāntikalpa, 13; Śāṅkhāyana Gṛhya Sūtra, i. 26.</F>

{@Dhanu@}¦ (fem.), ‘sandbank,’ occurs several times in the Rig- veda,<sup>1</sup> but only metaphorically of the clouds in the atmosphere. Dhanū is found in the Atharvaveda,<sup>2</sup> where it seems to denote a sandbag used to prevent bleeding.<sup>3</sup> {%Cf.%} {@Dhanvan.@} <F>1) i. 33, 4; 144, 5; viii. 3, 19; x. 4, 3; 27, 17.</F> <F>2) i. 17, 4.</F> <F>3) Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 411; Whitney, Translation of the Atharva- veda, 18; Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the%} {%Atharvaveda,%} 259, 260.</F>

{@Dhanus,@}¦ the ‘bow,’ frequently mentioned in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later,<sup>2</sup> was the chief weapon of the Vedic Indian.<sup>3</sup> The last act of the funeral rite included the removal of the bow from [Page1-389+ 53] the right hand of the dead man.<sup>4</sup> The weapon was composed of a stout staff bent into a curved shape ({%vakra%}),<sup>5</sup> and of a bow- string ({@Jyā@}) made of a strip of cowhide<sup>6</sup> which joined the ends. The tips of the bow, when the string was fastened, were called {@Ārtnī.@} Relaxed when not in actual use, the bow was specially strung up when needed for shooting.<sup>7</sup> The stages of the process are given in detail in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā:<sup>8</sup> the stringing ({%ā-tan%}) of the bow, the placing ({%prati-dhā%}) of the arrow, the bending ({%ā-yam%}) of the bow, and the shooting ({%as%}). The arrow was discharged from the ear,<sup>9</sup> and is hence called {%karṇa-yoni,%}<sup>10</sup> ‘having the ear as its point of origin.’<sup>10</sup> The making of bows was a regular profession ({%dhanuṣ-kāra,%}<sup>11</sup> {%dhanuṣ-kṛt%}).<sup>12</sup> For the arrow see {@Iṣu,@} and for the handguard {@Hastaghna.@} <F>1) viii. 72, 4; 77, 11; ix. 99, 1; x. 18, 9; 125, 6.</F> <F>2) Av. iv. 4, 6; 6, 6; v. 18, 8; vii. 50. 9; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xvi. 10; Pañca- viṃśa Brāhmaṇa, vii. 5, 6; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vii. 14; Śatapatha Brāh- maṇa, i. 5, 4, 6; v. 3, 1, 11, etc.</F> <F>3) Rv. vi. 75, 2. {@Dharma,@}¦<sup>1</sup> {@Dharman,@}<sup>2</sup> are the regular words, the latter in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> and both later,<sup>2</sup> for ‘law’ or ‘custom.’ But there is very little evidence in the early literature as to the administra- tion of justice or the code of law followed. On the other hand, the Dharma Sūtras<sup>3</sup> contain full particulars. <div n="P"/>(1) {%Criminal Law.%} — The crimes recognized in Vedic litera- ture vary greatly in importance, while there is no distinction adopted in principle between real crimes and what now are regarded as fanciful bodily defects or infringements of merely [Page1-391+ 80] conventional practices.<sup>4</sup> The crimes enumerated include the slaying of an embryo ({%bhrūṇa%}),<sup>5</sup> the slaying of a man ({%vīra%}),<sup>6</sup> and  the slaying of a Brahmin,<sup>7</sup> a much more serious crime. Treachery is mentioned in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>8</sup> as being punishable by death, as it was punished later.<sup>9</sup> But there is no trace of an organized criminal justice vested either in the king or in the people. There still seems to have prevailed the system of wergeld ({@Vaira@}), which indicates that criminal justice remained in the hands of those who were wronged. In the Sūtras,<sup>10</sup> on the other hand, the king's peace is recognized as infringed by crimes, a penalty being paid to him, or, according to the Brahminical textbooks, to the Brahmins. It may there- [Page1-392+ 54] fore reasonably be conjectured that the royal power of jurisdic- tion steadily increased; the references in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa to the king as wielding punishment ({@Daṇḍa@}) confirm this supposition. Whether, as the analogy of other systems suggests, the king was assisted in his judicial duties, as he undoubtedly was later, by assessors, presumably of the Brahmin caste, cannot be made out clearly.<sup>11</sup> <div n="P"/>The procedure adopted in deciding cases is quite uncertain. In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad<sup>12</sup> the ordeal of the red-hot axe is mentioned as applied in an accusation of theft. It must apparently be understood to have been inflicted by the direction of the king. But no other judicial ordeal is known to Vedic literature (see {@Divya@}). The punishment of theft was in some cases at least death, probably when the thief was taken red- handed;<sup>13</sup> in other cases binding to posts was the penalty,<sup>14</sup> presumably accompanied by the return of the stolen goods. In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad<sup>15</sup> the list of sins given as apparently equal in wickedness is stealing gold, drinking spirits, defiling a Guru's bed, and the murder of a Brahmin. <div n="P"/>(2) {%Civil Law.%} — There is little recorded as to civil law in Vedic literature. The relations of the family and the question of family property are dealt with under {@Urvarā, Kṣetra, Pati;@} succession and partition of property are treated under {@Dāya.@} As regards the transfer of chattels — for land as transferable {%inter vivos%} is hardly yet recognized, save exceptionally as a sacrificial fee ({@Dakṣiṇā@}), and then disapproved<sup>16</sup> — the recognized modes are gift ({@Dāna@}) and barter or sale ({@Kraya@}), which includes exchange. Original acquisition of land was no doubt brought [Page1-393+ 52] about by occupation and apportionment among the tribesmen,<sup>17</sup> while chattels were acquired by taking possession of them, provided that they were found on one's own land or on unoccupied land, and did not belong to any other person originally. The Sūtras<sup>18</sup> contain rules for the disposal of lost property, which tend to give it to the king, with the deduction of a percentage for the finder, unless the latter is a Brahmin, who keeps it all. As for contract, save in regard to money- lending (for which see {@Ṛṇa@}), practically nothing is to be gathered from Vedic literature, doubtless because of the primitive conditions prevailing in that early period. Much of the labour, which would in a more developed society have been done by workers for hire, would be performed by slaves ({%cf.%} {@Dāsa,@} {@Śūdra@}), while the technical workers of the village — of whom long lists are given in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā<sup>19</sup> and the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa<sup>20</sup> — may have been recompensed not by any sum based on each piece of work done, but by fixed allow- ances, much as the village servants are in modern times.<sup>21</sup> But this must remain a matter of conjecture, and it is uncertain what exact status the carpenter or smith held in the village. Similarly it is impossible to trace in the early literature any legal theory or practice as to torts, but rules as to penalties for insults appear in the Sūtras.<sup>22</sup> <div n="P"/>Very little is recorded as to procedure. The list<sup>23</sup> of victims at the Puruṣamedha, or ‘horse sacrifice,’ includes a {%praśnin,%} an {%abhi-praśnin,%} and a {%praśna-vivāka,%} in whom it is not un- reasonable to see the plaintiff, the defendant, and the arbitrator or judge: the terms may refer to what is probably an early [Page1-394+ 59] form of judicial procedure, a voluntary arbitration. The same idea may be conveyed by the word {%madhyama-śī,%} ‘lying in the midst,’ which occurs in the Rigveda,<sup>24</sup> and which Roth,<sup>25</sup> followed by Zimmer,<sup>26</sup> understood to mean an arbitrator or judge, the expression being derived from the judge acting with other judicial persons,<sup>27</sup> and being surrounded by the assembly of the people. But this interpretation is uncertain; Whitney<sup>28</sup> thinks that the word merely alludes to a chief round whom his men encamp. The king is later the chief civil judge, and may presumably have been so earlier, no doubt in conjunction with the elders of the tribe, but for this we are reduced to conjecture.<sup>29</sup> <div n="P"/>The use of witnesses as evidence is uncertain (see {@Jñātṛ@}), and the ordeal is not recorded as deciding any civil matter except the dispute between {@Vatsa@} and his rival as to the true Brahminical descent of the former, which was settled by his walking unharmed through the flame of a fire.<sup>30</sup> But it is probable on analogy that the ordeal may have been used for the purpose of deciding disputes. Whether the oath was so used cannot be certainly shown. It appears, however, that a Brahmin was preferred in legal matters to a non-Brahmin.<sup>31</sup> <div n="P"/>There are very few references to police officials: no doubt the king employed some of his dependents to execute sentences and arrest offenders (see {@Ugra, Jīvagṛbh@}). <div n="P"/>(3) {%Morality.%} — It is convenient to notice under this head [Page1-395+ 61] several points bearing on the moral condition of the people: ({%a%}) the exposure of children; ({%b%}) the exposure of the aged; ({%c%}) prostitution; ({%d%}) adultery; ({%e%}) incest. <div n="P"/>({%a%}) The exposure of girl infants is asserted by Zimmer<sup>32</sup> on the strength of a passage in the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā,<sup>33</sup> but it seems clear that the passage has been misunderstood,<sup>34</sup> and that it refers merely to laying the child aside, not exposing it, while a boy was lifted up. It is, however, true that the birth of a girl was not at all popular, not an unnatural sentiment in an early society, and paralleled among other Āryan peoples.<sup>35</sup> <div n="P"/>({%b%}) The exposure of the aged is also inferred by Zimmer<sup>36</sup> from a passage of the Rigveda,<sup>37</sup> and from the mention of persons exposed ({%ud-hitāḥ%}) in the Atharvaveda.<sup>38</sup> The latter passage may well refer merely to the bodies being exposed after death to the elements (as is done by the Parsis). The former passage merely refers to the individual case of some person who may have been cast out, and proves absolutely nothing as to a habitual or recognized custom, nor can such a custom be inferred from, {%e.g.,%} the legend of {@Cyavāna.@} <div n="P"/>({%c%}) That prostitution existed in Rigvedic times is certain, but its extent is disputed. Brotherless girls were frequently reduced to becoming prostitutes;<sup>39</sup> the putting away of an illegitimate child is referred to in the Rigveda;<sup>40</sup> besides the [Page1-396+ 61] terms {%puṃścalī%}<sup>41</sup> and {%mahānagnī,%}<sup>42</sup> which undoubtedly mean ‘harlot,’ there are other clear references to prostitution;<sup>43</sup> and expressions like {%kumārī-putra,%} ‘son of a maiden,’<sup>44</sup> and the ‘son of an unmarried girl’ ({%agrū%}), spoken of in the Rigveda<sup>45</sup> as exposed and attacked by animals, point in the same direction. The Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā<sup>46</sup> seems to recognize prostitution as a profession. Pischel<sup>47</sup> sees many references to Hetairai in the Rigveda, which as Geldner<sup>48</sup> insists reflects in its imagery the court life of Indian princes. But the correct- ness of the view of these two scholars on this point is not by any means certain.<sup>49</sup> <div n="P"/>({%d%}) Adultery was generally regarded among Āryan peoples as a serious offence against the husband of the woman affected. We accordingly find in the legal literature of India traces of the rule that an adulterer can be slain with impunity if taken in the act.<sup>50</sup> Weber,<sup>51</sup> however, has adduced some material indicating an indifference to these matters in Vedic times, and Ludwig<sup>52</sup> has adopted the same view. But, as Delbrück<sup>53</sup> has clearly shown, the evidence is not convincing; the cited pre- scriptions<sup>54</sup> forbidding connexion with another man's wife during a certain rite do not imply that such connexion would otherwise be allowed: the ritual of the Varuṇa-praghāsas,<sup>55</sup> when a wife names her lover or lovers, seems originally to have been a solemn means of banishing the evil brought on a family by a wife's fall; {@Yājñavalkya's@} famous saying<sup>56</sup> that no one [Page1-397+ 48] cares whether a wife is ‘unchaste’ ({%paraḥ-puṃsā%}) or not is a mere mistranslation,<sup>57</sup> the expression {%paraḥ-puṃsā%} really mean- ing ‘removed from the male persons.’ And the uncertainty asserted in some passages<sup>58</sup> as to origin from a Ṛṣi is not a sign of doubtful descent, but is due to the fact that Ṛṣihood was a difficult matter to ascertain. None the less woman's position was lowered by the prevalence of polygamy, and such stories as that of Ahalyā and Indra<sup>59</sup> are not compatible with a very high standard of morality. A similar conclusion is pointed to by references in the Yajurveda<sup>60</sup> to relations between the Ārya man and the Śūdrā woman, and by a spell given in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad<sup>61</sup> to expiate relations with the wife of a Śrotriya (Brahmin theologian). <div n="P"/>({%e%}) Incest was recognized in the marriage of brother and sister as appears from the legend of Yama and Yamī in the Rigveda,<sup>62</sup> which clearly shows that such a marriage was not approved by the feeling of the Vedic age. There is also another hymn<sup>63</sup> in which reference to such intercourse appears to be made. Mention is further made in the Rigveda<sup>64</sup> to the wedlock of Prajāpati and his daughter, which is, however, interpreted mythologically in the Brāhmaṇas,<sup>65</sup> an interpre- tation which may be correct.
