1. {@Dhava@}¦ is the name of a tree ({%Grislea tormentosa%}) mentioned, together with the {@Plakṣa, Aśvattha,@} and {@Khādira,@} in the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) v. 5, 5; xx. 137, 11. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 62.</F>

2. {@Dhava,@}¦ ‘man,’ is not found before the Nirukta.<sup>1</sup> The word clearly owes its existence merely to {%vidhavā,%} ‘widow,’ wrongly interpreted as {%vi-dhavā,%} ‘without a husband.’ <F>1) iii. 15. {%Cf.%} Naighaṇṭuka, ii. 3.</F>

{@Dhavitra,@}¦ occurring in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> and the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka,<sup>2</sup> denotes a ‘fan’ of hide or leather for blowing the sacrificial fire. <F>1) xiv. 1, 3, 30; 3, 1, 21.</F> <F>2) v. 4, 33.</F>

{@Dhānaṃ-jayya,@}¦ ‘descendant of {@Dhanaṃ-jaya,@}’ is the patronymic of {@Aṃśu@} in the Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 373. Under this patronymic he is frequently named by Lāṭyāyana Srauta Sūtra, i. 1, 25; ii. 1, 2; 9, 10, etc. (misread Dhānaṃ- japya in many manuscripts). {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indian Literature,%} 76, 77, 82.</F>

{@Dhānā,@}¦ always used in the plural, and frequently referred to in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later,<sup>2</sup> means ‘grains of corn.’ They were sometimes parched ({%bhṛjj%}),<sup>3</sup> and were regularly mixed with Soma.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) i. 16, 2; iii. 35, 3; 52, 5; vi. 29, 4, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. xviii. 3, 69; 4, 32. 34; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xix. 21, 22; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 5, 11, 2, etc.</F> <F>3) Rv. iv. 24, 7.</F> <F>4) Rv. iii. 43, 4; 52, 1; viii. 91, 2; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 1, 10, 2; Sata- patha Brāhmaṇa, iv. 4, 3, 9. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Schrader, {%Prchistoric Antiquities,%} 283.</F>

{@Dhānya@}¦ (neut.), a derivative from the preceding word,<sup>1</sup> denotes ‘grain’ in general. It is found in the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> and later.<sup>3</sup> According to the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad,<sup>4</sup> there are ten cultivated ({%grāmyāṇi%}) kinds of grain: rice and barley ({%vrīhi-%} {%yavāḥ%}), sesamum and beans ({%tila-māṣāḥ%}), Panicum Miliaceum and Italicum ({%aṇu-priyaṅgavaḥ%}), maize ({%godhūmāḥ%}), lentils ({%masūrāḥ%}), Khalvāḥ and Dolichos uniflorus ({%khala-kulāḥ%}). The [Page1-399+ 52] horse is called ‘corn-eating’ ({%dhānyāda%}) in the Aitareya<sup>5</sup> and Śatapatha<sup>6</sup> Brāhmaṇas, and men are mentioned as ‘purifying corn’ ({%dhānyā-kṛt%}) in the Rigveda.<sup>8</sup> <div n="P"/>7 Lit., ‘preparing corn.’ <F>1) Primarily as an adjective, ‘con- sisting of grain.’</F> <F>2) vi. 13, 4.</F> <F>3) Av. iii. 24, 2. 4; v. 29, 7; vi. 50, 1; Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, xi. 8; Ṣaḍviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, v. 5, etc.</F> <F>4) vi. 3, 22 (Mādhyaṃdina = 13 Kāṇva).</F> <F>5) viii. 21.</F> <F>6) xiii. 5, 4, 2.</F> <F>8) x. 94, 13.</F>

{@Dhānva@}¦ is the patronymic of {@Asita@} in the Śatapatha Brāh- maṇa.<sup>1</sup> In the Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra<sup>2</sup> the form of the name is Dhānvana. <F>1) xiii. 4, 3, 11; Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra, x. 7.</F> <F>2) xvi. 2, 20.</F>

{@Dhāman@}¦ denotes in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> ‘dwelling’ and ‘house,’ or sometimes<sup>3</sup> its inmates. The word is also<sup>4</sup> found in the sense of ‘ordinance,’ ‘law,’ expressing much the same as {@Dharman,@} especially in conjunction<sup>5</sup> with Rta, ‘eternal order.’ Hillebrandt<sup>6</sup> sees in one passage<sup>7</sup> the sense of {@Nakṣatra.@} <F>1) i. 144, 1; ii. 3, 2; iii. 55, 10; vii. 61, 4; 87, 2; x. 13, 1, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. iv. 25, 7; vii. 68, 1; xii. 1, 52; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, iv. 34; Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, ii. 7, 2.</F> <F>3) Rv. viii. 101, 6; ix. 63, 14; x. 82, 3; Av. ii. 14, 6. Many of the examples given in the St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v., C,%} are doubtful.</F> <F>4) Rv. iv. 55, 2; vi. 21, 3; vii. 63, 3; viii. 41, 10; x. 48, 11.</F> <F>5) Rv. i. 123, 9; iv. 7, 7; vii. 36, 5; x. 124, 3.</F> <F>6) {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 446.</F> <F>7) Rv. ix. 66, 2. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Geldner, {%Rigveda, Glossar,%} 92, 93.</F>

{@Dhārā@}¦ denotes the ‘edge’ of a weapon,<sup>1</sup> as of an axe ({%svadhiti%}),<sup>2</sup> or of a razor ({%kṣura%}).<sup>3</sup> See also {@Asi.@} <F>1) Rv. vi. 3, 5; 47, 10. {%Cf.%} viii. 73, 9; Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, iv. 38, 1, for metaphorical applications.</F> <F>2) Kauśika Sūtra, 44.</F> <F>3) Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, iii. 3, 2.</F>

{@Dhiṣaṇā,@}¦ according to the St. Petersburg Dictionary, denotes<sup>1</sup> an implement used in preparing the Soma, ‘bowl’ or ‘vat,’ and by metonymy also the Soma draught itself.<sup>2</sup> The dual, by [Page1-400+ 54] a metaphor,<sup>3</sup> also expresses the ‘two worlds,’ heaven and earth.<sup>4</sup> Hillebrandt,<sup>5</sup> however, thinks that the word properly means earth,<sup>6</sup> in the dual heaven and earth,<sup>7</sup> in the plural the triad, earth, atmosphere, and heaven,<sup>8</sup> while in some passages<sup>9</sup> Dhiṣaṇā denotes the Vedi, the excavated ground used as an altar. This is not, however, certain, while it seems clear that the Vājasaneyi<sup>10</sup> and Taittirīya<sup>11</sup> Saṃhitās understand the Dhiṣaṇās (dual) to be the planks over which the pressing of the Soma took place ({%adhiṣavaṇa-phalake%}).<sup>12</sup> Pischel<sup>13</sup> sees in Dhiṣaṇā a goddess of wealth akin to Aditi and the earth. <F>1) Rv. i. 96, 1; 102, 1; 109, 3, 4; iii. 49, 1; iv. 34, 1; 36, 8; viii. 61, 9; ix. 59, 2; x. 17, 12; 30, 6; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, i. 19; vi. 26, 35, etc.</F> <F>2) Rv. i. 102, 7; iii. 32, 14; 49, 4; vi. 19, 2; vii. 90, 3; viii. 15, 7; x. 96, 10, etc.</F> <F>3) Like {@Camū.@}</F> <F>4) Rv. i. 160, 1; vi. 8, 3; 50, 3; 70, 3; x. 44, 8; in the plural, ‘the three worlds,’ Rv. v. 69, 2. In other passages, Rv. i. 22, 10; iii. 56, 6; v. 41, 8; vi. 11, 3; x. 35, 7, the sense of ‘a genius of prosperity’ was assigned to Dhiṣaṇā by Roth.</F> <F>5) {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 175-181.</F> <F>6) Rv. i. 22, 10; 96, 1; 102, 1; iii. 31, 13; 56, 6; vi. 19, 2; vii. 90, 3; viii. 15, 7; x. 30, 6; 35, 7; 96, 10.</F> <F>7) See n. 3; also Rv. viii. 61, 2; {%nivid%} in Sāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, viii. 19, 4.</F> <F>8) Rv. iv. 36, 8; v. 69, 2; ix. 59, 2.</F> <F>9) Rv. i. 109, 3, 4; iii. 2, 1; 49, 4 (or perhaps ‘earth’); iv. 34, 1; v. 41, 8; vi. 11, 3; x. 17, 12.</F> <F>10) vii. 26.</F> <F>11) iii. 1, 10, 1.</F> <F>12) Mahīdhara on Vājasaneyi Saṃ- hitā, vii. 26; Sāyaṇa on Taittirīya Saṃhitā, {%loc. cit.%}</F> <F>13) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 82-87. {%Cf.%} Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} p. 124; Oldenberg, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 46, 120-122.</F>

{@Dhī,@}¦ ‘thought,’ is used several times in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> to denote the ‘prayer’ or ‘hymn of praise’ of the singer. One poet speaks of himself as ‘weaving’ such a prayer,<sup>2</sup> while another refers to his ‘ancient ancestral hymn,’ which he refurbishes presumably for use.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) i. 3, 5; 135, 5; 151, 6; 185, 8; ii. 3, 8 (where it is connected with {@Sarasvatī@}); 40, 5, etc.</F> <F>2) Rv. ii. 28, 5.</F> <F>3) Rv. iii. 39, 2. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 338.</F>

{@Dhīti@}¦ has in several passages of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> practically the same sense as {@Dhī,@} ‘prayer,’ or ‘hymn of praise.’ <F>1) i. 110, 1; iii. 12, 7; 52, 6; v. 25, 3; 53, 11; vi. 15, 9, etc.; Nirukta, ii. 24.</F>
{@Dhīra Śāta-parṇeya@}¦ (‘descendant of Śataparṇa’) is men- tioned in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (x. 3, 3, 1) as a pupil of {@Mahāśāla.@}

{@Dhīvan@}¦ occurs in the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> where it may either be taken with Roth,<sup>2</sup> Bloomfield,<sup>3</sup> and Whitney<sup>4</sup> as an epithet of ‘chariot-builders’ ({%ratha-kārāḥ%}), meaning ‘clever,’ or be con- strued with the scholiast as denoting ‘fishermen’ ({%dhīvara%}). The Paippalāda recension has {%takṣāṇaḥ,%} ‘carpenters.’ <F>1) iii. 5, 6.</F> <F>2) St. Petersbuig Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>3) {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 114.</F> <F>4) Translation of the Atharvaveda, 114. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indīsche Studien,%} 17, 194 {%et seq.;%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 252.</F>

{@Dhuṅkṣā@}¦ is the name of some sort of bird in the list of victims at the Aśvamedha, or ‘horse sacrifice,’ in the Yajurveda Saṃhitās.<sup>1</sup> See also {@Dhūṅkṣṇā@} and {@Dhvāṅkṣa.@} <F>1) Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 12; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 31. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 93.</F>

{@Dhuni@}¦ is the name of a foe of Indra, normally mentioned along with {@Cumuri@} in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> He and Cumuri seem to have been opposed to {@Dabhīti.@}<sup>2</sup> His name is probably that of an aboriginal chief.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) ii. 15, 9; vi. 18, 8; 20, 13; vii. 19, 4.</F> <F>2) Rv. x. 113. 9.</F> <F>3) Wackernagel, {%Altindische Grammatik,%} 1, xxii; Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} p. 162. {%Cf.%} Oldenberg, {%Religion des%} {%Veda,%} 157, 158.</F>

{@Dhur@}¦ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> denotes, according to the St. Petersburg Dictionary, that part of the yoke which is placed on the shoulders of the animals drawing the chariot or cart, whence they are called {%dhūr-ṣāh,%} ‘yoke-bearing,’ in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā.<sup>3</sup> In one passage of the Rigveda<sup>4</sup> the sense is uncertain: Roth<sup>5</sup> takes it to mean the pin at either end of the axle ({@Akṣa@}) which goes through the nave of the wheel, and would thus be equivalent to {@Āṇi,@} and Oldenberg<sup>6</sup> [Page1-402+ 42] seems to adopt the same view. Monier Williams<sup>7</sup> seems to think that ‘load’ is meant, but this is not probable. It is possible that Dhur has the sense of ‘pole,’<sup>8</sup> and then more generally still the pole and the axle together regarded as the drawing part of the chariot: this might explain the use in the doubtful passage of the Rigveda. <F>1) i. 84, 16; 100, 16; 134, 3; 164, 19; ii. 18, 7; iii. 35, 2; v. 55. 6; vii. 34, 4, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. v. 17, 18; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa vi. 18; Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 1, 2 10; 4, 4, 13, etc.; Aitareya Āraṇyaka i. 5, 2 (the Dhur is the end), etc.</F> <F>3) iv. 33. {%Cf.%} {@Uara.@}</F> <F>4) v. 43. 8.</F> <F>5) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.,%} 2.</F> <F>6) {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 339; Griffith. {%Hymns of the Rigveda,%} 1, 508. The {%akṣa-%} {%dhurau%} are mentioned in the Āpastamba Srauta Sūtra, xi. 6, 5; Kātyāyana Srauta Sūtra, viii. 3, 22. {%Cf.%} Caland and Henry. {%L'Agniṣṭoma,%} 31.</F> <F>7) Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>8) Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 246. Later, the word means the ‘end of the pole,’ a sense already found in the Aitareya Āraṇyaka (n. 2). This modi- fication of meaning seems to be due to the fact that the yoke is at the end of the pole. See also {@Dhūrṣad.@}</F>

{@Dhūṅkṣṇā@}¦ is the form in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> of the name of the bird elsewhere found as {@Dhuṅkṣā.@} It is glossed as ‘white crow’ ({%śveta-kākī%}). <F>1) v. 5, 19, 1. Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 93, gives the form as Dhūṅkṣṇa. perhaps in error. {%Cf.%} also {@Dhvāṅkṣa.@}</F>

{@Dhūma-ketu,@}¦ ‘smoke-bannered,’ is an epithet of Mṛtyu, ‘death,’ in the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> Zimmer<sup>2</sup> thinks that a comet is meant, but Whitney<sup>3</sup> considers this extremely improbable. Lanman<sup>4</sup> plausibly suggests that the smoke of the funeral pile is referred to. <F>1) xix. 9, 10.</F> <F>2) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 358.</F> <F>3) Translation of the Atharvaveda, 914.</F> <F>4) {%Ibid.%}</F>
{@Dhūmra@}¦ in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (i. 8, 21, 1) denotes ‘camel’ according to Böhtlingk's Dictionary.

{@Dhūr-ṣad@}¦ means, according to Roth,<sup>1</sup> ‘standing under the yoke’ and so ‘burden-bearing,’ and thus metaphorically ‘promoting,’ in the passages of the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> where it occurs. More probable, however, is the view<sup>3</sup> that it means ‘sitting on the pole,’ that is, ‘charioteer,’ with reference to the fact that [Page1-403+ 48] to get near his horses the charioteer might well go forward and sit on the pole or even on the yoke.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>2) i. 143, 7; ii. 2, 1; 34, 4 (but {%cf.%} Pischel. {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 301). In x. 132, 7, Roth renders ‘resting on the yoke.’</F> <F>3) {%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%Journal of the American%} {%Oriental Society,%} 13, 237 {%et seq.;%} Keith, {%Aitareya Āraṇyaka,%} 195.</F> <F>4) {%Cf.%} Mahābhārata, viii. 617: {%dhuryān dhuryagatān sūtān.%}</F>

1. {@Dhṛta-rāṣṭra@}¦ (‘having his kingdom firmly established’) is the name of a snake demon with the patronymic {@Airāvata,@} ‘descendant of {@Irāvant,@}’ in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and the Pañca- viṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) viii. 10, 29.</F> <F>2) xxv. 15, 3. {%Cf.%} Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa, iv. 26, 15; Weber, {%Indische%} {%Studien,%} 17. 257.</F>

2. {@Dhṛtarāṣṭra Vaicitra-vīrya@}¦ (‘descendant of Vicitra- vīrya’) is mentioned in a passage of the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā,<sup>1</sup> which is, unhappily, far from intelligible. But there is no ground for supposing that he was a Kuru-Pañcāla king; he seems rather to have lived at some distance from the Kuru- Pañcālas. There is no good reason to deny his identity<sup>2</sup> with the Dhṛtarāṣṭra of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>3</sup> king of {@Kāśi,@} who was defeated, when he attempted to offer a horse sacrifice, by {@Sātrājita Śatānīka.@} The fact that the latter was a {@Bharata@} also points to Dhṛtarāṣṭra's not having been a Kuru-Pañcāla at all. In the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā he appears as having a dispute with {@Vaka Dālbhi;@} but even assuming that the latter was a Pañcāla, there is nothing to hint that the former was a Kuru or that this dispute is a sign of an early hostility of Kuru and Pañcāla.<sup>4</sup> It is true that in the Epic {@Śantanu@} and Vicitravīrya and Dhṛtarāṣṭra himself are all connected, but this connexion seems to be due, as so often in the Epic, to a confused derange- ment of great figures of the past. <F>1) x. 6. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 3, 469 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>2) As does Weber, {%Indian Literature,%} 90, 114, 125; {%Episches im vedischen Ritual,%} 7, 8. Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.,%} treats them as identical.</F> <F>3) xiii. 5, 4, 22.</F> <F>4) Keith, {%Journal of the Royal Asiatic%} {%Society,%} 1908, 831 {%et seq.%} This argument is independent of the identification of the two Dhṛtarāṣṭras, but is confirmed by it.</F>

{@Dhṛṣṭi,@}¦ found in the dual in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka,<sup>1</sup> the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>2</sup> and the Sūtras,<sup>3</sup> seems to denote ‘fire- tongs.’ <F>1) v. 9, 8.</F> <F>2) xiv. 3, 1, 22.</F> <F>3) Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xxvi. 2, 10, etc.</F>

{@Dhenā@}¦ denotes a ‘milch cow,’<sup>1</sup> or in the plural, ‘draughts of milk.’<sup>2</sup> In two passages<sup>3</sup> Roth<sup>4</sup> takes the word to mean ‘mare,’ and in another the ‘team’ of Vāyu's chariot. Benfey,<sup>6</sup> on the other hand, renders it ‘lips’ in one passage,<sup>7</sup> with Sāyaṇa and with Durga's commentary on the Nirukta.<sup>8</sup> Geldner<sup>9</sup> assigns to the word the senses of ‘lips,’<sup>10</sup> ‘speech,’<sup>11</sup> ‘cow,’<sup>12</sup> ‘beloved,’<sup>13</sup> and ‘streams.’<sup>14</sup> <div n="P"/>5) Rv. i. 2, 3. <F>1) Rv. iii. 34, 3 (Macdonell, {%Vedic%} {%Mythology,%} p. 61); v. 62, 2. {%Cf.%} Geldner, {%Vedische Studien,%} 3, 114.</F> <F>2) Rv. iii. 1, 9; iv. 58, 6, etc.</F> <F>3) i. 101, 10; v. 30, 9.</F> <F>4) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>6) {%Orient und Occident,%} 3, 130.</F> <F>7) Rv. i. 101. 10.</F> <F>8) vi. 17. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches%} {%Leben,%} 249.</F> <F>9) {%Vedische Studien,%} 3, 35-43; 166; {%Rigveda, Glossar,%} 95.</F> <F>10) Rv. i. 101. 10; iii. 1, 9.</F> <F>11) Rv. iv. 58, 6; i. 55, 4; 141, 1; viii. 32, 22; x. 104, 3. 10.</F> <F>12) Rv. v. 62, 2, and Vāyu's cow of plenty, i. 2, 3.</F> <F>13) Rv. v. 30, 9.</F> <F>14) Rv. vii. 21, 3; iii. 34, 3. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Max Müller, {%Sacred Books of the%} {%East,%} 32, 441, 442.</F>

{@Dhenu@}¦ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> means ‘milch cow,’ which is often mentioned with special reference to the production of milk,<sup>3</sup> and is contrasted with the ‘bull’ ({%vṛṣabha,%}<sup>4</sup> {%pumāṃs,%}<sup>5</sup> {%anaḍvāh%}).<sup>6</sup> In the plural<sup>7</sup> the word denotes ‘draughts of milk.’ The derivative, {%dhenukā,%} means merely ‘female.’<sup>8</sup> <F>1) i. 32, 9 ({%saha-vatsā,%} ‘with her calf’); 134, 4; ii. 2, 2; 34, 8; vi. 135, 8, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. v. 17, 18; vii. 104. 1; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 6, 2, 3; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃ- hitā, iv. 4, 8; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xviii. 27; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 2, 1, 21, etc.</F> <F>3) Rv. vii. 33. 22; viii. 14, 3; Av. iv. 34, 8 ({%kāma-dughā,%} ‘milking desires,’ the later ‘cow of plenty’ of the Epic); Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, xii. 8, 2, 2.</F> <F>4) Rv. x. 5, 7.</F> <F>5) Av. xi. 1, 34.</F> <F>6) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xviii. 27; Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 1, 2, 21.</F> <F>7) Rv. iv. 22, 6; viii. 2, 6; 4, 8; ix. 61, 21; 72, 1, etc.</F> <F>8) Av. iii. 23, 4; Pañcaviṃśa Brāh- maṇa. xxv. 10, 23; Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xii. 6, etc.</F>
{@Dhenu-ṣṭarī@}¦ in the Kāṭhaka (xiii. 6) and Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā (ii. 5, 4) denotes a cow which has ceased to give milk.

{@Dhaivara@}¦ means a ‘fisherman,’ as a member of a caste,<sup>1</sup> in the list of victims at the Puruṣamedha, or ‘human sacrifice,’ in the Yajurveda.<sup>2</sup> {%Cf.%} {@Dhīvara.@} <F>1) This seems to be shown by the patronymic form, ‘descendant of a {%dhīvara.%}’</F> <F>2) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxx. 16; Tait tirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 15, 1.</F>

{@Dhmātṛ@}¦ (lit. ‘blower’) occurs twice in one passage of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> in the two forms, {%dhmātā,%} nom. ‘smelter,’ and {%dhmātarī,%} which, according to the Padapāṭha, stands for {%dhmātari,%} a locative probably meaning ‘in the smelting furnace.’<sup>2</sup> Geldner,<sup>3</sup> Bartholomae,<sup>4</sup> and Oldenburg<sup>5</sup> regard the latter form as a locative infinitive, ‘in the smelting.’ Ludwig<sup>6</sup> and Neisser<sup>7</sup> think {%dhmātarī%} is a nom. sing. masc. used in the same sense as {%dhmātā.%} Smelting is also clearly referred to,<sup>8</sup> and the smelter is described as using the wings of birds ({%parṇa śakunānām%}) to fan the flame.<sup>9</sup> That the art was widely applied is shown by the fact that reference is made to arrows with points of {@Ayas,@}<sup>10</sup> to kettles which were fashioned of the same metal and could be placed upon a fire,<sup>11</sup> and to Soma cups of beaten Ayas.<sup>12</sup> <F>1) v. 9. 5.</F> <F>2) Macdonell, {%Journal of the Royal%} {%Asiatic Society,%} 1893, 446.</F> <F>3) {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 146, n, 1.</F> <F>4) {%Indogermanische Forschungen,%} 1, 496. n. 2.</F> <F>5) {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 46, 388.</F> <F>6) {%Infinitiv im Veda,%} 9; Translation of the Rigveda, 4, 334.</F> <F>7) Bezzenberger's {%Beitrāge,%} 20, 40.</F> <F>8) Rv. iv. 2, 17. In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, vi. 1, 3. 5, {@Ayas@} is smelted from the ore ({%aśman%}), and gold from the Ayas.</F> <F>9) Rv. ix. 112, 2.</F> <F>10) {%Cf.%} {@Īṣu.@}</F> <F>11) Rv. v. 30, 15.</F> <F>12) Rv. ix. 1, 2. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 252; Schrader, {%Prchistoric Antiquities,%} 159.</F>

{@Dhrāji@}¦ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> denotes the ‘sweep’ of the wind, referring no doubt to the violent gales which often blow in India devastating the forests, and which figure in the descriptions of the Maruts, or storm gods.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) i. 164. 44; x. 97, 13; 136, 2.</F> <F>2) Av. iii. 1, 5; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, i. 2, 17; iv. 9, 5 Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, i 11, 19, etc.</F> <F>3) {%Cf.%} Max Müller, {%Sacred Books of the%} {%East,%} xxxii. xxiii {%et seq.;%} Macdonell. {%Vedic Mythology,%} p. 79.</F>

{@Dhruva@}¦ in the Sūtras<sup>1</sup> denotes the pole star, being mentioned in connexion with the marriage ritual, in which the star is pointed out to the bride as an emblem of constancy. In the [Page1-406+ 49] Maitrāyaṇī Upaniṣad,<sup>2</sup> a late work, the movement of the Dhruva ({%dhruvasya pracalanam%}) is mentioned, but this can hardly be interpreted as referring to an actual observed motion of the nominal pole star,<sup>3</sup> but rather to an extraordinary event, such as a destruction of the world, as Cowell understood the expression.<sup>4</sup> Jacobi<sup>5</sup> sees in the motion of the Dhruva the possibility of fixing a date, on the ground that the only star which could have been deemed a pole star, as ‘immovable,’ was one ({%a%} Draconis) of the third {{millenium->millennium||20210704|Dr. Sampada Savardekar|https://github.com/sanskrit-lexicon/csl-corrections/issues/67|}} B.C. But this attempt to extract chronology from the name of the star is of very doubtful validity.<sup>6</sup> <F>1) Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra, i. 7, 22; Sāṅkhāyana Gṛhya Sūtra, i. 17, 2 {%et seq.;%} Lāṭyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, iii. 3, 6, etc. It is to be noted that the marriage Mantras, of which we have a great many, do not include any reference to the Dhruva; but it is not possible to say definitely whether the practice is really an old one or not</F> <F>2) See Max Müller, {%Sacred Books of%} {%the East,%} 15, 289; Weber, {%Indische%} {%Studien,%} 2, 396.</F> <F>3) As understood by Weber, {%Indian%} {%Literature,%} 98, n. 103; Bühler, {%Indian%} {%Antiquary,%} 23, 245, n. 21; Jacobi, {%Zeit-%} {%schrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen%} {%Gesellschaft,%} 49, 228, n. 2.</F> <F>4) In his edition of the Upaniṣad, p. 244.</F> <F>5) {%Indian Antiquary,%} 23, 157; {%Zeitschrift,%} {%loc. cit.,%} 50, 69 {%et seq.; Journal of the%} {%Royal Asiatic Society,%} 1909, 721 {%et seq.;%} 1910, 461 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>6) Whitney, {%Journal of the American%} {%Oriental Society,%} 16, xc; Keith, {%Journal%} {%of the Royal Asiatic Society,%} 1909, 1102; 1910, 465 {%et seq.%}</F>

{@Dhruvā,@}¦ ‘fixed,’ as an epithet of {@Diś,@} ‘cardinal point,’ denotes the ground under one's feet. <div n="P"/>1) Av. iii. 27, 5; xii. 3, 59; xv. 6, 1; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, viii. 14 ({%cf.%} {@Madhya-@} {@deśa@}); Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, iii. 9, 25, etc.

{@Dhvaja@}¦ occurs twice in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> in the sense of ‘banner’ used in battle. It is characteristic of Vedic fighting that in both passages reference is made to arrows being discharged and falling on the banners. <F>1) vii. 85, 2; x. 103, 11. In Epic warfare banners are of vast importance -{%e.g.,%} Rāmāyaṇa, ii. 67, 26; they were attached to a pole on the chariot, Mahabhārata, vii. 3332, etc. The army was called {%dhvajinī,%} ‘bannered host,’ {%ibid.,%} i. 2875, etc.</F>
{@Dhvanya@}¦ is apparently the name of a patron, son of {@Lakṣ-@} {@maṇa,@} in a hymn of the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) v. 33, 10. {%Cf.%} Ludwig Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 155.</F>

{@Dhvasan Dvaita-vana@}¦ (‘descendant of Dvitavana’) is the name in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> of the king of the {@Matsyas@} who celebrated an Aśvamedha, or ‘horse sacrifice,’ near the {@Sarasvatī.@} <F>1) xiii. 5, 4, 9. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 211; {%Episches im vedischen%} {%Ritual,%} 6.</F>

{@Dhvasanti@}¦ is in one passage of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> mentioned together with {@Puruṣanti@} as having been aided by the Aśvins. There can be no doubt that this is the longer form of the name {@Dhvasra,@} which is found with Puruṣanti both in the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> and in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) i. 112, 23.</F> <F>2) ix. 58. 3 = Sv. ii. 409.</F> <F>3) xiii. 7, 12 (where the dual of Dhvasra appears as a feminine {%Dhvasre%}). <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Sieg. {%Die Sagenstoffe des Ṛgveda,%} 62, 63; Benfey, {%Sāmaveda,%} 105, 126, who is inclined to think that Dhvasanti and Puruṣanti are names of women.</F>

{@Dhvasra@}¦ is named with {@Puruṣanti@} in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāh- maṇa<sup>1</sup> as giving gifts to {@Taranta@} and {@Purumīḍha.@} These two, being kings, could not<sup>2</sup> properly accept gifts which Brāhmaṇas alone could accept, but by becoming authors of a verse of the Rigveda<sup>3</sup> they qualified themselves to accept them. The verse mentions the names in the dual as {%Dhvasrayoḥ Puruṣantyoḥ,%} ‘from the two, Dhvasra and Puruṣanti.’<sup>4</sup> In the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>5</sup> the names occur in the dual as {%Dhvasre Puruṣantī,%} a reading which is confirmed by the Nidāna Sūtra.<sup>6</sup> The former is necessarily a feminine form, though Sāyaṇa, in his comment on the passage, explains it as really an irregular masculine. According to Roth,<sup>7</sup> the feminine is a corruption based on the dual form in the verse of the Rigveda mentioned above; but the names may be those of women,<sup>8</sup> as Benfey<sup>9</sup> [Page1-408+ 47] inclines to believe. Weber<sup>10</sup> suggests that the two were demons, but this is, as Sieg<sup>11</sup> shows, quite unnecessary. Dhvasra is no doubt identical with {@Dhvasanti.@} <F>1) xiii. 7, 12. {%Cf.%} Jaiminīya Brāh- maṇa, iii. 139; Sāṭyāyanaka, {%apud%} Sāyaṇa, on Rv. ix. 58, 3.</F> <F>2) Mānava Dharma Śāstra, x. 75, 77.</F> <F>3) ix. 58, 3.</F> <F>4) Both words are in the dual, as if they were members of a Dvandva com- pound. {%Cf.%} Macdonell, {%Vedic Grammar,%} 261.</F> <F>5) {%Loc. cit.%}</F> <F>6) ix. 9.</F> <F>7) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} {%dhvasra.%}</F> <F>8) The first would in that case be Dhvasrā.</F> <F>9) {%Sāmaveda,%} 105. 126, under Dhvasanti and Puruṣanti.</F> <F>10) {%Episches im vedischen Ritual,%} 27, n. 1.</F> <F>11) {%Die Sagenstoffe des Ṛgveda,%} 62, 63. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rig- veda, 3, 139; Oertel, {%Journal of the%} {%American Oriental Society,%} 18, 39; Max Müller, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 32, 360, points out that the sense of the Rīgveda passage is quite uncertain, and that the two, Taranta and Puru- mīḷha, as they appear in Rv. v. 61, are rather donors than receivers (see, however, verse 9, {%Purumīṭhāya viprāva%}). See also Oldenberg, {%Zeitschrift der%} {%Deutschen Morgenlāndischen Gesellschaft,%} 42, 232; {%Ṛgveda-Noteu,%} 1, 354.</F>

{@Dhvāṅkṣa,@}¦ ‘crow,’ is mentioned twice in the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> and in the Sūtras.<sup>2</sup> Possibly the same bird is meant by the words {@Dhuṅkṣā@} and {@Dhūṅksnā.@} <F>1) xi. 9, 9; xii. 4, 8.</F> <F>2) Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra xxv. 6, 9. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 88.</F>

{@Dhvānta@}¦ is the name of some wind in the Yajurveda Saṃhitās<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, i. 7, 7, 2; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxxix. 7.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 7, 16, 1; Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, iv. 24, 1; 25, 1.</F>

{@Nakula,@}¦ ‘ichneumon,’ is mentioned in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> as being able to cut a snake in two and then join it up again. Its knowledge<sup>2</sup> of a remedy against snake poison is also mentioned. The animal figures in the list of sacrificial victims at the Aśvamedha, or ‘horse sacrifice,’ in the Yajurveda Saṃhitās.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) vi. 139, 5.</F> <F>2) Av. viii. 7, 23.</F> <F>3) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 12, 1; 21, 1; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 26. 2; Maītrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 7 In the Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vii. 3, 18, 1; Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya, xvii. 9, {%nakula%} denotes a colour — no doubt that of the ichneumon.</F>

{@Nakta,@}¦ ‘night,’ is found frequently in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> and sometimes later,<sup>2</sup> usually in the adverbial form {%naktaṃ,%} ‘by night’ <F>1) i. 13, 7; 73, 7; 96, 5; vii. 2, 6; x. 70, 6; adverbially, i. 24, 10; 90, 7; v. 76, 3; vii. 15, 15; 104, 17; viii. 96, 1.</F> <F>2) Chāndogya Upaniṣad, viii. 4, 2, adverbially, Av. vi. 128, 4; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 1, 4, 2; xiii. 1, 5, 5, etc.</F>

{@Nakṣatra@}¦ is a word of obscure origin and derivation. The Indian interpreters already show a great divergence of opinion as to its primary meaning. The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> re- solves it into {%na-kṣatra%} (‘no power’), explaining it by a legend. The Nirukta<sup>2</sup> refers it to the root {%nakṣ,%} ‘obtain,’ following the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa.<sup>3</sup> Aufrecht<sup>4</sup> and Weber<sup>5</sup> derived it from {%nakta-tra,%} ‘guardian of night,’ and more recently<sup>6</sup> the derivation from {%nak-kṣatra,%} ‘having rule over night,’ seems to be gaining acceptance. The generic meaning of the word therefore seems to be ‘star.’ <div n="P"/>{%The Nakṣatras as Stars in the Rigveda and Later.%} — The sense of ‘star’ appears to be adequate for all or nearly all the passages in which Nakṣatra occurs in the Rigveda.<sup>7</sup> The same sense occurs in the later Saṃhitās also: the sun and the Nakṣatras are mentioned together,<sup>8</sup> or the sun, the moon, and the Nakṣatras,<sup>9</sup> or the moon and the Nakṣatras,<sup>10</sup> or the Nakṣatras alone;<sup>11</sup> [Page1-410+ 55] but there is no necessity to attribute to the word the sense of ‘lunar mansion’ in these passages. <div n="P"/>On the other hand, the names of at least three of the Nakṣatras in the later sense occur in the Rigveda. Tiṣya,<sup>12</sup> however, does not seem to be mentioned as a lunar mansion. With {@Aghās@} (plur.) and {@Arjunī@} (dual)<sup>13</sup> the case is different: it seems probable that they are the later lunar mansions called Maghās (plur.) and Phalgunī (dual). The names appear to have been deliberately changed in the Rigveda, and it must be remembered that the hymn in which they occur, the wedding hymn of Sūryā, has no claim to great age.<sup>14</sup> Ludwig<sup>15</sup> and Zimmer<sup>16</sup> have seen other references to the Nakṣatras as 27 in the Rigveda,<sup>17</sup> but these seem most improbable. Nor do the adjectives {%revatī%} (‘rich’) and {%punarvasā%} (‘bringing wealth again’) in another hymn<sup>18</sup> appear to refer to the Nakṣatras. <div n="P"/>{%The Nakṣatras as Lunar Mansions.%} — In several passages of the later Saṃhitās the connexion of the moon and the Nakṣatras is conceived of as a marriage union. Thus in the Kāṭhaka<sup>19</sup> and Taittirīya Saṃhitās<sup>20</sup> it is expressly stated that Soma was wedded to the mansions, but dwelt only with Rohiṇī; the others being angry, he had ultimately to undertake to live with them all equally. Weber<sup>21</sup> hence deduced that the Nakṣatras were regarded as of equal extent, but this is to press the texts unduly, except in the sense of approximate equality. The number of the mansions is not stated as 27 in the story told in the two Saṃhitās: the Taittīriya has 33, and the Kāṭhaka no [Page1-411+ 56] number; but 27 appears as their number in the list which is found in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>22</sup> and elsewhere.<sup>23</sup> The number 28 is much less well attested: in one passage of the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa<sup>24</sup> Abhijit is practically marked as a new comer, though in a later book,<sup>25</sup> in the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā,<sup>26</sup> and in the Atharvaveda list,<sup>27</sup> it has found acceptance. It is perfectly possible that 28 is the earlier number, and that Abhijit dropped out because it was faint, or too far north, or because 27 was a more mystic (3×3×3) number: it is significant that the Chinese Sieou and the Arabic Manāzil are 28 in number.<sup>28</sup> Weber,<sup>29</sup> however, believes that 27 is the older number in India. <div n="P"/>The meaning of the number is easily explained when it is remembered that a periodic month occupies something between 27 and 28 days, more nearly the former number. Such a month is in fact recognized in the Lāṭyāyana<sup>30</sup> and Nidāna Sūtras<sup>31</sup> as consisting of 27 days, 12 months making a year of 324 days, a Nakṣatra year, or with an intercalary month, a year of 351 days. The Nidāna Sūtra<sup>32</sup> makes an attempt to introduce the Nakṣatra reckoning into the civil or solar ({%sāvana%}) year of 360 days, for it holds that the sun spends 13(1/3) days in each Nakṣatra (13(1/3)×27 = 360). But the month of 27 or 28 days plays no part in the chronological calculations of the Veda.<sup>33</sup> <div n="P"/>{%The Names of the Nakṣatras.%} — In addition to the two men- tioned in the Rigveda, the earlier Atharvaveda<sup>34</sup> gives the [Page1-412+ 61] names of Jyeṣṭhaghnī<sup>35</sup> (the later Jyeṣṭhā) and Vicṛtau,<sup>36</sup> which are mentioned as in close connexion, and of Revatīs (plural) and Kṛttikās.<sup>37</sup> With reference to possible times for the ceremony of the Agnyādhāna, or ‘laying of the sacred fires,’ the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā,<sup>38</sup> the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā,<sup>39</sup> and the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa<sup>40</sup> mention the Nakṣatras called Kṛttikās, Rohiṇī, Phalgunyas, Hasta; the latter Brāhmaṇa adds Punar- vasū, and in an additional remark<sup>41</sup> excludes Pūrve Phalgunī in favour of Uttare Phalgunī. The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>42</sup> adds Mṛgaśīrṣa and Citrā as possibilities. On the other hand, Punarvasū is recommended by all authorities<sup>43</sup> as suitable for the Punarādheya, ‘relaying of the sacred fires,’ which takes place if the first fire has failed to effect the aim of its existence, the prosperity of the sacrificer.<sup>44</sup> The Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā,<sup>45</sup> however, allows Anurādhās also. <div n="P"/>In the ceremony of the Agnicayana, or ‘piling of the fire- altar,’ the bricks are assumed to be equal in number to the Nakṣatras. The bricks number 756, and they are equated to 27 Nakṣatras multiplied by 27 secondary Nakṣatras, reckoned as 720 (instead of 729), with the addition of 36 days, the length of an intercalary month. Nothing can be usefully derived from this piece of priestly nonsense.<sup>46</sup> But in connexion with this ceremony the Yajurveda Saṃhitās<sup>47</sup> enumerate the 27 [Page1-413+ 50] Nakṣatras, and these lists<sup>48</sup> may be given {%in extenso%} as follows: <C n="1"/>{%Taittirīya Saṃhitā.%} <C n="2"/>{%Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhita.%} <C n="3"/>{%Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā.%} <C n="1"/>1. It runs as follows: Kṛttikās, Rohiṇī, Invakās, Bāhū (dual), Tiṣya, Āśleṣās, Maghās, Pūrve Phalgunī, Uttare Phalgunī, Hasta, Citrā, Niṣṭyā, Viśākhe, Anūrādhās, Rohiṇī, Mūlabarhaṇī, Pūrvā Aṣāḍhās, Uttarā Aṣāḍhās, Śroṇā, Śraviṣṭhās, Śatabhiṣaj, Pūrve Proṣṭhapadās, Uttare Proṣṭhapadās, Revatī, Aśvayujau, Apabharaṇīs. In a later book,<sup>50</sup> however, the list grows to 28, [Page1-414+ 50] and the full moon is inserted after number 14, and the new moon after number 28, as an attempt to bring the Nākṣatra (lunar) month into accordance with the Sāvana (solar) month of 30 days. The names in this second list are as in the Saṃhitās with the following exceptions. The seven stars of the Kṛttikās are named as Ambā, Dulā, Nitatnī, Abhrayantī, Meghayantī, Varṣayantī, Cupuṇīkā, names found also in the Taittirīya<sup>51</sup> and Kāṭhaka Saṃhitās.<sup>52</sup> Beside Mṛgaśīrṣa, Invakās are also mentioned.<sup>53</sup> Then come Ārdrā, Punarvasū, Tiṣya, Āśreṣās, Maghās (beside which Anaghās, Agadās, and Arun- dhatīs are also mentioned), Phalgunyas (but elsewhere in the dual, Phalgunyau),<sup>54</sup> Phalgunyas, Hasta, Citrā, Niṣṭyā, Viśākhe, Anūrādhās, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūla, Aṣāḍhās, Aṣāḍhās, Abhijit, Śronā, Śraviṣṭhās, Śatabhiṣaj, Proṣṭhapadās, Proṣṭhapadās, Revatī, Aśvayujau, Bharaṇyas, but also Apabharaṇīs.<sup>55</sup> Abhijit, which occurs also in an earlier part of the Brāhmaṇa,<sup>56</sup> is perhaps interpolated. But Weber's<sup>57</sup> argument that Abhijit is out of place in this list because Brāhmaṇa is here mentioned as the 28th Nakṣatra, loses some force from the fact (of course unknown to him) that the list in the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā<sup>58</sup> contains 28 Nakṣatras, including Abhijit, and adds Brāhmaṇa at the end as another. <div n="P"/>In another passage<sup>59</sup> the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa divides the Nakṣatras into two sets, the Deva Nakṣatras and the Yama Nakṣatras, being 1-14 and 15-27 (with the omission of Abhijit) respectively. This division corresponds with one in the third book of the Brāhmaṇa<sup>60</sup> where the days of the light half of the month and those of the dark half are equated with the Nakṣatras. The Brāhmaṇa treats the former series as south, the latter as north; but this has no relation to facts, and can only be regarded as a ritual absurdity. <div n="P"/>The late nineteenth book of the Atharvaveda contains a list<sup>61</sup> of the Nakṣatras, including Abhijit. The names here [Page1-415+ 53] given are: Kṛttikās, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, Punarvasū, Puṣya, Āśleṣās, Maghās, Pūrvā Phalgunyau ({%sic%}),<sup>62</sup> Hasta, Citrā, Svāti (masc.),<sup>63</sup> Viśākhe, Anurādhā,<sup>64</sup> Jyeṣṭhā, Mūla, Pūrvā Aṣāḍhās,<sup>65</sup> Uttarā Aṣāḍhās, Abhijit, Śravaṇa, Śraviṣṭhās, Śatabhiṣaj, Dvayā Proṣṭhapadā, Revatī, Aśvayujau, Bharaṇyas. <div n="P"/>{%The Position of the Nakṣatras.%} — There is nothing definite in Vedic literature regarding the position of most of the Nakṣatras, but the later astronomy precisely locates all of them, and its statements agree on the whole satisfactorily with what is said in the earlier texts, though Weber<sup>66</sup> was inclined to doubt this. 1. {@Kṛttikās@}¦ are unquestionably <lang n="greek">η</lang> Tauri, etc., the Pleiades. The names of the seven stars forming this constellation, and given above from Yajurveda texts,<sup>68</sup> include three — {%abhrayantī,%} ‘forming clouds’; {%meghayantī,%} ‘making cloudy’; {%varṣayantī,%} ‘causing rain’ — which clearly refer to the rainy Pleiades. The word {%kṛttikā%} possibly means ‘web,’ from the root {%kṛt,%} ‘spin.’ <F>68) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iv. 4, 5, 1; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xl. 4; Taittīrīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 1, 4, 1.</F>

2. {@Rohiṇī,@}¦ ‘ruddy,’ is the name of the conspicuously reddish star, <lang n="greek">α</lang> Tauri or Aldebaran, and denotes the group of the Hyades, <lang n="greek">α θ γ δ ε</lang> Tauri. Its identification seems absolutely assured by the legend of Prajāpati in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.<sup>69</sup> He is there represented as pursuing his daughter with incestuous intention, and as having been shot with an arrow ({@Iṣu Trikāṇḍā,@} ‘the belt of Orion’) by the ‘huntsman’ ({@Mṛgavyādha,@} ‘Sirius’). Prajāpati is clearly Orion (Mṛgaśiras being the name of the little group of stars in Orion's head). <F>69) iii. 33. {%Cf.%} Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 1, 2, 8; Tilak, {%Orion,%} 98 {%et seq.%}</F>

3. {@Mṛgaśīrṣa@}¦ or {@Mṛgaśiras,@} also called Invakā or Invagā, [Page1-416+ 47] seems to be the faint stars <lang n="greek">λ, φ<sup>1</sup>, φ<sup>2</sup></lang>, Orionis. They are called Andhakā, ‘blind,’ in the Śāntikalpa of the Atharvaveda, probably because of their dimness.<sup>70</sup> <F>70) Whitney, {%op. cit.,%} 401. {%Cf.%} Tilak, 102 {%et seq.%}</F>

4. {@Ārdrā,@}¦ ‘moist,’ is the name of the brilliant star, <lang n="greek">α</lang> Orionis. But the names by which it is styled, in the plural as Ārdrās in the Śāṅkhāyana Gṛhya Sūtra<sup>71</sup> and the Nakṣatrakalpa,<sup>72</sup> and in the dual as Bāhū, in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa,<sup>73</sup> point to a constellation of two or more stars, and it may be noted<sup>74</sup> that the corresponding Chinese Sieou includes the seven brilliant stars composing the shoulders, the belt, and the knees of Orion. <F>71) i. 26.</F> <F>72) 10.</F> <F>73) i. 5, 1.</F> <F>74) Whitney, {%op. cit.,%} 352, 401, n. 1.</F>

5. {@Punarvasū,@}¦ ‘the two that give wealth again,’ denotes the two stars, <lang n="greek">α</lang> and <lang n="greek">β</lang> Geminorum, on the heads of Castor and Pollux. The name is no doubt connected with the beneficent character of the Aśvins, who correspond to the Dioscuri.<sup>75</sup> <F>75) Oldenberg, {%Religion des Veda,%} 212; Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} p. 53.</F>

6. {@Tiṣya@}¦ or {@Puṣya@} includes the somewhat faint group in the body of the Crab, <lang n="greek">γ, δ</lang>, and <lang n="greek">θ</lang> Cancri. The singular is rather curious, as primarily one star would seem to have been meant. and none of the group is at all prominent.<sup>76</sup> <F>76) Whitney, {%op. cit.,%} 403, n. 1.</F>

7. {@Āśreṣās@}¦ or {@Āśleṣās,@} which in some texts<sup>77</sup> is certainly to be read Aśreṣās or Aśleṣas, denotes <lang n="greek">δ, ε, η, ρ, σ</lang>, and perhaps also <lang n="greek">ζ</lang>, Hydræ. The word means ‘embracer,’ a name which admirably fits the constellation. <F>77) Aśreṣās, Śāṅkhāyana Gṛhya Sūtra, i. 26; Śāntikalpa; Nakṣatrakalpa; Aśleṣās, Śāntikalpa, 2; Nakṣatrakalpa, 4. 48.</F>

8. {@Maghās,@}¦ the ‘bounties,’ are the Sickle, or <lang n="greek">α, η, γ, ζ, μ, ε</lang>, Leonis. The variants {@Anaghā,@} the ‘sinless one,’ etc., clearly refer to the auspicious influence of the constellation. <div n="P"/>9, 10. {@Phalgunī, Phalgunyau, Phalgū,@}<sup>78</sup> {@Phalgunīs, Phal-@} {@gunyas,@} is really a-double constellation, divided into Pūrve, ‘former,’ and Uttare, ‘latter.’ The former is <lang n="greek">δ</lang> and <lang n="greek">θ</lang> Leonis, the latter <lang n="greek">β</lang> and 93 new Leonis. According to Weber, the word denotes, like {@Arjunī,@} the variant of the Rigveda,<sup>79</sup> a ‘bright- coloured’ constellation. <F>78) Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, v. 1.</F> <F>79) x. 85, 13.</F>

11. {@Hasta,@}¦ ‘hand,’ is made up of the five conspicuous stars (<lang n="greek">δ, γ, ε, α, β</lang>) in Corvus, a number which the word itself suggests. According to Geldner,<sup>80</sup> the ‘five bulls’ of the Rigveda are this constellation. <F>80) {%Vedische Studien,%} 3, 177; Rv. i. 105, 10. {%Cf.%} below, p. 427, n. 156.</F>

12. {@Citrā,@}¦ ‘bright,’ is the beautiful star, <lang n="greek">α</lang> Virginis. It is mentioned in a legend of Indra in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa,<sup>81</sup> and in that of the ‘two divine dogs’ ({%divyau śvānau%}) in the Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa.<sup>82</sup> <F>81) Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 1, 2, 4-6.</F> <F>82) ii. 1, 2, 13-17.</F>

13. {@Svātī@}¦ or {@Niṣṭyā@} is later clearly the brilliant star Arcturus or <lang n="greek">α</lang> Bootis, its place in the north being assured by the notice in the Śāntikalpa,<sup>83</sup> where it is said to be ‘ever traversing the northern way’ ({%nityam uttara-mārgagam%}). The Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa,<sup>84</sup> however, constructs an asterismal Prajāpati, giving him Citrā (<lang n="greek">α</lang> Virginis) for head, Hasta (Corvus) for hand, the Viśākhe (<lang n="greek">α</lang> and <lang n="greek">β</lang> Libræ) for thighs, and the Anurādhās (<lang n="greek">β, δ,</lang>, and <lang n="greek">π</lang> Scorpionis) for standing place, with Niṣṭyā for heart. But Arcturus, being 30° out, spoils this figure, while, on the other hand, the Arabic and Chinese systems have respectively, instead of Arcturus, <lang n="greek">ι, κ</lang>, and <lang n="greek">λ</lang> Virginis and <lang n="greek">κ</lang> Virginis, which would well fit into the Prajāpati figure. But in spite of the force of this argument of Weber's,<sup>85</sup> Whitney<sup>86</sup> is not certain that Niṣṭyā here must mean a star in Virgo, pointing out that the name Niṣṭyā, ‘outcast,’ suggests the separation of this Nakṣatra from the others in question. <F>83) 3.</F> <F>84) i. 5, 2. {%Cf.%} Tilak, {%Orion,%} 204.</F> <F>85) {%Op. cit.,%} 2, 307, 308.</F> <F>86) {%Op. cit.,%} 409.</F>

14. {@Viśākhe@}¦ is the couple of stars <lang n="greek">α</lang> and <lang n="greek">β</lang> Libræ. This mansion is later called Rādhā according to the Amarakośa, and it is curious that in the Atharvaveda<sup>87</sup> the expression {%rādho%} {%Viśākhe,%} ‘the Viśākhe are prosperity,’ should occur. But probably Rādhā is merely an invention due to the name of the next Nakṣatra, Anurādhā, wrongly conceived as meaning ‘that which is after or follows Rādhā.’<sup>88</sup> <F>87) xix. 7.</F> <F>88) Lanman in Whitney's Translation of the Atharvaveda, 908. {%Cf.%} Thibaut, {%Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal,%} 63, 156.</F>

28. {@Apabharaṇīs, Bharaṇīs,@}¦ or {@Bharaṇyas,@} ‘the bearers,’ is the name of the small triangle in the northern part of the Ram known as Musca or 35, 39, and 41 Arietis. <div n="P"/>{%The Nakṣatras and the Months.%} — In the Brāhmaṇas the Nakṣatra names are regularly used to denote dates. This is done in two ways. The name, if not already a feminine, may be turned into a feminine and compounded with {%pūrṇa-māsa,%} ‘the full moon,’ as in {%Tiṣyā-pūrṇamāsa,%} ‘the full moon in the Nakṣatra Tiṣya.’<sup>103</sup> Much more often, however, it is turned into a derivative adjective, used with {%paurṇamāsī,%} ‘the full [Page1-420+ 52] moon (night),’ or with {%amāvāsyā,%} ‘the new moon (night),’ as in {%Phālgunī paurṇamāsī,%} ‘the full-moon night in the Nakṣatra Phalgunī’;<sup>104</sup> or, as is usual in the Sūtras, the Nakṣatra adjec- tive alone is used to denote the full-moon night. The month itself is called by a name derived<sup>105</sup> from that of a Nakṣatra, but only Phālguna,<sup>106</sup> Caitra,<sup>107</sup> Vaiśākha,<sup>108</sup> Taiṣya,<sup>109</sup> Māgha<sup>110</sup> occur in the Brāhmaṇas, the complete list later being Phālguna, Caitra, Vaiśākha, Jyaiṣṭha, Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, Prauṣṭhapada, Āśvayuja, Kārttika, Mārgaśīrṣa, Taiṣya, Māgha. Strictly speaking, these should be lunar months, but the use of a lunar year was clearly very restricted: we have seen that as early as the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa there was a tendency to equate lunar months with the twelve months of thirty days which made up the solar year (see {@Māsa@}). <div n="P"/>{%The Nakṣatras and Chronology.%} — (1) An endeavour has been made to ascertain from the names of the months the period at which the systematic employment of those names was intro- duced. Sir William Jones<sup>111</sup> refers to this possibility, and Bentley, by the gratuitous assumption that Śrāvaṇa always marked the summer solstice, concluded that the names of the months did not date before B.C. 1181. Weber<sup>112</sup> considered that there was a possibility of fixing a date by this means, but Whitney<sup>113</sup> has convincingly shown that it is an impossible feat, and Thibaut<sup>114</sup> concurs in this view. Twelve became fixed as the number of the months because of the desire, evident in the Brāhmaṇas, somehow or other to harmonize lunar with solar time; but the selection of twelve Nakṣatras out of twenty-seven as connected with the night of full moon can have no chronological significance, because full moon at [Page1-421+ 55] no period occurred in those twelve only, but has at all periods occurred in every one of the twenty-seven at regularly re- current intervals. <div n="P"/>(2) All the lists of the Nakṣatras begin with Kṛttīkās. It is only fair to suppose that there was some special reason for this fact. Now the later list of the Nakṣatras begins with Aśvinī, and it was unquestionably rearranged because at the time of its adoption the vernal equinox coincided with the star <lang n="greek">ζ</lang> Piscium on the border of Revatī and Aśvinī,<sup>115</sup> say in the course of the sixth century A.D. Weber<sup>116</sup> has therefore accepted the view that the Kṛttikās were chosen for a similar reason, and the date at which that Nakṣatra coincided with the vernal equinox has been estimated at some period in the third millennium B.C.<sup>117</sup> A very grave objection to this view is its assumption that the sun, and not the moon, was then regarded as connected with the Nakṣatras; and both Thibaut<sup>118</sup> and Oldenberg<sup>119</sup> have pronounced decidedly against the idea of connecting the equinox with the Kṛttikās. Jacobi<sup>120</sup> has contended that in the Rigveda<sup>121</sup> the commencement of the rains and the summer solstice mark the beginning of the new year and the end of the old, and that further the new year began with the summer solstice in Phalgunī.<sup>121</sup> He has also referred to the distinction of the two sets of Deva and Yama Nakṣatras in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa<sup>122</sup> as supporting his view of the connexion of the sun and the Nakṣatras. But this view is far from satisfactory: the Rigveda passages cannot yield the sense required except by translating the word {%dvādaśa%}<sup>123</sup> as ‘the twelfth (month)’ instead of ‘consisting of twelve parts,’ that is, ‘year,’ the accepted [Page1-422+ 61] interpretation; and the division of the Nakṣatras is not at all satisfactorily explained by a supposed connexion with the sun. It may further be mentioned that even if the Nakṣatra of Kṛttikās be deemed to have been chosen because of its coincidence with the vernal equinox, both Whitney<sup>124</sup> and Thibaut<sup>125</sup> are pre- pared to regard it as no more than a careless variant of the date given by the Jyotiṣa, which puts the winter solstice in Māgha. <div n="P"/>(3) The winter solstice in Māgha is assured by a Brāhmaṇa text, for the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa<sup>126</sup> expressly places it in the new moon of Māgha ({%māghasyāmāvāsyāyām%}). It is not very important whether we take this with the commentators<sup>127</sup> as the new moon in the middle of a month commencing with the day after full moon in Taiṣa, or, which is much more likely, as the new moon beginning the month and preceding full moon in Māgha. The datum gives a certain possibility of fixing an epoch in the following way. If the end of Revatī marked the vernal equinox at one period, then the precession of the equinoxes would enable us to calculate at what point of time the vernal equinox was in a position corresponding to the winter solstice in Māgha, when the solstitial colure cut the ecliptic at the beginning of Śraviṣṭhās. This would be, on the strict theory, in the third quarter of Bharaṇī, 6(3/4) asterisms removed from Śraviṣṭhās, and the difference between that and the beginning of Aśvinī= [Page1-423+ 48] 1(3/4) asterisms = 23(1/3)° (27 asterisms being = 360°). Taking the starting-point at 499 A.D., the assured period of Varāha Mihira, Jones<sup>128</sup> arrived at the date B. C. 1181 for the vernal equinox corresponding to the winter solstice in Māgha — that is, on the basis of 1° = 72 years as the precession. Pratt<sup>129</sup> arrived at precisely the same date, taking the same rate of precession and adopting as his basis the ascertained position in the Siddhāntas of the junction star<sup>130</sup> of Maghā, <lang n="greek">α</lang> Leonis or Regulus. Davis<sup>131</sup> and Colebrooke<sup>132</sup> arrived at a different date, B.C. 1391, by taking as the basis of their calculation the junction star of Citrā, which happens to be of uncertain position, varying as much as 3° in the different textbooks. But though the twelfth century has received a certain currency as the epoch of the observation in the Jyotiṣa,<sup>133</sup> it is of very doubtful value. As Whitney points out, it is impossible to say that the earlier asterisms coincided in position with the later asterisms of 13(1/3)° extent each. They were not chosen as equal divisions, but as groups of stars which stood in conjunction with the moon; and the result of subsequently making them strictly equal divisions was to throw the principal stars of the later groups altogether out of their asterisms.<sup>134</sup> Nor can we say that the star <lang n="greek">ζ</lang> Piscium early formed the eastern boundary of Revatī; it may possibly not even have been in that asterism at all, for it is far remote from the Chinese and Arabic asterisms corresponding to Revatī. Added to all this, and to the uncertainty of the starting-point —  582 A.D., 560 A.D., or 491 A.D. being variants<sup>135</sup> — is the fact that the place of the equinox is not a matter accurately determin- able by mere observation, and that the Hindu astronomers of the Vedic period cannot be deemed to have been very accurate observers, since they made no precise determination of the [Page1-424+ 78] number of days of the year, which even in the Jyotiṣa they do not determine more precisely than as 366 days, and even the Sūrya Siddhānta<sup>136</sup> does not know the precession of the equinoxes. It is therefore only fair to allow a thousand years for possible errors,<sup>137</sup> and the only probable conclusion to be drawn from the datum of the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa is that it was recording an observation which must have been made some centuries B.C., in itself a result quite in harmony with the probable date of the Brāhmaṇa literature,<sup>138</sup> say B.C. 800-600. <div n="P"/>(4) Another chronological argument has been derived from the fact that there is a considerable amount of evidence for Phālguna having been regarded as the beginning of the year, since the full moon in Phalgunī is often described as the ‘mouth ({%mukham%}) of the year.’<sup>139</sup> Jacobi<sup>140</sup> considers that this [Page1-425+ 54] was due to the fact that the year was reckoned from the winter solstice, which would coincide with the month of Phālguna about B.C. 4000. Oldenberg<sup>141</sup> and Thibaut,<sup>142</sup> on the other hand, maintain that the choice of Phālguna as the ‘mouth’ of the year was due to its being the first month of spring. This view is favoured by the fact that there is distinct evidence<sup>143</sup> of the correspondence of Phālguna and the beginning of spring: as we have seen above in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, the new moon in Māgha is placed at the winter solstice,<sup>144</sup> which puts the full moon of Phalgunī at a month and a half after the winter solstice, or in the first week of February, a date not in itself improbable for about B.C. 800, and corresponding with the February 7 of the {%veris initium%} in the Roman Calendar. This fact accords with the only natural division of the year into three periods of four months, as the rainy season lasts from June 7-10 to October 7-10, and it is certain that the second set of four months dates from the beginning of the rains (see {@Cāturmāsya@}). Tilak,<sup>145</sup> on the other hand, holds that the winter solstice coincided with Māghī full moon at the time of the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (B.C. 2350), and had coincided with Phālgunī and Caitrī in early periods — viz., B.C. 4000-2500, and B.C. 6000- 4000. <div n="P"/>(5) The passages of the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>146</sup> and the Pañca- viṃśa Brāhmaṇa,<sup>147</sup> which treat the full moon in Phālguna as the beginning of the year, give as an alternative the full moon in Caitra. Probably the latter month was chosen so as to secure that the initial day should fall well within the season of spring,<sup>148</sup> and was not, as Jacobi believes, a relic of a period [Page1-426+ 49] when the winter solstice corresponded with Caitra. Another alternative is the Ekāṣṭakā, interpreted by the commentators as the eighth day after the full moon in Maghās, a time which might, as being the last quarter of the waning half of the old year, well be considered as representing the end of the year. A fourth alternative is the fourth day before full moon; the full moon meant must be that of Caitra, as Ālekhana quoted by Āpastamba held, not of Māgha, as Āśmarathya, Laugākṣi and the Mīmāṃsists believed, and as Tilak believes.<sup>149</sup> <div n="P"/>(6) Others, again, according to the Gṛhya ritual, began the year with the month Mārgaśīrṣa, as is shown by its other name Āgrahāyaṇa<sup>150</sup> (‘belonging to the commencement of the year’). Jacobi and Tilak<sup>151</sup> think that this one denoted the autumn equinox in Mṛgaśiras, corresponding to the winter solstice in Phalgunī. But, as Thibaut<sup>152</sup> shows clearly, it was selected as the beginning of a year that was taken to commence with autumn, just as some took the spring to commence with Caitra instead of Phālguna.<sup>153</sup> <div n="P"/>(7) Jacobi has also argued, with the support of Bühler,<sup>154</sup> from the terms given for the beginning of Vedic study in the Gṛhya Sūtras, on the principle that study commenced with the rains (as in the Buddhist {%vassā%}) which mark the summer solstice. He concludes that if Bhādrapada appears as the date of commencing study in some texts, it was fixed thus because at one time Proṣṭhapadās (the early name of Bhadra- padās) coincided with the summer solstice, this having been the case when the winter solstice was in Phālguna. But Whitney<sup>155</sup> has pointed out that this argument is utterly illegitimate; we cannot say that there was any necessary connexion between the rains and learning — a month like Śrāvaṇa might be preferred [Page1-427+ 89] because of its connexion with the word Śravaṇa, ‘ear’ — and in view of the precession of the equinoxes, we must assume that Bhādrapada was kept because of its traditional coincidence with the beginning of the rains after it had ceased actually so to coincide.<sup>156</sup> <div n="P"/>{%The Origin of the Nakṣatras.%} — As we have seen, there is no evidence showing the process by which the Nakṣatras may [Page1-428+ 52] have originated in India. They are mentioned only as stars in the earlier parts of the Rigveda, then the names of three of them are found in the latest parts of that Saṃhitā, and finally in the later Atharvaveda and in the Yajurveda Saṃhitās the full list appears. It may also be noted that the Vedic Indians show (see {@Graha@}) a remarkably small knowledge of the other astronomical phenomena; the discovery of a series of 27 lunar mansions by them would therefore be rather surprising. On the other hand, the nature of such an operation is not very complicated; it consists merely in selecting a star or a star group with which the moon is in conjunction. It is thus impossible {%a priori%} to deny that the Vedic Indians could have invented for themselves a lunar Zodiac.<sup>157</sup> <div n="P"/>But the question is complicated by the fact that there exist two similar sets of 28 stars or star groups in Arabia and in China, the Manāzil and the Sieou. The use of the Manāzil in Arabia is consistent and effective; the calendar is regulated by them, and the position of the asterisms corresponds best with the positions required for a lunar Zodiac. The Indians might therefore have borrowed the system from Arabia, but that is a mere possibility, because the evidence for the existence of the Manāzil is long posterior to that for the existence of the Nakṣatras, while again the Mazzaroth or Mazzaloth of the Old Testament<sup>158</sup> may really be the lunar mansions.<sup>159</sup> That the Arabian system is borrowed from India, as Burgess<sup>160</sup> held, is, on the other hand, not at all probable. <div n="P"/>Biot, the eminent Chinese scholar, in a series of papers published by him between 1839 and 1861,<sup>161</sup> attempted to prove [Page1-429+ 48] the derivation of the Nakṣatra from the Chinese Sieou. The latter he did not regard as being in origin lunar mansions at all. He thought that they were equatorial stars used, as in modern astronomy, as a standard to which planets or other stars observed in the neighbourhood {{can be eferred->can be referred||20210704|Dr. Sampada Savardekar|https://github.com/sanskrit-lexicon/csl-corrections/issues/67|}}; they were, as regards twenty-four of them, {{selecte about->selected about||20210704|Dr. Sampada Savardekar|https://github.com/sanskrit-lexicon/csl-corrections/issues/67|}} B.C. 2357 on account of their proximity to the equator, and of their having the same right ascension as certain circumpolar stars which had attracted the attention of Chinese observers. Four more were added in B.C. 1100 in order to mark the equinoxes and solstices of the period. He held that the list of stars commenced with Mao (= Kṛttikās), which was at the vernal equinox in B.C. 2357. Weber,<sup>162</sup> in an elaborate essay of 1860, disputed this theory, and endeavoured to show that the Chinese literary evidence for the Sieou was late, dating not even from before the third century B.C. The last point does not appear<sup>163</sup> to be correct, but his objections against the basis of Biot's theory were rein- forced by Whitney,<sup>164</sup> who insisted that Biot's supposition of the Sieou's not having been ultimately derived from a system of lunar mansions, was untenable. This is admitted by the latest defender of the hypothesis of borrowing from China, Léopold de Saussure,<sup>165</sup> , but his arguments in favour of a Chinese origin for the Indian lunar mansions have been refuted by Oldenberg,<sup>166</sup> who has also pointed out<sup>167</sup> that the series does not begin with Mao (= Kṛttikās). <div n="P"/>There remains only the possibility that a common source for all the three sets — Nakṣatra, Manāzil, and Sieou — may be found in Babylonia. Hommel<sup>168</sup> has endeavoured to show that recent research has established in Babylonia the existence of a lunar zodiac of twenty-four members headed by the [Page1-430+ 120] Pleiades (= Kṛttikās); but Thibaut's researches<sup>169</sup> are not favourable to this claim. On the other hand, Weber,<sup>170</sup> Whitney,<sup>171</sup> Zimmer,<sup>172</sup> and Oldenberg<sup>173</sup> all incline to the view that in Babylonia is to be found the origin of the system, and this must for the present be regarded as the most probable view, for there are other traces of Babylonian influence in Vedic literature, such as the legend of the flood, perhaps the Ādityas,<sup>174</sup> and possibly the word {@Manā.@} <F>103) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 2, 10, 1. {%Cf.%} vii. 4, 8, 1. 2; Pañcaviṃśa Brāh- maṇa, v. 9, 1.</F> <F>104) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 6, 3. 11 {%et seq.;%} vi. 2, 2, 18; xiii. 4, 1, 4; Kausītaki Brāhmaṇa, i. 3; iv. 4; v. 1. {@Nakṣatra-darśa@}¦ (‘gazer at the lunar mansions’), an ‘astro- loger,’ is mentioned in the list of victims at the Puruṣamedha, or ‘human sacrifice,’ in the Yajurveda.<sup>1</sup> A notice in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> indicates that that work regarded the practice of choosing a particular Nakṣatra under which to set up the sacrificial fires as an idle one, because it decides in favour of choosing the sun as one's Nakṣatra. <F>1) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxx. 10; Tait- tirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 4, 1.</F> <F>2) ii. 1, 2, 19, and {%cf.%} the Kāṇva text in Eggeling, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} xii, 288, n. 3.</F>
{@Nakṣatra-vidyā,@}¦ the ‘science of the lunar mansions,’ ‘astronomy,’ is mentioned with other sciences in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (vii. 1, 2. 4; 2, 1; 7, 1).

{@Nakha@}¦ denotes either the ‘nail’ of a man,<sup>1</sup> or the ‘claw’ of a wild beast, such as a tiger.<sup>2</sup> The trimming ({%nikṛntana%})<sup>3</sup> of the nails was a regular part of the toilet of the Vedic Indian, especially on occasions of special sanctity, when it accompanied the cleansing of the teeth.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) Rv. i. 162, 9; x. 163, 5; Av. ii. 33, 6, etc.</F> <F>2) Rv. iv. 3, 3. {%Cf.%} x. 28, 10, of the eagle's talon.</F> <F>3) Chāndogya Upaniṣad, vi. 1, 6.</F> <F>4) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 5, 1, 7; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 6, 2, etc.; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 1, 3, 4.</F>
{@Na-ga@}¦ (‘not moving’), ‘mountain,’ is a word occurring only in a late book of the Atharvaveda (xix. 8, 1), and then in the Sūtras.

{@Nagara@}¦ is in early Vedic literature found only in the deriva- tive adjective, used as a proper name, {@Nagarin,@} but it appears in the sense of ‘town’ in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka (i. 11, 18; 31, 4), and frequently in the later language.
{@Nagarin Jāna-śruteya@}¦ (‘descendant of Janaśruti’) is men- tioned as a priest in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (v. 30), and as Nagarin Jānaśruteya Kāṇḍviya in the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa (iii. 40, 2).

{@Nagha-māra@}¦ and {@Naghā-riṣa.@} See 1. {@Kuṣṭha.@}

{@Na-ciketas@}¦ occurs in the well-known legend of the Taitti- rīya Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> (where he is a Gotama, the son of {@Vāja-@} {@śravasa@}), and in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad.<sup>2</sup> His historical reality is extremely doubtful: in the Upaniṣad he is called son of Āruṇi Auddālaki or Vājaśravasa, an impossible attribution, and one due only to a desire to give Naciketas a connexion with the famous Āruṇi. <F>1) iii. 11, 8.</F> <F>2) i. 1, etc. {%Cf.%} Geldner, {%Vedische%} {%Studien,%} 3, 154, n, 1; Weber, {%Indian%} {%Literature,%} 157; Macdonell, {%Vedic Myth-%} {%ology,%} p. 168.</F>

1. {@Naḍa,@}¦ ‘reed,’ is mentioned in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as growing in lakes, and in the Atharvaveda<sup>2</sup> is described as {%vārṣika,%} ‘pro- duced in the rains.’ Reeds were used, after being split, for making mats, a work carried out by women.<sup>3</sup> They are frequently mentioned elsewhere.<sup>4</sup> See also {@Nada.@} <F>1) viii. 1, 33.</F> <F>2) iv. 19, 1.</F> <F>3) Av. vi. 138, 5.</F> <F>4) Av. vi. 137, 2; xii. 2, 1, 19. 50. 54; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxv. 7; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 1, 4, 19; Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, vi. 7, 10. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 71.</F>

2. {@Naḍa Naiṣadha@}¦ is mentioned in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> where he seems to be<sup>2</sup> a human king who is compared with Yama, the god of death, because of his conquests. Being there identified with the southern sacrificial fire, he was pre- sumably a king of the south, just as Yama is connected with the south. <F>1) ii. 2, 2, 1. 2.</F> <F>2) Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 225-227, followed by Eggeling, {%Sacred Books of%} {%the East,%} 12, 338, notes 4 and 5. The printed text has Naiṣidha by error.</F>
{@Naḍvalā,@}¦ a ‘reed bed,’ is mentioned in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā (xxx. 16) and the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa (iii. 4, 12, 1).

{@Nada@}¦ is found in several passages of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> but its sense is still obscure. It is identified by Pischel<sup>2</sup> with {@Naḍa,@} being explained by him in one passage<sup>3</sup> as a reed boat, which is split, and over which the waters go; in another<sup>4</sup> as a reed whip, of which the sharp points ({%karṇa%}) are used to urge horses on; and in others<sup>5</sup> again as figuratively designating the penis. Roth<sup>6</sup> takes the sense to be ‘bull’ (either literally or meta- [Page1-434+ 45] phorically) in all passages. Once at least<sup>7</sup> the ‘neigher’ (from the root {%nad,%} ‘sound’) seems to be meant with reference to Indra's horse. In the phrase {%nadasya karṇaiḥ%}^8 the sense is, perhaps, ‘through the ears of the (side) horse’ (that is, by their being ready to hear the word of command) of their chariot, the Maruts ‘hasten on with their swift steeds’ ({%turayanta%} {%āśubhiḥ%}). <F>1) i. 32, 8; 179, 4; ii. 34, 3; viii. 69, 2; x. 11, 2; 105, 4. {%Cf.%} Nirukta, v. 2.</F> <F>2) {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgen-%} {%ländischen Gesellschaft,%} 35, 717 {%et seq.;%} {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 183 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>3) i. 32, 8. Here Caland and Henry, {%L'Agniṣṭoma,%} 312, n., would read {%naḷam.%} See also Wackernagel, {%Altindische Gram-%} {%matik,%} 1, 173.</F> <F>4) ii. 34, 3, followed by Max Müller, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 32, 301 (who, however, does not construe {%āśubhiḥ,%} ‘sharp,’ with {%karṇaiḥ%} as Pischel does in {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 190). He sees ‘reed’ also in x. 11, 2, but ‘horse’ in x. 105, 4.</F> <F>5) i. 179, 4; viii. 69, 2.</F> <F>6) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} The sense of ‘bull’ seems imperative in viii. 89, 2; it is admissible in i. 179, 4, where ‘bull’ may denote a man, and in x. 11, 2, and possibly in i. 32, 8, but ‘reed’ there seems far more likely.</F> <F>7) x. 105, 4. and in x. 11, 2. The latter passage suggests that ‘river’ may, after all, be the sense there. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Oldenberg, {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 32, 178, 215.</F>

{@Nadī,@}¦ ‘stream,’ is mentioned in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> Reference is made to shallows ({%gādha%})<sup>3</sup> in the river's bed, to the opposite bank ({%pāra%}),<sup>4</sup> and to the bathing of horses in streams.<sup>5</sup> Rivers are also mentioned in close connexion with mountains.<sup>6</sup> The title Nadī-pati, ‘lord of rivers,’<sup>7</sup> is once used to express ‘ocean’ or ‘sea-water.’ <F>1) i. 158, 5; ii. 35, 3; iii. 33, 4; v. 46, 6, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. iii. 13, 1; xiv. 1, 43.</F> <F>3) Rv. vii. 60, 7.</F> <F>4) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xi. 1, 6, 6.</F> <F>5) Rv. viii. 2, 2.</F> <F>6) Rv. v. 55, 7; x. 64, 8.</F> <F>7) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, v. 3, 4, 10.</F>

{@Nanā@}¦ is a familiar name for mother, parallel with {@Tata,@} for father, with which it is found in a verse of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> describing the occupations of the parents of the poet. <F>1) ix. 112, 3. {%Cf.%} Nirukta, vi. 6, and see {@Upala-prakṣiṇī.@}</F>

{@Nanāndṛ@}¦ is a word occurring only once in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> where it denotes, according to Sāyaṇa, the ‘husband's sister,’ over whom the wife is to rule. This interpretation is confirmed by the fact that the same position is ascribed to the husband's sister — no doubt while unmarried and living in her brother's care — by the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) x. 85, 46.</F> <F>2) iii. 22. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Delbrück, {%Die indogermanischen%} {%Verwandtschaftsnamen,%} 516. The native lexicographers recognize the word, though its occurrence in the later literature is very rare (it has been noted in the Uttararāmacarita). See the St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>

{@Napāt@}¦ in Vedic literature apparently has both the wider sense of ‘descendant,’<sup>1</sup> and the narrower one of ‘grandson’ in the Saṃhitās.<sup>2</sup> In the Brāhmaṇas the word seems hardly to have the sense of ‘descendant’ at all, while it denotes not only ‘grandson,’<sup>3</sup> but also ‘great-grandson’ in the sequence ‘sons, grandsons, great-grandsons’ ({%putrān, pautrān, naptṝn%}).<sup>4</sup> ‘Grandson’ is also expressed by Pautra (‘son's son’) in the Atharvaveda and later,<sup>5</sup> while the sense of ‘great-grandson’ is accurately conveyed as early as the Rigveda<sup>6</sup> by Pra-ṇapāt, used beside Napāt, ‘grandson.’ Naptī, the feminine, is practi- cally limited to the Saṃhitās,<sup>7</sup> and denotes ‘daughter.’ The use in the Veda throws no light on the original use of the word.<sup>8</sup> <F>1) It is equivalent to ‘son’ in a number of mythological epithets such as {%apāṃ napāt,%} ‘son of waters.’</F> <F>2) Rv. x. 10, 1, clearly ‘son’; vi. 20, 11, may be ‘grandson.’ Most passages, vi. 50, 15; vii. 18, 22; viii. 65, 12; 102, 7; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxi. 61; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxii. 2, require ‘de- scendant.’</F> <F>3) As in Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 48; {%putra-naptāraḥ.%} ‘sons and grandsons.’ {%Cf.%} Nirukta, viii. 5.</F> <F>4) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vii. 10, 3; Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra, x. 11, 5.</F> <F>5) Av. ix. 5, 30; xi. 7, 16; Aitarey Brāhmaṇa, vii. 10, 3; Taittirīya Brāh- maṇa, ii. 1, 8, 3.</F> <F>6) Rv. viii. 17, 13, with {%napāt.%}</F> <F>7) Rv. iii. 31, 1 (Nirukta, iii. 4); viii. 2, 42. {%Cf.%} i. 50, 9; ix. 9, 1; 14, 5; 69, 3; Av. i. 28, 4; ii. 14, 1; vii. 82, 6.</F> <F>8) Delbrück, {%Die indogermanischen Ver-%} {%wandtschaftsnamen,%} 403-405; Lanmann, {%Festgruss an Böhtlingk,%} 77.</F>
{@Naptrī,@}¦ as feminine of {@Napāt,@} is found in the Sāmaveda, Āraṇya (v. 13).
{@Nabha(s) Nabhasya.@}¦ See {@Māsa.@}

{@Nabhāka@}¦ is the name of a Ṛṣi who is referred to in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> The Anukramaṇī (Index) attributes to {@Nābhāka@} the composition of several hymns of the Rigveda (viii. 39-42). <F>1) viii. 40, 4. 5.</F> <F>2) vi. 24. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rig- veda, 3, 107.</F>

{@Nabhya,@}¦ the ‘nave’ of the wheel, is mentioned in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> See also {@Nābhi.@} <F>1) vi. 70, 3; xii. 1, 12.</F> <F>2) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, iv. 15; Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 5, 3, 20; Kauṣī- taki Brāhmaṇa, ix. 4; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, i. 3, 23, etc.</F>

{@Namī Sāpya@}¦ is the name of a man in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> Weber<sup>2</sup> thinks that he is mentioned as a priest, but the passages suit a king better, and in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> he appears as Namī Sāpya, {%Vaidcho rājā,%} ‘King of Videha.’ In one passage<sup>4</sup> he is represented as engaged in the contest against Namuci. <F>1) vi. 20, 6; x. 48, 9. Simply Namī in i. 53, 7.</F> <F>2) {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 231, 232.</F> <F>3) xxv. 10, 17.</F> <F>4) Rv. i. 53, 7. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rig- veda, 3, 149; Macdonell, {%Vedic Myth-%} {%ology,%} p. 161; Hopkins, {%Transactions of%} {%the Connecticut Academy of Arts and%} {%Sciences,%} 15, 49. Sāpya may be read Sāyya, but Sāyaṇa recognizes the {%p;%} Oldenberg, {%Zeitschrift der Deutscheu%} {%Morgenländischen Gesellschaft,%} 55, 328.</F>

{@Nara, Nṛ.@}¦ — The general name for ‘man’ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> is Nṛ, while Nara<sup>3</sup> is found occasionally in the later Saṃhitās and the Brāhmaṇas.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) i. 25, 5; 167, 20; 178, 3; ii. 34, 6; iii. 16, 4, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. ii. 9, 2; ix. 1, 3; xiv. 2, 9; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 34; vi. 27. 32, etc.</F> <F>3) This form of the word, common in the post-Vedic language, is secondary, having originated from cases like {%nar-%} {%am,%} understood as {%nara-m;%} but its origin goes back to the Indo-Iranian period. See Brugmann, {%Grundriss,%} 2, 106. {%Cf.%} Macdonell, {%Vedic Grammar,%} 318, {%a%} 5.</F> <F>4) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vii. 1, 12, 1; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, ix. 3, 1, 3; Nirukta, v. 1, etc.</F>
{@Narācī@}¦ occurs once in the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> perhaps meaning a poisonous plant. <F>1) v. 31, 4. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 18, 286.</F>
{@Narya@}¦ (‘manly’) is in two passages of the Rigveda (i. 54, 6; 112, 9) understood by the commentator Sāyaṇa as the proper name of a man. See also {@Nārya.@}

{@Nalada,@}¦ ‘nard’ ({%Nardastachys Jatamansi%}) is a plant mentioned in the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> in the Aitareya<sup>2</sup> and the Śāṅkhāyana<sup>3</sup> Āraṇyakas (where it is mentioned as used for a garland), as well as in the Sūtras. In the Atharvaveda<sup>4</sup> the feminine form of the word, Naladī, occurs as the name of an Apsaras, or celestial nymph. <F>1) vi. 102, 3.</F> <F>2) iii. 2, 4.</F> <F>3) xi. 4.</F> <F>4) iv. 37, 3. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 68, 69; Grohmann, {%Indische Studien,%} 9, 420; Caland, {%Altindisches Zauberritual,%} 177, n. 4.</F>

{@Navaka@}¦ is mentioned as having wished for a wife at the Sattra of the {@Vibhindukīyas@} in the Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) ii. 233 ({%Journal of the American Oriental Society,%} 18, 38).</F>

{@Nava-gva@}¦ occurs in several passages of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as a man, an Aṅgiras in the highest degree ({%Aṅgirastama%}),<sup>2</sup> appar- ently being the type of the Navagvas,<sup>3</sup> who appear as a mystic race of olden times, coupled with, and conceived probably as related to, the Aṅgirases. They are often associated with the {@Daśagvas.@}<sup>4</sup> <F>1) iv. 51, 4; ix. 108, 4; x. 62, 6.</F> <F>2) x. 62, 6.</F> <F>3) Rv. i. 62, 4; iii. 39, 5; v. 29, 12; 45, 7. 11; vi. 22, 2; x. 14, 6; 61, 10; 108, 8; Av. xiv. 1, 56; xviii. 3, 20, etc.</F> <F>4) Rv. i. 62, 4; iv. 51, 4; v. 29, 12; x. 62, 6, etc. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Ludwig. Translation of the Rig- veda, 3, 165; Macdonell, {%Vedic Myth-%} {%ology,%} pp. 144 (B), 170.</F>

{@Nava-nīta,@}¦ ‘fresh butter,’ is mentioned frequently in the later Saṃhitās<sup>1</sup> and the Brāhmaṇas.<sup>2</sup> According to the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> this is the kind of butter which is fitted for anointing an embryo ({%garbha%}), while the gods receive {@Ājya,@} men fragrant ghee ({@Ghṛta@}), and the fathers {@Āyuta.@} Elsewhere<sup>4</sup> it is contrasted with Ghṛta and {@Sarpis.@} <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā. ii. 3, 10, 1; vi. 1, 1, 5; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xi. 7; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 3, 4, etc.</F> <F>2) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 1, 3, 7. 8; v. 3, 2, 6; Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāh- maṇa, iii. 5, 3.</F> <F>3) i. 3.</F> <F>4) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 3, 10, 1, etc</F>

{@Nava-vāstva@}¦ appears in three passages of the Rigveda. In one<sup>1</sup> he seems to be a protégé of Agni; in another<sup>2</sup> as perhaps a son of {@Uśanas@} and favourite of Indra, but in the last he seems to be defeated, or even slain, by Indra.<sup>3</sup> But he may be a mythic figure altogether. {%Cf.%} also {@Bṛhadratha.@} <F>1) i. 36, 18.</F> <F>2) vi. 20, 11.</F> <F>3) x. 49, 6. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Bergaigne, {%Religion Védique,%} 2, 223; Griffith, {%Hymns of the Rigveda,%} 1, 581; Pischel, {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 128, 129; Ludwig, Translation of the Rig- veda, 3, 147; {%Uber die neuesten Arbeiten%} {%auf dem Gebiete der Ṛgvedaforschung,%} 160; Perry, {%Journal of the American Oriental%} {%Society,%} 11, 202; Macdonell, {%Vedic%} {%Mythology,%} p. 158.</F>

{@Nah@}¦ has been taken by Roth<sup>1</sup> and Grassmann<sup>2</sup> to be the stem, meaning ‘bond,’ of the dative form {%nadbhyas,%} which occurs once in the Rigveda,<sup>3</sup> and which Sieg<sup>4</sup> thinks means ‘sister's sons.’ But the sense of this dative is probably rather ‘to the grandsons.’<sup>5</sup> <F>1) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>2) {%Wörterbuch, s.v.%}</F> <F>3) x. 60, 6.</F> <F>4) {%Die Sagenstoffe des Ṛgveda,%} 129.</F> <F>5) Macdonell, {%Vedic Grammar,%} p. 56, 3{%b.%}</F>

{@Nahus@}¦ occurs several times in the Rigveda, but the exact sense is not certain. Ludwig<sup>1</sup> sees in the Nahus a tribe on the {@Sindhu@} (Indus)<sup>2</sup> or {@Sarasvatī,@}<sup>3</sup> rich in horses,<sup>4</sup> allied with the {@Bharatas@} and {@Śimyus,@}<sup>5</sup> connected with {@Kakṣīvant@} and the {@Vārṣāgiras,@}<sup>6</sup> and having as kings {@Maśarśāra@} and {@Āyavasa.@}<sup>7</sup> Roth,<sup>8</sup> on the other hand, sees in Nahus the general sense of ‘neighbour’ as opposed to a member of one's own people ({@Viś@}); this interpretation is supported by the occurrence of the phrase {%nahuṣo nahuṣṭara,%}<sup>9</sup> ‘closer than a neighbour.’ Nahuṣa has the same sense as Nahus in two passages of the Rigveda,<sup>10</sup> but in [Page1-439+ 58] one it seems to be intended for the proper name of a man.<sup>11</sup> Possibly Nahus was originally a man like Manu.<sup>12</sup> <F>1) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 206.</F> <F>2) Rv. i. 31, 11; vi. 22, 10; 46, 7; x. 80, 6.</F> <F>3) Rv. vii. 95, 2. {%Cf.%} ix. 88, 2; 91, 2.</F> <F>4) Rv. viii. 6, 24.</F> <F>5) Rv. i. 100, 18; vii. 18, 5.</F> <F>6) Rv. i. 100, 16. 17.</F> <F>7) Rv. i. 122, 15. {%Cf.%} also {%nahuṣo%} {%viśaḥ,%} Rv. vii. 6, 5; x. 49, 8; 99, 7, etc.</F> <F>8) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>9) Rv. x. 49, 8. {%Cf.%} also viii. 8, 3.</F> <F>10) i. 31, 11; v. 12, 6.</F> <F>11) Rv. viii. 46, 27.</F> <F>12) Oldenberg, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 46, 28; Bergaigne, {%Religion Védique,%} 2, 324. But Nahus, if it was originally the name of a mythic forefather, cannot have been that of a forefather recog- nized by all the tribes, for there is no passage in which it applies to all men. Geldner, {%Ṛgveda, Glossar,%} 92, regards Nahus as a tribe, Nahuṣa as a king. Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 128, leaves the question open. {%Cf.%} Muir, {%Sanskrit%} {%Texts,%} 1^2, 165, n. 7; 179 {%et seq.;%} 307 {%et seq.%}</F>

1. {@Nāka@}¦ denotes the ‘firmament’ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> It is often used with the epithet ‘highest’ ({%uttama%})<sup>3</sup> or ‘third’ ({%tṛtīya%})<sup>4</sup> referring to the threefold division of heaven, parallel to the threefold division of earth, atmosphere, and sky ({@Div@}). The Nāka is said to be on the third ridge ({%pṛṣṭha%}), above the luminous space ({%rocana%}) of the sky.<sup>5</sup> Elsewhere<sup>6</sup> the series earth, atmosphere, sky, and the firmament ({%nāka%}), heaven ({%svar%}), the celestial light ({%jyotis%}), occurs. The word {%nāka%} is explained in the Brāhmaṇas<sup>7</sup> as derived from {%na,%} ‘not,’ and {%aka,%} ‘pain,’ because those who go there are free from sorrow. <F>1) i. 60, 10; 125, 5; iii. 2, 12; iv. 13, 5; vii. 86, 1; 99, 2; viii. 103, 2; ix. 73, 4, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. vii. 18, 1; xviii. 2, 47; xiii. 1, 7; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xv. 10; Pañca- viṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xviii. 7, 10; Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, viii. 5, 3, 4, etc.</F> <F>3) Av. iv. 14, 6; xi. 1, 4; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, ix. 10; xii. 63.</F> <F>4) Av. vi. 122, 4; ix. 5, 1. 4; xviii. 4, 3.</F> <F>5) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xv. 50.</F> <F>6) Av. iv. 14, 3; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xvii. 67.
