In Rv. x. 121, 5, the earth and sky ({%dyauḥ%}), and heaven ({%svar%}), and the firmament ({%nāka%}), are all mentioned.</F> <F>7) Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, x. 1, 18; Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, viii. 4, 1, 24; Nirukta, ii. 14; and {%cf.%} Chāndogya Upaniṣad, ii. 10, 5. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} p. 9; Max Müller, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 32, 50, 56, 57.</F>

2. {@Nāka@}¦ is the name of a teacher in the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> Presumably he is identical with Nāka Maudgalya (‘descendant of Mudgala’), who is mentioned in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>2</sup> the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad,<sup>3</sup> and the Taittirīya Upaniṣad.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) iii. 13, 5.</F> <F>2) xii. 5, 2, 1.</F> <F>3) vi. 4, 4.</F> <F>4) i. 9, 1.</F>

{@Nākra@}¦ is the name of an aquatic animal included among the victims at the Aśvamedha, or ‘horse sacrifice,’ in the Yajurveda Saṃhitās.<sup>1</sup> Perhaps the animal meant is the crocodile, which later is called Nakra.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 13, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 2; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 35.</F> <F>2) Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 96, fol- lowing one version given by Mahī- dhara on Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, {%loc. cit.;%} Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 3, 21, n. 4.</F>

{@Nāga@}¦ appears once in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> in the form {%mahānāga,%} where ‘great snake’ or ‘great elephant’ may be meant. In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad,<sup>2</sup> and in a citation found in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> the sense of ‘elephant’ is clearly intended. In the Sūtras<sup>4</sup> the mythic Nāga already occurs. <F>1) xi. 2, 7, 12.</F> <F>2) i. 3, 24.</F> <F>3) viii. 22.</F> <F>4) Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra, iii. 4, 1. {%Cf.%} Winternitz, {%Sarpabali,%} 43; Mac. donell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} p. 153.</F>
{@Nāgna-jita,@}¦ ‘descendant of {@Nagnajit,@}’ is the patronymic of {@Svarjit@} in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (viii. 1, 4, 10).

{@Nāciketa,@}¦ ‘connected with {@Naciketas,@}’ is the title of a narrative ({%upākhyāna%}) in the Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad.<sup>1</sup> The word is also applied as an epithet to a special fire in that Upaniṣad<sup>2</sup> and in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) iii. 16.</F> <F>2) i. 18; ii. 10.</F> <F>3) i. 22, 11; 26, 3. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische%} {%Studien,%} 3, 386. The native lexicog- raphers give Nāchiketa and Nāciketu as synonyms of fire generally.</F>

{@Nāḍa-pit@}¦ occurs in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> as the birth- place of {@Bharata.@} The word may, however, be read as Nāḍa-pitī, the name of Bharata's mother,<sup>2</sup> but this is less probable. <F>1) xiii. 5, 4, 13.</F> <F>2) Weber, {%Episches im vedischen Ritual,%} 6, n. 3. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Leumann, {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen%} {%Morgenländischen Gesellschaft,%} 48, 81.</F>

1. {@Nāḍī@}¦ denotes a ‘vein’ or ‘artery’ in the human body in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and later,<sup>2</sup> a natural extension of the literal sense of ‘reed.’ <F>1) vi. 138, 4; x. 7, 15. 16.</F> <F>2) Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xii. 10; Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, x. 4, 5, 2; Bṛhad- āraṇyaka Upaniṣad, ii. 1, 21; iv. 2, 3, etc.; Chāndogya Upaniṣad, viii. 6, 1; Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad, iv. 19.</F>

2. {@Nāḍī@}¦ means a musical instrument, a ‘reed flute,’ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as well as the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā,<sup>2</sup> where in one passage it is mentioned along with the {@Tūṇava.@}<sup>3</sup> <F>1) x. 135, 7.</F> <F>2) xxiii. 4; xxxiv. 5.</F> <F>3) xxxiv. 5. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%Journal of the American%} {%Oriental Society,%} 13, 329.</F>
3. {@Nāḍī@}¦ in the Yajurveda Saṃhitās<sup>1</sup> seems to mean the box of the chariot wheel. <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 4, 8, 3; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxxvii. 12.</F>

{@Nāḍīkā@}¦ occurs once in the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> where the sense seems clearly to be ‘wind-pipe,’ with a reference also to the ‘shaft of an arrow’ made of reed. <F>1) v. 18, 8. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische%} {%Studien,%} 18, 229; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 251; Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 432.</F>

{@Nātha@}¦ in Vedic literature<sup>1</sup> appears only as a neuter meaning ‘protection,’ and is of rare occurrence.<sup>2</sup> Generally, too, very little appears in Vedic literature of practices such as those which produced Anglo-Saxon society or the Roman {%patronatus.%} <F>1) Av. iv. 20, 9; ix. 2, 17; xviii. 1, 13; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 6, 4, 1. Also in Av. xiii. 2, 37, {%nātha-kāma,%} ‘seeking help’; xi, 1, 15, {%nātha-vid,%} ‘finding help’; Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xiv. 11, 23, {%nātha-vindu,%} ‘procuring protection,’ as the name of a Sāman, or chant.</F> <F>2) In the post-Vedic literature, on the other hand, the word is a masculine, meaning ‘protector,’ and is very com- mon.</F>

{@Nāpita,@}¦ ‘barber,’ is mentioned in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> But the older word is Vaptṛ,<sup>3</sup> a derivative of [Page1-442+ 50] {%vap,%} ‘shave,’ with forms of which verb shaving is referred to as early as the Rigveda.<sup>4</sup> The dead were shaved before burial.<sup>5</sup> <F>1) iii. 1, 2, 2.</F> <F>2) Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, vii. 2, 8. 13; Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra, i. 17, etc.</F> <F>3) Rv. x. 142, 4.</F> <F>4) x. 142, 4. {%Cf.%} i. 65, 4; Av. vi. 68; v 2, 17, etc.</F> <F>5) Av. v. 19, 4. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 266; Max Müller, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 32, 265.</F>

{@Nābhāka,@}¦ ‘descendant of Nabhāka,’ is the name of a Ṛṣi, or seer, in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> The Anukramaṇī (Index) ascribes three or four hymns of the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> to him. According to Ludwig,<sup>3</sup> the man was an Āṅgirasa,<sup>4</sup> not a Kaṇva. <F>1) viii. 41, 2; Nirukta, x. 5.</F> <F>2) viii. 39-41, and doubtfully 42.</F> <F>3) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 107.</F> <F>4) viii. 40, 12.</F>

{@Nābhā-nediṣṭha@}¦ (‘nearest in descent’) {@Mānava@} (‘descendant of Manu’) is famous in the later Saṃhitās and the Brāhmaṇas<sup>1</sup> for the way in which he was treated when his father {@Manu@} divided his property among his sons, or they divided it: Nābhānediṣṭha was left out, but was solaced by obtaining, through his father's advice, cows from the Aṅgirases, a feat which is regarded in the Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra<sup>2</sup> as on a level with the exploits of other seers who celebrated their patrons in hymns, and as giving rise to the hymn, Rigveda x. 62. Nābhānediṣṭha's hymn is repeatedly mentioned in the Brāh- maṇas,<sup>3</sup> but beyond its authorship nothing is recorded of him. In the Saṃhitā<sup>4</sup> itself he seems to be spoken of as a poet in one passage, which is, however, of quite uncertain meaning. <div n="P"/>Nābhānediṣṭha is etymologically connected in all probability with Nabānazdiṣta in the Avesta, which refers to the Fravaṣi of the paoiryō-ṭkaēsha and the Fravaṣi of the Nabānazdiṣta. Lassen<sup>5</sup> saw in the legend a reminiscence of an Indo-Iranian split; but Roth<sup>6</sup> showed conclusively that this was impossible, and that Nābhānediṣṭha meant simply ‘nearest in birth,’ and [Page1-443+ 48] Weber<sup>7</sup> admits that the connexion of the words is not one of borrowing on either side, but that in the Avesta it has kept its original sense of ‘nearest relation,’ while in the Rigveda it has become a proper name. <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 1. 9. 4-6; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, v. 14. {%Cf.%} Muir, {%Sanskrit Texts,%} 1^2, 191 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>2) xvi. 11. 28-30.</F> <F>3) Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, xxviii. 4, merely refers to him as connected with the Aṅgirases. See also {%ibid.,%} xxx. 4; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vi. 30. 31; Pañca- viṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xx. 9, 4.</F> <F>4) x. 61, 18.</F> <F>5) {%Indische Alterthumskunde,%} 1, 520, and {%Addenda,%} p. lxxvii.</F> <F>6) {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgen-%} {%ländischen Gesellschaft,%} 6, 243 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>7) {%Episches im vedischen Ritual,%} 40-50. {%Cf.%} also {@Dāya.@}</F>

1. {@Nābhi@}¦ develops from the literal sense of ‘navel’ the figurative meaning of ‘relationship,’<sup>1</sup> or, concretely, ‘relation.’<sup>2</sup> <F>1) i. 105, 9; 164, 33; ii. 3, 9; 40, 4, etc.; Av. xii. 1, 40; Vājasaneyi Saṃ- hitā, x. 8; xi. 12; xx. 1, etc.</F> <F>2) Rv. i. 163, 12; vi. 47, 28; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xiii. 42-44. 50, etc.</F>

2. {@Nābhi,@}¦ ‘nave’ of a chariot wheel, is mentioned in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> See also {@Ratha,@} and {%cf.%} {@Nabhya.@} <F>1) v. 43, 8; vi. 39, 4; viii. 41, 6.</F> <F>2) Av. iii. 30, 6; x. 8, 34; xi. 7, 4; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xi. 4; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, ii. 5, 11; Chāndogya Upani- ṣad, vii. 15, 1; Aitareya Āraṇyaka, iii. 2, 4; Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad, iii. 8.</F>

{@Nāma-dheya,@}¦ ‘name,’ is found in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> and often in the later language.<sup>2</sup> See {@Nāman.@} <F>1) x. 71, 1.</F> <F>2) Av. vii. 109, 6; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 4, 9, 3; iii. 3, 4, 1; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 1, 6, 1; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, ii. 3, 11; vi. 4, 25; Chāndogya Upaniṣad, vi. 1, 4; Aitareya Upaniṣad, v. 2, etc.</F>

{@Nāman,@}¦ ‘name,’ is a common word from the Rigveda onwards. The Gṛhya Sūtras<sup>1</sup> give elaborate rules for the formation of the names of children, but more important is the distinction between the secret ({%guhya%}) and the ordinary name, though the rules as to the secret name are not at all consistent. The secret name is already recognized in the Rigveda,<sup>2</sup> and is referred to in the Brāhmaṇas,<sup>3</sup> one secret name, that of Arjuna for Indra, being given in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.<sup>4</sup> It is to be noted that the rule as to giving the [Page1-444+ 54] designation of a Nakṣatra (lunar asterism) as the secret name or otherwise is not illustrated by a single recorded name of a teacher in the Brāhmaṇas.<sup>5</sup> <div n="P"/>The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>6</sup> several times mentions the adoption of a second name with a view to securing success, and also refers to the adoption of another name for purposes of distinction.<sup>7</sup> <div n="P"/>In actual practice two names are usually found in the Brāhmaṇas, the second being a patronymic or a metronymic, as in {@Kakṣīvant Auśija@}<sup>8</sup> (if the story of the slave woman Uśij as his mother is correct), or {@Bṛhaduktha Vāmneya,@}<sup>9</sup> ‘son of Vāmnī,’ though the relationship may, of course, be not direct parentage, but more remote descent.<sup>10</sup> Three names are less common — for example, {@Kūśāmba Svāyava Lātavya,@}<sup>11</sup> ‘son of Svāyu, of the Lātavya (son of Latu) family,’ or {@Devataras@} {@Śyāvasāyana Kāśyapa,@}<sup>12</sup> where the patronymic and the Gotra name are both found. In other cases the names probably have a local reference — {%e.g.,%} {@Kauśāmbeya@} and {@Gāṅgya.@} Fre- quently the patronymic only is given, as {@Bhārgava, Maudgalya,@} etc., or two patronymics are used. The simple name is often used for the patronymic — {%e.g.,%} {@Trasadasyu.@}<sup>13</sup> In a few cases the name of the wife is formed from the husband's name,<sup>14</sup> as {@Uśīnarāṇī, Purukutsānī, Mudgalānī.@} <F>1) Weber, {%Naxatra,%} 2, 316 {%et seq.;%} Hillebrandt, {%Rituallitteratur,%} 46, 47; Jolly, {%Recht und Sitte,%} 152.</F> <F>2) {%Cf.%} x. 55, 2; 71, 1, as explained in Aitareya Āraṇyaka, i. 3, 3.</F> <F>3) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, vi. 1, 3, 9 (the name is given to a child at birth); Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, vi. 4, 25.</F> <F>4) ii. 1, 2, 11; v. 4, 3, 7; Weber, 2, 317, n. 3.</F> <F>5) Weber, 2, 318, 319. See {@Aṣāḍha,@} {@Rauhiṇa, Rauhiṇāyana.@}</F> <F>6) iii. 6, 2, 24; v. 3, 3, 14; ix. 4, 3, 3, which directs that the name should be derived from a feast performed by the person in question. See also Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxvi. 4; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 7, 17.</F> <F>7) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 4, 4, 4. {%Cf.%} vi. 1, 3, 9.</F> <F>8) Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xiv. 11, 17.</F> <F>9) {%Ibid.,%} xiv. 9, 38.</F> <F>10) Pargiter, {%Journal of the Royal Asiatic%} {%Society,%} 1910, 14; Hopkins, {%Transactions%} {%of the Connecticut Academy of Arts and%} {%Sciences,%} 15, 55, n. 2.</F> <F>11) Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, viii. 6, 8.</F> <F>12) Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa, iii. 40, 2.</F> <F>13) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, vi. 1, 2, 13; Hopkins, {%Religions of India,%} 201, n. 2.</F> <F>14) {%Cf.%} Macdonell, {%Vedic Grammar,%} p. 135. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%op. cit.,%} 2, 316-320; Hopkins, {%loc. cit.%}</F>

{@Nāmba@}¦ is the name of a kind of grain mentioned in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> Āmba is the form of the word in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>2</sup> and the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) v. 3, 3, 8.</F> <F>2) i. 8, 10, 1.</F> <F>3) xv. 15.</F>

{@Nāya@}¦ in two passages of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> is, according to the St. Petersburg Dictionary, probably a proper name. Sāyaṇa takes the word to mean ‘leader,’ while Pischel<sup>2</sup> considers it a gerund with passive sense. <F>1) vi. 24, 10; 46, 11.</F> <F>2) {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 41. For other explanations, see Oldenberg, {%Ṛgveda-%} {%Noten,%} 1, 123, 370.</F>

{@Nārada@}¦ is the name of a mythical seer mentioned several times in the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> In the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa he appears in conjunction with {@Parvata@} as priest of {@Hariścandra,@}<sup>2</sup> as teaching {@Somaka Sāhadevya,@}<sup>3</sup> and as anointing {@Āmbāṣṭhya@} and {@Yudhāṃśrauṣṭi.@}<sup>4</sup> In the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā<sup>5</sup> he is mentioned as a teacher, and in the Sāmavidhāna Brāhmaṇa<sup>6</sup> as a pupil of Bṛhaspati. In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad<sup>7</sup> he is coupled with Sanatkumāra. <F>1) v. 19, 9; xii. 4, 16. 24. 41.</F> <F>2) vii. 13. {%Cf.%} Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xv. 17.</F> <F>3) vii. 34.</F> <F>4) viii. 21.</F> <F>5) i. 5, 8.</F> <F>6) iii. 9 (the Vaṃśa, or ‘list of teachers,’ at the end).</F> <F>7) vii. 1, 1. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 204, n.</F>

{@Nārāśaṃsī@}¦ (scil. Ṛc), ‘(verse) celebrating men,’ is mentioned as early as the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> and is distinguished from {@Gāthā@} in a number of passages in the later literature.<sup>2</sup> The Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā,<sup>3</sup> while distinguishing the two, asserts that both are false ({%anṛtam%}). It is hardly probable that the two were abso- lutely distinct, for the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa<sup>4</sup> has the phrase ‘a Gāthā celebrating men’ ({%nārāśaṃsī%}). What such verses were may be seen from the Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra,<sup>5</sup> which enumerates the {%Nārāśaṃsāni%} at the Puruṣamedha, or ‘human [Page1-446+ 63] sacrifice.’ They may legitimately be reckoned as a source of the epic.<sup>6</sup> <div n="P"/>The term Nārāśaṃsī is restricted in some passages<sup>7</sup> to a particular group of three verses of the Atharvaveda,<sup>8</sup> but Oldenberg<sup>9</sup> must be right in holding that the restricted sense is not to be read into the Rigveda.<sup>10</sup> Not even in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>11</sup> is the technical sense certain, and the Bṛhaddevatā<sup>12</sup> gives the word a general application. <F>1) x. 85, 6.</F> <F>2) Av. xv. 6, 4; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vii. 5, 11, 2; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vi. 32; Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, xxx. 5; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, v. 5, 2; Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, ii. 10, etc.; Weber, {%Indische%} {%Studien,%} 5, 78. The passage, Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xi. 5, 6, 8, is uncertain. See Eggeling, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 44, 98, n. 5.</F> <F>3) xiv. 5; Weber, {%Indische Streifen,%} 1, 98.</F> <F>4) i. 3, 2, 6.</F> <F>5) xvi. 11, 1 {%et seq.;%} Weber, {%Episches%} {%im vedischen Ritual,%} 10 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>6) Hopkins, {%Journal of the American%} {%Oriental Society,%} 15, 264, n. Bloomfield, {%Atharvaveda,%} 100 ({%cf. Hymns of the Athar-%} {%vaveda,%} 688, 689), lays stress rather on their character as mere eulogies of donors, and that, no doubt, was one of their sides; but the other elements may have been more prominent in reality than the priestly tradition shows.</F> <F>7) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vi. 32; Kauṣī- taki Brāhmaṇa, xxx. 5. Possibly, in the other passages mentioned in note 2, the reference may be to the Atharva- veda verses, but this is not at all likely.</F> <F>8) xx. 127, 1-3 = Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xii. 14, 1-3. {%Cf.%} Scheftelowitz, {%Die Apokryphen des Ṛgveda,%} 155.</F> <F>9) {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgen-%} {%ländischen Gesellschaft,%} 42, 238.</F> <F>10) x. 85, 6.</F> <F>11) vii. 5, 11, 2.</F> <F>12) iii. 154. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Episches im Vedischen%} {%Ritual,%} 4 {%et seq.%}</F>

{@Nārī,@}¦ ‘woman,’ occurs in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> The word seems in the Rigveda<sup>3</sup> to have a distinct reference to a woman as a wife, because it occurs in several passages with distinct reference to matrimonial relations,<sup>3</sup> and in the later Vedic literature, where it is not common, it sometimes<sup>4</sup> has that sense. Delbrück,<sup>5</sup> however, thinks that it does not indi- cate marital relations, but merely the woman as the sexual complement of the man. <F>1) vii. 20, 5; 55, 8; viii. 77, 8; x. 18, 7; 86, 10. 11.</F> <F>2) Av. xiv. 2, 13; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiii. 36; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 34.</F> <F>3) i. 73, 3 ({%pati-juṣṭā,%} ‘dear to her husband’); vii. 20. 5; x. 18, 7 ({%avidhavāḥ%} {%supatnīḥ,%} ‘not widowed, with noble husbands’), etc.</F> <F>3) i. 73, 3 ({%pati-juṣṭā,%} ‘dear to her husband’); vii. 20. 5; x. 18, 7 ({%avidhavāḥ%} {%supatnīḥ,%} ‘not widowed, with noble husbands’), etc.</F> <F>4) Gautama Dharma Sūtra, ix. 28.</F> <F>5) {%Die indogermanischen Verwandtschafts-%} {%namen,%} 417, 439.</F>

{@Nārmara@}¦ occurs once in a corrupt verse of the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> Ludwig<sup>2</sup> regards the word as the proper name of the prince of a fort, {@Ūrjayantī,@} but Roth<sup>3</sup> as that of a demon. <F>1) ii. 13, 8.</F> <F>2) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 152.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>

{@Nārmiṇī@}¦ is found in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as an epithet of {@Pur,@} ‘fort’: it must apparently either be a proper name of the fort,<sup>2</sup> or mean ‘belonging to Narmin or Narmiṇa,’ some prince.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) i. 149, 3.</F> <F>2) Ludwig, Translation of the Rig- veda, 3, 204.</F> <F>3) Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} Possibly the expression may con- sist of two words — {%na,%} ‘not’ or ‘like,’ and {%armiṇī,%} whatever that may mean. See Oldenberg, {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 148; {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 46, 177.</F>
{@Nārya,@}¦ ‘descendant of {@Narya,’@} is the name of a generous donor in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) viii. 24, 29. {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 161, 162.</F>

{@Nārṣada,@}¦ ‘descendant of Nṛṣad,’ is the patronymic of Kaṇva ({%i.e.,%} a descendant of Kaṇva) in the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> and in one passage of the Rigveda,<sup>2</sup> where probably the same man is referred to in another passage<sup>3</sup> as a protégé of the Aśvins, and perhaps as the husband of {@Ruśatī.@} But in a third passage of the Rigveda<sup>4</sup> the name seems applied to a demon, though this is not certain. <F>1) iv. 19, 2.</F> <F>2) x. 31, 11.</F> <F>3) i. 117, 8.</F> <F>4) x. 61, 13. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rig- veda, 3, 108, 150; Bloomfield, {%Hymns%} {%of the Atharvaveda,%} 397.</F>

{@Nāva-prabhraṃśana,@}¦ the ‘sliding down of the ship,’ is read in Whitney and Roth's text of the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> and has been connected by Weber<sup>2</sup> and others<sup>3</sup> with Manor Avasarpaṇa, the name in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>4</sup> of the northern mountain on which Manu's ship settled on the subsidence of the deluge. But both Bloomfield<sup>5</sup> and Whitney<sup>6</sup> point out that this inter- pretation is highly improbable, and this view is accepted by [Page1-448+ 37] Macdonell.<sup>7</sup> The expression is analyzed as {%na ava-prabhraṃśana%} by the Pada text and the commentator alike, and is never found elsewhere with reference to the descent of a boat or ship.<sup>8</sup> <F>1) xix. 39, 8, where the reading {%nāva-%} {%prabhráṃśana%} is a conjectural emendā- tion, the manuscripts of the Saṃhitā text all having two accents, {%nāvapra-%} {%bhráṃśana%} (one of them reading {%nāvaḥ-%}).</F> <F>2) {%Indische Streifen,%} 1, 11.</F> <F>3) {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 198; Eggeling, {%Sacred Books%} {%of the East,%} 12, 218, n.; Zimmer, {%Altin-%} {%disches Leben,%} 30.</F> <F>4) i. 8, 1, 6.</F> <F>5) {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 679.</F> <F>6) Translation of the Atharvaveda, 961.</F> <F>7) {%Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society,%} 1907, 1107, where his acceptance of Weber's interpretation in his {%Sanskrit%} {%Literature,%} 144, is withdrawn.</F> <F>8) The word {%nau,%} ship, never occurs as the first member of a compound in the form of {%nāva,%} while {%pra-bhraṃś,%} ‘fall down,’ is never used of the gliding down of a boat, and would be inappropriately applied in that sense.</F>
{@Nāvā,@}¦ ‘ship,’ occurs once in the Rigveda (i. 97, 8). See {@Nau.@}
{@Nāvāja@}¦ (‘ship-propeller’), a ‘boatman,’ is mentioned in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (ii. 3, 3, 5).

{@Nāvyā@}¦ is found several times in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and the later literature<sup>2</sup> in the sense of a ‘navigable stream.’ <F>1) i. 33, 11; 80, 8; 121, 13.</F> <F>2) Av. viii. 5, 9; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxiii. 6; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, x. 5, 4, 14, etc.</F>

{@Nāhuṣa,@}¦ like {@Nahus,@} means, according to the St. Petersburg Dictionary, in some passages of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> ‘neighbouring’ as an adjective, and once<sup>2</sup> as a substantive ‘neighbour.’ If, on the other hand, Nahus is taken as a proper name, then Nāhuṣa no doubt denotes ‘belonging to the Nahus people,’ and, as a substantive, ‘King of the Nahus.’ <F>1) i. 100, 16; v. 73, 3; vi. 22, 10; viii. 6, 24.</F> <F>2) viii. 95, 2.</F>

{@Nikothaka Bhāya-jātya@}¦ (‘descendant of Bhayajāta’) is mentioned in the Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> as a pupil of {@Pratithi.@} <F>1) {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 373. {%Cf.%} Max Müller, {%Ancient Sanskrit Literature,%} 444.</F>

{@Nigada Pārṇa-valki@}¦ (‘descendant of Parṇavalka’) is men- tioned in the Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> as a pupil of Giriśarman. <F>1) {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 372. {%Cf.%} Max Müller, {%Ancient Sanskrit Literature,%} 443.</F>

{@Ni-gut@}¦ occurs in two passages of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> where Sāyaṇa takes it to mean ‘enemy,’ a possible interpretation. Ludwig<sup>2</sup> suggests that non-Āryan foes are meant. <F>1) ix. 97, 53, 54; x. 128, 6.</F> <F>2) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 164.</F>
{@Nigustha@}¦ is a term of unknown meaning applied in the Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra (xvi. 29, 6) to the peoples of Kāśi, Videha, and Kosala.

1. {@Ni-tatnī,@}¦ ‘striking downwards,’ occurs in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> as the name of an unknown plant which was used as a means of restoring the hair. <F>1) vi. 136; probably 137 also refers to this plant. {%Cf.%} Kauṣītaki Sūtra, xxxi. 28, with Caland's note in his translation; Bloomfield, {%Atharvaveda,%} 61; {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 536, 537; Whitney, Translation of the Atharva- veda, 383.</F>
2. {@Ni-tatnī@}¦ is the name of one of the seven {@Kṛttikās@} in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa (iii. 1, 4, 1). See {@Nakṣatra.@}
{@Ni-tāna Māruta@}¦ is the name of a man in the {@Kāṭhaka@} Saṃhitā (xxv. 10).
{@Ni-dāgha@}¦ (‘burning down’), ‘summer,’ is the name of one of the seasons in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (xiii. 8, 1, 4). See {@Naidāgha.@}

{@Ni-dāna@}¦ is the name of a Sūtra, which is referred to in the Bṛhaddevatā<sup>1</sup> apparently as containing a quotation from the Bhāllavi Brāhmaṇa. The quotation cannot be verified in the existing text of the Sūtra.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) v. 23, with Macdonell's note.</F> <F>2) Sieg, {%Die Sagenstoffe des Ṛgveda,%} 65. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 44; Max Müller, {%Ancient Sanskrit Literature,%} 111, etc.</F>
{@Ni-dhā,@}¦ ‘net,’ is mentioned in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) ix. 83, 4; x. 73, 11; Nirukta, iv. 2.</F> <F>2) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 19.</F>

{@Ni-dhi@}¦ means primarily ‘(place of) deposit,’ ‘store,’<sup>1</sup> and then ‘treasure’ generally.<sup>2</sup> In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad<sup>3</sup> Nidhi denotes some sort of science. <F>1) Rv. i. 183, 4; v. 43, 8; vii. 67, 7; 69, 3, etc.</F> <F>2) Rv. ii. 24, 6; viii. 29, 6; x. 68, 6; Av. x. 7, 23, etc.</F> <F>3) vii. 1, 2. 4; 2, 1; 7, 1. The St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.,%} and Böhṭlingk in his edition, take {%daivo%} {%nidhiḥ%} as one expression. See {@Daiva.@} Sāyaṇa takes each as a separate entity, and renders Nidhi as {%mahākālādinidhi-%} {%śāstram,%} presumably meaning some sort of chronology. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} for Nidhi as ‘treasure,’ Jolly, {%Recht und Sitte,%} 103, 104.</F>

{@Ni-nāhya@}¦ denotes in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (iii. 9, 2, 8) a ‘water jar,’ so called, according to the commentator, because it was buried in the ground.<sup>1</sup> Eggeling<sup>2</sup> explains it as ‘a vessel or cistern dug into the ground for keeping water cool.’ <F>1) As meaning etymologically ‘to be fastened or fixed down.’</F> <F>2) {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 26, 223, n. 4.</F>

{@Ninditāśva@}¦ (‘possessing contemptible steeds’) is the name of a patron in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> The name may suggest connexion with Iran, but such a reference is not at all necessary.<sup>2</sup> Sāyaṇa ingeniously turns the name — probably a nickname —  into a compliment by rendering it ‘one who puts to shame the horses of his rivals.’ <F>1) viii. 1, 30.</F> <F>2) Hopkins, {%Journal of the American%} {%Oriental Society,%} 17, 90. {%Cf.%} Ludwing, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 159.</F>
{@Ni-pāda@}¦ in the Rigveda (v. 83, 7) denotes ‘low ground,’. ‘valley,’ as opposed to ‘hill’ ({%udvat%}). {%Cf.%} {@Nivat.@}

{@Ni-mruc,@}¦ ‘sunset,’ is repeatedly mentioned in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> as a division of time. <F>1) i. 151, 5; 161, 10; viii. 27, 19; x. 151, 5.</F> <F>2) Av. xiii. 3, 21; Taittirīya Saṃ- hitā, i. 5, 10, 2; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxxvii. 10; Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, ii. 5, 2, etc.</F>

{@Nir-aṣṭa,@}¦ ‘castrated,’ is found in some of the later Saṃhitās<sup>1</sup> as applied to oxen, and in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> to horses. <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, i. 8, 9, 1; 17, 1; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xv. 4. 9.</F> <F>2) xiii. 4, 2, 5.</F>

{@Nir-āla@}¦ occurs once in the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> where Sāyaṇa regards it as the name of a disease. Bloomfield,<sup>2</sup> with the Padapāṭha, explains it as two words, understanding {%nir%} as an elliptical imperative, ‘(go) out,’ with the vocative {%āla,%} a kind of weed. Whitney<sup>3</sup> at first took {%āla%} to be a verbal form, but finally came to the conclusion that the expression is one word, {%nirāla,%} of unknown sense. <F>1) vi. 16, 3.</F> <F>2) {%Hymns of the Atharvavéda,%} 466.</F> <F>3) Translation of the Atharvaveda, 292.</F>

{@Nirukta,@}¦ ‘explanation’ of a word or passage, is found in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (viii. 3, 3), but does not appear as the name of a work before the later Upaniṣads. It is, however, probable that Yāska's Nirukta is not later than the rise of Buddhism. {%Cf.%} {@Nirvacana.@} <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 13, 17; 3, 260 {%et seq.; Indian Literature,%} 25, 26, 41, 42, etc.; Macdonell, {%Sanskrit%} {%Literature,%} 269, 270; Keith, {%Aitareya%} {%Āraṇyaka,%} 24, 25; Roth, {%Nirukta,%} xv. {%et seq.%}
{@Nir-yāsa@}¦ denotes the ‘exudation’ of trees. In the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (ii. 1, 5, 4) it is tabooed as food because of its red colour.

{@Nir-vacana@}¦ in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka<sup>1</sup> and the Nirukta<sup>2</sup> means ‘explanation,’ especially etymological. {%Cf.%} {@Nirukta.@} <F>1) i. 6, 3.</F> <F>2) ii. 1. {%Cf. a-nirvacanam,%} ‘not serving as an explanation,’ {%ibid.,%} vii. 24.</F>

{@Ni-vat@}¦ denotes ‘valley’ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) i. 161, 11; iii. 2, 10; vii. 50, 4; x. 127, 2; 142, 4.</F> <F>2) Av. vi. 22, 3; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 2, 4; 4, etc.</F>

{@Nivānya-vatsā@}¦ and {@Nivānyā@} in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> denotes a ‘cow with a calf to which she has to be won over,’ that is, with a calf substituted for one of her own which has died. Nivānyā<sup>2</sup> is a contracted form of the compound term. Similar expressions are {%abhivānya-vatsā,%}<sup>3</sup> {%abhivānyā,%}<sup>4</sup> {%vānyā,%}<sup>5</sup> and {%api-%} {%vānya-vatsā.%}<sup>6</sup> <F>1) xii. 5, 1, 4.</F> <F>2) ii. 6, 1, 6.</F> <F>3) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vii. 2.</F> <F>4) Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 6, 8, 4.</F> <F>5) {%Ibid.,%} ii. 6, 16, 2.</F> <F>6) Kauśika Sūtra, lxxxii. 22. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Lanman in Whitney's Translation of the Atharvaveda, 880.</F>

{@Ni-vid@}¦ denotes a brief invocation of the deity that is invited in a liturgy in honour of the god. The Brāhmaṇas<sup>1</sup> repeatedly mention Nivids as inserted in the Śastras (recitations), and the {@Khilas@} of the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> preserve among them a set of Nivids. But it is doubtful<sup>3</sup> whether the habit of using such brief formulas — the Nivid is usually not more than a Pada or quarter-verse in length — is known to the Rigveda, though it has been seen even there,<sup>4</sup> and the word Nivid is several times found in that Saṃhitā,<sup>5</sup> but hardly in the technical sense of the Brāhmaṇas. In the later Saṃhitās<sup>6</sup> the technical sense is common. <F>1) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 33. 34; iii. 10. 11; vi. 33. 35; Kauṣītaki Brāh- maṇa, xiv. 1; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 9, 3, 28; xiii. 5, 1. 9, etc.; Aitareya Āraṇyaka, i. 5, 2; Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇ- yaka, i. 3, etc.</F> <F>2) See Scheftelowitz, {%Die Apokryphen%} {%des Ṛgveda,%} 137-143.</F> <F>3) The antiquity of the Nivids was asserted by Haug, {%Aitareya Brāhmaṇa,%} 1, 26 {%et seq.,%} and often since, {%e.g.,%} by Tilak, {%Orion,%} 206; Scheftelowitz, {%op. cit.,%} 3. It is shown to be most improbable by Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 9, 265, 355, and Oldenberg, {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen%} {%Morgenländischen Gesellschaft,%} 42, 242 {%et seq.; Göttingische Gelehrte Anzeigen,%} 1907, 232, 233.</F> <F>4) i. 86, 4; Bezzenberger's {%Beiträge,%} 9, 192. So Oldenberg, {%Sacred Books of%} {%the East,%} 46, 119, 122, takes Rv. i. 96, 2, to refer to the Nivids in the technical sense, but not to the Nivids as pre- served.</F> <F>5) i. 89, 3; 96, 2; 175, 6; ii. 36, 6; iv. 18, 7; vi. 67, 10.</F> <F>6) Av. v. 26, 4; xi. 7, 19; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xix, 25, etc. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%Rituallitteratur,%} 102; Oldenberg, {%Religion des Veda,%} 387, n. 2; Muir, {%Sanskrit Texts,%} 1^2, 241.</F>

{@Nivid-dhāna,@}¦ ‘containing a Nivid,’ is found several times as an epithet of a hymn or verse in the Brāhmaṇas.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 17; Kauṣī- aki Brāhmaṇa, xxi. 6; xxiv. 4; Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 5, 1, 12; Aitareya Āraṇyaka, i. 2, 2; 5, 3.</F>

{@Ni-veśana,@}¦ ‘dwelling,’ occurs in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and the Sūtras. In the latter<sup>2</sup> the word is sometimes contrasted with {@Gṛha@} as the resting-place of animals. <F>1) iv. 19, 9; vii. 19, 5.</F> <F>2) Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra, iv. 6, etc.</F>

{@Ni-ṣaṅgathi@}¦<sup>1</sup> or {@Niṣaṅga-dhi@}<sup>2</sup> is found in the Yajurveda Saṃhitās. If the second form of the word is correct, the sense may be ‘sheath of a sword’ ({%niṣaṅga%}), as it is taken by the St. Petersburg Dictionary, but probably the first form is the correct one, the word then having the same meaning as {@Niṣaṅgin.@} <F>1) Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xvii. 11; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 9, 2.</F> <F>2) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xvi. 10.</F>

{@Ni-ṣaṅgin@}¦ is found three times in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> where, owing to its following in one passage<sup>2</sup> the words {%sudhanvāna%} {%iṣumanto,%} ‘having good bows and arrows,’ the sense of {%niṣaṅginaḥ%} as ‘having quivers’ seems quite certain. In the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā<sup>3</sup> it is taken by the commentator Mahīdhara to mean ‘having a sword,’ a sense which is quite possible both there and in the other passages<sup>4</sup> where it occurs. But the word far more probably means ‘having a quiver,’ for the bow was the Vedic weapon, not the sword ({@Asi@}). <F>1) iii. 30, 15; v. 57, 2; x. 103, 3.</F> <F>2) v. 57, 2.</F> <F>3) xvi. 20. {%Cf.%} Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xx, 2, 11, with the commentator.</F> <F>4) Sāmaveda, ii. 1199; Kāṭhaka Saṃ- hitā, xvii. 12; xxxvii. 11; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 9, 3; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iv. 5, 3, 1; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 4, 2, 5. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%Journal of the American%} {%Oriental Society,%} 13, 274.</F>

{@Ni-ṣāda@}¦ is found in the later Saṃhitās and the Brāhmaṇas.<sup>1</sup> The word seems to denote not so much a particular tribe, but to be the general term for the non-Āryan tribes who were not under Āryan control, as the Śūdras were, for Aupamanyava<sup>2</sup> took the five peoples ({%pañca janāḥ%}) to be the four castes ({%catvāro%} [Page1-454+ 56] {%varṇāḥ%}) and the Niṣādas, and the commentator Mahīdhara explains the word where it occurs in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā<sup>3</sup> as meaning a Bhilla, or Bhīl. A village of Niṣādas is men- tioned in the Lāṭyāyana Śrauta Sūtra,<sup>4</sup> and a Niṣāda {@Sthapati,@} a leader of some kind, is referred to in the Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra<sup>5</sup> and in a Brāhmaṇa cited by the scholiast on that passage. Weber<sup>6</sup> thinks that the Niṣādas were the settled aborigines (form {%ni,%} ‘down,’ and {%sad,%} ‘settle’), a view sup- ported by the fact that the ritual of the Viśvajit sacrifice<sup>7</sup> requires a temporary residence with Niṣādas; for the Niṣādas who would permit an Āryan to reside temporarily amongst them must have been partially amenable to Āryan influence. But the name might easily be applied to the whole body of aborigines outside the Āryan organization. Von Schroeder<sup>8</sup> thinks that the Niṣādas were most probably identical with the Nysæans, who, according to the Greek account, sent an embassy to Alexander when he was in the territory of the Aśvakas, but this identification is doubtful. <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iv. 5, 4, 2; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xvii. 13; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 9, 5; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xvi. 27; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, viii. 11; Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xvi. 6, 8, etc.</F> <F>2) In Yāska, Nirukta, iii. 8.</F> <F>3) xvi. 27. {%Cf.%} xxx. 8.</F> <F>4) viii. 2, 8.</F> <F>5) i. 1, 12; Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 10, 13.</F> <F>6) {%Indische Studien,%} 9, 340. {%Cf.%} 10, 13, 16.</F> <F>7) See Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, xxv. 15; Lāṭyāyana, {%loc. cit.;%} Pañcaviṃśa Brāh- maṇa, {%loc. cit.%}</F> <F>8) {%Indiens Literatur und Cultur,%} 366. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 39, 119. In the later system (Manu, x. 8) the Niṣāda is the offspring of a Brāh- maṇa and of a Śūdra woman, while the Bṛhatsaṃhitā of Varāhamihira (xiv. 10) recognizes a kingdom ({%rāṣṭra%}) of Niṣādas in the south-east of Madhyadeśa. In the Pāli texts (Fick, {%Die sociale Gliederung,%} 12, 160, 206 {%et seq.%}) they are wild hunters and fishers. {%Cf.%} also Muir, {%Sanskrit Texts,%} 1^2, 301, 303, 366, n. 164, 403, 481.</F>

{@Niṣka@}¦ is frequently found in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> denoting a gold ornament worn on the neck, as is shown by the two epithets {%niṣka-kaṇṭha%}<sup>3</sup> and {%niṣka-grīva,%}<sup>4</sup> ‘having a gold ornament on the neck.’ A Niṣka of silver is mentioned in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>5</sup> As early as the Rigveda<sup>6</sup> traces are seen of the [Page1-455+ 42] use of Niṣkas as a sort of currency, for a singer celebrates the receipt of a hundred Niṣkas and a hundred steeds: he could hardly require the Niṣkas merely for purposes of personal adornment. Later the use of Niṣkas as currency is quite clear.<sup>7</sup> {%Cf.%} also {@Kṛṣṇala.@} <F>1) ii. 33, 10; viii. 47, 15. etc.</F> <F>2) Av. v. 14, 3; vii. 99, 1; xx. 131. 8; Chāndogya Upaniṣad, iv. 2, 1. 2; v. 13, 2; Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāh- maṇa, i. 36, 7. 8; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 4, 1, 7. 11, etc.</F> <F>3) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, viii. 22.</F> <F>4) Rv. v. 19, 3; Av. v. 17, 14.</F> <F>5) xvii. 1, 14, as worn by the Vrātya {%Cf.%} Av. xv. 3.</F> <F>6) i. 126, 2.</F> <F>7) Av. xx. 127, 3; Lāṭyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, ix. 9, 20, etc. In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xi. 4, 1, 1. 8; Gopatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 3, 6; the sense of ‘coin’ is seen by Eggeling. {%Sacred Books of%} {%the East,%} 44, 50, 51, and by Geldner, {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 185. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 51, 259, 263; Geldner, {%op. cit.,%} 1, 268, n. 2; {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen%} {%Gesellschaft,%} 40, 127.</F>

{@Niṣkirīya@}¦ is the name of a school of priests who are men- tioned in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> as holding a Sattra, or ‘sacrificial session.’ <F>1) xii. 5, 14. {%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%Transactions of the Connecticut Academy of Arts and%} {%Sciences,%} 15, 58.</F>

{@Niṣṭya@}¦ means in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> an outsider or stranger. Hence the constellation usually known as Svāti (see {@Nakṣatra@}) is named Niṣṭyā in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa,<sup>3</sup> because it occupies a position markedly away from the ecliptic. <F>1) vi. 75, 19; viii. 1, 13; x. 133, 5.</F> <F>2) Av. iii. 3, 6; Vājasaneyi, v. 23; Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 6, 4, 17, etc.</F> <F>3) i. 5, 2, 2. 3; iii. 1, 1, 13. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Max Müller, {%Sacred Books of the%} {%East,%} 32, 215.</F>

{@Nihākā@}¦ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>2</sup> appears to denote some phenomenon of a storm, perhaps the ‘whirl- wind.’ <F>1) x. 97, 13.</F> <F>2) vii. 5, 11, 1 (following {%nīhāra%}).</F>
{@Nīkṣaṇa.@}¦ See {@Nekṣaṇa.@}

{@Nīcya@}¦ (‘living below’) is a designation of certain nations of the west. The Nīcyas are mentioned in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (viii. 14) as distinguished from the people of {@Madhyadeśa,@} and no doubt mean the inhabitants of the Indus and Panjab regions.

{@Nītha@}¦ (‘leading’), neut., means musical ‘mode’ and then ‘hymn of praise.’<sup>1</sup> The feminine form Nīthā occurs once in the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> meaning ‘artifice.’ <F>1) Rv. iv. 3, 16; vii. 26, 2; x. 92, 3; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 38. {%Cf. nīthāvid%} of singers ({%jaritṛ%}) in Rv. iii. 12, 5.</F> <F>2) i. 104, 5. {%Cf.%} the epithet {%śata-nītha,%} i. 100, 12; 179, 3; x. 69, 7; {%sahasra-%} {%nītha,%} iii. 60, 7; ix. 85, 4; 96, 18 (used of the poet's art, {%padavīḥ kavīnām%}). <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Muir, {%Sanskrit Texts,%} 1^2, 241.</F>
{@Nīnāha,@}¦ a word occurring once in the Atharvaveda (xix. 57, 4), seems to denote a ‘girdle’ or something similar, as derived from the verb {%nah,%} ‘fasten.’

{@Nīpātithi@}¦ occurs in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as the name of a man to whom a hymn<sup>2</sup> is ascribed by the Anukramaṇī (Index). A Sāman, or Chant, of his is mentioned in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) viii. 49, 9, where he appears as engaged in battle; viii. 51, 1, where he seems to be a sacrificer. Either a king or a seer may be meant.</F> <F>2) viii. 34. {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 140; Hopkins, {%Journal of the American Oriental Society,%} 17, 90.</F> <F>3) xiv. 10, 4.</F>

{@Nīlaṅgu@}¦ is the name of a species of ‘worm’ in the Yajurveda Saṃhitās<sup>1</sup> in the list of victims at the Aśvamedha, or ‘horse sacrifice.’ <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 11, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 11 ({%v.l.%} {%nīlāṅgu%}); Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 30. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 98.</F>

{@Nīla-śīrṣṇī,@}¦ ‘black-headed,’ is the name of an unknown animal in the list of victims at the Aśvamedha, or ‘horse sacrifice,’ in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) v. 5, 15, 1. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 99.</F>

{@Nīlāgalasāla,@}¦ or, as the Paippalāda version reads, {@Nīlākala-@} {@sālā,@} is the name, according to the commentator, of a grain- creeper in the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) vi. 16, 4. {%Cf.%} Whitney, Transla- tion of the Atharvaveda, 292, 293; Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 466.</F>

{@Nīvāra,@}¦ ‘wild rice,’ is mentioned in the Yajurveda Saṃhitās<sup>1</sup> and the Brāhmaṇas.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xii. 4; Maitrā- yaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 4, 10; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xviii. 12.</F> <F>2) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, v. 1, 4, 14; 3, 3, 5; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 3, 6, 7, etc. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 240.</F>

{@Nīvi@}¦ is the name of the ‘undergarment,’ probably a simple apron of cloth, worn by both men and women, but especially by the latter. It is mentioned in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) viii. 2, 16; xiv. 2, 50. {%Cf. nīvi-%} {%bhārya,%} ‘to be borne in the apron,’ viii. 6, 20.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vi. 1, 1, 3; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, iv. 10; Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 3, 3, 6; iii. 2, 1, 15, etc. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 262; Schrader, {%Prehistoric Antiquities,%} 331.</F>

{@Nīhāra,@}¦ ‘mist,’ occurs in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) x. 82, 7.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vii. 5, 11, 1; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxviii. 4; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxii. 26; xxv. 9; Av. vi. 113, 2; xviii. 3, 60; Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, i. 10, 7; vi. 4, 1; Chāndogya Upaniṣad, iii. 19, 2, etc.</F>
{@Nṛ.@}¦ See {@Nara.@}

{@Nṛti@}¦ in one passage of the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> seems to mean a bag of skin. But though the Paippalāda recension has the same text, it is clear that we must read {@Dṛti@} with Roth<sup>2</sup> and Whitney.<sup>3</sup> Ludwig<sup>4</sup> renders the word ‘dancer,’ which makes no sense in the context. <F>1) vi. 18, 3.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>3) Translation of the Atharvaveda, 294. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 5, 235; Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Athar-%} {%vaveda,%} 468.</F> <F>4) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 514.</F>

{@Nṛtū@}¦ occurs once in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> denoting a female ‘dancer.’ In another passage<sup>2</sup> Nṛti is found coupled with {%hāsa,%} ‘laughter,’ in the description of the funeral ritual; but though it is clear that a joyful celebration is meant (like the Irish ‘wake’ or the [Page1-458+ 47] old-fashioned feasting in Scotland after a funeral), it is difficult to be certain that actual dancing is here meant. Dancing is, however, often referred to in the Rigveda<sup>3</sup> and later. Nṛtta- gīta, ‘dance and song,’ are mentioned in the Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa<sup>4</sup> as found in the sixth world. See also {@Śailūṣa.@} <F>1) i. 92, 4 (where Uṣas, Goddess of Dawn, is compared to a dancer).</F> <F>2) x. 18, 3. {%Cf.%} 29, 2.</F> <F>3) i. 10, 1; 92, 4, etc. See Weber, {%Indian Literature,%} 196 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>4) i. 42 ({%Journal of the American Oriental%} {%Society,%} 15, 235).</F>

{@Nṛ-pati,@}¦ ‘lord of men,’ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> denotes a ‘king’ or a man of the ruling class ({@Kṣatriya@}). <F>1) ii. 1, 1. 7; iv. 20, 1; vii. 69, 1; x. 44, 2. 3.</F> <F>2) Av. v. 18, 1. 15; Taittirīya Āraṇ- yaka, vi. 3, 3; x. 77, etc.</F>

{@Nṛ-medha,@}¦<sup>1</sup> {@Nṛ-medhas,@}<sup>2</sup> is the name of a protégé of Agni in the Rigveda,<sup>3</sup> where he also appears with {@Sumedhas@} in a hymn that Griffith<sup>4</sup> with justice declares to be unintelligible. In the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> he is an unsuccessful rival of {@Parucchepa,@} and in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> he is an Āṅgirasa and a seer of Sāmans (Chants). <F>1) Rv. x. 80, 3; 132, 7; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 5, 8, 3.</F> <F>2) Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, viii. 8, 21 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>3) x. 80, 3.</F> <F>4) x. 132; Griffith, {%Hymns of the%} {%Rigveda,%} 2, 578, n. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 2, 160; Hopkins, {%Transactions of the Connecti-%} {%cut Academy of Arts and Sciences,%} 15, 61.</F> <F>1) Rv. x. 80, 3; 132, 7; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 5, 8, 3.</F> <F>2) Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, viii. 8, 21 {%et seq.%}</F>
{@Nṛ-ṣad,@}¦ ‘sitting among men,’ is the name of the father of {@Kaṇva@} in the Rigveda (x. 31, 11). {%Cf.%} {@Nārṣada.@}

{@Nekṣaṇa@}¦ occurs once in the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> where a ‘spit’ seems to be meant. In the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> Nīkṣaṇa occurs, and must have the same sense; Oldenberg<sup>3</sup> inclines to think that this word refers to the ‘inspection’ of food, to see if it is ready (as from {%ni-īkṣ,%} ‘look into’). <F>1) ix. 6, 17. {%Cf.%} Kauśika Sūtra, ii. 11; lxxxvii. 12; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 540.</F> <F>2) i. 162, 13.</F> <F>3) {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 155.</F>

{@Nemi@}¦ denotes in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> the ‘felly’ of a chariot wheel. It was required to be of good wood ({%su-drū%}),<sup>3</sup> and was bent into shape.<sup>4</sup> {%Cf.%} {@Ratha.@} <F>1) i. 32, 15; 141, 9; ii. 5, 3; v. 13, 6; vii. 32, 20; viii. 46, 23; 75, 5, etc.</F> <F>2) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 4, 2, 15; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, ii. 5, 15, etc.</F> <F>3) Rv. vii. 32, 20.</F> <F>4) Rv. viii. 75, 5. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 248.</F>

{@Neṣṭṛ,@}¦ the name of one of the chief priests at the Soma sacrifice, occurs in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> See {@Ṛtvij.@} <F>1) i. 15, 3; ii. 5, 5, etc.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, i. 8, 18, 1; vi. 5, 8, 5. 6; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vi. 3, 10, etc.; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 8, 2, 1, etc.; Pañcaviṃśa Brāh- maṇa, xxv. 15, etc. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 250, 261, 527.</F>

{@Naicā-śākha@}¦ is found in one passage of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> where Sāyaṇa renders it as ‘of low origin,’ but elsewhere<sup>2</sup> he explains it as the name of a place. The former sense is accepted by Grassmann and Ludwig in their versions, and by Zimmer,<sup>3</sup> but Hillebrandt<sup>4</sup> points out that the reference is rather to the ‘low-branched’ Soma plant. {%Cf.%} {@Kīkaṭa@} and {@Pramaganda.@} <F>1) vii. 53, 4.</F> <F>2) See St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>3) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 31.</F> <F>4) {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 14-18; 2, 241- 245, where he opposes Böhtlingk's view that it is a proper name.</F>

{@Naicu-dāra@}¦ occurs in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> meaning ‘composed of the wood of the Nicudāra.’ What tree is meant by the latter name is unknown. <F>1) xxi. 4, 13. {%Cf.%} Anupada Sūtra, vi. 4.</F>

{@Naitandhava@}¦ is mentioned as a place on the {@Sarasvatī@} in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> and the Sūtras.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) xxv. 13, 1.</F> <F>2) Lāṭyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, x. 19, 13; Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xiii. 29, 31; Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xxiv. 6, 23.</F>

{@Nai-dāgha@}¦ is the name of the ‘summer’ season in the later Saṃhitās and Brāhmaṇas.<sup>1</sup> {%Cf.%} {@Ṛtu@} and {@Nidāgha.@} <F>1) Av. ix. 5, 31; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 8, 4, 2; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 4, 1, 16, etc.; {%naidāghīya,%} ‘belonging to the summer,’ Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xxiii. 16, 8, etc.</F>

{@Nai-dāna@}¦ is a term applied in the Nirukta<sup>1</sup> to a class of Vedic interpreters. Roth<sup>2</sup> takes the Naidānas to be ‘etymo- logists,’ but Sieg<sup>3</sup> thinks they are the same as the {@Aitihāsikas@} or ‘legendarists.’<sup>4</sup> <F>1) vi. 9; vii. 12.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} But {%of.%} Nirukta, {%Erlāuterungen,%} 220, 221; Muir, {%Sanskrit Texts,%} 2^2, 176.</F> <F>3) {%Die Sagenstoffe des Ṛgveda,%} 29.</F> <F>4) The word seems to mean ‘one concerned with the original form’ ({%nidāna%}).</F>
{@Nai-dhruvi,@}¦ ‘descendant of Nidhruva,’ is the patronymic of {@Kaśyapa@} in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) vi. 4, 33 (Mādhyandina = vi. 5, 3 Kāṇva).</F>

{@Naimiśi@}¦ is the epithet of {@Śitibāhu Aiṣakṛta@} in the Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> It is probably to be taken as an indication that Śitibāhu came from the Naimiśa forest. <F>1) i. 363 ({%Journal of the American Oriental Society,%} 26, 192).</F>

{@Naimiśīya,@}¦<sup>1</sup> {@Naimiṣīya@}<sup>2</sup> denotes the dwellers in the Naimiśa forest. They are mentioned in the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā<sup>2</sup> and the Brāhmaṇas,<sup>2</sup> being clearly of special sanctity. Hence in the Epic the Mahābhārata is said to have been recited to the Ṛṣis dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xxv. 6, 4; Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 363 ({%Journal of%} {%the American Oriental Society,%} 26, 192).</F> <F>2) Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, xxvi. 5; xxviii. 4; Chāndogya Upaniṣad, i. 2, 13; Naimiṣya, Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, x. 6 ({%Indische Studien,%} 3, 469). The cerebrals seems to be universal later.</F> <F>2) Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, xxvi. 5; xxviii. 4; Chāndogya Upaniṣad, i. 2, 13; Naimiṣya, Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, x. 6 ({%Indische Studien,%} 3, 469). The cerebrals seems to be universal later.</F> <F>2) Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, xxvi. 5; xxviii. 4; Chāndogya Upaniṣad, i. 2, 13; Naimiṣya, Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, x. 6 ({%Indische Studien,%} 3, 469). The cerebrals seems to be universal later.</F> <F>3) Weber, {%Indian Literature,%} 34, 45, 54, 68, 70, 185.</F>

{@Nair-ukta@}¦<sup>1</sup> in the Nirukta<sup>2</sup> denotes a man who knows the true etymology of words, and explains their meaning accord- ingly. Yāska's Nirukta is the classic work of this school, and forms a commentary on an earlier Nirukta, the so-called Naighaṇṭuka, a glossary consisting of five collections of Vedic words. <F>1) ‘One concerned with etymological explanation’ ({%nir-ukta%}).</F> <F>2) i. 12; vi. 11; xi. 19. 29. 31; xii. 10; xiii. 9. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indian Literature,%} 26, 85; {%Indische Studien,%} 2, 39, n.; Sieg, {%Die%} {%Sagenstoffc des Ṛgveda,%} 10-13; Muir, {%Sanskrit Texts,%} 2^2, 165 {%et seq.%}</F>
{@Nai-ṣāda,@}¦ a ‘man of Niṣāda,’ is mentioned in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa (xxv. 15) and the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā (xxx. 8).

{@Naiṣidha@}¦ is the reading in the Śata atha Brāhmaṇa (ii. 3, 2, 1. 2) of the epithet of {@Naḍa,@} a king of the south. The later form of the name is Naiṣadha; the St. Petersburg Dictionarv suggests that its original form was Naiḥṣidha.

{@Nodhas@}¦ is the name of a poet who is mentioned in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> and to whom certain of its hymns are ascribed.<sup>2</sup> In the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> he is called {@Kākṣīvata,@} a ‘descendant of {@Kakṣīvant.@}’ Ludwig<sup>4</sup> regards him as con- temporary with the defeat of {@Purukutsa.@} He was a {@Gotama.@}<sup>5</sup> <F>1) i. 61, 14; 62, 13; 64, 1, and 124, 4, according to Nirukta, iv. 16.</F> <F>2) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vi. 18; Rv. i. 58-64 are ascribed to him in the Anukramaṇī (Index).</F> <F>3) vii. 10, 10; xxi. 9, 12. {%Cf.%} Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, iv. 27; viii. 12. 17; Av. xv. 2, 4; 4, 4.</F> <F>4) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 110.</F> <F>5) Rv. i. 62, 13; Max Müller, {%Sacred%} {%Books of the East,%} 32, 125. For the controversy as to the meaning of Rv. i. 124, 4, see Oldenberg, {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 137. {%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%Transactions of%} {%the Connecticut Academy of Arts and%} {%Sciences,%} 15, 33.</F>

{@Nau@}¦ is the regular word in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> for a ‘boat’ or ‘ship.’ In the great majority of cases the ship was merely a boat for crossing rivers, though no doubt a large boat was needed for crossing many of the broad rivers of the Panjab as well as the {@Yamunā@} and {@Gaṅgā.@} Often no doubt the Nau was a mere dug-out canoe ({%dāru%}).<sup>3</sup> It is certainly against the theory<sup>4</sup> of the existence in Vedic times of an extensive sea trade that there is no mention of any of the parts of a ship, such as masts and sails, except the oar ({@Aritra@}), Yet there are some allusions indicating a trade more extensive than that implied by boats used for crossing rivers. The Atharvaveda<sup>5</sup> compares the ruin of a kingdom where Brahmins are oppressed to the [Page1-462+ 49] sinking of a ship which is leaking ({%bhinnā%}); though the language here employed can be made to fit the theory that the ship was only a canoe, it cannot naturally be so interpreted. Moreover, there is mention made in the Rigveda<sup>6</sup> of men who go to the ocean ({@Samudra@}) eager for gain ({%saniṣyavaḥ%}). It is not altogether satisfactory to restrict such references with Zimmer<sup>7</sup> to the broad stream of the Indus after the union of that river with the tributaries of the Panjab. In the Rigveda<sup>8</sup> too it is said that the Aśvins rescued {@Bhujyu@} in the ocean with a ship of a hundred oars ({%śatāritra%}). It is not easy to refuse to recognize here the existence of larger vessels with many oars used for sea voyages. The Baudhāyana Dharma Sūtra,<sup>9</sup> at any rate, clearly refers to maritime navigation. See also {@Samudra.@} <F>1) i. 131, 2; ii. 39, 4; viii. 42, 3; 83, 3, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. ii. 36, 5; v. 19. 8; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 3, 10, 1; Vājasaneyi Saṃ- hitā, x. 19; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, iv. 13; vi. 6. 21; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 8, 1, 4; iv. 2, 5, 10, etc.</F> <F>3) Rv. x. 155, 3.</F> <F>4) Wilson, {%Rigveda,%} 1, xli.</F> <F>5) v. 19, 8. {%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%American%} {%Journal of Philology,%} 19, 139. So per- haps the passage, Rv. i. 32, 8, {%nadaṃ%} {%na bhinnam,%} refers to a ship. See {@Naḍa.@}</F> <F>6) Rv. i. 56, 2; iv. 55, 6.</F> <F>7) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 22, 23.</F> <F>8) i. 116, 3 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>9) i. 2, 4; ii. 2, 2. But it is not of very early date. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%op. cit.,%} 255-257.</F>

{@Nyag-rodha,@}¦ ‘growing downwards,’ is the name of the {%Ficus indica,%} a tree remarkable for sending down from its branches fibres which take root and form new stems. Though the tree is not mentioned by name in the Rigveda, it appears to have been known, as Pischel<sup>1</sup> has shown from a hymn<sup>2</sup> in which its characteristics may be recognized. It is frequently mentioned in the Atharvaveda<sup>3</sup> and the later literature.<sup>4</sup> The sacrificial bowls ({@Camasa@}) were made of its wood.<sup>5</sup> It was doubtless of the greatest importance, as in modern times, to the Vedic village. The sister tree, the {@Aśvattha@} ({%Ficus religiosa%}), already occurs in the Rigveda. <F>1) {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 113, 114.</F> <F>2) i. 24, 7, where {%stūpa%} seems to denote the crest or crown of the tree above the main trunk.</F> <F>3) iv. 37, 4; v. 5, 5.</F> <F>4) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vii. 30. 31; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, v. 3, 5, 13 xiii. 2, 7, 3; Chāndogya Upaniṣad, vi. 12, 1, etc.</F> <F>5) Taittirīya Samhitā, vii. 4, 12, 1; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiii. 13. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 58.</F>

{@Ny-aṅka@}¦ in the dual denotes in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> and Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> some part of the chariot, parallel with {@Aṅka.@} The Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> has Nyaṅkū, the dual of Nyaṅku. <F>1) i. 7, 7, 2.</F> <F>2) i. 3, 5, 4; ii. 7, 8, 1.</F> <F>3) i. 7, 5; Lāṭyāyana Srauta Sūtra, ii. 8, 9.</F>

{@Nyaṅku@}¦ is the name of an animal in the list of victims at the Aśvamedha, or ‘horse sacrifice,’ in the Yajurveda Saṃhitās.<sup>1</sup> It seems clear that a kind a ‘gazelle’ is meant, but the com- mentary on the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> suggests ‘bear’ ({%ṛkṣa%}) as a variant rendering. <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 17, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 9; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 27. 32. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 83. The metre {%nyaṅku-sāriṇī,%} ‘with a gazelle's gait,’ is already mentioned in the Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya, xvi. 31; Chandas, 5; Nidāna Sūtra, i. 2.</F> <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 17, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 9; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 27. 32. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 83. The metre {%nyaṅku-sāriṇī,%} ‘with a gazelle's gait,’ is already mentioned in the Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya, xvi. 31; Chandas, 5; Nidāna Sūtra, i. 2.</F>

{@Ny-astikā@}¦ seems in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> to denote a plant of some kind, identified by the scholiast with the Śaṅkhapuṣpikā ({%Andropogon aciculatus%}). <F>1) vi. 139, 1. {%Cf.%} Whitney, Transla- tion of the Atharvaveda, 385; Bloom- field, {%ymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 539, 540.</F>
{@Ny-ocanī@}¦ is found in the marriage hymn of the Rigveda (x. 85, 6), where some kind of ornament worn by women seems to be meant. The commentator Sāyaṇa interprets it as ‘female slave.’

{@Pakti@}¦ denotes a cooked object, probably a kind of ‘cake,’ in the Saṃhitās.<sup>1</sup> One who cooks food is called {@Paktṛ.@}<sup>2</sup> <F>1) Rv. iv. 24, 5. 7; 25, 6. 7; vi. 29, 4; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxi. 59, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. x. 9, 7. 11. 25; xi. 1, 17; xii. 3, 17; Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 3, 4, 17; x. 4, 2, 19.</F>

{@Paktha@}¦ is the name of a people in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> where they appear as one of the tribes that opposed<sup>2</sup> the {@Tṛtsu-Bharatas@} in the {@Dāśarājña.@} or ‘battle of the ten kings.’ Zimmer<sup>3</sup> compares [Page1-464+ 44] them with the tribe of <lang n="greek">Πάκτυες</lang> and their country <lang n="greek">Πακτυική</lang>, mentioned as in the north-west of India by Herodotus,<sup>4</sup> and with the modern Pakhthūn in Eastern Afghanistan, holding that they were a northern tribe; this is probable, since the Bharatas seem to have occupied the Madhyadeśa, or ‘Middle Land.’ In three passages of the Rigveda<sup>5</sup> a Paktha is referred to as a protégé of the Aśvins. The second connects him with {@Trasadasyu,@} whose tribe, the {@Pūrus,@} were aided by the Pakthas in their unsuccessful onslaught on {@Sudās.@} In the third passage he seems specified as {@Tūrvāyaṇa,@} and appears as an opponent of {@Cyavāna.@}<sup>6</sup> Probably, therefore, Paktha in all cases denotes the king of the Paktha people. <F>1) vii. 18. 7.</F> <F>2) Roth, {%Zur Litteratur und Geschichte%} {%des Weda,%} 95, thought that the Pakthas were allies of the Trtsus, but this view is certainly incorrect. {%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%Journal of the American Oriental Society,%} 15, 260.</F> <F>3) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 430, 431.</F> <F>4) vii. 65 new (<lang n="greek">Πάκτυες</lang>); iii. 102 new and iv. 44 (<lang n="greek">Πακτυική</lang>).</F> <F>5) viii. 22, 10; 49, 10; x. 61, 1.</F> <F>6) Pischel, {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 71-77.</F>

{@Pakva,@}¦ ‘cooked,’ is used substantively as meaning ‘cooked food’<sup>1</sup> or ‘cooked milk.’<sup>2</sup> The word is also used of ‘baked’ bricks.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) Rv. vi. 63, 9; Av. vi. 119, 2; xii. 3, 55; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 5, 1, 26; ii. 6, 1, 7, etc.</F> <F>2) Rv. i. 62, 9; 180, 3; ii. 40, 2; iii. 30, 14; vi. 44, 24, etc.</F> <F>3) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, vi. 1, 2, 22; vii. 2, 1, 7.</F>

{@Pakṣa@}¦ is, in the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> applied to some part of a house, either the ‘side posts,’ according to Roth,<sup>2</sup> Zimmer,<sup>3</sup> and Grill,<sup>4</sup> or ‘sides,’ as understood by Whitney<sup>5</sup> and Bloom- field.<sup>6</sup> The description of the roof ({@Chadis@}) in the Atharvaveda<sup>7</sup> as {%catuṣ-pakṣa,%} ‘four-sided,’ tells in favour of the second explanation. In the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa<sup>8</sup> Pakṣa is used of the sides of a chariot. For Pakṣa as the ‘half’ of a month, see {@Māsa.@} <F>1) ix. 3, 4.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>3) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 153.</F> <F>4) {%Hundert Lieder^2,%} 188.</F> <F>5) Translation of the Atharvaveda, 526.</F> <F>6) {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 597.</F> <F>7) iii. 7, 3.</F> <F>8) i. 5, 12, 5. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 17, 210.</F>

{@Pakṣas@}¦ is found in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> meaning the ‘sides’<sup>3</sup> of a chariot. In the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā<sup>4</sup> and the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa<sup>5</sup> it is used of the sides of a hut or chamber ({@Śālā@}). In the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā<sup>6</sup> it means the ‘wing’ of a door. In the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa<sup>7</sup> the ‘half’ of an army is so named, and in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāh- maṇa<sup>8</sup> it means the ‘half’ of a month, or ‘fortnight.’ {%Cf.%} {@Pakṣa.@} <F>1) viii. 8, 22.</F> <F>2) vii. 7.</F> <F>3) Whitney, Translation of the Athar- vaveda, 506; Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the%} {%Atharvaveda,%} 117.</F> <F>4) xxx. 5.</F> <F>5) i. 2, 3, 1.</F> <F>6) xxix. 5.</F> <F>7) ii. 9.</F> <F>8) xxiii. 6, 6.</F>

{@Pakṣin@}¦ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> denotes a ‘winged’ creature, more particularly a ‘bird.’ <F>1) i. 48. 5; 182, 5; x. 127, 5, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. iv. 34, 4; xi. 5, 21; xii. 1, 51; xiii. 2, 33; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxxiv. 8; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, iv. 23; Bṛhad- āraṇyaka Upaniṣad, ii. 5, 18, etc.</F>

{@Paṅkti,@}¦ originally a ‘set of five,’ denotes as early as the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> a ‘series’ generally. In the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka<sup>2</sup> the word is used of the series of a man's ancestors whom he purifies by certain conduct. <F>1) x. 117, 8, as taken by the St. Petersburg Dictionary.</F> <F>2) x. 38, 39.</F>

{@Pacata,@}¦ like {@Pakti,@} denotes ‘cooked food’ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) i. 61, 7; x. 116, 8.</F> <F>2) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxi. 60; xxiii. 13; Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, viii. 21, etc.</F>
{@Pacana@}¦ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and the Śatapatha Brāhamaṇa<sup>2</sup> denotes a ‘vessel for cooking’ food. <F>1) i. 162, 6.</F> <F>2) vi. 5, 43, 3. 4; xiv. 1, 2, 21.</F>

{@Pajra@}¦ is the name of the family from which {@Kakṣīvant@} sprang ({@Pajriya@}). It is mentioned several times in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> According to Pischel,<sup>2</sup> the epithet {%pṛkṣa-yāma%}<sup>3</sup> applied to them means ‘carrying out brilliant sacrificial performances,’ which won for them {@Śrutaratha's@} generosity. In two passages<sup>4</sup> Roth<sup>5</sup> sees a Pajra called Sāmaṅ. This is uncertain, but in any case a Pajra seems clearly alluded to. Elsewhere<sup>6</sup> it is very doubtful whether the word is a proper name at all. In the Śāṭyāyana<sup>7</sup> the Pajras are declared to be Aṅgirases. <F>1) i. 117, 10; 122, 7. 8; 126, 4. 5.</F> <F>2) {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 97, 98.</F> <F>3) Rv. i. 127, 8, where Roth (St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}) thinks this compound is probably a proper name.</F> <F>4) Rv. viii. 4, 17; 6, 47.</F> <F>5) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v. pajra.%}</F> <F>6) Rv. i. 190, 5, where the reference is clearly hostile and contemptuous.</F> <F>7) Cited by Sāyaṇa on Rv. i. 51, 4.</F>

{@Pajrā@}¦ occurs once in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> where Ludwig<sup>2</sup> sees in the word the name of the wife of the sacrificer, {@Pajra,@} while Roth<sup>3</sup> takes it to be an epithet (‘stout’) of the Soma plant. The sense is thus uncertain. <F>1) ix. 82, 14.</F> <F>2) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 110.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} {%pajra.%}</F>
{@Pajriya@}¦ ‘descendant of Pajra,’ is the patronymic<sup>1</sup> of {@Kakṣīvant@} in the Rigveda.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) {%Cf.%} {@Tugrya,@} n. 1.</F> <F>2) i. 116, 7; 117, 6; 120, 5.</F>

{@Pañca-janāḥ,@}¦ the ‘five peoples,’ are mentioned under various names in Vedic literature.<sup>1</sup> Who are meant by the five is very uncertain. The Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> explains the five to be gods, men, Gandharvas and Apsarases, snakes, and the Fathers. [Page1-467+ 60] Aupamanyava<sup>3</sup> held that the four castes ({@Varṇa@}) and the {@Niṣādas@} made up the five, and Sāyaṇa<sup>4</sup> is of the same opinion. Yāska<sup>5</sup> thinks that the five are the Gandharvas, fathers, gods, Asuras, and Rakṣases. No one of these explanations can be regarded as probable. Roth<sup>6</sup> and Geldner<sup>7</sup> think that all the peoples of the earth are méant: just as there are four quarters ({@Diś@}), there are peoples at the four quarters (N. E. S. W.), with the Āryan folk in the middle. Zimmer<sup>8</sup> opposes this view on the ground that the inclusion of all peoples in one expression is not in harmony with the distinction so often made between Āryan and Dāsa; that neither {%janāsaḥ,%} ‘men,’<sup>9</sup> nor {%mānuṣāḥ,%} ‘people,’<sup>10</sup> could be used of non-Āryans; that the Soma is referred to as being among the five tribes;<sup>11</sup> that the five tribes are mentioned as on the {@Sarasvatī,@}<sup>12</sup> and that Indra is {%pāñca-%} {%janya,%}<sup>13</sup> ‘belonging to the five peoples.’ He concludes that Āryans alone are meant, and in particular the five tribes of the {@Anus, Druhyus, Yadus, Turvaśas,@} and {@Pūrus,@} who are all mentioned together in one or perhaps two hymns of the Rigveda,<sup>14</sup> and four of whom occur in another hymn.<sup>15</sup> But he admits that the expression might easily be used more generally later. Hopkins<sup>16</sup> has combated Zimmer's view, but his own opinion rests mainly on his theory that there was no people named Turvaśa, but only a king of the Yadus called Turvaśa, and that theory is not very probable. [Page1-468+ 43] <div n="P"/>In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>17</sup> and the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>18</sup> the five peoples are opposed to the Bharatas, and in the former work<sup>19</sup> seven peoples are alluded to. <F>1) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 31; iv. 27; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, i. 6, 1, 2; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, v. 6; xxxii. 6; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, iv. 2, 9 ({%pañca-janāḥ%} as a compound). See also {%pañca mānuṣāḥ,%} Rv. viii. 9, 2; {%mānavāḥ,%} Av. iii. 21, 5; 24, 3; xii. 1, 15; {%janāḥ,%} Rv. iii. 37, 9; 59, 8; vi. 14, 4; viii. 32, 22; ix. 65, 23; 92, 3; x. 45, 6; {%kṛṣṭayaḥ,%} ii. 2, 10; iii. 53, 16; iv. 38, 10; x. 60, 4; 119, 6; Av. iii. 24, 3; {%kṣitayaḥ,%} Rv. i. 7, 9; 176, 3; v. 35, 2; vi. 46, 7; vii. 75, 4; 79, 1; {%carṣaṇyaḥ,%} Rv. v. 86, 2; vii. 15, 2; ix. 101, 9. See Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 204. Every book of the Rigveda has a mention of the five peoples: one such in ii. and iv.; two in i., v., vi., vii., viii.; three in iii. and ix.; four in x.</F> <F>2) iii. 31.</F> <F>3) In Yāska, Nirukta, iii. 8.</F> <F>4) On Rv. i. 7, 9, etc.</F> <F>5) Nirukta, {%loc. cit.%}</F> <F>6) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v. kṛṣṭi,%} {%Nirukta, Erläuterungen,%} 28. For his view, Av. iii. 24, 3, can be cited: {%pañca%} {%pradiśo mānavīḥ pañca kṛṣṭayaḥ,%} ‘the five directions, the five races of men.’</F> <F>7) {%Siebenzig Lieder,%} 18. See, however, {%Ṛgveda, Glossar,%} 103, where he recog- nizes the use of the phrase to denote five tribes, as well as all mankind.</F> <F>8) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 119-123. His view is accepted by Macdonell, {%Sanskrit%} {%Literature,%} 153; Muir, {%Sanskrit Texts,%} 1^2, 179, is doubtful.</F> <F>9) {%Cf.%} its use in Rv. ii. 12, {%sa janāsa%} {%Indraḥ,%} where the address must be to Āryan men.</F> <F>10) {%Cf.%} Rv. viii. 9, 2, and i. 52, 9, with viii. 70, 11; x. 28, 8.</F> <F>11) Rv. ix. 65, 23.</F> <F>12) Rv. vi. 61, 12 {%(pañca jātā). Cf.%} x. 53, 4.</F> <F>13) v. 32, 11. Agni is ‘of the five tribes,’ Rv. ix. 66, 20. Atri also is so described, Rv. i. 117, 3.</F> <F>14) Rv. i. 108, 8. In vii. 18, cited by Zimmer, 122, the five tribes do not occur {%eo nomine,%} for {@Yakṣu@} replaces Yadu. But it is probable that Yadu is meant by Yakṣu.</F> <F>15) Rv. viii. 10, 5.</F> <F>16) {%Journal of the American Oriental%} {%Society,%} 15, 260.</F> <F>17) xiii. 5, 4, 14.</F> <F>18) viii. 23.</F> <F>19) It is a conjecture of Weber's, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 202, that the five peoples are identical with the {@Pañcālas,@} and the seven mentioned in Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 5, 4, 23, with the Kuru-Pañcālas.</F>
{@Pañca-daśī,@}¦ ‘the fifteenth day of the month,’ is already mentioned in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa (i. 5, 10, 5).

{@Pañca-nada,@}¦ ‘having five streams,’ is not found until the epic period as the name of the Panjāb, which has no desig- nation in the earlier literature. The importance of the Panjāb as the home<sup>1</sup> of the Rigveda has been greatly diminished by recent research, Hopkins,<sup>2</sup> Pischel,<sup>3</sup> and Geldner<sup>4</sup> having on different grounds shown reason for believing that the Rigveda, at least in great part, was composed farther east, in the {@Madhyadeśa,@} which admittedly was the home of the later Vedic culture. Hillebrandt<sup>5</sup> considers that the Rigveda belongs in part to the Panjāb, or rather to Arachosia, and in part to the Middle Country. See also {@Kuru, Tṛtsu.@} <F>1) See, {%e.g.,%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 32 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>2) {%Journal of the American Oriental%} {%Society,%} 19, 19-28. {%Cf.%} Macdonell, {%Sanskrit Literature,%} 145, 441.</F> <F>3) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 218.</F> <F>4) {%Ibid.,%} 3, 152.</F> <F>5) {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 98 {%et seq.%} But see {@Divodāsa.@} {%Cf.%} also Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 189.</F>
{@Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.@}¦ See {@Tāṇdya.@}

{@Pañcāla@}¦ is the later name<sup>1</sup> of the people called {@Krivi@} in the Rigveda. The Pañcālas are rarely referred to except in con- nexion with the {@Kurus,@} and the kings of the Kuru-Pañcālas are mentioned in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> In the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā<sup>3</sup> the Pañcālas appear as the people of {@Keśin Dālbhya.@} [Page1-469+ 46] In the Upaniṣads and later<sup>4</sup> the Brahmins of the Pañcālas figure as taking part in philosophical and philological dis- cussions. The Saṃhitopaniṣad Brāhmaṇa<sup>5</sup> makes mention of the Prācya-Pañcālas. <div n="P"/>The Pañcālas, no doubt, included other tribes besides the Krivis. The name seems to refer to five tribes, and it has been suggested<sup>6</sup> that the Pañcālas represent the five tribes of the Rigveda, but the suggestion is not very probable. There is no trace in Vedic literature of the Epic division of the Pañcālas into northern ({%uttara%}) and southern ({%dakṣiṇa%}). The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>7</sup> mentions their town {@Paricakrā;@} other towns to which allusion seems to be made were {@Kāmpīla@} and kauśāmbī.<sup>8</sup> Of their kings and chiefs, as distinguished from kings of the Kuru-Pañcālas, we hear of {@Kraivya, Durmukha,@} {@Pravāhaṇa Jaivali,@} and {@Śona.@} <F>1) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 5, 4, 7.</F> <F>2) viii. 14</F> <F>3) xxx. 2 ({%Indische Studien,%} 3, 471).</F> <F>4) Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, vi. 1, 1 (Mādhyaṃdina = vi. 2, 1 Kāṇva); Chāndogya Upaniṣad, v. 3, 1; Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya, ii. 12, 44; Nidāna Sūtra, i. 6; Sāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xii. 13, 6, etc.</F> <F>5) 2. {%Cf. Indische Studien,%} 4, 375, n.; 8, 92, n. 1.</F> <F>6) Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 202; Geldner, {%Vedische Studien,%} 3, 108, n. 1. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%op. cit.,%} 1, 191 {%et seq.%}; {%Indian Literature,%} 10, 90, 114, 115, 125, 135, 136.</F> <F>7) xiii. 5, 4, 7.</F> <F>8) See {@Kauśāmbeya.@}</F>

{@Pañcāla-caṇḍa@}¦ is the name of a teacher in the Aitareya<sup>1</sup> and the Śāṅkhāyana<sup>2</sup> Āraṇyakas. <F>1) iii. 1, 6.</F> <F>2) vii. 18. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 391; {%Indian Literature,%} 50, 315, 326.</F>

{@Pañcāvi@}¦ occurs several times in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> in the sense of ‘aged five lamb-periods’ (of six months), that is, ‘thirty months old.’<sup>2</sup> <F>1) xviii. 26; xxi. 14; xxiv. 12; xxviii. 26.</F> <F>2) {%Cf.%} {@Tryavi.@}</F>

{@Pañcaudana@}¦ is an adjective in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> meaning ‘prepared with five rice-messes.’ The cooking of five rice dishes is referred to in the same Saṃhitā.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) iv. 14, 7; ix. 5, 8 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>2) ix. 5, 37.</F>

{@Paṭala@}¦ as early as the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> denotes ‘section’ of a work, a sense occurring in the Sūtras<sup>2</sup> and later. <F>1) i. 21. 22.</F> <F>2) Śāṅkhāyana Srauta Sūtra, xi. 9. 20; xiii. 21, 2; Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra, iv. 6. 7.</F>

{@Paṭharvan@}¦ appears to be the name of a man in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> According to Ludwig,<sup>2</sup> however, the word is Paṭharu, and is the name of a fort which was saved by a rain-storm from being set on fire. <F>1) i. 112, 17, with Sāyaṇa's note.</F> <F>2) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 204. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Griffith, {%Hymns of the Rigveda,%} 1, 147, 148.</F>

{@Paḍgṛbhi,@}¦ ‘seizing by the foot,’<sup>1</sup> is the name in the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> of either a man<sup>3</sup> or a demon. See also {@Paḍbīśa.@} <F>1) But it may mean ‘seizing with a cord.’ {%Cf.%} Macdonell, {%Vedic Grammar,%} p. 34 (top); Pischel, {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 236.</F> <F>2) x. 49, 5.</F> <F>3) Ludwig, Translation of the Rig- veda, 3, 165.</F>

{@Paḍ-bīśa,@}¦ the ‘foot-fetter’ of a horse in five passages, two in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> and one each in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad,<sup>2</sup> the Chāndogya Upaniṣad,<sup>3</sup> and the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka.<sup>4</sup> Elsewhere<sup>5</sup> its uses are metaphorical. According to Roth,<sup>6</sup> the literal sense is ‘foot-fastening’ ({%paḍ%} being = {%pad,%} ‘foot,’ and {%bīśa,%} written {%vīśa%} in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, being connected with the Latin {%vincire,%} ‘bind’). Pischel<sup>7</sup> objects that the sense of ‘foot-fastening’ involves the absurdity, in the Upaniṣad passages, of a fine horse from the {@Sindhu@} (Indus) being spoken of as tearing up the peg to which it is fastened. He suggests instead the meaning of ‘hobble,’ which must be right.<sup>8</sup> <F>1) i. 162, 14. 16 = Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iv. 6, 9, 1. 2; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxv. 38. 39.</F> <F>2) vi. 2, 13 (Mādhyaṃdina).</F> <F>3) v. 1, 12.</F> <F>4) ix. 7; Keith, {%Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka,%} 57, n. 3.</F> <F>5) Rv. x. 97, 16; Av. viii. 1, 4; xii. 5, 15; xvi. 8, 27; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 6, 10, 3; Mantra Brāhmaṇa, i. 3, 10.</F> <F>6) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>7) {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 233-236.</F> <F>8) He explains the first part of the word as derived from {%paś,%} ‘tie.’ {%Cf.%} Macdoneli, {%Vedic Grammar,%} p. 34 (top). But the form {%paḍ%} may be due to a false analogy, and the sense of ‘foot- fastener’ may express ‘hobble’ quite satisfactorily; it is not confined to a rope tied to a peg in the ground.</F>

{@Paṇa,@}¦ with {@Pratipaṇa,@} is found in a hymn of the Atharva- veda<sup>1</sup> denoting the process of bargaining and selling. The root {%paṇ,%} from which the word is derived, is employed in the later Saṃhitās and the Brāhmaṇas,<sup>2</sup> while Paṇana in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> denotes ‘trafficking.’ {%Cf.%} {@Vaṇij.@} <F>1) iii. 15, 4. 6 (in the Paippalāda recension; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 112).</F> <F>2) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, viii. 55; Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 3, 3, 1 {%et seq.;%} Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, i. 27. {%Cf.%} Tait- tirīya Saṃhitā, vi. 1, 10, 1.</F> <F>3) iii. 3, 2, 19. The root does not occur in the Rigveda, but its etymology is vouched for by the Greek <lang n="greek">πέρνημι</lang>, {%Cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 84, n. 3.</F>

{@Paṇi@}¦ in the Rigveda appears to denote a person who is rich, but who does not give offerings to the gods, or bestow {@Dakṣiṇās@} on the priests, and who is therefore an object of intense dislike to the composers of the Saṃhitā.<sup>1</sup> Hence the gods are asked to attack the Paṇis, who are also referred to as being defeated with slaughter.<sup>2</sup> The Paṇi is opposed to the pious sacrificer as a niggard,<sup>3</sup> and is spoken of as a wolf,<sup>4</sup> the symbol of enmity. In some passages<sup>5</sup> the Paṇis definitely appear as mythological figures, demons who withhold the cows or waters of heaven, and to whom Saramā goes on a mission from Indra.<sup>6</sup> Among the Paṇis {@Bṛbu@} was apparently important. In one passage of the Rigveda<sup>7</sup> they are described as {@Beka-@} {@nāṭas,@} or ‘usurers’ (?). In another<sup>8</sup> they are called {@Dasyus,@} and styled {%mṛdhra-vāc,%} probably ‘of hostile speech,’ and {%grathin,%} a word of uncertain meaning. Hillebrandt<sup>9</sup> thinks that the latter epithet refers to the continuous flow of a speech which [Page1-472+ 54] is not understood, and that {%mṛdhra-vāc%} means ‘śpeaking an enemy's speech,’ though not necessarily with reference to non-Āryans.<sup>10</sup> In two passages<sup>11</sup> the Paṇis appear as {@Dāsas,@} and in one<sup>12</sup> a Paṇi is mentioned in connexion with wer- geld ({@Vaira@}), being apparently regarded as equal to a man merely in the price put on his life, but in other respects as inferior. <div n="P"/>It is difficult to be certain exactly who a Paṇi was. Roth<sup>13</sup> thinks that the word is derived from {%paṇ,%} ‘barter,’ and that the Paṇi is properly the man who will give nothing without return, hence the niggard, who neither worships the gods nor rewards their priests. This view is accepted by Zimmer<sup>14</sup> and by Ludwig.<sup>15</sup> The latter scholar thinks the apparent references to fights with Paṇis are to be explained by their having been aboriginal traders who went in caravans — as in Arabia and Northern Africa — prepared to fight, if need be, to protect their goods against attacks which the Āryans would naturally deem quite justified. He supports this explanation by the references to the Paṇis as Dasyus and Dāsas. It is, however, hardly necessary to do more than regard the Paṇis generally as non-worshippers of the gods favoured by the singers; the term is wide enough to cover either the aborigines or hostile Āryan tribes, as well as demons. Hillebrandt,<sup>16</sup> however, thinks that a real tribe is meant, the Parnians of Strabo, and that they were associated with the Dahae ({@Dāsa@}). Moreover, he finds them associated in one passage<sup>17</sup> with the {@Pārāvatas,@} whom [Page1-473+ 45] he identifies with the <lang n="greek">Παρουῆται</lang> of Ptolemy,<sup>18</sup> and with {@Bṛṣaya,@} whom he connects with <lang n="greek">Βαρσαέντης</lang> of Arrian;<sup>19</sup> he also con- siders that the frequent<sup>20</sup> mention of the Paṇis as opponents of {@Divodāsa@} shows that the latter was on the Arachosian Haraqaiti ({@Sarasvatī@}) fighting against the Parnians and Dahae, as well as other Iranian tribes. But the identification of Paṇi and the Parnians is needless, especially as the root {%paṇ,%} which is found also in the Greek <lang n="greek">πέρνημι</lang>, shows a satisfactory deri- vation, while the transfer of Divodāsa to the Haraqaiti is improbable.
