{@Pari-kṣit@}¦ appears in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> as a king in whose realm, that of the Kurus, prosperity and peace abound. The verses in which he is celebrated are later<sup>2</sup> called {%Pārikṣityaḥ,%} and the Brāhmaṇas explain that Agni is {%pari-kṣit%} because he dwells among men. Hence Roth<sup>3</sup> and Bloomfield<sup>4</sup> regard Parikṣit in the Atharvaveda not as a human king at all. This may be correct, but it is not certain. Both Zimmer<sup>5</sup> and [Page1-494+ 45] Oldenberg<sup>6</sup> recognize Parikṣit as a real king, a view supported by the fact that in the later Vedic literature King {@Janamejaya@} bears the patronymic {@Pārikṣita.@} If this be so, Parikṣit belonged to the later period, since the Atharvan passage in which his name occurs is certainly late, and none of the other Saṃhitās know Parikṣit at all. The Epic<sup>7</sup> makes him grandfather of Pratiśravas and great-grandfather of Pratīpa, and Zimmer,<sup>5</sup> probably with justice, compares the Prātisutvana and Pratīpa found in another late Atharvan passage.<sup>8</sup> But {@Devāpi@} and {@Śantanu@} cannot be brought into connexion with Pratīpa.<sup>9</sup> <F>1) xx. 127, 7-10. See also Scheftelo- witz, {%Die Apokryphen des Veda,%} 156, 157, and the verses in the Vaitāna Sūtra, xxxiv. 9. The Vedic spelling is Parikṣit, not Parīkṣit.</F> <F>2) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vi. 32, 10; Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, xxx. 5; Gopatha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 6, 12; Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xii. 17.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>4) {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 690, 691. but see {%Atharvaveda,%} 101, n. 9.</F> <F>5) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 131.</F> <F>6) {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgen-%} {%lāndischen Gesellschaft,%} 42, 237; {%Buddha,%} 396.</F> <F>7) See Zimmer, {%loc. cit.%}</F> <F>5) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 131.</F> <F>8) xx. 129.</F> <F>9) Devāpi is really a Brahmin, son of Ṛṣṭiṣeṇa, and not connected directly with Śantanu. Yāska, Nirukta, ii. 10, identifies them as brothers and Kurus; but the former part of the identification is, no doubt, wrong.</F>
{@Pari-gha@}¦ denotes an iron bolt or bar in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (ii. 24, 6. 10. 15) as often later.

{@Pari-cakrā@}¦ is according to one reading the name of a {@Pañcāla@} town mentioned in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> and identified by Weber<sup>2</sup> with the later Ekacakrā, which was near {@Kāmpīla.@}<sup>3</sup> There is a various reading Parivakrā.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) xiii. 5, 4, 7.</F> <F>2) {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 192.</F> <F>3) Mahābhārata, i. 6094.</F> <F>4) Accepted by the scholiast and Eggeling, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 44, 397.</F>

{@Pari-cara@}¦ is found in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> in the sense of ‘attendant.’ In the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> {%pari-caraṇa%} has the same sense metaphorically, the other two Vedas (Sāma and Yajur) being said to be subsidiary to the Rigveda. <F>1) iv. 3, 5, 9. {%Cf. pari-caritṛ,%} Chāndogya Upaniṣad, vii. 8, 1.</F> <F>2) vi. 11; Max Müller, {%Ancient Sanskrit Literature,%} 457.</F>
{@Pari-carmaṇya@}¦ denotes a thong of leather in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa (vi. 12) and the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka (ii. 1).

{@Pari-takmyā@}¦ in a number of passages of the {@Rigveda@}<sup>1</sup> denotes ‘night’ according to the St. Petersburg {@Dictionary.@} [Page1-495+ 35] Sieg<sup>2</sup> thinks that in one place<sup>3</sup> at least the word signifies the decisive point of the race, something like the sense of {@Prapitva.@} But this is very doubtful. <F>1) i. 116, 15; iv. 41, 6; 43, 3; v. 30, 13; 31, 11; vi. 24, 9; vii. 69, 4.</F> <F>2) {%Die Sagenstoffe des Ṛgveda,%} 128. {%Cf.%} Geldner, {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 36; {%Rigveda,%} {%Glossar,%} 106.</F> <F>3) i. 116, 15.</F>

{@Pari-dā@}¦ in a few passages of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> has the sense of ‘giving oneself up to the mercy or protection of another.’ <F>1) ii. 4, 1, 11; ix. 2, 1, 17; 4, 2, 17; 4, 5; 5, 1, 53.</F>

{@Pari-dhāna@}¦ denotes ‘garment,’ probably ‘under garment,’ in the Atharvaveda (viii. 2, 16) and the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upani- ṣad (vi. 1, 10). A garment of saffron is mentioned in the Śānkhāyana Āraṇyaka (xi. 4).
{@Pari-pad@}¦ seems in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> to denote a pitfall used to capture lions. <F>1) x. 28, 10; metaphorically, viii. 24, 24.</F>

{@Pari-panthin,@}¦ ‘besetting the path,’ denotes ‘robber’ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> {%Cf.%} {@Taskara, Tāyu, Stena.@} <F>1) i. 42, 3; 103, 6; x. 85, 32.</F> <F>2) Av. i. 27, 1; iii. 15, 1; xii. 1, 32; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, iv. 34, etc.</F>
{@Pari-pavana@}¦ signifies in the Nirukta (iv. 9. 10) an instrument for winnowing grain.

{@Pari-mit@}¦ occurs once in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> in the description of a house, meaning perhaps the ‘crossbeams’ connecting the vertical posts.<sup>2</sup> {%Cf.%} {@Gṛha.@} <F>1) ix. 3, 1.</F> <F>2) Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Atharva-%} {%veda,%} 596; Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 158; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 525.</F>

{@Pari-moṣa@}¦ in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> signifies ‘theft,’ and {%parimoṣin%} in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> ‘thief.’ <F>1) ii. 5, 5, 1; vi. 1, 11, 5.</F> <F>2) xi. 6, 3, 11; xiii. 2, 4, 2, etc.</F>

{@Pari-rathya@}¦ occurs once in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> meaning either ‘road’<sup>2</sup> or a part of the chariot, perhaps as Ludwig<sup>3</sup> and Whitney<sup>4</sup> render it, the ‘rim.’ <F>1) viii. 8, 22.</F> <F>2) Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Atharva-%} {%veda,%} 587, following Nīlakaṇṭha's ex- planation of {%parirathya,%} Mahābhārata, viii. 1487.</F> <F>3) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 528.</F> <F>4) Translation of the Atharvaveda, 506.</F>
{@Pari-vakrā@}¦ is the reading accepted in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (xiii. 5, 4, 7) by the scholiast instead of the variant {@Paricakrā,@} which is supported by the Epic Ekacakrā.

{@Pari-vatsara@}¦ denotes in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> a ‘full year.’ It is often mentioned with other names of year (see {@Saṃvatsara@}), and in the later five year cycle counts as the second year. <F>1) x. 62, 2.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa i. 5, 5, 6; Mahābhārata, i. 3202, etc. So {%pari-%} {%vatsarīṇa,%} as an adjective, ‘relating to a full year,’ Rv. vii. 103, 8; Av. iii. 10, 3.</F>

{@Pari-vāpa@}¦ in the later Saṃhitās<sup>1</sup> and Brāhmaṇas<sup>2</sup> denotes ‘fried grains of rice.’ <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 1, 10, 1; vi. 5, 11, 4; vii. 2, 10, 4; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxxiv. 11; Vājasaneyi Saṃ- hitā, xix. 21. 22.</F> <F>2) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 24; Tait- tirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 5, 11, 2, etc.</F>

{@Pari-vitta@}¦ denotes an ‘elder brother who is not married when his younger brother is.’ The term occurs in the list of sinful persons in the Yajurveda Saṃhitās<sup>1</sup> as well as in the Atharvaveda,<sup>2</sup> where Ludwig<sup>3</sup> needlessly proposes to read {%parivettā,%} the ‘younger brother who marries before his eldest brother.’ The name for the younger brother in the older texts is Parivividāna.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxxi. 7; Kapiṣ- ṭhala Saṃhitā, xlvii. 7; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iv. 1, 9; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 2, 8, 11; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxx. 9.</F> <F>2) vi. 112, 3.</F> <F>3) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 470.</F> <F>4) So in the Kāṭhaka, Kapiṣṭhala, Maitrāyaṇī, and Vājasaneyi Saṃhitās, {%loc. cit.%} <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Delbrück, {%Die indogermanischen%} {%Verwandtschaftsnamen,%} 580 {%et seq.;%} Bloom- field, {%American Journal of Phīlology,%} 17, 430 {%et seq.; Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 522 {%et seq.;%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 315; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 362.</F>
{@Pari-vṛktā, Pari-vṛktī, Pari-vṛttī,@}¦ are variant forms of the name of the rejected one among the royal wives. See {@Pati.@}

{@Pari-veṣṭṛ@}¦ in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> denotes an ‘attendant,’ more especially one who serves up food, a ‘waiter.’ The feminine form Pariveṣṭrī signifies a ‘female attendant’ or ‘handmaid.’<sup>3</sup> <F>1) ix. 6, 51.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vi. 3, 1, 3; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, i. 2, 16; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, vi. 13; xxx. 12. 13; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 8, 1; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, viii. 21; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 5, 4, 6; iii. 8, 2, 3; vi. 2, 13, 3, etc.</F> <F>3) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xi. 2, 7, 4; Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad, ii. 1; Keith, {%Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka,%} 21, n. 2.</F>
{@Pari-vrājaka@}¦ (lit., ‘wandering about’) denotes in the Nirukta (i. 14; ii. 8) a ‘mendicant monk.’

{@Pari-ṣad@}¦ (lit., ‘sitting around’) denotes in the Upaniṣads<sup>1</sup> an ‘assemblage’ of advisers in questions of philosophy, and the Gobhila Gṛhya Sūtra<sup>2</sup> refers to a teacher with his Pariṣad or ‘council.’ In the later literature the word denotes a body of advisers on religious topics, but also the assessors of a judge, or the council of ministers of a prince.<sup>3</sup> But in none of these senses is the word found in the early literature, though the institutions indicated by it must have existed at least in embryo. <F>1) Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, vi. 1, 1 (Mādhyaṃdina = vi. 2, 1 Kāṇva); {%daivī%} {%pariṣad,%} Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa, ii. 11, 13. 14.</F> <F>2) iii. 2, 40.</F> <F>3) {%Cf.%} Jolly, {%Recht und Sitte,%} 136, 137; Foy, {%Die königliche Gewalt,%} 16-19; 33- 37; 66; Bühler, {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen%} {%Morgenländischen Gesellschaft,%} 48, 55, 56; Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 2, 124.</F>
{@Pari-ṣkanda@}¦ (lit., ‘leaping around’) occurs in the {@Vrātya@} hymn of the Atharvaveda (xv. 2, 1 {%et seq.%}) denoting, in the dual, the two footmen running beside a chariot.
{@Pari-ṣyanda@}¦ (with water ‘flowing around’) in two passages of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (ix. 1, 19; xiv. 3, 1, 14) denotes a sandbank or island in a river.
{@Pari-sāraka@}¦ is the name of a place, an island formed by the {@Sarasvatī@} ‘flowing around’ it, according to a story in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (ii. 19).

{@Pari-srut@}¦ is the name of a drink which is mentioned first in the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> and which was distinct from both {@Surā@} and {@Soma,@}<sup>2</sup> but was intoxicating. According to Mahīdhara,<sup>3</sup> the liquor was made from flowers ({@Puṣpa@}). Zimmer<sup>4</sup> thinks that it was the family drink, and this is supported by the fact that in the Atharvaveda it twice occurs as a household beverage.<sup>5</sup> Hillebrandt<sup>6</sup> is of opinion that it was very much the same as Surā. <F>1) iii. 12, 7; xx. 127, 9. {%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%Journal of the American Oriental Society,%} 17, 68.</F> <F>2) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, v. 1, 2, 14. {%Cf.%} v. 5, 4, 10; xi. 5, 5, 13; xii. 7, 1, 7; 8, 2, 15; 9, 1, 1.</F> <F>3) On Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, ii. 34.</F> <F>4) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 281, 282.</F> <F>5) See also Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xix. 15; xx. 59; xxi. 29; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 11, 2. Its nature is more elaborately explained in the Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xiv. 1, 14; xv. 10, 11; Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 10, 349, 350.</F> <F>6) {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 24, 8.</F>
1. {@Parī-ṇah@}¦ appears to denote a ‘box’ or something similar in the Atharvaveda (xix. 48, 1).

2. {@Parī-ṇah@}¦ is the name of a place in {@Kurukṣetra@} mentioned in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka,<sup>2</sup> and the Sūtras.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) xxv. 13, 1.</F> <F>2) v. 1, 1.</F> <F>3) Lāṭyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, x. 19, 1; Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xxiv. 6, 34; Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xiii. 29, 32.</F>

{@Parī-śāsa@}¦ is the name of an instrument of the nature of tongs, used to lift the sacrificial kettle off the fire.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiv. 1, 3, 1; 2, 1, 16; 2, 54; 3, 1, 20, etc.</F>

{@Paruc-chepa@}¦ is the name of a Ṛṣi to whom the Anukramaṇī (Index) attributes a series of hymns<sup>1</sup> in the Rigveda, and whose [Page1-499+ 60] authorship is asserted in the Aitareya<sup>2</sup> and the Kauṣītaki<sup>3</sup> Brāhmaṇas, as well as in the Nirukta.<sup>4</sup> In the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>5</sup> he appears as a rival of {@Nṛmedhas.@} <F>1) Rv. i. 127-139.</F> <F>2) v. 12. 13 (where hymns Rv. i. 128, 129, 130, 133, 135, 137, 139, are at- tributed to him).</F> <F>3) xxiii. 4. 5.</F> <F>4) x. 42.</F> <F>5) ii. 5, 8, 3. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rig- veda, 3, 116. Parucchepa's claim to authorship is very doubtful.</F>
{@Paruṣa@}¦ seems to mean ‘reed’ in the Atharvaveda (viii. 8, 4) and ‘arrow’ in the Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra (xiv. 22, 20).

{@Paruṣṇī@}¦ is the name of a river which is mentioned in the Nadī-stuti (‘Praise of Rivers’),<sup>1</sup> and in the song of Sudās’ victory over the ten kings,<sup>2</sup> which seems to have been made decisive by the rise of the river drowning the fugitives.<sup>3</sup> In these passages and one of the eighth book of the Rigveda,<sup>4</sup> where it is called a ‘great stream’ ({%mahenadi%}), the name is certainly that of the river later called Ravi (Irāvatī), as recog- nized by Yāska.<sup>5</sup> Pischel<sup>6</sup> sees a reference to it in two other passages of the Rigveda,<sup>7</sup> where ‘wool’ ({%ūṛṇā%}) is connected with the word {%paruṣṇī,%} and the allusion to the river is accepted by Max Müller<sup>8</sup> and Oldenberg,<sup>9</sup> though they are not fully agreed as to the exact sense of the passages in question. Pischel suggests that the name is derived from the ‘flocks’ ({%parus%}) of wool, not from the bends of the river, as understood by the Nirukta,<sup>5</sup> or from its reeds, as Roth<sup>10</sup> suggests. [Page1-500+ 47] <div n="P"/>The mention of the Paruṣṇī and the Yamunā in the hymn celebrating the victory of Sudās has given rise to the conjectures of Hopkins,<sup>11</sup> that the Yamunā in that hymn is merely another name for the Paruṣṇī, and of Geldner,<sup>12</sup> that the Paruṣṇī there is merely a tributary of the Yamunā (Jumna). But neither interpretation is either essential or even probable. The hymn is a condensed one, and may well be taken as celebrating two great victories of Sudās. There is a doubtful reference to the Paruṣṇī in the Atharvaveda.<sup>13</sup> <F>1) x. 75, 5.</F> <F>2) vii. 18, 8. 9.</F> <F>3) It is impossible to decide precisely what part the river played in the battle. It is usually held that the enemies of Sudās tried to divert the stream, but failed, and were drowned in its current. So Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 11; Macdonell, {%Sanskrit Literature,%} 154; Geldner, {%Rigveda, Kommentar,%} 103, holds that Sudās was caught between two opposing armies, and had to escape over the Paruṣṇī, that his enemies tried to divert it to render him more accessible to their attack, but failed, and were overwhelmed in the river. Hopkins, {%India, Old and New,%} 52 {%et seq.,%} may be right in rejecting {%in toto%} the theory of the attempted diversion of the waters, though in the {%Journal of the%} {%American Oriental Society,%} 15, 261 {%et seq.,%} he accepted the traditional view.</F> <F>4) viii. 74, 15.</F> <F>5) Nirukta, ix. 26.</F> <F>6) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 208-210.</F> <F>7) iv. 22, 2; v. 52, 9.</F> <F>8) {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 32, 315, 323.</F> <F>9) {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 348.</F> <F>5) Nirukta, ix. 26.</F> <F>10) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} 4{%a.%}</F> <F>11) {%Op. cit.,%} 52.</F> <F>12) {%Ṛgveda, Glossar,%} 106.</F> <F>13) vi. 12, 3. {%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Hymns%} {%of the Atharvaveda,%} 462; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 289.</F>

{@Parus@}¦ means first a ‘limb’ or ‘member’ of the body,<sup>1</sup> and is then applied metaphorically to the divisions of the sacrifice<sup>2</sup> or of the year<sup>3</sup> ({%cf.%} {@Parvan@}). <F>1) Rv. i. 162, 18; x. 97, 12; 100, 5; Av. i. 12, 3; iv. 12, 2. 3, etc.</F> <F>2) Rv. x. 53, 1; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 6, 9, 1.</F> <F>3) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 5, 6, 1.</F>

1. {@Parṇa@}¦ denotes the ‘wing’ of a bird in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> It also means the ‘feather’ of an arrow in a late passage of the Rigveda,<sup>3</sup> and more often later;<sup>4</sup> and the ‘leaf’ of a tree from the Rigveda onwards.<sup>5</sup> <F>1) i. 116, 15; 182, 7; 183, 1; iv. 27, 4, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. x. 1, 29; Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 6, 3, 5, etc.</F> <F>3) x. 18, 14. {%Cf.%} Lanman, {%Sanskrit%} {%Reader,%} 386.</F> <F>4) Av. v. 25, 1; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxv. 1; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, i. 25; iii. 26, etc.</F> <F>5) Rv. x. 68, 10; Av. viii. 7, 12; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 5, 1, 7; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xvi. 46, etc.</F>

2. {@Parṇa@}¦ denotes the tree {%Butea frondosa,%} later usually called {@Palāśa.@} It occurs in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> in connexion with the {@Aśvattha,@} and with that tree as well as the {@Nyagrodha@} in the Atharvaveda,<sup>2</sup> which mentions both amulets<sup>3</sup> and the cover of sacrificial dishes<sup>4</sup> as made from its wood. Its use for the [Page1-501+ 55] making of sacrificial implements like the ladle ({%juhū%}),<sup>5</sup> or sacrificial posts,<sup>6</sup> or the small ladle called {%sruva,%}<sup>7</sup> is mentioned. The Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>8</sup> ascribes its origin to the loss of a feather by the Gāyatrī when winning the Soma. The tree is also often mentioned elsewhere.<sup>9</sup> Reference too is sometimes made to its bark ({%parṇa-valka%}).<sup>10</sup> <F>1) x. 97, 5.</F> <F>2) v. 5, 5.</F> <F>3) iii. 5, 4. 8.</F> <F>4) xviii. 4, 53.</F> <F>5) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 59, 7, 2. {%Cf.%} Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iv. 1, 1.</F> <F>6) Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xxi. 4, 13.</F> <F>7) Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xv. 2. {%Cf.%} viii. 2; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 1, 3, 11; 7, 1, 9; 8, 7.</F> <F>8) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, {%loc. cit.,%} and {%cf.%} Kuhn, {%Die Herabkunft des Feuers und%} {%des Göttertranks,%} 148, 192; Bloomfield, {%Journal of the American Oriental Society,%} 16, 20, 24; {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 331, 332; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 91.</F> <F>9) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 3, 4, 10; vi. 5, 1, 1; xi. 1, 4, 2; 7, 28; Pañca- viṃśa Brāhmaṇa, ix. 5, 4.</F> <F>10) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 5, 3, 5; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 7, 4, 2, 18, etc. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altinadisches Leben,%} 59; Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 17, 194, 195.</F>

{@Parṇaka@}¦ is the name of a man included in the list of victims at the Puruṣamedha (‘human sacrifice’) in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> and the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> According to Mahī- dhara,<sup>3</sup> a Bhilla is meant — {%i.e.,%} presumably a wild hillman, for he glosses {@Niṣāda@} in the same way.<sup>4</sup> Sāyaṇa<sup>5</sup> explains the word as meaning ‘one who catches fish by putting over the water a {%parṇa%} with poison,’ but this is apparently a mere etymological guess. Weber's<sup>6</sup> rendering of the term as refer- ring to a savage ‘wearing feathers’ is ingenious, but uncertain. <F>1) xxx. 16.</F> <F>2) iii. 4, 12, 1.</F> <F>3) On Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, {%loc. cit.%}</F> <F>4) On Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xvi. 27.</F> <F>5) On Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, {%loc. cit.%}</F> <F>6) {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgen-%} {%ländiscnen Gesellschaft,%} 18, 281. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 119.</F>

{@Parṇa-dhi@}¦ in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> denotes the part of the shaft in which the feather of the arrow is fastened. <F>1) iv. 6, 5. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches%} {%Leben,%} 300; Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the%} {%Atharvaveda,%} 375; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 154.</F>

{@Parṇaya@}¦ is the name in two passages of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> either of a hero, as Ludwig<sup>2</sup> thinks, or of a demon<sup>3</sup> overcome by Indra. <F>1) i. 53, 8; x. 48, 2.</F> <F>2) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 149.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>

{@Pary-aṅka@}¦ is the name of the seat of the Brahman in the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad.<sup>1</sup> It seems to correspond to what is else- where called {@Āsandi;@}<sup>2</sup> as used in the Upaniṣad, it can, how- ever, hardly mean a long seat for reclining on, but rather a throne.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) i. 5.</F> <F>2) Av. xv. 3, 3. {%Cf.%} xiv. 2, 65; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, viii. 5, 6, 12.</F> <F>3) {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 397, 401; Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 155; Lanmar in Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 765, 776.</F>
{@Pary-āsa@}¦ is used in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (iii. 1, 2, 18) to denote the woof of cloth, the warp being called {%anuchāda.%}

1. {@Parvata@}¦ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and the Atharvaveda<sup>2</sup> is con- joined with {%giri%} in the sense of ‘hill’ or ‘mountain.’ From the Rigveda<sup>3</sup> onwards<sup>4</sup> it is common in this sense as connected with the waters of rivers which flow in the hills.<sup>5</sup> The legend of the mountains having wings is already found in the Saṃhitās.<sup>6</sup> In the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad<sup>7</sup> are mentioned the southern ({%dakṣiṇa%}) and the northern ({%uttara%}) mountains, evidently in allusion to the Himālaya and the Vindhya ranges. The plants ({%oṣadhi%}) and aromatic products ({%añjana%}) of the mountains are referred to in the Atharvaveda,<sup>8</sup> and their mineral treasures in the Rigveda.<sup>9</sup> <F>1) i. 37, 7; v. 56, 4.</F> <F>2) Av. iv. 6, 8; vi. 12, 3; 17, 3; ix. 1, 18; xii. 1, 11.</F> <F>3) i. 39, 5; 52, 2; 155; 1; 191, 9; ii. 12, 2, 3; 17, 5, etc.</F> <F>4) Av. i. 14, 1; iii. 21, 10; iv. 9, 8; viii. 7, 17; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 4, 5, 1; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xvii. 1; xviii. 13, etc.</F> <F>5) Rv. vii. 34, 23; 35, 8; viii. 18, 16; 31, 10; x. 35, 2; 36, 1, etc.; Pischel, {%Vedische Studien,%} i. 80; 2, 66.</F> <F>6) Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxxvi. 9; Mai- trāyaṇī Saṃhitā, i. 10, 13; and Rv. iv. 54, 5, as explained by Pischel, {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 174.</F> <F>7) ii. 13; Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 407; Keith, {%Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka,%} 28, n. 1.</F> <F>8) xix. 44, 6; 45. 7.</F> <F>9) x. 69, 6.</F>

2. {@Parvata@}¦ in one passage of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> denotes, according to Ludwing,<sup>2</sup> a sacrificer whose generosity is praised. But it is probable that the god Parvata, the spirit of the mountain, is meant.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) vii. 87, 8</F> <F>2) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 159.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>

3. {@Parvata@}¦ is mentioned several times in the Aitareya Brāh- maṇa<sup>1</sup> along with {@Nārada.@} The Anukramaṇī (Index) attri- butes to him the authorship of several hymns of the Rigveda.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) vii. 13, 34; viii. 21; Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xv. 17. 4.</F> <F>2) viii. 12, ix, 104; 105.</F>

{@Parvan@}¦ denotes the knots of the reed or the joints of a plant,<sup>1</sup> and more generally a part or limb of the body.<sup>2</sup> It also designates a period of time, probably with reference to the breaks in the month at new and full moon.<sup>3</sup> In one passage<sup>4</sup> Geldner<sup>5</sup> thinks the word indicates a song section of the Sāmaveda. <F>1) Av. xii. 3, 31; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, i, 1, 2, 1; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, vi. 3, 1, 31, and {%cf.%} Rv. x. 68, 9.</F> <F>2) Rv. i. 61, 12; iv. 19, 9; viii. 48, 5; x. 89, 8; Av. i. 11, 1; 12, 2; ii. 9, 1; vi. 14, 1; xi. 8, 12; xii. 5, 71; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 31; Śatapatha Brāh- maṇa, i. 6, 3, 35 {%et seq.;%} iii. 4, 4, 2; vi. 1, 2, 31; x. 4, 5, 2, etc.</F> <F>3) Rv. i. 94, 4; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xiii. 43; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 6, 3, 35; vi. 2, 2, 34, etc. {%Cf.%} {@Māsa.@} In the Sūtras the days of the four-monthly festivals ({%cāturmāsaya%}) are so called: Kātyāyana Srauta Sūtra, v. 2, 13; xxii. 7, 1. 16. 17; xxiv. 4, 30; Śāṅkh- āyana Śrauta Sūtra, xiv. 5, 6; 10, 4. 18; Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra, ix. 2, 3; and more often the periods of the change of moon: Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra. xxiv. 6, 4. 25. 30; Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, iii. 2, 1; 3, 1; Lāṭyāyana Srauta Sūtra, viii. 8, 46, etc.</F> <F>4) vii. 103, 5.</F> <F>5) {%Ṛgveda, Glossar,%} 107. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 364, who quotes Tacitus, {%Germania,%} 11.</F>
{@Parśāna,@}¦ ‘hollow,’ is mentioned several times in the Rigveda (vii. 104, 5; viii. 7, 34; 45, 41).

1. {@Parśu@}¦ denotes ‘rib’ in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> {%Cf.%} {@Śarīra.@} <F>1) ix. 7, 6; x. 9, 20; xi. 3, 12.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vii. 5, 25, 1; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxxi. 1; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, viii. 6, 2, 10; x. 6, 4, 1; xii. 3, 1, 6; Ṣaḍviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, i. 3, etc.</F>

2. {@Parśu@}¦ seems in some passages<sup>1</sup> to denote a ‘sickle,’ being apparently a variant of {@Paraśu.@} <F>1) Av. xii. 3, 31 (Kauśika Sūtra, i. 24. 25; viii. 11; lxi. 38. 39); perhaps vii. 28, 1 = Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 2, 4, 1. See Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 407, 408; Bṛhad- āraṇyaka Upaniṣad, vi. 4, 26 (where {%parśu%} is metrically needed), etc. {%Cf.%} Böhtlingk, Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>

3. {@Parśu@}¦ in the Nirukta<sup>1</sup> is explained in one passage of the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> as meaning the sides of a cistern ({%kūpa%}).<sup>3</sup> But the sense of ‘ribs’ is quite adequate there. <F>1) iv. 6.</F> <F>2) i. 105, 8; x. 33, 2.</F> <F>3) Oldenberg, {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 100; Geldner, {%Rigveda, Glossar,%} 107.</F>

4. {@Parśu@}¦ occurs in one passage in a Dānastuti (‘praise of gifts’) in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as the name of a man. It is not certain that he is identical with {@Tirindira,@} but the Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra<sup>2</sup> mentions Tirindira Pāraśavya as the patron of {@Vatsa@} {@Kāṇva.@} In another passage occurring in the Vṛṣākapi hymn,<sup>3</sup> Parśu Mānavī occurs, apparently as a woman, daughter of Manu, but who is meant it is quite impossible to say. Excepting these two, there are no other occurrences in which the word has with any probability the value of a proper name in the Rigveda. <div n="P"/>Ludwig,<sup>4</sup> however, sees in several other places an allusion to the Parśus. Thus in one passage of the Rigveda<sup>5</sup> he finds a reference to the defeat of {@Kuruśravaṇa@} by the Parśus; in another<sup>6</sup> he finds a reference to the Pṛthus and Parśus — {%i.e.,%} the Parthians and the Persians. He also sees the Parthians in {@Pārthava,@} a name found in one hymn.<sup>7</sup> The same view is taken by Weber,<sup>8</sup> who holds that historical connexions with the [Page1-505+ 38] Persians are referred to. But Zimmer<sup>9</sup> points out that this conclusion is not justified; the Parśus were known to Pāṇini<sup>10</sup> as a warrior tribe; the Pāraśavas were a tribe in south-west {@Madhyadeśa;@} and the {%Periplus%}<sup>11</sup> knows a tribe of Parthoi in north India. At most the only conclusion to be drawn is that the Indians and Iranians were early connected, as was of course the case. Actual historical contact cannot be asserted with any degree of probability. <F>1) viii. 6, 46.</F> <F>2) xvi. 11, 20.</F> <F>3) x. 86, 23. Apparently Vārttika 2, on Pāṇini, iv. 1, 177, where Parśu is explained as a feminine, Princess of the Parśus, refers to this passage. On the sense, {%cf.%} Geldner, {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 42; {%Rigveda, Glossar,%} 107; and Tait- tirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 2, 2, 2, where the expression occurs, but where the sense is very dubious.</F> <F>4) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 196 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>5) x. 33, 2. The sense here is, no doubt, ‘ribs.’ See Geldner, {%op. cit.,%} 2, 184, n. 3; Bergaigne, {%Religion Védique,%} 2, 362, n.</F> <F>6) vii. 83, 1, {%pṛthu-parśavaḥ,%} which really means either ‘with large ribs’ —  {%i.e.,%} ‘strong,’ as Roth, with Sāyaṇa, inclines to take it — or ‘with broad axes,’ according to Zimmer.</F> <F>7) vi. 27, 8.</F> <F>8) {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 379; {%Indian%} {%Literature,%} 4; {%Episches im vedischen%} {%Ritual,%} 36 {%et seq.%} He confines his view to the equation of Parśu in Rigveda, viii. 6, 46, and the Persians. Hille- brandt, who is inclined to see relations with Iran in early times (see {@Paṇi,@} {@Pārāvata, Sṛñjaya@}), does not in this connexion quote Parśu at all, and, though he mentions Pārthava, does not regard it as probably referring to a Parthian ({%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 105). Brunnhofer, in his various works ({%Iran%} {%und Turan,%} 1889; {%vom Pontus bis zum%} {%Indus,%} 1890, etc.), finds constant refer- ences in the Veda to events in Iran, but his theories must be regarded as definitely unscientific. See also Hop- kins, {%Journal of the American Oriental%} {%Society,%} 15, 264, n.</F> <F>9) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 134 {%et seq.;%} 433. {%Ibid.,%} 434, 435, he refutes conclusively Ludwig's extraordinary view that Pṛthu and Parśu are dialectical forms of the same word.</F> <F>10) v. 3, 117.</F> <F>11) c. 38.</F>

{@Parṣa@}¦ occurs in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> denoting in the plural ‘sheaves’ strewn over the threshing floor. {%Cf.%} {@Khala.@} <F>1) x. 48, 7; Nirukta, iii. 10. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 238. Per- haps {%parṣin,%} in the compound {%iṣu-parṣin%} in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 4, 2, 5, means ‘having a bundle (of arrows).’</F>

{@Palada@}¦ occurs twice in one hymn of the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> in the description of a house. It seems to mean bundles of straw or reeds used to thatch the house and render the sides wind and weather proof. <F>1) ix. 3, 5, 17. {%Cf.%} Zimmer. {%Altindisches Leben,%} 153; Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the%} {%Atharvaveda,%} 194, 195.</F>
{@Palasti.@}¦ See {@Palita.@}

{@Palāla@}¦ is found with Anu-palāla in the Atharvaveda (viii. 6, 2) as the name of a demon. The meaning of the word is ‘straw,’ in which sense it occurs in the Kauśika Sūtra (lxxx. 27), while the feminine form, Palālī, is found in the Atharvaveda itself (ii. 8, 3) as the straw of barley ({@Yava@}).

{@Palāva@}¦ is found in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa<sup>2</sup> in the sense of ‘chaff.’ <F>1) xii. 3, 19, where some manuscripts read {%palāvā.%}</F> <F>2) i. 54, 1</F>

{@Palāśa,@}¦ like {@Parṇa,@} denotes ‘leaf’ in the Brāhmaṇas.<sup>1</sup> It also<sup>2</sup> designates the tree {%Butea frondosa,%} of which Parṇa is the early name. <F>1) Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, x. 2; Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, i. 5, 4, 5; v. 2, 1, 17 etc.; Chāndogya Upaniṣad, iv. 14, 3.</F> <F>2) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 1; Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, i. 3, 3, 19; ii. 6, 2, 8, etc. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 59.</F>

{@Palita,@}¦ ‘grey-haired,’ occurs frequently from the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> onwards.<sup>2</sup> It is the distinctive sign of old age. Those who, like certain descendants of {@Jamadagni,@} do not grow old,<sup>3</sup> are said not to become grey-haired, while {@Bharadvāja@} is described as having in his old age become thin and grey-haired.<sup>4</sup> The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>5</sup> in one passage observes that grey hairs appear first on the head, and elsewhere<sup>6</sup> alludes to the hair on the arms having become grey. <F>1) i. 144, 4; 164, 1; iii. 55, 9; x. 4, 5, etc.</F> <F>2) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxx. 15, etc.</F> <F>3) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vii. 1, 9, 1; Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xxi. 10, 6. {%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%Transactions of the Connecticut%} {%Academy of Arts and Sciences,%} 15, 54, and Rv. iii. 53, 16, where {%palasti%} seems to mean {%palita.%}</F> <F>4) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 49.</F> <F>5) xi. 4, 1, 6. 14.</F> <F>6) iii. 8, 2, 25.</F>

{@Palpūlana@}¦ is found in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>2</sup> apparently meaning, properly, ‘lye,’ or water impreg- nated with some biting substance for washing clothes. In the Atharvan passage urine seems to be meant.<sup>3</sup> The verb {%palpū-%} {%laya,%} ‘to wash with alkaline water,’ occurs in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>2</sup> and the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa;<sup>4</sup> and the Sūtras refer to hides ({%carman%})<sup>5</sup> and garments<sup>6</sup> so washed. {%Cf.%} also {@Vāsaḥ-@} {@palpūlī.@} <F>1) xii. 4, 9. {%Cf.%} Kauśika Sūtra, xi. 16.</F> <F>2) ii. 5, 5, 6.</F> <F>3) Whitney, Translation of the Athar- vaveda, 695. {%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Hymns of%} {%the Atharvaveda,%} 74, 175.</F> <F>2) ii. 5, 5, 6.</F> <F>4) i. 3, 5, 2. 3.</F> <F>5) Kauśika Sūtra, 67.</F> <F>6) Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, iii. 8, 12. {%Cf.%} Baudhāyana Dharma Sūtra. i. 6, 13, 15; Böhtlingk, Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>

{@Palli-gupta Lauhitya@}¦ (‘descendant of Lohita’) is mentioned in a Vaṃśa (‘list of teachers’) in the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa (iii. 42, 1) as a pupil of {@Śyāmajayanta Lauhitya.@} [Page1-507+ 37] The name is obviously a late one, for Palli is not found in the early literature, and the name of the Lauhitya family is other- wise known in post-Vedic works only.

{@Pavana@}¦ (‘purifier’) in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> denotes an instrument for purifying grain from husks, etc.; either a ‘sieve’ or a ‘winnowing basket’ may be meant. In the Sūtras<sup>2</sup> it is mentioned as used for cleaning the bones of the dead after cremation. <F>1) iv. 34, 2; xviii. 3, 11. {%Cf.%} Nirukta, vi. 9.</F> <F>2) Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra, iv. 5, 7.</F>

{@Pavamāna@}¦ is a term very frequently applied in the Rigveda to the Soma ‘purifying itself’ by running through the sieve. Later it appears in a few passages<sup>1</sup> in the sense of ‘wind’ (as a purifier). <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vii. 5, 20, 1; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, vi. 17; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, i. 7.</F>
{@Pavasta@}¦ in one passage of the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> apparently denotes ‘covers.’ <F>1) iv. 5, 6. {%Cf.%} Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda. 156.</F>

{@Pavi@}¦ denotes the ‘tire’ of the wheel of a chariot in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> Reference is made<sup>3</sup> to the necessity for fastening it on firmly, and the epithet {%su-pavi,%} ‘having a good tire,’ is found in the Atharvaveda<sup>4</sup> with {%su-nābhi,%} ‘having a good nave,’ and {%su-cakra,%} ‘having a good wheel.’ The tires were, of course, of metal,<sup>5</sup> and being sharp,<sup>6</sup> could serve on occasion as weapons.<sup>7</sup> The St. Petersburg Dictionary in one passage of [Page1-508+ 54] the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā<sup>8</sup> takes Pavi to mean a metal rim on the stone for pounding Soma, but this seems improbable, because no such metal attachment is elsewhere alluded to. Hille- brandt<sup>9</sup> seems clearly right in accepting the sense of ‘sharp edge’ in this passage, especially as the stones in the Rigveda<sup>10</sup> are, in allusion to their rolling action, styled ‘rims without horses and without chariots’ ({%anaśvāsaḥ pavayo 'rathāḥ%}). <div n="P"/>The Nirukta<sup>11</sup> ascribes to Pavi the sense of arrow ({%śalya%}), but this is very uncertain. The St. Petersburg Dictionary cites for this use two passages of the Rigveda,<sup>12</sup> but in one the secondary sense of sharp-edged weapon with reference to the bolt of Indra is quite likely, and in the other, where the expression {%vāṇasya%} {%pavi%} occurs, the sharp-edged pounding-stone of the ‘reed,’<sup>13</sup> meaning the stalk of the Soma plant, may be meant. Hille- brandt<sup>14</sup> thinks a reference to the shape of the Soma plant is intended. Pavī-nasa, the name of a demon mentioned in the Atharvaveda,<sup>15</sup> seems to throw no light on this point, for while the St. Petersburg Dictionary takes it to mean ‘whose nose is like a spearhead,’ it is translated as ‘rim-nosed’ (presumably in allusion to the curved shape of the nose) by Whitney.<sup>16</sup> <F>1) i. 34, 2; 88, 2; 139, 3; 166, 10, etc.; Nirukta, v. 5.</F> <F>2) Sāmaveda, ii. 7, 1, 15, 3, etc.</F> <F>3) Rv. vi. 54, 3.</F> <F>4) Av. iv. 12, 6.</F> <F>5) Of gold in the case of the Aśvins and the Maruts, Rv. i. 64, 11; 180, 1.</F> <F>6) Rv. i. 166, 10.</F> <F>7) Rv. v. 52, 9. {%Cf.%} vi. 8, 5, and x 180, 2.</F> <F>8) vi. 30. {%Cf.%} Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 9, 4, 5. Mahīdhara, on the Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, takes {%pavinā%} as {%vajra-%} {%sadṛśena,%} ‘like a thunderbolt,’ and Eggeling, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 26, 239, 240, renders {%pavi%} by ‘bolt.’</F> <F>9) {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 44.</F> <F>10) v. 31. 5.</F> <F>11) xii. 30.</F> <F>12) ix. 50, 1; x. 180, 2.</F> <F>13) {%Cf.%} Rv. iv. 24, 9, where the ex- pression {%vāṇaṃ duhanti,%} ‘they milk out the reed,’ occurs.</F> <F>14) {%Op. cit.,%} 1, 43, 44.</F> <F>15) viii. 6, 21.</F> <F>16) Translation of the Atharvaveda, 497. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 248; Geldner, {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 12, n. 1.</F>

{@Pavitra@}¦ denotes in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> and later,<sup>2</sup> the sieve used for purifying the Soma, the only mode of purifying it certainly<sup>3</sup> known to the Rigveda. It seems clearly<sup>4</sup> to have been made of [Page1-509+ 53] sheep's wool, whether woven or plaited is not certain, for the expressions used are too vague to be decisive, though Zimmer<sup>5</sup> thinks {%hvarāṃsi%}<sup>6</sup> points to plaiting. <F>1) i. 28, 9; iii. 36, 7; viii. 33, 1; 101, 9, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. vi. 124, 3; ix. 6, 16; xii. 1, 30; 3, 3. 14. 25, etc.</F> <F>3) {%Cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 239, 240.</F> <F>4) {%Cf.%} the names of it: {%aṇva,%} Rv. ix. 16, 2; {%aṇvāni meṣyaḥ,%} 86, 47; 107, 11; {%avayaḥ,%} ii. 36, 1; ix. 86, 11; 91, 2; {%tvac%} with {%avya%} or {%avyaya,%} ix. 69, 3; 70, 7; {%meṣyaḥ,%} ix. 8, 5; {%rūpa avyaya,%} ix. 16, 6; {%roman,%} alone or with {%avyaya; vāra,%} alone or with {%avyaya,%} etc.</F> <F>5) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 278, n.</F> <F>6) ix. 3, 2; 63, 4.</F>

{@Pavīra,@}¦ according to the Nirukta,<sup>1</sup> denotes a ‘lance.’ The epithet derived from this word, {%pavīravant%} or {%pavīrava,%} which is found in the Atharvaveda<sup>2</sup> and the Yajurveda Saṃhitās,<sup>3</sup> is used of the plough, apparently in the sense of ‘having a metal share.’ The same epithet occurs in the Rigveda<sup>4</sup> applied to a man, in the sense of ‘having a goad’ or ‘having a spear.’ <F>1) xii. 30, In Rv. i. 174, 4, {%pavīrava%} seems to mean ‘thunderbolt.’</F> <F>2) iii. 17, 3.</F> <F>3) {%Pavīravant,%} Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xii. 71; {%pavīrava,%} Taittirīya Saṃhitā, 10, 2, 5, 6; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 7, 12; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xvi. 11.</F> <F>4) x. 60, 3. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 116.</F>
{@Pavīru@}¦ appears in a hymn of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as a {@Ruśama,@} being a prince or at least a wealthy noble. <F>1) viii. 51, 9 = Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxxiii. 82.</F>

{@Paśu@}¦ means ‘animal’ generally, including man. There is frequent mention<sup>1</sup> of the five sacrificial animals — the horse, the cow, the sheep, the goat, and man. Seven such domestic animals are spoken of in the Atharvaveda<sup>2</sup> and later;<sup>3</sup> probably, as Whitney<sup>4</sup> observes, merely as a sacred mystic number, not, as the commentator<sup>5</sup> explains, the usual five with the ass and the camel added. Animals are also referred to as {%ubhayadant%} [Page1-510+ 63] and {%anyatodant.%} They are further<sup>6</sup> classified as those which take hold with the hand ({%hastādānāḥ%}), man ({%puruṣa%}), elephant ({%hastin%}), and ape ({%markaṭa%}), and those which grasp by the mouth ({%mukhādānāḥ%}). Another division is that of biped ({%dvipād%}) and quadruped ({%catuṣpād%}).<sup>7</sup> Man is a biped;<sup>8</sup> he is the first ({%pra-%} {%thama%}) of the beasts;<sup>9</sup> he alone of animals lives a hundred years ({%śatāyus%}),<sup>10</sup> and he is king of the animals.<sup>11</sup> He possesses speech ({%vāc%}) in conjunction with the other animals.<sup>12</sup> In the Aitareya Āraṇyaka<sup>13</sup> an elaborate distinction is drawn between vegetables, animals, and man in point of intellect. <div n="P"/>Of animals apart from man a threefold division is offered in the Rigveda<sup>14</sup> — into those of the air ({%vāyavya%}), those of the jungle ({%āraṇya%}), and those of the village ({%grāmya%}), or tame animals. The division into {%āraṇya%} and {%grāmya%} animals is quite common.<sup>15</sup> In the Yajurveda Saṃhitās<sup>16</sup> is found a division into {%eka-śapha,%} ‘whole-hoofed’; {%kṣudra,%} ‘small’; and {%āraṇya,%} ‘wild,’ the two former classes denoting the tame animals.<sup>16</sup> The horse and the ass are {%eka-śapha;%}<sup>17</sup> the {%kṣudra%} are the sheep, the goat, and the ox: this distinction being parallel to that of {%ubhayadant%} and {%anyatodant.%}<sup>18</sup> Zimmer<sup>19</sup> sees in a passage of the Atharvaveda<sup>20</sup> a division of wild animals ({%āraṇya%}) into five classes: (1) those of the jungle described as the ‘dread beasts [Page1-511+ 43] which are in the wood’ ({%mṛgā bhīmā vane hitāḥ%}); (2) winged creatures, represented by the {@Haṃsa,@} ‘gander,’ {@Suparṇa,@} ‘eagle,’ {@Śakuna,@} ‘bird’; (3) amphibia — {@Śiṃśumāra,@} ‘alligator,’ and {@Ajagara,@} ‘crocodile’ (?); (4) ‘fish,’ {@Purīkaya, Jaṣa,@} and {@Matsya;@} (5) insects and worms (described as {%rajasāḥ%}). But this division is more ingenious than probable, and it is ignored by both Bloomfield<sup>21</sup> and Whitney.<sup>22</sup> <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iv. 2, 10, 1-4; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xvi. 17; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 7, 17; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xiii. 47-51, {%Cf.%} Av. xi. 2, 9; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iv. 3, 10, 1-3; v. 5, 1, 1. 2; vi. 5, 10, 1; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xiv. 28-31, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. iii. 10, 6.</F> <F>3) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 8, 4, 16; ix. 3, 1, 20; xii. 8, 3, 13 (where they are called {%jāgatāḥ,%} perhaps as number- ing 12); Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, x. 2, 7.</F> <F>4) Translation of the Atharvaveda, 103.</F> <F>5) On Av. iii. 10, 6. The St. Peters- burg Dictionary suggests ‘mule’ and ‘ass’ as the two making up seven ({%cf.%} Mahābhārata, vi. 165 {%et seq.%}). Zimmer's view ({%Altindisches Leben,%} 76) is that ‘goat,’ ‘sheep,’ ‘ox,’ ‘horse,’ ‘dog,’ ‘ass,’ and ‘camel’ or ‘mule,’ are meant.</F> <F>6) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vi. 4, 5, 7; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iv. 5, 7 (where {%puruṣa%} must be read for {%paruṣa%}).</F> <F>7) Rv. iii. 62, 14; Av. iii. 34, 1, etc. Zimmer, 73, n., suggests that the division is Indo-European, as the Inguvenic tables make a distinction between {%dupursus%} and {%peturpursus.%}</F> <F>8) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iv. 2, 10, 1, 2; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xvii. 47, 48.</F> <F>9) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, vi. 2, 1, 18; vii. 5, 2, 6.</F> <F>10) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 2, 6, 3; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, vii. 2, 5, 17.</F> <F>11) Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xx. 10; Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, iv. 5, 5, 7. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgen-%} {%ländischen Gesellschaft,%} 18, 274.</F> <F>12) Rv. viii. 100, 11.</F> <F>13) ii. 3, 2, with Keith's note.</F> <F>14) x. 90, 8.</F> <F>15) Av. iii. 31, 3. {%Cf.%} ii. 34, 1, with Whitney's note, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 78; xi. 2, 24; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 2, 3; 9, 7; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xiii. 12; Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, iii. 2, 29. 32; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 7, 1, 8; 2, 8. {%Cf.%} xi. 8, 3, 2, where there is reference to animals being tied up at night in their stalls.</F> <F>16) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iv, 3, 10, 2; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xiv. 30.</F> <F>16) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iv. 3, 10, 2; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xiv. 30.</F> <F>17) Zimmer, 74.</F> <F>18) {%Cf.%} Av. v. 31, 3; Taittirīya Saṃ- hitā, ii. 2, 6, 3, with Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 1, 1, 5: v. 1, 1, 3; 2, 6.</F> <F>19) {%Op. cit.,%} 77, 78.</F> <F>20) xi, 2, 24. 25, compared with xii. 1, 40, 51.</F> <F>21) {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 631.</F> <F>22) Translation of the Atharvaveda, 633, 634. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 72. 77.</F>

{@Paśu-pa@}¦ denotes ‘herdsman’ in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> Metaphori- cally the term is applied to Pūṣan.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) i. 114, 9; 144, 6; iv. 6, 4; x. 142, 2.</F> <F>2) vi. 58, 2. {%Cf.%} of Pūṣan and Revatī, Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 1, 2, 12.</F>

1. {@Paṣṭha-vāh@}¦ occurs in the Yajurveda Saṃhitās<sup>1</sup> meaning an ox, four years old, according to the commentators. This qualification is, however, very doubtful, for Paṣṭhauhī, ‘cow,’ a word occurring quite frequently,<sup>2</sup> is in one passage<sup>3</sup> accom- panied by the adjective {%prathama-garbhāḥ,%} ‘having a first calf,’ which disproves the theory of the age adopted by the com- mentators. <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iv. 3, 5, 2; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xiv. 9; xviii. 27; xxi. 17; xxiv. 13. 28. 29. etc.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā vii. 1, 6, 3; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xi. 2; xii. 8; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xviii. 27; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 7, 3, 3; 8. 3, 2; ii. 7, 2, 2, etc.</F> <F>3) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iv. 6, 1, 11.</F>
2. {@Paṣṭha-vāh@}¦ is mentioned as a seer of Sāmans in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) xii. 5, 11. {%Cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 2, 160.</F>

{@Pastya-sad@}¦ (‘sitting in the house’) occurs in one passage of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> where the sense seems to be ‘inmate,’ ‘com- panion.’ <F>1) vi. 51, 9. {%Cf.%} Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.;%} Pischel, {%Vedische%} {%Studien,%} 2, 211.</F>

{@Pastyā@}¦ (fem. pl.) is a word occurring in several passages of the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> Roth<sup>2</sup> ascribes to it the meaning of ‘house’ or ‘dwelling,’ in the wide sense of the term, as well as that of the ‘family’ living in the house; and this view is accepted by Zimmer.<sup>3</sup> On the other hand, Pischel<sup>4</sup> finds in two of the passages<sup>5</sup> usually referred to Pastyā the neuter Pastya, which appears in {@Pastya-sad@} and in {@Pastyā-vant@} (where the length of the second syllable is not primitive), and which is certainly found in the Rigveda<sup>6</sup> in the metaphorical sense of ‘dwelling,’ ascribed to it in the Naighaṇṭuka.<sup>7</sup> In the other passages<sup>8</sup> he thinks the word means ‘rivers’ or ‘waters’; in particular, where Soma in the middle of the Pastyās<sup>9</sup> is spoken of, the sees a reference to {@Kurukṣetra,@} with its several rivers,<sup>10</sup> {@Āpayā,@} {@Dṛṣadvatī,@} and {@Sarasvatī@} ({%cf.%} 2. {@Pastyāvant@}). In some passages<sup>11</sup> he sees in Pastyā the proper name of a stream, just as Sindhu primarily means ‘river,’ then the ‘Indus.’ <F>1) Rv. i. 25, 10; 40, 7; 164, 30; iv, 1, 11; vi, 49, 9; vii. 97, 5; ix, 65, 23; x. 46, 6. See also iv. 55, 3; viii. 27, 5, where Pastyā appears as a goddess.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>3) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 149. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Über den Rājasūya,%} 43, n. 4; 63.</F> <F>4) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 211-22. So Geldner, {%Rigveda, Glossar,%} 107.</F> <F>5) vi. 49. 9; vii. 97, 5, where the sense is ‘householder’ ({%gṛha-stha%} or {%gṛhin,%} as Sāyaṇa renders it).</F> <F>6) x. 96, 10. 11. In x. 96, 10, Roth takes {%pastyoḥ%} to denote the two parts of the Soma press, but Pischel, 2, 211, accepts Sāyaṇa's rendering ‘heaven and earth.’ In the compounds {%tri-%} {%pastya%} of Agni, Rv. viii. 39, 8; {%vāja-%} {%pastya%} of Pūṣan, vi. 58, 2, of Soma, ix. 98, 12; and {%vīra-pastya,%} v. 50, 4, the primitive word may very well be {%pastya,%} not {%pastyā.%}</F> <F>7) iii. 4, misquoted by Sāyaṇa on Rv. i. 151, 2, as applying to {%pastyā,%} whereas it really refers to {%pastya.%}</F> <F>8) Rv. i. 25, 10 = Taittirīya Saṃhitā, i. 8, 16, 1 = Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, i. 6, 2; ii. 6, 12; 7, 16; iv. 4, 6 = Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, x. 27; Rv. i. 40, 7; 164, 30 (used of Agni's home); iv. 1, 11; ix. 65, 23; x. 46, 6; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, i. 8, 12, 1 = Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 6, 8 = Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, x. 7.</F> <F>9) Rv. ix. 65, 23.</F> <F>10) Rv. iii. 23, 4.</F> <F>11) Rv. iv. 55, 3; viii. 27, 5; and in {%pastyāvant%} in ix. 97, 18.</F>

1. {@Pastyā-vant,@}¦ explained in the Pada text as Pastya-vant, occurs in several passages of the Rigveda. In two of them<sup>1</sup> [Page1-513+ 48] a rich householder seems meant, and in the two others reference to a ‘house’ is clear.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) i. 151, 2; ix. 97, 18; but the latter passage is explained by Pischel as referring to {@Pastyā,@} the river, and by Böhtlingk, Dictionary, {%s.v.,%} as ‘kept in the stall.’</F> <F>2) {%Barhis,%} Rv. ii. 11, 16, ‘of the house’; {%kṣayān pastyāvataḥ,%} iv. 54, 5, ‘abodes having (fixed) habitations.’ <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Pischel, {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 212.</F>

2. {@Pastyā-vant@}¦ occurs in one passage of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> in the locative parallel with {@Suṣoma, Śaryaṇāvant,@} and {@Ārjīka.@} It must apparently denote a place, as Pischel<sup>2</sup> argues, probably corresponding to the locality ‘in the middle of the streams’ ({%madhye pastyānām%}), elsewhere<sup>3</sup> referred to as the home of Soma. Pischel<sup>4</sup> suggests that Patiāla is meant, though he does not lay any stress on the similarity of name. In the north of Patiāla there are hills where the Soma might have grown. Roth<sup>5</sup> thought that something connected with the Soma press was meant. <F>1) viii. 7, 29.</F> <F>2) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 209.</F> <F>3) Rv. ix. 65, 23.</F> <F>4) {%Op. cit.,%} 2, 219.</F> <F>5) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} 2. Max Müller, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 32, 260, 398, 399, takes Pastyāvant as a place-name, but thinks that {%pastyā%} denotes ‘hamlet,’ or, as an epithet of Aditi, refers to her as a ‘housewife’ (Rv. iv. 55, 3; viii. 27, 5).</F>

{@Pāṃsu@}¦ in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> denotes ‘dust’ or ‘sand,’ usually in the plural. Among the portents enumerated in the Adbhuta Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> is a rain of dust or sand ({%pāṃsu-%} {%varṣa%}), a phenomenon not rare in India.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) vii. 109, 2; xii. 1, 26.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 6, 10, 2; Nirukta, xii. 19, etc.</F> <F>3) vi. 8 ({%Indische Studien,%} 1, 40). {%Cf.%} Varāhamihira, Bṛhatsaṃhitā, xxii. 6.</F> <F>4) The adjective {%pāṃsura%} is found in Rv. i. 22, 17, with a variant, {%pāṃsula,%} Sāmaveda, i. 3, 1, 3, 9. {%Cf.%} Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iv. 5, 1, 9.</F>

{@Pāka-dūrvā@}¦ is, in a verse of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> included with {@Kiyāmbu@} and {@Vyalkaśā@} among the plants used for growing on the spot where the corpse of the dead man has been consumed with fire.<sup>2</sup> The verse is repeated in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka<sup>3</sup> [Page1-514+ 38] with the variant Kyāmbu. In the Atharvaveda<sup>4</sup> the word is read Śāṇḍadūrvā. Pākadūrvā is probably, as Sāyaṇa-under- stands it, {%paripakva-dūrvā,%} ‘ripe or edible millet.’ Śāṇḍadūrvā is explained by the commentator<sup>5</sup> in various ways, as millet ‘having egg-shaped roots’ ({%i.e., sāṇḍa,%} not {%śāṇḍa%}), or as ‘having long joints,’ with the additional remark that it was called {%bṛhad-%} {%dūrvā,%} ‘large millet.’ In the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, on the other hand, the commentary explains Pākadūrvā as small millet. <F>1) x. 16, 13.</F> <F>2) See Bloomfield, {%American Journal%} {%of Philology,%} 11, 342-350; {%Journal of the%} {%American Oriental Society,%} 15, xxxix.</F> <F>3) vi. 4, 1, 2.</F> <F>4) xviii. 3, 6.</F> <F>5) Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 850. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 70.</F>

{@Pāka-sthāman Kaurayāṇa@}¦ is celebrated as a generous donor  in a hymn of the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> Ludwig<sup>2</sup> suggests, without much reason, that he may have been a king of the {@Anus.@} <F>1) viii. 3, 21. 24.</F> <F>2) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 160.</F>

{@Pākaru@}¦ is mentioned as a disease, together with {@Viṣūcikā@} and {@Arśas,@} ‘hæmorrhoids,’ in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā.<sup>1</sup> Its nature is unknown; the etymology<sup>2</sup> points to the sense of ‘developed sores,’ ‘ulcers.’ <F>1) xii. 97 {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches%} {%Leben,%} 393.</F> <F>2) From {%pāka,%} ‘maturity,’ and {%aru =%} {%arus,%} ‘sore.’</F>

{@Pāṅktra@}¦ is the name of an animal mentioned in the list of victims at the Aśvamedha, or ‘horse-sacrifice,’ in the Yajurveda Saṃhitās.<sup>1</sup> The ‘field-rat’ seems to be meant. <F>1) Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 7; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 26. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 85.</F>
{@Pāñca-janya,@}¦ ‘relating to the five peoples.’ See {@Pañcajanāḥ.@}

{@Pāñcāla@}¦ means a ‘king of the Pañcāla people,’ and is applied to {@Durmukha@} in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> and to {@Śoṇa@} in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> The term is also found in the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa.<sup>3</sup> See also {@Pañcāla.@} <F>1) viii. 23.</F> <F>2) xiii. 5, 4, 7.</F> <F>3) iii. 29, 1. {%Cf.%} Kāṭhaka Anukramaṇī in {%Indische Studien,%} 3 460.</F>

{@Pāñci,@}¦ ‘descendant of Pañcan,’ is the name of a teacher mentioned with disapproval in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) i. 2, 5, 9; ii. 1, 4, 27. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 434.</F>
{@Pāṭava,@}¦ ‘descendant of Paṭu,’ is a patronymic of {@Cākra@} in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (xii. 8, 1, 17; 9, 3, 1).

{@Pāṭā@}¦ is mentioned in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and in the Kauśika Sūtra.<sup>2</sup> It is assumed by the commentator to be identical with the later Pāṭhā, the plant {%Clypea hernandifolia,%} which was much used medicinally, and is still so used at the present day according to Roth.<sup>3</sup> Very possibly the word should be read as Pāṭhā. <F>1) ii. 27, 4.</F> <F>2) xxxvii. 1; xxxviii. 18. {%Cf.%} Ṛgvi- dhāna, iv. 12, 1.</F> <F>3) Quoted in Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 68. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 13, 190; 17, 266; Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 305, n. 1; {%Proceedings of the American%} {%Oriental Society,%} May, 1885, xlii-xliv.</F>

{@Pāṇi-ghna,@}¦ ‘hand-clapper,’ is enumerated among the list of victims at the Puruṣamedha (‘human sacrifice’) in the Yajur- veda.<sup>1</sup> Presumably a man who drives away birds from the fields by making a noise is intended. <F>1) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxx. 20; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 15, 1.</F>
{@Pāṇḍva@}¦ in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (v. 3, 5, 21) denotes an uncoloured woollen garment.

{@Pātalya@}¦ is found in one passage of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> meaning some part of the chariot. What it was is quite uncertain. Hopkins<sup>2</sup> suggests that, as in the Epic, it was possibly a piece of wood on the axle to hold the pole of the car. <F>1) iii. 53, 17.</F> <F>2) {%Journal of the American Oriental%} {%Socicty,%} 13, 242, 243; 20, 224. {%Cf.%} Zim- mer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 251; Geldner, {%Rigveda, Glossar,%} 108.</F>

{@Pātra,@}¦ primarily a ‘drinking vessel’ (from {%pā,%} ‘to drink’) denotes a vessel generally both in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> It was made either of wood<sup>3</sup> or clay.<sup>4</sup> In some passages<sup>5</sup> the word is, according to Roth, used to indicate a measure. The feminine Pātrī occasionally occurs<sup>6</sup> in the sense of ‘vessel.’ <F>1) i. 82, 4; 110, 5; 162, 13 (to hold the broth from the flesh of the horse); 175, 1; ii. 37, 4; vi. 27, 6, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. iv. 17, 4; vi. 142, 1; ix. 6, 17; xii. 3, 25. 36; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 1, 6, 2; vi. 3, 4, 1; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xvi. 62; xix. 86. etc.</F> <F>3) Rv. i. 175, 3.</F> <F>4) Av. iv. 17, 4.</F> <F>5) Av. x. 10, 9; xii. 3, 30; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 4, 1, 5; Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Śūtra, xvi. 1, 7, etc.</F> <F>6) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, viii. 17; Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, i. 1, 2, 8; ii. 5, 3, 6; 6, 2, 7; Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, v. 8, 2. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 271.</F>

{@Pāthya,@}¦ a word occurring only once in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> is either an epithet meaning ‘being in heaven’ ({%pāthas%}), or a patronymic, as Sāyaṇa interprets it, of {@Vṛṣan.@} <F>1) vi. 16, 15. {%Cf.%} Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, vi. 4, 2, 4; Max Müller, {%Sacred Books%} {%of the East,%} 32, 153.</F>

1. {@Pāda@}¦ in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> denotes the ‘foot’ of an animal, a bird, and other creatures. <F>1) xiv. 1, 60.</F> <F>2) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, viii. 5. 12; Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, xii. 8, 3, 6, etc.; Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad, i. 5.</F>

2. {@Pāda,@}¦ as a measure of length, denotes ‘foot’ in the Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> The term is occasionally<sup>2</sup> used to express a measure of weight. As a fraction it means a ‘quarter,’ a sense derived from that of ‘foot’ of a quadruped (just as {%śapha,%} the divided hoof, comes to mean an ‘eighth’). <div n="P"/>^3) Rv. x. 90, 3. 4. <F>1) vi. 5, 3, 2; vii. 2, 1, 7; viii. 7, 2, 17; Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra, vi. 10, etc.</F> <F>2) Nirukta, ii. 7; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, iii. 1, 2.</F>

3. {@Pāda@}¦ is the regular expression for a ‘quarter verse’ in the Brāhmaṇas.<sup>1</sup> This sense is merely a limitation of ‘quarter’ = the ‘foot’ of a quadruped <F>1) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, iv. 4; Kauṣī- aki Brāhmaṇa, xxvi. 5; Nirukta, vii. 9; xi. 6; Lāṭyāyana Srauta Sūtra, i. 2, 1; x. 6, 9, etc.</F>

{@Pāna,@}¦ ‘drink,’ occurs in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> and the Upaniṣads.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) xiii. 4, 2, 17.</F> <F>2) Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, iv. 1, 43; Chāndogya Upaniṣad, viii. 2, 7, etc.</F>

{@Pānta@}¦ occurs several times in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> apparently<sup>2</sup> meaning ‘drink,’ ‘beverage’ ({%cf.%} {@Pāna@}). Geldner,<sup>3</sup> however, thinks that in one passage^4 Pānta is the name of a prince. <F>1) i. 122, 1; 155, 1; viii. 92, 1; ix. 65, 28 (a very doubtful passage); x. 88, 1.</F> <F>2) So Nirukta, vii. 25; Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.;%} Olden- berg, {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 122, 123.</F> <F>3) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 139; {%Rigveda,%} {%Glossar,%} 108.</F>
{@Pān-nejana@}¦ in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> denotes a ‘vessel for washing the feet.’ <F>1) iii. 8, 2, 1; 9, 3, 27; xiii. 5, 2, 1.</F>
{@Pāpa-yakṣma.@}¦ See {@Yakṣma.@}
{@Pāpa-sama,@}¦ a ‘bad season,’ is in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> opposed to Puṇya-sama, a ‘good season.’ <F>1) iii. 3, 8, 4. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Naxatra,%} 2, 342.</F>

{@Pāman@}¦ occurs in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> as the name of a skin disease. The derivative adjective, Pāmana, ‘suffering from skin disease,’ is found in the later Saṃhitās and the Brāhmaṇas.<sup>2</sup> Since it is mentioned as an accompaniment of fever, probably a cutaneous eruption or scab consequent on fever is meant. <F>1) v. 22, 12. {%Cf.%} for the reading, Whitney, Translation of the Atharva- veda, 261. See also Chāndogya Upani- ṣad, iv. 1, 8.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vi. 1, 3, 8; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxiii. 4; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 2, 1, 31. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Grohmann, {%Indische Studien,%} 9, 401 {%et seq.;%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 388; Schrader, {%Prehistoric Antiquities,%} 421, n.; Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the%} {%Atharvaveda,%} 450, 451; {%Atharvaveda,%} 63.</F>
1. {@Pāyu,@}¦ meaning ‘guard,’ ‘protector,’ occurs several times in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) i. 147, 3; ii. 1, 7; iv. 2, 6; 4, 3. 12; vi. 15, 8; viii. 18, 2; 60, 19; x, 100, 9.</F>

2. {@Pāyu@}¦ is found in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as the name of a poet, a Bhāradvāja. In the Bṛhaddevatā<sup>2</sup> he is credited with assisting {@Abhyāvartin Cāyamāna@} and {@Prastoka Sārṅjaya@} by conse- crating their weapons with a hymn.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) vi. 47, 24. {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 128.</F> <F>2) v. 124 {%et seq.,%} with Macdonell's notes.</F> <F>3) vi. 75 (the ‘battle’ hymn).</F>

{@Pāra,@}¦ in accordance with its derivation ({%pṛ,%} ‘bring across’), denotes the ‘farther bank’ of a river or stream, in which sense<sup>1</sup> it occurs in the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> and later.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) It also often has the generalized sense of ‘extreme limit’ or ‘end,’ as in i. 92, 6 ({%tamasas,%} ‘of darkness’); v. 54, 10 ({%adhavanaḥ,%} ‘of a road’).</F> <F>2) i. 121, 13 ({%nāvyānām,%} ‘of streams’); viii. 96, 11 ({%nadīnām%}); i. 167, 2 ({%samud-%} {%rasya%}); x. 155, 3 ({%sindhoḥ%}), etc.</F> <F>3) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vii. 5, 1, 2. 3; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxxiii. 5; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 6, 2, 4 ({%salilasya%}); Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, viii. 21 ({%pāra-kāma,%} ‘desiring the farther bank’), etc.</F>
{@Pāraśavya,@}¦ ‘descendant of Paraśu,’ is the patronymic of {@Tirindira@} in the Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Śūtra (xvi. 11, 20). {%Cf.%} {@Parśu.@}

1. {@Pārāvata@}¦ occurs in the list of victims at the Aśvamedha (‘horse sacrifice’), in the Yajurveda,<sup>1</sup> meaning ‘turtle-dove.’ <F>1) Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 6; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 25.</F>

2. {@Pārāvata@}¦ occurs in several passages of the Rigveda. Roth<sup>1</sup> thinks that in most places<sup>2</sup> it means ‘coming from a distance,’ but in two passages<sup>3</sup> he regards it as the proper name of a people on the {@Yamunā@} (Jumna). It is certain that in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa the Pārāvatas are a people on that river ({%cf.%} {@Turaśravas@}). Hillebrandt<sup>4</sup> sees in all the passages<sup>5</sup> the name of a people, comparing the <lang n="greek">Παρυῆται</lang> of [Page1-519+ 52] Ptolemy,<sup>6</sup> who apparently were settled on the northern border of Gedrosia, or the <lang n="greek">Παροῦται</lang>, who were found in <lang n="greek">Αρεία</lang><sup>7</sup> He suggests that they were originally ‘mountaineers’ ({%Cf.%} {@Parvata@}). Ludwig<sup>8</sup> holds a similar view, and Geldner<sup>9</sup> recognizes a people as meant. The mention of the {@Sarasvatī@} in connexion with the Pārāvatas<sup>2</sup> in the Rigveda accords generally with their position on the Yamunā in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F> <F>2) Rv. v. 52, 11; viii. 100, 6; Av. xx. 135, 14; {%pārāvata-ghnī%} of the Sarasvatī, Rv. vi. 61, 2.</F> <F>3) Rv. viii. 34, 18; Pañcaviṃśa Brāh- maṇa, ix. 4, 11. {%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%Transac-%} {%tions of the Connecticut Academy of Arts%} {%and Sciences,%} 15, 53.</F> <F>4) {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 97 {%et seq.;%} 3, 310, following Brunnhofer, {%Iran und%} {%Turan,%} 99.</F> <F>5) See notes 2 and 3.</F> <F>6) vi. 20, 3. It is suggested by Hille- brandt that the <lang n="greek">Ἀπαρύται</lang> of Herodotus, iii. 91, may be the same.</F> <F>7) Ptolemy, vi. 17.</F> <F>8) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 162. 197.</F> <F>9) {%Rigveda, Glossar,%} 109. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%Journal of the American%} {%Oriental Society,%} 17, 91; Max Mūller, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 32, 316.</F> <F>2) Rv. v. 52, 11; viii. 100, 6; Av. xx. 135, 14; {%pārāvata-ghnī%} of the Sarasvatī, Rv. vi. 61, 2.</F> <F>3) Rv. viii. 34, 18; Pañcaviṃśa Brāh- maṇa, ix. 4, 11. {%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%Transac-%} {%tions of the Connecticut Academy of Arts%} {%and Sciences,%} 15, 53.</F>
{@Pārāśarī-kauṇḍinī-putra@}¦ is mentioned in the last Vaṃśa (list of teachers) of the Bṛhādāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (vi. 4, 30), in the Mādhyaṃdina recension, as a pupil of {@Gārgīputra.@}

{@Pārāśarī-putra,@}¦ ‘son of a female descendant of {@Parāśara,@}’ is mentioned in the last Vaṃśa (list of teachers) in the Bṛhad- āraṇyaka Upaniṣad as a pupil of {@Kātyāyanīputra,@}<sup>1</sup> of {@Aupasva-@} {@tīputra,@}<sup>1</sup> of {@Vātsīputra,@}<sup>2</sup> of {@Vārkāruṇīputra,@}<sup>3</sup> and of {@Gārgī-@} {@putra.@}<sup>4</sup> Different men are no doubt meant. <F>1) vi. 5, 1, Kāṇva.</F> <F>1) vi. 5, 1, Kāṇva.</F> <F>2) vi. 5, 2, Kāṇva.</F> <F>3) vi. 4, 31, Mādhyaṃdina.</F> <F>4) vi. 4, 30, Mādhyaṃdina.</F>

{@Pārāśarya,@}¦ ‘descendant of {@Parāśara,@}’ is mentioned in the first two Vaṃśas (lists of teachers) of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad as a pupil of {@Jātūkarṇya@}<sup>1</sup> or of {@Bhāradvāja.@}<sup>2</sup> A Pārāśarya is also mentioned as a pupil of {@Baijavāpāyana,@}<sup>3</sup> and {@Vyāsa Pārāśarya@} is the pupil of {@Viṣvaksena@} according to the Vaṃśa at the end of the Sāmavidhāna Brāhmaṇa.<sup>4</sup> See also {@Aṣāḍha, Jayanta, Vipaścit, Sudatta.@} <F>1) ii. 6, 3; iv. 6, 3, Kāṇva; ii. 5, 21; iv. 5, 27, Mādhyaṃdina.</F> <F>2) ii. 5, 20; iv. 5, 26, Mādhyaṃdina; ii. 6, 2; iv. 6, 2, 3. Kāṇva.</F> <F>3) ii. 6, 2, Kāṇva. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, i. 9, 2.</F> <F>4) Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa, iii. 41. 1.</F>

{@Pārāśaryāyaṇa@}¦ is mentioned in the first two Vaṃśas (lists of teachers) in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad<sup>1</sup> as a pupil of Pārāśarya. <F>1) ii. 5, 21; iv. 5, 27 (Mādhyaṃdina = ii. 6, 3; iv. 6, 3, Kāṇva).</F>
{@Pārikuṭa@}¦ is an obscure word — probably corrupt — occurring in a verse cited in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (viii. 22, 7), and apparently meaning ‘attendant.’

{@Pārikṣita,@}¦ ‘descendant of {@Parikṣit,@}’ is the patronymic of {@Janamejaya@} in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> and the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> The Pārikṣitīya appear in the Śatapatha Brāh- maṇa<sup>3</sup> and the Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra<sup>4</sup> as performers of the horse sacrifice. In a Gāthā there cited they are called Pāri- kṣitas. Apparently they were the brothers of Janamejaya, named {@Ugrasena, Bhīmasena,@} and {@Śrutasena.@} In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad<sup>5</sup> the question whither they have gone is made the subject of a philosophical discussion. It is clear that the family had passed away before the time of the Upaniṣad, and it is also clear that there had been some serious scandal mingled with their greatness which they had, in the opinion of the Brahmins, atoned for by their horse sacrifice with its boundless gifts to the priests. Weber<sup>6</sup> sees in this the germ of the Epic stories which are recorded in the Mahābhārata. <div n="P"/>The verses relating to Parikṣit in the Atharvaveda<sup>7</sup> are called Pārikṣityaḥ in the Brāhmaṇas.<sup>8</sup> <F>1) vii. 27 and 34; viii. 11.</F> <F>2) xiii. 5, 4, 1. {%Cf.%} Gopatha Brāh- maṇa, i. 2, 6; ii. 6, 12.</F> <F>3) xiii. 5, 4, 3.</F> <F>4) xvi. 9. 7.</F> <F>5) iii. 3, 1.</F> <F>6) {%Indian Literature,%} 125, 126; 135, 136. The later legend of the Pārikṣitas and Vāmadeva's mares is dealt with by Weber in {%Vedische Beiträge%} (1894).</F> <F>7) xx. 127, 7-10; Śāṅkhāyana Srauta Sūtra, xii. 17; Scheftelowitz, {%Die%} {%Apokryphen des Ṛgveda,%} 156, 157.</F> <F>8) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vi. 32, 10; Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, xxx. 5; Gopatha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 6, 12; Weber, {%op. cit.,%} 136, n. 144.</F>

{@Pāri-plava,@}¦ ‘cyclic,’ is a term applied to the {@Ākhyāna,@} or ‘tale,’ which is to be recited at the Aśvamedha (‘horse [Page1-521+ 35] sacrifice’), and to be repeated at intervals throughout the year. It is mentioned in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> and in the Sūtras.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) xiii. 4, 3, 2. 15.</F> <F>2) Āśvalāyana Srauta Sūtra, x. 6; Śāṅkhāyana Srauta Sūtra, xvi. 1, 26; 2, 36; Lāṭyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, ix. 9, 11.</F>

{@Pārī-ṇahya@}¦ denotes household utensils' in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā,<sup>1</sup> where it is said that the wife ({%patnī%}), as mistress of the house, has charge of all these.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) vi. 2, 1, 1.</F> <F>2) The word occurs {@later@} in the variant form of {%pāri-ṇāhya%} in Manu, ix. 11.</F>

{@Pārūṣṇa,@}¦ occurring in the list of victims at the Aśvamedha (‘horse sacrifice’) in the Yajurveda Saṃhitās,<sup>1</sup> appears to mean some kind of bird. <F>1) Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 4; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 24.</F>
{@Pārovarya-vid@}¦ in the Nirukta (xiii. 12) denotes ‘knowers of tradition.’

{@Pārṇa-valki,@}¦ ‘descendant of Parṇavalka,’ is the patronymic of {@Nigada@} in the Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 372; Max Müller, {%Ancient Sanskrit Literature,%} 443.</F>

{@Pārthava,@}¦ ‘descendant of {@Pṛthu,@}’ occurs once in the Rig- veda,<sup>1</sup> where the Pārthavas are mentioned as generous donors. The passage is somewhat obscure, as there is a reference<sup>2</sup> to a defeat of the {@Turvaśas@} and the {@Vṛcīvants@} by {@Sṛñjaya Daiva-@} {@vāta,@} followed in the next verse by the praise of the bounty to the singer of {@Abhyāvartin Cāyamāna,@} who was clearly a {@Pārthava,@} and who, in the earlier part of the hymn, has been referred to as victorious over {@Varaśikha.@} It is uncertain whether, as Zimmer<sup>3</sup> suggests, the two princes, Abhyāvartin [Page1-522+ 34] Cāyamāna and Sṛñjaya Daivavāta, are identical or not.<sup>4</sup> That Pārthava has any direct connexion with the Parthians, as held by Brunnhofer, is most improbable.<sup>5</sup> {%Cf.%} {@Parśu.@} <F>1) vi. 27, 8.</F> <F>2) vi. 27, 7.</F> <F>3) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 133, 134.</F> <F>4) {%Cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 105.</F> <F>5) {%Cf.%} Ludwing, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 196 {%et seq.%} Herodotos, iii. 93, mentions the <lang n="greek">Πάρθοι</lang>.</F>

{@Pārtha-śravasa,@}¦ ‘descendant of Pṛthu-śravas,’ is found as the name of a demon in the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) iv. 26, 15. This form of the name is supported by its occurrence in the Kauśika Sūtra, ix. 10; xvii. 27. But Pārthu-is also possible.</F>

{@Pārthya,@}¦ ‘descendant of Pṛthi,’ is the patronymic of some donor in a hymn of the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> The form of the name in the Aśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra<sup>2</sup> is Pārtha. <F>1) x. 93. 15.</F> <F>2) xii. 10. {%Cf.%} the Anukramaṇī on Rv. x. 93.</F>
{@Pārvati,@}¦ ‘descendant of Parvata,’ is the patronymic of {@Dakṣa@} in the Śatapatha (ii. 4, 4, 6) and the Kauṣītaki (iv. 4) Brāhmaṇas.

{@Pārṣada,@}¦ which first appears in the Nirukta,<sup>1</sup> denotes a text- book recognized by a school of grammarians. <F>1) i. 17. {%Cf.%} Max Müller, {%Ancient Sanskrit Literature,%} 128 {%et seq.;%} Weber, {%Studien,%} 3, 269; 4, 217.</F>
{@Pārṣad-vāṇa,@}¦ ‘descendant of Pṛṣadvāṇa,’ is mentioned as a wonder-worker in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) viii. 51, 2. {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 139.</F>
{@Pārṣṇa Śailana@}¦ is mentioned as a teacher in the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa (ii. 4, 8).

{@Pālāgala@}¦ occurs in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> apparently in the sense of ‘messenger,’ or ‘bearer of false news.’ <F>1) v. 3, 1, 11. Eggeling; {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 26, 64, renders it ‘courier.’</F>
{@Pālāgalī@}¦ is the name of the fourth and least respected wife of the king.<sup>1</sup> See {@Pati.@} <F>1) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 4, 1, 8; 5, 2, 8, etc.</F>

{@Pāvamānī@}¦ means the verses ({%ṛcas%}) in the ninth Maṇḍala of the Rigveda ‘relating to Soma Pavamāna’ (‘purifying itself’). The name is found in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and later,<sup>2</sup> possibly even in one hymn of the Rigveda itself.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) xix. 71, 1.</F> <F>2) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, i. 20; ii. 37; Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, xv. 1; Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, xii. 8, 1, 10; Nirukta, xi. 2; xii. 31; Aitareya Āraṇyaka, ii. 2, 2, etc.; Maitrāyaṇī Gṛhya Sūtra, ii. 14.</F> <F>3) ix. 67, 31. 32; Geldner, {%Vedische%} {%Studien,%} 3, 99. n. 3.</F>

{@Pāśa@}¦ denotes in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> a ‘rope’ used for fastening or tying up. Rope and knot ({%granthi%}) are mentioned together in the Atharvaveda.<sup>3</sup> Pāśa is in the Śatapatha Brāh- maṇa<sup>4</sup> used of the rope by which Manu's ship was fastened to the mountain. It is often employed metaphorically of the ‘fetter’ of Varuṇa.<sup>5</sup> <F>1) i. 24, 13. 15; ii. 27, 16; 29, 5. etc.</F> <F>2) Av. ii. 12, 2; ix. 3, 2; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, vi. 8. 45, etc.</F> <F>3) ix. 3, 2.</F> <F>4) i. 8, 1, 5.</F> <F>5) Rv. vi. 74, 4; vii. 88, 7; x. 85, 24; Av. iv. 16, 6; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 2, 5, 1, etc.</F>

{@Pāśin,@}¦ ‘having a noose,’ denotes a ‘hunter’ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and in the Atharvaveda.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) iii. 45, 1; ix. 73, 4. So of Nirṛti in Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, iv. 10.</F> <F>2) xvii. 1, 8.</F>

{@Pāśa-dyumna Vāyata@}¦ is the name of a king to whom the {@Vasiṣṭhas@} claim to have been preferred by Indra in one hymn of the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> Apparently he was, as Sāyaṇa says, son of Vayat, who may be compared with the {@Vyat of another@} passage of the Rigveda.<sup>2</sup> Ludwig<sup>3</sup> sees in him a priest of the {@Pṛthus@} and {@Parśus,@} but this is most improbable.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) vii. 33. 2.</F> <F>2) i. 122, 4.</F> <F>3) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 173.</F> <F>4) Geldner, {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 130, 139.</F>

{@Pāṣya@}¦ occurs in one passage of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> with reference to the defeat of Vṛtra, and apparently denotes ‘stone bulwarks.’ [Page1-524+ 40] In another passage<sup>2</sup> the word may mean the stones used for pressing Soma. <F>1) i. 56, 6.</F> <F>2) ix. 102, 2. {%Cf.%} Macdone, {%Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society,%} 1893, 457, 458.</F>

{@Pika,@}¦ the Indian ‘cuckoo,’ is mentioned in the list of victims at the Aśvamedha (‘horse sacrifice’) in the Yajurveda Saṃ- hitās.<sup>1</sup> {%Cf.%} {@Anyavāpa, Koka.@} <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 15, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 20; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 39. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 92.</F>

{@Piṅgā@}¦ is found in one passage of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> where it is explained by the St. Petersburg Dictionary with Sāyaṇa as ‘bowstring,’ but where Hillebrandt<sup>2</sup> thinks that a musical instrument of some kind is meant. <F>1) viii. 69, 9.</F> <F>2) {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 144, n.</F>

{@Pijavana@}¦ is the name of the father of {@Sudās@} according to the Nirukta.<sup>1</sup> Probably this statement is based on a mere con- jecture from the epithet Paijavana used of Sudās in a verse of the Rigveda,<sup>2</sup> but may very well be correct. <F>1) ii. 24.</F> <F>2) vii. 18, 19. So Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, viii. 21.</F>

{@Piñjūla@}¦ denotes a ‘bundle’ of grass or stalks, especially of {@Darbha.@} The word is only found in the Brāhmaṇa style.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxiii. 1; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, i. 3; Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, xviii. 8. It appears in the form of {%piñjula%} in Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iv. 8, 7; Pāraskara Gṛhya Sūtra, i. 15; of Puñ- jīla in Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vi. 1, 1, 7; 2, 4, 3; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 7, 6, 4; ii. 7, 9, 5.</F>
{@Piṭhīnas@}¦ is the name of a man, a friend of Indra, in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) vi. 26, 6. {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 156.</F>

{@Piṇḍa,@}¦ denoting specifically a ball of flour offered to the Manes, especially on the evening of new moon, occurs in the Nirukta,<sup>1</sup> and repeatedly in the Sūtras.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) iii. 4.</F> <F>2) Lāṭyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, ii. 10, 4, etc.</F>
{@Pitā-putra,@}¦ ‘father and son,’ is a compound of rare occur- rence.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Av. vi. 112, 2; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 2, 4, 4.</F>

{@Pitā-putrīya@}¦ (‘relating to father and son’), used with Sam- pradāna (‘handing over’) means the ceremony by which a father, when about to die, {{bequeathes->bequeaths||20210704|Dr. Sampada Savardekar|https://github.com/sanskrit-lexicon/csl-corrections/issues/67|}} his bodily and mental powers to his son. It is described in the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) ii. 15. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 408.</F>

{@Pitā-maha,@}¦ beside {@Tatāmaha,@} denotes from the Atharvaveda onwards<sup>1</sup> the ‘paternal grandfather,’ {{apparmtly->apparently||20210704|Dr. Sampada Savardekar|https://github.com/sanskrit-lexicon/csl-corrections/issues/67|}} as a ‘father in a higher sense.’<sup>2</sup> The great-grandfather is {@Prapitāmaha@} and {@Pratatāmaha.@}<sup>3</sup> It is significant that there are no corrésponding Vedic words for maternal grandparents, and that the words used in the latter language, such as Mātāmaha, are imitations of the terms for paternal relations. <div n="P"/>In one passage of the Rigveda<sup>4</sup> Delbrück<sup>5</sup> suggests that {%mahe pitre%} means ‘grandfather,’ a sense which would well suit the {%napātam,%} ‘grandson,’ following, but the sense of the whole passage is uncertain.<sup>6</sup> <div n="P"/>We learn very little from the texts of the position of grand- parents. No doubt they were entitled to marks of respect similar to those shown to parents,<sup>7</sup> as the epic expressly testifies.
