{@Saumāyana,@}¦ ‘descendant of Soma,’ is the patronymic of {@Budha@} in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa (xxiv. 18, 6).

{@Saumya@}¦ is a term of affectionate address (‘my dear’) in the Upaniṣads.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, iii. 1, 3; 2, 13 ({%varia lectia, somya%}); Chāndogya Upaniṣad, iv. 4, 4 {%et seq.%}</F>
{@Sau-yavasi,@}¦ ‘descendant of Suyavasa,’ is the patronymic of {@Ajīgarta.@}<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Aitareya Bṛāhmaṇa, vii. 15, 6; Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xv. 19, 29.</F>

{@Saurī@}¦ is given by Zimmer<sup>1</sup> as the name of an unknown animal at the Aśvamedha (‘horse sacrifice’) in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā.<sup>2</sup> But this is an error: {%saurī%} means ‘dedicated to the sun.’ <F>1) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 99.</F> <F>2) v. 5, 16, 1 = Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 33 = Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 14.</F>
{@Sau-varcanasa@}¦ is the patronymic of {@Saṃśravas@} in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (i. 7, 2, 1).

{@Sau-śravasa,@}¦ ‘descendant of {@Suśravas,@}’ is the patronymic of {@Upagu@} in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> and the {@Kaṇva@} Sauśravasas are mentioned in the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) xiv. 6, 8.</F> <F>2) xiii. 12 ({%Indische Studien,%} 3, 474).</F>

{@Sau-śromateya,@}¦ ‘descendant of Suśromatā,’ is the metro- nymic of {@Aṣāḍhi@} in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> {%Cf.%} {@Āṣādhi.@} <F>1) vi. 2, 1, 37. {%Cf.%} Eggeling, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 41, 171, n. 1.</F>
{@Sau-ṣadmana,@}¦ ‘descendant of Suṣadman,’ is the patronymic of {@Viśvantara@} in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (vii. 27, 1; 34, 7).

{@{{Skandhhyā->Skandhyā||20160113|Dr. Dhaval Patel|https://github.com/sanskrit-lexicon/CORRECTIONS/issues/189|Dh}},@}¦ fem. plur., is used in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> of a disease ‘of the shoulders,’ probably tumours of some kind. <F>1) vi. 25, 3. {%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 472, 473.</F>
{@Stanayitnu,@}¦ sing. and plur., denotes ‘thunder’ from the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> onwards.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) v. 83, 6.</F> <F>2) Av. i. 13, 1; iv. 15, 11; vii. 11, 1, etc.</F>

{@Stamba@}¦ in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> denotes a ‘tuft of grass,’ or more generally a ‘bunch’ or ‘cluster.’ <F>1) viii. 6, 14.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 6, 4, 1 (of {@Darbha@}); Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 7, 17, 3; iii. 2, 2, 4; 3, 3, 4; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, v. 23, 9, etc.</F>

{@Stambha,@}¦ ‘pillar,’ is found in the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā,<sup>1</sup> and often in the Sūtras. Earlier Skambha<sup>2</sup> is used, but only metaphorically. <F>1) xxx. 9; xxxi. 1.</F> <F>2) Rv. i. 34, 2; iv. 13, 5, etc.</F>
{@Starī@}¦ denotes a ‘barren cow’ in the Rigveda (i. 101, 3; 116, 22; 117, 20, etc.).
{@Sti.@}¦ See {@Upasti.@}
{@Sti-pā.@}¦ See {@Upasti.@}

{@Stukā@}¦ denotes a ‘tuft’ of hair or wool in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) ix. 97, 17.</F> <F>2) Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxv. 6; Av. vii. 74, 2; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 2, 1, 13, etc.</F>
{@Stuti@}¦ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> denotes a ‘song of praise.’ <F>1) i. 84, 2; vi. 34, 1; x. 31, 5.</F> <F>2) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, vii. 5, 2, 39</F>
{@Stupa@}¦ means ‘tuft of hair’ in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā (ii. 2; xxv. 2) and the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (i. 3, 3, 5; iii. 5, 3, 4). See {@Stukā.@}

{@Stūpa@}¦ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> denotes the ‘top-knot’ of hair as designating the upper part of the head. <F>1) vii. 2, 1. {%Cf.%} i. 24, 7.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 3, 6, 5; Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 4, 4.</F>

{@Stṛ@}¦ (used in the instrumental plural only) denotes the ‘stars’ of heaven.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) i. 68, 5; 166, 11; ii. 2, 5; 34, 2; iv. 7, 3; vi. 49, 3. 12. In i. 87, 1, it seems to denote a ‘star-like spot’ on the forehead of a cow or bull, but this is uncertain. {%Cf.%} Grassmann, {%Wörter-%} {%buch, s.v.;%} above, 1, 233.</F>

{@Stega@}¦ in the Yajurveda Saṃhitās<sup>1</sup> seems to denote a species of ‘worm.’ The word occurs in the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> also, where its sense is unknown, but may possibly be ‘ploughshare.’<sup>3</sup> <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 7, 11, 1; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxv. 1.</F> <F>2) x. 31, 9 = Av. xviii. 1, 39. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 98.</F> <F>3) Weber, Proceedings of the Berlin Academy, 1895, 833. {%Cf.%} Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 824.</F>

{@Stena@}¦ is a common word for ‘thief’ from the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> onwards.<sup>2</sup> See {@Taskara.@} <F>1) ii. 23, 16; 28, 10; 42, 3, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. iv. 3, 4, 5; 36, 7; xix. 47, 6; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, v. 30, 11, etc. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 178 {%et seq.%}</F>

{@Steya@}¦ denotes ‘theft’ in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> {%Cf.%} {@Dharma.@} <F>1) xi. 8, 20; xiv. 1, 57.</F> <F>2) Nirukta, vi. 27; Kauṣītaki Upani- ṣad, iii. 1. {%Cf. steya-kṛt,%} ‘thief,’ in Rv. vii. 104, 10.</F>

{@Stotṛ@}¦ denotes ‘praiser’ or ‘panegyrist’ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> The word often<sup>3</sup> occurs in connexion with patrons, the {@Maghavan@} or {@Sūri.@} <F>1) i. 11, 3; 38, 4; iii. 18, 5; vi. 34, 3, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. vi. 2, 1; xix. 48, 4.</F> <F>3) Rv. i. 124, 10; ii. 1, 16; v. 64, 1; vii. 7, 7; Nirukta, vii. 2.</F>

{@Stotra@}¦ denotes the ‘song’ of the Udgātṛ and his assistant priests (see {@Ṛtvij@}), just as {@Śastra@} denotes the ‘recitation’ of the {@Hotṛ@} and his assistants. The word has this technical sense quite frequently in the later Saṃhitās and the Brāhmaṇas.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 1, 2, 4; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxix. 2; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 37, 4; iii. 46, 8; iv. 12, 6; Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, xvii. 7; Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, iv. 1, 1, 7; viii. 1, 3, 4, etc. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 10, 353, and Caland and Henry, {%L'Agniṣṭoma,%} where the Stotras for that sacrifice are given at length.</F>

{@Stoma@}¦ denotes ‘song of praise’ in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> Later<sup>2</sup> the term has the technical sense of the typical forms in which the {@Stotras@} are chanted. <F>1) i. 114, 9; iii. 5, 2; 58, 1, etc.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 1, 2, 4; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, ix. 33; x. 10, etc. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 9, 229, 276; 10, 355; Hillebrandt, Ritual- litteratur, 101.</F>

{@Strī@}¦ is the ordinary word in poetry and prose for ‘woman,’ without special reference to her as a wife or as a maiden. {@Nārī@} has the same sense, but disappears in later prose, while {@Gnā@} refers only to the wives of the gods, and {@Yoṣit,@} with its cognate words, denotes the young woman as ripe for marriage.<sup>1</sup> In the Rigveda<sup>2</sup> Strī stands opposed to {@Pumāṃs,@} ‘man,’ and once to {%vṛṣan,%} ‘male person’; not until the Atharvaveda<sup>3</sup> does it mean ‘wife’ as opposed to {@Pati,@} ‘husband,’ and even in the Sūtras it is sharply opposed to {@Jāyā.@} <div n="P"/>In Vedic India by far the greater part of a woman's life was taken up in her marriage and marital relations (see Pati and {@Mātṛ@}). There is no trace in the Rigveda of the seclusion of women, which was practically complete in all but the earliest Epic:<sup>4</sup> the maiden may be assumed to have grown up in her father's house, enjoying free intercourse with the youth of the village, and sharing in the work of the house. Educa- tion<sup>5</sup> was not denied to them, at any rate in certain cases, for we hear in the Upaniṣads of women who could take no unimportant part in disputations on philosophical topics. Moreover, women were taught to dance and sing, which were unmanly accomplishments.<sup>6</sup> <div n="P"/>Of the exact legal position of daughters the notices are few and meagre. The Rigveda,<sup>7</sup> however, shows that in the place [Page2-486+ 60] of a father the brother was looked to for aid, and that brother- less maidens were apt to be ruined, though religious terrors were believed to await the man who took advantage of their defencelessness.<sup>8</sup> Moreover, women could not take an inherit- ance,<sup>9</sup> and were not independent persons in the eyes of the law, whether married or not. Presumably before marriage they lived on their parents or brothers, and after that on their husbands, while in the event of their husbands predeceasing them, their relatives took the property, burdened with the necessity of maintaining the wife.<sup>10</sup> Their earnings would be appropriated by their nearest relative — usually father or brother -in the few cases in which unmarried women could earn anything, as in the case of courtezans. <F>1) {%Cf.%} Delbrück, {%Die indogermanischen%} {%Verwandtsehaftsnamen,%} 417.</F> <F>2) Rv. i. 164, 16; v. 61, 8, etc. So also often later — {%e.g.,%} Maitrāyaṇī Saṃ- hitā, iv. 7, 4; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vi. 5, 8, 2.</F> <F>3) xii. 2, 39. {%Cf.%} Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 22, 1.</F> <F>4) Hopkins, {%Journal of the American%} {%Oriental Society,%} 13, 349, 350.</F> <F>5) {%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%op. cit.,%} 351, 352. See {@Gārgī Vācaknavī@} and others enumerated in the Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra, iii. 4, 4; Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 10, 118, 119.</F> <F>6) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vi. 1, 6, 5, Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 7, 3; Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 2, 4, 3-6.</F> <F>7) i. 124, 7. {%Cf.%} Av. i. 14, 2; 17, 1; Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 328; Hopkins, {%op. cit.,%} 341, and see {@Syāla,@} {@Putrikā.@}</F> <F>8) Rv. iv. 5, 5.</F> <F>9) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vi. 5, 8, 2; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iv. 6, 4; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iv. 4, 2, 13; Nirukta, iii. 4.</F> <F>10) {%Cf.%} the Attic <lang n="greek">ἐπίκληρος</lang>, Keith, {%Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society,%} 1912, 427.</F>

{@Stha-pati@}¦ is the name of a royal official mentioned in the Atharvaveda,<sup>1</sup> and often later.<sup>2</sup> {@Revottaras Cākra@} was the Sthapati of the exiled {@Duṣṭarītu Pauṃsāyana,@} a king of the {@Sṛñjayas,@} and succeeded in restoring him to his royal dignity.<sup>3</sup> The exact sense of the term is not certain: ‘governor’<sup>4</sup> is possible, but perhaps ‘chief judge’<sup>5</sup> is more likely; as in the case of the early English judges, his functions may have been both executive and judicial. He is inferior in position to the king's brother.<sup>6</sup> <F>1) ii. 32, 4; v. 23, 11 (of the chief of the worms in both cases).</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iv. 5, 2, 2; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xvii. 12; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 9, 3; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xvi. 19; Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xvii. 11, 6. 7; xxiv. 18, 2; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, v. 4, 4, 17, etc.</F> <F>3) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xii. 8, 1, 17; 9, 3, 1 {%et seq.%} Sthapati here is part, as it were, of the name of the man.</F> <F>4) In the Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, i. 1, 12; Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra, ix. 14, 12, is found Niṣāda-sthapati; perhaps ‘governor of {@Niṣādas.@}’ But it may also mean ({%cf.%} Weber, {%Indische%} {%Studien,%} 1, 207, n.) a Niṣāda as a Sthapati; thus, little can be deduced from this passage in particular. Eggel- ing, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 41, 111, renders it ‘governor.’ {%Cf.%} also St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.,%} and {@Aupo-@} {@diti.@}</F> <F>5) Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 10, 13, n. 3; 13, 203; 17, 200; 18, 260; {%Über%} {%den Rājasūya,%} 15, n. 6; {%Über den Vājapeya,%} 9, 10. {%Cf.%} Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, xxii. 5, 28; 11, 11; Lāṭyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, viii. 7, 11; Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra, xxii. 7, 6.</F> <F>6) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, v. 4, 4, 17.</F>

{@Sthavira,@}¦ literally ‘elder,’ is used as a sort of epithet of several men; Sthavira {@Śākalya@} occurs in the Aitareya Āraṇ- yaka<sup>1</sup> and the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka,<sup>2</sup> and Sthavira {@Jātūkarṇya@} in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa.<sup>3</sup> {%Cf.%} the names {@Hrasva@} and {@Dīrgha.@} <F>1) iii. 2, 1. 6.</F> <F>2) vii. 16; viii. 1. 11.</F> <F>3) xxvi. 5.</F>

{@Sthāgara@}¦ in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> is applied to an ornament ({%alaṃkāra%}) meaning ‘made of the fragrant substance Sthagara,’ which elsewhere<sup>2</sup> appears as Sthakara. <F>1) ii. 3, 10, 2; Apastamba Śrauta Sūtra, xiv. 15, 2.</F> <F>2) See Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 13, 198; Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Athar-%} {%vaveda,%} 311, n. 2; Muir, {%Sanskrit Texts,%} 5, 265.</F>
{@Sthāṇu@}¦ in the {@Rigveda@}<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> denotes a ‘stump’ or ‘post’ of wood. <F>1) x. 40, 13.</F> <F>2) Av. x. 4, 1; xiv. 2, 48; xix. 49, 10, etc.</F>
{@Sthātṛ@}¦ (‘he who stands’) in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> denotes the ‘driver’ of horses or a car. <F>1) i. 33, 5; 181, 3; iii. 45, 2, etc.</F>
{@Sthā-patya@}¦ denotes in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa (xvii. 11, 6. 7) the ‘rank or status of a {@Sthapati.@}’

{@Sthālī@}¦ denotes a ‘cooking pot,’ usually of earthenware, in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) viii. 6, 17.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vi. 5, 10, 5; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xix. 27. 86; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, i. 11, 8, etc. {%Sthālī-pāka,%} a dish of rice or barley boiled in milk, is mentioned in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, vi. 4, 18; Aitareya Āraṇyaka, iii. 2, 4; Śāṅkh- āyana Āraṇyaka, xi. 6, etc.</F>
{@Sthiraka Gārgya@}¦ (‘descendant of {@Garga@}’) is the name of a teacher in the Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 373.</F>

{@Sthivi@}¦ occurs once (used in the plural) in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> probably meaning ‘bushel.’ The word is also found once in the adjective {%sthivimant,%}<sup>2</sup> ‘provided with bushels.’ <F>1) x. 68, 3.</F> <F>2) Rv. x. 27, 15. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 238.</F>

{@Sthūṇā@}¦ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> denotes the ‘pillar’ or ‘post’ of a house. <F>1) i. 59, 1; v. 45, 2; 62, 7; viii. 17, 14; x. 18, 13 (of the grave).</F> <F>2) Av. iii. 12, 6 (of the {@Vaṃśa,@} ‘beam,’ being placed on the pillar); xiv. 1, 63; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiv. 1, 3, 7; 3, 1, 22, etc.; {%sthūṇā-rāja,%} ‘main pillar,’ iii. 1, 1, 11; 5, 1, 1. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 153.</F>

{@Sthūri@}¦ has in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> the sense of ‘drawn by one animal’ instead of the usual two (see {@Ratha@}), and always with an implication of inferiority. <F>1) x. 131, 3.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 8, 2, 4; iii. 8, 21, 3; Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xvi. 13, 12; xviii. 9, 7; Aitareya Brāh- maṇa, v. 30, 6; Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 3, 3, 9, etc.</F>
{@Sthairakāyaṇa,@}¦ ‘descendant of {@Sthiraka,@}’ is the patronymic of {@Mitravarcas@} in the Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 372 (where the word is spelt with {%n%}).</F>
{@Sthaulāṣṭhīvi,@}¦ ‘descendant of Sthūlāṣṭhīva,’ is the patro- nymic of a grammarian in the Nirukta (vii. 14; x. 1).

{@Snātaka,@}¦ the designation of the student ‘who has taken the bath,’ marking the termination of his studentship under a religious teacher, occurs in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (xii. 1, 1, 10), and repeatedly in the Sūtras. {%Cf.%} {@Brahmacārin.@}
1. {@Snāvanya,@}¦ used in the plural, denotes particular parts of the body of a horse in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (v. 7, 23, 1).
2. {@Snāvanya@}¦ appears to be the name of a people in the Baudhāyana Śrauta Sūtra.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) ii. 5 (in a Mantra). {%Cf.%} Caland, {%Über das rituelle Sūtra des Baudhāyana,%} 35.</F>

{@Snuṣā@}¦ denotes the ‘daughter-in-law’ in relation primarily to her father-in-law, but also to her mother-in-law. In the latter sense the word appears in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> in the epithet {%su-snuṣā,%} [Page2-489+ 37] ‘having a good daughter-in-law,’ used of Vṛṣākapāyī, while in the former it occurs in several passages, where the daughter- in-law's respect for her father-in-law is mentioned,<sup>2</sup> a respect which spirituous liquor alone causes to be violated.<sup>3</sup> See also {@Śvaśura@} and {@Pati.@} <F>1) x. 86, 13.</F> <F>2) Av. viii. 6, 24; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 22, 7; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 4, 6, 12.</F> <F>3) Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 4, 2; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xii. 12 ({%Indische%} {%Studien,%} 5, 260). <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Delbrück, {%Die indogermanischen%} {%Verwandtschaftsnamen,%} 414, 415.</F>

{@Spandana@}¦ in one passage of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> denotes a certain tree. Roth,<sup>2</sup> however, reads {%syandana,%} ‘chariot.’ <F>1) iii. 53, 19.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Aufrecht, {%Rigveda,%} 2, vi; Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 63.</F>
{@Sparśu@}¦ is apparently the name of a western people in the Baudhāyana Śrauta Sūtra (xxi. 13).
{@Spaś.@}¦ See {@Rājan.@}
{@Sphūrjaka@}¦ denotes a tree ({%Diospyros embryopteris%}) mentioned in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (xiii. 8, 1, 16).

{@Smad-ibha@}¦ is found once in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> where Roth<sup>2</sup> takes the word as perhaps the name of an enemy of {@Kutsa.@} {%Cf.%} {@Ibha.@} <F>1) x. 49, 4.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Oldenberg, {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 380; Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 3, 291, n. 5.</F>

{@Syandana,@}¦ ‘chariot,’ is found in the earlier literature only, if at all, in one passage of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> where {@Spandana@} is the received reading. <F>1) iii. 53, 19, according to Roth. A wood called Syandana seems to be meant in the Kauśika Sūtra, viii. 15.</F>

{@Syāla,@}¦ a word occurring in only one passage of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> appears to denote the brother of a man's wife, who is regarded as willing to protect her, and so secure a marriage for her.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) i. 109, 2.</F> <F>2) So Sāyaṇa on Rv., {%loc. cit.%} <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Delbrück, {%Die indogermanischen%} {%Verwandtschaftsnamen,%} 517; Pischel, {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 79.</F>
{@Syūma-gabhasti.@}¦ See {@Gabhasti.@}
{@Syūma-gṛbh,@}¦ used of a horse in the Rigveda (vi. 36, 2) seems to mean ‘grasping the bit between his teeth,’ as a horse does when anxious to break away from control.

{@Syūman@}¦ in one passage of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> denotes, according to Roth,<sup>2</sup> the strap fastening the door of a house, the Homeric <lang n="greek">ἱμάς, δεσμός</lang>. <F>1) iii. 61, 4.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%}</F>
{@Syūma-raśmi@}¦ is the name of a protégé of the Aśvins in the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) i. 112 16; viii. 52, 2. {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 150, 163.</F>

{@Srakti@}¦ is found in the description of the {@Dāśarājña@} in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> where Hopkins<sup>2</sup> thinks the sense of ‘spears’ essential. <F>1) vii. 18, 17.</F> <F>2) {%Journal of the American Oriental Society,%} 15, 264, n.</F>

{@Sraj,@}¦ ‘garland,’ is mentioned in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> as often worn by men when anxious to appear handsome, as at a wedding and so on. The Aśvins are described as ‘lotus- wreathed’ ({%puṣkara-sraj%}).<sup>3</sup> <F>1) iv. 38, 6; v. 53, 4; viii. 47, 15; 56, 3.</F> <F>2) Av. i. 14, 1 (where it means a ‘cluster of flowers’ from a tree); Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xvi. 4, 1; xviii. 3, 2; 7, 6; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xiii. 5, 4, 2, etc.</F> <F>3) Rv. x. 184, 3. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altin-%} {%disches Leben,%} 265.</F>

{@Srāktya@}¦ is an adjective describing an amulet ({@Maṇi@}) in the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> According to Weber,<sup>2</sup> it designates a crystal (literally ‘many-cornered’). The commentators,<sup>3</sup> however, agree in explaining the word to mean ‘derived from the Sraktya’ — {%i.e.,%} from the Tilaka tree ({%Clerodendrum phlomoides%}). <F>1) viii. 5, 4. 7. 8. {%Cf.%} ii. 11.</F> <F>2) {%Indische Studien,%} 13, 164.</F> <F>3) See Bloomfield, {%American Journal of%} {%Philology,%} 7, 477; {%Hymns of the Athar%} {%vaveda,%} 577.</F>

{@Sruc@}¦ denotes a ‘large wooden sacrificial ladle’ (used for pouring clarified butter on the fire) in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> It is of the length of an arm, with a bowl of the size of a hand and a beaklike spout. <F>1) i. 84, 18; 110, 6; 144, 1, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. v. 27, 5; vi. 114, 3; ix. 6, 17, etc. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} for its shape, etc., Max Müller, {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen%} {%Gesellschaft,%} 9, xli, lxxx; Eggeling, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 12, 67; 26, 20, 23.</F>

{@Sruva,@}¦ as opposed to {@Sruc,@} denotes in the ritual literature<sup>1</sup> a small ladle used to convey the offering ({@Ājya@}) from the cooking- pot ({@Sthālī@}) to the large ladle ({@Juhū@}). In the Rigveda,<sup>2</sup> how- ever, it was clearly used for the actual Soma libation. <F>1) Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra, i. 11, 10, etc.</F> <F>2) i. 116, 24; 121, 6, etc. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Max Müller, {%Zeitschrift der%} {%Deutschen Morgenländischen Gesellschaft,%} 9, viii; Caland and Henry, {%L'Agniṣṭoma%} xliv; Plate I., No. 9; Plate II., No. 11 Eggeling, {%Sacred Books of the East,%} 12, 68; 26, 20.</F>
{@Sreka-parṇa@}¦ in the Brāhmaṇas<sup>1</sup> seems to mean ‘like the oleander leaf.’ <F>1) Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 6, 6, 3; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 6, 15.</F>

{@Svaja@}¦ in the Atharvaveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> denotes the ‘viper.’ The word is explained by the commentators as {%sva-ja,%} ‘self- [Page2-492+ 48] born,’ but Roth,<sup>3</sup> Weber,<sup>4</sup> and Zimmer<sup>5</sup> prefer to derive it from the root {%svaj,%} ‘clasp,’ ‘encircle.’ In the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā<sup>6</sup> the {@Hariṇa@} is said to kill the viper. <F>1) iii. 27, 4; v. 14, 10; vi. 56, 2; x. 4, 10, 15, 17; xii. 3, 58.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 10, 2; 14, 1; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 26, 3.</F> <F>3) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.,%} gives the alternative {%vivipara.%}</F> <F>4) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, 2, 89, n.</F> <F>5) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 95.</F> <F>6) iii. 9, 3.</F>

1. {@Svadhiti@}¦ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> denotes the ‘axe’ or ‘knife’ used for dissecting the sacrificial horse. In all the other passages in that Saṃhitā<sup>2</sup> the sense of ‘axe’ for cutting wood is adequate; reference is made in one place<sup>3</sup> to sharpening the axe on the whetstone ({%kṣṇotra%}). In the Atharvaveda<sup>4</sup> the term seems once to denote the copper ({%lohita%})<sup>5</sup> knife used to mark the ears of cattle; the carpenter's knife or axe is also twice referred to there.<sup>6</sup> Later the word means ‘axe’ generally.<sup>7</sup> As a weapon it does not appear at all.<sup>8</sup> <F>1) i. 162, 9. 18. 20.</F> <F>2) ii. 39, 7; iii. 2, 10; 8, 6, 11; v. 7, 8; vii. 3, 9; viii. 102, 19; x. 89, 7. {%Cf.%} n. 8.</F> <F>3) ii. 39, 7.</F> <F>4) vi. 141, 2. {%Cf.%} Mantra Brāhmaṇa, i. 8, 7; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 386, 387; Geldner, {%Vedische%} {%Studien,%} 2, 159, who is inclined to com- pare {@Paraśu@} in Rv. iii. 53, 22.</F> <F>5) Geldner, {%loc. cit.,%} understands this word to mean ‘red-hot.’</F> <F>6) ix. 4, 6 (probably so to be taken); xii. 3, 33. In xviii. 2, 35, the sense is quite different. See Whitney, {%op. cit.,%} 845.</F> <F>7) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vi. 3, 3, 2; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, ii. 15 (the slaughtering- knife); v. 43 (the axe to fell the tree) etc.</F> <F>8) In Rv. x. 92, 15, Svadhiti may refer to the thunderbolt of Indra.</F>

2. {@Svadhiti@}¦ in certain passages of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> denotes, according to the St. Petersburg Dictionary, a great tree with hard wood. This interpretation seems probable. <F>1) v. 32, 10; ix. 96, 6. {%Cf.%} i. 88, 2.</F>

{@Svanad-ratha@}¦ (‘having a rattling car’) is taken by Ludwig<sup>1</sup> as a proper name of {@Āsaṅga@} in the Rigveda.<sup>2</sup> But the word is most probably only an epithet. <F>1) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 159.</F> <F>2) viii. 1, 32.</F>

{@Svanaya Bhāvya@}¦ is the name of a prince on the {@Sindhu@} (Indus) who bestowed gifts on {@Kakṣīvant,@} according to the Rigveda (i. 126, 1. 3). He is called Svanaya Bhāvayavya in the Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra (xvi. 11, 5).

{@Svapna,@}¦ ‘dream,’ is referred to in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> Evil dreams<sup>3</sup> are often mentioned. The Āraṇyakas of the Rigveda<sup>4</sup> contain a list of dreams with their signification, as well as of {%pratyakṣa-darśanāni,%} ‘sights seen with one's own eyes.’ <F>1) ii. 28, 10; x. 162, 6.</F> <F>2) Av. vii. 101, 1; x. 3, 6; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xx. 16; Śatapatha Brāh- maṇa, iii. 2, 2, 23, etc.</F> <F>3) Rv. ii. 28, 10; Av. x. 3, 6.</F> <F>4) Aitareya Āraṇyaka, iii. 2, 4; Śāṅkh- āyana Āraṇyaka, xi. 3. {%Cf.%} Kauśika Sūtra, xlvi. 9 {%et seq.;%} Atharvaveda Pari- śiṣṭa, lxviii.</F>

{@Svar@}¦ denotes the ‘sun’<sup>1</sup> and the ‘heaven of light’ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) i. 71, 2; 105, 3; 148, 1, etc.; Nirukta, ii. 14.</F> <F>1) i. 71, 2; 105, 3; 148, 1, etc.; Nirukta, ii. 14.</F> <F>2) Rv. iii. 2, 7; v. 83, 4; x. 66, 4. 9, etc.; Av. iv. 11, 6; 14, 2, etc.</F>

{@Svara@}¦ denotes in the Upaniṣads<sup>1</sup> the sound of a vowel: these are described<sup>2</sup> as being {%ghoṣavant,%} ‘sonant,’ and also as {%balavant,%} ‘uttered with force.’ The precise word for a mute is {%sparśa,%}<sup>3</sup> ‘contact,’ while {%ūṣman%} denotes a ‘sibilant,’ and {%svara%} a ‘vowel,’ in the Aitareya<sup>3</sup> and Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyakas.<sup>4</sup> The semivowels are there denoted by {%anta-sthā%} (‘intermediate’)<sup>5</sup> or {%akṣara.%}<sup>6</sup> Another division in the Aitareya Āraṇyaka<sup>7</sup> is into {%ghoṣa, ūṣman,%} and {%vyañjana,%} apparently ‘vowels,’ ‘sibilants,’ and ‘consonants’ respectively. {%Ghoṣa%} elsewhere in that Āraṇ- yaka<sup>8</sup> seems to have the general sense of ‘sounds.’ The Taittirīya Upaniṣad<sup>9</sup> refers to {%mātrā,%} a ‘mora’;<sup>10</sup> {%bala,%} ‘force’ of utterance, and {%varṇa,%} ‘letter,’ an expression found else- where<sup>11</sup> in the explanation of {%om,%} as compacted of {%a + u + m.%} [Page2-494+ 53] <div n="P"/>The Aitareya Āraṇyaka<sup>12</sup> and the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka<sup>13</sup> recognize the three forms of the Rigveda text as {%pratṛṇṇa,%} {%nirbhuja,%} and {%ubhayam-antareṇa,%} denoting respectively the Saṃ- hitā, Pada, and Krama Pāṭhas of the Rigveda.<sup>14</sup> The same authorities<sup>15</sup> recognize the importance of the distinction of the cerebral and dental {%n%} and {%s,%} and refer<sup>16</sup> to the {@Māṇḍūkeyas'@} mode of recitation. They also discuss<sup>17</sup> Sandhi, the euphonic ‘combination’ of letters. <div n="P"/>The Prātiśākhyas of the several Saṃhitās develop in detail the grammatical terminology, and Yāska's Nirukta<sup>18</sup> contains a good deal of grammatical material. The Śatapatha Brāh- maṇa<sup>19</sup> distinguishes the genders, and the Pañcaviṃśa Brāh- maṇa<sup>20</sup> the division of words in the Sāman recitation. <F>1) Chāndogya Upaniṣad, ii. 22, 5; Taittirīya Upaniṣad, i. 2, 1.</F> <F>2) Chāndogya Upaniṣad, {%loc. cit.%}</F> <F>3) iii. 2, 1, etc.</F> <F>3) iii. 2, 1, etc.</F> <F>4) viii. 1, etc.</F> <F>5) Aitareya Āraṇyaka, iii. 2, 1.</F> <F>6) Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka, viii. 1.</F> <F>7) ii. 2, 4.</F> <F>8) ii. 2, 2. {%Cf.%} Keith's edition, p. 213.</F> <F>9) {%Loc. cit.%}</F> <F>10) Also Aitareya Āraṇyaka, iii. 1, 5; Sāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka, vii. 13.</F> <F>11) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, v. 32, 2; Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, xxvi. 5; Āśval- āyana Śrauta Sūtra, x. 4; Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} v. 32.</F> <F>12) iii. 1, 3, 5.</F> <F>13) vii. 10, 12.</F> <F>14) Max Müller, {%Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya,%} ii. {%et seq.; Nachträge,%} ii; Oldenberg, {%Prolegomena,%} 380 {%et seq.; Sacred Books%} {%of the East,%} 30, 146 {%et seq.;%} Macdonell, {%Sanskrit Literature,%} 51.</F> <F>15) Aitareya, iii. 2, 6; Śāṅkhāyana, viii. 11.</F> <F>16) Aitareya, iii. 1, 1; 2, 6; Sāṅkh- āyana, vii. 2; viii. 11.</F> <F>17) Aitareya, iii. 1, 2. 3. 5; 2, 2 Śāṅkhāyana, vii. 13; viii. 1, 2.</F> <F>18) See Roth's edition (1852), p. 222, for a list of teachers cited by Yāska, especially {@Kautsa@} and {@Śākaṭāyana.@}</F> <F>19) x. 5, 1, 2. 3.</F> <F>20) x. 9, 1. 2. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} von Schroeder, {%Indiens Literatur%} {%und Cultur,%} 701 {%et seq.%}</F>

{@Sva-rāj,@}¦ ‘self-ruler,’ ‘king,’ is found frequently in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> It is the technical term for the kings of the west according to the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) i. 36, 7; 51, 15; 61, 9, etc. (of gods).</F> <F>2) Av. xvii. 1, 22; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 3, 6, 2; iv. 4, 8, 1; v. 5, 4, 1, etc.</F> <F>3) viii. 14. {%Cf.%} perhaps the republi- can form of government of which traces are seen in the Buddhist litera- ture by Rhys Davids, {%Buddhist India,%} 19.</F>

{@Svaru@}¦ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> or later<sup>2</sup> denotes a ‘post,’ or more precisely in the ritual a splinter of the Yūpa, or sacrificial post.<sup>3</sup> <F>1) i. 92, 5; 162, 9; iii. 8, 6, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. iv. 24, 4; xii. 1, 13, etc.</F> <F>3) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 3, 8; Tait- tirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 7, 1; vi. 3, 4 9, etc.; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 7, 1, 22; 8, 1, 5, etc.</F>

{@Svar-jit Nāgna-jita@}¦ (‘descendant of {@Nagna-jit@}’) is the name of a royal personage in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa,<sup>1</sup> a {@Gandhāra@} prince, whose views on the ritual are referred to with contempt. <F>1) viii. 1, 4, 10. {%Cf.%} Muir, {%Sanskrit Texts,%} 1^2, 515.</F>

{@Svar-ṇara@}¦ appears to be the proper name of a sacrificer in two verses of the Rigveda.<sup>1</sup> According to Geldner,<sup>2</sup> it every- where<sup>3</sup> means a specially sacred lake and the Soma-producing district around it. <F>1) viii. 3, 12; 12, 2. {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 160; Hopkins, {%Journal of the American Oriental%} {%Society,%} 17, 89.</F> <F>2) {%Rigveda, Glossar,%} 209.</F> <F>3) Rv. iv. 21, 3; v. 18, 4; 14, 1; viii. 6, 39; 65, 2; 103, 14; ix. 70, 6; x. 65, 4. Perhaps in viii. 12, 2, it means ‘coming from Svarṇara.’</F>

{@Svar-bhānu Asura@}¦ is the name, in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later,<sup>2</sup> of a demon supposed to have eclipsed the sun. See {@Sūrya.@} <F>1) v. 40, 5. 6. 8. 9.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 1, 2, 2; Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, iv. 5, 2; 6, 13; vi. 6, 8; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, v. 3, 2, 2; Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, xxiv. 3.</F>

{@Sva-sara,@}¦ according to the St. Petersburg Dictionary, denotes ‘cattle stall,’<sup>1</sup> and more generally ‘dwelling-place,’ ‘house,’<sup>2</sup> and then ‘nest of birds.’<sup>3</sup> Geldner,<sup>4</sup> however, shows that the real sense is the ‘wandering at will’ of cattle, more precisely their ‘grazing in the morning,’<sup>5</sup> and in the case of birds their ‘early flight’ from the nest,<sup>6</sup> while metaphorically it is applied first to the morning pressing of Soma and then to all three pressings.<sup>7</sup> <F>1) Rv. i. 3, 8; ii. 2, 2; 34, 8; v. 62, 2; viii. 88, 1; Sāmaveda, i. 5, 2, 3, 2.</F> <F>2) Rv. i. 34, 7; iii. 60, 6; 61, 4; vi. 68, 10; viii. 99, 1; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iv. 3, 5, 20.</F> <F>3) Rv. ii. 19, 2; 34, 5.</F> <F>4) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 110-115.</F> <F>5) Rv. i. 3, 8; ii. 2, 2; 34, 8; v. 62, 2; viii. 88, 1.</F> <F>6) Rv. ii. 19, 2; 34, 5.</F> <F>7) Rv. i. 34, 7; iii. 60, 6; vi. 68, 10; viii. 99, 1. In Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, {%loc. cit.,%} it is equivalent to ‘libation.’</F>

{@Svasṛ@}¦ is the regular word from the Rigveda onwards<sup>1</sup> for ‘sister.’ Like the word {@Bhrātṛ,@} the term sister can be applied [Page2-496+ 42] to things not precisely so related. For example, in the Rigveda the fingers and the seasons are ‘sisters,’ and night is the sister of dawn, for whom, as the elder, she makes way.<sup>2</sup> The {@Paṇis@} offer to adopt Saramā as their sister;<sup>3</sup> but this use is not applied — any more than in the case of Bhrātṛ — to ordinary human beings. <div n="P"/>The sister stood in a close relation to her brother. If the father was dead or feeble, the sister was dependent on her brother and on his wife, as appears from the Rigveda<sup>4</sup> and the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.<sup>5</sup> Moreover, maidens without brothers were apt to find marriage difficult, and to degenerate into Hetairai;<sup>6</sup> but it is not certain whether this was due, as Zimmer<sup>7</sup> thinks, to brothers being required to arrange marriages for orphan girls, or because sonless fathers were anxious to make their daughters {@Putrikās,@} in order that they themselves, instead of the husbands, should count the daughters' sons as their own.<sup>8</sup> See also {@Jāmi.@} <F>1) Rv. ii. 32, 6; vi. 55, 4. 5; viii. 101, 15; x. 108, 9, etc.</F> <F>2) Rv. i. 124, 8. See Delbrück, {%Die%} {%indogermanischen Verwandtschaftsnamen,%} 463; Rv. i. 62, 10; 64, 7, 71, 1, etc.</F> <F>3) Rv. x. 108, 9.</F> <F>4) x. 85, 46. {%Cf.%} ix. 96, 22.</F> <F>5) iii. 37, 5.</F> <F>6) Av. i. 17, 1; Rv. i. 124, 7; iv. 5, 5; Nirukta, iii. 5.</F> <F>7) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 328.</F> <F>8) {%Cf.%} Geldner, {%Rigveda, Kommentar,%} 22, 48, 49 (on Rv. iii. 31, 1 {%et seq.%}).</F>

{@Svasrīya@}¦ occurs in the sense of ‘sister's son’ in the descrip- tion of Viśvarūpa's ancestry in the Yajurveda Saṃhitās.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 5, 1, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 4, 1. {%Cf.%} Delbrück, {%Die indogermanischen Ver-%} {%wandtschaftsnamen,%} 485.</F>
{@Svātī.@}¦ See {@Nakṣatra.@}

{@Svādhyāya@}¦ (‘reciting to oneself’) in the Brāhmaṇas<sup>1</sup> denotes the study or repetition of the Vedic texts. The Sūtras give rules for it in great detail. {%Cf.%} {@Brāhmaṇa.@} <F>1) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 3, 6; iv. 6, 9, 6; xi. 5, 6, 3; 7, 1, 4, 7; Chāndogya Upaniṣad, i. 12, 1; 8, 15; Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad, i. 1.</F>
{@Svāyava,@}¦ ‘descendant of Svāyu,’ is the patronymic of {@Kūśāmba Lātavya@} in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa (viii. 6, 8).
{@Svā-rājya.@}¦ See {@Rājya.@}

{@Sveda-ja,@}¦ ‘born of sweat’ — that is, ‘engendered by hot moisture’ — is used in the Aitareya Upaniṣad (iii. 3, 3) as a term designating a class of creatures comprising vermin of all sorts. The Mānava Dharma Śāstra (i. 45) explains it as ‘flies, mosquitoes, lice, bugs, and so forth.’ <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Keith, {%Aitareya Āraṇyaka,%} 235.
{@Svaidāyana,@}¦ ‘descendant of {@Sveda,@}’ is the patronymic of a {@Śaunaka@} in the Brāhmaṇas.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xi. 4, 1, 2. 3; Gopatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 3, 6.</F>
{@Svaupaśa.@}¦ See {@Opaśa.@}

{@Haṃsa@}¦ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> denotes the ‘gander.’ These birds are described as dark in colour on the back ({%nīla-%} {%pṛṣṭha%});<sup>3</sup> they fly in troops,<sup>4</sup> swim in the water ({%uda-prut%}),<sup>5</sup> make loud noises,<sup>6</sup> and are wakeful at night.<sup>7</sup> The Haṃsa is credited with the power of separating Soma from water (as later milk from water) in the Yajurveda.<sup>8</sup> It is also mentioned as one of the victims at the Aśvamedha (‘horse sacrifice’).<sup>9</sup> <F>1) i. 65, 5; 163, 10; ii. 34, 5; iii. 8, 9, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. vi. 12, 1, etc.</F> <F>3) Rv. vii. 59, 7.</F> <F>4) Rv. iii. 8, 9.</F> <F>5) Rv. i. 65, 5; iii. 45, 4.</F> <F>6) Rv. iii. 53, 10.</F> <F>7) Av. vi. 12, 1.</F> <F>8) Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxxviii. 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 11, 6; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xix. 74; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 6, 2, 1.</F> <F>9) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 21, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 3; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 22. 35. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 89, 90; Lanman, {%Journal of the American%} {%Oriental Society,%} 19, 151; Macdonell, {%Sanskrit Literature,%} 150.</F>

{@Haṃsa-sāci@}¦ is the name of an unknown bird mentioned in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā<sup>1</sup> as one of the victims at the Aśvamedha (‘horse sacrifice’). <F>1) v. 5, 20, 1. {%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 93.</F>

{@Haya@}¦ denotes ‘horse’ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) v. 46, 1; vii. 74, 4; ix. 107, 25.</F> <F>2) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, vii. 47; xxii. 19, etc. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 231.</F>

{@Hara-yāṇa@}¦ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> is clearly the name of a man mentioned along with {@Ukṣaṇyāyana@} and {@Suṣāman.@} <F>1) viii. 28, 22; Nirukta, v. 15. {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 162.</F>

{@Hariṇa@}¦ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> denotes a ‘gazelle.’ It is at once a type of speed<sup>3</sup> and terror.<sup>4</sup> Its horns are used as amulets.<sup>5</sup> It is fond of eating barley ({@Yava@}).<sup>6</sup> In the Maitrā- yaṇī Saṃhitā.<sup>7</sup> it is said to kill vipers ({@Svaja@}). {%Cf.%} {@Kuluṅga,@} {@Nyaṅku.@} The feminine is Hariṇī.<sup>8</sup> <F>1) i. 163, 1; v. 78, 2.</F> <F>2) Av. vi. 67, 3, etc.</F> <F>3) Av. iii. 7, 1.</F> <F>4) Av. vi. 67, 3.</F> <F>5) Av. iii. 7, 1. 2.</F> <F>6) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vii. 4, 19, 2 ({%hariṇī%}); Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiii. 30; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 13, 1; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, Aśvamedha, iv. 8 (also {%hariṇī%}); Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 9, 7, 2 ({%hariṇī%}).</F> <F>7) iii. 9, 3.</F> <F>8) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vii. 4, 19, 2, and see n. 6. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 83; Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 336, 337.</F>
1. {@Harita@}¦ seems to mean ‘gold’ in a few passages of the Saṃhitās.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Av. v. 28, 5. 9; xi. 3, 8; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, viii. 5.</F>

2. {@Harita Kaśyapa@}¦ is mentioned as a teacher, a pupil of {@Śilpa Kaśyapa,@} in the last Vaṃśa (list of teachers) of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) vi. 4, 33 (Mādhyaṃdina = vi. 5, 3 Kāṇva).</F>
{@Hari-dru@}¦ in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (xiii. 8, 1, 16) is the name of a tree ({%Pinus deodora%}).

{@Hariman@}¦ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and the Atharvaveda<sup>2</sup> denotes ‘yellowness’ as a disease, ‘jaundice.’ <F>1) i. 50, 11 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>2) i. 22, 1; ix. 8, 9; xix. 44, 2. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 378, 388.</F>

{@Hari-yūpīyā@}¦ is mentioned in a hymn of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> as the scene of the defeat of the {@Vṛcīvants@} by {@Abhyāvartin Cāya-@} {@mana.@} It may denote either a place or a river, since many battles seem to have been fought on the banks of rivers. Ludwig<sup>2</sup> took it as the name of a town on the river {@Yavyāvatī,@} which is identified with it in Sāyaṇa's commentary on the passage. Hillebrandt<sup>3</sup> thinks that it is the river Iryāb (Haliāb), a tributary of the Kurum ({@Krumu@}), but this is not at all probable. <F>1) vi. 27, 5.</F> <F>2) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 158.</F> <F>3) {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 3, 268, n. 1. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 18, 19; Kaegi, {%Rigveda,%} n. 328.</F>

{@Hari-varṇa Aṅgirasa@}¦ (‘descendant of Aṅgiras’) is the name of the seer of a Sāman or chant in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) viii. 9, 4. 5. {%Cf.%} Hopkins, {%Transactions of the Connecticut Academy of Arts%} {%and Sciences,%} 15, 63.</F>

{@Hari-ścandra Vaidhasa@}¦ (‘descendant of Vedhas’) {@Aikṣvāka@} (‘descendant of {@Ikṣvāku@}’) is the name of a probably mythical king whose rash vow to offer up his son {@Rohita@} to Varuṇa is the source of the tale of {@Śunaḥśepa@} in the Aitareya Brāhmana (vii. 14, 2) and the Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra (xv. 17).

{@Harmya@}¦ denotes the Vedic ‘house’ as a unity including the stabling<sup>1</sup> and so forth, and surrounded by a fence or wall of [Page2-500+ 52] some sort.<sup>2</sup> It is several times referred to in the Rigveda<sup>3</sup> and later.<sup>4</sup> {%Cf.%} {@Gṛha.@} <F>1) Rv. vii. 56, 16. {%Cf.%} x. 106, 5.</F> <F>2) Rv. vii. 55, 6. Geldner, {%Vedische%} {%Studien,%} 2, 278, n. 2, takes {%harmyeṣṭhāḥ,%} ‘standing on a house’ (Rv. vii. 56, 16), to refer to princes on the roof of a palace.</F> <F>3) i. 121, 1 (the people, {%viśaḥ,%} of the house); 166, 4; ix. 71, 4; 78, 3; x. 43, 3; 73, 10, etc.</F> <F>4) Av. xviii. 4, 55 (a palace of Yama); Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 7, 6, 3, etc. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 149.</F>

{@Halikṣṇa@}¦<sup>1</sup> or {@Halīkṣṇa@}<sup>2</sup> is mentioned as one of the victims at the Aśvamedha (‘horse sacrifice’) in the Yajurveda Saṃhitās. The commentator Mahīdhara<sup>3</sup> thinks that it is a kind of lion, Sāyaṇa<sup>4</sup> that a green Caṭaka bird or a lion ({%tṛṇa-hiṃsa%})<sup>5</sup> is meant. In the Atharvaveda<sup>6</sup> Halīkṣṇa seems to be some par- ticular intestine, but Weber<sup>7</sup> thinks it may mean ‘gall.’ <F>1) Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 12; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 31.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 12, 1; 7, 23, 1.</F> <F>3) On Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, {%loc. cit.%}</F> <F>4) On Taittirīya Saṃhitā, {%loc. cit.%}</F> <F>5) {%Tṛṇa-siṃha%} is not much more in- telligible.</F> <F>6) ii. 33, 3.</F> <F>7) {%Indische Studien,%} 13, 206. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 79.</F>

{@Havir-dhāna@}¦ (‘oblation receptacle’) denotes primarily the cart on which the Soma plants are conveyed to be pressed,<sup>1</sup> then the shed in which these Soma vehicles were kept.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 1, 3, 1; vi. 2, 9, 1. 4, etc.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vi. 2, 11, 1. 4, etc. <div n="P"/>See {@Gṛha;@} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 154.</F>

{@Haviṣ-kṛt Āṅgirasa@}¦ (‘descendant of {@Aṅgiras@}’) is the name of the seer of a Sāman or chant according to the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> and the Taittirīya Saṃhitā.<sup>2</sup> See the following. <F>1) xi. 10, 9. 10; xx. 11, 3.</F> <F>2) vii. 1, 4, 1. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 2, 160; Hopkins, {%Transactions of the Con-%} {%necticut Academy of Arts and Sciences,%} 15, 62.</F>

{@Haviṣmant Āṅgirasa@}¦ is mentioned along with {@Haviṣkṛt,@} in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā and the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa,<sup>2</sup> as the seer of a Sāman or chant. <div n="P"/>^1) vii. 1, 4, 1. <F>2) xi. 10, 9. 10; xx. 11, 3.</F>

{@Havis@}¦ is the general term for an offering to the gods, ‘oblation,’ whether of grain, or Soma, or milk, or clarified butter, etc. It is common from the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> onwards.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) i. 24, 11; 26, 6; 170, 5, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. iii. 10, 5; vi. 5, 3, etc.</F>
{@Hasta.@}¦ See {@Nakṣatra.@}

{@Hasta-ghna@}¦ denotes in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> a ‘hand-guard,’ a covering used as a protection of the hand and arm from the impact of the bowstring. The word is of remarkable and still unexplained formation.<sup>2</sup> Lāṭyāyana<sup>3</sup> has {%hasta-tra%} and the Epic {%hastāvāpa%}<sup>4</sup> as its equivalent in sense. <F>1) vi. 75, 14; Nirukta, ix. 14. The reading is assured by the parallels in the Saṃhitās: Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iv. 6, 6, 5; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 16, 3; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxix. 51.</F> <F>2) Pischel, {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 296; Oldenberg, {%Ṛgveda-Noten,%} 1, 416.</F> <F>3) Śrauta Sūtra, iii. 10, 7.</F> <F>4) Hopkins, {%Journal of the American%} {%Oriental Society,%} 13, 308.</F>
{@Hastādāna.@}¦ See {@Paśu.@}

{@Hastin,@}¦ ‘having a hand,’ with {@Mṛga,@} ‘beast,’ denotes in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and the Atharvaveda<sup>2</sup> the ‘elephant.’ Later the adjective alone comes to mean ‘elephant.’<sup>3</sup> The animal was famed for its strength<sup>4</sup> as well as its virility.<sup>5</sup> It is mentioned with man and monkey as one of the beasts that take hold by the hand ({%hastādāna%}), as opposed to those that take hold by the mouth ({%mukhādāna%}).<sup>6</sup> It was tamed, as the expression {@Hastipa,@} ‘elephant-keeper,’ shows, and tame elephants were used to catch others (see {@Vāraṇa@}). But there is no trace of its use in war, though Ktesias and Megasthenes both record such use for [Page2-502+ 46] their times.<sup>7</sup> The Atharvaveda<sup>8</sup> alludes to its being pestered by mosquitoes. <F>1) i. 64, 7; iv. 16, 14.</F> <F>2) xii. 1, 25. Elsewhere Hastin is used alone: iii. 22, 3; iv. 36, 9; vi. 38, 2; 70, 2; xix. 1, 32.</F> <F>3) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 11, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 8; Vāja- saneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 29; Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, vi. 8, 8; xxiii. 13, 2; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, iv. 1, 14; v. 31, 2; vi. 27, 2; Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, iii. 1, 3, 4, etc.; Chāndogya Upaniṣad, vii. 24, 2 (coupled with gold), etc.; Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa, iii. 22, 1.</F> <F>4) Rv. {%loc. cit.;%} Av ii. 22, 1, 3.</F> <F>5) Av. iii. 22, 6; vi. 70, 2.</F> <F>6) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vi. 4, 5, 7; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iv, 5, 7.</F> <F>7) Von Schroeder, {%Indiens Literatur und%} {%Cidtur,%} 434.</F> <F>8) Av. iv. 36, 9. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 80.</F>

{@Hasti-pa,@}¦ ‘elephant-keeper,’ is mentioned as one of the victims at the Puruṣamedha (‘human sacrifice’) in the Yajurveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxx. 11; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 4, 9, 1.</F>
{@Hasrā@}¦ (‘laughing woman’) in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> denotes a courtesan according to Pischel.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) i. 124, 7.</F> <F>2) {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 196, 308.</F>

{@Hāyana@}¦ denotes a ‘year,’ usually in compounds.<sup>1</sup> In the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā<sup>2</sup> and the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>3</sup> the term appears as a designation of a species of red rice. As an adjec- tive in the sense of ‘lasting a year’ or ‘recurring every year,’ it is applied to fever in the Atharvaveda.<sup>4</sup> <F>1) Av. viii. 2, 21; {%śata-hāyana,%} ‘a hundred years old,’ viii. 2, 8; 7, 22; {%hāyanī,%} xii. 1, 36 (probably corrupt).</F> <F>2) xv. 5.</F> <F>3) v. 3, 3, 6 (the Taittirīya Saṃhitā, i. 8, 10, 1, has instead {%mahā-vrīhi,%} ‘great rice’).</F> <F>4) xix. 39, 10. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Schrader, {%Prehistoric Antiquities,%} 301.</F>

{@Hārikarṇī-putra,@}¦ ‘son of a female descendant of Hari- karṇa,’ is the name of a teacher, a pupil of {@Bhāradvājī-putra,@} in the last Vaṃśa (list of teachers) in the Mādhyaṃdina recen- sion of the Brhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (vi. 4, 30).

{@Hāridrava@}¦ is the name of a yellow bird in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> perhaps the ‘yellow water-wagtail.’<sup>2</sup> Geldner<sup>3</sup> compares the Greek <lang n="greek">χαραδριός.</lang> <F>1) i. 50, 12; viii. 35, 7.</F> <F>2) Sāyaṇa on Rv. i. 50, 12; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 7, 6, 2, treats it as the name of a plant ({%cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altin-%} {%disches Leben,%} 62). But on Av. i. 22, 4, he takes it as {%gopītanaka,%} ‘wagtail.’</F> <F>3) {%Rigveda, Glossar,%} 213. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Bloomfield, {%Hymns of the Athar-%} {%vaveda,%} 264, n. 1; 266; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 23.</F>
{@Hāridravika@}¦ is the title of a work by Hāridravin mentioned in the Nirukta.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) ix. 5. See Roth, {%Nirukta,%} xxiii; von Schroeder, Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, 1, xiii.</F>
{@Hāri-drumata,@}¦ ‘descendant of Haridrumant,’ is the patro- nymic of a {@Gautama@} in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (iv. 4, 3).
{@Hāliṅgava,@}¦ ‘descendant of Haliṅgu,’ is the name of a teacher in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (x. 4, 5, 1).
{@Hitā@}¦ in the Brāhmaṇas<sup>1</sup> is the name of certain ‘veins.’ {%Cf.%} {@Hirā.@} <F>1) Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, ii. 1, 21; iv. 2, 4; 3, 20; Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad, iv. 19.</F>

{@Hima,@}¦ denoting ‘cold,’ ‘cold weather,’ is quite common in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> but less frequent later.<sup>2</sup> As ‘snow’ the word appears as a masculine in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa,<sup>3</sup> and often later as a neuter.<sup>4</sup> {%Cf.%} {@Hemanta.@} <F>1) i. 116, 8; 119, 6; viii. 32, 26, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. vii. 18, 2; xiii. 1, 46; xix. 49, 5 (night as mother of coolness), etc.</F> <F>3) iii. 12, 7, 2.</F> <F>4) Saḍviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, vi. 9, etc. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 3, 192-195.</F>

{@Himavant,@}¦ ‘snowy,’ appears as an epithet of mountains in the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> It is also used both there<sup>2</sup> and in the Rigveda,<sup>3</sup> as well as later,<sup>4</sup> as a noun. There seems no reason to deny that in all the passages the word refers vaguely to the mountains now called Himālaya, though it is possible that the name may include mountains not strictly in that system, like the Suleiman hills.<sup>5</sup> See also {@Mūjavant@} and {@Trikakubh.@} <F>1) xii. 1, 11.</F> <F>2) vi. 95, 3. See also iv. 9, 9; v. 4, 2. 8; 25. 7; vi. 24, 1 (where reference is made to the rivers of the Himālayas); xix. 39, 1.</F> <F>3) x. 121, 4.</F> <F>4) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 11, 1; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 30; xxv. 12; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, viii. 14, 3 (the {@Uttara Kurus@} and {@Uttara Madras@} live beyond it; perhaps in Kaśmīr), etc.</F> <F>5) Ludwig, Translation of the Rig- veda, 3, 198. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leven,%} 29; Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 18, 12, who inclines to see a reminiscence of the Caucasus.</F>

{@Himā@}¦ denotes ‘winter’ in the combination a ‘hundred winters’ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and elsewhere.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) i. 64, 14; ii. 33, 2; v. 54, 15; vi. 48, 8.</F> <F>2) Av. ii. 28, 4; xii. 2, 28; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, i. 6, 6, 3; Vājasaneyi Saṃ- hitā, ii. 27.</F>

{@Hiraṇin,@}¦ ‘rich in gold,’ is apparently an epithet of {@Trasa-@} {@dasyu@} in one verse of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> referring to the golden raiment or possessions of the king. Ludwig,<sup>2</sup> however, thinks the word is a proper name, possibly of Trasadasyu's son. <F>1) v. 53, 8.</F> <F>2) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 155.</F>

{@Hiraṇina@}¦ is found in one passage of the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> where Ludwig<sup>2</sup> takes the word as a name of {@Śāṇḍa.@} But it seems to be an adjectival form of {%hiraṇin,%} ‘golden.’ <F>1) vi. 63, 9.</F> <F>2) Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 158.</F>

{@Hiraṇya@}¦ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> denotes ‘gold.’ It is hardly possible to exaggerate the value attached to gold by the Vedic Indians. The metal was, it is clear, won from the bed of rivers. Hence the Indus is called ‘golden’<sup>3</sup> and ‘of golden stream.’<sup>4</sup> Apparently the extraction of gold from the earth was known,<sup>5</sup> and washing for gold is also recorded.<sup>6</sup> <div n="P"/>Gold is the object of the wishes of the Vedic singer,<sup>7</sup> and golden treasures ({%hiraṇyāni%}) are mentioned as given by patrons<sup>8</sup> along with cows and horses. Gold was used for ornaments for neck and breast ({@Niṣka@}), for ear-rings ({@Karṇa-śobhana@}), and even for cups.<sup>9</sup> Gold is always associated with the gods.<sup>10</sup> [Page2-505+ 62] <div n="P"/>In the plural Hiraṇya denotes ‘ornaments of gold.’<sup>11</sup> <div n="P"/>A gold currency was evidently beginning to be known in so far as definite weights of gold are mentioned: thus a weight, {%aṣṭā-prūḍ,%} occurs in the Saṃhitās,<sup>12</sup> and the golden {%śatamāna,%} ‘weight of a hundred ({@Kṛṣṇalas@})’ is found in the same texts.<sup>13</sup> In several passages,<sup>14</sup> moreover, {%hiraṇya%} or {%hiraṇyāni%} may mean ‘pieces of gold.’ <div n="P"/>Gold is described sometimes as {%harita,%}<sup>15</sup> ‘yellowish,’ some- times as {%rajata,%}<sup>16</sup> ‘whitish,’ when probably. ‘silver’ is alluded to. It was obtained from the ore by smelting.<sup>17</sup> Mega- sthenes<sup>18</sup> bears testimony to the richness in gold of India in his time. <F>1) i. 43, 5; iii. 34, 9; iv. 10, 6; 17, 11, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. i. 9, 2; ii. 36, 7; v. 28, 6; vi. 38, 2, etc.</F> <F>3) Rv. x. 75, 8.</F> <F>4) Rv. vi. 61, 7; viii. 26, 18.</F> <F>5) Rv. i. 117, 5; Av. xii. 1, 6. 26. 44.</F> <F>6) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vi. 1, 7, 1; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, ii. 1, 1, 5.</F> <F>7) Rv. vi. 47, 23; viii. 78, 9; Pischel and Geldner, {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, xxiv.</F> <F>8) {%Cf.%} also {@Hiraṇyastūpa@} as a proper name.</F> <F>9) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 7, 1, 3; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 3, 3, 7; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, v. 1, 2, 19; 5, 28.</F> <F>10) All that is connected with them is of gold; the horses of the sun are {%hiraṇya-tvacas,%} ‘gold-skinned’ (Av. xiii. 2, 8), and so on.</F> <F>11) Rv. i. 122, 2; 162, 16; ii. 33, 9; v. 60, 4; Av. iv. 10, 6; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xv. 50; xx. 37; also in the singular, Av. i. 35, 1; xviii. 4, 56.</F> <F>12) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 4, 1, 4; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xi. 1; xiii. 10; von Schroeder, {%Zeitschrift der Deutschen%} {%Morgenländischen Gesellschaft,%} 49, 164.</F> <F>13) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, v. 5, 5, 16; xii. 7, 2, 13; 9, 1, 4. {%Cf.%} xiii. 1, 1, 4; 2, 3, 2; 4, 1, 13; 2, 7. 13; xiv. 3, 1, 32; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 3, 11, 5; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, viii. 5; xxii. 8; Weber, {%Indische Streifen,%} 1, 101. Geldner, {%Vedische Studien,%} 1, 268, is inclined to think that a gold unit is alluded to in the vague phrases ‘thousands,’ etc., of the Rigveda. See viii. 1, 13; 65, 12; x. 95, 3, etc.</F> <F>14) Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 4, 7, 4; iii. 8, 2, 2; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xii. 7, 1, 7; xiii. 4, 1, 6, etc.</F> <F>15) Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, x. 4; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xii. 4, 4, 6; Ṣaḍviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, ii. 9.</F> <F>16) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, i. 5, 1, 2; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, xii. 4, 4, 7; xiii. 4, 2, 10, etc.</F> <F>17) Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, vi. 1, 3, 5. {%Cf.%} ii. 2, 3, 28; xii. 4, 3, 1; Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xvii. 6, 4 ({%niṣ-ṭap,%} ‘heat’); Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 10 ({%Journal of%} {%the American Oriental Society,%} 16, 234, ccxliii); Lāṭyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, iii. 1, 9, etc.; Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāh- maṇa, iii. 34, 6.</F> <F>18) See Diodorus Siculus, ii. 36; Strabo, pp. 703, 711. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 49-51; Macdonell, {%Sanskrit Literature,%} 151.</F>

{@Hiraṇya-kaśipu@}¦ in the Brāhmaṇas<sup>1</sup> denotes a ‘golden seat,’ probably one covered with cloth of gold. <F>1) Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 9, 20, 1; Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, vii. 18, 12. {%Cf.%} the word as an adjective with the sense of ‘having a golden cloth,’ Av. v. 7, 10.</F>

{@Hiraṇya-kāra@}¦ denotes a ‘worker in gold’ mentioned in the list of victims at the Puruṣamedha (‘human sacrifice’) in the Yajurveda.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxx. 17; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 14, 1.</F>

{@Hiraṇya-dant@}¦ (‘gold-toothed’) {@Vaida@} (‘descendant of Veda’) is the name of a teacher in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (iii. 6, 3) and the Aitareya Āraṇyaka (ii. 1, 5). The name presumably refers to the use of gold to stop the teeth; see {@Dant.@}

{@Hiraṇya-nābha@}¦ is the name of a {@Kausalya@} or Kosala prince, whose horse sacrifice appears to be alluded to in the Śāṅkhā- yana Śrauta Sūtra (xvi. 9, 13). He is also referred to in the Praśna Upaniṣad (vi. 1), and may have been connected with {@Para Āṭṇāra.@} {%Cf.%} {@Hairaṇya-nābha.@}

{@Hiraṇya-stūpa@}¦ is the name of a man in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.<sup>2</sup> He is called an {@Āṅgirasa@} in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa,<sup>3</sup> which credits him with the authorship of a Rigvedic hymn.<sup>4</sup> The Anukramaṇī (Index) ascribes to him several other hymns.<sup>5</sup> <F>1) x. 149, 5.</F> <F>2) i. 6, 4, 2.</F> <F>3) iii. 24, 11.</F> <F>4) i. 32.</F> <F>5) i. 31-35; ix. 4, 69. {%Cf.%} Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 104, 141.</F>

{@Hiraṇya-hasta@}¦ is in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> the name of a son given by the Aśvins to {@Vadhrimatī@} (who, as her name denotes, was the wife of a eunuch). <F>1) i. 116, 13; 117, 24; vi. 62, 7; x. 39, 7. He appears to be called {@Śyāva@} in x. 65, 12. {%Cf.%} Macdonell, {%Vedic Mythology,%} p. 52.</F>
{@Hirā@}¦ in the {@Atharvaveda@}<sup>1</sup> denotes ‘vein,’ like {@Hitā.@} <F>1) i. 17, 1; vii. 35, 2; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxv. 8. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Omina%} {%und Portenta,%} 346.</F>
{@Hṛtsv-āśaya Āllakeya@}¦ is mentioned in the Jaiminīya Upani- ṣad Brāhmaṇa (iii. 40, 2) in the Vaṃśa (list of teachers) as a pupil of {@Somaśuṣma Sātyayajñi Prācīnayogya.@}

{@Hṛdayāmaya,@}¦ ‘disease of the heart,’ is mentioned in the Atharvaveda in connexion with {@Yakṣma@}<sup>1</sup> and with {@Balāsa.@}<sup>2</sup> [Page2-507+ 45] Zimmer,<sup>3</sup> who thinks that {@Balāsa@} is consumption, connects the name with the later view of the medical Saṃhitās,<sup>4</sup> that love is one of the causes of the disease. But it would be more natural to see in it a disease affecting the heart. <F>1) v. 30, 9.</F> <F>2) vi. 14, 1; 127, 3.</F> <F>3) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 387.</F> <F>4) Wise, {%Hindu System of Medicine,%} 321, 322.</F>

{@Hṛd-yota@}¦<sup>1</sup> (for {@Hṛd-dyota@}) and {@Hṛd-roga,@}<sup>2</sup> ‘heart disease,’ are mentioned in the Atharvaveda and the Rigveda respec- tively. Zimmer<sup>3</sup> identifies the disease in the Atharvaveda with {@Hṛdayāmaya,@} ‘consumption caused by love.’ In the Rigveda this is not at all likely: later in the medical Saṃhitās the word probably denotes {%angina pectoris.%}<sup>4</sup> <F>1) Av. i. 22, 1. {%Cf.%} vi. 24, 1.</F> <F>2) Rv. i. 50, 11.</F> <F>3) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 388.</F> <F>4) Wise, {%Hindu System of Medicine,%} 321.</F>

{@Heman@}¦ (used only in the locative singular) denotes ‘winter’ in the later Saṃhitās and the Brāhmaṇas.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 6, 1, 1; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxxvi. 6; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 4, 10, 10; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, i. 5, 4, 5; xi. 2, 7, 32.</F>

{@Hemanta,@}¦ ‘winter,’ occurs only once in the Rigveda,<sup>1</sup> but often in the later texts.<sup>2</sup> Zimmer<sup>3</sup> is inclined to trace differences of climate in the Rigveda: he thinks that certain hymns,<sup>4</sup> which ignore winter and insist on the rains, indicate a different place and time of origin from those which refer to the snowy mountains.<sup>5</sup> It is, however, quite impossible to separate parts of the Rigveda on this basis. It is probable that that text owes its composition in the main to residents in the later {@Madhyadeśa;@} hence the references to cold and snow are rather a sign of local than of temporal differences. It is otherwise with the later expansion of the three into four seasons, [Page2-508+ 36] which represents clearly the earlier advance of the Indians (see {@Ṛtu@}). <div n="P"/>The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa<sup>6</sup> describes winter as the time when the plants wither, the leaves fall from the trees, the birds fly low and retire more and more. <F>1) x. 161, 4.</F> <F>2) Av. vi. 55, 2; viii. 2, 22; xii. 1, 36; Taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 7, 2, 4; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xiii. 58; Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xxi. 15, 2; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, i. 4, 10, 10; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, x. 4, 5, 2 etc.</F> <F>3) {%Altindisches Leben,%} 40.</F> <F>4) Rv. vii. 103; x. 90.</F> <F>5) Rv. x. 68, 10; 121, 4 (both these are not early hymns).</F> <F>6) i. 5, 4, 5.</F>

{@Haita-nāmana,@}¦ ‘descendant of Hitanāman,’ is the patro- nymic of a teacher apparently called Āhṛta in the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā,<sup>1</sup> though the verse is a strange one. <F>1) iii. 4, 6. See Pāṇini, vi. 4, 170, Vārttika, and von Schroeder, Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, 2, ix.</F>
{@Hairaṇya-nābha,@}¦ ‘descendant of {@Hiraṇyanābha,@}’ is the patronymic of {@Para Āṭṇāra,@} the {@Kosala@} king, in a {@Gāthā@} occurring in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (xiii. 5, 4, 4).

{@Hotṛ@}¦ is the name of one of the oldest and most important priests of the Vedic ritual, the counterpart of the Zaotar of the Avestan priesthood.<sup>1</sup> The word must be derived from {%hu,%} ‘sacrifice,’ as was held by {@Aurṇavābha;@}<sup>2</sup> this indicates a time when the Hotṛ was at once sacrificer (the later Adhvaryu) and singer. But the functions were already clearly divided in the Rigveda, where the Hotṛ's chief duty was the recitation of the {@Śastras.@} He was also in the older period often the {@Purohita@} of the king, an office later filled by the {@Brahman@} priest. <F>1) Rv. i. 1, 1; 14, 11; 139, 10, etc.; {@Hotra,@} the ‘Hotṛ's office,’ Rv. ii. 1, 2; 36, 1; 37, 1, etc.</F> <F>2) Nirukta. iv. 26. {%Cf.%} Oldenberg, {%Religion des Veda,%} 380 {%et seq.%}</F>

{@Hotraka@}¦ in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa<sup>1</sup> denotes ‘assistant of the Hotṛ’ priest. <F>1) ii. 36, 5; vi. 6, 2. In the Sūtras it is variously used — sometimes in this sense, sometimes more widely — so as to include all the priests except the four chief priests ({%cf.%} Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra, v. 6, 17).</F>
{@Hyas@}¦ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> denotes ‘yesterday.’ <F>1) viii. 66, 7; 99, 1; x. 55, 5.</F> <F>2) Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xi. 9, 3.</F>

{@Hrada@}¦ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later<sup>2</sup> denotes a ‘lake’ or ‘pond.’ <F>1) i. 52, 7; iii. 36, 8; 45, 3; x. 43, 7; 71, 7; 102, 4; 142, 8, etc.</F> <F>2) Av. iv. 15, 4; vi. 37, 2; Pañca- viṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xxv. 10, 18; Śata- patha Brāhmaṇa, iv. 1, 5, 12; 4, 5, 10; xi. 5, 5, 8, etc.</F>

{@Hrade-cakṣus@}¦ in one passage of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> is thought by Jackson<sup>2</sup> to mean ‘will of the wisp.’ <F>1) x. 95, 6.</F> <F>2) {%Proceedings of the American Oriental Society,%} May, 1890, iv.</F>

{@Hrasva Māṇḍūkeya@}¦ (‘descendant of Maṇḍūka’) is the name of a teacher in the Aitareya Āraṇyaka.<sup>1</sup> <F>1) iii. 1, 5; 2, 1. 6. {%Cf.%} Weber, {%Indische Studien,%} 1, 391. The word must be regarded as a proper name, given from a personal characteristic, much as {@Sthavira@} is used.</F>
{@Hrāduni@}¦ denotes ‘hail’ in the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> and later.<sup>2</sup> <F>1) i. 32, 13; v. 54, 3.</F> <F>2) Taittirīya Saṃhitā, vii. 4, 13, 1; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxii. 26; xxvi. 9, etc.</F>

{@Hrūḍu@}¦ is a word of unknown meaning applied to {@Takman@} in the Atharvaveda.<sup>1</sup> It is variously spelled in the manuscript as {%hruḍa, hūḍu, rūḍu,%} and so forth; the Paippalāda recension reads {%huḍu,%} ‘ram.’ Henry<sup>2</sup> has conjectured that the word is the equivalent of a proto-Semitic {%ḥarāḍu,%} ‘gold’ (Assyrian {%huraçu%} and Hebrew {%ḥarāç%}), while Halévy<sup>3</sup> suggests that it may be the Greek <lang n="greek">χλωρός,</lang> ‘greenish-yellow’; but both conjectures are highly improbable.<sup>4</sup> Weber<sup>5</sup> thinks ‘cramp’ is meant. <F>1) i. 25, 2. 3.</F> <F>2) {%Journal Asiatique,%} 9th series, 10, 513.</F> <F>3) {%Ibid.,%} 11, 320 {%et seq.%}</F> <F>4) Macdonell, {%Journal of the Royal%} {%Asiatic Society,%} 1907, 1106.</F> <F>5) {%Indische Studien,%} 4, 420. <div n="P"/>{%Cf.%} Lanman on Whitney, Transla- tion of the Atharvaveda, 26; Bloom- field, {%Hymns of the Atharvaveda,%} 273.</F>

{@Hvaras@}¦ in three passages of the Rigveda<sup>1</sup> denotes, according to Roth,<sup>2</sup> a part of the Soma sieve, perhaps the part through which the Soma juice flowed. But Geldner<sup>3</sup> thinks that in all these cases the sense is merely ‘hindrance.’ <F>1) ix. 3, 2; 63, 4; 106, 13.</F> <F>2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, {%s.v.%} 1; Zimmer, {%Altindisches Leben,%} 278, n.; Hillebrandt, {%Vedische Mythologie,%} 1, 203.</F> <F>3) {%Vedische Studien,%} 2, 20</F>
